#1. Someone Hacked Tons of French Supermarket Refrigerators and Set Them to Defrost. It’s Clever—and Alarming.

The fridge heist exposed a hidden plan to turn grocery coolers into giant grid batteries.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

On Monday, October 12, bleary-eyed workers pulling the morning shift at hundreds of supermarkets across France were met with a shocking, foul-smelling surprise. Overnight, hackers compromised internet-connected controllers operating on software provided by the Danish company Danfoss, and set thousands of fridges to “defrost,” sending temperatures inside the units soaring to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122°F). In some cases, the hack sparked small fires in the refrigerators.

“When I opened the freezers, there was no more cold — just hot air coming out,” Cyril Scheubel, a manager at an Intermarché supermarket outside of Dijon told NPR. “All of our computer data is very well-protected…these hackers hit the only vulnerable point of our stores.”

Ars Technica reports that all three controllers targeted in the attack—Danfoss (Denmark), Dixell (Italy), and Copeland (U.S)—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow hackers full system rights, as if they were administrators. Remarkably, the controllers sat on the public internet with no virtual private network (VPN) shielding remote access. The U.S.-based Copeland company also says the devices impacted were “a discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers.”

Whatever the cybersecurity lapses, the result was likely millions of dollars’ worth of spoiled food, and the search is on for the culprits behind the attack. However, this strange story raises another question: Why were these refrigerators on the internet in the first place?

Travel to any supermarket in the U.S., and you’ll likely witness rows and rows of freezers and refrigerators continually chilling or freezing, well, pretty much everything—and those systems use a lot of energy in aggregate. In 2015, the Environmental Protection Agency’s National Center for Environmental Economics reported that refrigeration consumed 40 to 60 percent of the energy in a typical U.S. supermarket—enough, collectively, to account for up to three percent of all commercial building energy use in the country. Worse, the hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) inside them are potent greenhouse gases in their own right, more than doubling these systems’ climate impact.

Naturally, with that much electricity on the line, supermarkets want their refrigeration running as efficiently as possible. The key reason, at least in the case of France, is that internet controllers allowed technicians to track cooling levels without having to be physically at the store. However, researchers in recent years have explored even grander ambitions for connecting these refrigerators online.

In 2018, for example, a pilot project in northern Finland tested the concept of demand response, where supermarket fridges could be cut off from power for up to 30 minutes without damaging food or the systems themselves. In a way, these big cold boxes became a kind of battery that would chill food when demand was low and then disconnect from power when demand was high. Part of this project was in preparation for a renewable power system that might provide energy during the day but less energy at night. The researchers found that while regular grocery stores consumed 600 kWh/m2, energy-efficient stores topped out at only 240 kWh/m2, which amounted to roughly $200,000 in savings per year.

The following year, U.K. supermarket chain Tesco partnered with the University of Lincoln to test a similar system, timing the fridges’ defrost cycles to match power availability on the national grid. The appeal is that refrigeration accounts for more than 14 percent of electricity demand in the U.K. at any given moment, and roughly a third of a typical grocer’s energy costs. Tesco alone has some 112,000 refrigeration systems under central software control, so adjusting them in unison has a significant effect on the national grid.

Because the thermal mass of a loaded refrigerated case stores cold like a battery, it can safely coast without power for tens of minutes, allowing supermarkets to chill hard when energy is cheap and pause when it isn’t. However, using refrigeration as grid storage requires precise control to avoid two critical limitations. First, cutting power while a case recovers from its daily defrost cycle severely delays its return to temperature. Second, restarting thousands of compressors simultaneously can cause massive electrical surges on the grid.

Despite these challenges, supermarkets are actively grappling with how to lower their greenhouse gas emissions and electricity costs. A 2025 report by the Environmental Investigation Agency recommended that natural refrigerants can help keep things cool, save money, and avoid HFC pollution. According to the report, Carrefour, one of the chains hit by the hack, spent nearly $90 million on low-GWP refrigeration technology in 2022. The investment now returns roughly $30 million a year and cuts some 67,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide annually.

The connectivity that makes a supermarket’s freezers useful to the grid is also what allowed hackers to switch thousands of them to “defrost.” Advances in supermarket refrigeration could both prop up the grid and drastically cut energy use and greenhouse gas emissions. But the near-term challenge is simpler: keeping those fridges—and the internet-connected gadgets that control them—out of the wrong hands.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#2. APOD: 2026 October 20 – An Anticrepuscular Rainbow Fan

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Explanation: This is an unusual rainbow. For one thing, the rainbow is not complete, appearing only in a sunlit fan -- but that by itself is not very unusual. What is most unusual is the fake location of the Sun. The Sun appears to be toward the front, just below those hills -- but it is not. That is not how rainbows work. Rainbows involve a backward reflection from falling rain, so that the Sun must really be behind you. In this case, gaps between clouds near the setting Sun allowed rays to cross the entire sky and appear to converge in front, an unusual phenomenon called anticrepuscular rays. The photo was taken with a phone last week at sunset in Presenzano, Italy. The seemingly reverse rainbow was noticed when hanging up laundry.Tomorrow's picture: open space

#3. Scientists finally uncover why statins can cause muscle pain

Statins are among the most important medications for preventing cardiovascular disease. By lowering cholesterol, they have helped save millions of lives and reduce the likelihood of heart attacks and strokes. However, these benefits can come with unwanted effects. Some patients develop muscle pain or weakness, while a small number experience serious muscle breakdown that can potentially cause kidney failure.

Scientists at the University of British Columbia (UBC), working with colleagues at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, have identified a molecular mechanism that helps explain these complications. Their findings, published in Nature Communications, could guide the development of safer statins that maintain their cholesterol-lowering benefits while minimizing muscle damage.

How Statins Trigger a Harmful Calcium Leak

To investigate what happens inside muscle cells, the researchers used cryo-electron microscopy, an advanced imaging method that allows scientists to examine protein structures in remarkable detail. Their investigation centered on the ryanodine receptor (RyR1), a protein that regulates the movement of calcium within muscle cells.

Under normal conditions, this protein functions as a controlled gateway, releasing calcium when muscles need to contract. The researchers found that statins can interfere with this process by holding the channel open. As a result, calcium escapes continuously into areas where it should be carefully regulated, creating conditions that can injure muscle tissue.

"We were able to see, almost atom by atom, how statins latch onto this channel," said lead author Dr. Steven Molinarolo, a postdoctoral researcher in UBC's department of biochemistry and molecular biology. "That leak of calcium explains why some patients experience muscle pain or, in extreme cases, life-threatening complications."

Three Statin Molecules Reveal the Mechanism Behind Muscle Damage

The researchers concentrated on atorvastatin, a commonly prescribed medication for lowering cholesterol. Although this particular drug was the main focus, their results suggest that similar interactions could occur with other medications in the statin family.

One of the most striking discoveries was the unusual way statin molecules attach to the calcium channel. Rather than acting individually, three molecules occupy a specific pocket within the protein. The first binds while the channel is closed, making it more likely to open. Two additional molecules then enter the pocket and hold the channel open, allowing calcium to continue leaking.

"This is the first time we've had a clear picture of how statins activate this channel," said Dr. Filip Van Petegem, senior author and professor at UBC's Life Sciences Institute. "It's a big step forward because it gives us a roadmap for designing statins that don't interact with muscle tissue."

This detailed understanding could give drug developers a way to address the problem at its source. By modifying the specific features of statin molecules that interfere with muscle proteins, scientists may be able to reduce unwanted effects without compromising the drugs' ability to control cholesterol.

A Potential Path Toward Safer Cholesterol Drugs

More than 200 million people worldwide use statins. Although severe muscle injury occurs in only a small percentage of patients, less serious problems such as soreness, weakness, and fatigue are considerably more widespread. These symptoms can be disruptive enough that some people discontinue their medication, potentially losing important protection against cardiovascular disease.

The discovery could eventually help researchers create treatments that are easier to tolerate, allowing more patients to continue taking medications that reduce their risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Achieving this level of understanding required exceptionally detailed imaging. Working with the high-resolution macromolecular cryo-electron microscopy facility at UBC's faculty of medicine, the team was able to observe precisely how statin molecules interact with the muscle protein. These structural insights connect a longstanding drug safety concern to a specific molecular process, providing valuable information for future medication development.

"Statins have been a cornerstone of cardiovascular care for decades," Dr. Van Petegem said. "Our goal is to make them even safer, so patients can benefit without fear of serious side effects."

Although additional research and drug development will be needed before these findings translate into new treatments, they offer a promising direction. For millions of people who depend on statins to protect their hearts, future medications with fewer muscle-related complications could make treatment more comfortable and improve everyday quality of life.

Materials provided by University of British Columbia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4. A quantum computing feat brings the ‘megaquops’ era a step closer

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Error correction creates qubits that glitch only 5 out of a million times

A quantum chip made by Quantinuum (shown) demonstrated a qubit that made errors only five times out of a million.

Quantum computers capable of doing a million reliable operations could bring about a new stage of quantum calculation. That “megaquop” regime — as it’s called — isn’t here yet. But scientists just took a significant step toward it.

A quantum computer built by the company Quantinuum has error rates so low that it could perform a million operations with only about five errors, researchers report in a paper posted October 19 on the company’s website and arXiv.org.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“These statistics are consistent with this being a good building block for that megaquop machine,” says quantum physicist David Hayes of Quantinuum, who is based in Broomfield, Colo. In order to reach that regime, however, such computers will need to be scaled up.

Quantinuum’s computer, known as Helios, is made of electrically charged atoms, called ions, hovering over a chip. Those ions serve as the 98 quantum bits, or qubits, of the computer. But, like all qubits, those ions are finicky. Their states are delicate and can flip unintentionally and mess up calculations, like a 0 randomly switching to a 1.

A technique called quantum error correction tackles this by combining multiple error-prone qubits into one, forming a supercharged unit called a logical qubit that is less prone to mistakes. (For those who grew up on 1990s TV, it’s a bit like how Captain Planet is born from the combined powers of the gang of Planeteers.)

Logical qubits come in different sizes, integrating a given number of physical qubits — the ions, in this case. Each time a logical qubit is scaled up, going, say, from seven physical qubits to 19, the error rate drops by a factor called lambda. A previous demonstration of error correction by Google, reported in Nature in 2024, had a lambda of about 2, meaning errors were cut in half each time the logical qubits were scaled up.

Quantinuum’s computer has a lambda of about 10. So errors dropped quickly when the researchers made larger logical qubits. A logical qubit composed of 37 physical qubits had just 5 errors in a million operations — close to what would be needed for the megaquop regime. However, that experiment involved only a single logical qubit. Reaching the megaquop regime could possibly involve around 50 to 100 logical qubits.

The large value of lambda means that achieving a desired error rate takes fewer physical qubits, says Ken Brown, a quantum engineer at Duke University and a scientific adviser for the company Logiqal who was not involved with the research. “That’s a huge savings in the overall number of qubits you would need. So that’s what’s exciting.”

Live Science sat down with the European Space Agency's Simonetta Cheli to discuss the importance of Earth observation, how NASA budget cuts have changed the picture, and how the proliferation of private satellites could hinder our ability to view the planet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

FRASCATI, Italy — Observing Earth from space provides a much-needed insight into the evolution of our planet's health. This is particularly important in the face of climate change, as environmental degradation, food insecurity and extreme weather events can all reveal themselves in stark images taken from high above our planet's surface.

Simonetta Cheli is the director of Earth observation programs at the European Space Agency (ESA) and the head of the European Space Research Institute (ESRIN) in Frascati, Italy. With nearly 40 years of experience in the field, she is one of the world's leading experts on Earth observation.

Live Science spoke with Cheli on a recent visit to ESRIN to talk about why Earth observation is so important, how NASA budget cuts and political changes have altered the picture, and why private space satellites risk our ability to view the planet clearly.

Live Science spoke with Cheli on a recent visit to ESRIN to talk about why Earth observation is so important, how NASA budget cuts and political changes have altered the picture, and why private space satellites risk our ability to view the planet clearly. She also discussed how new supercomputers, like ESRIN's newly operational Space HPC, are helping to process vast amounts of data like never before — and shared her favorite recent satellite snap of our planet

Simonetta Cheli became ESA's director of Earth observation programs and head of ESRIN on Jan. 1, 2022, more than three decades after joining the agency. She was born in Siena, Italy, and went on to study law and economics at Yale University before gaining a degree in political sciences at the University 'Cesare Alfieri' in Florence, Italy. She also holds a diploma of advanced studies from the Centre d’Etudes Diplomatiques et Stratégiques in Paris.

Harry Baker: Why is observing Earth from space so important?

Simonetta Cheli: It's important because we need to know today what is the state of our planet, if it's healthy or if it's in danger, if it's stressed or not.

It's important to have objective information on many different variables, such as deforestation, the quality of the air that we breathe, the evolution of the oceans or the melting of ice masses. Basically, we need to be aware of what the situation is on Earth today, so we can preserve it tomorrow.

HB: How has ESA's Earth observation program changed throughout your career?

SC: When I started at ESA [in 1988], we were relying on missions from partners, including the Americans and Japanese. We didn't have our own missions.

We launched the first mission [ERS-1] in 1991. Today, just here at ESRIN, we manage over 20 missions and are planning more than 40 more. We have also launched three different missions in the last three weeks — one to look at how oceanography impacts extreme weather events [International Report for an Innovative Defence of Earth]; one to monitor the fluorescence and health status of vegetation [Fluorescence Explorer]; and one to measure temperature on land and sea [Sentinel-3C], which was a super useful thing this summer.

Cheli is one of the world's leading experts on Earth observation and currently oversees more than 20 different missions that are monitoring our planet from above.

Europe is now a leading power in this domain worldwide. We have evolved a lot.

HB: How important is it to cooperate with other countries when observing our planet from above?

SC: Well, I must say, in ESA, it's in the DNA of our work. ESA includes 23 countries today, so we work together daily. We also work very closely with other commercial partners and the European Union, as well as international partners like NASA, Brazil, India and Africa. So this is part of our job, and very much also in the domain I'm managing.

We used to go to the climate conferences together. We are not anymore.

To tackle climate and environmental stability, you cannot just do things alone at the national level. You have to share data and work with everybody in the world, where you have to have common objectives. For example, what happens to Greenland affects everybody on Earth, not just the people who live there. So the collaboration, I think, is very much inherent in our daily job at ESA and between our partners.

HB: Given the recent cuts to NASA's funding, including its Earth observation budget, does ESA feel a bigger responsibility to step up and fill the gap?

SC: I think we certainly have a bigger opportunity in the sense that today, with the systems we have and the satellites we have and the missions we have, even before the political context. For example, we were already leading the U.S. with data on emissions.

Live Science recently visited Frascati to see ESRIN's newly-operational Space HPC supercomputer.

We have a very good working-level collaboration with our American partners. This is somehow preserved, although politically it is, of course, more delicate. We used to go to the climate conferences together. We are not anymore.

HB: ESA just launched the latest batch of satellites in the IRIDE constellation (an Italian funded network of Earth-observing spacecraft designed and operated by ESA). What makes these satellites so special? And how are they helping your research?

SC: We launched the latest eight [satellites] last night! (The IRIDE satellites launched on Oct. 1, the day before this interview took place.)

Sixty-eight satellites are planned overall in this constellation, and we have launched quite a few [39] already, and plan to launch some more before the end of the year.

On Sept. 14, ESA also launched the Sentinel-3C satellite on board at Vega rocket that lifted off from the agency's launch site in French Guiana.

The network will collect a lot of data from the optical radar spectrum that will support different user needs: for example, in the civil protection area, in coastal erosion monitoring, in coast guard operations and in environmental stress analysis. And so this system will certainly be a big contribution to the wider European Earth observation setup.

HB: The number of private satellites, like in SpaceX's Starlink constellation, is increasing fast. Are you worried about the impacts that this might have on your scientific spacecraft?

SC: We are worried because we see that the anti-collision maneuvers are increasing and increasing. When my mission manager tells me we have to move the satellite because there is a risk of collision with another satellite, we have to go check with ESO [European Southern Observatory] in Germany, and then the operations center moves the satellite. And the number [of times we've done this] has certainly increased in the last four or five years due to the increased number of satellites up there.

For the moment, the technical collaboration with partners is going quite well. So when we see someone else's satellite, we actually try to organize things as best we can, and technically it's working well. But what we need for the future is a clear framework at the legal level, which is engaging everybody.

"Everybody" in space is no longer only the institutional partners; it's not just the space agencies of the world that should engage. Today, you have private actors, like Starlink, and if they don't engage in the same rules, you risk having a delicate situation. But this is something that we are discussing daily, and we're tackling.

HB: The whole point of Earth observation is to protect our planet. How do you feel about some of the negative impacts of launching satellites, such as exhaust plumes, metal pollution and space junk?

SC: There is a very strong objective linked to sustainability at ESA. It is not just about using the data to better preserve our planet; it's also about being sustainable in the daily work we do.

Chelli has been working at ESA for nearly 40 years, and believes that global cooperation is essential in Earth observation.

This is linked to, for example, trying to have a space debris policy; trying to have enough propellant on board of the satellites that we build to make sure that once they finish their lifetime, they come back with a re-entry assist and they don't stay there in orbit. And the same is true in the launcher domain, where there's a very strong effort from our partners in French Guiana [where ESA's only active launch site is located] to lessen our impact as much as possible on the environment with the launch setup.

There's a really dedicated team doing all this.

HB: How will AI systems and advanced computers, like Space HPC, help researchers process data? And what sort of things could that help you do?

SC: We have today a wealth of data that is continually increasing. Just in the Copernicus program [Europe's biggest Earth observation initiative], we receive 500 terabytes of data per day.

We also have big volumes of data in the archives here at ESRIN from science missions of international partners, including Japan, India, the U.S. and others. This "heritage data" guarantees that archival data of missions that have ended are preserved, which is super important.

Chelli (center right) was one of the people chosen to cut the ribbon at the opening of ESRIN's Space HPC supercomputer on March 12, 2025.

So instruments like SpaceHPC, which have high computing capability, help us a lot to process those datasets faster.

HB: What is your favorite satellite photo of Earth?

SC: I have too many favorite satellite photos, I must say. But this summer, the one I really found striking was a thermal image of Europe's heatwaves because, in that image, you see that the temperature on land and on sea was increasing so much.

This photo, captured by ESA's Sentinel-3B satellite in June 2026, shows land and sea surface temperatures spiking across Southern Europe. While it is concerning, Cheli says that the image gives her hope about our ability to monitor such extreme weather events in the future.

It was captured by Sentinel-3B [a predecessor of the recently launched Sentinel-3C], and you see the red in the sea, and you see the red on the land, and I think it gives the feeling of the heat wave that we've all been living through this summer. We had, I would say, the hottest summer ever.

But it makes me feel that we can do a lot about it. It makes me feel that we have tools and certainly information capabilities to support, help, and also raise awareness about this topic.

So right now that is a favorite, but there are so many [other photos].

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#8. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the October Hunter’s Moon, which occurs at 12:12 a.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in October. The Full Moon this month will be on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Tuesday, October 20Sunrise: 7:16 A.M.Sunset: 6:13 P.M.Moonrise: 3:32 P.M.Moonset: 1:11 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (73%)

Sunrise: 7:17 A.M.Sunset: 6:11 P.M.Moonrise: 3:56 P.M.Moonset: 2:15 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (81%)

Thursday, October 22Sunrise: 7:18 A.M.Sunset: 6:10 P.M.Moonrise: 4:18 P.M.Moonset: 3:20 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (89%)

Friday, October 23The nearly Full Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 11 P.M. EDT, creating a celestial triangle with the ice giant and nearby gas giant Saturn. Our satellite and Neptune share the constellation Pisces, while Saturn floats in northwestern Cetus.

By early evening, the trio stands above the southeastern horizon, and by local midnight they are high in the south. Neptune is 4° south of (below) the Moon, while Saturn is 8° to our satellite’s southeast (left). Only the latter planet is visible to the naked eye, as Neptune requires binoculars or a telescope to view.

Sunrise: 7:19 A.M.Sunset: 6:09 P.M.Moonrise: 4:41 P.M.Moonset: 4:26 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (95%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#9. Archaeologists Just Found the Lost Church From a Saint’s 1,600-Year-Old Letter.

The fourth-century church and bishop’s palace may explain how Venice rose from a dying city.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Excavations that revealed a fourth-century C.E. church in the ancient city of Altino have finally substantiated a letter written by Saint Jerome in 396 C.E., and they help illustrate the rise of Venice in the wake of Altino’s demise.

Experts had long suspected that a church stood in the ancient Italian city of Altino, thanks to St. Jerome’s letter, but no physical evidence had ever supported the claim, despite ongoing work at the Altino Archaeological Park. The new discovery not only uncovered the rectangular church building but also exposed a bishop’s palace connected to it. Together, the two structures help tell the story of the population shift from Altino to Torcello, the launching point for the rise of Venice.

“For the first time, we can say with a very high degree of confidence where the church and the bishop’s palace of Altino stood,” Diego Calaon, excavation director with Ca’ Foscari University of Venice, said in a translated statement. “Written sources told us they must have existed. Now we have archaeological evidence to support this.”

Those written sources begin with Letter 60, addressed by St. Jerome to Heliodorus, the first bishop of Altino. In it, Jerome describes the site and the care the priest Nepotian lavished on the church, even documenting its altar, walls, floors, curtained doorways, and sacred vessels.

The newly excavated building matches that picture. Roughly 1,600 years old, the late antique church measured 100 feet long and 65 feet wide. Its hall does not align with the Roman street grid, instead facing east, and its lack of an apse fits traditional northern Adriatic architecture. Immediately to the east, excavations revealed the bishop’s palace: the foundations of what was likely a two-story porticoed structure built with stones reused from Roman roads. The residence featured internal walls and annexes, with the second story probably housing clergy and the ground floor hosting privileged burials.

That reuse of trachyte Roman road paving stones—laid upside down—is one of the site’s most telling details, because it establishes the bishop as a key figure in the city. University experts noted that Roman law protected roads as public infrastructure, so repurposing the stone suggests the bishop held considerable sway.

Elisa Possenti, excavation co-director from the University of Trento, said the finds open fresh perspectives. “Thanks to these discoveries, the city can now be considered alongside other major episcopal centers in late antique northeastern Italy,” she said. “What we could only imagine from descriptions in written sources is finally taking physical form. This will help us reassess the lives and roles of Altino’s earliest bishops, whose histories have largely been shrouded in legend.”

Work at the site continues, and the team hopes to uncover more of the church and the bishop’s palace, including the baptistry.

Pinpointing Altino’s early Christian heritage also helps illustrate the demographic movement to Torcello and the shift of the episcopal seat. Once believed to have been a sudden change, the move now appears to have been both gradual and deliberate. Excavations at Torcello show that the island served as Altino’s port, and an inscription in the baptistry there dates the church to 639 C.E. With Torcello on the rise, Altino became a major source of reusable building material, and that trade eventually paved the way for the move to Rialto and the growth of Venice.

“This analysis allows us to tell the story of the transition from Altino to Torcello and Venice in a new way,” Calaon said, “not as a sudden flight, but as a long, managed transformation in which the ancient city and its inhabitants actively shaped economic and political decisions. At the same time, the buildings and spaces of ancient Altino became a source of materials that helped create a new way of inhabiting the lagoon.”

That recycling may also explain the church’s disappearance: experts believe the Altino church and palace were lost to the stripping of stones and bricks for reuse in construction at Torcello and Venice.

Marianna Bressan, director of the National Archaeological Museums of Venice and the Lagoon, said the excavations add important information for understanding these ancient cities. “Research at Altino provides an opportunity to view the city’s history in a broader context,” Bressan said, “tracing the Venetian area’s transformation from antiquity to the formation of the lagoon as we know it today.”

#10. Hurricane warning maps are improving, but a dangerous problem remains

An updated hurricane forecast map is making it easier for people to identify areas threatened by storms, but new research reveals a concerning limitation. Even when people can recognize where hurricane watches are in effect, they may not feel more at risk or become more inclined to take precautions.

Researchers at Florida State University examined whether changes to the National Hurricane Center (NHC) forecast graphics improve public understanding of hurricane threats. The study involved faculty from the School of Communication within the College of Communication and Information and the Department of Geography.

The researchers evaluated an experimental graphic that expands the traditional hurricane forecast cone to include tropical storm and hurricane watches and warnings for inland areas. The familiar cone has historically placed greater emphasis on coastal regions, even though dangerous storm conditions can extend far from the shoreline.

The findings revealed mixed results. Although the revised graphic helped people without specialized weather knowledge recognize inland areas under hurricane or tropical storm watches, it did not significantly influence how dangerous they believed the storms would be or whether they intended to take protective measures. Participants also showed no improvement in identifying areas covered by storm warnings.

The updated format was developed by the NHC in 2024, and the findings were published in the American Meteorological Society journal Weather, Climate, and Society.

"The National Hurricane Center has made a number of thoughtful changes to improve how hurricane information is communicated," said Assistant Professor Elizabeth Ray, the study's lead author. "We had a simple question. Do those changes actually help people understand what the graphic is telling them about the risk they face?"

Why People Misunderstand Hurricane Forecast Maps

To investigate how the public interprets hurricane forecasts, the research team surveyed residents of Florida and Georgia. Participants were shown either the conventional hurricane cone graphic or the newer experimental version that includes additional information about inland storm threats.

People who saw the revised map were more successful at identifying locations under hurricane or tropical storm watches. However, that improvement in recognizing watch areas did not lead to greater concern about the potential danger or stronger intentions to take safety precautions.

The results also highlighted a persistent misunderstanding surrounding the familiar hurricane "cone of uncertainty." Many people incorrectly interpret the width of the cone as an indication of a storm's physical size, rather than understanding what the graphic is intended to communicate about the uncertainty in its projected track.

"For years, research has shown that people often mistake a wider cone for a bigger storm," Ray said. "Our findings suggest that even with an updated graphic, that misconception can be hard to shake."

Why Better Hurricane Warnings May Not Be Enough

The NHC introduced its expanded forecast graphic in 2024 to help people recognize that hurricane dangers are not limited to communities along the coast. Flooding, tornadoes, and destructive winds can threaten areas well inland, making it important for residents beyond coastal evacuation zones to understand their potential exposure.

By adding inland hurricane and tropical storm watches and warnings to the traditional forecast cone, the updated graphic provides a more complete picture of where dangerous conditions could develop.

However, the study suggests that adding useful information to a forecast does not automatically make people more aware of their personal risk or more likely to respond appropriately.

The researchers stressed that their findings do not call into question the quality of the NHC's weather predictions, which they consider highly accurate. Instead, the results underscore the difficulty of presenting complex meteorological information in a way that people can readily interpret and use when making safety decisions.

"Our question wasn't whether the science is good," said co-author Patrick Merle, professor and director of the School of Communication. "The science is excellent. The question is how we communicate that science so people who aren't meteorologists understand the risk they're facing.

If people find information credible but still don't understand it well enough to take protective action, then communication has fallen short. The goal is to empower people with information they can use to stay safe."

The findings point to the importance of looking beyond a single forecast image when preparing for a hurricane. Although the cone can provide valuable information about a storm's expected path, it cannot communicate every hazard that a particular community might experience.

The researchers recommend using hurricane forecast graphics alongside local weather predictions and detailed information about possible impacts. Understanding the specific threats to an area, as well as the protective steps residents should consider, can provide a more useful basis for making decisions.

"Our findings are a reminder that one graphic can only tell you part of the story," Ray said. "Don't rely on the cone alone. Pair it with clear, local information about what impacts to expect and what actions to take. That gives you a fuller picture of what the storm could mean where you live and what to do next."

The study received funding through an internal Florida State University SEED grant. The research was also informed by discussions with the NHC, which supplied the experimental forecast graphics evaluated by the team.

Bradford Johnson, an assistant professor in the Department of Geography, contributed as a co-author.

#12. The Human Fingerprint on Earth’s Water Cycle

Human activities have become intertwined with how water is distributed across the continents. A new study brings their effects into sharper focus.

Humans are exerting increasing influence over how water moves through lakes, rivers, soil, and the subsurface, and a new NASA study shows where those effects are greatest. Using more than two decades of satellite measurements of subtle changes in Earth’s gravity, the researchers sharpened the picture of how—and why—terrestrial water storage has changed.

This map encapsulates their findings, depicting changes in terrestrial water storage from April 2002 to November 2025. Beyond the influence of climate variability, the scientists identified 40 regions where the changes also aligned with human activities such as irrigation, reservoir impoundment, and land-use change. These activities were significantly related to terrestrial water storage trends on every nonpolar continent except Australia.

In some areas, the effects of human activities were especially strong. “In four continental regions, an anthropogenic variable showed a stronger relationship with the storage trends than any climate variable did,” said Mary Michael O’Neill, a hydrologist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and lead author of the study.

They include well-known spots such as California’s Central Valley and northern India, where farmers’ heavy reliance on groundwater has drawn down storage—in India’s case, faster than earlier estimates suggested. Elsewhere, some types of farming and water management appear to have done the opposite.

The data behind the map come from the GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) and GRACE-FO (GRACE Follow-On) missions, each of which consists of two satellites that fly in tandem. As the lead satellite passes over an area with greater mass, the slight change in gravity tugs at it, and instruments aboard the satellites measure the change in distance between them. Since water and ice are heavy and shift around regularly, scientists can use GRACE data to infer gains and losses.

The satellites’ data are typically processed into monthly maps that show broad patterns of water storage. But over more than 20 years, the satellites have passed over most of the planet many times. By combining all of those passes, the researchers could map long-term water trends with five to 10 times more spatial detail than previous analyses. The tradeoff was a loss of temporal detail. They then applied statistical techniques to weigh the importance of various anthropogenic and climatic factors in the storage trends and to pinpoint where human activities may have contributed.

The improved spatial resolution uncovered some human impacts that had not been previously detected, said Matthew Rodell, deputy director of Earth Sciences for Hydrosphere, Biosphere, and Geophysics at Goddard and one of the study’s authors. The analysis also showed that some known trends were stronger than previously realized.

Across several continents, groundwater-irrigated farmland was strongly associated with declines in terrestrial water storage. In North America, these declines appeared in California’s Central Valley, the southern High Plains of the U.S., and Chihuahua, Mexico, where long-term droughts have increased farmers’ reliance on groundwater. Groundwater pumping also drove declines in northern India, where the refined analysis showed a steeper downward trend than previously realized. Consistent with previous findings, retreating Himalayan glaciers accounted for only 15 percent of the decline there.

Other types of agriculture had a different relationship with water storage trends. In parts of sub-Saharan Africa, for example, some increases occurred where rainfed cropland has expanded. There, swaths of native savanna were replaced by millet cultivation throughout the study period, and water tables rose despite below-average precipitation. A similar pattern emerged in northern Brazil’s Maranhão state, where soybean fields have replaced forests and shrublands. The resulting water storage trend might be explained in part by the efficient water use of cereal and legume plants and by Indigenous practices that help direct water into shallow aquifers, the researchers said.

Water storage and diversion projects also came into focus on the new map. Hundreds of large reservoirs were filled during the study period, the authors note, but the coarse spatial resolution of gravity measurements previously made them difficult to track. In the new analysis, the Boguchany Reservoir on Russia’s Angara River, the second-largest reservoir filled in the 21st century, produced the strongest water storage trend in nonpolar northern Asia.

The map also resolves smaller reservoirs and other hydrologic engineering projects. The Karakum Desert in Turkmenistan registered water storage gains stemming from the long, largely unlined Karakum Canal running through it. The canal diverts river water to support desert agriculture, but enough seeps into the ground during its journey to alter the water picture in the desert. The map’s finer resolution allows for better monitoring of such hydrologic changes in remote areas where other measurement options may be limited.

Moving forward, O’Neill wants to capture how dams, diversions, irrigation, and other controls on Earth’s water affect storage downstream, and to disentangle the influence of local and non-local activities. “I’d also like to recover more of the temporal picture,” she said. One way to do that is by combining the higher-resolution data with standard monthly products or by applying the recent technique over shorter timeframes. “This could help track how localized trends evolve in response to specific events like droughts or policy changes.”

The process has improved in recent years, but it still produces a voice that can sound unnatural. Jules Rodriguez did this as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, left his own voice diminished. But he wasn’t happy with the sound.New technology that uses artificial intelligence allowed Jules to create a voice clone, one that sounds like his old voice. With breaths, intonations and even stutters, these voice clones capture the quirks of a human voice. Jules’ voice clone was so realistic that his wife cried the first time she heard it.

Sanders: ALS forces families to confront tough medical decisions about life and death. Jules and MA had thought very carefully about how they’d approach the future. Jules had been getting by with just an external oxygen mask to help keep his body going. He had decided that he didn’t want to take a next big step of having a tracheostomy, a life-extending procedure that leaves a small tube in his throat connected to a ventilator. With a trache tube, Jules would need round-the-clock care, and he would lose his voice permanently.MA: He was someone who didn’t want to do a tracheostomy. Like, he was opting for, once I’m done, like, that’s it. And that was our plan.

Sanders: In the summer of 2024, not too long after he had cloned his voice, Jules had reached a very tough spot.MA: September, we went to the hospital again and we had one evening where we really thought like that was it, like he was going to, he was going to pass away that night. I remember texting his family and saying, you know, I don’t know that it’s going to happen right now, but we’re, I feel like we’re really close. And he went through this like crisis moment. And then on the other side, when they were able to like stabilize him again, he looked at me and he was like, babe, well, if the tracheostomy can help me live, then I think I’d change my mind. I want to do it. Let’s talk to the doctors about it.

Sanders: This decision to have a trache tube placed in his throat meant that Jules’ voice, diminished as it already was, would be gone. Remember, this is a couple who built their relationship on long, deep talks. Their intimate, funny, thoughtful conversations were so meaningful to them that they started an entire podcast based on them. But this decision, a proactive choice to fully and permanently lose the capacity to talk, represented a hard stop. A definitive end to talking. What you’re about to hear is a tough conversation. MA is telling me about a moment before the surgery.

MA: So I remember the night, the day, yeah, he was, the operation was like in the evening when they did it, and me recording like a last little video of us talking because I was like, I just want to capture your voice one more time. And he was like, oh babe, you know, being all like, and I haven’t even looked at that video, but it’s there. And so that was a big, it was a big transition.

Sanders:  You can’t see it, of course, but maybe you can hear it. As we talk, we’re both crying.

MA: I think I mentioned when we spoke last time how of all the things from the very beginning that I was like, oh, he’s going to lose the ability to this and this and this and this and this. I was like, oh, my God, when he loses the ability to speak, like, I’m going to really, really, really, really, really have a hard time. And all of the abrupt changes and the way you have to adapt to them kind of prepare you for the next things. And so usually the fear of the thing happening is more than when it actually happens. And then you’re there and you’re like, okay, we’re here and we’ll adapt to it. That’s usually been the case for pretty much everything. But yeah, it was big.

Sanders: But there was something that made the final and complete loss of Jules’ voice easier. Jules’ new digital voice. This was a very realistic AI-generated recreation of his old voice, the one that his family knew and loved. The existence of this new voice factored into Jules’ decision to get a trache.

MA: I really do believe that the AI voice and the ability for him to actually communicate in that way is one of the things that helped him decide to keep living.

Sanders: It wasn’t everything, of course. A decision like this depends on so many moving pieces. But it was big.

MA: I firmly believe that it had an enormous positive impact in him considering it, like, as a way of you know having certain goals and experiences that he thought, you know, wouldn’t have been there, had it not been for the cloned voice. So I’ve I’ve gone as far to say that if it wasn’t for the clone voice, I don’t think he, I don’t think he would have chosen the trache. Yeah, then that moment anything could happen, but he was pretty, a pretty like no, I don’t want the tracheostomy kind of guy from the beginning. And then all of that changed. And so I think it was a huge driver.

Sanders: At the time of Jules’ hospitalization and surgery, they talked to their son Skylar about what was going on.

MA: The whole like communicating with him afterwards, because I said, you know, now he’s going to lose his voice completely. He’s like, we have the computer. That’s great. And I was like, okay, yeah, true. The things he’s told us over time are like bonkers. How he sees, the perspective he has on things, is incredible. So that was a really big, pivotal time for like what it means to like use your voice, to keep your voice, to fight for your voice and to express yourself in ways that you didn’t even think you would before. That takes a lot of courage and willingness.

Sanders: And what is your voice? I mean, to Skylar, it didn’t matter because his voice was still there.

Sanders: To Jules’ son, the voice clone was his dad’s voice. That’s really all there was to it.

MA: He had his tracheostomy October, October 1st, and he was in the hospital for another two weeks. And then, mid-November, he was performing at, you know, an improv at one of our local comedy clubs.

Jules: In all seriousness, thanks for coming out. My name is Jules and because of the advancements in AI, I now have the ability to come up here and do this again with my original voice.

Sanders: Jules was back. Jules, with his voice clone, can laugh and sing and start trouble with his wife.

Jules: One thing in particular is how it inserts tone and inflections on words. Sometimes my wife will get mad because my response can come off with some sass.

Sanders: I asked Jules if he can swear with it.

Jules: [Beep] yeah, I can. With the latest version of this technology, I have more control of how I sound with prompts. That includes laughing, whispering, and even singing. I could never sing, even though my wife and I met at a karaoke bar.

Sanders: I think you can sing. Anyone who wants to sing can sing.

Sanders: Cave has been a speech therapist for decades, but even he was won over by the capabilities of these newer AI-generated voice clones.

Cave: I was really pleasantly surprised. These voices were the most authentic sounding I’d ever heard from this technology. It actually sounded like the people I was working with. And so it really changed my world. And because I was known for voice banking, I was getting a lot of inquiries. And I ended up spending so much time on answering questions about ElevenLabs. What really, really excited me was that many people reported that their social networks was being strengthened again, that more people were coming to talk to them and to reflect on times past and times current. And that to me is gold. That’s what voice banking is or should be, to maintain social and work networks.

Sanders: I’d say that we’ve now gone well beyond almost human, as Stephen Hawking put it. Today’s voice clones are fluid, individual, and in many ways, seamless. My synthetic voice says certain words the exact same way I would say them.

[Sanders voice clone] My real voice says certain words the exact same way I would say them. It’s spooky.

Sanders: The stories I’ve heard of how people are using these voices back this up. I emailed with Peggy Merrill, who lost her voice from ALS. She uses her voice clone to read to her  grandkids, teach yoga, and lead guided meditation.

Peggy: My name is Peggy and it is my honor to share this guided yoga nidra meditation with you.

Sanders: Peggy wrote to me, “It renews my sense of self to use and hear my own voice.” And there’s Patrick Darling, who you heard from in an earlier episode. He’s a composer and musician, and he’s been writing new songs and performing them with his voice clone.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it, even though I was not actually singing.

Patrick: It’s hard to explain. There’s just this strange energy about it and you feel like a performer again.

Sanders: Patrick’s description of feeling physically connected to his voice, I think, might be a big hint about why this voice cloning technology is so powerful. These realistic voices are able to create connections both within people and between people. These connections were lost, and then they’re remade. And they matter because of not just the big heavy conversations, but the little everyday stuff too.

Jules still has to use eye-tracking technology to type out what he wants to say. He has a device that senses where he’s looking on a screen and uses his gaze to write. Only then does his voice clone say what he wants it to say. That takes a lot of time and focus. Scientists are working on ways to get the words out faster by using signals earlier in the speech process.

On the next episode…researchers want to pull words straight from the brain.

Casey Harrell: And the more I read and I thought, why not me? And why not now?

Sanders: What does it feel like to have your thoughts turned into words?

Leigh Hochberg: The first thing that he said was something along the lines of, you know, is this thing on? And then the second thing that we decoded was, I’m looking for a cheetah. And it’s the second day. You know, there’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using an implanted brain computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah. You know,  that’s obviously a decoding error, and that’s fine. Except for the fact that his four-year-old daughter had just walked into the room dressed as a cheetah.

"Low Earth orbit looks like lots of other resources that we have trashed as economic actors."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The space around Earth is turning into a junkyard. Researchers think a refundable deposit scheme could force satellite operators to clean up their act before a tipping point is reached.

For years, space sustainability experts have warned that the growing number of satellites in orbit and the quantity of dead metal left behind threatens to trigger a dangerous cascade of collisions known as the Kessler Syndrome. Predicted in the 1970s by NASA physicist Donald Kessler, this chain of orbital smashups could make the space around Earth unusable and unsafe.

The dangerous tipping might be nearer than some think. Humankind's utilization of space is at an inflection point, as companies such as SpaceX, Blue Origin and Amazon plan to launch constellations of hundreds of thousands of telecommunication satellites and orbiting data centers in the coming years.

"Low Earth orbit looks like lots of other resources that we have trashed as economic actors," Daniel Kaffine, a professor of environmental and resource economics at University of Colorado Boulder, told Space.com.

"Waiting until it gets really, really bad to start implementing any of these types of policy interventions has historically been what we have done," Kaffine added. "But maybe we can think about things we can do right now."

In a paper published last month in the journal Nature Communications, Kaffine and his collaborators propose a scheme that would require satellite operators to post a bond of $200,000 before launch, refundable with interest upon the completion of a successful deorbit. Companies that fail to remove their junk would lose the money, which could go toward a shared pool funding active debris-removal missions, the researchers said.

"You could possibly raise billions of dollars by that," said Kaffine. "We think it's a very neat policy that doesn't require international coordination."

International bodies, such as the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee, ask satellite operators to remove their spacecraft from orbit within 25 years after the mission's end. The American Federal Communications Commission (FCC) imposes an even stricter standard — a five-year requirement for satellites in low Earth orbit. Still, a staggering 60% of satellites remain in place when their propellant runs out, the researchers say, as no consequences ensue if they fail to deorbit.

Solving the problem on the international level would be difficult, as international bodies have no powers to enforce compliance. Moreover, the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), which sets down rules for the peaceful exploration of outer space, requires the unanimous support of every member state to pass new regulations, which is nearly impossible to achieve.

"The policy we propose could be implemented on a national level, which is why we think it's interesting," Indigo Brownhall, a space sustainability researcher at University College London and the paper's lead author, told Space.com. "Any country in Europe can request satellites registered with them to follow this bond policy."

To put it simply, no satellite registered in a given country gets to space before putting the money into the kitty. The researchers acknowledge that it might be hard to persuade major players historically averse to regulations, such as the U.S., to roll out such a scheme. But they say a more environmentally conscious block, like the European Union (EU), could enforce compliance by limiting market access to those who observe their rules.

"The consumer market in Europe is massive, like 300 to 400 million people," Brownhall said. "And the EU can request anyone who wants to sell space data or any products in the EU to follow their rules. They did this with GDPR [General Data Protection Regulation]. And you can imagine that somebody like Starlink [SpaceX's satellite-internet subsidiary] surely wants to sell Starlink terminals to Europeans."

The authors estimate that, even if the scheme only covered 20% of global satellite launches, it would reduce the number of derelict satellites careening around the planet by 18%.

Currently, more than 57,000 pieces of space debris larger than 4 inches (10 centimeters) hurtle around Earth completely out of control, according to estimates by the European Space Agency. That's double the figure from less than 10 years ago. Most of these fragments were generated by explosions and orbital collisions that shattered satellites and used rocket stages into clouds of dangerous debris.

"Leaving big satellites that no longer work up there is like a ticking time bomb," Brownhall said. "Active satellites can move out of the way, but when two derelict satellites are going to hit each other, there is nothing you can do but watch it."

Kaffine said the policy could be modelled on U.S. oil operators' bond scheme, in place since the 1960s, which ensures that oil giants plug used oil wells after ceasing extraction.

"If the oil operators clean up after completing the oil production job, they get the money back," said Kaffine. "If they don't, the money goes into a fund, which the government then uses to clean up orphan wells. It's quite an analogous situation to what we see in space."

In the meantime, evidence of the worsening orbital situation is coming thick and fast. Space situational awareness companies such as U.S.-based LeoLabs, which use networks of ground-based radars and telescopes to monitor traffic in space, report increasing numbers of disintegration events — incidents involving either an explosion or a collision between old satellites, fragments and rocket bodies. In the past six months, LeoLabs has reported at least four fragmentation events in space, which together created hundreds of new pieces of space debris.

#16. Oct. 20, 2018: BepiColombo launches

BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, launched Oct. 20, 2018. The spacecraft is actually two satellites in one, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), commissioned with investigating one of the least-visited planets in our solar system.

To reach its final position, BepiColombo received assistance from the gravity of the two inner planets, flying by Venus twice and Mercury six times. That sixth flyby of Mercury occurred Jan. 8, 2025, setting the spacecraft up to reach its destination in November 2026. When it arrives, the two orbiters will separate: The MPO will investigate Mercury’s surface and geophysical makeup, particularly its unusually large core. The MMO will examine the planet’s magnetic field and how it’s generated – another unusual feature of Mercury, since its slow rotation suggests its field should not be possible.

#17. He Used a Nuclear Submarine to Lure an Alien Spacecraft—and Found Something That Defied Physics

Jay Stratton led the classified operation that tried to trap something that wasn’t from Earth.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

When Jay Stratton joined the military barely out of high school, he saw himself as an infantryman. Nothing in those early days pointed anywhere but toward a rifle and a rucksack. Stratton could never have predicted that someday, beyond camo and combat boots, he would end up on the front lines of something far more bizarre and unearthly than any battlefield.

It began with a video. After he had risen in the ranks of the Defense Intelligence Agency to become chief of air and space warfare, Stratton found himself in his office in Washington, D.C., when a colleague appeared at his door and asked him to make sense of classified footage. He was suddenly watching what could have easily been a scene from a science fiction movie. Hovering near a nuclear missile silo was an unidentified flying object that appeared vaguely menacing. How it had managed to enter one of the most restricted regions of U.S. airspace is still unknown. Its eerie yellowish glow left a visible trail, carving turns through the air that no engine or airframe should allow. The craft traversed the skies in complete silence, then accelerated faster than Han Solo could ever dream of pushing the Millennium Falcon in Star Wars—and vanished.

This would be the start of a UAP (unidentified anomalous phenomena) hunting mission that spanned nearly two decades. Stratton went on to co-found the Defense Intelligence Agency’s Advanced Aerospace Weapons Application Program (AAWSAP) and the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program (AATIP), then rose to director of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force (UAPTF), where he led the first UAP investigation to reach across the entire federal government. For the final sixteen years of his military career, he chased occurrences that no earthly explanation could cover: silent craft, impossible accelerations, objects that moved through air and water with equal ease. The infamous undersea “tic tac” craft was only the most famous. Nothing in the human catalog of engineering, Stratton concluded, could account for what he was seeing.

“The plan was bold as it was straightforward,” Stratton says of luring UAPs in his new memoir, Out of the Shadows. “It was an efficient expedition and our strategy was built on our educated opinion that UAP were drawn to nuclear energy. Our bait could be a nuclear submarine. Its reactor running hot would create a huge nuclear signature, and it would suffice as a pre-selected area within US waters known for past UAP activity. The goal, exploit a decades-old pattern. Draw a UAP close enough to monitor, track, or if possible, capture or recover.”

The encounters themselves baffle even skeptics. One pilot was on patrol when he caught sight of a floating sphere, roughly six feet in diameter, drifting through the darkness at 20,000 feet as if the violent winds hitting it simply weren’t there. The crew turned their radar on the object, and it fled so abruptly it might as well have been a hallucination. Roswell raises the same questions on a far larger scale. The city that inspired a paranormal TV series in the late ‘90s and still trades on aliens and flying saucers as unofficial mascots was the site of a 1947 crash that many dismiss as a failed military experiment. The debris made sensational headlines before officials wrote it off as a fallen weather balloon. Stratton says the balloon was just a cover story.

What the recovery team hauled out of the desert, Stratton writes, went well beyond crumpled metal. It included bodies that were not human. An unidentified source told him that some of these beings died on impact while others survived the crash but not much longer, refusing food and refusing to communicate. The aftermath never reached the public. Witnesses inside the intelligence services were traumatized enough that many resigned, several suffered breakdowns, and a few, haunted by what they had seen, took their own lives. The wreckage itself is long gone, beyond the reach of any modern analysis—but Stratton points to more recent events that unsettle him just as much. In one case, top gun instructors—pilots selected for their composure under pressure—recorded four encounters in a single week. They came away shaken.

The incidents recounted in Out of the Shadows drew backlash from several directions. Stratton had just returned from an investigation in Nevada when a colleague pulled him aside and warned him that entangling himself in such things carried dire consequences. Then came the hard questions. If aliens had really touched down on Earth, where are the images to corroborate the alleged video evidence? Why did no one run lab tests on the bodies recovered at Roswell? Why does every account offer everything but a scientific explanation? The pressure was not all professional. Glowing balls of light hovered outside the family’s windows after dark, and Stratton lived with the sense that someone was always a step behind him. Only retirement brought any relief.

“Anytime I’ve ever done anything related to UAP or UFO, that’s been my job,” Stratton told 8 News Now Las Vegas in an interview. “And what I mean by that [is] I didn’t really have a passion growing up, I didn’t have all the books, I didn’t watch all the TV shows. I stepped into a job for the Defense Intelligence Agency where some things came across the desk…[for] all the stories you hear, there’s probably an office that deals with this.”

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

The head of ESA's Earth observation program tells Live Science why a striking image of a recent heat wave scorching Southern Europe gives her hope that we can properly monitor ‪— and eventually prevent ‪— similar extreme weather events in the future.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Southern Europe and North Africa

What's in the photo? Land and sea surface temperatures during one of Europe's record-breaking summer heat waves

Which satellite took the photo? Sentinel-3B

This striking satellite snap shows the scorching land and sea surface temperatures that hit Southern Europe during one of the continent's record-breaking heat waves this summer.

The image was created using data from the Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR) on board the European Space Agency's (ESA) Sentinel-3B satellite. It was selected for this week's edition of Earth from space by Simonetta Cheli, director of Earth observation programs at ESA and head of the European Space Research Institute (ESRIN) in Frascati, Italy.

Live Science recently visited Frascati to see ESRIN's newly operational Space HPC supercomputer and sat down with Cheli for an in-depth discussion about Earth observation. When asked about her favorite satellite image, Cheli highlighted this photo as one that caught her eye this year.

In the thermal image, dark reds highlight terrestrial temperatures in excess of 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 degrees Celsius) across most of Spain and parts of France and Italy, while dark purple spots show highs above 104 F (40 C) across patches of Spain and North Africa. The image also reveals sea surface temperatures spiking across the Mediterranean Sea. (The colors in the image do not represent the same temperatures on land and sea. For example, orange indicates temperatures of around 86 F (30 C) on land but around 73 F, or 23 C, at sea.)

Cheli said that assessing how terrestrial and marine environments interact during extreme weather events is really important and that including both in the same image is the only way to appreciate the true scale of this heat wave: "You see the red in the sea, and you see the red on the land, and I think it gives the feeling of the heat wave that we've all been living through this summer," she said.

ESA launched the Sentinel-3C satellite in September, on board a Vega rocket that lifted off from the agency's launch site on French Guiana. It will help the agency monitor future extreme weather events in even greater detail.

While many people may find such images related to human-caused climate change disheartening, Cheli sees it as a sign of hope that orbiting spacecraft can monitor otherwise-invisible changes to our planet's surface in such detail.

"It makes me feel that we can do a lot about it," she said. "It makes me feel that we have tools and certainly information capabilities to support, help and also raise awareness about this topic."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Cheli told Live Science that ESA's ability to monitor extreme weather events like this will only improve as the agency launches new-and-improved spacecraft into orbit. In September, ESA successfully launched Sentinel-3C, the successor to the spacecraft that snapped this image, which has already captured its first photos of Earth and will help study future heat waves in greater detail.

Between late May and mid-August, parts of Europe were hit by at least five separate heat waves, meaning temperatures stayed unusually high throughout the season. "We had, I would say, the hottest summer ever," Cheli said.

The peak heat occurred in June, when the average temperature for that month reached 69 F (20.7 C) — its highest in Western Europe's recorded history, according to the World Meteorological Organization. (This average includes nighttime temperatures, which is why it seems relatively low compared to other temperatures mentioned so far.)

Eight countries — Austria, Belarus, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia — recorded their highest land surface temperature of all time at various points throughout this summer, and several others had record temperatures for a specific month or region.

The extreme weather caused widespread droughts across the continent, some of which are still ongoing, and helped trigger several wildfires, including a series of particularly large blazes in France. Experts think the high temperatures resulted in at least 35,000 excess deaths across Europe, although the true number is expected to be much higher, according to The Guardian.

Simonetta Cheli is the director of ESA's Earth observation programs, and has been working at the agency for nearly 40 years. She described this summer's heat waves as the hottest she can remember.

The heat waves were caused by "heat domes," which are pockets of high pressure in the atmosphere that trap warm air beneath them, like placing a lid on top of a boiling pot. These are also linked to higher sea surface temperatures.

The ongoing super El Niño began in May and has already led to record temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, but it did not contribute to the European heat waves, according to ESA. Instead, the record temperatures are a continuation of recent global warming trends.

However, El Niño could lead to more extreme weather this winter, in Europe and in North America.
