#19. Astronomers uncover new secrets of the Universe’s first five minutes

Scientists have measured the amount of helium produced during the Universe's first five minutes with unprecedented precision, offering a clearer picture of the conditions that existed shortly after the Big Bang. The achievement, made by an international research team that includes scientists from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, represents a major advance in precision cosmology.

The findings, presented in five papers published in The Astrophysical Journal, are based on 130 hours of observations using the Large Binocular Telescope. By analyzing distant galaxies, the researchers reduced the uncertainty in this fundamental measurement to just 0.5%, making it three times more precise than previous estimates.

The improved accuracy provides scientists with a powerful new tool for investigating the origins of the Universe and testing the Standard Model of physics. Such fundamental tests have a long history of advancing scientific understanding and contributing to technological breakthroughs.

"This is a physics experiment on a grand scale and one of the biggest findings in my entire 40-year career," said Evan Skillman, University of Minnesota College of Science and Engineering Distinguished Professor in the School of Physics and Astronomy. "It's a fundamental number that tells us specifically about the conditions of our Universe in its first five minutes. It has diagnostic power that speaks directly to the Standard Model of Physics."

According to the Big Bang theory, the Universe began expanding from an extraordinarily hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago. Three major lines of evidence support this explanation: the continuing expansion of the Universe, the cosmic microwave background radiation, and the amounts of light elements such as helium and deuterium that formed during its earliest moments.

Although cosmic expansion and the microwave background have been studied extensively, measurements of primordial helium have historically received less attention. Determining its original abundance more accurately allows researchers to investigate the physical conditions that prevailed when the Universe was only minutes old.

To achieve their new level of precision, the team departed from the conventional method of estimating primordial helium. That approach involves observing large numbers of galaxies and extrapolating the results to determine how much helium existed before later generations of stars altered their chemical composition.

Instead, the researchers selected 15 exceptionally pristine, small, distant galaxies. These galaxies have undergone relatively little chemical evolution, making them valuable cosmic "time capsules" that preserve clues about the Universe's early composition.

Powerful Telescopes Deliver Record Precision

The team used sophisticated spectrographs developed at Ohio State University to examine more than 10 helium spectral lines and 15 hydrogen lines simultaneously. Studying these signals together made it possible to identify and correct subtle sources of measurement error that earlier studies could largely overlook.

Such small effects become especially important when researchers are trying to reduce uncertainty to less than 1%. Accounting for them was essential to achieving the new 0.5% precision.

"The MODS spectrographs took 12 years to build from conception to first light on sky," said Richard Pogge, College of Arts and Sciences Distinguished Professor of Astronomy at Ohio State University. "This is the kind of project we designed them to do, and to see them deliver is enormously satisfying. It's not every day you can help build instruments that measure something fundamental about our Universe."

Beyond refining estimates of the Universe's earliest chemical composition, the new measurement provides an important test of the Standard Model of physics. The amount of helium created shortly after the Big Bang depends on the physical conditions at that time, including the types of elementary particles present.

Using their precise helium measurement, the researchers were able to calculate the number of neutrino families in the early Universe. Neutrinos are extremely light subatomic particles, and their behavior plays an important role in scientists' understanding of fundamental physics.

The results therefore do more than strengthen existing evidence for the Big Bang. They also offer a more precise way to check whether established physical theories accurately describe the Universe during its first few minutes.

"We promised a half-percent uncertainty in our proposal, and we got there," added Skillman. "In the unpredictable world of science, that doesn't happen very often."

The international collaboration brought together scientists from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, Ohio State University, Gonzaga University, Northwestern University, The University of Texas at Austin, Indiana University, University of California Santa Cruz, University of Illinois, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, and TRIUMF.

#21. Curiosity Blog, Sols 5036-5042: Watching the Clouds Go By

Mars Science Laboratory Mission Team Members

Written by Alex Innanen, Atmospheric Scientist at York University

Earth planning date: Friday, Oct. 9, 2026

Happy New Mars Year! We mark the start of a new year on Mars at the beginning of the northern hemisphere spring, or the vernal equinox. We then keep track of the seasons by counting degrees of solar longitude — each season is 90 degrees as Mars completes the whole 360 degrees of its orbit. The start of Mars year 39 at a solar longitude of 0 degrees (or Ls=0°, pronounced “ell-sub-ess-zero” if you want to sound like a Martian) came at the end of September on Earth. The new year also means it’s now autumn in Gale Crater, just south of the equator.

As Michelle talked about last week, we rang in the Martian new year with our drill campaign at “Basque Lakes.” This week was dedicated to wrapping up drill activities before we drive away on the weekend. After the team got a chance to see the results of last week’s lab activities, the SAM team decided on an additional GCMS (Gas Chromatograph/Mass Spectrometry) experiment. While GCMS tends to be an energy-intensive activity, we had four whole sols in Monday’s plan to play with, so we still had room for a slew of remote-sensing activities from Mastcam and ChemCam and contact science of the drill tailings — the bits of rock and minerals that are left over from our drill sample. This weekend’s plan gives us a couple more sols to wrap up drill activities at Basque Lakes and collect any last contact- or remote-science targets we want here before we begin a drive back toward the neat crystal forms we saw in the “Chiu Chiu” region.

While all this is happening, the atmosphere around us continues to go through its seasonal changes. Autumn means the return of high-altitude twilight clouds, which the low sun angle at sunset illuminates beautifully. While twilight cloud activity will pick up as the autumn progresses, our late afternoon cloud movies on Wednesday of this week already caught our first high-altitude clouds of the season, as you can see at the top of this post. Most of the clouds we tend to see at Gale Crater are suboptical, or too thin to be seen with either human eyes or with Curiosity’s robotic “eyes,” but these twilight clouds are bright enough that we can see them in the raw Navcam images. I’m looking forward to another Martian autumn of watching all these different clouds go by.

#22. Keeping jumping genes in place: New role for protein complex discovered

As much as half of the human genome is composed of so-called "jumping genes." These DNA sequences can make copies of themselves that are inserted back into the genome at another location, playing a significant functional role in creating the diversity that drives evolution and in regulating how other genes are turned on or off. However, their jumps can also make the genome less stable and create mutations that have been associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, autoimmune disease and cancer.

#23. These tiny snakes cartwheel to escape danger

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

New videos reveal, step by step, how the snakes pull off these rare acrobatics

This Pseudorabdion saravacense snake looks like it’s ready to slither, but new video captures its wildly acrobatic way of moving.

Cartwheeling seems like it should require both arms and legs. But some itty-bitty snakes in Southeast Asia manage it without either.

Scientists first shared snapshots of a dwarf reed snake (Pseudorabdion longiceps) cartwheeling away from danger in 2023. Now, videos of three Pseudorabdion species hightailing it down a racetrack in the lab have offered a closer look at this rare and strangely acrobatic behavior.

Each snake starts with its body curled into a C shape, head lifted off the ground and facing the way it’s going. It then whips its tail out behind it, briefly becoming airborne. The snake flips its tail forward and down past its head. When the snake’s tail hits the ground in front of it, another roll begins, researchers report October 19 in Current Biology.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“What a cool snake behavior,” says Jessica Tingle, a biologist at Brown University in Providence, R.I., not involved in the work. “I find it especially amazing that an elongate animal like a snake can manage to roll, especially given that they do it in such an explosive way, which probably asks a lot of their muscles and bones.”

Yosuke Kojima was equally surprised when a colleague in Sarawak, Malaysia recounted witnessing this “very weird” behavior in 2019. So the researchers collected snakes from Malaysia’s Kubah National Park. They scooped up 11 P. saravacense, one P. collaris, one P. longiceps, plus six Calamaria reed snakes for comparison.

Finding the snakes was no easy task. They were only about 11 to 28 centimeters long. “They always hide under the leaves,” says Kojima, an ecologist at Toho University in Chiba, Japan. But were any of the snakes able to cartwheel away from the researchers? “No,” Kojima laughs. “We are quicker than them.”

The team set up a 2.2-meter-long racetrack and placed the snakes one at a time at one end. A gentle tap coaxed the snakes to move and cameras above and beside the track recorded the action. None of the Calamaria snakes cartwheeled, but all of the Pseudorabdion snakes did. At full tilt, they tumbled at 1.7 to 3.7 meters per second — about six to 13 kilometers per hour.

Through it all, the snakes held their heads fairly steady — reminiscent of how flying snakes hold their heads stable while launching into the air, the researchers say.

A cartwheeling snake first rolls its body along the ground to whip its tail out behind its head. Then, it swings its tail up and over its head. Finally, it brings its tail down on either the left or right side of its head. Once it the tail hits the ground, the snake is ready for another roll. In the cartwheel seen on top, the snake brings its tail down on the left side of its head, angling its whitish belly toward the viewer. In the cartwheel on the bottom, the snake’s tail lands on the right side of its head, showing its darker back to the viewer.

“I am very curious how such a strange and possibly demanding movement evolved … whether dwarf reed snakes have something special in their anatomy, physiology or neural control that lets them do it when their close relatives apparently can’t or don’t,” Tingle says. “Are their brains different in some way to let them coordinate a fast and unusual movement? Or do all snakes have the basic equipment, and they just don’t use it?”

Those may be open mysteries. But catching snakes cartwheeling on camera does tie up one loose end for Tingle.

“Some writers in the 1800s talked about ‘hoop snakes’ and described their motion as rolling, but that seemed pretty fantastical to me, and I chalked it up to overly inventive imaginations,” Tingle says. Those 19th century authors may or may not have been describing the exact behavior Kojima’s team recorded. “Either way, it’s neat to find out a real animal does something reminiscent of a fantastical old story.”

#24. The Sky Today on Tuesday, October 20: Lovely spiral NGC 7331

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

October 19: Feast your eyes on the Southern Fish

Located in northern Pegasus, NGC 7331 is a bright galaxy that is the largest in a group of five galaxies collectively known as the Deer Lick Group. It’s best viewed in early evening, standing highest around 10 P.M. local daylight time, when it is more than 80° above the southwestern horizon.

You’ll find NGC 7331 glowing at 10th magnitude just 4.4° north of 3rd-magnitude Matar (Eta [η] Pegasi). Stretching some 11’ long and 4’ wide, this lovely galaxy has a large, bright nucleus with no bar, surrounded by delicate spiral arms. Even though the galaxy is nearly edge-on, larger scopes will allow you to see exquisite detail in those arms.

We see NGC 7331 from a distance of 40 million light-years, but it’s not the only galaxy in sight. Again, a larger scope (11 inches or more) is needed, but will reveal at least three of the Deer Lick Group’s other members, collectively called the “fleas” because they appear much smaller than NGC 7331, clustering around it. But these aren’t smaller dwarf galaxies swarming a larger central body — instead, the fleas are not physically associated with NGC 7331 at all, but lie far beyond it, at distances some 290 million to 370 million light-years away.

Sunrise: 7:16 A.M. Sunset: 6:13 P.M. Moonrise: 3:32 P.M. Moonset: 1:11 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (73%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

The Orionid meteor shower peaks the morning of October 21 — the perfect time to watch for shooting stars, as Earth turns into the meteoroid stream of dusty debris responsible for the show.

The best time to do some meteor-watching is between 2 A.M. local daylight time and dawn, as the radiant in Orion rises higher and the Moon has already set. Around 5 A.M., the Hunter stands above the southern horizon, his famous three-star Belt easy to find. Meteors in the Orionid shower appear to originate just to the upper left  (northeast) of Betelgeuse, the bright red giant that serves as one of Orion’s shoulders. Once you’ve found this star, cast your gaze some 40° to 60° to either side, away from it — that’s where you’ll see meteors with the longest trains.

This year’s shower is expected to produce some 15–18 meteors per hour in the early-morning hours. And if you aren’t able to get out in the morning, you can try again late tonight after Orion rises and overnight into tomorrow morning. Even though the peak has passed, meteor rates will still be higher than the sporadic six or so per hour that are visible even without any showers active.

#25. The 5 Best Snowblowers for Digging Yourself Out This Winter

These tested snowblowers will help make quick work of clearing driveways and walkways this winter.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Winter is almost here, and for many of us, that means the chance of snow in the forecast is going up. Will you be ready for whatever weather is headed your way? Now's the perfect time to check out what you've got in the garage or shed and prepare for the months ahead. The Old Farmer's Almanac is predicting widespread wintry weather with dramatic swings.

If you’re tired of shoveling, need to replace an aging snowblower, or are looking for something bigger and better, a new snowblower could take some of the chill out of snow removal and might be the best way to manage the cold, snow-filled months ahead. Whatever your mission, we have snow removal options right here.

Our recommendations run the gamut of sizes and include both battery- and gas-powered models. Read on to find the best machine to help you clear snow more quickly and efficiently.

We are gearing up for our 2026 snowblower testing, and the models below represent several of the models we’ll be evaluating. These models represent the breadth of options available right now and are some of the most reliable and effective you can buy.

When we test snowblowers ahead of snowfall season, we use wet sawdust to evaluate how these machines perform. We had a load delivered to our office and mixed with water until we arrived at a snow-like consistency. When we first conducted this test, we weighed one cubic foot of our imitation snow and found it was exactly 21 pounds. Average wet snow weighs about 20 pounds per cubic foot, so we were in the right ballpark.

Once the test area was set up, we ran the machines through the sawdust just like we would if we were blowing snow off our driveways. It’s important to note that wet sawdust, while it is similar enough for testing purposes, is not snow. It’s heavier than most snow and less slippery. So our test is a bit tougher on these machines than the snow most users will encounter. We should also note that cordless models are more sensitive to the heavier material than the gas machines. We fully expect these machines to perform better when used in actual snow.

The steel-framed Power+ is very much like gas-powered units of its size, except for the electric motor and two 56-volt, 7.5-Ah batteries. Those two things give the Power+ some distinct advantages in the noise and weight departments, being both quieter and lighter than its gas-fueled counterparts. Using it won’t hurt your hearing or wake the neighbors, and you won’t be laboring to move it around in the garage to store.

Ego claims a run time long enough to clear an 18-car driveway—that’s an area about 130 by 12 feet—of 8 inches of snow. This may be true with light, dry powder, but keep in mind that the heavier and wetter the snow, the shorter the run time. Clearing our test area of sawdust—significantly heavier than all but the wettest snow—used up between 25 and 30 percent of the battery. It’s important to note that we operated the auger in turbo mode to throw the sawdust as far as possible, a distance of 31 feet, but it does have a variable-speed control. So you can adjust the auger as needed for the conditions and to preserve battery.

Using the Power+ is a breeze. With a differential in the axle and its relatively light weight, we found it very easy to maneuver. We like how freely the discharge chute moves through its 200-degree arc. But with a separate control for the deflector, it’s not as quick to adjust on the fly. Other features include four LEDs, adjustable plastic skid shoes that won’t mar garage floor coatings or walkway pavers, and adjustable handle height. The Power+ is one of very few cordless snowblowers with two stages, and overall, we were impressed with its capabilities. It threw wet sawdust well, which means it will have no problems in real snow.

Snowblowers are an investment, but whereas many two-stage snow blowers are priced over $1,000, this model from Champion Power Equipment lists at $899. Even at this lower price, it carries a number of features others have, including push-button electric start, a self-propelled drive system, remote chute control, and an LED headlight.

With a 24-inch width and a 20.5-inch height, it can handle deep snowfall, and the height is adjustable, so you can set it to handle gravel paths without damaging the blades. Plus, 180-degree turning wheels help make tighter turns. The 209-cc engine is slightly less powerful than some of the two-stage gas snowblowers we’ve reviewed, but that still should be enough to tackle deep snowbanks.

Ryobi power tools do a good job of making things a bit more affordable, and this single-stage cordless snow blower is no exception. With a list price of $849, it’s a few hundred dollars less than comparable blowers, but it’s sized to handle moderate snowfall. It offers a clearing path of 21 inches wide and 11.5 inches high and can throw the snow up to 35 feet away.

This model comes with two 40-volt, 8-amp-hour batteries, which should keep things running for up to 2.5 hours, though that can decrease depending on how deep and wet the snow gets. The other benefit of this model is that you can use its batteries with any other Ryobi 40-volt power tools, making them useful for other work you have around the house in just about any season.

Ego claims its 21-inch Power+ snow blower can throw snow up to 40 feet with a 180-degree, adjustable chute, which is pretty far for a cordless machine. In the wet sawdust test, we were able to throw material 24 feet—longer distances are certainly achievable with lighter, drier snow. It took the Power+ 4 minutes 16 seconds to clear the sawdust down to the pavement in our area test.

Like most single-stage blowers, the Power+ is not self-propelled. In our dense, heavy sawdust, pushing the machine required some effort to make forward progress. It’s not a bad thing, though, as it makes it easier to prevent the machine from digging in too deeply and bogging down. In wet or ice-packed snow, we expect you’ll have to put in a similar effort.

The Power+ has a variable speed auger, so we were able to adjust speed for the conditions and conserve battery when less power was needed. There isn’t too much to worry about in the battery department, since it comes with two 5-Ah batteries, enough to clear 8 inches of snow on a 12-car driveway—that’s six cars long by two cars wide.

The Power+ comes with a dual-port charger, so the two batteries can be charged simultaneously to get you ready for the next round faster. Ego rounds things out with front-mounted LEDs for low-light and dark conditions, plus an easy folding handle for stowing the unit when not in use.

This single-stage snowblower from Toro is well-suited for medium-sized properties that get guaranteed snowfall each year, but don’t present a ton of ground to cover—just a driveway and some sidewalks. Its 212-cc engine should cut through even wet snow and it can throw it up to 40 feet away. Plus, it’s self-propelled to help you push through the snow.

It also simplifies things with some smart controls like a trigger and slide that can change the direction of the discharge chute and push-button electric start. This blower is aimed at clearing snowfall up to 9 inches, so northern regions that see more severe snowstorms may want to opt for a two-stage model, but this model will work well if you only have a few moderate snow events each winter.

The big limiting factor for cordless battery-powered snowblowers is how long they’ll run. If the battery dies, there are two options: Put a second battery in, if you have one, or put it on the charger and wait. Battery options do have their advantages, though. They produce no fumes, emit very little noise, are simple to operate, and can be stored anywhere in your home. There is also very little maintenance required with them.

Large gas snowblowers can easily handle snow 20 inches deep or more and, with enough gas, run for hours on end. And if you do run out of gas, just add fuel and keep going. The downsides with gas models are that they're noisier, do produce fumes, and require routine engine maintenance.

The choice comes down to how much snow you typically get, and how much space you have to clear.

Much like the choice between gas or battery power, choosing a single- or two-stage machine has a lot to do with snow volume and the area to be cleared. Single-stage blowers are so called because they have one curved paddle that collects the snow and ejects it through the chute. This is the limiting factor in how far the snow can be thrown, as well as the volume that can pass through the machine.

Single-stage units are simple to operate, lightweight, easy to maneuver, and typically less expensive than two-stage machines. Two-stage units have a horizontal auger that collects snow and pushes it to a separate, rotating impeller that ejects it. Two-stage machines can throw snow 30 to 60 feet, which makes it easier to clear large areas without piling snow that you’ll just have to move again.

The main purpose of a drive system is to adjust and convert engine revolutions per minute to an appropriate speed to drive the machine forward in various conditions. There are two basic types of transmissions: friction disc and hydrostatic.

Friction-disc transmissions are simple, mechanical devices that employ a rubber edged wheel that presses on the face of a large pulley. By repositioning the wheel on the face of the pulley, the machine will speed up or slow down—closer to the center for slower, close to the outside edge for faster. Snowblowers with friction discs will often have six forward speeds and two reverse, controlled by a lever on the dashboard. And these machines typically have a live axle, which means both wheels are attached to a solid axle and will always spin at the same rate.

Hydrostatic transmissions pump hydraulic fluid through hydraulic motors, which convert the flow to mechanical rotation. On these machines, drive speed is independent of engine speed and there is no fixed number of “speeds.” The lever controlling speed can be positioned at any point in its range. “Hydro”-drive machines are capable of slower speeds than those with friction disc drives, which is good for very deep or heavy snow. Due to the complexity of hydrostatic transmissions, they can be significantly more expensive than friction-disc units.

There are two features that help improve steering. The first uses triggers under each handle to control clutches that disengage the wheel on the corresponding side. The opposite wheel continues to drive, turning the machine in the direction of the stopped wheel. The other feature incorporates a differential gear on the axle, which allows the wheels to spin at different speeds.

Tracks provide greater grip and stability, which make them very good on slopes, loose surfaces like gravel, or areas that tend to get icy snowpack. They are often easier to keep going nice and straight. Wheels work well in most situations but can often slip on hills and small patches of ice. It takes more parts to manufacture a track drive than a wheeled drive, so tracked units tend to be more expensive. In the end, the decision comes down to budget and terrain.

Under no circumstances, reach into a running machine to clear snow jammed in the auger or chute. That's the biggest one. If you are using a gas-powered machine, we strongly suggest hearing protection be worn.

If the machine has pneumatic tires, be sure to pump them up to the proper pressure before using— low tire pressure can make them more difficult to maneuver. Also, for those machines with grease fittings on auger bearings or gearbox, be sure to lube each season with low temp grease.

Run the auger at the lowest possible speed that will clear the snow, and turn the auger off anytime you aren't actually blowing snow.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX just launched its mysterious "Starfall" return capsule for the second time ever.

Starfall was one of 32 payloads on the company's Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission, which launched atop a Falcon 9 rocket at 7:04 a.m. EDT (1104 GMT) today (Oct. 20) from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

SpaceX has been relatively quiet about Starfall, which debuted this past June on a Falcon 9 launch from the Cape.

That June 23 flight was a dedicated demonstration mission for Starfall, designed to show that the capsule can fly in a controlled fashion and survive the harrowing downward trip through Earth's atmosphere.

And those will be Starfall's main jobs. The vehicle "will enable affordable, routine access to the microgravity environment for scientific research and in-space manufacturing," SpaceX in a June 23 X post, one of the few public statements the company has made about Starfall.

Indeed, most of the details that we have about the capsule come from an environmental assessment that was published by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in May.

According to that document, the disk-shaped Starfall is roughly 2.5 feet (0.75 meters) tall and 10.2 feet (3.1 m) wide. It weighs about 4,600 pounds (2,100 kilograms) and can bring 2,200 pounds (1,000 kg) of payload back down to Earth.

Starfall wasn't the only return capsule that went up on Bandwagon-5. Among the other 31 payloads on the flight was W-Series 7, the latest orbital "mini-factory" built and operated by the California company Varda Space Industries.

The W-Series capsules are designed to both host the production of valuable goods such as pharmaceuticals and bring them safely down to Earth, Varda has said.

The other payloads on Bandwagon-5 are a mix of "cubesats and microsats," according to SpaceX's mission description. Among the latter is Pelican-12, a sharp-eyed Earth-observation satellite built by the San Francisco company Planet.

If all goes according to plan today, the 32 payloads will be deployed over a nearly two-hour span beginning about 57 minutes after launch. Starfall will be the last to separate, releasing from the Falcon 9's upper stage two hours and 48 minutes post-liftoff.

The Falcon 9's first stage, meanwhile, came back to Earth as planned on Bandwagon-5. It touched down about nine minutes after launch, coming down in the Atlantic Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "A Shortfall of Gravitas." It was the 19th mission for this particular booster, according to the company.

Bandwagon is one of two SpaceX rideshare programs. The other, known as Transporter, has been busier, flying 18 missions to date.

The first Transporter mission, which lifted off in January 2021, delivered 143 payloads to Earth orbit, a single-launch record that still stands.

#28. NASA Improves Shock, Vibration Analysis

Rockets vibrate, shake, and flex intensely as they climb into space, and spacecraft packed with delicate scientific instruments must survive those forces. Before any rocket leaves the ground, NASA engineers work to predict how those stresses will affect every part of a spacecraft.

To do that, engineers in the Dynamic Environments Group with NASA’s Launch Services Program Office at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida have streamlined how they ensure spacecraft and rockets can withstand harsh vibration, shock, stress, or other physical forces, strengthening mission safety in the process.

Using a commercial digital software tool in a new way, the engineers developed a standardized modeling workflow for finite element modeling to strengthen shock and vibration analysis and ensure hardware is prepared for the extreme environments of launch and ascent.

“This computer-based method helps predict how rockets and spacecraft behave under extreme conditions before hardware is built and helps identify weak spots and potential failure risks early so the team can address the findings,” said Brian Beaver, chief of the Flight Analysis Division with the Launch Services Program Office at NASA Kennedy.

The team recently used the software for the first time while certifying a commercial launch provider’s rocket selected for a NASA mission. The commercial partner provided vibration testing but not shock testing. The Dynamic Environments Group determined shock testing was needed and used a template the group created to run what-if comparisons, visualize structural behavior, and answer complex questions that would have required extensive manual modeling in the past. The team verified the company’s testing results for flight environments, and the analysis provided new insights addressing shock during transport.

“We are using a tool that’s existed for decades, but it’s not normally used by the dynamic environments disciplines,” said Alex Hardt, aerospace engineer with the Launch Services Program Office at NASA Kennedy. “But we’re changing that. We’re using it in a relatively new area of dynamics.”

Although rockets and spacecraft are designed to absorb shocks and vibrations, those forces can cause wear and tear or potentially flight failures, especially during launch and ascent.

“We define how severe the random vibration levels and shock levels are, and then we verify that all the parts going on future rockets have been tested to those levels, maximizing their longevity,” Hardt said.

For decades, engineers have estimated shock and vibration environments using rules of thumb or by scaling previous data to estimate how each rocket component or spacecraft equipment would be impacted once assembled and flown. The approach worked, but relied heavily on engineering judgment and simple approximations drawn from past missions.

Because most dynamic environments engineers use finite element modeling tools infrequently, they often need to re-learn complex workflows. The software replaces older tools and provides a standard template that guides engineers more quickly and thoroughly through vibration profiles and shock conditions.

Finite element analysis is a powerful simulation technique that breaks a complex structure into smaller components so computers can accurately predict how a spacecraft or rocket could respond to specific forces or launch environments. This is important because issues can be addressed on the ground; once the rocket leaves the launch pad, most problems cannot be repaired or corrected, making early identification essential.

“We’ve used it to get really valuable insight very quickly into verifying a provider’s system,” Hardt said. “It’s already provided some really deep insight into something that normally takes a lot of effort.”

Hardt says having the ability to visualize non-intuitive dynamics problems using finite element models also highlights the software’s valuable impact on learning, efficiency, and alignment with NASA’s people focused culture. The workflow can help the engineers share knowledge, refine assessments with additional flight data, and increase proficiency with modeling tools. This capability already has saved months by allowing the team to run analysis independently without having to request and wait for analysis reports or data, and by helping them identify risks that weren’t previously considered.

NASA’s Launch Services Program Office is responsible for launching rockets delivering spacecraft that observe the Earth, visit other planets and explore the universe, from weather satellites to space telescopes to Mars rovers. The team is constantly adopting new tools like this to give the agency the highest practical chance of success for each mission.

NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery.

The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22. Here's how to see "shooting stars" from Halley's Comet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of the best fall meteor showers peaks this week, when pieces of the famous Halley's Comet streak across Earth's atmosphere as fast-moving "shooting stars."

The Orionid meteor shower will peak overnight Wednesday (Oct. 21) through Thursday (Oct. 22), potentially producing around 20 meteors per hour under a dark sky, according to Time and Date. The Orionids are caused when Earth passes through the debris left by Halley's Comet, which last passed through the inner solar system in 1986 and will return in 2061.

Halley's Comet is presently beyond the orbit of Neptune, according to The Planets Today, but it doesn't need to be close to Earth to cause "shooting stars." Every time the comet travels through the inner solar system, heat from the sun causes it to shed dust and rocky particles along its orbital path. Earth's own orbit takes the comet through streams of that ancient debris several times a year, with the particles vaporizing as they slam into our planet's atmosphere.

The Orionids are particularly fast meteors, striking Earth's atmosphere at around 41 miles per second (66 kilometers per second). They can produce bright streaks, occasional fireballs (extremely bright, sometimes colorful meteors) and "persistent trains" — glowing trails that remain visible briefly after a meteor has disappeared. The best way to view them is with the naked eye, although a nice pair of stargazing binoculars or a small backyard telescope will help you enjoy more sights during peak skywatching season this fall.

Halley's Comet produces not one but two annual meteor showers. Its orbit comes close to Earth's at two different points, so our planet encounters the comet's debris twice each year — once during the Orionids in late October, and again during the Eta Aquariid meteor shower in early May.

There's a slight complication with the Orionids this year. A 71%-illuminated waxing gibbous moon will brighten much of the night, making it harder to spot meteors. However, the moon will set early Thursday morning, creating a valuable window of darkness before dawn. That's also when the constellation Orion will be high in the sky, making the predawn hours the best time to watch.

You can trace the paths of Orionid meteors back to their radiant: the famous red supergiant star system Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion. (That's why the shower is called the Orionids.) However, there's no need to look directly at Orion. Meteors seen farther from the radiant can produce longer streaks across the sky; each one comes from a tiny piece of Halley's Comet completing a journey that began many centuries ago.

#30. Scientists discover a surprising link between vitamin C and cancer survival

Vitamin C plays an important role in keeping the immune system healthy, helping wounds heal, and protecting cells from damage. However, people with precancerous blood disorders and blood cancers often have persistently low vitamin C levels. Researchers have been investigating whether correcting this deficiency could improve their health and treatment outcomes.

New findings from the phase 2 EVITA clinical trial suggest that vitamin C supplementation may offer important benefits for people with precancerous blood conditions and early-stage blood cancers. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study was conducted by the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer® Epigenetics Dream Team.

The results, published in the American Cancer Society journal CANCER, revealed that patients who received 1,000 mg of oral vitamin C every day for one year experienced fewer adverse events during the study and its follow-up period. The supplement also changed the levels of certain immune signaling molecules, known as cytokines, in ways associated with more favorable outcomes. These changes suggest that vitamin C could influence inflammation-related processes involved in the growth and progression of abnormal blood cells.

Although vitamin C did not significantly affect the rate at which abnormal blood cells expanded, the researchers identified an encouraging result. An exploratory analysis showed that participants who received vitamin C were significantly more likely to be alive after approximately three years of follow-up than those who took a placebo. Scientists emphasize that this potential survival benefit must be verified in a larger phase 3 clinical trial.

Vitamin C Shows Promise for Patients at Risk of Leukemia

"We are tremendously excited and cautiously optimistic that our results could one day translate into a simple way to improve care and outcomes for people with pre-leukemia disorders," said Peter A. Jones, Ph.D., D.Sc. (hon), a distinguished professor at Van Andel Institute. Jones is also a co-corresponding author of the research and co-leader of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team.

"Our approach reflects a growing emphasis on cancer interception -- intervening before cancer becomes established. We are working to build on the trial findings by exploring how exactly vitamin C interacts with pre-cancerous cells, including the idea that it may help restore normal epigenetic function in blood cells at risk of becoming leukemia."

The international research effort was led by Kirsten Grønbæk, M.D., Ph.D., a leading hematologist, professor at the University of Copenhagen, and member of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team.

"These exciting preliminary findings lay the groundwork for a larger clinical trial to explore vitamin C as a possible way to improve patient outcomes," said Grønbæk. "It is too early to make definitive recommendations based on our results, but we are hopeful that a more expansive study will provide further insights."

First Clinical Trial Tests Daily Vitamin C for Precancerous Blood Disorders

The study enrolled 109 patients with either clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance (CCUS) or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). Both conditions can develop into acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive form of blood cancer that is often difficult to treat. The likelihood of developing CCUS and related blood disorders rises with age, making these conditions particularly common among older adults.

Currently, no approved treatment can prevent CCUS from progressing to leukemia. Although stem cell transplantation is an option for treating MDS, many patients cannot undergo the procedure because of age or other medical conditions. None of the people enrolled in the trial were receiving cancer treatment when the study took place.

To determine whether vitamin C might offer benefits, researchers randomly divided participants into two groups. One received 1,000 mg of vitamin C by mouth each day for 12 months. The other received a placebo designed to be indistinguishable from the supplement in appearance, taste, and smell, but containing no vitamin C.

Neither the participants nor the clinical staff knew who was receiving vitamin C until the study concluded. This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled approach is considered the gold standard in clinical research because it reduces potential bias and allows investigators to assess treatment effects more objectively.

The research was carried out at four hospitals: Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen University Hospital-Herlev, Aalborg University Hospital, and Keck Hospital of the University of Southern California.

What makes EVITA particularly notable is that it was the first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to investigate oral vitamin C in patients with conditions that can precede leukemia or with lower-risk myeloid cancers. Earlier studies had primarily examined vitamin C administered intravenously and had focused on solid tumors rather than precancerous blood disorders or early-stage blood malignancies.

EVITA instead evaluated a daily oral dose comparable to that available in many over-the-counter vitamin C supplements.

More Than Half of Patients Had Low Vitamin C Levels

Blood samples collected throughout the study allowed researchers to track participants' vitamin C concentrations and determine whether supplementation corrected deficiencies.

At the beginning of the trial, more than half of the participants had insufficient vitamin C levels. Among those assigned to the supplementation group, blood concentrations returned to normal after they began taking vitamin C.

For patients living with conditions that could eventually develop into leukemia, the possibility of an accessible intervention is especially important. In many cases, physicians have little choice but to monitor the disease and watch for signs that it is progressing.

"The standard approach for patients with pre-cancer blood disorders is to monitor their blood cell counts over time. This is, understandably, very frustrating -- no one wants to hear that they have a condition that increases leukemia risk but there's nothing that can be done other than watch and wait," said Casey O'Connell, M.D., FACP, the Lawrence and Jane Kelly Chair in Hematology at the University of Southern California and lead clinician at USC's trial location.

"The EVITA trial took on this challenge by exploring vitamin C's potential to address the underlying factors that drive leukemia development."

How Vitamin C Could Influence Cancer Development

Scientists have investigated whether vitamin C could play a useful role in cancer treatment for more than seven decades. For much of that time, the evidence remained uncertain because studies produced inconsistent findings and employed different experimental methods.

During the past decade, however, improved research technologies have revealed that vitamin C has important functions beyond its familiar roles in nutrition and immunity. In particular, scientists have uncovered its involvement in controlling gene activity and guiding normal cell development.

One of the most important discoveries concerns TET2, an enzyme that helps prevent cancerous growth by controlling whether particular genes are switched "on" or "off." Vitamin C supports the activity of this enzyme, which helps maintain normal patterns of gene regulation.

Mutations affecting TET2 are frequently found in leukemia and related blood disorders. When the enzyme's normal function is disrupted, abnormal cells can gain an opportunity to multiply and potentially develop into cancer.

Experiments using cancer models have provided additional evidence of vitamin C's possible protective effects. These studies found that supplementation could interfere with cellular changes associated with cancer and slow the progression of leukemia. Notably, the strongest effects appeared when vitamin C was introduced before cancer had become established.

This research helped inspire the idea of using vitamin C as a form of early intervention, potentially targeting the biological changes that precede the development of leukemia.

Before launching EVITA, the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team conducted a pilot clinical study in 2016 to determine whether taking vitamin C orally could meaningfully raise its concentration in the blood.

The initial findings suggested that oral supplementation was a practical approach. Encouraged by those results, the researchers launched the phase 2 EVITA trial in 2017.

"This early work was critical because it offered a foundation from which to develop the present trial," said Stine Ulrik Mikkelsen, M.D., Ph.D., the study's first author and a clinician researcher in Grønbæk's laboratory.

"Vitamin C is important because it is involved in a range of biological functions, including the activity of enzymes that regulate normal cell function."

Researchers are continuing to examine the EVITA data to better understand the biological processes that might explain why patients receiving vitamin C showed improved survival.

Although the findings offer a promising direction for future research, additional clinical studies will be essential to determine whether vitamin C supplementation can reliably improve outcomes for people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers.

Other authors include Ali Al-Mousawi, M.D., Amalie Bach Puglisi, M.D., Anders Pommer Vallentin, M.D., Astrid Østergaard Mortensen, Heidi Naomi Ottesen, Linn Gillberg, M.Sc., Ph.D., Morten Tulstrup, M.D., M.Sc., Ph.D., Jakob Werner Hansen, M.D., Ph.D., and Mette Klarskov Andersen, M.D., D.MSc., of the University of Copenhagen and Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet; Zachary Madaj, M.S., Toshinori Hinoue, Ph.D., Stacey L. Thomas, Ph.D., Christine N. Isaguirre, Ryan D. Sheldon, Ph.D., Marie Adams, M.S., Ryan Burgos, and Peter W. Laird, Ph.D., of Van Andel Institute; Jakob Schmidt Jespersen, M.Sc., Ph.D., Niels Richard Hansen, M.Sc., and Jens Lykkesfeldt, Ph.D., D.MSc., of the University of Copenhagen; Stephen Baylin, M.D., of Johns Hopkins University and Van Andel Institute; Bo Kok Mortensen, M.D., Ph.D., of Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet and Copenhagen University Hospital-Herlev; and Marianne Tang Severinsen, M.D., Ph.D., of Aalborg University Hospital.

Funding for the study was provided by Van Andel Institute through the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer® Epigenetics Dream Team, the Danish Cancer Society, and Greater Copenhagen Health Science Partners.

#32. Japan sends MMX toward the martian moons

On Monday, Oct. 19, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) successfully launched its Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission aboard an H3-24L rocket from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan at 3:41 p.m. EDT. MMX will study the martian moons Phobos and Deimos and is designed to return a sample from Phobos by 2031.

RELATED: Japan prepares to launch sample return mission to Phobos

On Tuesday, Oct. 20, SpaceX will launch its Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida at 6:30 a.m. EDT. Bandwagon flights carry customer satellites to mid-inclination orbits tilted partway between the equator and the poles, which SpaceX says offer “higher revisit rates” for satellites, meaning they pass over the same point on Earth more frequently. The Falcon 9 booster is expected to land on the droneship A Shortfall of Gravitas in the Atlantic Ocean.

Later on Tuesday, Oct. 20, SpaceX will launch the Starlink Group 15-15 mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 6:14 p.m. EDT, adding another batch of broadband internet satellites to the company’s Starlink constellation. The booster is slated to land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

Closing out Tuesday, Oct. 20, Chinese commercial launch company Galactic Energy is scheduled to fly a Ceres-1S — the sea-launched version of its small Ceres-1 rocket — from the Haiyang Oriental Spaceport off China’s eastern coast at 11:35 p.m. EDT. The payload has not been publicly identified, according to NextSpaceflight.

On Wednesday, Oct. 21, Rocket Lab is targeting 1:00 a.m. EDT for “We’re Not Hawking Around” aboard an Electron rocket from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula. The rocket will carry three satellites for Virginia-based private defense firm HawkEye 360’s satellite constellation — a radio-frequency spectrum monitoring system that collects data for national defense interests.

Late on Wednesday, Oct. 21, the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), the country’s main state-owned space contractor, will launch a Long March 8A from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on Hainan Island at 10:57 p.m. EDT. The payload is undisclosed, according to NextSpaceflight.

On Friday, Oct. 23, CASC plans a doubleheader. A Long March 6A is scheduled to lift off from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in northern China at 6:15 a.m. EDT, followed by a Long March 4B from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi Desert at 3:25 p.m. EDT. Neither payload has been identified, according to NextSpaceflight.

Wrapping up the week on Saturday, Oct. 24, SpaceX will launch the Starlink Group 15-16 mission from Vandenberg at 1:29 a.m. EDT. The booster is expected to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Monday, Oct. 12, SpaceX launched the Starlink Group 15-25 mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base at 8:28 p.m. EDT, with the booster landing on Of Course I Still Love You. The Falcon 9 booster returned to Landing Zone 40 at Cape Canaveral.

#33. The Makita 40V Max XGT Chainsaw Is One of the Most Powerful Saws We’ve Tested

A 20-inch electric saw that’s every bit as capable as a gas saw

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Makita’s newest 40V Max XGT 20-inch chainsaw is a beast. The brand claims it offers the power of a 50cc gas saw, and I’m inclined to believe it. When I first pulled the trigger, I was surprised by the speed and sound of the chain whizzing around. And it wasn’t just the noise that was impressive—in testing, it positively tore through logs.

At 20 inches, the 40V Max XGT chainsaw is among the biggest battery-powered chainsaws we test. A saw this size will give you the ability to tackle bigger jobs, and it appears to have the power to do so. The saw we tested came as a kit with everything you need, including an 8.0-Ah battery and charger. The kit isn’t cheap, but if you’re already on the Makita 40-volt XGT platform, you can save $500 and buy the chainsaw as a tool only.

It’s important to note that we test at the highest power/speed settings, and for a saw this big, that’s overkill on 6-inch logs. Using the three mode settings to match the power needed to the job at hand, it’s possible to greatly extend run-time.

Using the 40V Max XGT for practical tasks like felling trees or cleaning up fallen trees after a storm, confirmed its power. I tackled logs as big as 18 inches, and the saw left nothing to be desired—it handled everything I used it on, without faltering.

Picking up and examining the 40V Max XGT, it was obvious that it was well made. The plastic saw housing is tightly fitted and sturdy, with a removable mesh filter to keep dust out of the cooling vents. Adding to the impression of solid construction is the saw’s weight at 16.8 pounds—this is a little heavy, but it is a bigger saw with a large, high-output 8.0-Ah battery.

Unlike many battery-powered saws, the 40V Max XGT has removable metal bucking spikes to positively engage logs when cutting. It also has a clear window in the bar oil reservoir so you can check the level by looking at the side of the saw.

Other than the trigger throttle and chain brake, which are largely the same as those of any traditional gas saw, the 40V Max XGT has two buttons and a display to manage and monitor saw functions. One button is used to turn the saw on, while the other allows you to toggle through the three modes to adjust chain speed—something you can confirm by checking the LED display below the forward handle.

The 40V Max XGT is a powerful, high-quality saw that appears to be built to last. It’s capable of bigger jobs, those you might normally reserve for a gas saw. With it, you’ll be able to fell trees or clean up storm fall. Battery run-time is fair to good—to extend it, you’ll want to be careful to use the appropriate cutting mode.

The expense for this saw is considerable, so it may be best for people already committed to Makita’s XGT 40-volt platform. For comparison, Stihl’s MSA 300 C-O with a 20-inch bar is slightly more expensive as a tool only, but the battery and charger are less, so the cost is similar. While I might pick the Stihl in a vacuum, this saw’s merits make it a worthy recommendation, and its value increases if you are already invested in the XGT platform for other tools or plan to in the future.

#34. Japan’s sample return mission to Phobos may also collect some Mars dust

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

With NASA’s Mars sample plans in limbo, Japan tackles the next best thing — a Mars moon

This artist’s depiction shows the MMX spacecraft preparing to land on the Martian moon Phobos.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For decades, scientists have dreamed of getting Martian rocks into Earth’s laboratories — a Herculean feat that would revolutionize our knowledge of the Red Planet. An audacious mission from the Japanese space agency might offer the next best thing: rocks from Mars’ larger moon, Phobos.

That’s the task confronting the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft. The mission, which launched October 19, aims to crack the long-standing mystery of how Mars got its two odd moons by delivering a sample of Phobos to Earth in 2031. These rocks are no substitute for true Martian material — but given that NASA’s plans to fetch the Perseverance rover’s prized samples are in limbo, scientists are eager for even an indirect glimpse of Mars.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“It’s a chance to get a totally different sample and view of Martian materials,” says planetary scientist Briony Horgan of Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., who is not involved in the MMX mission. “It’ll be a great contribution to our sample collection back here on Earth.”

If it’s successful, MMX will be the first mission to reach Phobos. Three previous spacecraft from Russia failed.

The MMX itinerary is action-packed: The spacecraft will spend about one year cruising out to Mars, then slip into orbit around Mars alongside Phobos for about three years. During its stay, the spacecraft will deploy a small rover named Idefix to scout the moon for good sampling sites. The main spacecraft will then make two landings to grab 10 grams of sample, about the weight of four U.S. pennies. It will use two different devices to snag the sample: One will drill two centimeters down into the rock, while the other will blow pressurized gas at the surface to collect loose material.

Once loaded up, MMX will zip past the smaller moon Deimos before making the one-year trek home to drop its cargo in Australia’s outback, just as Japan’s two previous asteroid sample-return missions have done. After the Japanese space agency JAXA sorts and catalogs the samples, it will share portions of them with other institutions.

Such a small handful of rock may not sound impressive, but it’s enough to thrill researchers. “A few grams of sample are going to be a real bonanza for scientists,” says planetary scientist Michael Zolensky of NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where 15 percent of the sample will eventually end up.

MMX is designed to reveal the enigmatic origins of Phobos and Deimos — the only moons in the inner solar system besides our own. “The Martian moons are so different from [the] terrestrial moon: They are two, very small [and] very dark,” says planetary scientist Tomoki Nakamura of Tohoku University in Sendai, Japan.

The strange objects look like rocks that wandered in from the outer asteroid belt and got trapped around Mars. But their tidy circular orbits suggest they coalesced after a massive collision tore material off the Red Planet. Or perhaps they came about some other way that scientists simply haven’t imagined, says planetary scientist Kiyoshi Kuramoto of Hokkaido University in Sapporo, Japan. “The natural world often reveals aspects that exceed our expectations,” he says.

Studying the features and composition of Phobos’ surface could solve the mystery. But although MMX carries sophisticated instruments to explore Phobos, those observations may not suffice. Hence bringing rock back to Earth’s labs, where scientists can enlist equipment far too large or delicate to ever send to space.

Although sample analysis will focus on understanding Phobos, researchers will also be able to use the rocks to fine-tune our understanding of Mars. For example, pinpointing the material’s age will allow scientists to calibrate the chronology of cosmic collisions in the neighborhood of Mars. Currently, scientists estimate ages on Mars based on a timeline based on our moon, which may not apply at the Red Planet.

Scientists even have reason to hope that stray grains from Mars will be hidden amid the MMX treasure. This material could be ancient relics of the two bodies mixing during a moon-forming process, potentially including grains that hail from deeper in the Martian crust than scientists have seen so far in rare meteorites the cosmos has delivered us. No matter how Phobos formed, the material could also include fresher debris flung off the Red Planet by cosmic collisions.

The biggest challenge may be positively identifying which grains came from Mars. Such lucky samples would lack valuable geologic context and be far from pristine. “They’re material that’s been blasted off Mars from some unknown location, micron-sized things, sitting on the airless body Phobos, getting irradiated by space,” says planetary scientist Nancy Chabot of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Md. Nonetheless, scientists are prepared to get creative and use the latest technology to tease out every secret they can manage in any sample they can snag.

MMX offers a very different type of sample return than what NASA has initiated with the Perseverance rover, which has spent years squirreling away fresh material drilled from the most interesting outcrops it can find. That’s all in hopes of a future mission ferrying the rock to Earth for scientists to hunt for signs of ancient microbes. But the U.S. Congress has axed funding for that successor due to spiraling costs and concerns about feasibility — particularly of accomplishing the first ever launch from Mars.

Even if MMX can’t give scientists the satisfaction of an ultimate Mars sample return, there’s still plenty to learn, says planetary scientist Vicky Hamilton of the Southwest Research Institute in Boulder, Colo., who is not involved in the mission. “It’s always a happy day when we’re getting a sample from another object in space and bringing it back to Earth to study,” she says.

#36. Software

Research teams at NASA’s Glenn Research Center are involved in developing theory and software to predict the noise from aircraft engines. This software helps engineers to design and analyze new and improved aircraft propulsion systems. Copies of our software can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog.

Development of jet noise prediction codes is multifaceted. Since JeNo predicts jet noise using Lilley’s Acoustic Analogy and the mean flow solutions from a Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) code, accurate acoustic predictions hinge on accurate aerodynamic predictions. This is why acoustic source modeling and turbulence modeling, together with the development of advanced measurement systems, are the leading areas of research in jet noise prediction at NASA Glenn. RANS-based jet noise prediction schemes based on Lilley’s Acoustic Analogy offer relatively quick answers compared to those from alternative methods like Large-Eddy Simulations (LES) or Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS).

The JeNo jet noise prediction code calculates the far-field sound spectral density produced by axisymmetric jets at a user-specified observer location and frequency range. Currently, JeNo has been validated for subsonic and low supersonic, unheated axisymmetric jets. Copies of the JeNo code can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog.

Development of the MGBK code preceeded JeNo. Researchers at NASA GRC have used MGBK to predict trends in jet noise for complicated aircraft engine exhaust nozzles. MGBK was used to analyze the noise reduction benefits of chevrons–serrations on teh edge of turbofan nozzles–which are a familiar site on many commercial aircraft engines today. Copies of the MGBK codes can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog.

Predicated on simplistic models of the fan flow and geometry, V072 has been proven useful in studying rotor/stator interaction tone noise. When you need to design a low-noise fan stage, tone noise level predictions from V072 can help you make smart choices for such important design parameters as blade and vane counts, rotor-stator spacing, and stator vane sweep and lean. When you’re after quick noise estimates early in the design cycle, V072 may be your tool of choice. Copies of V072 can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog.

Taking rotor/stator interaction noise prediction to the next level, not only can TFaNS calculate the tone noise levels generated by rotor/stator interaction it can also account for the blade row acoustic coupling effects such transmission and reflection and can propagate those tones to the far field. Like V072, TFaNS runs quickly and can be used in early design stages for studying trends. Copies of TFaNS can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog

When simple models are too simple, an analysis with Linflux gives you the power to study realistic, 3-D flows and blade geometries. Compared with V072 and TFaNS, Linflux requires significantly more computational resources since it models much more of the physics involved. Linflux predicts rotor/stator tone noise and, like all the software developed by the NASA Glenn Acoustics Branch, has been rigorously validated against experimental data. Copies of Linflux can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog.

Using estimates of turbulence intensity and characteristic length scale as input, BFANS can be used to calculate the broadband noise generated by turbulence impinging on the leading edges of the rotor blades and stator vanes. Calculations with BFANS, combined with experimental data from tests at facilities like NASA Glenn’s 9’x 15’ Low Speed Wind Tunnel, can be used to hunt down the noisiest components in a fan stage. Copies of BFANS can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog.

RSI is a computer code for calculating the spectrum of broadband noise produced as a result of the interaction of the fan rotor wake turbulence with the fan exit guide vanes. The software computes the spectra of acoustic power upstream and downstream of the stator on a mode-by-mode basis at each frequency of interest given information about the incident turbulence characteristics. The target frequencies are arbitary and need not be harmonics of the blade passing frequency of the fan. Copies of RSI can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog.

Propeller noise can be strongly affected by any inflow that leads to unsteady blade loading. The WOBBLE code computes the tone noise associated with propellers with varying inflow angle and predicts the axial and circumferential directivity. Inflow angle is specified in terms of yaw, pitch, and roll angles of the aircraft. The acoustic model is exact and accounts for all unsteady sources such as thickness and loading effects from the blades. Copies of WOBBLE can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog.

Multiple pure tone noise (aka “buzz saw” noise), created by rotor locked shocks present when the fan blade tip speed is supersonic, can be estimated with the MPT code. The MPT codes also use flow predictions from a Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) code as input. This tool can be used by engineers to study the real-world effects of blade-to-blade difference caused during fabrication (manufacturing variations) or during hot-running operation (blade setting angle and untwist variations). Copies of the MPT code can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog.

Developed by the Allison Engine Company under contracts with Glenn Research Center, ADPAC solves tightly coupled internal/external flows through future-concept short-duct turbofan engines. ADPAC is one of our flexible validated CFD tools. Characteristics of the problems that can be modeled with ADPAC include: 2D/axisymmetric/3D/mixed, steady/unsteady, inviscid/viscous, rotating/non-rotating/mixed components, with bleeds, leakages, and injection. ADPAC was developed specifically for propulsion system aerodynamic analysis Copies of the ADPAC code can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog.

#40. Scientists discover a bizarre Jurassic “squid” unlike anything ever seen

Two extraordinarily rare fossils found in Wyoming have revealed a strange new species of squid relative that lived approximately 160 million years ago, during the Jurassic Period.

Named Wyoteuthis linsterorum, the prehistoric creature belonged to an extinct group of marine animals known as belemnites, which were related to modern squid and octopuses. What makes this species particularly remarkable is its unusually thick, barrel-shaped internal skeleton, earning it the distinction of being the "chunkiest" or "fattest" belemnite ever identified.

An international research team from the United States, United Kingdom, and New Zealand, including Dr. Dean Lomax, an Honorary Research Fellow at The University of Manchester, detailed the discovery in the scientific journal Papers in Palaeontology.

An Unusually Thick Jurassic Squid Relative

Belemnites are among the most frequently discovered fossils in the world. They are best known for their distinctive, bullet-shaped internal skeletal structures, called rostra or guards, which are often the only parts of the animals that survive in the fossil record.

Wyoming's Sundance Formation, which preserves evidence of an ancient inland sea that once stretched across much of the western United States, has yielded millions of these fossils. According to Wyoming paleontologist and study coauthor Jessica Lippincott, they are commonly nicknamed "squid butts" in the region.

Most belemnite fossils from Wyoming have a narrow, bullet-shaped appearance, typically measuring between 5 and 10 centimeters in length and just 1 to 2 centimeters across. The newly identified species is dramatically different. Its rostrum measures approximately 10 centimeters long but reaches an extraordinary 6 centimeters in width, making it the thickest known example of its kind.

Scientists estimate that the living animal, including its arms, could have reached a total length of approximately 60 centimeters, or about two feet.

Rare Fossils Reveal a Surprising Evolutionary Secret

Wyoming paleontologist Bill Wahl, who has devoted much of his career to searching for fossils across the state, recognized that the unusual specimen deserved closer examination. He said the belemnite "stuck out like a sore thumb" compared with the countless others found in the region.

Wahl assembled an international team to investigate the fossils, bringing in specialists including belemnite expert Alexey Ippolitov, a PhD student now based at Victoria University of Wellington in New Zealand.

The researchers used computed tomography (CT) scanning to investigate the fossils' internal structures without damaging the specimens. These detailed scans revealed an unexpected connection to an ancient belemnite family that scientists had believed disappeared millions of years before this animal lived.

Ippolitov said he was "deeply surprised" to encounter such an unusual specimen from a group that has already been studied extensively. Belemnites have been the subject of paleontological research for more than 200 years, making the identification of such a radically different species especially remarkable.

The creature's unusual proportions may also offer clues about how it lived and hunted.

Ippolitov explains: "A possible explanation is that their relatively large size gave them an advantage when hunting co-occurring smaller belemnites of the genus Pachyteuthis. Modern squid, after all, are hardly picky when it comes to prey: they readily hunt not only other species of cephalopods, but sometimes even their own kind."

A Fossil Discovery Nearly 30 Years in the Making

Although the species has only now been formally described, its discovery began almost three decades ago.

The first known specimen was found in the late 1990s by Dr. Burkhard Pohl, founder of the Wyoming Dinosaur Center. While examining fossils, Pohl noticed a belemnite that was considerably larger than any he had previously encountered.

Despite its unusual appearance, the specimen remained unstudied in a museum collection drawer for many years.

A breakthrough came when fossil collector Cliff Linster discovered a second specimen near Ten Sleep, Wyoming. He donated the fossil to the Wyoming Dinosaur Center in 2019, providing researchers with another example of the mysterious animal.

With two specimens available for comparison, scientists finally had enough evidence to recognize and formally describe an entirely new species.

The genus name Wyoteuthis means "a squid from Wyoming," while the species name linsterorum recognizes Cliff Linster and his family for their contributions. Linster discovered one of the only two known examples and ensured it was available for scientific research.

Lippincott emphasized how extraordinary the discovery was, even for researchers familiar with Wyoming's abundant belemnite fossils.

"After spending years fossil hunting in Wyoming and collecting countless fossils of the common Pachyteuthis belemnites here in Wyoming, this one is unlike anything I have ever seen! It goes to show that we are still finding new species of fossils all the time, and people who rockhound or collect invertebrate fossils can also contribute to science."

Honoring a Fossil Hunter's Remarkable Legacy

Sadly, Cliff Linster passed away in June before the research was published. He had been aware that scientists were investigating his discovery and was enthusiastic about seeing the unusual fossil receive formal scientific recognition.

The Linster family already had an impressive history of fossil discoveries, including their association with the famous dinosaur Bambiraptor.

For British paleontologist Dr. Dean Lomax, the discovery also carries considerable personal meaning. Lomax, an Honorary Research Fellow at The University of Manchester and an 1851 Research Fellow at the University of Bristol, first worked alongside Cliff and his wife, Sandy, while excavating dinosaur fossils as a teenager.

He said: "I met Cliff and Sandy in 2009, when I spent a week digging up a dinosaur bonebed on their property in northern Montana. I have fond memories of that dig, listening to Cliff share his passion for fossils, including this belemnite. I'm honored to help name this fossil after Cliff. It's bittersweet that he didn't get to see it published, but it's wonderful that we can immortalize him and his family name in the history of paleontology. The find is incredibly rare, which might be due to some ecological adaptations to the environment at the time. Perhaps its rarity is a result of narrow specialization."

Lomax has extensive experience studying Wyoming's prehistoric animals, including collecting fossils and excavating plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs from the Sundance Formation. He is also the author of the recently published book "The Secret Lives of Dinosaurs," which features fossils from Wyoming.

The discovery highlights how even well-studied fossil groups can still hold major surprises, particularly when unusual specimens are preserved and made available for scientific investigation.

Both known fossils of Wyoteuthis linsterorum are now on display at the Wyoming Dinosaur Center in Thermopolis, Wyoming, where visitors can see the extraordinary remains of one of the Jurassic seas' most unusual squid relatives.

The findings are published in the international journal Papers in Palaeontology.
