OSIRIS-REx was the first U.S. mission to collect a sample from an asteroid and return it to Earth.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Sept. 30, NASA formally concluded OSIRIS-REx, the historic first U.S. mission to pluck a pristine piece of an asteroid and deliver it safely back to Earth.

The van-sized OSIRIS-REx spacecraft — whose name is short for Origins, Spectral Interpretation, Resource Identification, Security-Regolith Explorer — visited and sampled Bennu, an ancient space rock holding pristine remnants from the dawn of our solar system more than 4.5 billion years ago. Among those cosmic relics are raw organic building blocks, the kind that may have seeded life on Earth.

"I have known this day was coming for a long time, but it is still difficult to see it arrive," OSIRIS-REx Principal Investigator Dante Lauretta, who's based at the University of Arizona, said in a post on LinkedIn. "I feel enormous pride in what we accomplished together, and real sadness that this journey has come to an end."

For the mission team, the farewell capped a decade of high-stakes engineering, on-the-fly troubleshooting and nail-biting close calls that ultimately delivered to Earth the largest asteroid sample ever collected in space, one that held secrets from the early solar system.

Long before launch, the team faced obstacles that nearly thwarted the endeavor — chiefly, two rejections from NASA — before finally securing the green light for the $1 billion project under the New Frontiers Program in 2011.

When OSIRIS-REx launched on Sept. 8, 2016, on a two-year journey across the inner solar system, Bennu was little more than a point of light in telescopes. Scientists expected the asteroid’s surface to be a smooth, sandy sphere where OSIRIS-REx could seamlessly touch down. Much to their surprise, however, when the probe arrived at the asteroid in late 2018, it revealed Bennu to be a treacherous, loosely bound amalgamation of jagged boulders.

"Our expectations about the asteroid's surface were completely wrong," Lauretta said in an Oct. 7 statement from the University of Arizona. "There was no obvious place to collect a sample anywhere."

When OSIRIS-REx touched down on a small crater named Nightingale, Bennu offered so little structural resistance that scientists said its surface reacted more like fluid than a hard, rocky shell. The spacecraft's sampling head sank directly into the asteroid, stopping after burrowing 20 inches (51 centimeters) deep by firing its thrusters at the right time to pull away, with the precious sample in hand.

Then came another nail-biting moment: The sample collector lid got jammed in a partially open position because so much material was scooped up, allowing fragments of the precious cargo to escape. In a race against time to prevent further loss, the mission team quickly stowed the sampler head directly inside the return capsule, securing the cosmic treasure for its journey back to Earth.

Even the final return to Earth, on Sept. 24, 2023, kept the team on edge: A parachute failed to deploy properly during reentry, forcing a tense but ultimately safe landing in the Utah desert.

"Successful exploration missions are not those that avoid surprises; they are those that are deliberately designed to adapt to them," Lauretta said in the statement, quoting a line from the mission's final report to NASA.

"That certainly describes OSIRIS-REx," he said. "Again and again, the mission presented us with circumstances we had not expected, and again and again, this team found a way forward."

The mission's triumphs began long before the samples reached Earth. For example, the probe set a Guinness World Record when it slid into orbit around the 1,610-foot-wide (490 meters) Bennu, which became the smallest object ever circled by a spacecraft.

The scientific payoff that followed included remote-sensing work that confirmed Bennu's surface is coated in carbon-bearing compounds. Those observations also revealed that Bennu was once part of a much larger, water-rich parent asteroid that shattered in a catastrophic collision in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

The returned sample — which weighs 4.29 ounces (121.6 grams) here on Earth, more than twice the mission's requirement — continues to thrill and occupy scientists.

A wave of research papers, now topping 200, continues to piece together the composition and history of the ancient space rock. Among other findings, Bennu's pristine material has revealed amino acids and sugars that, on Earth, are essential for life, alongside a history of exposure to liquid water that could have served as the "broth" for these compounds to interact.

More discoveries are likely to come. Most of the returned Bennu sample is being preserved for future generations of scientists, who will study it "with questions and instruments we cannot yet anticipate," Lauretta said in the statement.

Though its OSIRIS-REx chapter is closed, the spacecraft itself is far from retired. Renamed OSIRIS-APEX (OSIRIS-APophis EXplorer), the probe is using its remaining propellant to head toward Apophis, another near-Earth asteroid and a different type of space rock from Bennu. It is scheduled to arrive in 2029.

Archaeologists in Russia unearthed a flat wooden "pizza paddle" that had a board game carved into it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed an 11th-century wooden kitchen gadget with an ancient board game carved into the back. Medieval bakers may have used the wooden paddle not just to transfer bread into an oven but also to pass the time while they waited for the food to cook, the researchers said.

"We discovered a fragment of a fairly large shovel," Sergey Toropov, director of Novgorod State University's Center for Archaeological Research, said in a translated statement. "Most likely, it was a bread shovel, which was used to bake bread in an oven. On the reverse side, however, three squares have been carved, one inside the other."

The "bread shovel" — also known to contemporary home bakers as a wooden bread peel, a pizza paddle or a pizza peel — was found at the archaeological site of Pyatnitsky in the center of Staraya Russa, a medieval town between Moscow and St. Petersburg where last month, archaeologists reported their discovery of a "snake amulet."

Archaeologists discovered a wooden baking implement — likely a pizza-paddle-like tool — dating back to medieval times.

The preserved portion of the bread peel measures about 12 by 16 inches (30 by 40 centimeters), and it was likely crafted from oak. While one side is flat, likely for baking tasty treats, the other side had been carved with a board for the ancient game known as merels, merrelles, mills, nine-men's morris or cowboy checkers.

The origin of the game is unknown, but historical records and archaeological artifacts suggest a similar two-person logic game was played by the ancient Romans two millennia ago — and the game may be even older than that. In the Middle Ages, merels became particularly popular across Europe and Asia, possibly because it requires little equipment and can be set up quickly.

A typical merels (also known as nine-men's morris, mills or merrelles) board and pieces.

A typical merels board has three nested squares connected by horizontal and vertical lines. Each player has nine pieces of the same color. The goal is to arrange the pieces into columns of three along the lines. When a player forms a line, they can remove any one of their opponent's pieces. In this way, merels is a mixture of tic-tac-toe and checkers. A player wins when their opponent has only two pieces left or is completely blocked. (You can play an online version here.)

"Perhaps special boards for playing merels existed in antiquity," Toropov said, "but more often, one finds playing boards scratched or carved into the flat surfaces of household objects."

The archaeologists are not sure whether the wooden bread peel served two functions or whether it was repurposed as a game board after it broke and was no longer useful.

"At any moment, one could mark out a board on a flat surface, find suitable pieces — for example, small stones lying underfoot, and while away some time," Toropov said.

Merel boards and playing pieces have been recovered from ninth-century archaeological sites in the kingdom of the Rus', whose ancestors were Vikings who arrived in what is now Russia in the eighth century, according to the statement, but "a find as well-preserved as the one from Staraya Russa is practically unique."

#45. Horned dinosaurs’ weapons evolved to handle the forces of combat

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

3-D skulls reveal biomechanics of ceratopsians’ headgear, giving new insight into combat methods

Triceratops (depicted here) may have had horns adapted for the strain of interlocking during battles.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Triceratops’ massive skulls were built for horn-to-horn grappling. The rhino-like Centrosaurus could withstand stabbing its nose horn up and down. And the parrot-faced Psittacosaurus would have been wise to avoid a fight: Its head was ill-suited to handle blows.

New simulations using 3-D models of the heads of five different horned dinosaurs reveal what forces the skulls could withstand in battle. The results provide insight into how these dinosaurs evolved to use their face-based armory in combat, researchers report September 24 in PeerJ.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Ceratopsians — horned dinosaurs like Triceratops — have been hypothesized to use their imposing headgear as armaments for battling with other members of the species.Fossilized facial injuries consistent with head-to-head violence have provided physical clues. “We know from many fossils that ceratopsian skulls tended to get banged up a little bit … in very particular spots on the frill or on the cheek,” says Andrew Farke, a paleontologist at Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, California. But little else was known about how ceratopsians actually used their horns in battle.

Studying the biomechanics of the animals’ weaponized skulls could provide information on what movements and forces the dinosaurs evolved to tolerate. Such biomechanics research had previously been done on the bite stresses of theropod dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus and on the forces felt by the club tails of armored dinosaurs, says vertebrate paleontologist Eric Austin Ames Jr.

Ames and his colleagues at the University of Bristol in England developed digital 3-D models of six skulls across five ceratopsian species spread across the group’s evolutionary tree. They simulated the combat stress experienced across the skull, varying the direction of attack and how the weaponry was used. Higher stresses in the skull meant a greater risk of mechanical failure, Ames says. The dinosaurs are more likely to have evolved to fight in a way that was well-tolerated by the skull’s mechanics.

The team found that early members of the group from about 125 million years ago — like the hornless, husky-sized Psittacosaurus — didn’t have skulls well-suited for combat of any type. The pig-sized Protoceratops had a skull that tolerated ramming fairly well. Larger, later-diverging species  like Centrosaurus and the three-horned Triceratops and Spiclypeus appeared adapted to a wider range of combat styles.

Centrosaurus may have been a specialized stabber, lunging its head to jab at opponents. “When we tested [the skull] with vertical forces, it actually handled the stresses really well,” Ames says. “But when we tried side-to-side, it did not perform very well.”In contrast, Triceratops and Spiclypeus had skulls that tolerate the forces generated by interlocking horns and wrestling.

Ames thinks ceratopsians’ horns and frills probably first evolved for social and sexual display, but were soon used for full contact purposes. “Throughout their evolutionary history, their [horns’ traits] started to really explode in diversity and that coincided with different intraspecific combat styles,” he says. “This is something we see in modern herbivores.”

Much like with the antlers and horns of modern deer, buffalo or antelope, these weapons could have easily been turned on predators as well. “These adaptations are kind of like a Swiss Army knife,” Ames says. “They can be used for multiple things.”

The team created its 3-D models from surface scans of fossilized skulls. More detailed models that better simulate the complicated internal structure of these dinosaurs’ immense, bizarre skulls could provide even more insight to this prehistoric fight club, Farke says.

#46. The Best Paper Shredders Destroy Sensitive Documents in Seconds

Get rid of personal data, credit cards, medical information, old IDs, and CDs securely … by turning them into confetti.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There are two types of people who have a paper shredder at home: Most folks are what I like to think of as “casual” shredders, who shred paper bank statements, medical notices, snail mail credit-card or life insurance offers from time to time. Home-office workers, gig workers and freelancers, small business owners, retirees, and anyone wary of identity theft. Then there are the “serious” shredders—doctors, lawyers, accountants, government workers, or anyone who regularly handles no-one-else-needs-to-know information—who may need to obliterate foot-high stacks of documents day after day, which requires a powerful, secure, durable machine that can monotonously masticate without jamming or overheating.

Whether you’re a “casual” or “serious” shredder, everyone wants to find a home office workshop that doesn’t cost too much, but can handle their workload swiftly, smoothly, and securely. Within both camps, there are significant features that can make or break a shredder: longer run and shorter cooldown times, bigger bins, quieter motors, safety features, casters, and compact designs that let you tuck an infrequently used shredder discreetly under your desk. There are also special features that can make life easier, like anti-jam protections and solutions, ever-smaller particles, and automatic paper feeding. It’s easy to pick a paper shredder, bring it home, and hope for the best: But if you’re reading this guide, chances are you’d rather not leave your information security to chance.

And that’s why we’ve tested many of the most popular shredders on the market. We’ve found the best options for a wide spectrum of specialties. Whether you need to crush a foot-high pile of papers every morning or a few envelopes every week, we’ve found a shredder whose power, capacity, conveniences, and price all cater to your needs.

Paper shredders are more home office tech than conventional consumer electronics: Most of us don’t plan on upgrading our paper shredders regularly. As a result, the tech inside evolves far more slowly than gear like laptops, phones, and even printers. As a result, many of the best models stay at the top of the heap for years.

Given that reality, I try to look for the best of the best, not the “latest and greatest.” Ideally these are machines that you can invest in and trust them meet your needs for years and years. In fact, I’ve owned and used my personal shredder, an old Fellowes MS-450Cs shredder, for two decades.

While selecting which shredders match specific purposes for this guide, we considered mostly real-world factors as well as tech specs, such as:

Since our last roundup, I’ve tested an expanding range of models, from cheap shredder-mechanism-over-trash-bin designs to full-fledged micro-cut and auto-feed machines. I also widened my search beyond familiar shredder brands to lesser-known and retailer-exclusive models where performance, features, price, and consumer history warranted consideration. Some of these often-unknown brands can be surprisingly difficult to contact, which makes where a shredder is sold—and what help that retailer provides if something goes wrong—part of our value equation.

The Fellowes Powershred LX220 is the most versatile shredder I’ve tested, and works equally well in a home office, pulverizing an occasional pile of household paperwork, or tackling the more substantial workload of a professional team. My testing revealed its stated specs met or even exceeded its rated 20-sheet capacity and 30-minute runtime. Plus, Fellowes’ IntelliBar provides visual feedback on bin fullness, runtime, and sheet capacity, while SafeSense stops the cutters when hands approach the paper opening.

Best of all, Fellowes’ proactive “100-percent Jam Proof” system is designed to detect overambitious stacks and head off paper jam interruptions before they happen.

Notice, I said designed to. During our testing, we did manage to jam the supposedly 100-percent-jam-proof LX220. In its defense, I was actively trying to choke it rather than accidentally overstuffing it in a fit of shredding enthusiasm.

Under more normal conditions, Fellowes’ anti-jam system works incredibly well. Combined with the LX220’s other talents and relatively few shortcomings, it’s still the shredder we’d recommend to the widest variety of buyers.

For $75, the Sam’s Club-exclusive Member’s Mark C249-A delivers a robust set of functional and convenience-minded features, including some options you’d expect only on a higher-priced shredder.

It has a rather surprising skill set, anchored by a 12-sheet capacity, P-4 micro-cut security, 30-minute runtime, and an auto-reverse to help clear jams. It also has a “safety interlock/shred safe” feature—a helpful safety precaution that prevents operation when the bin is missing or not seated correctly. It’s common in high-end shredders, but a huge get at this price.

Surprisingly, it also handles nearly all the non-paper office detritus likely to find its way into a shredder—staples, credit cards, CDs, and what Sam’s Club describes as “small” paper clips. Again, this kind of power is normally reserved for more expensive models.

Not only do you get capacity, stamina, security, and convenience for not a lot of money, but you have the convenience of taking it back to Sam’s Club if something should go wrong with it.

If your shredding needs lean toward the occasional, choose one that won’t hog otherwise valuable floor space. Better yet, get a shredder that’s essentially invisible when not in infrequent use. At roughly 15 inches tall, and barely a foot wide, this compact Aurora AU870MZ may not be a ninja, but its ability to simply slide beneath your desktop makes it as unobtrusive as a shredder can be.

Not only does this Aurora—not to be confused with its older and less capable sibling, the AU870MA—disappear beneath most desks or easily slip into a closet, it can also make up to eight sheets disappear at a time.

There are some compromises. This Aurora’s 3.9-gallon bin will fill faster, and its five-minute runtime won’t be enough time to take care of even a small pile of accumulated scraps in one session. But if you consider this a JIC shredder, being able to hide it is likely more important to you than its lack of workhorse attributes.

While compact, this Aurora doesn’t skimp on shredding security or capability. You get a P-4 micro-cutting mechanism that also can chomp non-paper credit cards, staples, and small paper clips.

Nearly everyone would rather do almost any other kind of office work than shredding. So, instead of feeding and watching, this HP (made by Royal and sometimes listed as the 91032T and/or the AF809), lets you load up to 80 sheets into its clever fold up/down automatic feeder which frees you up to do something more important, like grab a snack or cup of coffee.

However, in the real world, the small 3.8-gallon bin doesn’t hold the bits from all 80 shredded pages without some help. Once I reached around 50 pages shredded, the HP stopped and waited until I pulled out the bin and leveled its shredded contents. After shoving the bin back in, the HP finished the remaining 30 pages without any trouble. But even with this bin shuffling, the 80 sheets got chewed up in just around five minutes.

Other than its mismatched auto-feed and bin capacities, this surprisingly affordable, speedy, and compact machine—it’s less than 17 inches tall—includes P-4 micro-cut security and can also masticate credit cards, staples, paper clips, and CDs through its 9-sheet manual feed slot.

If you’re the paranoid type—rather extra extra careful like me—about completely obliterating confidential documents—purchase a shredder that’s capable of mincing personal papers into the most minuscule, irrecoverable particles possible at a price that doesn’t require a bond issue.

The relatively new Effeluviate Q9 deploys P-7 cutters—a shredding security level normally associated with much pricier specialist machines and here for something approaching a consumer price—pulverizes a document into tiny 1 × 1.7mm particles (3/64 x 5/64, or 0.05 x 0.08, of an inch), a fraction of the size of a P-5 shredder produced particle.

Other than its ultra-secure P-7 rating and its resulting paper powder, this Q9’s remaining specs are almost boringly conventional: a relatively low seven-sheet manual feed, a decent 30-minute runtime, and a mid-range 5.23 gallon bin (not 6 gallons, as rated). And while the Q9 can crush plastic credit cards, staples, and CDs, it’s apparently allergic to paper clips.

Its sub-56dB noise rating, however, makes the Q9 about 10dB quieter than most shredders so mincing documents won’t disturb your co-habitants either day or night. I’m a little skittish about recommending a relatively unknown brand, but the specs are incredibly impressive.

If you must macerate massive masses of documents on a daily basis, the Bonsen S9221 is about to become your new best friend. Lift up its top, load up to 320 sheets into its flatbed feeder, and walk away. In 30 minutes, all 320 sheets will be transformed into tiny 2 × 10mm specks.

The S9221’s 8.1-gallon pull-out bin is appropriately roomy for the kind of 320-sheet jobs its auto feeder invites. Although you can leave large jobs to the auto feeder, a separate manual slot handles up to 10 sheets in smaller batches along with staples, paper clips, and credit cards—but not CDs.

One thing to keep an eye out for when you go to buy: There’s an older version of the S9221 with a slightly lower 300-page capacity and only P-4 micro-cut security instead of P-5. Since it has the same name and similar features to the new model, it would be very easy to buy the old model without noticing. Please make sure to check the listing before clicking “buy.”

I recently evaluated the top shredders under $100, and there are a few sub-$100 models that work great, and are more widely available than the Member’s Mark, including the Amazon Basics 12-Sheet Cross-Cut ($59), the Staples ST62150 ($82), which is loaded with safety features, and the Bonsaii C275-A 12-Sheet Cross-Cut ($65) ideal for infrequent emptying.

You may not be able to control where your digital data ends up. But you know exactly how you can securely dispose of your paper records. The trick is deciding which shredder will best satisfy your serious or casual shredding needs, which usually comes down to a handful of features.

Once you start your shredding chore, you’d rather not be interrupted by problems with your shredder. Runtime tells you how long you can keep feeding paper into a shredder before its motor overheats and shuts down, forcing you to wait 30 to 45 minutes, depending on the model, for the machine to catch its mechanical breath.

A small personal shredder may run for only five or 10 minutes, which is plenty if you dispatch only a few documents at a time. If you’re regularly confronted by larger piles to pulverize, look for a runtime of 30 minutes or more.

Once you choose a shredder with longer runtimes, don’t obsess over the advertised cooldown time. You may fill the bin before the shredder overheats and, by the time you’ve disposed of all that confetti, the motor already has had a chance to cool before you return with an empty bin.

A shredder is still largely a mechanical device, a motor driving a set of cutters, augmented in many models by sensors and electronic controls. And as with any mechanical object, failure is often less a question of if than when. Long-term owner shredder reviews are especially useful for spotting recurring problems with motors, sensors, switches, and other parts that may not misbehave during short-term testing.

Unfortunately, getting help directly from some shredder brands can be harder than clearing a paper jam. During our ongoing shredder research, we’ve encountered multiple manufacturers failing to respond to repeated emails and phone calls. Some brands don’t even provide a U.S. customer-service number.

That doesn’t automatically make shredders from these contact-resistant brands a bad buy. Purchasing from an established store or online retailer with a clearly stated return or replacement policy gives you a more reliable resource to turn to if your new shredder turns out to be a lemon. Before buying—particularly from an unfamiliar brand—check both the manufacturer’s warranty and especially the retailer’s return/replace policy.

Unlike the shredders you may remember from old movies, most modern machines no longer turn documents into long linguini-like strips. Cross-cut shredders slice paper both lengthwise and crosswise into small rectangular scraps. Micro-cut models slice and dice those scraps into even tinier bits, leaving hundreds or even thousands of petite particles.

For most home and home-office use, either cutting method provides plenty of protection. Most shredders these days offer micro-cut machines with either P-4 security, which makes reconstructing a document the most puzzling jigsaw puzzle ever, or P-5 security, whose even more diminutive document destruction methods are favored by MDs, CPAs, JDs, or by other professionals with initials in their titles.

The larger and more powerful your shredder, the more sheets it can generally chew through at one time. Just don’t treat the number printed on the box as a dare.

Manufacturers’ rated sheet capacities are best-case numbers, usually based on neatly aligned standard-weight bond paper. Thicker stock, folds, staples, uneven piles, and stuffed envelopes can quickly turn a “12-sheet” machine into something more comfortable with eight or nine. Feeding a few sheets below the rated maximum is one of the easiest ways to avoid jams and unnecessary strain.

Manual shredders require you to stand there feeding paper in batches. Auto-feed machines let you load a stack, walk away, and get something else done while the shredder eats.

Here again, don’t take the rated auto-feed sheet capacity too literally. An “80-sheet” or “200-sheet” auto feeder may accommodate that many pristine sheets under ideal conditions, but real paperwork is rarely pristine. Wrinkles, folds, different paper weights, staples, and uneven stacks can reduce how much you can reliably leave it to swallow unattended. Plus, the bin on a high-capacity auto-feed model may fill before the maximum number of sheets are fed into it.

Auto-feed mechanisms also add more rollers, sensors, and jam-clearing compartments. And more moving mechanical parts create more places for something to eventually go wrong.

However, if you routinely accumulate large piles, the time a highly rated auto feed shredder saves can easily outweigh the added complexity and potential mechanical issues.

A bigger bin means fewer trips to empty it, but gallon capacity tells only part of the story. Pull-out drawers are lighter and easier to clean and empty. Bins that require lifting the often heavy shredder mechanism off the top of a wastepaper basket can potentially scatter loose particles still in the cutter mechanism.

Also pay attention to what happens when you pull that drawer out. Paper confetti has an impressive ability to cling to plastic, pile up behind a bin, and otherwise escape the container designed to hold it. An easy-to-remove bin that keeps most of its shredded paper actually in the bin will save you emptying and clean-up aggravation, especially if you don’t wait until the bin is filled to its brim.

Shredders may look sturdy and impervious, but most are actually quite finicky eaters. Nearly every shredder will eventually jam if you feed it too much at one time or feed it the wrong type, shape, or mix of paper. More advanced models with more advanced anti-jam systems sense an overload before one occurs, or either automatically reverse or allow you to manually reverse to relieve the jam before you need to perform paper-removal surgery from the cutters with tweezers or needle-nose pliers.

The cheapest jam protection, however, is restraint. If a machine claims 12 sheets, regularly feeding it eight or nine instead will lower your odds of spending quality time violently tugging mangled paper back out of its teeth.

Most current shredders can swallow staples and paper clips, and many can also chew up plastic credit cards. CDs and other thicker media such as metal cards are less universally welcome.

Check the manufacturer’s instructions before you buy for what non-paper materials a shredder can successfully chew and before feeding anything other than paper into its cutters. A shredder capable of mincing a stack of tax records can object like a microwave forced to cook metal to something it wasn’t designed to eat.

Probably less than you think. For most people who dispatch a few bills, receipts, financial statements, or junk-mail offers every few days, well under $100 can buy a perfectly capable shredder.

Spending more generally buys stamina, convenience, and durability: longer runtimes, larger bins, higher sheet capacities, auto-feed, better jam protection, sometimes finer-cut security, and years if not decades of service. Those features become worth paying for as the amount and frequency of your shredding increase.

As with nearly all things, don’t be penny wise and pound foolish. You will find you will shred more than you anticipated—it’s just human nature to use a new device more than you though you would. Overall, shredders costing several hundreds of dollars make the most sense for people who regularly devour large stacks or have a specialized need. Don’t decide what to spend simply by asking how private your paperwork is; ask how much of it you need to turn into confetti and how often both now and in the future.

The most important shredder “spec” may be how little time it forces you to spend with it. Sheet capacity, runtime, security level, and bin capacity are the headline numbers I’d look at first. Runtime is particularly useful because it tells you something about how much work the machine can comfortably handle before demanding a rest.

But some of the things that most determine whether you’ll love or hate a shredder aren’t specs at all. Nearly every decent modern shredder can reduce ordinary documents beyond casual recognition. The bigger differences are how often it jams, how easily those jams clear, how cleanly the bin empties, and how much confetti winds up everywhere except inside it.

Check owner reviews for recurring complaints about jams, overheating, finicky sensors, messy bins, and other annoyances. AI agents on online sites can summarize customer reviews to answer many of these before-you-buy questions.

With shredders, old doesn’t necessarily mean obsolete. Sometimes it means proven.Unlike most consumer electronics, shredders don’t become outdated because they lack this year’s faster processor, new operating system, wireless standard, or other bleeding-edge technology. An older model that’s still attracting buyers and good reviews may actually offer something a brand-new machine can’t: years of accumulated evidence about how well it holds up.

Before buying an older model, check whether the manufacturer has introduced a newer or revised version. When shopping online, search the manufacturer’s current lineup or, if the retailer provides an AI or shopping assistant, ask whether there’s a newer version of the model you’re considering. Then compare old to new rather than automatically assuming new means better.

The best shredder maintenance is self-restraint. Don’t continually stuff the cutters to their rated maximum, allow the bin overflow, or feed the machine materials it wasn’t designed to digest.

Lubrication requirements vary. Some manufacturers recommend shredder oil applied at regular intervals, others suggest pre-lubricated oil sheets, and some models claim to require little or no lubrication at all. Follow the instructions for your particular machine rather than assuming every shredder requires the same type of mechanical TLC.

Beyond that, maintenance should be pretty painless: empty the bin before the paper snow reaches the cutters, occasionally clean dusty sensors if the manufacturer recommends it, and clear jams rather than repeatedly hammering the reverse button and hoping for divine intervention.

Despite the name, most modern “shredders” no longer shred paper into long strips. While cross cut and micro cut are clues for how small the ultimate shred pieces will be, P-ratings, part of the DIN 66399 security standard, put an actual number on “small.”

P-ratings run from P-1 through P-7; the higher the number, the smaller the pieces produced. For ordinary household paperwork, P-3 is already plenty secure. A cross-cut P-3 machine reduces a document to hundreds of pieces, which is more than enough discouragement for anyone contemplating reconstructing your bills, junk mail, receipts, or other everyday paperwork. After all, a document pieced back together like a taped mosaic isn’t likely to fool many people.

P-4 is the sweet spot for buyers who want their paperwork diced considerably finer without spending much more, and P-4 is common among consumer micro-cut shredders. P-5 turns documents into even tinier bits and makes sense for especially sensitive financial, legal, medical, or professional paperwork. P-6 and P-7 go further still, into security levels intended for documents whose contents matter considerably more than last month’s Visa bill.

For most of us, then, P-3 is plenty, P-4 buys extra peace of mind, and P-5 is for paperwork you’d really rather nobody put back together.

Stewart Wolpin, based in New York City, has been writing about, reporting on, and reviewing consumer technology for nearly 40 years. #49. NASA’s Simulated Mars Crew Marks One Year Inside Habitat

The four crew members in NASA’s simulated Mars mission have spent the past year living and working in isolation in a confined habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. For the past 365 days, the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) Mission 2 crew members have operated as though they were on the Red Planet, growing crops, managing limited resources, navigating communication delays, and conducting suited extravehicular activities on a simulated Martian surface.

Crew members include Ross Elder, mission commander; Ellen Ellis, medical officer; Matthew Montgomery, science officer; and James Spicer, flight engineer. They entered their 1,700 square foot 3D-printed habitat Oct. 19, 2025. Leading up to the one-year mark of their 378‑day mission, science teams at NASA prepared to process health and performance data collected on the crew. This critical data can help NASA balance priorities and develop methods that counter spaceflight risks during future long-duration missions on Mars.

“We are extremely proud of the crew for their commitment and achievements over the last year on such a fast-paced, highly demanding mission,” said Grace Douglas, CHAPEA principal investigator. “The entire CHAPEA team is excited to congratulate the crew in person.”

The crew will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, to conclude their mission. They will have a chance to reconnect with their families, who they’ve only spoken with via email over the course of their mission with a Mars-like communication delay. The crew will then begin two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefs with NASA scientists.

These debriefs and evaluations will help scientists learn what it takes for crews to adapt to the routines and demands of daily life on long-duration missions, giving NASA insight into what future explorers may need to stay healthy, productive, and connected during missions far from Earth.

For example, data could shed light on how limited food and exercise systems will influence NASA’s ability to achieve mission objectives, including spacewalks on the surface of Mars. Some data also could help NASA foster autonomy and build decision-making support systems that best aid crew with communication delays lasting up to 45 minutes each way.

“This mission has been incredibly valuable in starting to teach us how to understand requirements for year-long missions, including medical and psychological care, via communication delays,” said Michael Stenger, chief scientist for NASA’s Human Research Program. “When combining this Mars-realistic mission analog with a suite of physiological, psychological, and performance measures in a rigorously controlled environment, we’ll be able to translate the knowledge from these experiences to Moon Base and beyond.”

To watch the CHAPEA Mission 2 egress ceremony on Oct. 31, visit:

NASA’s Human Research Program pursues methods and technologies to support safe, productive human space travel. Through science conducted in laboratories, ground-based analogs, commercial missions, the International Space Station and Artemis missions, the program scrutinizes how spaceflight affects human bodies and behaviors. Such research drives the program’s quest to innovate ways that keep astronauts healthy and mission ready as human space exploration expands to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery.

#50. Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable

Growing older is often associated with memory loss and declining mental abilities. However, scientists are questioning whether these changes tell the whole story. Rather than simply becoming less capable, the brain may be adapting to a new stage of life in which accumulated knowledge, wisdom, and understanding become more important than remembering every detail.

Researchers at the University of Arizona have proposed a different way of understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on findings from molecular biology and brain imaging, they suggest that the changes occurring in older brains may reflect a natural stage of human development rather than deterioration alone. Their work, published in Perspectives on Psychological Science, offers a new perspective on why thinking and memory change with age.

The researchers call their proposed explanation the adaptive aging hypothesis. It suggests that the brain gradually adjusts its priorities to make better use of a lifetime of accumulated experience. This could help explain why older adults often have valuable strengths in teaching, mentoring, storytelling, and passing knowledge to younger generations.

"If we look at normative aging as a story of just decline, we are really missing the boat," said study coauthor Fabian-Xosé Fernandez, an associate professor of cognition and neural systems at the University of Arizona. "The older brain is optimized for different things than the younger brain, predominantly the sharing of stored expertise and social relationships."

How the Brain Shifts From Memory to Meaning

Two brain regions play important roles in how people remember and interpret their experiences. The hippocampus helps preserve specific information about events, including their details and circumstances. The frontal cortex, meanwhile, is more involved in extracting broader meaning, recognizing patterns, and understanding the central message of an experience, sometimes called its "gist."

According to the researchers, the balance between these systems changes during healthy aging. As people grow older, the brain tends to place less emphasis on activity in the hippocampus and rely more on the frontal cortex. This shift may allow the brain to focus more on interpreting information through existing knowledge rather than recording every new experience in precise detail.

"The fact that you see this across people and animal models suggests there is an evolutionary driving force," Fernandez said. "One could argue you are developing your entire life, and development occurs in lockstep with the needs of your brain. When you're younger, the hippocampus turns on because you don't have a knowledge base or know how the world works. A kid absorbs information like a sponge because they are building an archive of information. In early life, the balance is tilted toward recollecting declarative memories with precision, detail, and context."

Young brains need to gather enormous amounts of new information because they are still building a foundation for understanding the world. By later adulthood, however, people have already developed extensive stores of memories, concepts, and experiences. Connecting new information to what they already know may become more useful than retaining every individual detail.

The researchers suggest that this changing balance reflects a shift in how the brain processes experience. Instead of concentrating primarily on collecting detailed memories, it increasingly emphasizes understanding relationships, identifying underlying meaning, and applying previously acquired knowledge.

Why Evolution May Favor Wisdom in Older Adults

Evidence of similar changes in animal models raises the possibility that this transition has an evolutionary explanation. Fernandez suggests that the aging brain may be adapting to help individuals preserve and share the knowledge they have acquired throughout their lives.

From this perspective, the ability to draw on decades of experience could be especially valuable for making judgments, guiding others, and transferring important information between generations. Older adults may therefore play a distinct role in supporting younger people through mentorship, teaching, and storytelling.

"Given those goals, it makes sense that you aren't interested in nitty-gritty details," Fernandez said. "You are interested in safeguarding the vast knowledge you already have. Evolution may be saying that if you make it long enough, there's a need to transmit this information, so we put into motion biological changes that enforce and protect your semantic and autobiographical memories."

Under this hypothesis, changes in memory and thinking are not necessarily signs that the brain is functioning less effectively. They may instead reflect a different set of priorities, with greater emphasis on preserving meaningful knowledge and using it to understand new situations.

Why Healthy Brain Aging Is Different From Alzheimer's

The adaptive aging hypothesis could also provide scientists with another way to examine the differences between normal cognitive aging and Alzheimer's disease.

Although both involve changes in memory, Fernandez emphasizes that Alzheimer's should not be understood as ordinary aging taken to an extreme. The biological processes involved are fundamentally different.

"When I was in grad school, people thought about Alzheimer's as a more intense version of cognitive aging, but that is just not the case," Fernandez said. "They are completely different."

During typical aging, the brain's gradual shift away from relying heavily on the hippocampus and toward greater involvement of the frontal cortex generally unfolds between the fifth and seventh decades of life. In Alzheimer's disease, however, abnormal processes involving proteins such as amyloid and tau may interfere with this transition.

One important distinction involves activity in the hippocampus. While healthy aging is generally associated with reduced emphasis on this region, Alzheimer's can involve unusually high levels of hippocampal activity. Rather than supporting the normal progression of cognitive development, disease-related changes may disrupt the brain networks responsible for memory and understanding.

"In normative aging, hippocampal activation is deemphasized, which is probably what should be happening in a 70-year-old. But in many cases of Alzheimer's, it turns out the hippocampus is hyperactive," he said. "This beautiful developmental transition is completely disrupted in Alzheimer's disease by pathological processes that mess with episodic memory and interfere with circuits that allow you to think about your own life, lexicon, and vocabulary."

These disruptions can affect the ability to recall personal experiences and access stored knowledge, including words and their meanings. Understanding how these changes differ from the adaptations associated with healthy aging may help researchers develop a clearer picture of normal brain development and neurodegenerative disease.

Embracing the Hidden Strengths of the Aging Brain

The researchers argue that society may need to reconsider what successful brain aging looks like. Encouraging older adults to process information exactly as younger people do may not always be the most productive approach.

Fernandez suggests that placing excessive emphasis on remembering precise details could work against the brain's changing priorities. "For many individuals, the weight of how you process information should probably not be so hippocampal-centric by the sixth or seventh decade."

Instead of judging older adults primarily by abilities that tend to weaken with age, the researchers encourage greater recognition of the capabilities that may become especially valuable later in life.

Creating more opportunities for social interaction could be one way to support these strengths. Relationships between older and younger generations may be particularly beneficial because they provide opportunities to exchange experiences, share expertise, and preserve knowledge that might otherwise be lost.

"People see older individuals and look at them as not being on par with younger individuals across a lot of metrics," Fernandez says. "The way I look at it is that you've got someone with a brain that has been active for several decades and has seen a lot. There is tremendous value there, and we don't do a good job of unlocking it."

The central message of the adaptive aging hypothesis is that growing older may involve more than a gradual reduction in cognitive abilities. Although some mental skills become less reliable with age, the brain may also be adapting to make better use of the knowledge and experience accumulated over a lifetime. Recognizing those strengths could change how society understands aging and the contributions older adults can make.

#52. The 7 Best Wood Chippers for Faster Yard and Storm Cleanup

Fall cleanup season is here. From storm-damaged limbs to mountains of leaves and branches, these tested wood chippers will save you hours of hauling and countless trips to the curb.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve been putting off yard cleanup, the calendar is going to force your hand. With various fall weather events occurring randomly and temperatures dropping and winter approaching, you probably want to get your yard in order while there’s still a vague idea of warmth outside. A wood chipper won’t stop the next storm from knocking limbs off your trees, but it will make cleaning up afterward a whole lot easier.

Like a generator or a snowblower, the time to buy one of these isn’t after the event has happened, but before, when items are still well-stocked. It’s also the best time to think about what to do with all of that woody debris once it drops. Instead of dragging branches to the curb, a quality wood chipper can turn those into useful mulch while saving you time, money, and annoying trips across the yard.

Powered by either a gas or electric motors, wood chippers use a set of blades that shred just about anything that falls from a tree to your lawn, from dead leaves to thick branches, into bite-sized pieces that you can use as mulch, which helps fertilize the soil and block weeds from growing in your landscaping.

While many of us think of wood chippers as industrial-strength tools for tree removal companies, there are smaller models suitable for homeowners with wooded properties and sustainable lawn care goals. These wood chippers are fairly portable. In fact, many come on wheels so you can bring them out from your shed or garage without a hassle. And I would know: I’ve tested some of the most promising wood chippers out there to find the best ones that are recommended here. Read on to decide which one is right for you.

Tony Carrick lives on a partially wooded lot in North Carolina, so he’s used to trees dumping branches, twigs, leaves, and other debris on his property. For this round of wood chipper testing, he tested four new models and found them all worthwhile to recommend.

Carrick selected these chippers for testing based on previous chipper tests performed by the Popular Mechanics test team as well as his own past wood chipping experience. He used each machine to break down dry branches of varying sizes, up to 3 inches thick, and evaluated how they handled thicker branches without stalling out or clogging. He also used each model’s mulching function to break down twigs and dead leaves.

Wood chippers usually deposit their chopped-up wood into a collection bag, so Carrick measured each chipper’s bag capacity and assessed how easy it was to unload and reset after the job was done. He also evaluated the chips themselves, checking each model’s ability to break down material into small pieces for mulching.

After testing for each machine was complete, Carrick weighed each model’s performance with its price tag to determine value. He made sure to highlight both small electric wood chippers for lighter-duty needs and larger gas models for more heavily wooded properties, so there’s a great option for every homeowner who needs one.

Champion’s 3-inch portable wood chipper strikes a good balance between size, chipping capacity, and price, which is why it’s our pick for best all-around wood chipper for homeowners.

For starters, the Champion’s compact size lends itself to homeowner use. Large wheels and wide handlebars made it easy to wheel from the garage, around the house, through a gate, and into the backyard. We do wonder how well the plastic wheels will stand up to the test of time, though that concern is as of now unfounded.

Despite its smaller size, the Champion has just as much cutting capacity as larger options. It chewed through 3-inch-diameter branches without clogging or stalling, whether cramming it with soft pine or harder maple branches. After a heavy day of rain, the material running through the Champion was saturated. Wet wood typically makes for tough sledding for a wood chipper, but this chipper was unfazed, grinding through soaked branches with ease.

As with the other wood chippers we tested, the Champion portable wood chipper features dual intakes—along with a chute for branches, there’s also a hopper on the top for leaves and twigs.

If there’s a gripe to be had with the wood chipping function on the Champion, it’s with the stiff rubber gasket that covers the chute opening, which created some resistance when feeding branches. These were small issues that didn’t really impact performance in testing, but we could see them slowing things down if a large stack of branches was fed into the chipper.

Champion’s 3-inch chipper is, above all else, a well-balanced option. It isn’t the most powerful chipper you can buy, but it’s a strong performer for what we’d call an average workload. When you factor that in with a lower price tag than those of other comparable models, it’s the right move for homeowners who need a chipper to break down yard waste from trees periodically and help with leaf cleanup in the fall.

Read the Full Review of the Champion Here »

The SuperHandy Mini feels affordable for what it offers: A powerful, gas-powered chipper that doesn’t take up too much space. Most gas wood chippers weigh more than 100 pounds, but the SuperHandy is significantly lighter—just 85 pounds. It’s also one of the only chippers we selected that sits on air-filled tires, which do a better job of absorbing bumps, making it easier to move over uneven ground. Those tires, along with the machine's compact build, make it far easier to wheel around the yard than most gas chippers.

And while it has a smaller 212-cc engine, it’s still capable of chipping branches up to 3 inches in diameter down to pieces that are small enough to mulch. It just takes longer to work through those thicker branches.

Keep in mind that this is just a wood chipper. There is no separate hopper for mulching leaves and twigs. If you want a wood chipper that can do both, look elsewhere. But, if you don’t mind separating your branches from your leaves and twigs, this is a reasonably priced and capable wood chipper.

We’ve tested both Earthquake’s K32 and K33 wood chippers, and both are impressive. While the K33 offers nominally better chipping ability, we’re partial to the K32, which still offers ample power but at a more homeowner-friendly price.

The K32 uses a high-performing gas engine that we found to be surprisingly easy to start, firing up after just a couple of pulls. Its 212-cc engine, though smaller than the K33’s 301-cc engine, is powerful enough to power the machine through branches up to 3 inches in diameter. We shoveled leaves and twigs into its hopper, all of which it quickly reduced into a fine mulch, though not without the need for a push stick to work it through its small opening. Its wood chipping performance was impressive as it chewed through 1- to 2-inch limbs faster than we could load them.

The K32 features a spacious top hopper, allowing you to easily dump armloads of dry leaves into it, making it an excellent companion for fall leaf cleanup. Its large collection bag is supported by a rod extending from the side of the chipper, which helps prevent clogging as the bag fills up.

Complementing its powerful chipping is a rock-solid build. It’s made from heavy-gauge steel and feels sturdy. Like all chippers, it’s pretty hefty at 118 pounds, but it sits on large 11-inch wheels and has a large sturdy handle that makes maneuvering it around manageable. It’s an impressively built wood chipper for homeowners who deal with a larger amount of tree debris on their properties.

The Popular Mechanics test team recommends both Patriot’s smaller 1.5-hp electric chipper as well as its more powerful 5-hp model, which is sold exclusively on the company’s website. There is a significant power difference, but both wood chippers offer many of the same features. We got a chance to conduct a hands-on review of both models.

With the 5-hp motor model, it ripped through 3-inch-thick branches, snatching them quickly and gobbling them up with near-frightening speed. This beast tore through limbs faster than we could feed them into the intake, making every test go quickly.

Less thrilling was the hopper for leaves. The opening is large, but it funnels down to a tight space before reaching the cutting blades, which clogged when a pile of leaves was dumped into it. Using a stick to push them through worked, but the job was more of a chore than it should have been.

All of that power comes with a few trade-offs. For starters, this Patriot chipper is heavy, weighing 173 pounds (the 1.5-hp model is much lighter at 95 pounds). It’s fairly compact, though. And while we wouldn’t say it was easy to move, having large 10-inch wheels and never-flat rubber tires made rolling it from garage to backyard surprisingly manageable.

The biggest issue, though, for the 5-hp model is that it requires a 240-volt outlet to power it—the same electric hookup you’d use for a dryer or electric stove, or that can be found on some generators. I hooked it up by connecting a long extension cord to our dryer outlet for testing, which was fine at the time, but is less than ideal for regular use. That inconvenience, combined with the chipper’s substantial price tag, makes it a niche pickup: It’s a superpowered electric chipper, so it’s low-maintenance and quieter than a similarly powerful gas alternative. If those two things are priorities for you, this may be a good fit.

If you don’t need a chipper with as much power, Patriot’s smaller 1.5-hp model, which impressed us during testing, is also a decent option. Plus, it runs on a standard 120-volt outlet, which makes things easier. It may not be as fast as the 5-hp version, but it’s reliable and half the cost.

The latest generation of Sun Joe’s lightweight wood chipper is a robust electric option for folks with only one or two trees in the yard. We were pleased with how the brand’s previous model handled twigs and small branches when tested a couple of years back, but the CJ603E is a step up. It features a pressure plate that pushes branches up against a rotary blade for better cutting. As a result, it can handle larger branches of up to about 1.73 inches, compared to the 1.5-inch max of its predecessor.

The effects of that upgrade were apparent in testing, with this model handling sticks and twigs up to its max capacity quickly. Also impressive is how it actually pulls material into it, eliminating the need to manually feed branches into the blade. In fact, at one point, we were able to continuously load sticks, one after the other, without the Sun Joe missing a beat.

At the same time, keep in mind that the CJ603E is expressly designed as a light-duty wood chipper. It has a lower maximum capacity than our other recommendations, and chews through wood far more slowly. The chips also fall short of Sun Joe’s estimated reduction ratio: At 21:1, the chips should have been finer than what they actually produced. That makes sense, given that it’s a lower-wattage electric model, but it’s definitely worth keeping in mind. If you plan to use your mulch for compost, we recommend spending the extra money on a more powerful chipper.

In keeping with its light and easy design, this Sun Joe's construction is less durable than that of many of my favorite wood chippers, with more plastic parts than we’d normally like. While it’s nice to be able to rapidly load it with material, using it that way for too long might wear it out.

This Sun Joe is far more affordable than other wood chippers and weighs only 38 pounds. After lugging around many chippers weighing well above 100 pounds, wheeling this one into position felt like pulling a cloud. It also took up far less space in the garage. While it doesn’t match the shredding ability of our other recommendations, there are plenty of homes that would benefit from this model for light cleanup jobs.

If you have a larger property to manage and a riding mower or ATV at your disposal, then a towable wood chipper is the way to go. DK2’s smallest towable option offers excellent build quality at an affordable price. It sits on large 13.75-inch ATV-style wheels that make it easy to pull over uneven ground and roots over a larger property. It’s also built to bounce around off-road with its steel frame and hardened steel chipping blades.

Its 212-cc engine is comparable to the engine found on other 3-inch capacity wood chippers and it’s equipped with a larger top hopper, which is a benefit when dumping in armloads of leaves and smaller debris. There are also handy features like a quick-release latch that opens the swing chute, which simplifies clearing any jams, and an adjustable discharge chute so you can direct where the chips end up.

One knock on the DK2 is its 10:1 reduction ratio. This means that it produces chips that aren’t as fine as other wood chippers, something to note if you’re planning to use this wood chipper to create usable mulch. If you have a large wooded property to cover and an ATV or lawn tractor in the shed, then this towable DK2 wood chipper is a great option.

A gas wood chipper can be a beast to pull around the yard. The Landworks wood chipper is slightly lighter than other wood chippers, yet doesn’t compromise power or cutting capacity. At 96 pounds, it’s about 30 to 40 pounds lighter than other wood chippers with similar engine sizes and chipping capacity. This by no means makes it a lightweight tool, but it does make it far more manageable to wheel around your property than those heavier models. There is a compromise for that lightweight design and that’s in functionality. Whereas other models operate as a combination shredder and chipper, the Landworks is a dedicated chipper with no leaf hopper.

Unlike those combination models, however, the Landworks gas wood chipper has a long discharge chute that extends away from the machine. This prevents chips from piling up around it so you don't have to stop frequently to clear them or reposition the wood chipper. The discharge is also adjustable from 90 to 145 degrees, which allows you to direct where the wood chips go. This design makes it especially useful for spreading chips for ground cover. If you’re looking for a lightweight alternative to other wood chippers and don’t need a machine that can shred leaves, then the Landworks 7-HP wood chipper is a good choice.

Electric wood chippers work best for cleaning up branches around small- to medium-sized yards. They’re quieter and easier to start and maintain than gas models, and don’t produce exhaust. Unlike many types of yard machines, though, electric wood chippers still feature a power cord, requiring you to plug into an electrical outlet: That generally means their power draw is capped at what they can pull from a 15-amp wall outlet, or 1,800 watts (W).

Practically speaking, that means most affordable electric models are limited to chipping branches up to 1.75 inches in diameter. They also have lower throughput than gas models, making them more likely to bog down or clog more easily with thick, wet or fibrous material. There are a few exceptions that can chip larger 2.5-inch branches and handle denser foliage, but they’re pricey machines, some of which require a larger 240V outlet.

Ultimately, though, you aren’t going to find a heavy-duty electric chipper with the power to match the wood-chipping capabilities of a gas engine. If you do choose an electric wood chipper, make sure to adhere to the manufacturer’s requirements for extension cords to avoid declines in performance, overheating, or tripping a breaker.

If you need to process larger fallen branches, portable gas wood chippers for homeowners usually feature a 4- to 10-horsepower engine, so chipping branches up to 3 inches in diameter is effectively the standard. Some gas wood chippers also function as shredders with hoppers for breaking down leaves and small twigs.

Manufacturers measure horsepower inconsistently, so we recommend skipping the spec and checking out the size of the engine, measured in cubic centimeters (cc), to get a sense of a chipper’s power, though blade design, engine speed, and the feed system will also impact its performance.

As a general rule, a chipper with a larger engine will have an easier time processing larger and harder materials. It’s also less likely to jam. Despite their size and heft, gas chippers are technically more portable than electric models, since they can operate without access to an external power supply, though they are also significantly heavier. Gas machines are also significantly louder and produce exhaust.

Keep in mind that, across the board, yard machines with gas engines require more maintenance than electric units: You’ll need to change the oil and clean or replace the air filter regularly. You’ll also need to stabilize the fuel in the tank if you’re putting it away for the season or don’t know when you’ll use it again. Still, gas is the way to go if you have a lot of ground to cover and/or a large number of trees.

The primary measurement of a wood chipper’s efficiency, the “reduction ratio,” gives you an estimate of how finely a chipper can break down branches and sticks. For example, a mulcher with a 10:1 ratio can reduce a branch down to about a tenth of its original size. The higher the ratio, the smaller the wood chips.

If you plan on using your wood chips for compost or mulch, you want your chipper to produce smaller pieces, so it’s important to look for a more powerful mulcher with a high ratio—at least 10:1.

We’ve found that manufacturers often exaggerate the mulching ratio of their machines on the spec sheet. If you want a more technical, grounded way of assessing a chipper, you should also take a look at the size of its motor or engine. Reduction ratio is dictated, in large part, by your chipper’s power. Looking for a larger electric motor or gas engine ensures that your chipper has the muscle to make finer mulch quickly and easily.

The second important measurement on a wood chipper is its capacity, which tells you the largest branch size it can process. Capacity refers to the diameter of a branch, so we’re talking about thickness, not length.

Most electric wood chippers max out at around 1.5 inches, while more powerful gas chippers can chew through branches up to 3 inches thick. There are industrial-grade chippers that can grind up branches that are quite a bit larger than what our picks can handle, but most people don’t need that kind of power regularly. Keep in mind that hardness, moisture, forks in the wood, side branches, and blade conditions can also impact the wood chipper’s capacity.

While a more powerful chipper sounds great on paper, keep in mind that a bigger engine makes for a larger, heavier wood chipper. Most electric wood chippers designed for homeowners typically weigh between 30 and 40 pounds, and tend to be relatively compact compared to gas-powered models, so they’re easier to store.

Gas wood chippers generally offer better reduction ratios and greater capacity, but they also weigh a lot—130 to 150 pounds or more. Given that, we’d urge you to bring home a chipper with just enough power to handle the kind of lawn debris you typically find lying around your yard.

You should avoid putting wet wood in a chipper. Wet wood clumps more easily as the blade chops it up, making it harder to cut. Too much wet wood can clog your chipper. Wait for branches and sticks to dry fully before processing them.

The simplest thing to do with wood chips is to put down a layer of mulch to provide nutrients for your soil, but there are other ways to make use of your yard waste. You can spread them to create a pathway in your garden or to make a soft surface under your child’s playground.

Wood chips can also help control erosion, preventing soil from running off during heavy rains. If you’re chopping up hardwoods, like hickory, cherry, oak, or apple, you’ve just made chips for your grill or smoker.

We wouldn’t recommend it—no. Wood chippers aren’t designed to handle acorns. They’re small and hard, so they can potentially jam or clog a chipper.

Pine cones are softer, so a powerful chipper should be able chop them up. But it would need at least a 2-inch capacity for a pine cone to fit. All the same, it would be better to bag them up and throw them out with whatever leaves and lawn debris aren’t going into a mulcher.

Avoid putting rocks, soil, metal, wood containing nail, treated or painted wood, vines and fibrous plants into a wood chipper as they can either damage or clog a wood chipper. Check the wood chipper's manual for a complete list of what to avoid putting in the chipper.

Pay attention to the wood chipper’s performance to determine whether its blades need sharpening. Slower feeding, larger ragged wood chippers, and increased vibration are all signs that the blades are likely dull.

Paul Russell Smith is a former NYC ironworker turned screenwriter (Grace Point) and home renovation specialist. In her free time, Jamie is in a yoga class, searching for the perfect matcha latte, or walking the boards.

A gene variant called APOE4 is the biggest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Scientists are finally figuring out how it works.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A gene variant called APOE4 dramatically increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's disease, the most common form of dementia. Now, emerging research is revealing APOE4's true role in the condition, and a new study pinpoints a possible way to treat it.

Historically, scientists studying Alzheimer's disease have focused on two proteins that accumulate in patients' brains: amyloid-beta and tau. However, there's a "third thing that people didn't pay attention to, until recently," said study co-author Li-Huei Tsai, a neuroscientist at MIT. That third thing is the accumulation of droplets of fat, or lipids, in the brain, she told Live Science.

The APOE gene makes proteins responsible for transporting fat around cells throughout the body and brain. A version of the gene called APOE4, which increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's three- to 12-fold, makes proteins that are less efficient at this function, Tsai said. But how APOE4 affects different brain cells was not clearly understood.

Tsai's team has been working to close that gap for about a decade.

"APOE4 can influence many different cell types," she emphasized. "It's not just one cell type."

In past laboratory research, Tsai's team found that APOE4 causes a buildup of cholesterol in astrocytes, star-shaped brain cells that support the function of neurons. Genetic analyses suggested that the gene variant may mess with how these cells process fat.

Another study zoomed in on oligodendrocytes, cells that help insulate neurons' outgoing wires with a fatty material called myelin. This material helps neurons send messages more efficiently. APOE4 caused the oligodendrocytes to accumulate cholesterol. So, in lab mice, the team used a drug to help the cells get rid of that extra cholesterol, and it improved the cells' ability to make myelin and the mice's performance on cognitive tests.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In their latest research, published Thursday (Oct. 15) in the journal Cell Stem Cell, Tsai's team dug into the question of why APOE4 causes fat to accumulate in the first place.

They used stem cells to grow APOE4-carrying oligodendrocytes and then turned specific genes on or off, to see if they increased or decreased the formation of fat droplets. This screening pointed to a major group of genes involved in cell-to-cell communication, called the Wnt signaling pathway. This included a key gene called DKK1, which acts as a brake on this signaling system.

Disabling DKK1 — essentially lifting the brake — reduced the concentration of fat droplets in the cells, the team found.

In brain tissue samples from organ donors with APOE4, the team also found signs of low Wnt signaling. This finding "establishes a very strong link" between the signaling pathway and formation of fat droplets, said Rosie Jackson, a cell biologist at the University of Dundee who was not involved in this study.

Myelin (orange) is a fatty material that coats the outgoing wires of many neurons, helping the cells send signals more efficiently.

The researchers then investigated exactly how Wnt signaling was disrupted in oligodendrocytes.

APOE4 seemed to decrease the cells' supply of a protein that helps relay Wnt signals. That helpful protein was being broken down by an enzyme whose levels had been boosted by the APOE4. In mice, the team used a drug to block that extra enzyme, and the treatment ultimately restored normal Wnt signaling, reduced fat buildup, and helped the cells make myelin properly.

This could change how scientists think about treating Alzheimer's disease, Jackson said. It "opens up a new wave of potential therapeutics" that could target the accumulated fats, rather than going after only amyloid-beta and tau, she said.

"I think that this is becoming a really common idea in the field — that we're going to need multiple medications that target slightly different elements," she told Live Science. "And targeting lipids will be a really important part of that."

That said, the findings have not been confirmed in humans yet.

"It's very encouraging that facilitating lipid clearance and lipid movement is a potential therapeutic avenue," said study co-author Joel Blanchard, a neuroscientist at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. The question is how we can do that in a safe and effective manner in humans, he said.

Blanchard has led other research that underscores APOE4's effects beyond fats and myelin. The gene variant may affect cells that support blood vessels in the brain by driving scarring and contributing to amyloid-beta buildup. It may also mess with the "trash collectors" inside astrocytes, again leading to a buildup of harmful proteins.

While cells with other versions of the APOE gene can put a lot of energy toward breaking down the proteins, APOE4-carrying cells put all their energy toward fat storage, Blanchard said.

But more research is needed to understand how to fix the problem, he said. Hopefully, targeting fat storage "could rescue not just one thing but multiple things that go wrong in the course of Alzheimer's disease," he told Live Science.
