#54. Artemis II results show how much science people can do at the moon

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The crew’s observations highlight what human eyes can add to lunar exploration

The Artemis II astronauts got views of our home planet and satellite that are normally impossible to see, such as the rugged moon and crescent Earth seen in this image taken on April 6.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Six months after the Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the moon, the value of their closeup view is coming into focus. The first science results, released on October 7, reveal details of the moon’s array of colors, how often it gets hit by tiny rocks and lessons for squeezing as much science as possible out of future human lunar missions.

“We worked extremely hard to make sure we were able to maximize lunar science return from wherever we could in this mission,” said Artemis II flight science operations lead Kelsey Young at a virtual Lunar Surface Science Workshop meeting on October 7. “This is creating yet another tool in our toolbox as planetary scientists to understand our moon, our solar system, even our own planet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon in April — the first time humans had been anywhere near our natural satellite in more than 50 years. Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen spent about seven hours in close proximity to the moon taking scientific observations, describing the moon’s surprising colors and textures and witnessing a solar eclipse from space.

Almost all of that event was livestreamed. But the astronauts took thousands of photos, notes and audio recordings that weren’t immediately made public. Part of the science team’s job was to digest those observations and release the data to anyone who wants to study them within six months of splashdown on April 10.

With three days to spare, the team released three reports and a massive data archive on October 7, the 67th anniversary of when the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft took the first photograph of the farside of the moon. The results offer a rare test of what trained human observers can add to lunar research and what NASA can learn for future missions to the lunar surface.

“We’re really excited to release all of this data,” earth scientist Sara Schmidt of NASA Johnson Space flight Cener in Houston said during the meeting. After six months of hard work, “this is enabling science to happen for the next, I don’t know, 60 years, if not more.”

Surprisingly, the most valuable data from the mission were not the mind-blowingly gorgeous photos, but the astronauts’ verbal and written descriptions of what they were seeing.

Before launch, the astronauts had extensive training in lunar geology and science observations. They were an extension of the science team, said field geologist Cindy Evans also of NASA Johnson Space Flight Center, one of the astronauts’ instructors.

“You could hear it in their voices. They understood the language of geology,” she said.

That training was meant to help answer a question Young hears often: What can humans add that a camera can’t?

During the flyby, the astronauts worked in pairs. Two of them spoke to mission control on the ground, giving periodic updates to the science team on what they were seeing. The other two recorded themselves describing their observations and reactions and used a stylus to annotate specially made maps of the moon that had been uploaded to their tablets during flight. Those notes, doodles and recordings were not made public until now.

The idea was to give the crew high tech field notebooks, Young says.

“If you have any field experience, you know your field notebook is your best friend,” she said in the meeting. On Earth, geologists capture nuance and context in written and spoken words, as well as sketches, she said. “We wanted to provide the ability to capture that nuanced information from the crew.”

One example of this was when Koch sketched her view of the Orientale basin, detailing differences in texture and layers around the crater.

“Sketches can be so powerful,” Young says. “They’re quick and dirty and that’s exactly the right thing to do. You’re capturing that nuance really quickly before it leaves your brain.”

Some of the most unique observations came during the 54 minutes when the moon eclipsed the sun, giving the astronauts a view of the solar corona, interplanetary dust and other stars and planets. That was a favorite moment for planetary scientist Jennifer Heldmann of NASA’s Ames Research Center in California.

“That audio showed their sheer joy and amazement in what they were seeing and where they were,” Heldmann says. “They were so blown away by what they were seeing, while also taking very relevant science observations.”

But some of the most affecting moments were when words failed. When Glover and Koch saw the Earth emerge from behind the moon, for a while all they could say was “Oh my gosh!”

“I guess I should be trying to describe it, but I mean, good grief,” Glover’s tablet recorded him saying.

“No, I tried, but it’s impossible,” Koch agreed. “You might be able to fly a spaceship and talk, but if you can see that and talk, you just ain’t right.”

Another thing the astronauts were able to see during the eclipse were impact flashes — tiny blips of light marking where bits of rock hit the moon.

“It’s a pinpoint of light,” Hansen said in his recorded observations. “It’s not like a meteor, you didn’t see anything else, it’s just like a bloop.”

Before launch, the science team identified and prioritized observations they hoped the crew would be able to make during the flyby. Impact flashes were at the top of the list. Seeing the flashes would give scientists a way to estimate how often the moon is struck by incoming rocks, and how large those rocks are. That’s an important thing to know for protecting future missions where astronauts will walk on the surface or build a long-term moon base.

Scientists didn’t know whether the astronauts would see any flashes at all. They saw five. The flashes were “pinpricks of light lasting less than a second, with no color associated with the flash,” Heldmann said at the meeting.

Comparing the number of flashes per minute to theoretical models of how many impacts the moon might experience, scientists determined that the incoming rocks were tiny, about 8.5 grams and just over 4.5 centimeters across — about the size of a golf ball.

“With these observations, we believe that the Artemis II crew set a record for the smallest meteorites ever optically observed to impact the moon,” Heldmann said.

The resulting craters are probably less than a meter wide, too small for cameras on NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to see.

That’s good news for future astronauts. Artemis IV, planned for 2028, is supposed to bring astronauts to the lunar surface for the first time since Apollo. If successful, it will be a two-week mission using landers from spaceflight companies Blue Origin or SpaceX. The probability of dangerous impact during such a mission is less than 1 in 10 million, Heldmann said. For a larger moon base meant to last a decade, the probability is higher, but still low.

“Now we can start to quantify those impact probabilities, which turns out are very very low,” she says. “Crews will be very safe.”

The moon’s muted colors were another high-priority observation for the science team. Lunar hues and brightnesses can change with terrain roughness, surface temperature and mineralogy — and they’re much more discernable with human eyes than with cameras. The crew also saw how colors changed as the viewing angle and light levels changed.

“This is such a cool demonstration of the value of human eyes as scientific sensors,” said planetary scientist Ariel Deutsch, also of NASA Ames.

Combining the crew’s observations with other data going back to the 1970s let scientists connect colors to composition. Blues were associated with titanium-rich volcanic rocks. Browns reflect different iron levels. Greens are from glass formed during volcanic eruptions or asteroid impacts.

Future astronauts could use this information to create terrain maps and to find specific materials on the moon for sample collection or resources.

The crew also was enamored with the terminator, the boundary between light and dark, which revealed lunar topography in a new way.

“Even as rugged as the far side looks … man, when you look at the terminator, it is just, like, impossibly rugged,” Wiseman said during the flight. “And it reminds you that the whole farside is that way. It’s just the terminator is really bringing out the shadows and the hills and the valleys. And it is just — it’s unbelievable.”

The lighting at the terminator is similar to what future astronauts might expect at the moon’s south pole, where the sun will be low on the horizon and may cast dramatic shadows.

“We want to make sure we have a good handle on that for both science and operations and exploration,” Heldmann said.

With the lessons from Artemis II in hand, now it’s the next astronauts’ turn.

Some recommendations coming out of Artemis II focus on improving conditions in the spacecraft and weaving science into mission planning better. For example, due to time constraints, the astronauts’ cameras were not calibrated before flight. The team is now trying to calibrate them back on Earth, but it can’t re-create how the windows affected images because the windows were charred on the way back through Earth’s atmosphere.

Another takeaway from Artemis II is to continue to refine and train astronauts in descriptive notetaking. The audio notes will be even more important for the first landed missions, where astronauts in spacesuits will not be able to write in a notebook.

“We want to train astronauts to be field scientists, regardless of the landing site, regardless of the mission that they’re given,” Young says.

The buddy system of two astronauts at the windows, two talking to the ground, led to better science, the team concluded.

“The crew had scientific discussions and tried to understand what they were viewing,” Heldmann says. For surface missions, where time is limited and choices must be made quickly, that collaboration will be even more important.

The crew also commented on how helpful it was.

“When we actually do go down there to the surface, I know for safety reasons that we would never send someone alone, but I just want to really emphasize how important the discussion time was,” Glover said. “When we started to talk, we not only got better science discussion, we got better human connection.”

#55. The Sky Today on Monday, October 19: Feast your eyes on the Southern Fish

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Hanging over the southern horizon this evening is the constellation Piscis Austrinus the Southern Fish. Although you might not have heard much about this particular star pattern, you’ve likely seen its luminary, the bright star Fomalhaut. Shining at magnitude 1.2, it is the 18th brightest star in the sky. It’s easy to find, too, because there aren’t many notable stars in the surrounding area: simply turn south around 10 P.M. local daylight time, and Fomalhaut is shining some 20° above the horizon. The only object that can rival it is Saturn, far to the upper left in Cetus, glowing at magnitude 0.3. To Fomalhaut’s upper right is the waxing Moon, but even our satellite can’t overpower the bright star.

Fomalhaut is a young star, still surrounded by a disk of debris from which astronomers believe planets could form. However, the (now in)famous Fomalhaut b, which astronomers once believed was a planet and tracked for roughly a decade, is in fact a cloud of debris that is now dispersing, perhaps the result of a collision of planetlike objects in the disk.

Piscis Austrinus comes in 60th in terms of size among the 88 official constellations, covering about 245 square degrees of sky.

#58. Instrumentation

To measure airflow and sound, research teams at the NASA Glenn Research Center use special instrumentation like particle image velocimetry, hot wire anemometry, Raman spectroscopy, microphones in phased arrays or continuously rotating rakes. The global aviation noise reduction community relies on data from NASA GRC experiments to validate theory and noise prediction software.

Hear an annoying tone from your turbofan engine? Engineers might prescribe an advanced liner or specially tuned active noise control system to quiet it down.

To get it right, though, more information about the modal content of the tone is needed. This kind of data can’t be measured with a stationary microphone, which is why NASA Glenn engineers pioneered procedures using rotating microphones in the 1990s.

Rotating Microphone Rakes have been used by NASA Glenn researchers in a wide variety of tests ranging from low-speed proof of concept tests in the Advanced Noise Control Fan Rig and 9- by 15-Foot Low Noise Wind Tunnel to full-scale turbofan engine ground tests.

In a phased array system, microphones are placed in a 1D, 2D or 3D arrangement and when sound measurements from these microphones are properly processed, noise sources can be pinpointed.

NASA Glenn has an Array48 microphone system that has been used extensively to locate noise sources in scale-model jet flows, a counter-rotating open rotor fan model, and even a full-scale F404 military engine. Through NASA funding, a method has been developed to use microphones embedded in the fan duct of an engine to determine the location of noise sources on the rotating blades.

We know that annoying tone noises can be created by periodic disturbances, such as when the wake from a fan blade interacts with a downstream stator vane. We also know that broadband noise is generated when an aircraft engine ingests turbulent air. Therefore, we must be able to record detailed velocity measurements of the air passing through an experimental propulsor so we can identifying noise sources and work to mitigate them. We must use special instrumentation like hotwire probes and Laser Doppler Velocimeters (LDV) to measure the air velocity upstream, downstream, and between the rotor and the stator of an experimental propulsor. Plots of the velocity measurements can be made which allow us to visualize the disturbances that the rotor created. Hotwire and LDV data are routinely used to validate calculations used to estimate noise from turbofan engines.

#59. Scientists find a way to fight Alzheimer’s brain damage without removing toxic tau

Protecting brain cells from destruction remains one of the biggest challenges in treating Alzheimer's disease and related neurodegenerative conditions. These disorders, known as tauopathies, involve the buildup of abnormal tangles of a protein called tau inside the brain. As the tangles accumulate, nearby neurons begin to die. However, growing evidence suggests that tau itself may not be responsible for most of the damage. Instead, the immune system's reaction to the protein appears to play a major role in the loss of brain cells, memory, and independence.

Scientists at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis have now identified a promising strategy for interrupting this damaging immune response. In mice with tau accumulation similar to that seen in Alzheimer's, researchers used an antibody to block a protein called CXCR3, which helps immune cells known as T cells enter the brain. After several months of treatment, the number of T cells inside the brain had fallen by approximately half.

The results were striking. Compared with untreated mice, animals receiving the antibody retained roughly 40% more tissue in brain regions involved in memory and performed better on a memory test. These improvements occurred even though the amount of accumulated tau remained unchanged.

The findings were published September 28 in the journal Neuron.

"In tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease, there's no treatment right now that actually decreases neurodegeneration," said David M. Holtzman, MD, senior author of the study and the Barbara Burton and Reuben M. Morriss III Distinguished Professor in the Department of Neurology at WashU Medicine. "If we can show that we're really decreasing brain cell death, it's certainly worth trying to pursue that pathway to prevent the most devastating consequences of these diseases."

Why Immune Cells May Be a Key to Alzheimer's Brain Damage

Current Alzheimer's treatments primarily focus on removing amyloid, another protein associated with the disease. Two approved medications, lecanemab and donanemab, target amyloid plaques that develop between brain cells during the early stages of Alzheimer's. These deposits interfere with communication between neurons, contribute to the formation of tau tangles inside cells, and ultimately lead to neuronal death.

Although these medications can slow cognitive decline, they have not been shown to prevent brain cells from dying. They also offer no treatment for primary tauopathies, conditions in which tau accumulates without the presence of amyloid. Alzheimer's is classified as a secondary tauopathy because both abnormal amyloid and tau are present.

Holtzman's laboratory has been investigating whether the immune system offers another way to address these diseases. In a 2023 study published in Nature, the researchers discovered that T cells enter the brains of mice with abnormal tau accumulation, concentrating in regions containing the most tau and contributing to neurodegeneration.

A related study published earlier this month in Nature Neuroscience provided another important clue. It showed that the signals directing these T cells originate in lymph nodes located outside the brain.

"For this therapeutic approach, if it is safe, you wouldn't have to design the drug to get into the brain -- which is a big deal since most molecules don't cross the blood-brain barrier well -- and you don't have to get rid of the tau to get this therapeutic effect."

Scientists Identify the Pathway That Guides Immune Cells Into the Brain

Despite these earlier discoveries, researchers still needed to understand how activated T cells found their way into the brain.

T cells navigate through the body by following chemical signals known as chemokines. Earlier experiments in Holtzman's laboratory had identified unusually high levels of one such signal, CXCL10, in mice with tau accumulation. Other researchers had also reported elevated CXCL10 levels in people with Alzheimer's disease.

Activated T cells carry a surface receptor called CXCR3 that recognizes CXCL10, allowing the cells to follow its chemical signals. This relationship suggested that the CXCL10 and CXCR3 pathway might be responsible for guiding harmful T cells into the brain.

To investigate, the researchers studied mice that developed abnormal tau deposits resembling those associated with Alzheimer's. The team included co-senior author Jason Ulrich, PhD, a professor of neurology at WashU Medicine, and first author Joshua T. Emmerson, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher in Holtzman's laboratory.

The experiments revealed that T cells could not infiltrate the brain when mice lacked either CXCL10 or its matching receptor, CXCR3, on T cells. This protection persisted even when the scientists deliberately triggered inflammation to stimulate an immune response.

Experimental Treatment Preserves Brain Tissue and Memory

With the pathway identified, the team tested whether blocking CXCR3 with an antibody could reduce brain damage.

The researchers selected young mice that already had tau deposits in their brains but had not yet experienced substantial loss of brain cells. They administered the antibody once every five days for three and a half months.

By the end of the experiment, treated mice had approximately half as many T cells in their brains as untreated animals. They also showed less evidence of neuronal injury and retained substantially more brain tissue, including roughly 40% more tissue in memory-related regions. Their performance on a memory test was also better.

Importantly, these protective effects occurred without any detectable reduction in tau tangles. The treated and untreated mice had similar amounts of abnormal tau, suggesting that limiting the immune response could reduce neurodegeneration even when the underlying protein deposits remain.

Another finding could have major implications for future drug development. The antibody reached the boundary of the brain but did not enter the brain tissue itself.

This suggests that it may be possible to reduce neurodegeneration by targeting immune activity from outside the brain. Such an approach could avoid one of the major difficulties in developing neurological treatments: getting drugs across the blood-brain barrier, which prevents many substances from entering brain tissue.

A Potential New Direction for Alzheimer's Treatment

Although the results are encouraging, the treatment has so far been tested only in mice. Additional research will be needed to determine whether the approach is safe and effective enough to evaluate in people.

Holtzman suggested that medications already used to control T cells in other diseases could provide a starting point. Certain treatments for multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune conditions, in which the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy tissue, might be worth investigating for their potential to reduce Alzheimer's-related brain damage.

This would represent a significant shift in treatment strategy. Rather than concentrating exclusively on the abnormal proteins associated with neurodegeneration, researchers could also target the immune responses that contribute to the destruction of neurons.

"Tauopathies aren't thought of as autoimmune disorders, so they haven't been treated the same way, but this study shows for the first time in an animal model that these diseases respond to a specific T-cell therapy," said Holtzman, who also directs WashU's Hope Center for Neurological Disorders and the Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center at WashU Medicine.

"For this therapeutic approach, if it is safe, you wouldn't have to design the drug to get into the brain -- which is a big deal since most molecules don't cross the blood-brain barrier well -- and you don't have to get rid of the tau to get this therapeutic effect."

The findings raise the possibility that protecting the brain from harmful immune activity, rather than removing tau itself, could become an important strategy for treating Alzheimer's and other tauopathies.

#61. I Put Several Cordless Drills to the Test in My Workshop—These 10 Were the Best

No home workshop is complete without one of these top cordless drills.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

No workshop is complete without a good cordless drill. This essential power tool is your workhorse, responsible for drilling holes and driving in fasteners—tasks that almost every home repair or woodworking project requires.

Today's cordless drills are more powerful than ever, with premium models producing torque surpassing 2,000 inch-pounds and speeds of more than 2,000 rpm. That’s enough to bore large holes through wood, metal, and even concrete.

Along with power, there are other factors to consider when shopping for a cordless drill, including size, weight, and features. In an effort to identify the top drills for a range of applications, I put eight models from some of the most reputable tool brands out there, including Milwaukee and DeWalt, to the test by drilling through lumber and masonry.

Below are my reviews of each model, including my pick for the best cordless drill worth investing in.

I started my initial research by searching for drills I thought would suit all types of users. After selecting six tools, I ran each through a series of tests. For my first test, I bored ten holes through a 2x4—five one-inch holes with a spade bit and five 1/2-inch holes with a twist bit. I considered the speed at which the drills completed these holes, as well as how smoothly the drill operated and how cleanly it was able to drill the hole.

Next, I tested the drills with fasteners by using each model to drive three-inch wood screws into stacked 2x4s. Finally, I took the hammer drills in the group outdoors and proceeded to drill holes into a slab of concrete. Along with performance, I also assessed each drill’s weight and size to determine ease of use.

For this story’s latest update, I added two new models—the Bosch 12-Volt pocket driver, which is one of the lightest and most compact drill/drivers we’ve tested, and the versatile Skil PWRCORE flip drill, which has a unique two-collet design that makes it ideal for jobs that require drilling pilot holes.

Milwaukee packs tremendous performance into a surprisingly compact tool with this 1/2-inch hammer drill. It pumps out a whopping 1,400 inch-pounds of torque and can reach a lightning-quick top speed of 2,100 rpm. Though not quite the fastest on our list, the drill blazed through my 1/2-inch drill bit and 1-inch spade bit tests. It posted similarly impressive performance, drilling 1/4-inch holes into concrete. Milwaukee’s hammer drill also has three speed settings (most only have two), which allowed me to dial back all that speed and power to drive screws.

What’s so impressive about this drill is that it packs all that power into such a small package. It’s just under 7 inches from tip to tail and weighs a relatively light 3.3 pounds. Plus, it comes equipped with an auto-stop feature that shuts off the motor to prevent over-rotation should the drill bit become bound up.

This Milwaukee drill may not be the fastest or most powerful tool on the list, but when you factor in its weight, size, and features, it’s the best all-around.

Full Milwaukee M18 2904 Hammer Drill Review

The Skil PWRCore drill produces a surprising amount of power for its size and at a fraction of the price of the premium cordless drills on our list. It took an impressive 3 seconds to drill a 1/2-inch hole into a 2x4. Its ability to drill holes with a 1-inch spade bit was mixed, however. During testing, the bit became hopelessly bound in the wood every couple of holes. When used as a driver, it had no problems driving in three-inch screws.

This drill weighs just 2.23 pounds, not including the battery. Couple that with a narrow profile, and the Skil was one of the easiest 20-volt drills to use. While it doesn’t offer the bells and whistles you’ll find on premium drills, it does give you two speed settings and an LED worklight. And while a premium cordless drill kit costs $300 or more, the Skil 20-volt drill kit is just $80. That low price, coupled with its solid performance, makes it a great budget pick.

FLEX’s cordless tools are known for their impressive power output and this cordless drill is no exception. With its 1,400 inch-pounds of torque and max 2,500 rpm speed, it blazed through our tests, drilling five holes with a 1/2-inch twist bit and five 1-inch holes with a spade bit each in under 3 seconds smoothly and with no hesitation. Interested to see just how much it could handle, I took it to a block of cement and set about drilling holes with a 3/8-inch bit. Where most cordless drills would fail at this point, the FLEX just kept on chugging, burrowing through cement with no hesitation.

With its 24-volt motor and battery, the FLEX isn’t light, weighing just under 4 pounds bare and nearly 6 pounds with the included 5.0Ah battery. Its head, meanwhile, is a relatively short 7.1 inches.

The FLEX is loaded with features. Along with a turbo button that allows you to boost torque to reach its max output, there’s also a rotation protection that stops the drill if it over-rotates to protect your wrist and arm. The FLEX cordless drill is a serious power tool that costs more than most other options on our list. But if you’re serious about power, look no further.

Ryobi keeps upping the ante with its cordless drill/driver. The latest iteration boasts a max speed of 2,150 rpm and max torque of 850 inch-pounds, which are both notably more than the brand’s previous hammer drill.

The increased speed and torque showed during testing, as I was able to bore five 1-inch holes with a spade bit in just under 4 seconds per hole, a full second faster than when I tested the older version. I also recorded markedly faster times with larger fasteners and had an easier time drilling into concrete. This model’s performance puts the Ryobi in the ballpark of the best drills I tested. There is one caveat: Our testing was done with Ryobi’s high-performance 18-volt battery, which delivers better performance than its standard, 2Ah battery.

In terms of size, the Ryobi hammer drill is bulkier than others I tested with a bare weight of 3.1 pounds and a head length of 7.5 inches. That said, its outstanding performance makes it a great option for anyone looking for serious power out of an affordable drill/driver.

The flagship drill of DeWalt’s line of cordless drills is impressive in its raw power and versatility. We bore a 1/2-inch hole through a 2x4 with a standard bit in about half a second and a 1-inch hole with a paddle bit in 3 seconds flat. Both times were the fastest I recorded for all of the drills I tested. I was also impressed by all the options for controlling that power. With three speed options, I was able to dial its speed way back. That, coupled with the ability to drop the torque, allowed me to drive in screws without stripping the screw head.

Among other features I appreciated about the DeWalt XR drill included an anti-rotation safety feature that shuts off the motor if it senses too much rotational motion, saving your wrist, and a built-in worklight you can aim.

The XR isn’t particularly light at 4.1 pounds (not including a battery), but it is relatively short with a head length of 7.6 inches, which means it can fit into tighter spots than many other cordless drills.

Makita’s flagship hammer drill packs quite a punch in a compact size, producing 1,250 inch-pounds of torque with a maximum speed of 2,100 rpm. Not surprisingly, it had no problem handling both of my drill bit tests. It easily drove a 1-inch spade bit and 1/2-inch drill bit through a 2x4. I also found success using its hammer drill function to bore 5/8-inch holes into concrete.

The Makita hammer drill also serves as a very capable driver. Once I dialed back the speed and torque to prevent it from stripping screw heads, I was able to consistently drive 3-inch wood screws into our stacked 2x4s. With all that power, the XPH14 still manages to stay compact with a head length of 7 inches, though it’s one of the heaviest drills I tested with a bare tool weight of 5.5 pounds.

Bosch is known for the ergonomics of its drill/drivers, which are frequently more compact and lighter than those made by other brands. Its 18V brushless hammer drill/driver has a bare tool weight of just 2.5 pounds and a narrow profile with a short head that makes it easier to handle and fit into tighter spots.

Its 575 inch-pounds of torque won’t match the others we tested on paper. But in practice? It handled the tasks I threw at it without trouble. I drove longer, 3-inch screws into wood with relative ease and had no problem drilling 1-inch holes into wood with a paddle bit. Switched to hammer mode, I was even able to drill 1/2-inch holes into concrete.

It also has some nice user features, including an auto shutoff that prevents over-rotation and a rapid mode selector that lets you quickly cycle through its drilling, driving, and hammer mode with the push of a button.

I love the drill/driver that comes in this kit so much that I’m willing to overlook the fact that it’s not available by itself. You’ll need to purchase the full kit, which includes an impact driver, to get it. That will understandably be a deal breaker for those who don't need an impact driver, but the Ridgid drill/driver's product specs speak for themselves.

With 1,250 inch-pounds of torque and a max speed of 2,000 rpm, this tool is up there with the top of the line brands when it comes to power and speed. It also comes with features you expect to see on pro level drills, including kickback control to protect your wrist.

The Ridgid’s impressive specs played out in our testing as it performed similarly to our top pick when it came to drilling holes with larger paddle bits and boring into denser materials like concrete. The Ridgid hammer drill/driver is a little on the bulky side, but it’s a drill worthy of your arsenal.

Very little has changed with the Bosch 12V PS21-2A Pocket Driver since it debuted years ago, and that’s just fine. With its light weight, compact size, and pistol grip, it’s one of the most comfortable drill/drivers I’ve picked up. It has 265 inch-pounds of torque and operates at a maximum speed of 1,300 RPM. While that won’t match the power and speed of 18V models, it’s on the high end for a 12V drill.

During testing, I had no trouble driving in several dozen 3-inch screws into two stacked 2x4s. With its nimble size, it excelled in tight spaces. It was compact enough to work screws in the engine bay of my truck, and I had no problem accessing screws inside cabinetry in my kitchen.

It does have its limitations—it barely finished driving in 3-inch lag bolts and refused to remove them. But, such a job is really meant for an 18V tool.

The versatile Skil Flip Drill has two 1/4-inch collets on a chuck that rotates at the push of a button, allowing you to quickly switch from drilling pilot holes with a drill bit to driving in screws in seconds. This eliminates the need to change bits or carry two separate drill/drivers, and while it might sound gimmicky, it really works.

I was able to drill pilot holes and then in quick succession drive in a fastener far faster than by changing out bits, though it’s worth noting that the drill doesn’t improve your ability to drill pilot holes accurately. It’s simply an efficiency improvement, but that’s fine.

There’s also a magnet that conveniently holds the screw on deck as you drill the pilot hole. It produces 1,700 RPMs and 350 inch-pounds of torque and has a digital clutch with nine torque settings and two speed options. It performed well with drill bits up to 1/2 inch and fasteners up to 3 inches long, making it a handy drill for light-duty projects around the house.

Like all cordless tools, the voltage of the motor determines the cordless drill’s power output. Cordless drills come in 12-, 18-, 20-, and 24-volt models. Generally speaking, the higher a drill’s voltage, the greater the amount of speed and torque it produces, but there is a caveat here.

Motor efficiency and battery technology vary from brand to brand. Some high-end, 18-volt models, including our top performer, the Milwaukee 2904-20 Hammer Drill, actually outperformed some 24-volt models in our tests.

It’s worth keeping in mind that cordless drills with greater voltage are generally bulkier and heavier than those with lower-voltage motors. Case and point, the Bosch 12V Max Two-Speed Pocket Driver Kit weighs just 1.8 pounds, while the FLEX 24V Brushless Cordless Hammer Drill weighs about twice as much at 3.9 pounds. If navigability and ease of use are priorities for you, it may be worth sacrificing some power.

A cordless drill’s ability to make larger diameter holes, drive in fasteners, and bore into concrete is largely dependent on its torque and speed outputs. Torque, which refers to the twisting force the drill generates, ranges from 500 inch-pounds for lighter-duty drills up to 2,500 for the most powerful cordless drill on our list, the FLEX 24V Brushless Cordless Hammer Drill.

Speed, which is measured in the RPM of the drill chuck, ranges from around 1,500 to 2,400. The greater the amount of torque and speed, the better the drill handles larger drill bits, bores into denser materials, and drives in longer screws.

The weight and size of a cordless drill determines how easy it is to hold and fit into compact spaces, such as inside cabinetry or between wall studs.

Lighter drills, such as the Skil PWRCORE Drill Driver, typically weigh around 2 pounds, while heavier cordless hammer drills weigh closer to 4. The battery also adds anywhere from 0.5 to 1.5 pounds to a cordless drill's overall weight (depending on its capacity).

Head size, which is the measurement from the tip of the cordless drill’s chuck to the back of its head, determines how tight a space a cordless drill can fit into. Head length ranges from around 6 to 8 inches.

These days, cordless drills come with a bevy of features that give you more control over their performance. Most cordless drills allow you to reduce the speed of the drill to avoid stripping out screw heads when using the drill as a driver. You can also reduce a cordless drill’s speed to increase torque, which is useful when drilling with larger bits.

Other features include autostop, which automatically cuts off the cordless drill in the event it binds into the wood and starts turning the drill body, which can cause wrist and arm injuries. You’ll find this feature in drill/drivers that produce greater amounts of torque, such as the Makita 18V LXT 1/2-Inch Cordless Hammer Drill/Driver.

Many of the cordless drills I selected also have a hammer drill feature, which adds an impacting action to the drill’s rotational movement that helps when you drill into denser materials, such as concrete.

#62. Oct. 18, 1977: The enigma of Chiron

On Oct. 18, 1977, Charles Kowal was at the 1.2-meter Schmidt telescope at Palomar Observatory in California – reportedly his favorite equipment at the facility to observe with – when he unwittingly discovered an entirely new class of objects.

Kowal was conducting a survey for slow-moving objects beyond the Main Belt, taking two plates of the same location a few hours apart and searching them for differences using a blink comparator. He spotted one such difference – an 18th-magnitude object moving at a rate of only 3 arcminutes per day between Saturn and Uranus that was initially designated an asteroid, 2060. (Later, Kowal would name it Chiron, after a mythological centaur who was the son of Saturn and grandson of Uranus.) Chiron was a puzzle, with an orbit and size that didn’t fit its location. It would eventually be recognized as the first in a new class of cosmic objects: Centaurs. These travelers dislodged from the Kuiper Belt are the bridge between small planetesimals and full-fledged planets, making them a valuable evolutionary link for understanding planet formation.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

An AI-operated drone learned to fly from scratch and navigated a race course at speeds over 60 mph, using a single camera.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A drone powered by artificial intelligence (AI) has completed a championship race course faster than some of the world's best human drone pilots.

In a study published Oct. 14 in the journal Science Robotics, scientists created an AI system capable of pushing a quadcopter through a demanding course at over 60 mph (100 km/h), using little more than a single forward-facing camera, an inertial measurement unit, and a tiny onboard computer.

The system, called MonoRace, even won the 2025 Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League drone racing competition, outperforming every rival autonomous team and posting faster times than three former human world-champion drone pilots.

MonoRace accomplished this without the aid of GPS, external motion-capture systems, stereo cameras, or a preloaded map of the course. The system is an onboard autonomous flight model created by researchers at the Delft University of Technology's Micro Air Vehicles Lab in the Netherlands. Its name reflects its central design feature; "mono" refers to its monocular vision. The drone relies on a single rolling shutter camera and monitors its own motion with an internal measurement unit (IMU) that gauges acceleration and rotation.

The limited sensor package feeds a neural network, a machine-learning model that uses interconnected artificial neurons to learn patterns from data. This neural network identifies racing gates and estimates the drone's position and motion to generate motor commands. Then, it sends the commands to the four propellers at a rate of 500 times per second through the drone's flight controller.

The system fits a drone that weighs a mere 966 grams (2.13 pounds) and measures approximately 11.8 x 11 x 3.9 inches (30 x 28 x 10 centimeters). Because the MonoRace hardware was so compact, lightweight and computationally efficient, the team was able to operate it entirely aboard the drone.

On the Abu Dhabi course, MonoRace completed two laps around 11 gates in 16.56 seconds, hitting a top speed of approximately 63 mph (102 km/h).

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A recently released video tracks MonoRace's development and performance in the competition, with real flight sequences demonstrating how the drone banks sharply, accelerates through gates, and navigates a course without human assistance.

However, some of the sequences are computer-generated. Study co-author Guido de Croon, a professor at the Delft University of Technology, said those are intentional visual effects. The only fully simulated imagery appears at about the two-minute mark, during the segment showing the training process.

"Here we show the gates in a visual simulator for the video but the real training happened in a stripped-down, pure physics simulator that ran really fast," de Croon told Live Science in an email. "Simulating vision was not done during training, as the control neural network receives an estimated state as input, which comes from a different perception and state estimation process."

The rest of the footage is real, although some shots include overlays showing how the drone interprets its camera feed. A convolutional neural network segments the white gates, sometimes displaying them as red in the normal camera image. Small circles mark detected gate corners, red lines indicate gate edges, and a blue overlay shows the portion of the image where the drone expects to find the next gate.

Scientists trained the MonoRace model with reinforcement learning, a machine learning method in which an agent repeatedly attempts a task and receives feedback based on its success or failure.

"The reinforcement learning ran in simulation, because it needs lots of trial and error — like millions of tries," de Croon said. "It actually learns to fly from scratch."

The network learned to translate the drone's position on the track, velocity and orientation directly into motor commands. According to de Croon, early training focused on the basics, like avoiding crashes and reaching the first gate. As the training progressed, the system learned to advance farther along the course and fly at higher speeds.

The researchers didn't train the system on a single aircraft. Instead, they varied dimensions such as weight, voltage, drag, sensor noise and propeller condition so the AI model could cope with real-world variations and imperfections.

"That ensures that the trained network can control different drones," de Croon said.

MonoRace could become a training tool for human drone pilots, "a bit like powerful chess programs have also inspired humans playing the game," de Croon said.

Its broader significance lies in demonstrating advancements in physical AI, especially how a robot can perceive, decide and act at high speeds despite limited sensing and computing power. The control network runs on a microcontroller-class chip, meaning that sophisticated control doesn't require a large computer.

De Croon noted that a similarly sized network could optimize for minimal energy use rather than minimum lap time. Because most machines rely on small processors and conventional controllers, energy-optimal neural control could eventually reduce power consumption in everyday robotics, he said.

Bahnam, S. A., Ferede, R., Blaha, T. M., Lang, A. E., Lucassen, E., Missinne, Q., Verraest, A. E. C., De Wagter, C., & De Croon, G. C. H. E. (2026). MonoRace: Robust monocular AI for champion-level drone racing. Science Robotics, 11(119). https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.aee9250

#66. Martian Dawn

NASA’s Curiosity captures the dawn on Mars – as well as elongated ridges formed by wind erosion, or yardangs – in this close-up from a panorama released on Oct. 6, 2026. This is the most detailed view yet of distant, wind-carved Martian cliffs, highlighting features the mission’s scientists have long been waiting to see up close.

The panorama was captured by Curiosity’s Mastcam on Aug. 11, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission, and comprises six individual images that were stitched together after being sent to Earth.

Brick by brick ... the truth is out there. You can now own a little piece of that with this 1,478-piece Lego set

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Millennials get a lot of flak for being overly nostalgic, but I don't think that's fair. When the modern-day world has nothing to offer us but AI slop, shrinkflation and a sad acceptance that we can't be bothered to do anything about global warming. It's easy to see why we yearn for the days of Pogs, the Backstreet Boys, and Saved by the Bell.

One area that we definitely had it good in the 90s was sci-fi, when legendary shows like Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stargate SG-1, and — of course — The X-Files ruled our TV screens long before the age of streaming services. You can relive those glory days of alien conspiracies, spooky happenings and cell phones the size of a brick with the Lego Ideas The X-Files set.

This 1478 piece set is essentially two dioramas crammed into a single display piece. The top of the model depicts a spinning UFO floating above one of those iconic coniferous forests that dominated 90s sci-fi. Why? Because — thanks to some generous tax credits — it was cheaper to shoot in Vancouver, so that's where they all flocked.

Catch Mulder and Scully in every season of The X-Files on Hulu, which is available bundled with Disney+ for only $11.99/month for the first six months, then increasing to $12.99/month.

Beneath the woodland scene, though, is the real star of the show: Mulder's office, squirrelled away in the basement of the FBI's J. Edgar Hoover Building in Washington, D.C. This dingy little office is where Scully meets "Spooky Mulder", kicking off a glorious sci-fi odyssey that would last for eleven seasons (and two movies).

Mulder's dingy little base of operations has been stunningly recreated here, with both overt references and subtle nods that X-Files fans will appreciate. The iconic "I want to believe" poster adorns the wall, alongside photographs of crop circles and a newspaper clipping from a paper called "The Lone Brickman" — a nice nod to "The Lone Gunmen". There's even an actual X-File sitting on the desk, and a cute Lego spoof of the "Face on Mars", with a photo on the wall that shows a Lego head on the moon.

Prefer to actually own your media? Make your way through this X-Files Complete Boxset on DVD. Just bear in mind that you will need a region-free DVD player to watch it with.

It's been a hot minute since I watched The X-Files (that DVD box set beside my TV is calling to me), but even so, I had a blast building my way down memory lane, remembering episodes as I assembled the diorama. I love the little touches, like the display cabinets filled with artifacts, the VHS tapes scattered around the office and the black oil spillage on the floor.

As with most Lego sets, the minifigures are half the joy. You get Mulder and Scully, obviously, with the dynamic duo of FBI agents both rocking flashlights (no smartphones with built-in lights back in the 90s). Mulder is wearing dark blue, while Scully is rocking an orangey brown suit, with both of them sporting an FBI badge.

Outside of the principal pair, you also get Skinner, Mr X, and the Cigarette Smoking Man. Mulder's partner-turned-nemesis Alex Krycek also gets a suitably devious-looking minifig. It's the gloves, they just make him look like a bad man (which, to be fair, he is). Finally, to ramp up the paranormal scale, we also get a pair of monster minifigs: a grey alien and Flukeman minifigures. The grey alien was a must-have, especially given the UFO floating atop this display piece, but the one-off monster of the week, Flukeman, felt like a weird choice.

Also, this John Doggett erasure will not stand. Sure, he could never replace Mulder, but Robert Patrick's seasons eight and nine run was excellent and he deserved a spot here.

And while I'm voicing minor gripes, the usual Lego FOMO tricks were in force with this set; if you pre-ordered, you got an exclusive gift set — Scully's Lab — free of charge. This extra little diorama isn't necessary, but it does feel like the collection is incomplete without it and it's not for sale separately, so you'll have to try your luck with eBay scalpers if you want it.

Speaking of Scully, Gillian Anderson has stated that after season 11 wrapped in 2018, she was done with the role. That wasn't entirely accurate, though, as she donned the lab gloves one more time for the Lego X-Files set advert. It's a short bit of fan service, but a nice touch, and, once again, it sparks those 90s neurons.

All these delicious Member Berries come at a price, though, and that's the price. This blast from the past will set you back $199 (£179 in the UK). That's no small chunk of change. But then again, anyone who wants this set is in their thirties or forties and can probably afford that outlay for the nostalgia trip. And look at it this way: when The X-Files debuted back in 1993, the price would only have been about $86.

I had a great time building the Lego X-Files set and if you're a fan of the series, you will too. Nostalgia often feels like a cheat code to our hearts, but there's nothing wrong with that. We deserve to remember the good times and the truth is that The X-Files was about as good as it ever got for sci-fi fans.

You can buy the Lego X-Files set now, available for $199/£179 from the Lego store.

#69. Scientists discover a way to kill dangerous gut bacteria without killing the good

A dangerous intestinal infection may soon have a more targeted treatment option. Scientists have identified a natural compound that can kill the bacteria responsible for severe gut infections while leaving much of the beneficial gut microbiome unharmed.

The bacterium Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) is naturally found in the intestines of many people and generally causes no problems when present in small amounts. However, antibiotics that target a wide range of bacteria can upset the delicate balance of microorganisms in the gut. This disruption allows C. difficile to multiply rapidly, potentially causing severe intestinal inflammation that can become chronic.

C. difficile infections (CDI) are among the leading causes of diarrhea associated with antibiotic treatment. The bacteria produce toxins that can trigger dangerous and sometimes life-threatening inflammation in the intestines. Because these infections frequently return after treatment, scientists are searching for more effective ways to eliminate the pathogen without causing additional damage to the gut microbiome.

A team led by Prof. Rolf Müller, department head and scientific director at HIPS, has now identified a promising drug candidate that specifically targets C. difficile while preserving much of the gut's beneficial microbial community. HIPS is a site of the Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research (HZI) that operates in collaboration with Saarland University.

Natural Compound Targets Dangerous Gut Bacteria

The researchers found that argyrin B, a naturally occurring antibacterial substance, was highly effective against C. difficile in laboratory tests and experiments involving infected mice. Importantly, the compound showed little activity against the beneficial microorganisms that help maintain a healthy digestive system.

"We were able to show that the natural compound argyrin B is highly effective against CDI: both in laboratory experiments and in a mouse model of the infection, where it significantly reduces the bacterial load," says Dr. Jennifer Herrmann, senior scientist in the department "Microbial Natural Products" at HIPS. "An antibacterial target of the argyrins had previously been identified and characterized in the notorious hospital-acquired pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Now we have been able to show that argyrin B also acts on this target in C. difficile and exhibits particularly high efficacy in doing so. In contrast, the argyrins have virtually no effect on the beneficial microorganisms in our digestive tract. The gut microbiome could therefore be spared during treatment with argyrin and restored to a healthy state more quickly."

A Bacteria-Killing Substance Found in Soil

Argyrins were originally discovered in myxobacteria, microorganisms that inhabit soil. These bacteria produce natural substances that help them attack other microbes and use them as a source of food.

Although argyrin B has demonstrated promising antibacterial activity, researchers must also determine whether its pharmaceutical properties make it suitable for use as a medicine. That includes understanding how the compound behaves inside the body and whether it could cause unwanted effects.

One particularly encouraging finding emerged when the team examined what happens after mice receive argyrin B orally. Very little of the compound entered their bloodstream. Instead, most of it remained in the large intestine, where C. difficile infections occur.

By concentrating in the gut rather than circulating throughout the body, argyrin B could potentially reduce the risk of side effects affecting other organs. Together with its selective activity against C. difficile, this characteristic makes the compound a promising candidate for a treatment that may be better tolerated.

Could It Help Prevent Recurring Gut Infections?

One of the biggest challenges in treating C. difficile is its tendency to return. Patients who experience multiple relapses are often treated using fecal microbiota transfer (commonly known as a stool transplant). This procedure aims to restore a healthier balance of gut microorganisms, but it can be complicated to perform and unpleasant for patients.

A medication developed from argyrin could eventually provide another treatment option. By eliminating the harmful bacteria without extensively disrupting the rest of the microbiome, such a therapy might reduce the likelihood of further infections and relapses. That could also help some patients avoid the need for stool transplants.

More research is needed before argyrin B can be considered for clinical use. The scientists plan to investigate which dosage produces the strongest antibacterial effect and use additional experimental models to determine whether the compound can also combat recurring C. difficile infections.

#70. The 6 Best Pre-Lit Christmas Trees for Easy Holiday Decorating

All is calm, all is bright with these traditional, realistic models we tested and recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Any artificial Christmas tree makes holiday decorating easy, but pre-lit models are even more convenient. They come with bright lights already woven into the branch tips and don’t require much more than an hour of your time to set up and fluff.

The best pre-lit Christmas trees are designed to look like the real deal but without uneven branches, bald spots, or needles that shed constantly. You don’t have to remember to water them, and with lights already integrated, there’s no hassle of untangling and stringing. While they may cost more upfront than a real tree, they last for many years.

Pre-lit Christmas trees range in styles, sizes, and features—everything from classic blue spruces to snowy white flocked trees. That’s why we put models from trusted brands like Balsam Hill, National Tree Company, and Puleo International to the test. Read on for our reviews, recommendations, and everything you need to know before you add to cart.

This Douglas Fir won our top spot because it’s realistic, easy to set up, and well-priced for what you get.

There are 650 lights pre-strung, which is more than most of the other models we tested, along with hundreds of branch tips that are down-swept, which helps give the tree a more tapered, natural appearance.

The tree also has two different types of tips, so you get similar versatility as you would on a real tree. Fluffing took some time, but by the end of setup we achieved a full-looking Christmas tree that brought us some early holiday cheer.

The only potential drawback (not a dealbreaker in our opinion) is that the tree is on the bulky side if you have limited storage.

One of our favorite features on this blue spruce is that instead of having to connect cords between each section, the lights connect through the tree trunk. That means there’s only one cord to plug into the wall outlet.

There are 500 pre-strung lights, and over 1200 branch tips, so we were able to disguise the hinges. The tree is divided into three sections that came labeled, and they were easy to insert into the base.

You also get a massive storage bag, gloves, and a metal stand for the tree, so it’s a great value.

Multicolor lights can be a step up from traditional white lights, adding more vibrancy and festiveness to your holiday decor.

This pre-lit Winchester pine has several hundred branch tips and is decked in 500 multicolor lights. Similar to our other National Tree Company selection, the branches are two different textures to give it a more realistic feel. The branches are pre-attached and hinged, so they fold up and down easily.

This tree is 7.5-feet tall, so it may take longer to fluff and decorate than a shorter model.

If you want a traditional tree with a smaller footprint, opt for a slim design. This model doesn't look too pencil-like, and it has more fullness than other trees that we've reviewed or tested.

The setup process is very simple. The tree is divided into three sections, all of which are labeled to help you differentiate. The lights are pre-strung, so all we had to do was release the hinged branches and fluff.

The green wires from the lights are a little noticeable, but they can easily be covered by ornaments.

This snow-flocked, full-bodied Christmas tree is a great way to bring winter wonderland aesthetics to your home. There are 1200 snowy branch tips, and it's pre-lit with 550 warm, white incandescent lights.

The tree is divided into three sections that attach to the metal tree trunk, and the branches are hinged so that they fall into place once they’re set up. Just fluff and decorate and you’re ready to celebrate.

A foldable metal stand is included, along with plastic caps to prevent it from scratching hardwood or laminate floors.

A pre-decorated pre-lit Christmas tree means less holiday decor to store off-season. This model is fully dressed in pine cones, berries, snow-flocked tips, along with 250 incandescent lights that are evenly dispersed throughout.

There are 818 branch tips in total on the tree, which is on the lower end compared to other models of the same size. Still, it may be a good choice for those who like to decorate with garland, tinsel, and lots of ornaments. The manufacturer suggests between 30 to 45 minutes of setup time to get the full effect.

Pre-lit trees come in different heights and shapes to accommodate the room in which they’re used. Most ceilings are 8 feet high, so a tree between 6.5 to 7.5 feet leaves enough clearance at the top and still fills in the space. Larger trees are typically 8 feet and up to roughly 12 feet. Make sure to factor in the tree stand height and have the room dimensions on hand.

Once you know the ideal height, it’s a good idea to measure the area around the tree to ensure the branch tips don’t rub against walls or furniture. Tree widths vary by style, size, and manufacturer. Slim trees have a narrow build and are around 2.5 to 3.5 feet wide at the base. Traditional, full-sized trees are wider with an average width of 4 to 5 feet. Overall, artificial trees are largest at the base, so allow yourself some extra wiggle room towards the bottom.

The number of branch tips on a pre-lit Christmas tree determines how full-bodied it is. Higher tip counts can also give a more realistic appearance, without leaving gaps even after fluffing. The number of branch tips is relative to the tree’s height—the taller the tree, the more branch tips.

This number varies depending on the tree’s style. For instance, slim trees generally have fewer tips than full-sized trees of the same height. A 6- to 7-foot slim tree with around 800 to 1200 tips can give a full appearance while maintaining balance, like the Fraser Fir from Puleo International. Full-sized Christmas trees, like the Blue Spruce from Balsam Hill, should have 1200 or more branch tips for a traditional, lush build.

Bulb count is another important consideration while shopping for a pre-lit Christmas tree. If you want a bright, well-lit tree, then aim for around 100 lights per foot of tree height. Our best overall pick, the Douglas Fir from National Tree Company, is 6.5 feet tall and has 650 lights.

Artificial trees typically have LEDs or incandescent lights. LEDs are more energy-efficient and last longer, and they’re cool to the touch. Incandescent lights offer a warmer, amber glow, but they use more energy and may need replacing over time. There are models with both LEDs and incandescents in our roundup.

We took a look at our guide to the best artificial Christmas trees to find models that we have previously reviewed and wanted to try out. For the trees we got to test, we fluffed each one for about 40 minutes or slightly longer if we noticed sparse areas. During the fluffing process, we were able to get a feel for branch texture. (The ‘Feel Real’ Douglas Fir was a standout with different types of branches that added more dimension to the overall appearance.) Once the trees were fully set up, we moved them around in their stands, and all held them in a stable, upright position, even with some jostling.

We then evaluated the trees on how easy they were to set up and take down. We noted the amount of time it took to separate each section and then flatten the branches to see how well they compressed for storage. We looked for high-quality trees with ample tip count and lights, considering different styles and heights. We also took into account how vibrant they were when lit, along with any additional features that might be useful, like lighting connections or pedal buttons to turn lights on and off. Our selection includes trees to suit a variety of budgets, home sizes, and aesthetics.

#71. The Sky Today on Sunday, October 18: Another Tethys transit

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Tiny Tethys is transiting the disk of Saturn beginning around 9:35 P.M. EDT, most easily visible from the eastern half of the U.S.

Saturn is easy to locate in Cetus the Whale — it’s the brightest light in the southeast around 9 P.M. local daylight time. Through any telescope, you’ll easily see Saturn’s disk and broad rings, as well as its brightest moon, Titan, which now lies far to the planet’s east. You might also spot its three next-brightest moons, 10th-magnitude Tethys, Dione, and Rhea. Tethys is closing in on the planet’s northeastern limb, while Rhea sits southeast and Dione southwest of the planet.

Tethys will be easy to track until the transit begins — then it grows much harder, as the tiny disk offers little contrast with Saturn’s much brighter cloud tops. The moon’s journey is followed by its equally tiny shadow, which appears just northeast of Tethys around 9:50 P.M. EDT. Both moon and shadow will only be visible to astroimagers using advanced video-capture techniques. Tethys finally leaves the northwestern limb shortly after midnight EDT.

Even if you can’t watch Tethys’ transit, you can still admire Saturn’s stunning rings and its other visible moons. Note that Dione is moving closer to Saturn’s southeastern limb — it will disappear behind the planet in an occultation just before 12:45 A.M. EDT (the 19th in the Eastern time zone only). And once the transit is through, visual observers should be able to pick up Tethys once more as it moves away from the planet, now on the western side of the planet, north of the rings.

Tesla has unveiled a new version of its Roadster EV that can briefly take to the air using SpaceX tech. Whether it actually qualifies as a flying car is another matter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tesla has unveiled a new "flying" version of its Roadster electric vehicle (EV) that uses SpaceX tech to pull off seemingly impressive airborne acrobatics.

During a filmed demonstration at the SpaceX rocket testing facility in Texas Thursday (Oct. 15), the second-generation Tesla Roadster was shown accelerating up a curved ramp before launching itself into the air, performing a 180-degree barrel roll and touching back down to Earth.

In another stunt, the vehicle leapt over a row of parked Teslas. For safety reasons, the vehicle was operated remotely in both instances.

"Turns out, the future does have flying cars," Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X following the demonstration.

The Roadster's airborne capabilities are made possible by a system of cold-gas thrusters developed using technology from Musk's aerospace company, SpaceX. These thrusters release bursts of high-pressure gas to generate thrust, allowing the vehicle to accelerate rapidly and, according to Tesla, become airborne for short periods.

The new Roadster will come in three variants: Performance, Thrust and Rocket. Only the Rocket is capable of flight. The Performance model is a two-seater equipped with a suction system that's designed to improve traction and handling (or drive up inverted ramps, as in Tesla's demo), while the Thrust model adds rear-mounted thrusters that Tesla claims can propel the vehicle from 0 to 60 mph (97 km/h) in under a second.

The highest-end model, Rocket, features SpaceX cold-gas thrusters positioned around the vehicle to enable short bursts of flight and in-air control. This single-seat model will be available by invitation only, according to Tesla.

On the company's website, Tesla representatives explicitly stated that the Rocket isn't approved for use on public roads and that availability depends on regional regulations. During the reveal, Musk told the audience that the Rocket "is not necessarily a safety-optimized car."

Tesla hasn't disclosed how far or for how long its EV can remain airborne, nor is it the first company to develop a hybrid road-air vehicle. There is also skepticism from outside viewers on whether the demonstration could be replicated outside of controlled scenarios.

Artificial intelligence (AI) scientist Yann LeCun ‪— a professor of data science, computer science, neural science and electrical engineering at New York University ‪— described the demonstration on X as a "marketing stunt" and questioned whether the vehicle would work in practice.

"Even assuming that 50% of the mass of the car is the compressed air, that gives you less than 10s of useful thrust (with thrust-to-weight ratio larger than 1.0). Probably more like 5 seconds, actually," he posted on the social media platform. "So the car must be an empty, lightweight shell containing big compressed air tanks. Cute demo, but totally impractical. But of course, you knew that."

He likened it to SpaceShipOne, which debuted in 2004 as the first privately funded spacecraft and made three record-setting flights before being retired.

California-based Alef Aeronautics, which is developing its own flying EVs, marked Tesla's unveiling by releasing footage of its vehicle flying over an earlier Roadster model. Alef representatives said the demonstration marked its 1,000th logged flight.

"Welcome Tesla to the flying car race, we've been here alone for eleven years," Alef CEO Jim Dukhovny said in a statement emailed to Live Science. "Having competition is a good thing, especially from such a major company as Tesla."

Unlike Tesla's compressed-gas tech, Alef's vehicle uses electric propellers for vertical takeoff and landing, with a rotating cabin and body designed to support forward flight.

Production of the new Roadster is scheduled for 2028, but Tesla doesn't have the best track record of meeting its deadlines. The company has delayed production of its Optimus humanoid robot a few times since first unveiling the machine in 2021, for example, with an initial start in 2023, before being pushed back. Only in recent months has production begun to scale to a few hundred units per week.

This unusual radio structure extends over 2 million light-years and resembles a common musical symbol -- but has its visible light hidden by our own Milky Way Galaxy. #76. Many American diets may not include enough of this essential nutrient

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Salt iodization was a public health victory that calls for renewed attention today

Iodized salt hit store shelves in 1924 in the United States, and companies heralded the health benefits, like in this 1925 Morton’s Salt Company ad. The body needs iodine to make thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can cause an enlarged thyroid gland, called a goiter.

University of Michigan Center for the History of Medicine

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Grocery store shelves are bursting with fancy salts: Himalayan, kosher, sea salt and more. Considering these choices, it can be easy to forget about the public health victory found in basic, iodized table salt.

The nutrient iodine is a crucial component of thyroid hormones, necessary for fetal and early childhood brain development and health throughout life. At the start of the last century, iodine deficiency was a rampant and visible public health problem in the United States, with the telltale sign of enlarged thyroid glands, called goiters, especially prevalent in much of the north. A series of steps taken by a medical society in Michigan and U.S. salt producers brought iodized salt to tables across the country, and by the 1950s, occurrences of goiters had dropped precipitously.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But more recently, the United States appears to be backsliding on iodine nutrition. In 2017 and 2018, 24 percent of women and 30 percent of men, aged 14 and older, weren’t getting an adequate amount of the nutrient. That’s about twice as many as in 2001 and 2002, researchers reported in the Journal of Nutrition in 2025. Breaking the data down further, nearly half of pregnant women haven’t been getting enough iodine. The study reflects an estimated, short-term look at population iodine levels.

Long-term, a consistent dearth of iodine robs the body of the ability to produce sufficient amounts of thyroid hormones. If iodine levels in the population continue to trend down, that could eventually result in more goiters and harm brain development in children.

“The group that has the most severe potential consequences of iodine deficiency is pregnant women,” says Elizabeth Pearce, an endocrinologist at Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine. “Even mild degrees of iodine deficiency in pregnancy may be associated with measurably lower IQ in children.”

Yet women of reproductive age, at the U.S. population level, are on the cusp of mild iodine deficiency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stated in its 2026 Nutrition Report.

With all of the ways that diets, salt intake and noniodized options have changed over time, the importance of iodine nutrition may not be top-of-mind for the general public like it was a century ago. “Iodine deficiency is the leading cause worldwide of preventable developmental delay,” says Monica Serrano-Gonzalez, a pediatric endocrinologist at Hasbro Children’s and Brown University’s Warren Alpert Medical School in Providence, R.I. “People have kind of forgotten this is a risk.”

When iodine deficiency keeps the thyroid gland from making enough hormones, the body calls for more, which stimulates and enlarges the gland. That supersized gland, called a goiter, bulges at the neck. In the United States, goiters were extremely common a century ago in the Northwest, Great Lakes and Appalachians; together, the area became known as the “goiter belt.” Iodine naturally occurs in seawater and soil. But in the noncoastal northern part of the country, soils and water sources have little iodine, so the crops produced in these inland areas lack the nutrient.

An examining physician for the World War I draft reported in 1918 that 30 percent of almost 600 men from a northern Michigan county had goiters, some large enough to be disqualifying. A 1922 Michigan Department of Health study of schoolchildren in four counties revealed that close to 50 percent had goiters. “It would have been a really visible public health problem at that time,” Pearce says.

In response to the state’s iodine issues, the Michigan State Medical Society recommended the addition of the nutrient to table salt. The minimal expense for iodization meant this common kitchen staple would remain affordable. Companies introduced iodized salt in Michigan in the spring of 1924. By the fall, the Morton Salt Company, a major producer, was selling iodized salt nationwide. Over time, the goiters of the “belt” dwindled.

Salt iodization has been linked to rising IQ in the United States. For example, for men born in areas without natural sources of iodine, there was a significant jump in World War II Air Force acceptances, based on a qualifying exam, after widespread salt iodization. The increase did not occur among men born in areas with adequate natural sources of the nutrient, researchers reported in the Journal of the European Economic Association in 2017.

Adding iodine to salt was never mandated by the U.S. government. But for a long time, the voluntary approach — combined with how most people consumed salt and other dietary habits — did the trick to get people enough iodine. Today, different meal practices and available food options are tearing holes in the iodine safety net. “Iodized salt is important, but it may not be reaching everybody anymore,” Pearce says.

There are many more noniodized salt options today, with one analysis reporting that only 53 percent of table salt sold in U.S. stores is iodized. People get much of their salt from prepared, processed and packaged foods, which generally are made with noniodized salt. Milk can provide iodine, due to iodine-supplemented feed and the use of an iodine cleanser on cows’ udders. But the amount of iodine in milk can vary greatly, a recent analysis found, probably because industry practices can differ. Diets that restrict dairy may also put people at risk of consuming too little iodine.

The U.S. recommended dietary allowance for iodine for adults is 150 micrograms per day, which rises to 220 mcg for pregnant people and 290 mcg for those breastfeeding. The amount of the nutrient that iodized salt contains can vary, but will be listed on the container’s label. Based on a 2023 federal report on food iodine content, one teaspoon of salt has around 300 mcg of added iodine. (The American Heart Association recommends a limit of 2,300 milligrams of sodium per day; one teaspoon of salt has 2,400 mg of sodium.)

The American Thyroid Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend that pregnant and breastfeeding people, as well as those planning to become pregnant, take a daily supplement with 150 micrograms of iodine. Sufficient iodine is especially important in the first trimester of pregnancy, when a developing embryo relies solely on the mother’s supply.

When choosing table salt, “look for salt that’s iodized,” Pearce says. For people on a low-salt diet, it’s better to cut out packaged and prepared foods, Serrano-Gonzalez says. “We do want to have moderation with salt intake, but we need a little bit” of iodized salt, she says.

People have largely forgotten why it’s important to choose iodized salt, Pearce says. It’s not a decision that many people have to make globally: One hundred and twenty-six countries mandate salt iodization, while only 21 have voluntary polices.

An observational study of an iodine crisis in Ethiopia indicates the catastrophic consequences of losing the nutrient. The country adopted a salt iodization policy in the 1990s, and by 1995, 80 percent of households reported using iodized salt. But the country’s stock came from Eritrea, and in 1998, a conflict between the two countries closed the border and interrupted the supply of iodized salt. By 2005, the Ethiopian population was severely iodine deficient, with up to 40 percent of school-aged children and 36 percent of women of reproductive age developing goiters. Ethiopia’s government was able to reinstate mandatory salt iodization in 2012, and household coverage climbed to 85 percent by 2015.

But the severe iodine disruption during the war had a devastating effect on the children born and raised in that period. In rural areas, which had very low soil iodine levels, mortality among children in the first two years of life reached 25 to 30 percent, compared with 10 percent in other areas, researchers reported in Nature Food in September. The children from rural areas who reached secondary school scored lower on national exams. The study team took other effects of the conflict into account, to focus on the impact of the iodine nutrition emergency.

In the United States, the worst manifestation of iodine deficiency was the long ago “goiter belt.” “There needs to be public health education,” Pearce says, “so people understand again what the dangers are if we don’t have adequate iodine nutrition, and how to just ensure that they’re protected.”
