#77. NASA solves a strange mystery hidden inside asteroid Bennu’s boulders

NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission encountered an unexpected mystery when it arrived at asteroid Bennu in 2018. Instead of the relatively smooth terrain that earlier observations had suggested, the spacecraft found a rugged landscape dominated by enormous boulders, with very few areas suitable for collecting samples.

"When OSIRIS-REx got to Bennu in 2018, we were surprised by what we saw," said Andrew Ryan, a scientist at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory, who led the mission's working group responsible for analyzing the physical and thermal properties of its samples. "We expected some boulders, but we anticipated at least some large regions with smoother, finer regolith that would be easy to collect. Instead, it looked like it was all boulders, and we were scratching our heads for a while."

The discovery was especially confusing because of what astronomers had previously learned about Bennu's ability to retain heat. Measurements from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope in 2007 indicated that the asteroid's surface warmed and cooled rapidly as it rotated through sunlight and darkness.

Scientists describe this property as low thermal inertia. Materials with low thermal inertia, such as beach sand, quickly gain heat in sunlight and lose it once the Sun disappears. Large, solid rocks behave differently. Much like concrete, they typically hold on to warmth and release it gradually.

Bennu's boulder-covered surface appeared to contradict those earlier measurements, leaving researchers with a puzzling question: How could an asteroid covered in massive rocks cool so quickly?

Hidden Cracks Reveal the Secret of Bennu's Boulders

Observations collected by OSIRIS-REx while surveying Bennu offered an early clue. The asteroid's boulders might contain far more empty space than scientists had assumed, allowing them to lose heat faster than ordinary solid rocks.

When samples from Bennu were returned to Earth, researchers finally had an opportunity to examine that possibility directly.

Ryan and his colleagues used several laboratory techniques to investigate tiny rock fragments collected from the asteroid. Their findings, published in Nature Communications, confirmed that the rocks were indeed highly porous. However, porosity alone could not fully explain Bennu's unusually rapid heat loss.

The researchers discovered another important feature. Many of the rock particles contained extensive networks of cracks running through their interiors.

To investigate how these fractures influence the movement of heat, researchers at Nagoya University in Japan examined the samples using a technique called lock-in thermography. This method uses a laser to heat a tiny area of a sample while measuring how the heat spreads through the surrounding material, much like ripples expanding across the surface of a pond.

"That's when things became really interesting," Ryan said. "The thermal inertia measured in the lab samples turned out to be much higher than what the spacecraft's instruments had recorded, echoing similar findings obtained by the team of OSIRIS-REx's partner mission, JAXA's (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) Hayabusa-2."

The difference between laboratory measurements and spacecraft observations suggested that the size and internal structure of Bennu's rocks were essential to understanding their behavior.

Because the returned samples were much smaller than the enormous boulders covering Bennu, scientists needed a way to determine how heat would move through the material on a much larger scale.

NASA Uses 3D Scans to Look Inside Asteroid Rocks

At NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, researchers prepared the samples for detailed X-ray imaging while taking special precautions to prevent contamination.

Inside a glove box filled with protective nitrogen gas, team members sealed individual rock particles in airtight containers. They then transported the containers to a laboratory for X-ray computed tomography, or XCT scanning. After imaging, the particles were returned to the glove box without being exposed to Earth's environment.

"The sample goes into its own 'spacesuit,' gets a CT scan, and then comes back to its pristine environment, all without having any exposure to the terrestrial environment," said Nicole Lunning, lead OSIRIS-REx sample curator within the Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science division at NASA Johnson and one of the study's co-authors. "We can image right through these airtight containers to visualize the shape and internal structure of the rock that's inside."

The scans gave scientists a detailed view of the samples' interiors, revealing structures that could not be examined simply by looking at their surfaces.

"X-ray computed tomography allows us to look at the inside of an object in three dimensions, without damaging it," said study co-author and NASA Johnson X-ray scientist Scott Eckley.

Each scan also produced a permanent three-dimensional digital record of the particle's exterior and internal features. These records were added to a publicly accessible database, allowing the samples to be studied without repeatedly handling the original material.

Ryan's team then incorporated the X-ray scan data into computer simulations designed to track how heat travels through asteroid rocks. By extending the calculations from individual particles to the much larger boulders found on Bennu, they were able to reproduce the low thermal inertia observed by the spacecraft.

A Discovery That Could Change How Scientists Study Asteroids

The results resolved a key mystery about Bennu's unusual surface. Scientists had previously considered whether the asteroid's boulders might be extremely porous, with a soft, fluffy, or even sponge-like internal structure.

Although the rocks do contain substantial pore space, the researchers found that their widespread internal fractures were equally important to understanding how they retain and release heat.

"It turns out that they're really cracked too, and that was the missing piece of the puzzle," Ryan said.

The discovery has implications beyond Bennu. Astronomers frequently rely on measurements of how an asteroid absorbs and releases heat to estimate the physical properties of its surface. Until now, interpreting those observations has been difficult without actual rock samples to examine.

Ron Ballouz, a scientist at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Maryland, and the study's second author, explained that the findings provide a valuable connection between measurements made remotely and the true internal structure of asteroid material.

"We can finally ground our understanding of telescope observations of the thermal properties of an asteroid through analyzing these samples from that very same asteroid," Ballouz said.

#78. Oct. 17, 1956: Birth of Mae Jemison

Born Oct. 17, 1956, in Decatur, Alabama, and raised in Chicago, Mae Jemison showed a passion and talent for science from early in her childhood. After graduating high school by the age of 16, Jemison attended Stanford University and earned a B.S. in chemical engineering and a B.A. in African American studies. She went on to Cornell Medical College, and after completing her M.D. in 1981, worked for several years as a medical officer in the Peace Corps.

Watching Sally Ride become the first American woman in space inspired Jemison to pursue her lifelong dream of becoming an astronaut, and on June 4, 1987, she became the first Black woman admitted into NASA’s training program. On Sept. 12, 1992, she launched as a mission specialist on the Space Shuttle Endeavor, becoming the first woman of color in space. During her eight-day flight, she conducted experiments that capitalized on her background as a medical doctor, including research on motion sickness and on bone density in space. Since her return to Earth, Jemison has focused on education and technology access and integration, including teaching at Dartmouth and founding a science camp for children – and even made a guest appearance on Star Trek: The Next Generation.

#79. The 8 Best Table Saws to Rip Boards with Accuracy and Precision

Whether you’re looking for a portable or stationary model, these are the tested and researched options we love most.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A table saw isn’t just another tool—it’s the one that decides whether your work looks intentional or as if you were guessing. I’ve spent enough time on job sites and in workshops to know the difference. The best table saws, from the most compact portable models to hulking stationary ones, disappear under you. You stop thinking about the tool and start focusing on the work.

A bad saw does the opposite. Every cut feels like a negotiation, and you check it with every pass. And that frustration inevitably leads to mistakes.

Most people chase horsepower and price when they shop for table saws. While those elements are important, stability, accuracy, safety, and how repeatable your cuts are matter just as much. The table saws we’ve chosen aren’t just popular—they’re the ones that hold up again and again when you actually need to lean on them.

I’ve spent years working with tools on job sites, in shops, and on projects where repeatable accuracy isn’t an option. That experience shaped the methods I used to evaluate every table saw in this guide.

To test these saws, I put them through the kinds of cuts I would make most often: ripping 5/8-inch plywood, crosscutting 2x lumber, full blade extension on pressure-treated 4x4s, and locking bevel cuts on trim. While my experience in building cabinetry is limited, I have packed out plenty of framing and installed a great deal of trim work over the years—jobs that call for repeated cuts of high accuracy.

Every saw went through the same evaluation process. I looked at setup time, ease of use, and how confidently each tool handled core tasks. Fence stability was also a major factor—if a fence doesn’t lock down square to the blade, little else matters. I also paid close attention to rip capacity and how stable each saw felt during longer cuts.

Mobility was another big consideration. Many of these saws are designed to move—whether that’s lifting it in and out of a truck or setting up in a tight garage. I evaluated stand design, wheel durability, overall weight, and how easy each saw was to deploy and break down without turning the setup into a full-blown job of its own.

Usability matters more than people think, so I evaluated key details like blade guard design, bevel adjustments, and onboard storage—features that either slow you down or keep your job moving. I also considered specs like blade size, RPM, weight, and motor type—not just on paper—but in how they translate into real-life performance and use.

This table saw really has it all. The assembly from box to saw-mounted stand took less than 20 minutes. Moving away from the conventional “kickstand” configuration, the DeWalt saw employs four folding legs that conveniently engage with the squeeze of a lever. This gives the saw a base of unparalleled sturdiness.

Every accessory has a proper home onboard the saw itself, and DeWalt’s inclusion of a table side release lever makes swapping riving knives and blade guards an absolute breeze. The fence—maxing out at 32-1/2 inches—was dead-on accurate from the jump. Tracking was consistent straight through the cut.

I’m a fan of the push stick mounted inside the fence itself for easy access when making cuts close to the blade. Rip cuts (both straight and beveled) were clean and accurate, but dust control is merely average. My other complaints with this saw are that the bevel and blade height gearing feel a bit stiff, and I’d love to see a bed extender option beyond the blade for handling longer materials better.

Full DeWalt DWE7491RS 10-Inch Jobsite Table Saw Review

This Skil saw makes a strong case for stretching your dollar where it counts—as long as you don’t mind carrying the saw from place to place. This saw lacks wheels, but has four legs that fold out from under it, card-table style. For less than $350, you get a full 10-inch saw with the stability–if not the mobility—of a jobsite saw.

The legs are simple and effective—they lock in solid when you set them up and tuck away without turning the whole unit into a bulky mess. It’s a smart design that makes it easy to store or throw in the truck without thinking twice about it.

Looking beyond the stability design, this saw really shines where table saws should—in its cutting ability. The fence was dead-on accurate to the blade straight out of the box, a factor that assists the powerful Skil motor in delivering repeat cuts effectively. I was especially taken with the blade quality, which routinely ripped through 1x trim like a razor, leaving barely a mark to sand away later. Dust exhaust was equally impressive as I watched a steady flow of debris cascade from the rear port. Where other saws tend to accumulate dust in the body of the saw, I saw none of that here.

For a saw that cuts this well and stands on its own stable platform, this one is a huge win at this price and likely ideal for those looking to expand their tool corral without going over budget.

Full Skil 15-Amp 10-Inch Portable Table Saw Review

Like most jobsite table saws, this one comes with a 10-inch blade and a legitimate 32-1/2-inch rip capacity, which is more than you’ll need for most light-duty cutting work and much more than I expected considering this saw’s price.

What surprised me most, though, is the saw’s stand. It has folding legs and 6-inch wheels, so you can simply roll it from the garage to wherever you’re working. When you’re done, it tucks up nicely without taking over your entire storage space.

Assembling the Kobalt saw was a little more complicated than others—it took me a solid 45 minutes to build. Once built, you notice how much lighter it is than bigger jobsite saws. It’s not quite as planted as the heavier DeWalt or Bosch models, but it is lighter on your wallet. For occasional use, this saw gets you in the game without burning a serious hole in your wallet.

Bosch really nailed the balance with this saw. It rides on a gravity-rise stand, and it’s clearly built for those who need to move their saw around but still expect it to perform like a burly stationary beast.

The stand’s open-frame design acts as its own base when folded and stood upright, which makes storage a whole lot easier. Add in the solid rubber wheels, and it’s as nimble as a hunting dog. While the assembly wasn’t my favorite part of this experience—the moving parts of the gravity rise system relies on precise alignment—the saw was up and making cuts in less than 45 minutes, which is pretty fair. That said, the system is well worth the assembly patience. Just hit the foot pedal, and the entire unit lifts smoothly into working position.

Once you’re cutting, there’s very little compromise on this tool. You get a full 32-1/8-inch rip capacity, and the motor regulates blade speed so it doesn’t struggle as much when you have to lean into it. But what I really like is the automatic blade brake, which kicks in about 3 seconds after you cut the power. If you’re doing a bunch of repeat cuts, the difference between those 3 seconds and the time it normally takes for a blade to spin down adds up quickly.

Of all the saws I set up straight from the box, this one gave me the most trouble. I attribute much of that to the rather poor schematics in the instructions, so I highly recommend this YouTube video, which helps with the visuals. Once assembled, this saw is a beast in both size and power. Even the wheels are huge (16 inches), which is something you have to account for when you return the saw to its storage position. That added circumference increases the speed of the drop. Be warned—it drops down fast!

The shining feature of this saw is Skil’s patented worm-drive motor, which is self-cooling and powerful enough to rip through pressure-treated 4x4s without a hitch (the only saw on our list to clear that depth in a single pass). While the motor spins faster than other saws at 5,000 RPM, the gearing converts that speed to higher torque and lower blade speed under load, which makes cuts through heavy, damp lumber easier.

The fence—in spite of a less-than-sturdy release latch—glides across the rack-and-pinion gearing with ease, extending out to 30-1/2 inches, which is fine for larger sheet materials. The saw has a powerful, fast start-up and a quick braking system, and the table ruler is right on the money in terms of accuracy.

We were introduced to the Evolution R10TBLX via the comments section of one of our social media posts of the previous version of this buying guide. It seemed like fans of this saw were adamant that we were overlooking a real contender by not including this saw. So, we listened and called it in for testing.

While the rolling buck is not as sturdy as those on other saws I’ve tested, it rolls well across terrain and locks in horizontally at the push of the pedal. Once in place, this table saw is a workhorse like I’ve rarely used before.

First, the saw is capable of cutting a variety of materials including wood, plastic, laminates, and steel. Yes, you read that right—steel. And that’s all without changing the 28-tooth tungsten carbide blade that’s included. The saw also boasts dual rack-and-pinion tracking (to better maintain fence-to-blade alignment), table extenders, leveling feet, and dado-cutting capabilities. But the truly unique element of this saw is the built-in crosscut sled, which offers an added element of safety when making those risky cuts.

The Evolution is a great choice for someone who routinely bridges materials in their work. Don’t expect furniture-quality cuts from the general-use blade—especially over time if you’re running through a lot of metal (or lumber with nails embedded)—but this unique saw certainly earns its spot on our list.

At just 45 pounds, this saw makes other portable models seem stationary. The frame doubles as a carrying handle, so it feels more like grabbing a piece of gear than wrestling with a tool. And unlike a lot of cordless table saws, this one actually comes with a 12.0Ah battery (though if you’re already on the Milwaukee M18 platform, you can buy this tool-only and save about $350.)

Light as it is, this saw is surprisingly solid. I set mine up on an old picnic table, and it didn’t budge while I cut with it, even while running plywood and 1x hardwood through it all day. Best of all, it delivers very clean, accurate cuts repeatedly.

Of course, considering its compact size, you do give up a bit of capacity with this saw. The 8-1/4-inch blade means less cut depth than you get with a full 10-inch saw, and the 24-1/2-inch rip capacity isn’t huge, generally around six to ten inches less than larger jobsite saws.

But that’s not really what this kind of saw is meant for. This one is about mobility and convenience—grabbing it, setting it up anywhere, and getting to work without dragging a cord around behind you.

If compact size is a priority, or you just want a corded table saw that transports relatively easily, consider the small but mighty DeWalt DWE7485. Weighing a hair over 50 pounds and with a 27-by-27-inch footprint, this saw is well-suited to smaller workshops, temporary workspaces, and casual woodworkers who might want to minimize clutter by stashing it out of the way until needed.

Despite its compact size, the DWE7485 still provides the same convenient onboard storage perks found on beefier models with dedicated spaces for a blade guard, riving knife, anti-kickback pawls, blade change wrench, miter gauge, and push stick. The metal roll cage also gives this saw a durable, heavy-duty feel, although compared to the larger, 10-inch DeWalt saw, some components (like the cord wrap) felt a little less durable.

Yes, the 8-1/4-inch blade doesn't give it a 30-inch rip capacity, nor the cut depth you get from the 10-inch version, but as long as you have a decent idea of the scope of cuts you’re planning on doing, the superior storage and portability benefits potentially make this the more practical choice.

The average table saw has a blade that’s 10 inches in diameter, but some 8-1/4-inch options are available for smaller saws like the Milwaukee M18 FUEL 8-1/4-inch Table Saw. Larger saw blades offer more cutting depth, which helps them slice through thicker materials without resistance, but any blade larger than 10 inches should be reserved for huge, commercial table saws that aren’t practical for the average homeowner.

To “rip” means to cut a wooden board along the grain. In simple terms, rip capacity refers to the distance between the edge of the blade and the edge of the saw’s fence. This determines the maximum width you can cut with that saw and indicates the types of projects you can tackle effectively with it.

For example, most furniture projects require just a 30-inch rip capacity (achievable with any of the 10-inch models listed above), while those in the market for a table saw that will break down larger sheet goods for cabinetry should look for one with a 52-inch rip capacity. Larger rip capacities generally correspond to a higher price tag, so choosing a saw with more rip capacity than you need may not be worth it.

The large, exposed blade of a table saw deserves your utmost respect, so follow all recommended guidelines provided in your saw’s instruction manual. Beyond that, look for a saw that includes features that encourage safe operation and enhanced user protection. Blade guards provide an extra layer of defense between your fingers and the blade, and riving knives prevent kickback and keep your workpiece from jamming.

Regardless of the saw you choose, look for one that includes its own push stick—a tool used to guide wood through the blade while keeping your fingers at a safe distance—like the DeWalt DWE7491RS. These are essential when ripping narrow boards, cuts that would otherwise require you to place your fingers extremely close to the blade.

This is your go-to tool for any woodworking project where precision matters most. Use one for building kitchen cabinets, bookshelves, or creating dado and rabbet cuts for joinery and shelf slots, as table saws deliver the consistent accuracy you need for professional-looking results (and, more importantly, they do almost all the work for you).

A table saw excels at ripping lumber to exact widths, making repetitive crosscuts for trim work, and handling large sheet goods like plywood that would be unwieldy with handheld tools or things like jigsaws or circular saws.

From constructing furniture components to creating custom storage solutions, table saws handle both fine woodworking and heavy-duty construction tasks with equal confidence, making them rather indispensable.

A circular saw with a track saw attachment can sometimes be a more convenient solution (although a lot less user-friendly), allowing you to bring the saw to the workpiece instead of the other way around. I’ve seen guys use this to rip the edges of deck boards this way more than once.

Table saw safety starts before you even flip the switch. First of all, always wear safety glasses and avoid loose hair, clothing, or jewelry that could catch and get pulled into the blade. Keep your hands well away from the cutting area by using push sticks or push blocks, especially when ripping narrow pieces.

Never remove the blade guard unless absolutely necessary and always use the rip fence or miter gauge to guide your workpiece. Never try to cut freehand.

Before each cut, ensure the blade is properly aligned and the workpiece is flat against the table. Then—regarding body positioning—stand to the side of the blade, not directly behind it, to avoid kickback injuries. Most importantly, if something feels wrong or the wood starts binding, turn off the saw immediately. A moment of caution beats a lifetime of regret when working with these powerful machines.

To keep your table saw running smoothly and cutting accurately (and safely) for years to come, regular maintenance is a must. After each cutting session, be sure to clear excess sawdust from the motor housing and internal components since buildup can result in overheating over time. You can use an air compressor for this, but if you don’t have one of those, a regular shop vac will do the trick (most have a setting that can blow air out of the nozzle instead of sucking it in).

You should also check the blade alignment periodically, adjust the fence to ensure accuracy, and lubricate moving parts according to the manual’s recommended schedule. Since they can strain the motor and cause dangerous kickback situations, always replace blades when they become worn and dull.

Japan's groundbreaking mission to Mars is officially underway, headed to the Red Planet's mysterious moons Phobos and Deimos for a historic sample-return attempt.

The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission launched today (Oct. 19) from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan, riding an H3 rocket that lifted off from Pad-2 at Tanegashima's Yoshinobu Launch Complex at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan on Oct. 20).

The JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency)-led MMX mission is bound for Mars orbit, where it will study the planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos. If everything goes according to plan, MMX will become the first spacecraft to land on and return samples from Phobos for study back on Earth, which scientists think could shed light on a decades-old mystery about the moons' origins and reveal clues about the formation of the early solar system.

It was the 10th liftoff of Japan's expendable, two-stage H3 rocket, which was jointly developed by JAXA and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. After clearing its launch pad today, the 207-foot-tall (63 meters) launch vehicle flew a nominal trajectory through its ascent corridor over the Pacific Ocean, jettisoning its four solid boosters in pairs just before the flight clock reached two minutes. The rocket shed its payload fairings about one minute and 20 seconds later, exposing MMX to the vacuum of space for the first time.

H3's first stage, powered by two LE-9 rocket engines, channels a mixture of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to produce a combined thrust of 331,000 pounds (1,471 kN), according to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. As the mission clock approached T+5 minutes, H3 executed its main engine cutoff procedure and separated from the second stage, which ignited its engines for a 5.5-minute burn about 10 seconds later.

All continued to go to plan after that. The H3's upper stage ignited its engine for a second time for a trans-Mars injection burn about one hour and four minutes after liftoff, a maneuver that lasted roughly six minutes and 25 seconds and took MMX to a maximum velocity of about 24,145 mph (38,858 kph).

MMX was released from the rocket's upper stage right on schedule, about one minute after the completion of that burn and roughly 71 minutes after liftoff. The success elicited loud cheers in mission control, which viewers saw and heard on JAXA's launch webcast.

MMX is now under its own power, and on course for Mars. The interplanetary transit will last about 10 months, with the spacecraft scheduled to arrive at the Red Planet in August 2027. When it does, MMX's propulsion module will execute an orbital insertion burn to place itself in a quasi-satellite orbit (QSO) around Phobos, which places MMX within the space around the moon as both circle Mars.

MMX will spend about three years in the Martian system, devoting much of that time to studying the 14-mile-wide (22 km) Phobos with its science instruments. The spacecraft also carries the IDEFIX rover, a joint effort of the space agencies of France and Germany, which is scheduled to deploy to the surface of Phobos in late 2028 or early 2029.

After a mapping campaign to select suitable landing sites, MMX will perform two separate touchdowns on Phobos to collect and stow samples in the spacecraft's return capsule. Following its second landing and sample collection, MMX will briefly return to QSO with Phobos before transferring to a more elongated orbit around Mars that intersects with the planet's smaller moon, Deimos, which is just 8 miles (14 km) in diameter.

During the last several months of its time around Mars, MMX will perform a series of Deimos flybys before departing for Earth in November 2030. If all goes according to plan, the MMX sample-return capsule will land in Australia in 2031.

Scientists are counting on those samples, and other data collected during MMX's time around Mars, to answer a decades-old question surrounding the Martian moons' origins. Competing theories and conflicting evidence point to two possibilities for how Mars got its moons.

Their near-circular, equatorial orbits suggest a narrative similar to how Earth's moon is thought to have formed — as a result of a massive planetary impact between Mars and some other giant space rock, which broke off pieces of the planet that eventually coalesced to form the natural satellites that orbit there today.

Neither Phobos nor Deimos is spherical, isntead; both are oblong and lumpy, like potatoes. That fact — along with their chemical composition, as far as we have been able to tell using telescopic spectroscopy — point to the possibility that Phobos and Deimos were asteroids from the early solar system that were captured by Mars' gravitational pull. Figuring out the moons' true origin story would provide key clues about Mars' geological past, the solar system's early history and the formation of the inner planets, mission team members have said.

Once the MMX samples are safely returned to Earth, scientists will study their composition and mineralogy, then compare such chemical fingerprints with those of Martian rocks and asteroid material. These analyses, combined with data collected by MMX during its mission, will help nail down the origin of Phobos — and by extension, Deimos. — by

While JAXA leads MMX, the mission is an international effort, with interagency partnerships between JAXA, NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA), as well as U.S. and European companies, which supplied a handful of the spacecraft's scientific hardware and communications equipment.

NASA's contributions to MMX include the Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE, pronounced "meh-gah-nay") device, which is a gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL); a Honeybee Robotics-built pneumatic sampler; and communications support using the agency's Deep Space Network.

NASA has also invested approximately $87 million through the end of the mission, which includes funding for United States scientists and astromaterials experts on the MMX team. The agency is getting something concrete for such contributions: At least 15% of the planned 10-gram (0.35 ounces) returned Phobos sample will be reserved for NASA's study. Those materials will be transferred and maintained at the agency's Johnson Space Center in Houston for analysis and long-term preservation.

MMX is not the first Phobos sample-return project to take flight, by the way. That distinction goes to Russia's Phobos-Grunt ("Phobos-Soil") mission, which launched in November 2011 but failed to get out of Earth orbit due to a rocket glitch. The 14.5-ton spacecraft eventually crashed back to Earth over the Pacific Ocean in January 2012.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 5 p.m. ET on Oct. 19 with news of MMX's successful separation from the H3 rocket's upper stage.

#82. Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find

A new study suggests that even low levels of physical activity could protect the brain from Alzheimer’s disease – but not in the way scientists expected.

The researchers tracked almost 300 older adults with early brain signs of Alzheimer’s for nine to 11 years using pedometers. They found that physical activity didn’t reduce the toxic amyloid plaques that most Alzheimer’s treatments now target.

Instead, in people who already had these plaques, physical activity reduced the accumulation of misfolded tau proteins in specific brain areas. These proteins appear later in Alzheimer’s disease and are more closely linked to cognitive and functional decline. These signs of dementia were reduced by almost half in more active participants.

Benefits appeared at just 3,000 steps – roughly half an hour of walking at a moderate pace. The optimal range was 5,000 to 7,500 steps daily, after which the effect plateaued. More steps didn’t necessarily mean greater protection, which suggests a realistic target for older, sedentary people, rather than the often-cited 10,000 steps.

The study had limitations, however. It involved a fairly small group of mostly white, well-educated people in the US, and it didn’t take other lifestyle or health factors into account. Also, there may be other protective mechanisms of walking at play. But it does support other research suggesting that being physically active may lower the risk of dementia.

A UK study of 1,139 people over 50 found that those who were moderately to vigorously active had a 34-50% reduction in dementia risk when followed over eight to ten years. Among those who developed dementia, staying active reduced their memory decline, particularly in older women.

A larger 2022 UK study tracked 78,430 people for seven years using wrist accelerometers. It found a 25% reduction in dementia risk with just 3,800 steps daily, rising to 50% at 9,800 steps.

However, people who walked more also had better cardiovascular health – lower cholesterol, better sleep and blood pressure and reduced diabetes risk. Since these heart and stroke risk factors also increase dementia risk, the picture is complex.

Healthy habits often go together. People who exercise are more likely to eat well, not smoke, look after their heart health and have fewer financial stresses. This makes it hard to know which factor is having the biggest effect. The researchers tried to account for this, but because these habits are so closely linked, it’s difficult to say that exercise alone is responsible.

However, there is a strong case for this as there are multiple ways exercise might support the brain: improving cardiovascular health, increasing blood flow and boosting chemicals that promote brain-cell connections.

One such substance is irisin, a hormone produced by muscles that acts on almost all faulty brain mechanisms associated with Alzheimer’s, including inflammation. This and other chemicals, such as BDNF, associated with exercise, provide plausible biological pathways for how physical activity might directly influence brain health beyond its cardiovascular benefits.

But the relationship might work in reverse, too. People may become less active because of early Alzheimer’s symptoms. Those with hearing problems, for instance – itself a dementia risk factor – often report barriers that make them stop being active before other dementia symptoms appear.

Reduced activity then accelerates memory decline. This creates a vicious circle. Early disease symptoms – such as not hearing – can affect self-esteem and reduce engagement in physical activity, which in turn worsens cognitive decline.

Brisk walking might be particularly beneficial. A small trial of 15 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer’s who did Nordic walking (an enhanced walking technique that uses poles to work your upper body as well as your legs) maintained brain function over 24 weeks, with some functions even improving.

The 15 who received only standard care showed decline or no improvement. Though small, the trial suggests that even people already diagnosed with Alzheimer’s might benefit from increased physical activity, including brisk walking.

Getting outside, particularly in nature, may be especially beneficial for preventing dementia – possibly because it improves mood and sleep while reducing isolation – all dementia risk factors. The combination of physical movement, natural light exposure and social interaction when walking outdoors may create multiple protective effects that complement each other.

The challenge now is helping people overcome barriers to outdoor activity, such as safety concerns, fear of falling, or simply preferring the comfort of the sofa – particularly during wetter, colder months. But the evidence suggests that even a few minutes of walking could make a difference, and that modest, achievable targets – a half-hour stroll rather than a marathon training regime – may offer substantial protection against cognitive decline.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Eef Hogervorst, Professor of Biological Psychology, Loughborough University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#83. The 7 Best Miter Saws for Cutting Precise, Accurate Angles

These crosscutting models, including our top choice from Bosch, make possible an endless array of woodworking projects.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Not too long ago, making precise angled cuts meant using a simple miter box—a block with pre-cut 90- and 45-degree slots—and a squat little saw with more teeth than a piranha. Those old-school setups still have their place, especially for ultra-clean trim cuts without tearout, but they’ve largely been replaced by the more powerful and versatile miter saw.

When it comes to angled cuts for trim, framing, or furniture, few tools match a good miter saw. A circular blade mounted on a hinged, pivoting arm delivers fast, consistent, and precise cuts at a wide range of angles—something hand saws and circular saws can’t replicate as easily.

The best models combine clean cutting power with accurate miter and bevel adjustments, smooth sliding action, and enough stability to stay precise while cutting dense wood. Features like clear cutline indicators, effective dust collection, and easily adjustable fences also make a huge difference when you’re making cuts all day.

Whether you’re building a garden bed or installing window trim, a miter saw is the fastest way to get accurate, repeatable results.

When selecting potential options for the original version of this article, author Alex Rennie, a former residential and commercial carpenter in New York City, first put together a rough collection of options based on brands and saw types he had found to be most useful to him over the years. After paring that list down, he put each saw through a comprehensive series of tests.

Paul Smith updated this article most recently with the Milwaukee M18 FUEL 18V Sliding Compound Miter Saw, which impressed him during testing. He is in the process of testing more models and will update this article with the results of those tests when they are available. In the meantime, those models are included below as recommended miter saws based on reputation, product specs, features, price point, and online customer reviews.

Unlike most sliding saws that use rails to slide the blade forward and backward, this Bosch miter saw uses an axial-arm mechanism that eliminates the need for rear clearance. This unique design (also used by this Bosch model) allows the saw to take up considerably less space on your workbench without compromising overall cut capacity.

We loved the lever locks that secure the arm in place during transport (although we weren’t as much of a fan of the saw’s hefty 65-pound weight), and the smoothness of the arm, combined with the rubber handle grip, made this an especially comfortable saw to operate.

It’s worth noting that while the clear blade guard (compared to the black of the DeWalt models) provides a clearer view of the cutline, this saw lacks a shadow or laser line feature.

What the Skil 10-inch dual-bevel miter saw lacks in refinement—things like pro-level build quality, multiple bevel detents, and high-end dust collection—it makes up for in capability and cost. At about half the price of most major brands, it delivers consistently clean cuts on a stable, well-constructed turntable.

The motor spins the blade up to 4,800 rpm quickly, so there’s little wait between cuts. In use, cuts were smooth along the rails as I cut through 2x12s, with no tearout or flyaway pieces. The saw is capable of bevels up to 48 degrees left and 45 degrees right—important if you’re making compound miter cuts for things like crown molding. There is a preset detent at 45 degrees left—a common cutting angle—but any bevel angle in between is easily locked down via the rear bevel knob. Even so, it proved accurate across those settings—I had no trouble dialing in compound miters—cuts that employ both miter and bevel cuts—for crown molding that lined up cleanly from both sides.

Ergonomics are a highlight. The trigger sits naturally within the grip, and it’s the only saw I tested that feels equally comfortable left- or right-handed. That might seem minor, but when you’re stretched out on a tricky compound cut, being able to switch hands makes a real difference. Finally, at less than 50 pounds, this saw is no trouble to move around your yard during setup changes or throw in your truck at the end of the day.

This dual-bevel, 10-inch saw packs a lot of power and features into one relatively small and comparatively inexpensive package. With nine positive miter stops and a cutting capacity of 12 inches on the bed, you’ll get up to 500 cuts on a single battery charge.

LED line indicators ensure precision, and a bevel pivot that's as easy to access as it is to operate rounds out this saw's top features. While it's not the most powerful saw, even compared to other cordless options, this one holds its own among the arguably bigger names that populate this list in every other way.

This DeWalt miter saw provides serious power and performance. We found that it maintained speed and power really well during our cut tests, but because it’s cordless, you don’t need to sacrifice mobility when you’re working with it.

The included stabilizer bar ensured that the saw felt sturdy and stable while we cut, and the included LED work light created a convenient, precise shadow line to maximize accuracy. We also appreciated how well the instruction manual walked us through all the different operations, giving us comprehensive instructions on a variety of cuts.

At a little over 50 pounds (without the 20V battery, which you’ll have to buy separately) and with a top-mounted carrying handle, this was one of the easier saws to transport during testing. Plus, this saw’s dust port was located on the side, instead of the rear, which made it easier to fit on a smaller workbench.

With dual-bevel capabilities, smooth gliding rails, and user-friendly controls and adjustment knobs, this cordless powerhouse handles everything from 13.5-inch-wide cuts to 6.5-inch-tall baseboards.

This saw won’t be your go-to if you’re working with large lumber. Nothing bigger than a 2x4 is recommended here, but if that type of work isn’t on your horizon, this saw is as easy to maneuver as it is to operate.

Its small size and extremely accurate blade make it ideal for using indoors to cut trim, flooring, and picture framing. And at just over 14 pounds, it’s a breeze to move from room to room as you work. We also like the gooseneck type of LED built into the blade housing for throwing light on your entire cut. And the 64-tooth blade delivers a clean, precise cut every time.

If you believe you get what you pay for, this Makita 8-1/2-inch miter saw makes the case. Tools should solve problems—and this one addresses a big one in its category: size versus capability. A 12-inch saw powers through 4x4s but is heavy and space-hungry; a compact 6-inch is portable but limited. This Makita saw lands squarely in between.

This 40V cordless saw delivers corded-level power in a lighter package—roughly 10 to 20 pounds less than larger models—while still handling 12-inch crosscuts. Its forward-facing rails save valuable workspace, letting it sit flush against a wall without the usual rear clearance.

Build quality stands out immediately. The heavy aluminum turntable feels rigid under load, with precise detents that lock in smoothly at common angles—no fighting to find your mark. Preset bevel stops on both sides add convenience, and the front-mounted bevel lock means no awkward reaching over the saw.

Makita also includes dual dust collection options: a standard bag or a ducted port for a dedicated system. Pair it with Makita’s AWS technology and pulling the trigger wirelessly activates a compatible vacuum—an easy, thoughtful upgrade for shop workflow.

Prior to using this saw, I read that some users had issues with the out-of-the-box accuracy of the table in relation to the blade. This situation is problematic when cutting trim, for instance, because it needs to fit perfectly.

I personally experienced none of that. I cut a variety of woods with this saw—from 2x10s to MDF trim—and the results completely satisfied me. Cuts were clean, splinter-free, and above all, accurate at connection.

The saw is powerful, thanks in part to its brushless motor and impressive battery, which Milwaukee claims makes 330 cuts per charge, but I honestly ran out of wood before that number (and according to the battery indicators, I still had half a charge remaining).

Milwaukee puts a lot of effort into getting its shadow line system clear and precise, and I appreciate that when it comes to eyeing up my cuts. As an added bonus, I find the LED field is the best of any saw I’ve used, cordless or otherwise. My only complaints are that the rear bevel is a little clunky to maneuver and the table extenders have an underwhelming feel to them. If you’re expanding your Milwaukee cordless platform, this saw is a great add.

The three main types of miter saws are compound, dual compound, and sliding. Each variation performs specific functions and cuts better than the others, so it’s important that you understand their differences and also have a decent idea of how you plan on using your saw.

In addition to lowering straight down for perpendicular crosscuts, the blade of a compound miter saw also pivots from side to side for angled “miter” cuts and it tilts to one side for bevel cuts. A “compound” cut utilizes both of these functions in one motion and is commonly used to create things like picture frames or to cut crown molding for installation.

Instead of tilting to only one side for bevel cuts, dual compound saws (also called “double” or “double-bevel” compound saws) tilt in both directions. This makes work much faster than using a standard compound saw because while a compound saw technically makes all the same cuts as a dual compound saw, its single-bevel design means you spend more time flipping workpieces around to cut opposite angles.

These two non-sliding types are solid options for homeowners who want a reasonably compact and portable machine.

A standard compound miter saw drops straight down onto the board. It’s great for narrow stock but limited by the diameter of the blade. A sliding compound miter saw adds rails that let the blade travel forward and backward during the course of the cut. This feature dramatically increases the width of material the saw can handle—making it possible to cut wider boards in a single pass. If you’re cutting a lot of shelving, flooring, or wide trim, a sliding miter saw, such as the DeWalt 20V MAX XR Dual-Bevel Sliding Miter Saw, is usually worth the extra cost and size.

When shopping for a miter saw, you’ll also need to decide what type of power source you prefer.

Cordless miter saws have improved dramatically over the last few years, mostly due to the evolution of high-capacity lithium-ion batteries and the inclusion of brushless motors. Today’s 18- and 20-volt models offer plenty of power for trim work and general carpentry without sacrificing the portability that makes cordless power tools appealing in the first place.

I like knowing I can set up the saw anywhere and get to work without worrying about finding power or running an extension cord through an open door or window. That said, corded saws still hold the edge when it comes to cutting ability and run time.

Most miter saws come with 10- or 12-inch blades, and that difference has a big impact on what type of cuts and tasks the saw excels at.

A 10-inch saw, like the Metabo HPT Single Bevel Compound Miter Saw, is typically lighter and easier to move around your shop or from room to room. It’s more than capable of cutting trim, flooring, and smaller dimensional lumber.

A 12-inch saw, on the other hand, gives you significantly more cutting capacity—especially when you’re working with wider boards or tall trim pieces like crown molding. 12-inch saws, like our Best Overall choice, the Bosch GCM12SD Dual-Bevel Sliding Miter Saw, are a bit more awkward to move around the workplace.

A large saw also adds bulk and takes up more room in the shop or truck. But the trade-off to those negatives is that you’re far less likely to run into a job that you simply can’t handle. I’d rather deal with the extra footprint than discover upon starting a project that my saw is undersized. If you have the space, it’s often better to size up.

Blade speed, measured in rpm (revolutions per minute), is another important performance indicator. Most miter saws operate between 3,000 and 5,500 rpm, and naturally, higher speeds increase your cutting efficiency. Some saws, like the Hilti Nuron 22V miter saw, even allow you to customize your speed to a specific task, which makes it uniquely versatile.

That said, the relationship between the saw blade diameter and rpm makes comparing the speed of two miter saws a little more complex. Two saws running at the same rpm, but using different-sized blades—let’s say 7¼-inch and 12-inch—will not cut at the same speed. That’s because even though the center of each blade is spinning at the same speed, the outer edge of the 12-inch blade will turn faster than the edge of the 7¼-inch one.

Things get even more complicated when we bring the blade’s tooth count into the mix, with higher-tooth blades reducing speed. As a beginner, you can drive yourself a little crazy trying to determine the perfect combination of blade factors, so I’d recommend relying on your saw’s instruction manual for basic guidance.

Modern miter saws often include features designed to help you cut more accurately and consistently. Some use laser guides to project the cut line, while others use LED systems that cast a shadow from the blade, so you can see exactly where it will land. Detents at common angle stops around the saw table—like 22.5 degrees and 45 degrees—also make it faster to dial in repeated cuts. These features aren’t essential, but they make a noticeable difference when you’re making dozens of cuts in a row.

Archaeologists discovered a first-century-B.C. military camp that was erected during Emperor Augustus' Cantabrian Wars.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed a Roman military camp in Spain, where they found fragments of weapons and metal tacks from soldiers' shoes. The camp was used during the Cantabrian Wars fought by Emperor Augustus as he expanded the Roman Empire in the first century B.C.

The fortified military camp is made up of an earthen platform roughly 39 feet (12 meters) wide, which is surrounded by a stone perimeter wall about 5 feet (1.5 m) thick, according to a translated statement. Uncovered during excavations earlier this year, the camp is situated about one-third of a mile (500 m) from where an Iron Age settlement was once inhabited by the Cantabri people, a group of Celtic tribes that lived among the Cantabrian Mountains in modern-day northern Spain.

The Cantabri fiercely resisted Roman rule for a decade, but in 19 B.C., they were conquered by the military commanded by Emperor Augustus. The Cantabrian Wars marked the end of local control over the territory, as the Iberian Peninsula then came under control of the Roman Empire.

Archaeologists work at the site of the Roman fort.

"It's not easy to find a camp associated with a hill fort in this condition," Eduardo González Gómez de Agüero, an archaeologist at the University of León who co-directed the excavation project, said in the statement.

Among the well-preserved remains at the camp were metal weapon fragments and small iron tacks known as hobnails, which were hammered into the bottom of Roman soldiers' leather military sandals to help provide traction on rocky and muddy terrain. These objects are evidence that the Roman military was prepared to attack and subdue the Iron Age community, according to the statement.

The archaeologists also uncovered evidence of a major fire that destroyed most of the pre-Roman settlement, including two temples. González Gómez de Agüero suggested that the Romans may have deliberately set the fire as part of their conquest.

"It's not just about defeating the enemy, but about humiliating them, erasing their identity, and breaking their connection to the land," he said in the statement.

Researchers are still working on establishing the chronology of the Romans' final attack on the Cantabri and want to understand if the settlement was destroyed in a single event or over time. Previously, another research team found 66 Roman camps in northern Spain, showing the immensity of the empire's attacks against the Cantabri.

The latest find is helping researchers understand the scale and location of Rome's fight for control of the Iberian Peninsula.

"It is an important step in understanding how the conquest was carried out on the Cantabrian slope of León, an area where it was necessary to link the Roman camps with Iron Age settlements," Carlos Fernández Rodríguez, an archaeologist at the University of León, said in the statement.

Can you identify these historical objects of war? Test your smarts with our weapons of the world quiz!

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

The ExoMars 2016 orbiter survived the Mars arrival. Sadly, its Schiaparelli lander did not.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars mission arrived at Mars!

ExoMars 2016 consists of the Trace Gas Orbiter and the Schiaparelli lander. The orbiter and lander traveled there together and separated on Oct. 16, three days before the orbiter entered orbit around Mars, and the lander touched down on the planet's surface. But something went wrong during the lander's descent, and it crashed into the ground.

Schiaparelli did not survive the accident, but the Trace Gas Orbiter is still functional. It is currently circling the planet, looking for methane and other gases in the Martian atmosphere that could be evidence for possible biological activity.

ExoMars 2016 was a landmark mission for the European Space Agency and designed to be the vanguard of a two-flight ExoMars program to send an orbiter, lander and rover to Mars.

Launched in March 2016, ExoMars 2016 aimed to achieve two goals for ESA and Russia. First, the mission aimed to use the Schiaparelli lander to test landing techniques that would be vital on a planned ExoMars 2018 rover. Second, the mission would deliver a critical orbiter around Mars to study the planet's atmosphere and serve as a communications link for that future Mars rover.

In the end, ExoMars 2016 was just a partial success, with ESA officials calling it "96% successful." due to the loss of the lander.

While Schiaparelli separated smoothly from the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter spacecraft, it stopped communicating with Earth just 1 minute before its planned landing on Oct. 19. Photos from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter at Mars later revealed what appeared to be its crash site and, nearby, its jettisoned parachute. Officials suspect Schiaparelli did not fire its descent thrusters as designed in order to slow itself enough for a safe landing. A data glitch was cited as its cause.

The Trace Gas Orbiter, meanwhile, continues to study Mars to this day and has spent 10 years and counting studying the Martian atmosphere.

The launch of ExoMars 2018, which includes the Mars rover Rosalind Franklin, was delayed by the Schiaparelli failure, as well as the loss of its Russian Proton rocket when ESA severed its partnership with Russia over that country's war on Ukraine.

The ExoMars rover is now expected to launch no earlier than 2028, with a landing on Mars expected in 2030.

In 2026, another country took aim at Mars on this day.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency attempted to launch the ambitious Martian Moons eXploration mission (called MMX) to land a probe on the Mars moon Phobos and return samples to Earth.

#87. A telling hole in a Neandertal bone hints at a bitter end

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

But a shattered tooth suggests a more nuanced tale of life

A hole in this 75,000-year-old shoulder blade suggests that this Neandertal was stabbed by a spear around the time they died.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A new set of remains found in modern-day Iraq suggests that one Neandertal probably suffered a devastating blow to the face before dying at the point of a spear many years later.

The size and structure of a puncture wound in a shoulder blade suggest that it was made by a wooden spear shortly before or after death, researchers write October 15 in Scientific Reports. But violence isn’t all this Neandertal may have known. A shattered tooth found with the remains hints that the deceased suffered a facial injury at some point in their life. Surviving this injury indicates that Neandertals may have helped each other in times of need, the study authors speculate.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

These remains with visible trauma are “super cool,” because “there’s a lot of ways to die that leave absolutely no mark on your skeleton,” says Libby Cowgill, a biological anthropologist at the University of Missouri in Columbia who wasn’t involved with the study.

Neandertals were often injured throughout their lives, probably from hunting. But archaeologists have also uncovered occasional signs that Neandertals and other hominids — modern humans and their extinct cousins — were stabbing and pummeling each other, maybe even intentionally, as far back as 430,000 years ago. Signs of injuries caused by other hominids have included another Neandertal at the same Iraq site whose rib was probably stabbed.

During an excavation that began in 2019 at Shanidar, the famous Neandertal burial site in Iraqi Kurdistan, researchers uncovered remains from at least three previously unknown individuals. The set included ribs, hand bones, teeth and a perforated shoulder bone that probably belonged to a single individual who lived around 75,000 years ago.

At first, the team had no idea what caused the hole, says Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge. “It’s so round, it’s like, what is it?” she recalls thinking at the time.

The team removed the shoulder blade with the surrounding sediment and tested for evidence that roots or insects had damaged the fossil. But that didn’t fit the nature of the damage.

Instead, they found fragments of bone from the shoulder blade in the dirt that suggested it had been pierced when the individual, which the team named Shanidar A, was alive. The team also didn’t see any signs of healing around the puncture wound when they analyzed the bone under the microscope and using X-rays — suggesting that the injury had occurred around the time of death.

The next task was to find out what instrument might have caused the injury. The team compared the puncture with the fossilized remains of butchered animals found alongside human tools, as well as wounds created by archaeologists stabbing animal corpses with re-created Paleolithic weapons. Stone-tipped spears usually create a diamond-shaped hole. Wooden spears, on the other hand, tend to leave round puncture wounds.

The wound was “absolutely, without any question,” made by a wooden spear, says Bruno Maureille, an anthropologist at the University of Bordeaux in France who wasn’t on the study team.

The team also found a broken incisor alongside the rest of the remains. The tooth was so shattered that Shanidar A probably experienced a serious injury to their face. Tartar buildup suggests that the tooth splintered in half years before Shanidar A died, meaning they lived with their disability for a long time.

“Given it would have affected their ability to eat, to drink — they’d have been in massive amount of pain at first — it’s likely [to] have needed some care,” Pomeroy says. That one set of remains suggest both violence and care show that Neandertal “behavior is complex,” Pomeroy says. “Like us.”

#88. Scientists Discover Exercise Changes the Body in Ways We Never Fully Understood

Salk Institute researchers have created a molecular map of how healthy mice respond to exercise, offering clues that could help improve performance and reduce injury risk.

Exercise can help the body resist disease and dysfunction and recover from illness. Studies have also linked it to more than 30 percent lower mortality from all causes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. Explaining those benefits is harder, partly because studies in people generally rely on blood and muscle samples, leaving researchers with an incomplete picture of how exercise changes other organs.

Researchers at the Salk Institute turned to mice to follow those changes through more of the body. They compared young male and female mice that ran voluntarily on a wheel for eight weeks with mice that remained sedentary, creating a first-of-its-kind molecular atlas spanning 22 tissues. The study was published in Cell on October 15, 2026.

Exercise altered the activity of nearly half the genes examined in at least one tissue, yet no single gene’s activity changed in all 22. Those comparisons came from bulk RNA sequencing, which measures gene activity across whole tissue samples. Rather than revealing one response shared everywhere, the analysis showed that tissues adapted in different ways.

The researchers also cataloged the small molecules that cells use and produce during metabolism in eight tissues and plasma, the liquid part of blood. Alongside this metabolomics analysis, they used proteomics to measure protein levels in four specific leg muscles, examining a hamstring muscle, two calf muscles, and the quadriceps.

“Exercise doesn’t just change our muscles, it changes many of our organs and cells at different levels—some short-term, some long-term,” says co-first and co-corresponding author Geraldine Maier, PhD, a staff scientist at Salk. “Our experimental setup allows us to capture that detail across tissues, and sexes, and in muscle, down to the individual cell types.”

Skeletal muscle accounted for most of the changes in gene activity, and the strong responses in leg muscles prompted the researchers to examine three of them more closely. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing, they could distinguish neighboring cell types and compare their gene activity instead of averaging their responses together. They also conducted the first single-cell analysis of DNA methylation in muscle after exercise.

In some muscle cell types, training changed chemical marks on DNA that help regulate gene activity, while other cell types showed no such changes. These marks are added through a process called DNA methylation. Changes in their pattern can be more persistent than shifts in RNA or protein levels, allowing this form of epigenetic regulation to have lasting effects on how particular cell types and whole tissues behave.

“Exercise impacts the whole body, not just your muscles, so an atlas like ours that looks more holistically at many tissues is key to understanding the true impact of exercise,” says co-first author Manoj Hariharan, PhD, a former senior staff scientist at Salk. “That’s also why single-cell studies are so important—there are so many cell type-specific changes that get lost in bulk sequencing. I hope our work highlights that and encourages more single-cell atlases, and especially multi-omic single-cell atlases, moving forward.”

Female mice showed broader changes in gene activity and distinct expression patterns compared with males. The epigenetic response to training also differed strongly by sex.

To capture variation across daily biological rhythms, the researchers collected tissues during both the active and resting phases of the mice’s circadian cycle. Most tissues showed greater exercise-related changes when sampled during the active phase, with the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung as exceptions.

“Our atlas provides a comprehensive resource for understanding the systemic molecular adaptations to endurance exercise,” says co-first author Ramesh Ramasamy, PhD, a former computational biologist at Salk. “Now that we have all this data, researchers can begin developing strategies that harness exercise—either alone or in combination with other interventions—to ensure we all live long, healthy lives.”

The researchers have already used the gene activity dataset to develop a 51-gene exercise signature, a pattern that distinguishes exercise-trained muscle from sedentary muscle in both mice and humans. It could help identify biomarkers, measurable indicators of a biological state, and support research into muscle disuse and dysfunction.

By establishing a healthy baseline, the atlas gives researchers a reference for investigating how tissues adapt to exercise. The differences by sex and circadian phase could eventually inform more personalized exercise routines, while closer investigation of particular tissues and cell types may point to ways of improving performance, recovery, and muscle health.

“Now that we have the data,” adds Maier, “labs can identify one gene or metabolic pathway they find interesting, then dissect that mechanism. Our atlas gives the field a shared foundation to build on.”

How long those molecular changes last remains unresolved. Researchers still need to determine how long training must continue before lasting changes develop and whether cells retain a memory of exercise for months or years.

Reference: “Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise” by Geraldine Maier, Manoj Hariharan, Ramesh K. Ramasamy, Aidan Glina, Laura van Rosmalen, Suraj J. #89. Why painful arthritis can return stronger after cancer treatment

For some cancer patients, the effects of immunotherapy can linger in an unexpected place: their joints. Painful arthritis may return repeatedly, sometimes becoming more severe with each episode. Now, scientists have uncovered a possible explanation involving the immune system's ability to remember previous attacks.

Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have found evidence that arthritis triggered by certain cancer immunotherapies behaves like a disease driven by immune memory. Rather than launching an entirely new inflammatory response during each flare, the immune system appears to reactivate cells involved in earlier episodes.

The discovery could eventually help doctors identify patients at risk of recurring arthritis and develop treatments that control joint inflammation without interfering with the immune system's ability to fight cancer.

The study, published in Cancer Immunology Research, was led by scientists at UT MD Anderson and Yale University. The research team included Roza I. Nurieva, Ph.D., professor of Immunology; Synat Keam, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the Nurieva Laboratory; and Yuanteng Jeff Li, M.D., assistant professor of General Internal Medicine. Sang Taek Kim, M.D., Ph.D., an assistant professor at Yale University, also co-led the investigation.

"Cancer immunotherapy works by creating a lasting immune response against tumors, but that same persistence may also contribute to recurring inflammatory side effects that can be debilitating for patients," Nurieva said. "By identifying the immune cells that drive recurrent arthritis, we can inform treatment strategies that reduce the risk of future flares while preserving the therapy's effectiveness against cancer."

Why Cancer Immunotherapy Can Trigger Painful Arthritis

Immune checkpoint inhibitors are widely used cancer treatments that help the body's natural defenses recognize and attack tumor cells. These drugs are a form of immunotherapy that works by removing some of the molecular restraints that normally keep immune activity under control.

Although this approach can help the immune system destroy cancer cells, it can sometimes cause immune cells to attack healthy tissues as well. When the joints become targets, patients may develop inflammatory arthritis, a condition that causes pain, swelling, and inflammation.

For some patients, the problem does not disappear after the first episode. Approximately 20% to 50% of patients who develop this complication experience repeated arthritis flares, and symptoms can persist for months or even years after immunotherapy ends.

These recurring episodes are often more intense than the initial attack, raising an important question: Why does the immune system continue to produce inflammation, and why can its response become increasingly aggressive?

Scientists Discover Immune Cells That Remember Previous Attacks

To investigate, the researchers examined fluid taken from the joints of six patients during both their first arthritis episode and a later recurrence.

Their analysis revealed two distinct populations of immune cells that appeared during both flares. One consisted of inflammatory CD8 T cells, while the other was a specialized group of CD4 T cells expressing two markers known as PD-1 and CXCL13.

T cells are immune cells that help coordinate the body's defenses and respond to potential threats. Some can also persist after an initial immune response, allowing the immune system to react more quickly when it encounters a familiar target.

The presence of the same immune cell populations during separate arthritis attacks suggests that recurring inflammation may arise from cells already involved in the earlier episode. Instead of starting from scratch, the immune system appears to reactivate an established inflammatory response.

This immune memory mechanism could help explain why arthritis can repeatedly return even after cancer treatment has stopped.

Why Arthritis Flares May Become More Severe

The researchers also found that the recurring immune cells appeared more active during subsequent arthritis episodes. They produced increased amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, which immune cells use to communicate and influence one another.

Another finding was particularly unexpected. Regulatory T cells, which normally act as a braking system to prevent excessive immune activity, also began producing inflammatory molecules during recurring flares.

This suggests that some of the cells responsible for keeping inflammation under control may instead contribute to it, potentially weakening the body's ability to shut down the response.

The researchers also identified extensive communication networks connecting inflammatory cells within affected joints. These signaling networks became more pronounced during the second arthritis episode.

Together, the findings suggest that recurring flares involve a coordinated and increasingly active inflammatory environment, rather than just a handful of immune cells acting independently.

Could Immune Memory Help Predict Future Arthritis Flares?

Despite growing recognition of inflammatory arthritis as a complication of cancer immunotherapy, scientists still do not fully understand why it affects certain patients while others never develop the condition.

The newly identified immune cell populations could provide an important starting point. Future studies may determine whether these cells can serve as biomarkers, meaning measurable biological indicators that help doctors recognize patients who are more likely to experience recurring arthritis.

Understanding which immune cells sustain the inflammation could also guide the development of more precise treatments. Ideally, such therapies would prevent or reduce painful arthritis flares while leaving the beneficial cancer-fighting effects of immunotherapy intact.

Because the investigation examined samples from only six patients, additional research will be needed to confirm the findings and establish whether the identified immune cells can reliably predict future episodes.

Still, the results offer a promising explanation for a difficult complication of cancer treatment: an immune system trained to remember and fight tumors may also retain inflammatory responses that continue to harm the joints.

This work received support from the Wilkes Family Melanoma Autoimmune Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Advanced Technology Genomics Core Facility, the Rheumatology Research Foundation Fund, the National Cancer Institute (NCI), the Andrew Sabin Family Fellowships, the Gateway for Cancer Research, the U.S. Department of Defense, the Kidney Cancer Association, the V Foundation for Cancer Research, the Finneran Family Endowment in Translational Research, philanthropic donations from the family of Mike and Mary Allen, and institutional funding from UT MD Anderson.
