#90. The 8 Best Paint Sprayers Give You Even Coverage—and Fast Results

We tested the best models out there to help you maximize efficiency and save time on your next project.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve ever painted an entire room—or worse, a whole exterior—using a cheap roller, you already know the moment when painting stops feeling like a weekend project and starts feeling like a self-imposed punishment. That’s usually when your mind starts drifting toward that paint sprayer you eyeballed at the home improvement store recently.

Used right, a good paint sprayer can turn hours of painting into a fast, even coat that actually looks professional. But here’s the part people don't tell you: They’re not magic. There’s a learning curve to using a paint sprayer—especially when it comes to setup and cleanup. This is not to dissuade or frighten anyone from adding a paint sprayer to their workshop or tool shed. Far from it. Once you get the hang of using one properly, it’s hard to go back to a standard brush and roller as a process.

We’ve spent time testing a range of paint sprayers, from small handheld units for detail work to airless rigs that blast through gallons of paint for larger jobs in a hurry, to find the ones that are actually worth your time.

I’ve used plenty of paint sprayers over the years, both in my own home and on client renovation projects, so I was less interested in spec-sheet claims and more focused on how these tools behave in real situations. That means looking at things like how easy each sprayer is to set up, how consistent the spray pattern stays over time, and how much effort it takes to clean everything when you’re done.

If you’re replacing a few pieces of base trim in a room, for example, it might be faster to paint them with a brush or roller before installation so you don’t have to deal with the setup and cleanup of a sprayer. But if you’re trimming out an entire finished basement? Pre-painting with a sprayer prior to installation is a major time saver.

One thing that stood out this time around: The latest cordless sprayers have come a long way over the past year. A few of the models I tested delivered solid finish quality at lightning-fast speeds, with the kind of mobility that makes them genuinely useful for smaller jobs or quick projects where dragging a hose behind you just slows things down.

While I’ve used the Graco UltraMax, our pick for Best for Touch-Up Work, a few times with great success, this testing process saw the first use of our Best Overall pick—the Titan Control Backpack—as well as Graco’s Ultra QuickShot Airless sprayer, our pick for Best for Trim and Cabinetry. The end result of our testing process is a mix of sprayers that cover a range of projects and budgets.

This backpack-style airless sprayer is designed for mobility on large interior and exterior jobs. Its 18V battery system and 9-foot hose allow for fully untethered spraying while still delivering the pressure needed for unthinned paints and stains.

Full disclosure: I tested the more commercially oriented Titan Impact X120 (check out my full review here), but the ControlMax is so similar in design that I felt comfortable placing it atop this list. The only differences between the two sprayers are pressure and flow rate, and the ControlMax's specs are really the most appropriate for the average homeowner.

The backpack reservoir holds 1.25 gallons of paint, so it’s especially useful for fences, siding, and multi-room interiors that are the same color. High-efficiency airless technology reduces overspray compared to traditional airless rigs, while the self-contained design eliminates the need for long hoses or extension cords. Though tip maintenance is key to preventing clogs, true convenience and portability make this a great option for those looking for freedom of movement without sacrificing performance.

The relatively short supply hose means that you can go far on a single gallon, refilling as needed. Standing on those elements alone, this sprayer bridges the use gap between smaller units and the larger airless rigs. And while the rubber lid latches require some decent finger strength to open and close, it’s finally the sprayer that can go anywhere and do anything.

The Graco TrueCoat 360 Variable Speed is a solid handheld sprayer that marries affordability with performance, especially for smaller projects. Setup is quick and simple—fill the paint bag, give it a squeeze to prime the pump, and you’re up and painting. Again, Graco’s handy quick-start guide delivers the basics in a straightforward and clear manner.

In use, this sprayer is more capable than you might expect given the wide area of coverage. I was able to spray at different angles, including upside down, without any sputtering, and the multiple speed settings give you a decent amount of control depending on the material and the desired finish. I dialed in the pressure at the “2” setting (out of 10) and coated a large area of plywood in seconds. So be warned—a little goes a long way.

That said, it’s not without a few quirks. The transition from priming to spraying is a bit clumsy at first. And since everything is self-contained, the weight adds up over a painting session and you’ll feel it in your arms and wrists the longer you paint with it. Still, for furniture, trim, and small-to-medium sized jobs, it’s a reliable option that delivers great results.

Full Graco TrueCoat 360 Paint Sprayer Review

Furniture, doors, shutters, and weekend DIY paint projects are where the Flexio 5000 feels most at home. Its HVLP (High Volume Low Pressure) design makes it especially convenient for smaller jobs where quick setup and easy cleanup matter just as much as the finish.

The Flexio 5000 delivers solid results for the price. It’s not the smoothest sprayer out there—you might notice a bit of inconsistency at the edges—but if you pay close attention to keeping a proper overlap, it’s certainly manageable. Where it really earns its keep is usability. The turbine design keeps things relatively self-contained, cleanup is quick and simple, and the whole setup tucks neatly into the included case.

It’s not a precision tool, and it’s not what I’d reach for if I need to do high-end finish work, but if cost is just as important (or more so) than quality, this is a very capable sprayer.

If you’ve got an entire floor of walls and ceilings to paint, the Magnum X5 strikes an excellent balance between power and simplicity. Its stand-mounted design keeps the paint supply in one place while the 25-foot hose gives you plenty of reach through each room, which improves the painting experience in terms of both time and convenience. As a free-standing unit, you’re able to position the unit directly over a 1- or 5-gallon container of paint and pump straight to the spray nozzle. If your project includes painting multiple rooms in a uniform color or ceilings in a common “ceiling white” color, I recommend buying your paint in a 5-gallon bulk container and adding a roller attachment to the Magnum X5 nozzle mount to save both time and money.

Setup is about as straightforward as it gets: Hook up the hose, prime it, and you’re spraying. Once you have the nozzle dialed in to match your paint, movement, and experience, this sprayer lays down a smooth, consistent coat. It’s not the lightest setup, and cleanup still takes a little time, but that comes with the territory of airless sprayers which require a garden hose hookup in order to flush the pump and supply line with water. If you want a sprayer that can handle a variety of projects without becoming overly complicated, the Magnum 5X is a solid choice.

If you’re planning to repaint the exterior of your house, the Graco Magnum ProX17 is the sprayer I’d reach for. It’s more than capable of handling multiple rooms or long runs of fences too, but after spending several days repainting my own home, I came away convinced that exterior painting is where the ProX17 really makes its mark.

At around 38 pounds, it’s not at all light, but the wheeled cart and upright design made it easy enough to move around my grassy terrain. Setup is quick—especially if you follow Graco’s laminated quick guide (a nice bonus)—and once it’s up and running, the high flow rate lays down fast, consistent coverage. While it’s a bit unwieldy, the 50-foot hose is a huge advantage here, as it allows you to cover a lot of ground with limited movement of the pumping unit.

It’s important to understand that this isn’t a casual, weekend-use tool, and its size and scope don’t work in its favor for faster, smaller jobs. That said, if you’ve got serious square footage to cover, this is the kind of sprayer that earns its place in your toolshed pretty quickly.

Full Graco Magnum ProX17 Cart Airless Paint Sprayer Review

Sometimes the idea of dragging out an entire paint sprayer setup to paint over a few small dings, scuffs, and marks is exhausting to even consider. Raising three kids in a small house, those touch-up tasks never seem to end for me. Graco’s Ultra Max Cordless sprayer is perfect for those moments. From touch-up work after a remodel to painting a single door, built-in cabinet, or section of trim, its cordless design makes setup practically effortless. For pros and DIYers who are always tackling “just one more spot”, that convenience alone can justify the price.

Designed around Graco’s proven airless pump system and powered by DeWalt’s 20V battery platform, the Ultra Max is prized for its consistent spray pattern and durable build quality. Cleanup is straightforward, and the lightweight handheld design makes it easy to maneuver in tight spaces. It’s a premium-priced tool that requires priming with each refill of paint–a common annoyance with handheld sprayers– but the finish quality and reliability it offers are hard to beat.

The Wagner Flexio 2500 isn’t the most powerful sprayer in the lineup, but where it really stands out is how much time it saves you, both up front and after painting concludes. Setup is quick and pretty forgiving—everything locks together intuitively, and the controls are simple enough that you’re not spending half your time trying to dial it all in.

It’s light and easy to handle, even with a full paint reservoir, which makes it a good fit for smaller projects. The spray pattern isn’t quite as refined as what you’ll get from higher-end, airless models, but with a little practice, you’ll get a solid, even finish. I like an easy-to-use sprayer like this if I’m pre-coating trim before hanging it, as I simply follow up with a brush to smooth out any gaps or spatters.

Cleanup is where this one really shines, though. A quick rinse and flush is usually all it takes. No flushing of pumps or discharging of hoses. Convenience matters, and this model certainly delivers.

Graco’s Ultra QuickShot found a sweet spot that didn’t really exist a few years ago. A compact and fully cordless airless sprayer, this one outshines other “small project” sprayers when it comes to performance. In my testing, it delivered a clean, beautiful finish beyond my expectations for cabinets, trim, and doors—without the hassle of dragging around a hose, setting up a full-size rig, or trying to maneuver a bulky, paint-filled handheld unit.

What really stood out for me is the level of control I had over both the sprayer and the paint. The pump and paint cup are separated from the nozzle by about 6 feet of supply hose—a length that doesn’t hold so much usable paint as to make it self-defeating, as larger sprayers do. The QuickShot also comes with a belt strap that the pump clips to, making the whole setup suitably mobile. This makes everything very lightweight, which makes a huge difference when you’re trying to be precise over long stretches.

Though it’s pricier than any other sprayer we’ve used, I think it’s worth the cost, especially if you expect to complete a number of painting projects in the near future. You won’t paint the entire house with this tool, but for furniture restoration, detail work, and smaller touch-up projects where achieving a high level of finish quickly matters, it’s one of the most impressive sprayers I’ve used.

This is the first fork in the road for most folks with paint sprayers on the brain, and it matters more than anything else.

High-volume low-pressure (HVLP) sprayers, like the Wagner Flexio 5000, are slower and more controlled, meaning the user generally experiences less overspray. This makes them the better choice for cabinets, furniture, trim, and anything else where the finish truly matters. You’ll spend a little more time getting coverage, but you’ll have a lot more control over paint output.

Airless sprayers are built for speed. If you’re painting a deck, a fence, or the side of your house, choosing one of these, like our Best Overall, the Titan ControlMax 18V Backpack Paint Sprayer, is the right move. They push a lot of paint out quickly, but they’re less forgiving—especially if you’re new to paint spraying.

This used to be an easy call: Corded for power, end of story. That’s not entirely true anymore.

Some of the newer cordless sprayers, like the Graco Ultra Max Cordless Handheld Paint Sprayer, are more than just capable, especially for smaller jobs. The mobility alone makes a huge difference when you’re operating around furniture, working outside, or just trying to avoid dragging a hose or extension cord behind you all the time.

That said, if you’re tackling bigger projects or planning to spray for long stretches, corded models still win out in terms of consistency and runtime.

More power isn’t always better; it just depends on what you’re spraying. Thicker materials like exterior paint or primer need more pressure to atomize properly. This is where airless sprayers shine. But for thinner paints and finishes, too much pressure can actually work against you, leading to both overspray and wasted material.

The key is having enough control to dial things in. A sprayer that only does one thing well, like the Wagner Flexio 2500, is a lot less useful than one you can quickly adjust to meet your needs and technique of movement.

It’s a good idea to pay attention to how the sprayer in question holds paint. Smaller, handheld units usually have built-in cups, which are fine for detail work but need frequent refilling. Additionally, those cups often speed up the cleaning process thanks to built-in disposable liners, much like the kind commonly found in handheld paint pails.

Larger sprayers either pull from bigger containers or siphon directly from a paint bucket—some as large as 5 gallons—which is a lot more efficient for larger jobs. Again, it’s important to keep in mind that jobs requiring a gallon or 2 of paint, like a single room, can be a little misleading in terms of paint consumption with large-capacity sprayers, as up to a quart of paint is continually used in the supply hose, resulting in substantial loss of available product.

For example, if you’re painting multiple rooms in your home of the same color, you’ll save money by buying five gallons at a time. Swap out the spray nozzle for a roller attachment, and you’ll make short work of an otherwise long, tedious job. But use the same sprayer and roller attachment for a single room requiring a gallon of paint and you’ll likely wonder why your paint disappeared so fast.

Size is not just about capacity—it’s about how often you want to stop what you’re doing to reset, refill, and make any necessary adjustments.

This is the part that nobody thinks about until they’re standing over a sink with a sprayer full of half-dried paint. Some models break down quickly and rinse clean without much hassle. Others just don’t. And if cleanup is a pain, you’re less likely to break out the sprayer again when you want to use it in future jobs.

I find that HVLP sprayers are infinitely easier to clean in general than airless sprayers, as the sprayer and paint are mostly self-contained in one unit. They tend to have chunkier, easier to remove and rinse parts, although they do tend to be a little messier in the process.

Cleaning airless sprayers is a bit more of a job—higher capacity machines require a garden hose hookup to flush the paint supply hose out—but once you’ve conquered the learning curve, it’s all fairly simple.

If you’re tackling a one-time project, or you aren’t sure if you’ll take to the learning curve of a paint sprayer, consider renting one from a paint or hardware store. Rental prices vary, but they’re certainly much lower than what it costs to purchase a sprayer that you may end up never using again.

That said, if you regularly tackle painting projects in your home, a sprayer is a great investment.

The tip of the nozzle affects the amount of material forced out, as well as the size and shape of the coverage area (also known as the “fan”). Since paint sprayers apply a range of materials like lacquer, shellac, and stains—in addition to paint—tip type is a very important factor.

While consumer-grade HVLP sprayers commonly come with adjustable tips, airless sprayers use interchangeable tips of all different sizes. Tips with larger openings (also called the orifice) are best for thicker substances, while smaller openings are designed to accommodate lacquers and stains. Tips that produce wider fans cover more surface area with each pass, which is great for efficiently coating large surfaces, while narrower fans are best for more precise applications.

Airless tips use a three-digit numerical system to indicate their fan width and opening size, and once you understand how it works, it’s easy to find the best one for you and your material. The first number represents one-half of the fan width in inches when sprayed 12 inches from the painting surface. The next two numbers represent the opening size in thousandths of an inch. So, a 515 spray tip produces a 10-inch fan and an opening of 0.015 inches.

If you’re not sure which tip to use with your specific product, the packaging on your paint or stain should have an accurate suggestion.

Paint sprayers naturally produce overspray, a fine paint mist that lands on surfaces behind the one you’re attempting to spray. In order to protect furniture and flooring around the area you’re painting, make sure to use tarps and tape to cover anything you don’t want painted.

If you’re just starting out, practice your spray first on some scrap wood or another surface you don’t mind getting paint on. Or, if you’re using an airless sprayer, use water instead of paint. This is fine for the machine and allows you to practice maintaining the proper distance and pressure setting to get the coverage you want.

To avoid clogs and time-consuming scrubbing, it’s imperative that you thoroughly clean your sprayer, hose, filter, and tips after each use.

If you have an airless sprayer that uses a suction tube to pull paint from a bucket into the machine, look for one that’s compatible with a garden hose. This allows you to quickly and easily flush the system of paint when you’re finished for the day.

Full cleaning and maintenance procedures come with your paint sprayer’s instructions. Make sure you follow these closely to avoid damaging the machine while you clean it. Also, keep an eye on the performance of your sprayer tip, as it wears down over time. A tip’s recommended lifespan—represented in gallons of paint—is typically indicated on its packaging.

#91. Scientists Unlock the Secret of One of the World’s Smallest Flowering Plants

Tiny aquatic plants are attracting scientific attention for their untapped potential as future food sources, including for space missions.

Some of the world’s smallest flowering plants have found a way to fit the basic architecture of much larger species into a body just a few millimeters (about 0.1 inch) across. Researchers at the University of Nottingham discovered that duckweed retains essential structures found in larger plant shoots, but these components are tightly compressed and fused rather than lost.

Using advanced microscopy and gene expression analysis, the scientists examined how duckweed organizes its remarkably compact body. Their findings, published in Current Biology, challenge the assumption that extreme miniaturization necessarily involves losing parts of a plant’s original structure.

Dr. Anthony Bishopp, who led the research, explained: “We were interested to find out how a complete plant body plan can be packed into such a tiny space. While miniaturization in animals is often associated with the loss of organs or body structures, we have revealed that duckweeds have taken a different route.”

“What surprised us is that, when we looked closely, the basic organization of the shoot was still there. Rather than throwing away parts of the blueprint, duckweed appears to have compressed and fused its components into an incredibly compact plant. That gives us a new way of thinking about how plants can evolve to become so small.”

Despite their miniature size, duckweeds belong to a group of flowering plants whose relatives include some of the largest herbaceous species. Scientists are increasingly investigating duckweed as a potential source of food and protein, both on Earth and during future space missions.

Unlike major agricultural crops, which have undergone thousands of years of domestication and selective breeding, duckweed remains largely unexplored as a cultivated food source. Its unusual anatomy has also been poorly understood, making it difficult to fully explain how the plant grows and develops. The new findings provide a foundation for investigating these processes and identifying traits that could eventually be improved for cultivation.

Dr. Alex Ware, a co-author of the study, said: “Duckweeds are astonishingly small, so it is tempting to think of them as either primitive plants or simply as having lost parts, but this is not the case. Our research adds to growing evidence from across the research community about this plant and will help efforts to turn them into a future crop.”

Reference: “Miniaturization of duckweeds occurred through compression of the angiosperm body plan” by Alexander Ware, Emily Chan, Rahul Bhosale and Anthony Bishopp, 7 October 2026, Current Biology. DOI: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.035

#93. JWST Tracks Shifting Water Clouds and Churning Gases on the Coldest Known Brown Dwarf

When picturing a star, typically people think of giant balls of burning gas in the sky that emit enough light they are hard to miss. Planets, on the other hand, come in one of two general categories - rocky worlds like Earth or gas giants similar to Jupiter. But there is a third category of astronomical object that doesnât really fit either of those descriptions, and also doesnât exist in our own solar system. Known as a brown dwarf, they are sometimes called a âfailed starâ as they form the same way stars do, but never reach the critical mass of material to create active fusion in the cores. They are also much too massive to be considered a regular planet. But a new paper from researchers led by Brittany Miles of the University of Arizona describes one similarity between the coldest known brown dwarf and some of the planets in our solar system - it has water-ice clouds.

Discovered in 2014 by Kevin Luhman, using NASAâs Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE), WISE J085510.83-071442.5 - which the astronomy community has thankfully shortened to just WISE 0855 - is the third closest âsystemâ to our own solar system, sitting just 7.2 light years away in the constellation Hydra. It also holds the title for the coldest known brown dwarf in the universe, sitting at an average upper atmosphere temperature of around 265 K (-8â). This squarely puts it in the category of a âYâ dwarf, the coldest category of brown dwarfs, most of whom fall into categories that are much hotter.

So how did we find this object if itâs not a star, and itâs not orbiting a star to reflect its light or gravitationally pull on it? Brown dwarfs themselves, even the cold ones, emit infrared radiation, otherwise known as heat. With that signature, we can track WISE 0855 as it moves throughout the galaxy. We also know that it is about the same physical size as Jupiter, but weighs between three and ten times our largest planetâs mass. It also sits in a unique position in atmospheric physics.

Fraser talks about how phosphine was found in a brown dwarf.

Normally we refer to a âGoldilocks zoneâ when referring to an exoplanetâs orbit around its parent star - where liquid water is possible on its surface. But in atmospheric physics, there is also a âGoldilocks zoneâ, where an atmosphere is too cold for molten iron to form clouds, but just cold enough for water vapor to form ice clouds, and warm enough that ammonia stays as a gas. That temperature is precisely where WISE 0855 lies. But astronomers have been questioning for a decade whether WISE 0855 actually does have water clouds.

The problem comes down to data interpretation. WISE 0855 is just a single point of light to our sensors. Astronomers can split the infrared light it emits into a rainbow of wavelengths to track which chemicals are absorbing light at specific wavelengths, in a process known as spectroscopy. However, there has been a debate over whether the spectral signature of this frigid world could be explained by water clouds that were blocking light from warmer, deeper layers, or something called âdisequilibrium chemistryâ, where updrafts cause the upper atmosphere to be flooded with chemicals like carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and phosphine, which could also mimic the spectral signature that WISE 0855 gives off.

To solve this mystery, the research team turned to the James Webb Space Telescope. They managed to get an astonishing 11 hours of time on the Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) instrument, utilizing its Bright Object Time-Series (BOTS) mode. Every 15 minutes, the instrument would record a new infrared spectrum between 2.87 and 5.27 microns in wavelength.

Fraser talks to Dr. Joanna Barstow about exoplanet atmospheres.

Lining up those 44 back-to-back snapshots allowed the researchers to watch as WISE 0855âs brightness changed over time. There were three very noticeable discoveries to come from this time series. First, the strongest brightness swings over the 11 hours happened between 4.5 and 4.8 microns in wavelength - right where carbon monoxide absorbs light. As the brown dwarf rotated, this band swung up or down by 10%.

The second discovery was that, in spectral regions that werenât blocked by common upper-atmospheric gases like methane or ammonia, the team saw lots of variations from carbon dioxide and phosphine. A third discovery was that the spectral signature of water didnât really change brightness at all.

From this data, the researchers isolated two separate patterns that operated at different depths of the atmosphere. First, accounting for around 60.5% of the objectâs variability of its brightness, thereâs an apparent dimming and brightening pattern that accounts for the overall surface temperature variation, which wobbles between 0.6 to 1.3 degrees, and, potentially, changes in water ice clouds. A second pattern, accounting for around 4.7% of the variability, appears in the absorption bands of carbon monoxide and phosphine, which differs from the overall brightness curve, meaning this feature is probably coming from much deeper in the atmosphere.

Fraser talks about the discovery of the first "steam world", discussing it with guest Eshan Rual

With those data points, the team tested two cutting-edge atmospheric computer models - PICASO and coolTLUSTY. Both models clearly showed that including water clouds fit the data vastly better than any model without them. Specifically, it appears that when we are looking at WISE 0855, we are looking at patchy water clouds located near the top of the atmosphere at a pressure of around 1 to 4 bar. Meanwhile, much further down toward the objectâs surface, updrafts are pulling carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and phosphine up from the depths.

In terms of how WISE 0855 would physically appear if we were allowed to see it up close, with a pair of infrared goggles, it would show up as a striped world with fast-moving equatorial jet streams wrapped in frigid water ice clouds. But, unfortunately, we still donât know how fast it is rotating. Gas moving around its surface obscured the objectâs actual rotation. But the researchers think they can determine WISE 0855âs rotational speed, if only they can get around 20 more hours of time on the JWSTâs instrumentations. Given the demand for time on the worldâs foremost infrared telescope, thatâs a tall ask. But thereâs a chance we can unlock even more secrets about this close-by cool neighbor if they do manage to get that time - and doing so would provide even more information about how these cool brown dwarfs work.

Discovered in an Indigenous grave in Georgia nearly 150 years ago, the "Birdman" copper plate may actually depict a woman ceremonially dressed as a warrior.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This hammered copper artifact depicts an Indigenous person wearing a bird costume and holding a severed head and a mace.

What it is: A copper plate with a hammered decoration

Where it is from: Cahokia Mounds, Illinois

This copper plate was discovered in the late 19th century in a prehistoric Native American burial at the Etowah Indian Mounds archaeological site in Georgia, but it was likely made hundreds of miles away at Cahokia Mounds in Illinois. While the decorative plate showcases long-distance trade and a shared ritual culture among early Indigenous groups in the southeastern United States, the nature of the human figure depicted on the artifact has been debated for over a century.

The "Birdman" relic is one of two hammered copper plates that Smithsonian archaeologist John P. Rogan unearthed in the 1880s while digging in a burial mound at Etowah, a centuries-old village occupied by thousands of Native Americans from 1000 to 1550. Etowah was part of the "mound-building," or Mississippian, phase of Indigenous occupation; other famous sites include Moundville in Alabama and Cahokia in Illinois. These groups had extensive trade networks and shared a common artistic and ceremonial tradition known as the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex.

This copper artifact, known as Rogan Plate 1 or the "Birdman" plate, is in the collection of the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C. The plate is roughly 11 inches (28 centimeters) tall and had been buried with a high-status person who likely died at Etowah in the mid-14th century. But experts believe the copper plate was an heirloom made decades earlier, at Cahokia, and traded south to Etowah.

A human figure dominates the copper plate with its elaborate bird costume. The person carries a severed head by the hair in their left hand, while their right hand holds a club or mace. The figure also wears a pleated skirt or loincloth that may have been made from human scalps. This bird-human figure is commonly depicted in the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex and has been called a dancing warrior, eagle warrior, eagle dancer, hawk dancer, falcon dancer and falcon warrior. But more often, the figure is called Birdman or Morning Star, a prehistoric Mississippian hero associated with agriculture and rebirth.

Archaeologists' interpretations of the Birdman plaque from Etowah have long assumed that the represented figure is a male warrior. In a 2004 study, for example, archaeologist Adam King wrote that "this plaque would have served as an emblem of office awarded to a chieftain, and would have accompanied him as a sign of his strength among the ancestral spirits."

But the sex of the skeleton in the Etowah burial is unclear, and there were high-status graves of both men and women at Etowah, archaeologist Billie Follensbee and art historian Katie Buford wrote in a 2017 study. Although experts previously assumed that both Rogan Plate 1 and Rogan Plate 2 represented male warriors, Follensbee and Buford found that the figures have slender bodies with prominent right breasts, suggesting the "Birdman" may have actually been female.

"A female bird-human warrior could have represented a gender variant individual in the form of the well-known Native American phenomenon of the 'manly-hearted woman,' a woman who has assumed the usually male role and the garb of a combat soldier," Follensbee and Buford wrote. In addition to the historic term "manly-hearted woman," third-gender or gender-variant individuals in Indigenous North America are often referred to as "two-spirit," a broad term Indigenous people coined in 1990 to describe people who take on gender-nonconforming roles.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The commemoration of a two-spirit individual on a copper artifact, as well as the use of the artifact as a high-status grave good, "not only demonstrates the Native American cultural acceptance of such gender variant roles but also further serves to celebrate the elite status and achievements of these 'manly-hearted women,'" Follensbee and Buford wrote.

One new study shows how much the moon has diminished over time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The moon is shrinking, and scientists are narrowing in on exactly how much our natural satellite has dwindled over the years.

The moon is thought to have formed from a violent collision between a massive object and our young Earth roughly 4.5 billion years ago, and its interior is still gradually cooling off from this ancient collision. As it cools, the moon contracts, leading to a long, slow shrinking process. Now, in a new study, scientists think that they have figured out how much smaller the moon is actually getting.

In this new study, scientists analyzing images snapped by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) have spotted over 10,000 young faults, or cracks across the moon's surface. This helped them to figure out how much the moon has contracted over time, and they now estimate that the moon's radius has decreased by about 148 feet (45 meters) over the past 400 to 800 million years.

"The number of these young faults revealed in LROC images is much greater than I ever imagined," study lead Thomas Watters, a geologist and scientist emeritus at the Center for Earth and Planetary Studies at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum, said in a statement. "As the interior of the moon continues to cool and contract, it is expected that the growth of existing faults and formation of new faults continues today."

With these LROC observations, researchers in this study saw a variety of different types of cracks and landforms across the lunar surface. This included lobate scarps, or long, curved structures that form when the moon's surface contracts, cracks and is pushed upwards; and small mare ridges, or narrow "wrinkles" in the lunar surface, across the dark plains on the moon.

Tectonic activity on the moon looks a lot different than it does on Earth. On our own planet, there are about 15 major tectonic plates. On the moon, there are no tectonic plates at all. Instead, the moon has a single-plate body meaning its outer shell is a single piece only broken by faults or other such cracks created by the moon contracting. This means that instead of faults or cracks appearing at tectonic plate boundaries, they are instead scattered all over the moon.

By mapping these thousands of different features, all created from the moon cooling and contracting over time, the researchers are piecing together lunar history. In addition to finding the extent to which the moon has shrunk over time, they also found that some areas of the moon are covered in many more faults than other areas, and the areas with fewer cracks and faults have thicker moon crust.

This led them to conclude that not only are these areas with thicker crust more stable, but they suggest that a great deal of the widespread cracks in the lunar surface were created later in the moon's history as, in its earlier years, its thick crust would have insulated the moon's warm interior and prevented cooling, contracting and cracking.

This work was described in a study published Oct. 14 in The Planetary Science Journal.

#97. Scientists reach the ultimate quantum limit on a surface

Scientists at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Light (MPL) have achieved a breakthrough in quantum physics, developing a way to study individual molecules on a surface with extraordinary precision. For the first time, researchers have demonstrated that molecules attached to a surface can reach the ultimate quantum limit of optical coherence, overcoming a major obstacle that has long restricted molecular quantum research.

The findings, published in Science, could open new possibilities for investigating how molecules interact with surfaces and developing advanced quantum technologies.

Why Surfaces Have Been a Major Obstacle in Quantum Physics

Many emerging quantum technologies depend on extremely small objects, such as individual atoms and molecules, that interact with light. Known as quantum emitters, these tiny systems can produce single particles of light called photons, store quantum information, and help establish quantum connections between distant systems. These capabilities are important for future applications in quantum computing and secure quantum communication.

To study a single quantum emitter, scientists must keep it stable and confined to one location for extended periods. Traditionally, researchers have accomplished this by trapping atoms or molecules in a vacuum or embedding them inside solid materials.

Placing quantum emitters directly on a surface, however, offers an intriguing advantage. Scientists could potentially manipulate individual molecules by "touching them" with an extremely sharp probe. Techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) already use tips with atomic precision to investigate matter at incredibly small scales.

The difficulty is that surfaces are rarely as clean and stable as quantum experiments require. Contaminants from the surrounding environment can accumulate on them, creating disturbances that interfere with the delicate quantum behavior of nearby atoms and molecules. Until now, researchers had struggled to preserve the quantum optical properties of individual emitters attached to surfaces.

Scientists in MPL's Nano-Optics Division have now found a way around this problem.

A Clever Crystal Cleaning Method Solves the Problem

The research team, led by Prof. Vahid Sandoghdar, director at MPL and head of the "Nano-Optics" Division, developed an unusual cleaning method that takes advantage of a natural property of organic crystals.

At room temperature, the crystal material gradually evaporates through a process known as sublimation, in which a solid transforms directly into a gas without first becoming a liquid.

The researchers placed a small crystal inside a vacuum chamber equipped for extremely low temperatures, called a cryostat. As the crystal's uppermost layers slowly evaporated, they carried away unwanted contaminants, leaving behind a remarkably clean surface.

The team then cooled the crystal to just a few degrees Kelvin above absolute zero, the lowest theoretically possible temperature. This extreme cooling halted further sublimation and helped maintain the pristine surface.

Finally, the scientists used a tiny, specially fabricated oven to evaporate molecules onto the cold crystal, allowing them to settle on the clean surface.

Molecules Reach the Ultimate Quantum Limit

With this exceptionally stable environment in place, the researchers could investigate whether the molecules retained their fragile quantum properties.

Dr. Alexey Shkarin, a researcher in the Nano-Optics Division at MPL, explained: "The quality of quantum emitters can be evaluated by their coherence times, which indicate how long they keep their quantumness."

Coherence time describes how long a quantum system can maintain the properties needed for quantum behavior. The longer this coherence persists, the better the emitter can perform in applications that depend on precise interactions with light.

However, there is a fundamental physical restriction on how long coherence can last. Known as the Fourier limit, this boundary is determined by the time required for a quantum emitter to release its energy into its surroundings.

In an unstable or 'noisy' environment, disturbances can cause coherence to disappear hundreds or even thousands of times faster than this theoretical limit allows.

The scientists discovered that molecules deposited on their exceptionally clean crystal surface consistently reached the Fourier limit. This demonstrated that the surrounding environment was sufficiently quiet and stable to preserve the molecules' quantum coherence for the maximum physically permitted duration.

It is the first time researchers have achieved this fundamental limit with molecules attached to a surface.

New Possibilities for Controlling Individual Molecules

The breakthrough also allowed the team to investigate how a crystal surface influences the molecules resting on it.

Further experiments revealed that interactions with the surface can cause molecules to align in particular directions and alter their energy levels. The researchers also found indications that the surface might influence the molecules' shapes or the ways they vibrate.

These effects could provide valuable clues about how matter behaves at the molecular scale, while also offering new opportunities to control quantum systems.

"Our future work will focus on combining this method with AFM and STM to gain local nanometer control over individual quantum emitters," says Vahid Sandoghdar.

By combining their ultra-clean surface technique with powerful microscopy methods, the researchers hope to manipulate individual quantum emitters with precision measured in billionths of a meter.

Such capabilities could reveal previously inaccessible details about interactions between molecules and surfaces, while laying the groundwork for engineering new quantum states of matter and advancing future molecular quantum technologies.

#98. Brain implants are helping people who’ve lost their voice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The technology could get those with ALS, Parkinson’s disease and brain injuries “talking” again

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

On paper, my interview with Casey Harrell looks like any other.

I ask the questions, he answers them. He tells me about his background as a climate activist, his Southern roots and his daughter, who as a preschooler loved to dress up like a cheetah and roar around the house. “My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit,” Harrell says.

The transcript tells the story of our conversation. But between the lines is an entirely different story — the story of where Harrell’s words come from.

Harrell started losing his ability to speak in his early 40s, nearly six years ago. He talked to me using a brain implant that can decode his words directly from his thoughts. The device, called a brain-computer interface, is experimental. But it has transformed Harrell’s life. And it could soon transform others. Advances in computing power and AI, lessons gleaned from patient experience and investments from neurotechnology companies are starting to yield real progress on brain-computer interfaces for people who can no longer talk. In other words, Harrell’s new voice might not be so singular in the future.

“There’s a lot of excitement and hope in the field right now,” says Matthew Willsey, a neuro­surgeon and biomedical engineer at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, who recently implanted a new type of speech interface in a woman’s brain. For years, Willsey says, scientists didn’t know whether attempts to decode speech would be successful; now, a body of research results points clearly to yes. “They’re thinking, ‘Wow, this is actually a usable technology that addresses a real problem that people suffer from.’”

Harrell has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. The progressive neurodegenerative disease, which affects an estimated 35,000 people in the United States, kills nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord that control muscles. As the neural connections between Harrell’s brain and body began to falter, he gradually lost his ability to move his muscles, leaving him confined to his bed or a wheelchair. Some of those dropped signals directed the muscles in his throat and mouth, the ones that allow him to speak.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020,” Harrell says. After that, it was “a slow-motion car crash” as fewer and fewer people could understand him. “[My voice] is the most important thing I have lost in this whole disease,” he says.

In a stroke of luck, Harrell learned through a family member about a clinical trial happening at the University of California, Davis — one that attempted to restore speech with a brain-computer interface. In 2023, Harrell had four small devices implanted on the left side of his brain. These grids of electrodes reside on Harrell’s speech motor cortex, a stretch of brain along the precentral gyrus that controls the movements required for speech.

Today, Harrell uses his system for about 10 to 14 hours daily, making him, as he puts it, “the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.” Hard data suggest he’s right. A recent count shows that Harrell has used his system to communicate nearly 2 million words, the scientists working with him reported in June in Nature Medicine.

“I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020 … [My voice] is the most important thing I have lost in this whole disease.”

The very existence of Harrell’s words shows it may be possible to restore speech for people with ALS, as well as for those whose speech is impaired by stroke, paralysis, cerebral palsy and Parkinson’s disease. “This kind of technology has the potential to dramatically change the conversation,” says David Brandman, a UC Davis neurosurgeon and neuroscientist who works with Harrell.

Harrell’s interface still has room for improvement. It’s bulky, relatively slow and limited in what sorts of nonword sounds it can decode.

But it is a “beginning,” says Leigh Hochberg, a neuroscientist at Brown University who works with Harrell. “It’s still early days. There’s a lot of research to happen, and it’s going to be very exciting.” The end game, Hochberg says, is a world in which people could use a device to communicate seamlessly, quickly, clearly — and in their former voices.

Success would mean restoring more than just people’s words, Brandman says. It would mean restoring their ability to connect in all the ineffable ways that make us human. “Speech is so fundamental to who we are,” he says. “Imagine living in a world where you couldn’t tell someone you’re in pain, or you couldn’t say that you love them … It’s not hard to imagine how devastating that would be for your quality of life.”

On the path to a technology that enables fast, natural speech, scientists first had to answer a more basic question: Could the brain’s electrical chatter be decoded and translated into action outside of the head?

Nerve cells speak to each other with tiny pulses of electricity, signals that can be picked up with electrodes. The existence of this electrical language raised the tantalizing idea that electrical messages could be decoded straight from where they originate in the brain, bypassing damaged links to the rest of the body.

“This has really started as early as the 1950s, the first time scientists put electrodes into brains to record neural activity,” says Sergey Stavisky, a neuroscientist and neural engineer at UC Davis. “You can record the electrical activity of brain cells or parts of the brain. And that’s really when modern neuroscience started trying to study, how does the brain compute? How does it allow us to move our muscles?”

Figuring out how to decode simple neural commands was the first step. Animal studies paved the way, including experiments in which rhesus monkeys consciously controlled the movements of a robotic arm using only brain signals detected by implanted electrodes.

What if you lost your voice? Today, AI can re-create it, and brain implants can turn thoughts into speech. This season of The Deep End follows people living through these vocal transformations — and asks what these remarkable technologies can teach us about why our voices matter in the first place.

By 2004, scientists had enough confidence in the approach to launch a clinical trial in humans called BrainGate. Researchers implanted a grid of electrodes in the brain of a paralyzed man named Matthew Nagle. A former star athlete, Nagle was able to control a computer cursor with his thoughts alone. “That was really the starting gun of the modern version of the brain-computer interface field,” Stavisky says.

From there, attempts to link brain activity with some physical outcome — such as moving a computer mouse, a wheelchair or a robotic arm — blossomed. Some of these efforts focused on the brain signals and regions that controlled movements of the hands and arms. Others focused on a very tricky version of the same basic problem: talking.

A brain-computer interface that could detect the intention to say a word and bypass the muscles needed to say it would be a powerful workaround for people with diseases like ALS or brain injuries. And it is no small thing to people who can no longer talk. “Losing their speech is way more devastating than losing their mobility,” says Jessica Pietrowski, a speech and language pathologist at UC Davis who has worked with many such patients. “Speech is how they maintain their identity in their relationships.”

Harrell emphasizes this point. “What does my voice mean to me? It means so much,” he says. “It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends.”

Talking feels effortless to most of us, but just saying hello involves a sweeping array of actions — and upwards of 100 muscles. “It’s incredibly complex and intricate, and really, an incredible human feat,” Pietrowski says.

Consider the “h” sound in “hello.” Known as a glottal fricative, it involves an orchestra of tiny movements. First, the diaphragm contracts to fill the lungs with air. Chest and abdominal muscles push air up through relaxed vocal cords and surrounding tissues. This puff of air then travels to the mouth, where lips, jaw and tongue execute complex sequences of movements that create the rest of the sound. Finally, air waves, perfectly shaped, ripple from the mouth. Then, and only then, “you have speech,” Pietrowski says.

But the beginnings of this nearly miraculous transformation start in the brain, where tiny electrical nerve pulses command the body to speak. In Harrell’s trial, he would attempt to speak words, prompting his motor cortex to send signals to his body. The implanted electrodes would detect the patterns and send them to a computer to interpret. With this work-around, it didn’t matter that Harrell’s muscles didn’t get the message; the computer would.

After Harrell recovered from surgery, researchers began testing the system in his home. They collected his neural data and streamed it to computers on a nearby cart, where machine learning algorithms attempted to match Harrell’s brain activity patterns to those that predictably occur with certain sounds. Called phonemes, these sound units are the building blocks of words. The algorithm assembled the phonemes into words, as it made its best guess about what Harrell was trying to say. To limit the computational power required, the algorithm used a vocabulary of just 50 words.

When the system was plugged in and ready to go, scientists asked Harrell to try and say a specific, random sentence built from that library: “What good is that?”

Harrell got to work. His eyebrows shot up as he saw the words appear on a screen in front of him in response to his thoughts. The decoder worked.

Everyone paused. Some of the researchers started to cry. Harrell and his family became emotional. Being in the room when the switch was flipped on was “incredible,” Brandman says. “The majority of my adult life was working up to that moment, and to see it come to fruition was an incredible experience. But more than that was seeing what impact it immediately had for Casey and his family.”

“Imagine living in a world where you couldn’t tell someone you’re in pain, or you couldn’t say that you love them … It’s not hard to imagine how devastating that would be for your quality of life.”

Harrell remembers his feelings that day, too: “Pure joy.” Even though he wasn’t choosing his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”

The second day of testing was even more profound, but in a personal way. This time, the system’s algorithm was using a vocabulary of over 125,000 words. This would be more challenging for the decoder, but it would give Harrell more autonomy to say what he wanted.

Harrell started the session with a joke, Hochberg recalls, along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” But his next line was a real puzzler: “I’m looking for a cheetah.”

Hochberg, who had joined remotely on a video call, was sure it was a mistake. “There’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using a brain-to-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah,” Hochberg says. “That’s obviously a decoding error.”

But there was something the scientist couldn’t see. Harrell’s 4-year-old daughter had bounded into the room, dressed as a cheetah.

The discovery was big scientifically, but it was bigger for what it represented to Harrell. Brain technology could restore not just his words, but also the spontaneous exchanges that had once made up his everyday life.

“It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond to my daughter,” Harrell says, “especially because that was lacking completely from my life.”

Hochberg says moments like that represent the promise that brain-computer interfaces hold. “To me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living,” he says, “but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child.”

Casey Harrell’s brain-computer interface extracts neural signals from his brain and, through a few key steps, transforms them intowords. Electrodes implanted in Harrell’s speech motor cortex detect neurons’ electrical signals (1), generating raw neural data (2). Advanced machine learning efforts (3) map chunks of the data to phonemes, the building blocks of words (4). Those phonemes are then assembled into sentences by a predictive language model, or LM (5), and put on a screen where they can be read or spoken.

Harrell uses his interface to send email and Slack messages and play Wordle with his wife and child. He uses it to work; in fact, he’s just getting started on a new climate consultancy project. Harrell’s interface has connected him to the world in a way that would have been impossible even a few years ago.

But the system is still a research device. And like any early design, it comes with limitations. First, it isn’t portable; Harrell has wires coming from a port that sits on the top of his head, and he can use it only at home. And it is slow by the standards of typical conversation. You can’t tell from the written transcript of our interview, but our conversations always came with built-in delays.

For example, as we chatted, we discovered that we had both worked in the same part of Washington, D.C. I asked him if he remembered his old address. The answer came some two minutes later.

“I make a very simple analogy where I talk about having the brain-to-computer interface being akin to trying to catch a train, running to get the last car before it leaves the station,” Harrell says. With the current interface, “if people are patient and wait for my sentence correction, I can [catch the train and] be a part of the conversation.”

Harrell’s system translates his neural activity into words on a screen. If he chooses to do so, he can then use a computerized voice to say the words out loud. “It is brain-to-text, and then it gets translated to the voice,” Harrell says. A brain-to-voice system, in which a person’s thoughts are translated directly into spoken words, he adds, “is the holy grail of what this will become.”

Harrell and the scientists working with him are getting closer to this very type of real-time communication. Last year in Nature, they debuted a new algorithm that attempted to turn Harrell’s brain signals straight into sounds. The results: He could speak his mind with a delay of just 10 milliseconds. That’s very close to a real-time conversation. But the sounds Harrell made were hard to understand, with just over half of them being intelligible to listeners.

The next generation of devices aims to do better. Willsey, the University of Michigan neuro­surgeon, is working on one such device, a fully implantable array. In June, he implanted what’s called the “cortical module,” about the size of a dime, in the brain of a 68-year-old woman. Like Harrell, the woman could no longer talk in a way that most people could understand.

Unlike the BrainGate system, this new device — made by Austin, Texas–based neurotechnology company Paradromics — is portable. Surgeons implanted it in a stretch of brain tissue that made up the woman’s speech motor cortex, along the precentral gyrus. The cortical module collects neural data and sends it to another device implanted in the chest called a transceiver. From there, signals shoot to a receiver on her chest, where the data gets transformed into sounds — spoken words that play out of speakers on a nearby computer.

Paradromics’ priority is to test whether the implant is safe. If so, scientists can turn to the goal of restoring speech in real time. “The moment that you’re thinking the words, you don’t have to wait for the sentence to complete,” says Willsey, who, like Brandman, is a site investigator for the Paradromics clinical trial. “You can let the words kind of flow out as they would in a normal conversation.”

Scientists also want to decode more than words. Qualities of voice, such as pitch, are important for marking questions, says Vikash Gilja, a Paradromics neuroscientist. Speakers can also alter or pace their conversation to show sarcasm or concern. These sounds are all made by moving muscles, Gilja says, and can therefore be decoded from the brain.

“Our near-term goal right now is just to restore speech,” says Paradromics neurosurgeon Stephen Ryu. “But eventually, we’re hoping that we can actually restore someone’s ability to be fully involved in a conversation, to basically decode things like their timing, their emotions, their personality.”

Other researchers are trying to incorporate the gestures that many of us use to communicate.

“Some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up,” says bioengineer Samantha Brosler of the University of California, San Fransico. Gestures can also change the meaning of words; a “maybe” with a head nod is close to a yes, for instance. “I think of gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech,” Brosler says.

In a new study, Brosler and colleagues enabled two people with paralysis who had lost their speaking ability to instead use their brain signals to control both the words and gestures of digital avatars. The advance, reported in September in Nature Neuroscience, adds to the repertoire of signals that could be decoded and turned into action.

And as all this is happening, scientists are creating smaller, more stable types of electrodes to embed in the brain; more powerful computational algorithms to handle larger amounts of data; and better models of how those signals relate to sounds, words and gestures, Gilja says. “We can see all the pieces coming together.”

“It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond to my daughter, especially because that was lacking completely from my life.”

There are many reasons to be optimistic about the future, says Brandman, who is an investigator for the clinical trial led by Paradromics. “I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation,” he says. “‘Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate.’”

That conversation is tantalizing. But there are no guarantees that these systems will work as hoped, or that they will be widely available. Such implants would probably come with hefty price tags, invasive brain surgeries and perhaps more demand than the few capable clinicians and technologists could meet.

And there are underlying questions about the brain itself. One concern is that changes to the brain over time might render neural signals unreliable, especially as diseases progress. If that happens, a person’s interface might produce a scrambled message — or be left without enough neural data to decode.

“These are real challenges, and the field is working on them,” Stavisky says. “But they’re not solved yet.”

Despite these hurdles, the push for voice-restoring technology can’t come soon enough for people who have lost theirs. In September, researchers reported that the woman with the Paradromics implant had a message for them. “OK,” she used her brain-computer interface to tell researchers. “I have a lot to say.” With her system, she was able to call her grandchildren on the telephone.

And Harrell is now living a life that looks very different from the one he might have imagined six years ago. Although his disease keeps him close to home, he can now share his thoughts with the world — and his family — instead of locking them away inside.

“The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress, the ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear,” Harrell says. “These are the things that life is all about, and when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs. And this is why this is good enough for now.”

But he too has a vision, a day when these devices are commonplace, “when I am one of many, instead of being one of one.”

For more about the human voice and to hear from Casey Harrell himself, listen to The Deep End podcast Season Two, called Talk to Me. It’s free wherever you get your podcasts.

#99. Antarctica’s Sea Ice Has Gone From Record Highs to Near-Record Lows

Antarctica’s sea ice has plunged from record highs to its third-lowest winter peak, revealing a dramatic reversal in the frozen continent’s recent history.

Antarctic sea ice reached one of its lowest winter peaks ever recorded in 2026, continuing a striking shift in ice coverage around the frozen continent. Its annual maximum was the third lowest since satellites began tracking sea ice in the late 1970s.

Antarctica and the Arctic have very different geographies. The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by land, while Antarctica is a massive continent encircled by ocean. This allows Antarctic sea ice to spread across a much larger area during winter. However, as the ice extends into warmer waters farther from the continent, it becomes more vulnerable to melting when summer arrives. Antarctic sea ice typically reaches its greatest extent in September, near the end of the Southern Hemisphere’s winter, before shrinking to its annual minimum in February.

NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) reported that Antarctic sea ice likely reached its annual maximum on September 14 (above). At its peak, the ice covered approximately 17.59 million square kilometers (6.79 million square miles). That made 2026 the year with the third-lowest winter maximum in the satellite record.

For decades, Antarctic sea ice appeared to be moving in the opposite direction of Arctic sea ice. Between 1979 and 2014, the total extent of Antarctic sea ice grew by approximately 1 percent per decade. However, scientists remain uncertain whether this increase reflected a significant underlying trend, since ice coverage around Antarctica can fluctuate substantially from one year to the next.

The growth was particularly notable between 2012 and 2014, when Antarctic winter sea ice set new records for three consecutive years. During the same period, Arctic sea ice was experiencing a steep decline.

That pattern changed dramatically after 2014. Antarctic sea ice stopped expanding in 2015, and substantial declines began appearing in 2016. Although ice coverage has occasionally recovered somewhat, it has generally remained below normal in the years since.

The most extreme conditions occurred in 2023, when Antarctica recorded both its lowest summer minimum and lowest winter maximum in the satellite record. Researchers are continuing to track these changes to determine whether the persistent decline represents a lasting transformation in Antarctic sea ice or could still be explained by statistical fluctuations.

Scientists track the extent of Antarctic sea ice using satellites equipped with passive microwave sensors. These instruments detect microwave energy naturally released by Earth’s surface. Because frozen sea ice emits more microwave energy than open ocean water, researchers can distinguish between the two and calculate how much of the ocean is covered by ice.

One major advantage of this technology is its ability to detect sea ice through clouds. Unlike conventional optical imagery, microwave observations are not blocked by cloud cover, allowing scientists to monitor Antarctica’s frozen waters consistently even when weather conditions are poor.

The continuous satellite record began in late 1978 with measurements from NASA’s Nimbus-7. Observations later came from satellites operated under the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP), beginning in 1987, and NASA’s Aqua satellite from 2002 through 2011.

In 2025, researchers began incorporating observations from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s GCOM-W satellite, helping maintain the long-running record of Antarctic sea ice changes.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using data from the National Snow and Ice Data Center.

#101. The Chemistry in Stellar Nurseries is Complex, and a New 3D Model Highlights It

Molecular hydrogen is the raw stuff of star formation. Stars form in massive clouds of it called Giant Molecular Clouds (GMCs). When young stars form, their radiation shapes the clouds they formed in. Stars need cold, dense hydrogen gas to form, and the young stars heat up and disperse the surrounding gas, creating a barrier against further star formation. This much is known.

But there's still much more to learn about stellar feedback and how it shapes GMCs and their chemistry. There's a lot of complex chemistry inside what are called photodissociation regions, and new research shows how they shape the overall structure of a GMC.

The new research examines photodissociation regions in the Orion Bar, a ridge of gas and dust in the Orion Nebula. The research is "Resolving dense photodissociation regions: The structure of photochemical fronts in three-dimensional gas distributions," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. The lead author is Dr. Brandt Gaches from the University of Duisburg-Essen.

"For decades, the Orion Bar has been the prototypical photodissociation region (PDR)," the authors write. "Viewed nearly edge-on, it offers a unique window into the stratified chemical structure of the atomic-to-molecular transition of the interstellar medium." According to the authors, understanding the photochemistry in the Orion Bar is important in order to "interpret key observations originating from dense PDRs."

ALMA and the JWST have observed the region and discovered that the molecular hydrogen (H2) photodissociation front overlaps with another important feature: the C+ recombination front. The front is like a layer in the Orion Bar where another transition occurs. Ionized carbon (C+) converts to neutral C there.

The takeaway from this concerns modelling. When trying to understand GMCs and how stellar feedback shapes them, researchers don't rely solely on observations. They build models and watch to see what happens, and how close the models line up with observations. In the case of PDRs, 1D models use stratified layers. But ALMA and the JWST shows that layers actually overlap one another. Since the models are based on the current understanding of GMC's and feedback, and since observations don't agree with them, there's work to do.

"Despite considerable theoretical effort, existing modeling approaches based on simplified geometrical assumptions have difficulties reproducing the spatial emission structure," the authors write. "We investigate the response of photochemistry in realistic three-dimensional density distributions using the Orion Bar as a representative application."

The Orion Bar is nearly a perfect place to do this work, both because we see it from an advantageous angle, and because it's only about 1,350 light years away.

âThe Orion Bar is an ideal natural laboratory for studying these processes,â lead author Gaches said in a press release. âWe see it nearly edge-on, so its different chemical layers are particularly easy to distinguish. That makes it a benchmark for testing models of photon-dominated regions."

The researchers created the "first fully three-dimensional high-resolution model of an Orion Bar analog," that captures the complex, clumpy, even messy reality of GMCs. Its high-resolution reveals more detail of how intense radiation from nearby stars drives changes in star-forming regions.

This rendering shows the the location of the H2 dissociation front and the C+ recombination front. The H2 dissociation front is shown in red and the C+ recombination front is shown in cyan. Unlike previous work, it shows how H2 and C+ co-exist in some regions. Image Credit: Gaches et al. 2026. A&A

The overlap of H2 and C+ is important in astrochemistry. It drives what's called 'excited-state hydrocarbon chemistry.' That means that chemical pathways that are usually forbidden are open. It can create compounds like methane, acetylene, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH). PAH can be important building blocks for organic matter, and act as an important carbon reservoir.

But this work is mostly about the morphology in GMCs, and how photodissocation helps shape it.

"Our three-dimensional model can reproduce the complex morphology of H2 emission seen in observations, in particular, the arc- and filament-like features, and it provides a physical explanation of its chemistry," the authors write.

"The three-dimensional structure of the gas makes a crucial difference,â said Gaches. "It creates shadows and shields parts of the cloud from the intense radiation. That changes the chemistry and leaves a clear signature in the infrared- to radio- wavelengths of light we observe."

This JWST image of the Orion Bar highlights some of the features. The bottom right panel shows the filaments and arcs in the Bar. The new model reproduced some of these features. Image Credit: NASA / ESA / CSA / PDRs4All ERS Team / SalomÃ© Fuenmayor.

When scientists create models whose results match observations, they know they're on the right track to a better understanding. That's what happened in this case, even though that wasn't necessarily what they set out to do.

"We note that while the main objective was not to provide an optimized fit to the Orion Bar, our three-dimensional chemical model was able to reproduce many of the features found in observations of the Bar," the authors write in their conclusion. They determined that the spatial dimensions of the PDR front plays a critical role in determining the emissions at the front.

"Our results mark a turning point for astrochemistry, where three-dimensional steady-state models can deliver fundamentally new insights into the chemistry and fundamental structure of the interstellar medium," the researchers explain.

"Future works can now investigate gas morphologies induced by different physical mechanisms and examine their photochemistry and emissions in three dimensions," they conclude.

#102. AI May Have Uncovered the Zodiac Killer’s Identity. Could It Crack History’s Greatest Mysteries?

What comes next could reshape our understanding of the world—ancient and modern.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story...

In 2007, Alex Baber saw Zodiac, David Fincher’s movie about the serial killer of the same name, and became obsessed with cracking one of the murderer’s unsolved ciphers, known as Z13. Out of the four ciphers the Zodiac Killer left behind, it’s the shortest, comprised of only 13 characters prefaced by the phrase “My name is…” So the 50-year-old West Virginian began poring over college-level textbooks, teaching himself forensic science and cryptography, the science of breaking codes, while working as a bodyguard outside Charleston.

Then, a couple of years ago, Baber also started learning how to code using artificial intelligence (AI) and successfully prompted his AI program to come up with potential names that fit the 13-character cipher. It produced 71 million possibilities. Cross-referencing those names against historical records like social security numbers and birth certificates, “we found out about 93 percent of [them] were never living, breathing people,” Baber explains, “so the list became considerably smaller,” about a couple thousand people. After the program eliminated those who didn’t match the Zodiac’s physical traits—white, middle-aged, about six feet tall—the amateur code breaker was left with an answer to the 67-year-old cipher: Marvin Merrill.

To Baber’s surprise, the name was familiar. It was an alias used by Marvin Skipton Margolis, a suspect in the infamous 1947 murder of Elizabeth Short, a 22-year-old aspiring actress whose decapitated body a pedestrian found slashed in half in a Los Angeles park. Short’s dark hair and wardrobe earned her the nickname “the Black Dahlia,” and her unsolved case has been a fascination of true crime fanatics ever since.

Baber’s sleuthing garnered international attention and attracted the interest of crime reporter and novelist Michael Connelly, who hosts a podcast series about Baber’s Zodiac/Black Dahlia theory. “I have no doubts,” he told the New York Times.

Other cryptographers, however, have plenty of doubts.

Klaus Schmeh, a German computer scientist who has written more than a dozen books about cryptology, says Z13 is virtually unsolvable because of its brevity. “The message is just too short. There are just too many possibilities.”

What is certain, Schmeh says, is the potential of AI to solve decades-old and even ancient mysteries.

“At the moment, cipher solutions are falling like ripe fruit from the trees,” according to Schmeh. “The autumn of 2026 will undoubtedly go down in the history of cryptology. Thanks to AI-assisted methods, cryptographic cold cases that have resisted solution for decades are suddenly being cracked one after another.”

For instance, in late September, Eren Bozbulut, a 22-year-old cybersecurity researcher from Turkey, used AI to crack five encrypted messages that the German spy Walter Koehler left behind during World War II. Using OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Daybreak Blue models to explore possible solutions, Bozbulut discovered a trove of WWII-era ciphers that the U.S. Coast Guard solved—and they happened to look a lot like one of Koehler’s uncracked messages. Combining the two ciphers, AI found the key that Koehler had based his code on: a single page in a Dutch prayer book published in 1893.

A few weeks later, an unrelated Russian engineer—Anton Zaytsev—successfully cracked an encrypted message found inside a glass bottle in Kaliningrad (formerly Königsberg) during the height of the Cold War. Zaytsev instructed his AI program to compare the letter frequencies of the cipher with those of known texts, and it quickly turned up the key: a song from East Germany that was especially popular with a socialist youth organization called the Freie Deutsche Jugend, or the Free German Youth.

AI has also shown potential in translating ancient cuneiform as well as Linear A, an undeciphered writing system the Minoan civilization used some 3,000 years ago. Google’s DeepMind Ithaca is helping scholars interpret damaged Greek inscriptions by predicting the missing text. Historians stand to learn a lot about bygone societies should AI prove successful in decoding dead or classical languages.

While the developments are exciting, Elonka Dunin, a cryptology expert and author, is quick to point out that AI is also “remarkably good at making things up. It hallucinates and fills in blanks,” she says. A solution that looks right “isn’t necessarily a solution. You have to be able to demonstrate how you got there.”

Additionally, while AI has been getting all the credit for cracking old ciphers and translating dead languages, humans are still very much at the helm, Dunin says. “It’s a prompt-and-response relationship. You still have to give AI some sort of prompt to get it rolling, you still need a human.”

Schmeh agrees, “AI is making progress and because people are making progress in using AI,” to sort through massive amounts of data infinitely quicker than a human could.

Dunin is confident AI will never take all the guesswork out of codebreaking. “Even after all the AI platforms pound on all of them, there will still be unsolved ciphers out there,” she says. “And the question will be: is this a fraud or is it just using a technique that neither humans nor AI have figured out yet?”

In the meantime, whether they’re cracking ancient mysteries or recent cold cases, humans will just have to rely on their own wit and diligence.
