As climate change fuels extreme temperatures and makes severely hot days more frequent, doctors are concerned about the health impacts on pregnant people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rising temperatures around the globe are contributing to a range of health risks, from infectious disease to food insecurity and wildfire smoke. Extreme heat is another major public health concern, as climate change drives up both average temperatures and the frequency of extremely hot days. This August was the world's hottest on record, and it drove upticks in heat-related emergency visits and deaths in various U.S. states.

Hotter weather is expected to pose dangerous health risks for millions, and pregnant people are especially vulnerable to its impacts, experts caution.

"Pregnant people are physiologically more vulnerable to heat," Dr. Susanna Esposito, a pediatrician at the University of Parma in Italy, told Live Science. "Climate adaptation should treat pregnant people as a priority population."

Extreme heat is linked to adverse birth outcomes that can be fatal for both mothers and newborns. Heat can also hinder fetuses' development, contributing to long-term health and cognitive effects.

Scientists and public health experts are working to identify the thresholds between safe and dangerous heat for maternal and prenatal health. As the planet warms, how will that affect the risks associated with pregnancy? And how can those risks be countered?

When the body tries to cool down, blood moves to the extremities to dissipate heat through the skin's surface. Some studies suggest that, in a pregnant person, this may reduce blood flow to the placenta, which in turn reduces the organ's supply of oxygen and nutrients. This is thought to contribute to low birth weight, which is associated with a heightened risk of illness and death shortly after birth, as well as cognitive and mental-health challenges later in life.

Heat stress may also spike the body's levels of cortisol beyond what they should be in a healthy pregnancy, studies in lab animals suggest. This may expose developing fetuses to more cortisol than usual, affecting some aspects of development and functions of the placenta. This mechanism is not fully understood in humans yet, though.

That said, several studies in humans support the notion of a link between heat exposure and low birth weight. Mothers who were pregnant during a 2003 heat wave in France were more than twice as likely to have a baby of low birth weight than mothers whose pregnancies did not coincide with the extreme heat. The trend was especially strong when the heat wave hit during a person's first trimester.

In a study conducted in Arizona, hotter temperatures during the third trimester were also associated with lower birth weight, said study co-author Kristin Mickelson, a sociologist who studies public health at the Arizona State University.

Exposure to extreme heat has been linked to a higher chance of babies being born at a low weight. The reasons why are still being studied, however.

Preterm delivery — before 37 weeks of gestation — is one of the most concerning health outcomes that's been linked to heat, Esposito told Live Science. The risk of neurological and developmental disabilities is higher in preterm babies than in full-term babies.

"If you're born preterm, you have a heightened risk of all sorts of adversities throughout infancy, but then also extending into childhood and even longer term," said Clara Heil, health researcher at Lund University in Sweden.

Severe heat may make preterm birth more likely. A review of 70 studies suggests that the chance of preterm birth is 16% higher when a multiday heat wave hits during the final weeks of pregnancy. Regarding average temperatures across an entire pregnancy, each additional 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit (1 degree Celsius) boosts the risk of preterm birth by 5%, the same review found.

High temperatures have also been tied to early births, which occur after 37 weeks of pregnancy but before 39 completed weeks. Early birth is associated with an increased risk of hospitalizations through childhood and slower neurologic development.

A study analyzing 56 million U.S. births across two decades suggested there was about 1 more early birth per 100,000 pregnancies on days with a maximum temperature above 90 F (32.2 C), compared to 60 to 70 F (15 to 21 C). Deliveries on hot days were typically about six days earlier than anticipated, but some were up to two weeks early.

With average temperatures continuing to rise, early and premature births could become more common. The United Nations predicts that the world is set to cross the 1.5 C (2.7 F) threshold of warming compared with pre-industrial levels, likely within the next five years, and we may even surpass the 2 C (3.6 F) threshold in that timeframe.

"We can probably expect to see these temperatures, or worse, in the upcoming years," Lizbeth Burgos Ochoa, statistician at Tilburg University in the Netherlands, told Live Science.

Maternal heat exposure has also been associated with an increased risk of preeclampsia, a pregnancy complication related to blood pressure that can be fatal. In a 2011 study conducted in France, hotter temperatures during the first trimester were associated with a slightly increased risk of severe preeclampsia, although more research is needed to understand why.

Heat exposure has also been linked to other conditions of pregnancy, including gestational diabetes and hypertension, as well as increased emergency hospital admissions during pregnancy, overall.

Additional studies have highlighted potential risks for developing fetuses and newborns. For example, following a heat wave in Canada, the risk of a baby being born with critical heart defects was 6% higher, one study found. Babies with the highest risk had been exposed to temperatures of 86 F (30 C) or higher for at least 15 days during the first trimester of pregnancy.

Extreme heat waves may also raise the chance of stillbirth, according to a study conducted across six U.S. states. Four consecutive unusually hot days — exceeding the 97.5th percentile of temperature for a given county — in the last week of pregnancy was linked to a 3% increase in the risk of stillbirth.

These studies are observational, so they show links between heat and pregnancy outcomes but cannot directly show that the heat spurred the increased risks. They also don't take into account study participants' home environments or strategies for cooling off, so they don't provide a full picture of how much heat they were exposed to.

Studies suggest that both maternal, prenatal and newborn health can be negatively impacted by exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy.

Researchers are still working to understand what temperatures pregnant people should be most concerned about.

"It would be [helpful] to understand what level of heat becomes dangerous to women," Heil said. "Is there a threshold where it becomes difficult for the body to dissipate heat? And especially for the pregnant body, which is different from the non-pregnant body, to cope with that heat?"

Heil and her research team synthesized over 100 studies on heat and poor birth outcomes, such as stillbirth, preterm birth, placental abruption and preeclampsia. The studies varied considerably in that they covered different timeframes, focusing on just one trimester or all three, for instance. But in general, their results converged on a pattern: The risk of poor outcomes rose as temperatures hit about 87 F (30.5 C). At 102 F (39 C), the combined risk of poor outcomes rose by 20%.

This summer, daytime maximum temperatures in the continental U.S. averaged a record-breaking 88.6 F (31.4 C). The number of days per year over 105 F (35 C) is expected to triple in the U.S. by midcentury.

Heat's detrimental effects on birth outcomes are even more extreme for those with disadvantaged socioeconomic conditions, Burgos Ochoa noted. People with lower incomes are less likely to have air conditioning, and neighborhoods with a lower median income tend to have less green space, which contributes to trapped heat in their immediate surroundings. Expanding green spaces and adding bodies of water can help cool down neighborhoods and mitigate heat impacts on health, she said.

Heil's research team has developed a phone app for pregnant people and those who have recently given birth that forecasts the risk of heat stress and suggests actions to take to mitigate those risks, such as hydrating or changing clothing. Heil is hopeful that the app and similar early-warning systems can make a difference.

"Maternal health should be at the top [of our concerns], because it is about the next generation," Mickelson said. "If we don't take care of the mothers that are giving birth to the next generation, that's going to have long-term consequences down the road."

#104. NASA reveals 16 stunning galaxies hiding cosmic chaos

Some galaxies glow with sweeping spiral arms, while others are shaped by violent collisions, powerful black holes, and explosive bursts of star formation. A newly released collection of 16 images from NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory and other telescopes reveals the extraordinary diversity of these cosmic structures.

Like precious gemstones, galaxies come in many shapes and sizes, each with characteristics that tell a story about its history. Astronomers generally classify them into three major groups. Spiral galaxies, including our Milky Way, have winding arms extending from their centers. Elliptical galaxies typically contain older stars and are often thought to form through galactic mergers. Irregular galaxies have less orderly structures and can display a wide variety of cosmic activity.

Much as gemstones preserve clues about the geological processes that shaped Earth over billions of years, galaxies hold evidence of the forces that have shaped the universe. Studying these distant systems helps astronomers piece together the Milky Way's history and better understand what may await our galaxy in the distant future.

NASA Combines Chandra, Webb, and Hubble to Reveal Galactic Secrets

The new gallery features 16 images that bring together observations from some of the world's most powerful telescopes. Each includes X-ray measurements gathered by Chandra during its decades of operation in space.

These observations are combined with data from NASA's James Webb and Hubble Space Telescopes, IXPE (Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, NuSTAR (Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array), and additional observatories operating on Earth and in space.

X-ray observations are especially valuable because they reveal extreme activity that other types of light can miss. Chandra can detect enormous clouds of gas heated to millions of degrees by powerful winds from massive stars, material expelled by supermassive black holes, and debris from stellar explosions. These processes also help spread chemical elements through space, including elements that ultimately become part of planets, the air we breathe, and our own bodies.

By combining X-rays with observations at other wavelengths, astronomers can see more of what is happening inside galaxies. The resulting images reveal how these vast systems form stars, interact with their surroundings, and change over billions of years.

Spiral Galaxies Reveal Explosive Star Formation

Several images highlight the remarkable activity taking place inside spiral galaxies. Messier 33 and NGC 3938 are viewed almost directly from above, allowing astronomers to examine their sweeping arms and identify regions containing energetic pairs of stars and the aftermath of stellar explosions.

Other galaxies reveal how their internal structures can help drive the birth of new stars. NGC 1672 and NGC 1385 are barred spiral galaxies, meaning they contain elongated central structures made of stars, gas, and dust. These bars can channel material toward the inner regions, providing fuel for intense episodes of star formation.

NGC 4725 demonstrates another way galaxies can produce new stars. Its observations reveal how an earlier encounter with another galaxy can disturb gas and stimulate star formation.

The collection also includes dramatic side views of NGC 4631 (the Whale Galaxy) and Messier 82 (the Cigar Galaxy). These galaxies feature enormous halos and powerful winds of gas heated to millions of degrees. Driven by intense stellar explosions, these outflows can carry material thousands of light-years into space, spreading important chemical elements into the regions between galaxies.

Supermassive Black Holes Blast Energy Across Galaxies

Some of the most dramatic features in the gallery come from the enormous black holes lurking at the centers of galaxies.

When these black holes actively consume surrounding material, their central regions become extremely energetic. Known as active galactic nuclei, these bright and powerful galactic cores can launch jets of particles and enormous outbursts that influence conditions across their host galaxies.

Centaurus A provides a striking example. Observations from Chandra and IXPE reveal a powerful stream of high-energy particles shooting tens of thousands of light-years into space from the galaxy's central region.

In Messier 106, jets launched from the central supermassive black hole interact with and heat surrounding gas. This activity produces unusual spiral structures that differ from the familiar arms normally associated with spiral galaxies.

The famous Sombrero Galaxy (Messier 104) offers another remarkable view. A supermassive black hole sits within its immense central concentration of stars, while Chandra's X-ray observations reveal a widespread halo of gas heated to millions of degrees and the hot remains of stars. These features surround the galaxy's prominent bands of dust, providing a deeper look at the energetic environment hidden within its elegant appearance.

Violent Galaxy Collisions Offer a Glimpse of the Milky Way's Future

Not every galaxy evolves peacefully. Some undergo enormous transformations as gravity pulls neighboring galaxies together, distorts their structures, or strips away the gas needed to create new stars.

Arp 143 captures the aftermath of a particularly dramatic encounter. A direct galactic collision produced an expanding ring, similar to ripples spreading outward after an impact. The disturbance also triggered waves of new star formation.

Other images show the chaotic consequences of galaxies merging. NGC 3256 and II Zw 096, the latter containing a powerful burst of star formation hidden behind thick dust, provide examples of the violent interactions that were especially common in the early universe.

These collisions also offer clues about the Milky Way's possible future. Our galaxy is expected to merge with the neighboring Andromeda galaxy billions of years from now, and observing other galactic mergers helps scientists understand how such an encounter could unfold.

The gallery includes several other unusual systems. NGC 1569 serves as a nearby example for investigating the intense episodes of star formation that occurred in young galaxies billions of years ago. NGC 660 displays a rare "polar ring" structure, with a ring of stars orbiting around the galaxy's poles rather than following its main plane.

Messier 90 illustrates a different kind of galactic transformation. As it travels through the Virgo Cluster, the galaxy is losing the gas it needs to form new stars. Its movement through the cluster strips away this material, potentially changing how the galaxy evolves.

Together, these 16 cosmic portraits show that galaxies are far from static collections of stars. They are constantly influenced by gravity, stellar explosions, black holes, and interactions with neighboring systems. By revealing these processes in remarkable detail, NASA's Chandra and its partner telescopes are helping astronomers understand the forces that shape galaxies, including our own.

#105. Can math stay human in the age of AI?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

When AI companies value competition over collaboration, we may lose out on understanding

AI is getting better at solving difficult math problems. But for mathematicians, the value of a proof can lie in more than the answer — it can also be in what the reasoning reveals.

Wikimedia Commons; Kieran Stone/Moment/Getty Images (laptop); Moor Studio/DigitalVision Vectors/Getty Images (brain); Aviral Sood, Adapted by J. Hirshfeld

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

“Exponentially exploding,” mathematician Thomas Bloom told me by phone, describing the flood of new results in his field. Little did he know that hours later, OpenAI was going to post 722 mathematical manuscripts an unreleased AI model had produced.

The firehose of new work lends new urgency to the question: How is AI changing mathematical discovery? In their race for headline-grabbing breakthroughs, AI companies typically do not disclose their methods and data. That competition among AI companies threatens to overwhelm human collaboration and understanding.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

This tension had been playing out in miniature on a website Bloom runs that tracks progress on more than 1,000 problems originally posed and collected by Paul Erdős, one of the 20th century’s most prolific mathematicians. Here, people used to collaborate to discuss open problems, or ones for which the best solution either hasn’t been found or isn’t known to the greater math community. But increasingly, visitors were competing to close open problems with AI proofs that they often didn’t understand. Bloom, a mathematician at the University of Manchester in England, doesn’t want to spend his days refereeing AI-generated work. So, soon after we spoke, and before he knew that OpenAI would be announcing its latest results, Bloom posted that he’d no longer tag problems as open or solved, and he also closed comments.

It’s definitely exciting that AI can tackle so many open problems so quickly. But can it help mathematicians understand the answers and build on them?

Just two days after OpenAI’s deluge of results, the peer-reviewed edition of a Google DeepMind study became public. First reported in a preprint earlier this year, it offers an inside look at how one AI system tackles open math problems. The system called AlphaProof Nexus solved 9 Erdős problems and made a number of other interesting mathematical advances, researchers report October 8 in Science.

The report includes a detailed description of how the results were obtained. Plus, human mathematicians vetted many of the proofs. That’s “quite different” from how OpenAI and Anthropic are handling their math results, Bloom says.

“The ultimate objective of any AI for math research,” says research scientist and study co-author Swarat Chaudhuri of Google DeepMind in London, should be “to advance mathematics as done by human mathematicians.”

In the recently published study Chaudhuri and his colleagues tested different configurations of their system. To tackle a collection of 353 open Erdős problems, they used multiple agents powered by the Gemini language model. These could call on AlphaProof, an AI model specially trained to do math, and the inspiration for the name of the overall system, for difficult steps. The agents also relied on Lean, math software that identifies steps that remain unproven, to check their logic. The agents shared their work, circulating promising proof attempts and discarding ones that weren’t going well.

The team also tested a simpler setup on the nine problems the full system solved. Independent Gemini agents worked through proofs using Lean’s feedback, without sharing attempts or consulting AlphaProof. That setup solved all nine, too. It was cheaper—using fewer computing resources—than the full system on easy problems and more expensive on the two toughest ones. The team did not establish whether the simpler setup would solve any of the problems the full system had missed.

The fact that the simpler setup could solve the same nine problems as the full system surprised Chaudhuri. It suggests that increasingly capable language models can tackle research mathematics with relatively simple checking tools.

But computer-checking comes with a caveat. Lean checks only the statement it’s given, as it is written in its code. And a mathematical statement may be incorrectly translated to or from Lean code. An October 6 preprint shows why this translation matters. In the paper, the researchers pinpoint mismatches between parts of OpenAI’s written Navier–Stokes proof and its Lean counterpart. The mismatches do not mean the written proof is wrong, the team writes, but they note that a valid Lean proof does not automatically validate an AI-generated math paper.

That’s why the vetting human mathematicians did for the DeepMind publication is so important. “The human mathematician has to really think through the problem and set goals for the system,” Chaudhuri says. And even if the system failed to finish a proof, its checked steps helped mathematicians focus on the remaining gaps. “Math is ultimately a human art,” Chaudhuri says. “The system enhances the human user’s insights, and the human user is able to guide the system with new ideas.”

The mathematical results that the AlphaProof Nexus system achieved are “not really at the top level of importance,” says Bloom, who wasn’t involved with the work. But that underscores the team’s more measured approach. Google DeepMind, he says, is “trying to be more responsible with the science,” while companies like OpenAI are using math to showcase their software. OpenAI’s papers and accompanying Lean proofs were entirely AI-generated, leaving it up to the math community to work out what’s useful or useless.

OpenAI says they worked with an independent advisory group to develop best practices on how to share their AI math results. But that group has said their advice was to not test unreleased AI models on advanced math, guidance the company clearly ignored.

The company’s fast-moving, competitive approach continues to alienate mathematicians such as Bryna Kra of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill. She says the company made some improvements in their efforts to cite past literature. And she’s excited about AI’s potential to solve important problems in math. But there is widespread concern, she says, that AI models have accessed people’s unpublished work. “We had a healthy, collaborative, sharing culture that is being destroyed,” she says. “Now, people are wary of sharing their ideas.”

Not all mathematicians feel this way about AI. The technology is “making math more accessible,” says Andrew Turner, who wonders why a small group of mathematicians should get to decide how we solve problems. Turner, who studied math and physics and is Now CTO of the company Plasma AI, based in New York City thinks “math is becoming engineering.” And doing math with machines will allow people to “answer questions previously unfathomable.”

A few days after Bloom shut down the competition on his website, Plasma AI announced a new website to track progress on Erdős problems. They will welcome AI results.

Bloom doesn’t see math as a Silicon Valley–esque move-fast-and-break-things competition. I agree, and hope that curious people will continue to explore problems they care about, with AI helping rather than taking over. At the end of his post announcing the changes to his website, Bloom wrote something that makes me tear up every time I read it. I hope everyone, even the most enthusiastic AI users, can find the time for this type of work: “Be confused, be stuck, be inspired. Find a messy proof, then find a better one,” he wrote. “Get tired, get hungry, get into a flow state. Argue, laugh, give up, drink some coffee and attack it again. Be human. Let your brain be open.”

#106. The Amazon Is Burning Again, and NASA Warns the Worst Is Yet To Come

A dangerous El Niño-driven wildfire cascade has reached the Amazon, and NASA scientists warn that the worst may still be ahead as hidden fires spread beneath the rainforest canopy.

El Niño is fueling a chain reaction of wildfires across the tropics, with fires first emerging in equatorial Asia before spreading to the central and eastern Amazon rainforest.

While tornadoes and thunderstorms can cause widespread damage in a matter of minutes, El Niño influences weather conditions over the course of months. In 2026, the climate pattern has intensified drought across the Amazon, leaving vast areas of rainforest increasingly vulnerable to fire. Scientists warn that the region is only beginning what could become an unusually long and destructive fire season.

Satellite observations have revealed a dramatic increase in fires and smoke emissions across the central and eastern Amazon since September 2026. The surge is apparent in several monitoring systems, including NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), and NASA Worldview. The affected area extends from the forests surrounding Manaus and Santarém, two important commercial and transportation hubs, eastward toward the mouth of the Amazon River.

On October 12, 2026, NASA’s Aqua satellite captured an image showing enormous plumes of smoke rising from fires on both sides of the Amazon River. The image was recorded by MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer), one of the satellite’s Earth-observing instruments.

That same day, Manaus, the capital of Brazil’s Amazonas state, was engulfed in dense smoke. City officials reported dangerously polluted air, with concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exceeding 135 micrograms per cubic meter. That level placed air quality in the second-worst category of a regional air quality index.

The smoke brought significant disruptions to the city of more than 2 million residents. Schools shut down, public events were called off, and children’s sports leagues suspended activities as authorities issued warnings about unhealthy air conditions, according to news reports.

According to Douglas Morton, an Earth system scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, the fires around Manaus and Santarém are part of a much larger pattern. He describes it as a “cascade” of tropical wildfires driven by changes in rainfall associated with El Niño.

The sequence typically begins near the equator, where dry conditions contribute to peat fires in Indonesia. Increased burning then develops in the central and eastern Amazon. Morton and researchers from the University of California, Irvine; Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam; and the University of Maryland documented this connection in a 2017 study examining the devastating wildfire season associated with the 2015–2016 El Niño. A similar sequence occurred in 2023.

The wildfire activity unfolding in 2026 appears to be following that same progression. Since August, parts of Indonesia have experienced persistent drought, widespread fires, and heavy smoke. In October, wildfires destroyed hundreds of homes, while thick smoke covered entire islands on most days.

“Now, in the Amazon, we’re seeing the second domino in the cascade fall,” Morton said, referring to the growing number of fires in the Brazilian states of Pará and Amazonas.

Scientists expect the next phase of the wildfire cascade to develop farther north during November and December. Areas at risk include the Brazilian states of Roraima and Amapá, northern Pará, and parts of Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname.

The danger could then shift southward. Morton predicts that drought and wildfire risk will reach their highest levels in the southern Amazon regions of Brazil and Paraguay around August and September 2027.

“It’s so striking—and frustrating—that this is happening all over again,” said Morton.

One particularly troubling aspect is that many of the forests now burning were also damaged during the El Niño events of 2015 and 2023. Fire can be especially destructive in tropical rainforests because most native plants and animals have not evolved to withstand frequent burning.

Previous wildfires have also weakened parts of the forest, leaving behind damaged and partially charred trees. Morton explained that these changes make the remaining vegetation more vulnerable, potentially allowing some fires to burn with greater intensity than before.

For communities around Manaus and Santarém, relief may not arrive until seasonal rains return in December 2026 or January 2027. However, Morton emphasized that regions farther north and south still have an opportunity to reduce their risk.

“Given the intensity of this El Niño, this really is the year for people to avoid burning at all costs,” Morton said.

Despite the enormous number of wildfires affecting the Amazon, lightning is responsible for very few of them. The Brazilian Amazon is normally so wet that lightning starts less than 1 percent of fires. According to Morton, human activity is responsible for the overwhelming majority of the fires currently burning there.

What makes 2026 especially dangerous is the severity of the drought, which has been intensified by El Niño. Brazil’s National Institute of Meteorology reported that rainfall in Manaus was 95 percent below normal in August and 60 percent below normal in September.

Many of the major fires began as controlled burns used to manage agricultural land, such as clearing unwanted vegetation from pastures or removing crop remnants from fields. But with the forest floor unusually dry, some of those fires escaped their intended boundaries and spread into the rainforest’s understory.

Shane Coffield, an assistant research scientist at the University of Maryland who works at NASA Goddard, said satellite analysis suggests that between 50 and 70 uncontrolled fires are currently burning in the Santarém area alone.

The true extent of the burning may be even greater than official fire monitoring systems suggest.

Through a NASA Earth Action project, Coffield is examining observations from VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) to find fires that fall below the detection thresholds used for official FIRMS fire data.

These additional detections, referred to as “candidate fires,” could help researchers build a more complete picture of wildfire activity. Coffield intends to provide their locations to scientists at MapBiomas, a collaborative network of universities, nongovernmental organizations, and technology companies that tracks fires and changes in land use throughout the Amazon.

“For the area around Santarém, we’ve identified about 40 percent more fires than you’ll see in active fire counts from FIRMS,” said Coffield.

Detecting every fire from space is difficult, particularly in dense tropical forests. Heavy smoke, cloud cover, and thick tree canopies can interfere with satellite sensors by obscuring the infrared heat signals emitted by flames. Smaller, less intense fires moving through vegetation beneath the forest canopy are especially easy to overlook.

This means that some of the days with the thickest smoke can produce surprisingly few satellite fire detections, even when extensive burning is taking place.

“On some of the smokiest days, we have very few detections from MODIS and VIIRS, and we know that isn’t right.”

#107. Webb Captures This Golden Galaxy Cluster in All it's Glory

The NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has provided something truly wonderful for its latest Picture of the Month. While observing the famous MACS J0454.1-030 galaxy cluster, Webb captured brilliant golden galaxies in great and glorious detail! Light from these galaxies traveled about 6 billion light-years to reach us and is warped by the gravitational lens created by the galaxy cluster.

In essence, the cluster's enormous mass warps spacetime around it, causing light from more distant objects to bend and magnify. Astronomers routinely exploit this effect to observe distant objects that telescopes cannot see under normal conditions. This technique, known as Gravitational Lensing, has opened new windows into the cosmos and made this image possible, especially when combined with next-generation instruments like Webb.

Based on various analyses of this image, astronomers estimate that some objects in the lensed area are magnified by a factor of more than 300. Whereas the golden galaxies are part of the cluster, which existed when the Universe was 8 billion years old, those that appear in the lensed areas (orange and red) predate them considerably. The red galaxies in particular existed when the Universe was just 2 billion years old.

Astronomers have also determined that one galaxy in the image existed just 800 million years after the Big Bang. Analysis of this galaxy's light suggests it was undergoing a merger that triggered an enormous burst of star formation. Our current cosmological models suggest this is how galaxies in the early Universe grew and became more complex, eventually becoming the elliptical and lenticular galaxies astronomers regularly observe near the Milky Way.

Using NASA’s SPHEREx spacecraft, astronomers have studied a host of "failed stars," also known as brown dwarfs.

These strange cosmic bodies straddle the line between planets and stars, possessing a mass between 13 and 80 times that of Jupiter (0.013 to 0.08 times the mass of the sun). They get the nickname failed stars because they form like stars from collapsing clouds of gas and dust but fail to gather enough mass to trigger the fusion of hydrogen to helium in their cores, the process that powers actual stars.

This formation process also means that brown dwarfs are cosmic loners, wandering the darkness of space alone, bereft of the light of a parent star. That description might sound like lyrics from a Type O Negative song ("Black No. 1," anybody?). And that's apt, according to the leader of the new study, which reveals that, chemically speaking, the atmospheres of these dark and cloudy worlds are not unlike those of our solar system's gas giant planets.

"They’re kind of goth," Zafar Rustamkulov, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Unlike exoplanets, free-floating brown dwarfs are completely independent celestial objects that will fade into eternity alone. We’re still learning how complex they are."

Rustamkulov added that, from Earth orbit, SPHEREx — short for Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer — sees wavelengths of light that are nigh-impossible to see with telescopes on the ground because water in Earth’s atmosphere absorbs them. That is important for bringing brown dwarfs into the light.

"We are picking up light from the deep, red clouds of brown dwarfs all over the sky," he said.

Brown dwarfs have been somewhat mysterious since their discovery in the 1990s, due to the fact that the small amount of nuclear fusion that occurs within them causes them to emit no more than a faint glow. That means that our understanding of their makeup, their storms, and their evolution really only comes from theory.

To help lift this observational darkness, the team turned to data from SPHEREx. They studied 37 nearby brown dwarfs in a spectrum of light including 102 wavelengths, from the deepest red our eyes can see to the invisible infrared light. These local failed stars spanned the full temperature range for brown dwarfs — from 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit (2,200 to minus 20 degrees Celsius).

Considering that the temperature of the sun is about 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit (5,500 degrees Celsius), you could definitely say brown dwarfs run cold.

The spectra of brown dwarfs seen by SPHEREx allowed the team to determine that their atmospheres are chemically rich in water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane.

"We’re seeing the signatures of these molecules and how they change from object to object across the entire temperature regime," said team member J. Davy Kirkpatrick, also of Caltech. "Our paper concentrated on just three dozen, but we have thousands more that we are in the process of analyzing.

"I really want to see what bounds the universe places on the variety of brown dwarfs."

Brown dwarfs have been routinely observed by other telescopes, including NASA's James Webb Space Telescope and the agency's now-retired Spitzer Space Telescope, but the wide wavelength coverage of SPHEREx has made it particularly useful in observing these failed stars. That's good news for astronomers waiting for change in the atmospheres of brown dwarfs as they age and grow cold.

The researchers found that some brown dwarfs observed by SPHEREx are at a stage of extreme change in which their clouds are clearing, creating atmospheres rich in methane.

The team may have discovered significant new details about brown dwarfs, but they are still on the proverbial mystery street when it comes to these strange celestial objects,

"The state-of-the-art models are capturing the general chemical trend, but when it comes to these cloudy transitions, the models are struggling to match the data," said Rustamkulov. "No two brown dwarfs are alike. Even at the same temperature, their spectra look quite distinct."

"This journey has turned many of us into accidental meteorologists. We know how hard it is to predict weather on our own planet, and we realize it's going to be just as challenging to explain the phenomena we see in these bizarre, cold objects," Kirkpatrick said. "The findings are a call to action to explore even more of these dark worlds."

As astronomers resond to that call to action, I will ponder how I could have worked Bauhaus' Goth classic "Bela Lugosi is Dead" into this article.

The team's research was published on Sept. 28 in The Astrophysical Journal.

Amazon has a knack for discounting sets when something is trending. Spider-Man fits that bill, with the latest movie hitting theaters a couple of months ago. This isn’t a Brand New Day set, but it’s nonetheless pretty sick. It’s one of the top-rated Marvel sets on Amazon, and it’s now at a 365-day low. And with the new Avengers film around the corner, you can’t go wrong, especially if Tobey Maguire’s Spidey makes his rumored appearance.

The holidays are right around the corner, and you can never go wrong gifting flowers. They also don’t have to be real. Lego flower arrangements are arguably more thoughtful, especially for a Lego fanatic. Plus, they won’t ever wilt, which is always a good thing. We’d consider those baked-in savings.

This set is surprisingly hard to come by. It’s been rereleased in recent years, but I couldn’t get my hands on it for a while. Not only is it available on Amazon, but it’s even on sale. It’s one of the pricier options on this list, but we’ll take the $30 off any day of the week. We love the 80s nostalgia—not to mention the only opportunity to get Christopher Lloyd in minifigure form. That right there is priceless.

A review of 41 studies found that higher exposure to air pollution was linked to greater odds of glaucoma and cataracts, with PM2.5 pollution showing the clearest association.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Aging is one of the biggest risk factors for developing glaucoma or cataracts — but as scientists look more closely at what happens to the eyes over a lifetime, they are finding that people's exposure to air pollution also plays a role in whether they develop these eye conditions.

Glaucoma, which affects about 80 million people worldwide, is a group of diseases that damage the optic nerve, which carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It can lead to permanent vision loss, usually affecting peripheral vision at first and later central vision. Cataracts are even more common, affecting more than 94 million people globally; the condition occurs when the eye's lens becomes cloudy, causing blurred vision and, eventually, blindness.

Aging raises the risk of both diseases, as do certain medical conditions, such as diabetes. But now, a review of 41 studies suggests that people who are exposed to higher levels of air pollution may also face a greater risk of these diseases. The research, presented in September at the 44th Congress of the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons in London, brought together evidence from dozens of studies collectively involving millions of people across East Asia and the U.K.

The studies were observational, meaning they can only draw a link between air pollution and the eye conditions, rather than prove that air pollution causes the diseases. But still, "this reframes glaucoma and cataract as conditions shaped by where you live and breathe, not just how long you've lived," said study co-author Dr. Ahmed Alnabihi, an ophthalmologist at King Khaled Eye Specialist Hospital and Research Center in Saudi Arabia, who presented the findings. These environmental exposures may compound age-related decline in the eye as they do in cardiovascular disease, he said.

The researchers examined exposure to several pollutants, including different sizes of particulate matter (PM), such as fine PM2.5 and larger PM10. They also looked at nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, ozone and carbon monoxide.

Most studies included in the review estimated people's long-term exposure based on the pollution levels around their homes and in their communities. They used a range of methods, including government monitoring systems, satellite data and computer models designed to estimate pollution levels. A few studies examined short-term exposure and its relation to more sudden eye issues, such as acute angle-closure glaucoma, a medical emergency that can quickly cause vision loss.

Using this wealth of data, the team compared pollution exposure with rates of glaucoma, cataracts and age-related macular degeneration (AMD), another common eye condition that impairs vision. PM2.5 — tiny particles that measure 2.5 micrometers or smaller — showed the clearest associations with glaucoma and cataract risk.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

People with the highest exposure to PM2.5 had 70% higher odds of glaucoma, compared to those with the least exposure. Plus, an increase in PM2.5 exposure equivalent to the difference between the 25th and 75th percentiles of exposure within each study was associated with 8% higher odds of glaucoma and a 4% higher hazard of cataracts.

Smoke from burning agricultural residue contains fine particulate matter. In a review of 41 studies, higher PM2.5 exposure showed a strong association with glaucoma and cataract.

The evidence was less consistent for air pollution and age-related macular degeneration, which damages the central part of the retina that's responsible for sharp, detailed vision. And unlike the clear connection seen with PM2.5, other pollutants showed less consistent links to eye disease. For instance, nitrogen dioxide was not significantly tied to AMD, ozone was not tied to cataracts, and neither pollutant was linked to glaucoma. Sulfur dioxide and PM10 showed no significant associations with any of the three conditions.

The association between PM2.5 and glaucoma was relatively consistent across the reviewed studies, said Nidhi Singh, an environmental epidemiologist at the IUF-Leibniz Research Institute for Environmental Medicine in Germany, who was not involved in the study. The findings for PM2.5 and cataracts were moderately consistent, albeit more variable than the glaucoma data; still, she said that the analysis seems to support a link.

Singh did caution that the underlying evidence is observational. "Therefore, the results demonstrate an association, not by themselves a causal effect of PM2.5 on glaucoma or cataract," she told Live Science.

The exact biological mechanisms behind these links remain unclear, but Alnabihi noted that fine particulate matter is small enough to be absorbed into the body. This can trigger oxidative stress, in which harmful molecules overwhelm natural defenses and cause damage. It also drives chronic, low-grade inflammation, in which the immune system stays mildly activated for long periods, he explained.

In the eye's lens, these processes can "damage the crystallin proteins that keep it transparent, causing them to misfold and cloud, which is what a cataract is," Alnabihi said.

In the optic nerve, the same processes are thought to damage retinal ganglion cells, a special type of neuron that relays information from the retina to the brain. This can contribute to glaucoma independent of internal eye pressure, he said, which is another big risk factor.

"Unlike the lungs or gut, its [the eye's] surface is in direct, continuous contact with outdoor air, giving pollutants a uniquely direct route that might cause damage," he added.

Other studies have found clues that support the link between PM2.5 and eye damage. Mice that were exposed to ambient PM2.5 for nine months developed elevated pressure inside their eyes, a glaucoma risk factor. The researchers observed both oxidative stress and nitrative stress — a similar phenomenon — in the tissues that drain fluid from the eye, which may help to explain the rise in pressure.

Studies of humans and human cells have uncovered similar patterns. In data from more than 480,000 people in the UK Biobank, a large repository of health information, those exposed to higher PM2.5 were more likely to develop glaucoma over time. In another study, scientists exposed lab-grown human retinal tissue made from stem cells to PM2.5. The particles disrupted retinal cell development, including that of retinal ganglion cells, while increasing cell death.

These studies offer pieces of a possible mechanism, but for now, how those pieces fit together in people remains unclear.

#113. Researchers Discover What Reading for Pleasure May Be Doing to Your Brain

Reading for pleasure may offer surprising benefits for the brain, with research linking the habit to better mental health, stronger cognitive abilities, and a lower risk of dementia.

Reading for pleasure may do far more than provide entertainment. A scientific review published in Psychological Medicine links the habit to better mental health, stronger cognitive abilities, and a lower risk of dementia. Research also suggests that reading is associated with measurable differences in brain structure, although scientists are still investigating whether reading directly causes these changes.

Researchers from the University of Cambridge and The Queen’s Reading Room examined evidence spanning childhood through old age. Their findings suggest that reading for enjoyment, whether alone or with others, may support brain health in several ways, with some benefits potentially appearing after just a few minutes.

Some of the strongest evidence comes from a study involving more than 10,000 young people. Children who began reading for pleasure at an early age tended to perform better on tests of attention, memory, and executive function, the mental abilities involved in planning, decision-making, and controlling behavior. They also showed stronger academic performance, fewer mental health problems, healthier sleep habits, and less screen time.

Reading is closely associated with literacy development, but its relationship with learning extends to mathematics. Both activities rely on overlapping cognitive processes, including working memory, language comprehension, and executive control. Despite these potential advantages, surveys indicate that recreational reading among children and teenagers has fallen to its lowest recorded levels, particularly among adolescent boys and children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

Reading may also provide psychological benefits throughout adulthood. Surveys associate reading for enjoyment with lower stress, greater relaxation, stronger empathy, and more openness to different perspectives. In one survey, nearly two in five adults (38%) identified reading as their preferred way to unwind.

A neuroscience study commissioned by The Queen’s Reading Room in 2024 reported that just five minutes of reading fiction could reduce stress by up to 20%. The research also identified improvements in concentration and problem-solving, alongside reduced feelings of loneliness. These results suggest that even brief reading sessions may offer benefits, although the size and persistence of those effects require further investigation.

Brain imaging studies have found associations between reading and several features of brain anatomy. These include greater volume and cortical surface area in regions involved in language, learning, emotional regulation, and executive control. Researchers have also observed stronger white matter connections supporting language processing and increased cortical thickness in areas important for reading and comprehension.

Most of these findings are observational, so they cannot establish whether reading produces the anatomical differences or whether existing brain characteristics influence reading habits. However, intervention studies offer preliminary evidence that reading-related training can alter brain structure. In one small study, 11 children with dyslexia aged 7 to 11 completed eight weeks of training involving mental imagery, speech articulation, and tracing letters and words. Their reading abilities improved alongside increases in gray matter volume in specific brain regions. Because the intervention involved specialized training rather than recreational reading, its findings cannot be directly applied to reading for pleasure.

The potential benefits of reading extend into later life, when preserving memory and thinking abilities becomes increasingly important. In a study of nearly 5,500 adults aged 55 and older, participants who frequently engaged in mentally stimulating activities, including reading, were significantly less likely to develop cognitive impairment during five years of follow-up.

Another study associated reading newspapers, magazines, and books with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease. These findings support a possible relationship between mentally stimulating activities and healthier cognitive aging, but they do not establish that reading prevents dementia. Other factors, including education, general health, and lifestyle, may contribute to the observed associations.

Reading with other people may provide advantages beyond those associated with reading alone. Book clubs, family reading sessions, and community reading groups combine intellectual engagement with social interaction, potentially helping participants feel less isolated and more connected. Social connection is itself associated with better mental and physical health, particularly among older adults.

“Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction,” said Professor Barbara Sahakian of the University of Cambridge. The Queen’s Reading Room has also introduced shared reading programs in homeless shelters and domestic violence refuges, where books are used as part of therapeutic recovery efforts.

Sahakian and Cambridge researcher Dr. Christelle Langley began examining the broader benefits of reading while writing their 2025 book, Brain Boost: Healthy Habits for a Happier Life. They found evidence linking recreational reading to numerous positive outcomes, but also discovered that the subject had received relatively limited scientific investigation.

Together with Vicki Perrin, CEO of The Queen’s Reading Room, the researchers argue that encouraging people to read for enjoyment could support well-being across the lifespan. They emphasize that reading does not have to involve traditional novels. Comics, graphic novels, and books connected to a person’s existing interests may help make reading more accessible, particularly for children who otherwise show little interest in it.

Reference: “Reading and associations with brain health, cognition, well-being, and mental health” by Barbara J. Sahakian, Vicki Perrin and Christelle Langley, 15 September 2026, Psychological Medicine. DOI: 10.1017/S0033291726105625

#114. The ESA's Euclid Space Telescope Has Discovered A New Comet

The ESA's Euclid Space Telescope has discovered its first comet, a result that's not part of its primary mission. The telescope was launched at the beginning of July, 2023, and its mission is to observe about 1.5 billion galaxies out to redshift z=2, which corresponds to seeing around 10 billion years into the past. The goal is to measure the redshift of a massive amount of galaxies, to shed light on the expansion history of the Universe and the force that drives it, dark energy.

The space telescope has observed other comets, but this is the first time it's discovered one. The comet was found in multiple images captured between September 16th and 24th, 2026. For a telescope built to take deep images of distant galaxies, discovering a rapidly moving comet in the Milky Way is a surprising bonus.

The comet didn't announce its presence. The discovery relied on new software designed by Mikko PÃ¶ntinen of the University of Helsinki. PÃ¶ntinen, together with the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium, discovered it.

âI was excited to see my software flag a âstreakâ smeared across several images â the result of a fast-moving object," PÃ¶ntinen said in an ESA press release. "By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas.â

Comets are dusty, icy bodies left over from the earliest days of the Solar System, more than four billion years ago. They come from the Oort Cloud and the Kuiper Belt. When a comet approaches the inner Solar System, the Sun heats it up, and some of its frozen volatiles form a hazy cloud around the comet called a coma, as well as a tail. Astronomers are interested in comets because they're pristine material from the Solar System's formative years, and hold clues to the process of Solar System formation. They may be especially relevant as deliverers of water to the inner Solar System, including to Earth.

PÃ¶ntinen compared the discovery with known cometsâand asteroidsâand found no match with existing Solar System objects. He reported the discovery to the Minor Planet Center, the body responsible for identification, designation and orbit computation of Solar System objects. Ground-based follow-up observations helped confirm the comet, and the MPC gave it the name C/2026 S1 (Euclid), following convention.

C/2026 S1 (Euclid) is about 1.3 billion km (808 thousand miles) away from Earth, or roughly the distance from the Sun to halfway between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn. It's a long-period comet that takes thousands of years to complete one orbit.

Most asteroids and comets follow the plane of the Milky Way. But Euclid purposely avoids observing this part of the sky. It's full of dust that makes deep-sky imaging difficult. So the telescope is not expected to find anything new in the Milky Way.

But C/2026 S1 (Euclid) follows an odd orbit. Rather than orbiting along the same plane the planets follow, it arches over top of the galaxy. This means it travelled through one of Euclid's fields of observation.

Euclid observes the sky in wide and deep surveys. It found the comet in its Euclid Deep Field North in the constellation Draco. The Deep Field North was chosen because it overlaps with a deep field region of the sky surveyed by NASA's now-defunct Spitzer Space Telescope, an infrared observatory. The telescope observed the comet in five separate sub-fields with two to four exposures per view, for a total of 16 exposures.

This figure shows Euclid's wide and deep fields. The wide field is in blue, while the deep fields are in yellow. Euclid found C/2026 S1 (Euclid) in its Deep Field North, the yellow region near the image's top left. Euclid avoids observing along the plane of the Milky Way due to the presence of so much problematic dust. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA/Planck Collaboration/A. Mellinger â Acknowledgment: Jean-Charles Cuillandre, JoÃ£o Dinis and Euclid Consortium Survey Group. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO

âVery few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid so it was a happy coincidence that the combination of the cometâs orbit and Euclidâs scanning over those days captured the object in multiple images,â said Bruno Altieri, Euclid Archive Scientist, and part of the discovery team.

âWhile this particular comet is not a suitable candidate for Comet Interceptor, the process of discovery and alert gives us a real test case for how our two mission teams will coordinate in the future. And we are of course happy to have discovered a previously unknown comet for the Solar System community to follow-up on,â added Valeria Pettorino, Euclid Project Scientist.

#115. Alaska’s monster tsunami sent water 1,580 feet up a mountain

On the evening of Aug. 9, 2025, passengers on the Hanse Explorer finished taking selfies and videos of the South Sawyer Glacier, and the ship headed back down the fjord. Twelve hours later, a landslide from the adjacent mountain unexpectedly collapsed into the fjord, initiating the second-highest tsunami in recorded history.

We conduct research on earthquakes and tsunamis at the Alaska Earthquake Center, and one of us serves as Alaska state seismologist. In a new study with colleagues, we detail how that landslide sent water and debris 1,580 feet (481 meters) up the other side of the fjord – higher than the top floor of the Taipei 101 skyscraper – and then continued down Tracy Arm. The force of the water stripped the fjord’s walls down to bare rock.

It was just after 5 o’clock in the morning on a dreary day, and fortunately, no ships were nearby. In the months after, some cruise lines started avoiding Tracy Arm. However, the conditions that led to this event are not at all unique to this fjord.

Landslides are common in the coastal mountains of Alaska where rapid uplift, caused by tectonic forces and long-term ice loss, converges with the erosive forces of precipitation and moving glaciers. But a curious pattern has emerged in recent years: Multiple major landslides have occurred precisely at the terminus of a retreating glacier.

Though the mechanics are still poorly understood, these mountains appear to become unstable when the ice disappears. When the landslide hits the water, the momentum of millions of tons of rock is transferred into tsunami waves.

This same phenomenon is playing out from Alaska to Greenland and Norway, sometimes with deadly consequences. Across the Arctic, countries are trying to come to terms with this growing hazard. The options are not attractive: avoid vast swaths of coastline, or live with a poorly understood risk. We believe there is an obvious role for alert systems, but only if scientists have a better understanding of where and when landslides are likely to occur.

The Tracy Arm landslide is a powerful example.

The landslide occurred in August, when warm ocean waters and heavier precipitation favor both glacier retreat and slope failure. The glacier below the landslide area had experienced rapid calving – large chunks of ice breaking off and falling into the water – and it had retreated more than a third of a mile in the two months prior. Heavy rain had been falling. Rain enters fractures in the mountain and pushes them closer to failure by increasing the water pressure in cracks.

Most provocative are the thousands of small seismic tremors that emanated from the area of the slide in the days prior to the mountainside collapsing.

We believe that this combination of signs would have been sufficient to issue progressive alerts to any ships in the vicinity and homes and businesses that could have been harmed by a tsunami at least a day prior to the failure – had a monitoring program existed.

Escalating alerts are used for everything from terrorism and nuclear plant safety to avalanches and volcanic unrest. They don’t remove the risk, but they do make it easier for people to safely coexist with hazards.

For example, though people are still killed in avalanches, alert systems have played an essential role in making winter backcountry travel safer for more people. The collapse at Tracy Arm demonstrates what could be possible for landslides.

We believe that the combination of weather and rapid glacier retreat in early August 2025 was likely sufficient to issue an alert notifying people that the hazard may be temporarily elevated in a general area. On a yellow-orange-red scale, this would be a yellow alert.

In the hours prior to the landslide, the exponential increase in seismic events and telltale transition to what is known as seismic tremor – a continuous “hum” of seismic energy – were sufficient to communicate a time-sensitive warning for a specific region.

These observations, recorded as a byproduct of regional earthquake monitoring, warranted an “orange” alert noting immediate concern. The signs were arguably sufficient to recommend keeping boats and ships out of the fjord.

Our research over the past few years has demonstrated that once a large landslide has started, it is possible to detect and measure the event within a couple of minutes. In this amount of time, seismic waves in the surrounding area can indicate the rough size of the landslide and whether it occurred near open water.

A monitoring program that could quickly communicate this would be able to issue a red alert, signaling an event in progress.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s tsunami warning program has spent decades fine-tuning rapid message dissemination. A warning system would have offered little help for ships in the immediate vicinity, but it could have provided perhaps 10 minutes of warning for those who rode out the harrowing tsunami farther away.

There is no landslide monitoring system operating yet at this scale in the U.S. Building one will require cooperation across state and federal agencies, and strengthened monitoring and communication networks. Even then, it will not be fail-proof.

Alert systems do not remove the risk entirely, but they are a better option than no warning at all. Over time, they also build awareness as communities and visitors get used to thinking about these hazards.

Many of the most alluring places on Earth come with significant hazards. Arctic fjords are among them. The same processes that create this hazard – glacier retreat, steep terrain, dynamic geology – are also what make these landscapes so compelling. The mix of glaciers, ice-choked waters and steep mountains is exactly what draws people to these places. People will continue to visit and experience them.

The question is not whether these places should be avoided altogether, but how to help people make more informed decisions. We believe that stronger geophysical and meteorological monitoring, coupled with new research and communication channels, is the first step.

On Aug. 9, visitors unknowingly passed through a landscape on the cusp of failure. An alert system might have given tour companies and people in the area the information they needed to make more informed choices and avoid being caught by surprise.

#117. The 8 Best Tool Sets for Basic Home and Auto Repairs

Everything you need to hang a frame, fix a leak, or change your spark plugs in one sturdy case.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note—Friday, September 4, 2026: For this article’s latest update, I tested two new tool sets. The Kobalt 228-piece set offers a large, well-curated collection that has absolutely everything you need for furniture assembly projects (and most of what you’d need for other household work). Craftsman’s 102-piece household tool set, meanwhile, is free of filler and includes some of the highest-quality hand tools I’ve tested, including a set of screwdrivers, two sets of pliers, a hammer, and a socket set. It was this build quality that landed the Craftsman set as my new pick for Best Overall.

There’s nothing more annoying than needing a handful of basic tools—like a hammer, screwdriver, pliers, and wrench—to complete a job at home and finding none of them were put back where they belong. That’s rarely the case if you invest in a high-quality home tool set. They bring together all of your essential tools and store them neatly in a solid carrying case (or sturdy bag) that’s small enough to fit inside a closet or even a kitchen utility drawer.

The tools themselves in many of these sets lack the build quality and durability you’ll find when you purchase individual tools, so you might not want to use them when, for example, building a deck or renovating a kitchen. But they offer exceptional value for homeowners looking to mount a TV, hang pictures, change out a light fixture, and complete other similar odd jobs. Along with these general tool sets, there are also great tool sets designed for specific purposes like working on vehicles or bicycles.

I put several of the most popular tool sets out there to the test in my house and garage, using them to tighten screws, hammer nails, cut wires, and turn bolts, all in an effort to see which ones performed the best.

As someone who has spent years testing tools, not to mention working on home projects and performing basic auto maintenance, I understand what’s essential in a good tool set and what’s more of a luxury. I used this experience to identify what looked worthy of inclusion among the best tool sets, specifically choosing from brands that have a reputation for making quality tools, and I then set about testing each set around my home. I turned screws, hammered nails, and worked bolts in order to assess each tool in each set. While testing, I evaluated ease of use, performance, and build quality. I also evaluated each set on how well-organized it is and whether its case seemed like it could withstand the rigors of regular use and transport.

Whereas the tools in many home tool sets feel like lighter-duty, smaller versions of full-size hand tools, most of the pieces in this set are designed and built well enough that they could be sold on their own. The 16-ounce hammer features a molded, rubberized grip, and I had no problem using it to drive 16d nails into a pair of stacked 2x6s. The screwdrivers have precision tips and large molded handles that allowed me to generate enough torque to turn 2½-inch carpentry screws into pine. There are also three sets of pliers that have a heavy, sturdy feel to them and open and close easily.

While these tools are impressive, it's the kit’s socket set that truly stands out. The sockets feature knurling on the sides for hand turning, as well as radius corners that grip tightly to bolt heads. With their short swing arcs and beefy build quality, the two 90-tooth socket wrenches could go toe-to-toe with ratchets I’ve tested in higher-end mechanic’s socket sets.

All in all, this set’s above-average and excellent tools far outnumber its disappointing, lighter-duty ones, but there are a few duds—specifically the flimsy, 12-foot tape measure and undersized utility knife that you will almost certainly need an alternative for. And, as with many of the home tool sets I’ve tested, I wish Craftsman had included an 8-inch crescent wrench versus the smaller, 6-inch model you get in this set, as the longer version allows you to generate considerably more leverage and therefore makes it a more versatile tool.

Many budget-priced home tool sets have tools that vary in quality or omit essentials in favor of tools or supplies you’ll likely never use. Kobalt’s home tool set is an exception. All of the tools selected for the set are ones you’ll actually use, including screwdrivers, a hammer, utility knife, pliers, wire cutters, bit driver, and a small socket set. There’s even a set of utility scissors and a torpedo level.

I also like the build quality of this tool set (both in terms of the tools and case that holds them). The handles on all of the hand tools, including the hammer, screwdrivers, pliers, and ratchet, are overmolded with plenty of rubberized grip, making them comfortable to use. The hammer, though a smaller, 10-ounce model, doesn’t feel flimsy or undersized like hammers I typically find in these value tool sets. Plus, everything fits securely into the molded plastic case (although some were so secure that I found them difficult to get out).

Full Kobalt 158-Piece Household Tool Set Review

This is a comprehensive mechanics tool set that won’t break the bank. It comes with three drive sizes and a nice collection of both standard and deep sockets in both SAE and metric sizes.

Craftsman has long had a reputation for high-quality hand tools, and that holds true with this set. The sockets have a sturdy feel and radius corners that allow you to create a lot of torque without rounding off bolt heads. The oval ratchet handles fit nicely in the hand and turn smoothly. There is also a full slate of extenders and joints, which make it easier to work bolts in tight spaces.

Along with sockets, the set also includes a full set of 12 combination wrenches and a bit driver with assorted Phillips, Torx, and other fastener types commonly found on vehicles. All of the pieces fit securely into a solid molded plastic carrying case.

Full Craftsman 159-Piece Mechanics Tool Set Review

WorkPro’s large tool set includes just about everything a homeowner would need to handle beginner and intermediate jobs around the house. There’s a cordless drill, multiple sets of pliers, a hammer, torpedo level, and a full set of screwdrivers. It’s one of the best-curated tool kits I’ve seen, and it will help you handle everything from installing shelves to fixing a leaky faucet to changing a light fixture. While it does come with some filler in the form of zip ties and anchors, it’s one of the more affordable large sets I’ve seen.

I also like the quality and user-friendly design of this kit. Everything from the hammer to the pliers to the screwdrivers has molded, oversized grips that feel good in the hand. Even the cordless drill has a light, mobile feel to it.

All of the pieces fit into a well-made canvas bag that’s easy to carry and is small enough to store in a closet.

This mechanic’s tool set includes all the essentials for the home mechanic. The highlight of this set is its collection of ratchets. They operate smoothly and with precision. I was able to work bolts on my truck and ratchet lag bolts into a set of wood shelving in my workshop with ease.

Each piece shows DeWalt’s attention to detail. The sockets and drivers are designed with a knurled grip for hand-threading bolts, and radius corners on the sockets prevent them from rounding off bolt heads. The kit also comes with a bit driver (plus assorted bits) and a full set of metric and SAE hex wrenches. It even comes with a separate case that includes adapters, so you can use the sockets with the bit driver or even an impact driver.

The carrying case is rugged and has two metal latches that securely hold it together. It’s important to note, though, that this is not a general home tool set. If you go with this kit, you’ll need to purchase other essential tools, like a hammer and pliers, separately.

Black and Decker’s budget tool set consists of the essential hand tools anchored by a surprisingly powerful cordless drill. The kit comes with an ambitious set of paddle bits and hole saws that, quite frankly, I wasn’t sure the drill could handle, but it drilled large holes through a sheet of plywood during testing with surprising speed and power. While the drill/driver won’t compare with the top cordless drills out there, it’s certainly no slouch and more than enough for casual DIYers.

While the cordless drill is the star of this set, the kit also comes with a nice selection of hand tools, including two sets of pliers, screwdrivers, a hammer, a utility knife, and a tape measure. These hand tools have molded grips that make them comfortable to use and perform well, though it’s clear they’re only designed to handle lighter-duty jobs.

This kit is perfect for hanging pictures and changing out a light fixture. And with the cordless drill, it will also handle bigger jobs, like mounting a flat-screen TV or installing curtain rods.

This tool kit offers a complete set of bike-specific specialty tools at a reasonable price. It comes with all the essentials, including a full set of hex wrenches for adjustments and tire levers for changing flats. There are also the tools you’ll need for larger repairs or bike assembly, like a crank puller, chainring nut wrench, and bottom bracket wrench.

I’ve owned this tool kit for more than a year and have used it for everything from minor overhauls to assembling new bikes. The tools are not as high-quality as those from brands that professional bike mechanics use, but those kits cost five times as much. The quality is certainly good enough to meet the needs of more casual cyclists who like to work on their own bike rather than send it to the local shop.

The tools have well-made grips, and all the pieces fit into a compact carrying case that’s easy to store or take with you on a weekend cycling trip. If I have a complaint with this kit, though, it’s with a carrying case. Some pieces don’t stay securely in their spot, and some tools you’ll use most often, such as the hex wrenches, fit behind tools you won’t use very often, which is inconvenient. Setting these complaints aside, however, this is a comprehensive and very reasonably priced kit for the DIY bike mechanic.

The most important part of any tool set is the selection of tools that it includes. A good tool set should give you everything you need to fix a leaky faucet, change out a light switch, tighten a doorknob, or hang a picture. These include a hammer, tape measure, pliers, adjustable wrench, screwdrivers, utility knife, and Allen wrenches.

There is a caveat here. Some tool sets are designed to meet specific needs. For example, the DeWalt 142-Piece Mechanics Tools Kit and Socket Set is designed with the home mechanic in mind, while the Cyclists 23-Piece Bike Tool Kit includes tools for working on bikes that you simply won’t need around your home.

Tool set manufacturers love to use the number of pieces included in the set to highlight its value. Take this number with a grain of salt, however, as many sets will inflate this number with cheap, consumable supplies like zip ties, drywall anchors, screws, and other “pieces” that don’t add much value. Pay less attention to the size of the set and look carefully at what’s in it. Sets like the Kobalt 158-Piece Blue Household Tool Set include very little filler.

Build quality varies considerably from tool set to tool set and even among tools inside a set. I’ve seen sets with high-quality socket sets that are paired with undersized hammers, flimsy tape measures, or screwdrivers with uncomfortable grips. Look for sets that have consistent quality across all the tools. Pay attention specifically to tool handles. They should be molded with rubberized grips that allow you to hold the tool firmly and comfortably while you’re working.

Keep in mind that home tool sets are generally designed for lighter-duty work, so don’t expect pro-level build quality. You won’t be framing a shed, building a deck, or renovating a bathroom with one of these sets.

All tool sets come in a handy case that not only keeps all the pieces together and organized but also makes it easier to transport and store. Note the dimensions of these cases. Some are small enough to fit inside a utility drawer while others may require a larger space like a closet. Tool sets come in either hard or soft cases. Soft cases are more comfortable to carry than hard cases but don’t organize tools with the same precision as a molded hard case that has specific spots for each tool.

Tony Carrick is a full-time freelance writer who specializes in technology, home improvement, DIY, home security, and outdoor recreation. He’s tested and written about everything from home security systems to power tools to gas grills. His product guides, how-to articles, and feature stories can be found in such publications as Bob Vila, Angi, U.S. News and World Report, Field & Stream, Futurism, and Switchful. When Tony isn’t writing, he can be found working on his latest home improvement effort at his home in North Carolina.
