#118. Tiny implants can use the body itself to talk to each other

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The network could let tiny implants sense symptoms and trigger treatments

An implant, small enough to inject through a syringe, can send electrical signals to a wearable device through the body’s own tissue

Candler Hobbs, Georgia Institute of Technology

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Medical implants are getting smaller and smarter. But getting them to talk to each other remains tricky.

Now, researchers have developed a way for tiny implantable devices to send electrical signals through the body’s own tissues. The approach could offer a low-power way for implants to work together, with one detecting a symptom and another delivering treatment, the team reports September 24 in Science.

Currently, getting devices to communicate through tissue comes with trade-offs. Some medical devices, such as insulin pumps linked to glucose monitors, use Bluetooth, which relies on radio signals. Receiving those signals requires power even when a device is only listening, increasing the need for battery power and making devices harder shrink. Radio signals also weaken as they travel through body tissue, limiting how far apart communicating devices can be.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The new network called SWANS, the Smart Wireless Autonomous Networking System, works differently. A wearable external hub or implant generates an electric pulse that produces a small current in the surrounding tissue. Tiny implants can detect those electrical signals while using almost no power when they are only listening. And without large batteries, those implants can be small enough to inject through a syringe.

To demonstrate how the network works, the team attached motion sensors to the front legs of rats. When the animals moved their front legs, the system’s external hub sent signals through their bodies to neurostimulator implants in the sciatic nerves, causing muscles in the back legs to contract.

The synchronized limbs weren’t really the point. The experiment was designed to show that signals could travel through the body, linking different kinds of devices, says Alex Abramson, a biomedical engineer at Georgia Tech in Atlanta. It was “a proof of concept showing that you can really connect this system to anything.”

Abramson says a network of smart implants could automatically deliver a drug or stimulate a neuron exactly when needed to treat complex conditions like Parkinson’s disease. Simple signals can be sent from one implant to another, while an external hub can coordinate more complex networks of sensors and devices, possibly using artificial intelligence.

Before the new network can be used in humans, researchers will need to show that the electrical signals do not cause unintended problems like heart rhythm disruptions. Such issues  have not turned up in the experiments in rats yet, but the technology will need to be tested over longer periods of time and in larger animals, Abramson says.

Materials engineer Amir Alavi says the network’s potential could grow as other technologies improve, including wearables, AI systems and miniature, battery-free implantable sensors like those his lab is developing. “There are now several really interesting directions converging,” says Alavi, of at the University of Pittsburgh’s Swanson School of Engineering. “If those pieces eventually come together, you could have implants that are much smaller, simpler, longer-lived, and more connected than what we have today.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

R. Ghanim et al. An in-body networking system for communication between wearable and implantable therapeutics. Science 2026. doi: 10.1126/science.adz5300

J. Luo et al. Wireless electronic-free mechanical metamaterial implants. Materials Today, 2025. doi: 10.1016/j.mattod.2024.12.018

The incredible beauty of Antarctica is evident from space .

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Antarctica is a magnificent sight, and that beauty is visible all the way from space.

Orbiting planet Earth, the European Space Agency's (ESA) Copernicus Sentinel-3 mission captured a close-up of West Antarctica.

Winter is ending in the Southern Hemisphere, meaning this is the peak of icy weather and sea ice in the Arctic.

In this image snapped by Sentinel-3, you can see a massive swath of ice which includes Elephant Island on the left-hand side. An ice-covered island off the Antarctic coast, Elephant Island floats in the Southern Ocean. It got its name both from the island's shape, which some liken to that of an elephant's head, and the fact that the island is home to a community of elephant seals.

While a seal-inhabited island on the left floats near the Antarctic coast, across the water is a vast, frozen landscape. In just this snapshot, you can see about between 746 and 1,056 miles (1,200 to 1,700 kilometers) of the icy continent.

This image was captured on Sept. 30, 2026. In the Southern Hemisphere, that was just past the end of winter. The absolute peak for sea ice in Antarctica fell just a couple weeks before, on Sept. 14, according to the National Snow and Ice Data Center, ESA reported.

So in this one snapshot, we can see a near-maximum for sea ice in the Antarctic, spanning hundreds of miles. In observing our own planet from space, we are able to peer across vast landscapes, capturing important observational data. This is especially critical for the Antarctic as, with the progression of climate change, this sea ice continues to dwindle, adding to sea level rise among other serious consequences across the planet.

Researchers have found that during the Black Death, when a third of Europe's population was wiped out, biodiversity fell. Understanding the farming practices of the time could help us increase diversity in modern agriculture.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When millions of people died in Europe during the Black Death, biodiversity suffered too, new research suggests. The findings suggest that human activities once promoted biodiversity in the landscape — and experts say we could use these findings to boost biodiversity in our modern agricultural landscapes.

The 14th century was a tumultuous time for the people of Europe. Persistent cold, wet weather at the beginning of the century led to widespread agricultural failures and unprecedented levels of starvation in what became known as the Great Famine from 1315 to 1317.

This was followed by the Black Death, an epidemic of bubonic plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that killed more than a third of Europe's population. As a result of the widespread deaths and resultant social upheaval, large swaths of agricultural land were abandoned. Population levels didn't begin to recover until the 16th century.

The Black Death era is the perfect opportunity to look at the effects of humans on biodiversity over a longer period, Jonathan Gordon, a paleoecologist at the Leverhulme Centre for Anthropocene Biodiversity at the University of York and first author of the paper, told Live Science.

In the study, which was published March 4 in the journal Ecology Letters, the researchers compared more than 100 European pollen records that included about 4,600 samples. The records came from sites ranging from the lowlands of France and uplands of the southwest United Kingdom to the Swiss Alps.

The pollen records "give us information on the past diversity of the plant records," Gordon said.

For example, cereal grains ‪—‬ such as wheat, barley and rye ‪—‬ were a fundamental part of medieval agriculture. The representation of pollen from these types of crops in the pollen record points to historic land use.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers divided the pollen data into three categories based on the presence of cereal pollen: places where agricultural production went up, places where it went down, and places where there was no evidence of cereal cultivation.

"We found a decline in biodiversity overall, but the decline overall was driven by those landscapes that declined in agricultural production," Gordon said.

"In those landscapes where agricultural production went down, there was a reduction in biodiversity of around 40%. Then, after about 150 years, as populations started recovering and landscape disturbances started increasing again, biodiversity went up to slightly above the level it was before."

Many people think there was a "stable and pristine world in which the entry of people has only one result: net loss of species and homogenization," Erle Ellis, an agroecologist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email. "The paleoecologists have always known the story is far more complicated."

There is a growing body of evidence showing that people's long-term cultural shaping of their landscapes often creates more diverse habitats, known as "mosaics," that can sustain more species than simple homogenous landscapes can, he said.

Whereas modern agriculture focuses on single crops on plots of land, in previous centuries, "you had all these different types of agriculture operating within the same landscape," Gordon said.

"In that landscape, you had lots of natural features that remained from the Middle or Early Holocene (which began after the last Ice Age about 12,000 years ago)," he added. "You had old bits of woodland, you had heaths, you had ponds, and bits of secondary forest. It was all interlaced with these agricultural mosaics, and that led to raised biodiversity because there were more habitats for different plant species to exploit."

Modern farming often uses monoculture, where one crop species is grown over a large area. This lowers biodiversity in the area.

The findings highlight the differences between medieval and modern land use practices — and their consequences for biodiversity. Research suggests that during the 20th century, global biodiversity declined by up to as much as 11% and human activities‬, such as land-use changes, pollution, and climate change‬, are the major culprits. In agriculture, the practice of monoculture — where a single crop species is grown over a large area — reduces biodiversity.

"What this work contributes to showing is that, until relatively recently, even in Europe, very different forms of land management and interaction were practiced than exist today," Patrick Roberts, director of Department of Coevolution of Land Use and Urbanisation at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, told Live Science in an email.

"Rather than the monoculture, plantations, or uniform changes to landscapes we see in the 20th and 21st centuries, emphasis was placed on maintaining 'mosaics,'" said Roberts, who was not involved in the new research.

In the study, "we can see how relationships between people and biodiversity have changed through time and how people can actively use landscapes while maintaining biodiversity and mixed ecosystem functions," he said.

There is still more to understand about how humans' disappearance from landscapes in the Black Death era affected the natural world, Gordon said. "There are a lot of other types of diversity ‪—‬ not just the number of types, but what the different types present actually do." There may be a hundred types of plants in a landscape, but if they do the same thing, "you have low functional diversity," he said.

Functional diversity "is super important for how ecosystems adapt to changes in climate and how resilient they are, which is something we need for future-proofing our agricultural system," Gordon said.

Gordon, J. D., Fagan, B., Finch, J., Gillson, L., Milner, N., & Thomas, C. D. (2026). Black death land abandonment drove European diversity losses. Ecology Letters, 29(3), e70325. https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.70325

#121. Scientists Restore Memory in Mice With Alzheimer’s by Boosting a Single Brain Protein

Boosting a protein restored brain rhythms and improved memory in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease, pointing to a potential treatment strategy focused on how brain cells coordinate.

The brain relies on rapid electrical rhythms called gamma oscillations when focusing on a task, learning a skill, or retrieving a memory. These rhythms cycle 30 to 90 times a second, and scientists have known for decades that they weaken in Alzheimer’s disease. What remained unclear was how individual brain cells coordinate their activity to generate them, and why that coordination fails.

Researchers at Gladstone Institutes have now watched specialized brain cells called parvalbumin (PV) interneurons organize these rhythms in awake mice. Their study, published in Neuron, found that the cells take precisely timed turns firing. In mice engineered to develop Alzheimer’s-like disease, that sequence broke down. More cells fired together, yet the gamma rhythms grew weaker.

“Gamma oscillations are essential for clear thinking and memory, but we’ve lacked a complete picture of how the brain creates them,” says Jorge J. Palop, PhD, a Gladstone investigator and senior author of the study. “What makes this discovery so exciting is that we didn’t just figure out how healthy cells pass the baton; we discovered a way to reset their timing when Alzheimer’s related processes throw them off beat.”

In healthy mice, each burst of gamma oscillations involved successive groups of PV cells. The first cells to respond fired strongly, followed by groups with progressively weaker activity. Roughly a third of the cells stayed quiet.

The Alzheimer’s mice lost that balance. Cells that normally responded first were sluggish, later participants were overactive, and fewer cells remained silent. With more cells firing at the same time and at similar activity levels, the orderly sequence gave way to excessive synchrony, weakening the rhythm.

“The important thing here is that more activity is not always going to produce better oscillations or better cognition,” says first author Keran Ma, PhD, who led the work as a postdoctoral scholar at Gladstone and is now an assistant professor at UTHealth Houston. “The dynamics of the cells are most important.”

The recordings also captured epileptic spikes after sudden drops in PV interneuron activity. That observation could help explain why more than a quarter of people with Alzheimer’s show epilepsy-like activity in the brain, although the relationship still needs investigation in humans.

Seeing how individual cells participated required a different approach from earlier experiments. Scientists had previously used methods such as optogenetics, which uses light to activate cells, to switch on PV interneurons simultaneously and demonstrate that they can generate gamma rhythms.

“Turning on all the cells at once shows you what they can do, but not how they naturally work together or how they’re recruited to generate spontaneous gamma oscillations,” Ma says. “Until now, no one has actually been able to image these cells and look at gamma oscillations at the same time in an awake animal during natural behavior.”

The Gladstone team combined real-time electrical recordings with imaging of living cells, allowing them to track brain rhythms alongside the activity of individual PV interneurons. They engineered the cells to glow fluorescently whenever they fired an electrical pulse and monitored awake mice running on a treadmill, an activity that naturally prompts attention-related brain rhythms.

“The relationship between the PV cells and the gamma oscillations was much more dynamic and complex than we expected going into this,” Palop says. “Rather than all the cells contributing to the rhythm at once, each cell contributes for just a brief moment, and those small contributions add up to create the larger brain rhythm. It’s less like a military lockstep march and more like a flock of birds in the sky—each responding to the others, shifting turns and trajectories, yet together creating a remarkably coordinated pattern.”

Palop’s lab had previously identified a molecular change that could affect this timing. Levels of Nav1.1, a sodium channel protein on the surface of PV cells that helps them fire electrical pulses, were reduced in both Alzheimer’s mouse models and people with the disease.

For the new study, the researchers engineered the Alzheimer’s mice to produce more Nav1.1, then monitored their PV cells and brain activity. The additional channels restored the normal waves of interneuron activity and strengthened gamma oscillations. They also reduced epileptic activity and amyloid plaques, a pathological hallmark of Alzheimer’s, while improving the mice’s memory, cognition, and lifespans.

Those benefits were demonstrated in mice. More work is needed to understand the connection between PV cell failure and Alzheimer’s in humans, as well as how Nav1.1 levels or activity could be increased.

“We still don’t know why interneuron dysfunction happens early in Alzheimer’s disease,” Ma says. “But this is another study underscoring that a lot of the pathology of the disease could arise downstream of disrupted interneurons and the abnormal brain rhythms this disruption produces.”

Even in healthy brains, the researchers do not yet know what determines which PV cells participate at any given moment.

“It could be that different thoughts or brain processes are regulated by different assemblies of PV cells,” Palop says. “A lot of interesting questions remain to be answered in the future as we continue our research.”

The ability to target these cells specifically could help researchers pursue treatments. To pinpoint PV interneurons, the team used genetic tools developed at the Allen Institute. Study co-authors Boaz P. Levi, PhD, and Jonathan T. Ting, PhD, helped design these delivery vehicles to reach particular brain cell types across different species.

“One of the most exciting aspects of this work is our ability to target a single cell type out of the hundreds in the brain,” Levi says. “Because these tools work in both mice and humans, they help us bridge the gap between understanding how individual cells fail in disease and developing targeted treatments to fix them.”

“This collaboration illustrates where this field is headed,” Ting adds. “By combining precise delivery tools with a deep understanding of Alzheimer’s, we can start designing treatments that act only on the specific cells responsible for restoring healthy brain function.”

Palop and his team are now working to develop small-molecule Nav1.1 enhancers designed to boost interneuron activity in Alzheimer’s disease and other disorders, moving toward potential therapies while continuing to investigate how the cells coordinate brain rhythms.

Reference: “Parvalbumin cell state dynamics regulate gamma oscillations and are disrupted in Alzheimer’s disease” by Keran Ma, Kyerl Park, Patrick S. #122. New Observations Show How Black Holes Stir Up Material Surrounding A Galaxy

Supermassive black holes are powerful engines. They can rip stars apart and feed upon them. They blast jets of ionized gas at near-light speeds. On the other hand, these gravitational beasts are rather small. Though they can be millions or billions of solar masses, they are localized to within the size of a stellar system. The galaxies they call home span more than 100,000 light-years and can be more than 100 billion solar masses. So how do these localized powerhouses have such a large impact on galactic evolution? This is the focus of a new study in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

We know from observations that black holes and their galaxies are intimately connected. We are still figuring out just how they interact. Much of the research focuses on the central region of a galaxy. After all, that's where the black hole is and where most of the stars, gas, and dust are located. This new study focuses on the outer region of a galaxy.

Although the stellar region of a galaxy is the part we easily see, galaxies also have a large region of gas surrounding them known as the circumgalactic medium (CGM). Over time the CGM cools and falls inward, providing a source of material for new stars. But surveys of CGM regions find that much of it remains at the outer edge of a galaxy. The question is why, and the answer seems to be the galactic black hole.

The powerful jets of a supermassive black hole carry material to the outer edge of the galaxy, but only along the polar axis of the black hole. It has been thought that much of the circumgalactic material wouldn't be affected by it. This new study finds a subtle interaction.

The team looked at H-alpha regions around hundreds of galaxies with active jets. H-alpha emissions are caused by ionized hydrogen. Anywhere you see the H-alpha signal, you know the region is warm enough to ionize hydrogen. Using data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) survey and the LOFAR Two-meter Sky Survey (LoTSS), the authors found H-alpha regions close to the jets as expected, but they also found that the light of the jets ionizes regions farther away as well. This means the jets heat the CGM more than we thought. The team also looked at an absorption line of magnesium, which indicated a lower overall temperature within the CGM. Thus, the heating is clearly driven by the jets themselves.

What this means is that active jets stir the pot. Heat is exchanged to the circumgalactic material, reducing the amount that falls inward to the galaxy. As a result, there is less material available for stars to form. There are other factors that drive star production, but this study shows how some interactions are subtle.

Galactic black holes are deadly to stars that stray too close, but they can also prevent some distant stars from being formed in the first place.

Reference: Roy, Namrata, et al. "Lighting Up the Circumgalactic Medium: Strong, Jet-aligned H Î± Emission around Radio Galaxies." The Astrophysical Journal Letters 1009.2 (2026): L34.

Brian Koberlein is an astrophysicist and author of the books Astrophysics Through Computation and Radio Sky: 40 Years of the Very Large Array. You can find more of his work on his website.

#123. Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene

Some people carry one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease yet never develop it, remaining mentally sharp well into their 80s. For years, scientists have wondered what protects these individuals despite their increased genetic vulnerability.

Now, researchers at Columbia University have uncovered a biological mechanism that could help explain this remarkable resistance. Their findings point to a rare genetic mutation that protects the brain's blood vessels from damage, potentially opening a new path toward Alzheimer's treatments.

The discovery builds on research the team published two years ago involving APOE ε4, a gene variant strongly associated with Alzheimer's risk. The scientists found that some people carrying APOE ε4 also possess a rare protective mutation in the fibronectin (FN1) gene.

Fibronectin is a protein that helps support the structure of tissues. However, in people with APOE ε4, excessive amounts can accumulate around blood vessels in the brain, potentially compromising a critical protective system known as the blood-brain barrier. The rare FN1 mutation appears to limit this buildup and the damage associated with it.

That earlier discovery suggested an intriguing possibility: What if scientists could develop a treatment that recreates the protection provided by this rare mutation?

A new study published in Nature Aging brings that possibility closer by identifying how excess fibronectin damages the brain's protective barrier and revealing potential ways to interrupt the process.

"This new study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism," says Caghan Kizil, the study's corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer's Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

"We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer's, but we didn't know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism -- and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection."

How an Alzheimer's Risk Gene Weakens the Blood-Brain Barrier

The blood-brain barrier serves as a protective boundary between the bloodstream and the brain. Made up of tightly connected cells surrounding the brain's blood vessels, it carefully regulates which substances can enter brain tissue while helping maintain conditions necessary for removing potentially harmful waste.

When this barrier becomes damaged or excessively permeable, substances that would normally be kept out can enter the brain more easily. Such disruptions may contribute to inflammation and other processes involved in neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's.

To investigate the role of fibronectin, the Columbia team combined several advanced research approaches. They examined human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, using genetic and epigenetic analyses to explore changes in DNA and gene activity.

Their investigation also included single-cell sequencing, which reveals the activity of individual cells, and spatial imaging to examine where biological changes occur within tissues. Additional experiments involved human stem-cell models, three-dimensional cultures of blood vessels, and studies in zebrafish and mice.

Despite the variety of methods, the findings consistently pointed to the same mechanism: APOE ε4 promotes the production and accumulation of fibronectin around the brain's blood vessels.

In mice engineered to carry human APOE ε4, researchers measured nearly twice as much fibronectin in the brain as in mice carrying APOE ε3, another common version of the gene. The greater accumulation was accompanied by evidence that the blood-brain barrier had become leaky.

Scientists Discover How Fibronectin Causes Brain Damage

One experiment provided especially important evidence that fibronectin does more than simply accumulate in damaged blood vessels.

The researchers increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes, specialized support cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier and keep the brain functioning properly.

Increasing fibronectin in these cells was enough to disrupt the barrier, allowing it to become more permeable. Conversely, reducing fibronectin improved the barrier's ability to function normally.

These results provided experimental evidence that excess fibronectin can directly contribute to blood-brain barrier damage rather than merely appearing alongside it.

"The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association," says co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved."

The team then investigated the molecular events responsible for the damage.

They found that excessive fibronectin interferes with communication between cells by activating abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that help cells sense and respond to their surroundings, and an enzyme known as focal adhesion kinase.

These abnormal signals disrupt a network of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. Although growth factors are often associated with cell development and repair, these particular signaling molecules also help astrocytes and blood vessel cells coordinate their activities to maintain a healthy blood-brain barrier.

When their communication becomes disrupted, the barrier can lose its integrity, potentially leaving brain tissue more vulnerable to damage.

"Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain's blood vessels," says co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer's tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling."

Evidence From Human Brains Strengthens the Alzheimer's Connection

Importantly, the researchers found signs of similar biological disturbances in human samples, suggesting that the process identified in laboratory experiments may also contribute to Alzheimer's disease in people carrying APOE ε4.

Analyses of brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid showed that elevated fibronectin levels were associated with inflammation in astrocytes.

Genetic and gene-regulation analyses also connected FN1 to blood vessel disease and changes involving VEGFA, a growth factor that plays an important role in maintaining healthy brain blood vessels.

Together, these findings provide multiple lines of evidence linking excess fibronectin to the vascular damage associated with APOE ε4.

"The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process," says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on this discovery of the FN1 mutation.

A Rare Genetic Defense Could Inspire New Alzheimer's Treatments

The potential implications are significant because APOE ε4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Approximately one in five people carries at least one copy of this gene variant.

Although carrying APOE ε4 does not guarantee that someone will develop Alzheimer's, it increases their likelihood of developing the disease. Understanding why certain carriers remain unaffected could reveal new opportunities for prevention and treatment.

The latest findings suggest several possible approaches.

One strategy would be to prevent harmful amounts of fibronectin from accumulating around the brain's blood vessels. Another would involve blocking the abnormal cellular signals triggered by excess fibronectin. A third possibility would be to restore the growth factor signaling that allows astrocytes and blood vessel cells to maintain the blood-brain barrier.

Researchers are already investigating these possibilities through laboratory experiments.

However, translating the discovery into a treatment will require considerable care. Fibronectin performs essential functions throughout the body, including supporting tissue structure and helping damaged tissues heal. Any future therapy would therefore need to target its harmful accumulation or effects without disrupting these beneficial activities.

By identifying the molecular mechanisms involved, scientists now have a more precise framework for designing such treatments. The findings may also help researchers determine when interventions would be most effective and how to measure whether they are successfully protecting the brain.

"By showing how fibronectin contributes to early vascular damage, this study gives us new therapeutic targets and potential ways to measure whether treatments are working," says Richard Mayeux, chair of the Department of Neurology and a collaborator on the project. "Clinically, it connects a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's to an early disease process that may be possible to modify."

Although these potential therapies remain experimental, the discovery offers a promising new direction in Alzheimer's research. Rather than focusing only on the damage that develops as the disease progresses, scientists may eventually be able to reproduce a natural genetic defense that helps protect vulnerable brains before significant damage occurs.

Materials provided by Columbia University Irving Medical Center. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#124. Juvenile striped bass maintaining average abundance in Virginia waters in 2026

Preliminary results from an ongoing long-term survey conducted by William & Mary's Virginia Institute of Marine Science (VIMS) suggest that an average year class of young-of-year striped bass was produced in the Virginia tributaries of the Chesapeake Bay in 2026. Striped bass are an important top predator in the Chesapeake Bay ecosystem and a valuable resource for commercial and recreational anglers. The 2026 year class, representing fish hatched this spring, will reach fishable sizes in three to four years.

#125. Voyager 1 is nearly one light-day from Earth. What’s out there?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The spacecraft is finding the sun’s reach extends farther than expected

(Left) Engineers test Voyager 1 in a clean room in California in November 1976. (Right) The spacecraft launched from Cape Canaveral, Fla., on September 5, 1977. Voyager 2 had already launched, but it followed a longer path.

JPL-Caltech/NASA; JPL-Caltech and KSC/NASA

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has been breaking distance records for decades. Launched almost 50 years ago, it became the farthest human-built object from Earth when it overtook the pathfinding Pioneer 10 probe in 1998. It was the first spacecraft to leave the solar system’s protective bubble, and it will be humankind’s first emissary to the stars.

The cameras on Voyager 1, along with those on its twin spacecraft, Voyager 2, captured powerful megastorms in the outer solar system, the first images of dozens of moons and never-before-seen details of the gossamer rings around Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and Uranus. The images and data sent home have shaped theories of how the solar system formed and evolved, inspired subsequent missions and posed enough new questions to keep space scientists busy for decades.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

And this month, Voyager 1 will set another big record. On November 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern Standard Time, it will become the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth: the distance light travels in 24 hours. That’s a journey of 25.9 billion kilometers, or more than four times the distance from the sun to Pluto. At that point, signals from Earth will take a full day to reach Voyager 1; it will take another day to hear back.

“I just never imagined [the mission] would last that long,” says Linda Spilker, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., who began working on Voyager shortly before the probes launched in 1977. Spilker was in Cape Canaveral, Fla., for the first launch. She even planned the births of her children, now in their 40s, around mission milestones. After stepping away to lead another mission, she is now back as Voyager head scientist.

Two other scientists have been with Voyager since the beginning. Others weren’t yet born when the spacecraft launched. “Voyager, to this day, is a multi-generational mission,” Spilker says. But it isn’t a mission of nostalgia. There’s still a world of discovery out beyond the solar system’s edge.

“Every piece of data, every day that goes by that we get data from the Voyagers, tells us something new,” says physicist Jamie Rankin of Princeton University, who started her Ph.D. in August 2012, the same month that Voyager 1 left the solar system for the cold, calm seas of interstellar space. “Every day, it’s in places nobody’s ever explored before.”

The original mission of the Voyager probes was to explore the outer parts of our solar system, which until then had remained largely mysterious. A rare planetary alignment meant that a spacecraft launched in the late 1970s could swoop past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, getting a gravitational boost from each planet that it passed. With these gravitational assists, the spacecraft could complete the tour in less than 15 years. Such an alignment won’t happen again until the 2150s.

The project was a bold step for its time. When work began in the early 1970s, no spacecraft had gone farther than Mars. NASA set a conservative goal for the mission: flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1972 and 1973, NASA launched two Pioneer probes, which made sure the trek was possible and gathered data along the way. As with Voyager, there were two spacecraft in case one failed.

After nail-biting launches and a wait of nearly two years, the Voyagers began uncovering many of Jupiter’s and Saturn’s long-held secrets, including the volcanoes on Jupiter’s moon Io, details of Jupiter’s Great Red Spot and hints of geologic activity on Saturn’s moon Enceladus.

Mission accomplished, Voyager 2 went on to pass Uranus and Neptune. It took the first images of the planets’ rings and discovered more than a dozen moons along the way. The spacecraft also spotted a perpetually churning storm on Neptune and erupting geysers on Neptune’s moon Triton.

“The highlights of Voyager were clearly the planetary encounters,” said Ed Stone, the mission’s original head scientist, in a NASA interview before his death in 2024. “We had a lifetime of discovery packed into each one.”

The uncontested stars of these encounters were the images shared in news reports and TV broadcasts as the planets and their moons came into view. Jupiter’s moon Io turned out to be a shocking splotchy orange color that looked like a pizza.

A humble navigation image of that moon led to one of the most surprising discoveries of the entire mission. Four days past Voyager 1’s closest approach to Jupiter, after the excitement had died down, project astronomer Linda Morabito of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory started processing additional images of Io. These images had been taken after the flyby, when Voyager was looking back over its shoulder.

As Morabito enhanced one image’s brightness, she spotted an odd bulbous formation protruding from Io’s edge. “What’s that?” she asked herself. Her supervisor had the same reaction: “Jesus, what’s that?” she later recalled him saying.

The bulb turned out to be a volcanic plume — an erupting fire fountain extending 250 kilometers above Io’s surface. It was the first discovery of active volcanism anywhere other than Earth, and it transformed our view of the outer solar system. Instead of a cold, inert icebox, this was a bubbling and dynamic region.

The findings inspired many future missions. While visiting Jupiter from 1995 to 2003, the Galileo probe found that Europa may have a subsurface ocean that could be hospitable to life. When the Cassini probe orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, it discovered that the moon Enceladus also has a potentially habitable ocean that spews icy geysers into space.

In 1990, with Voyager 1 about 6 billion kilometers from the sun, astronomer Carl Sagan convinced mission leaders to turn the spacecraft backward for one last look at the planets. Voyager 1 took a family portrait in which Earth appeared faintly as a “pale blue dot,” Sagan said. “Everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives … on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam,” he wrote in the 1994 book Pale Blue Dot.

To save power, Voyager 2’s cameras were shut off in 1989. After the family portrait, Voyager 1’s cameras were also turned off. Where the spacecraft were headed, there wouldn’t be much to see.

The probes were now on their way out of the solar system along their own separate paths, both headed toward a mysterious boundary that no human emissary had ever crossed. In this next phase of their voyage, no one knew what to expect. How long would the spacecraft keep communicating? How far would the powerful forces that drive the sun reach? And what would it be like to taste interstellar space?

For its first 35 years in space, Voyager 1 was swaddled in the solar wind. This stream of hot, charged particles flows constantly from the sun, forming a vast bubble called the helio­sphere. The bubble surrounds the solar system, protecting it from cosmic radiation; it extends billions of kilometers past the planets up to a boundary called the heliopause. Heliophysicists consider this boundary, where the solar wind bumps into interstellar space, the edge of the solar system, although the sun’s gravitational influence extends much farther.

Scientists expected the Voyagers to cross the heliopause, but they didn’t know when — or what the spacecraft would find when they did. Rankin had just started her Ph.D. at Caltech when in August 2012 Voyager 1 detected an abrupt jump in the number of high-energy cosmic rays alongside a drop in solar particles, hinting that the spacecraft had crossed the boundary. But magnetic field measurements suggested other­wise. Instead, those measurements indicated that the sun still exerted some influence. The interstellar magnetic field diverted around the heliosphere like a river around a rock.

A Voyager instrument that could have settled the question of whether the probe had passed the heliopause was no longer working. But scientists got a lucky break in April 2013 when an eruption on the sun sent a pressure wave rippling outward. It set the electrons around Voyager 1 vibrating, which allowed scientists to estimate the density of charged particles nearby.

The results showed that Voyager 1 had in fact crossed the heliopause on August 25, 2012, when it was about 18 billion kilometers away, or 120 times Earth’s distance from the sun. Data from Voyager 2 later backed up that finding. “This is the beginning of a new era of exploration for us,” Stone told Science News in 2013.

But the line between our solar system and interstellar space isn’t solid. The sun’s reach extends farther than anyone expected, and “this boundary is not very sharp or very thin,” says physicist Jeewoo Park of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md.

With Voyager on the other side of the heliopause, particle speeds and gas temperatures have dropped. The magnetic field is weaker. Even dust particles are about half as abundant compared with inside the heliosphere. “For the most part, it’s been very quiet and very consistent,” Rankin says.

But it’s not entirely silent. In four instances, scientists saw spikes in the magnetic field strength and particle density measurements around the probe. After the fourth, in mid-2020, those numbers have remained high. No one knows why. Perhaps Voyager 1 continues to ride the aftershocks of solar eruptions, says Park, who reported on the events in June in the Astrophysical Journal.

Where pure interstellar space begins is still an open question. So is the heliosphere’s shape. Most scientists think it is elongated, like a comet, but others think it is a sphere or even a croissant.

Space telescopes launched in 2008 and 2025, the Interstellar Boundary Explorer and Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe, could help answer that question.

Meanwhile, the Voyager probes are silently sailing onward. Scientists estimate that the onboard power sources that keep the crafts’ instruments running will dry up in 10 to 15 years, preventing them from sending data back to Earth. Our conversation will come to an end. But the journey goes on.

Voyager 2 will approach a red dwarf star known as Ross 248 in about 42,000 years, coming within 700 light-days. It will be 44,000 years before Voyager 1 next encounters another star, Gliese 445, at a similar distance. “The Voyagers become our silent ambassadors, a little bit of us that continues into space,” Spilker says.

They carry a message, should anyone find it, contained on the Golden Record. A copy of the phono­graph record, which is plated in gold, rides on each of the probes. The long-distance dispatches feature sights and sounds of Earth, including a map of the solar system; images of Earth’s monuments; greetings in dozens of languages; and the sounds of whale song, laughter, classical composers and Navajo chants.

That time capsule captures the optimism and promise of the mission, Spilker says. “It may well outlast humanity.”

#126. Reddit Users Are Experimenting With an Unapproved Weight-Loss Drug. AI Found Something Surprising

An AI analysis of nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments offers the first systematic look at symptoms people attribute to gray-market retatrutide, showing how social media could guide drug safety research.

People are buying unapproved versions of retatrutide, a next-generation GLP-1 weight-loss drug, and sharing their experiences on Reddit before the drug has received approval for use. The products they describe taking are not intended for human consumption, but their posts offer researchers a way to examine experiences that conventional drug-safety monitoring may miss.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania used AI to analyze nearly 150,000 posts and comments from roughly 40,000 Reddit users, producing the first systematic look at the potential symptoms reported by people claiming to take these unapproved products. In their study, published in JAMA Network Open, increased appetite was the most frequently reported symptom among users whose reports could be classified, after expected effects such as weight loss and appetite suppression were excluded.

That finding contrasts with retatrutide’s Phase 2 clinical trials, which demonstrated weight-loss effects and identified nausea and other gastrointestinal complaints as the most common side effects. The drug is currently in Phase 3 trials, the final stage of clinical testing before possible FDA approval. The Reddit accounts, however, cannot establish that retatrutide caused the reported symptoms or that these users’ experiences reflect those of clinical trial participants.

“We can’t say that retatrutide is causing these symptoms, or even that Reddit users are actually taking genuine retatrutide, since the drug is not legally available, and gray market formulations vary,” says Lyle Ungar, a professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS) at Penn and a study co-author.

Retatrutide also acts differently from the better-known drugs semaglutide and tirzepatide. Semaglutide activates one hormone receptor involved in regulating appetite and blood sugar, while tirzepatide activates two. Retatrutide activates three, giving the researchers a reason to investigate whether reports from people claiming to use it might show a different pattern of symptoms.

Compared with the team’s earlier analysis of Reddit discussions about semaglutide and tirzepatide, posts about gray-market retatrutide contained proportionally more reports of appetite-related symptoms, sleep disturbances, increased heart rate, and muscle-related changes. Reports of nausea and other gastrointestinal symptoms were proportionally less common.

“Retatrutide works differently from existing GLP-1 drugs, so it’s possible that its effects on the body are different, too,” says Jena Shaw Tronieri, a senior research investigator at Penn’s Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a study co-author.

“But the people discussing it on Reddit also may be different,” she notes. “Users willing to obtain an unapproved medication on the gray market likely differ from other clinical populations. Some may be taking multiple experimental peptides, and we can’t verify exactly what they’re taking. We need more research to understand what, if anything, these differences in self-reported symptoms mean.”

To identify accounts of personal use within the larger Reddit dataset, the researchers used AI tools to find users who described taking an unapproved version of retatrutide. Approximately 14,000 users met that description. The tools then extracted symptoms those users attributed to the product and matched their descriptions to standardized medical terminology. After excluding expected effects such as weight loss and appetite suppression, the analysis included 7,823 users who reported at least one classifiable potential symptom.

“A researcher might be able to examine a few thousand Reddit posts by hand, but looking at nearly 150,000 would be an enormous undertaking,” says Neil Sehgal, the study’s first author and a doctoral student in CIS at Penn. “AI makes it possible to analyze these conversations at scale, identifying patterns in what people are sharing that would otherwise be difficult to recognize.”

The approach grew out of the Penn team’s earlier work using large language models, or LLMs, to examine more than 400,000 Reddit posts about semaglutide and tirzepatide. That analysis identified potential side effects, including menstrual irregularities, that may not have been fully captured in clinical trials or regulatory documents. “We wanted to apply the same methodology to gray-market retatrutide,” says Sehgal.

The new results should be treated as leads for further research, rather than evidence of previously unrecognized side effects. “This is the first glimpse into the experiences of a population that is otherwise outside conventional drug safety monitoring because they are taking unapproved versions of a drug that has yet to finish clinical trials,” says Sehgal.

“Our goal is to identify hypotheses in online conversations that we could test. AI helps us find recurring patterns in people’s self-reports, including experiences that may be missed by conventional drug-safety monitoring,” says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, a research associate professor in CIS, director of Penn’s Computational Social Listening Lab, and the paper’s senior author.

The researchers hope this approach can identify potential safety concerns earlier and give clinicians and public health researchers a starting point for investigation. Sehgal points to what happened after the team reported menstrual irregularities in its earlier GLP-1 study. Another research group was inspired to examine the same symptoms using the FDA’s adverse-event database. Its subsequent study in Obstetrics & Gynecology also found disproportionate reports of certain menstrual changes, adding evidence that those symptoms merit investigation.

“That’s what we hope will happen with this study,” says Sehgal. “Other researchers can take what we find on Reddit and look for the same patterns in other datasets, using entirely different methods. Whether those signals hold up or not, the goal is to build a better understanding of what people are actually experiencing.”

Reference: “Self-Reported Adverse Effects Among Social Media Users Taking Nonapproved Retatrutide” by Neil K. R. Sehgal, Jena Shaw Tronieri, Benjamin Rader, Lyle Ungar and Sharath Chandra Guntuku, 14 October 2026, JAMA Network Open. DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.38929

This project was funded in part by the University of Pennsylvania’s Penn Medical Communication Research Institute.

#127. Achievement Unlocked: Microblazar Confirmed

In this Universe, nothing can travel faster than light. Only light itself can reach lightspeed, as far as we know. But some things get awfully close to the speed of light, and when these things are detected, astrophysicists take note.

Researchers found electrons with extremely high energies travelling at close to the speed of light, coming from an unusual source. The source is a microblazar, the first one ever detected. What's a microblazar?

Understanding microblazars starts with understanding supermassive black holes (SMBH), active galactic nuclei, and quasars, which are all facets of the same thing.

When a SMBH in the center of a galaxy is actively feeding and drawing gas and dust toward itself, it's called an active galactic nuclei (AGN). The material gathers in an accretion disk rotating around the SMBH, where it heats up and emits energetic light. The brightest of these AGN are called quasars.

Not all of the gas and dust in the accretion disk finds its way into the SMBH. Some of the material drawn toward the SMBH is ejected in a pair of massive energetic jets that are emitted in opposite directions from the SMBH's axis of rotation.

When one of these jets is aimed at Earth, we call it a blazar. In this case, the object the researchers found is a microblazar, and the difference between it and a blazar is largely a matter of scale. A blazar is extragalactic, and powered by another galaxy's SMBH, while a microblazar is within the Milky Way.

A microblazar consists of a stellar-mass black hole rather than a SMBH. (Instead of a black hole, there could be a neutron star, another extremely dense astrophysical object.) In a microblazar, the black hole or neutron star has a companion star, which is the source of material that forms the accretion ring. The same type of high-energy jets are emitted as in a quasar, just on a smaller scale. To be a microblazar, one of the jets must be pointed at Earth, just like with a blazar.

Both blazars and microblazars are also called x-ray binaries. The system contains two bodies interacting with one another that produce powerful x-ray radiation, and even the more powerful gamma-rays.

Astrophysicists have theorized about the existence of microblazars, and now, new research in Astronomy and Astrophysics presents the first one ever detected. The jets from the microblazar could be powering the fastest particles in the Milky Way.

The research is titled "A Galactic microblazar as a potential accelerator of ultra-high-energy particles," and the first author is Jose Marti. Marti is a professor of astronomy and astrophysics at the University of JaÃ©n in JaÃ©n, AndalucÃ­a, Spain.

"Persistent jets from X-ray binaries that are aligned very close to the line of sight could be considered Galactic equivalents of blazars, or âmicroblazarsâ," the authors write. "They are also expected to power gamma-ray sources."

An object named IRAS 18293â0941 is a candidate microblazar. Astronomers first detected it back in 1989, when it was identified as an infrared source. More detailed study of the objects was held up for years. It's in the plane of the Milky Way, where gas and dust obscure its true nature. But as telescopes became more powerful and astronomical methods more advanced, they brought IRAS 18293â0941 into clearer view.

"We carried out an intense, multi-wavelength observational and theoretical study on our proposed candidate source," the authors write. They used MeerKAT, the VLA, and other telescopes, along with spectroscopes and x-ray observatories to examine the source more thoroughly.

Their results show that IRAS 18293â0941 has a black hole with about 10 solar masses, and a massive star, either a blue giant or a blue supergiant. It's about 11,700 light years away, in the constellation Scutum. The combined masses of the pair of objects classifies it as high-mass x-ray binary. At some point in the past, both objects were massive stars. But one of them exploded as a supernovae and became a black hole.

The powerful jets are a critical part of this discovery. The fact that they're long-lasting, continuous, and high-energy, rather than a short-term phenomenon, helps identify the object as a microblazar.

This image highlights how the jets terminate. The receding jet terminates in a star-forming molecular cloud, where it will affect star formation. It also creates a non-thermal hotspot, a sort of natural laboratory to study high-energy particles. Image Credit: MartÃ­ et al. 2026. A&A

"The inferred jet power and sustained activity imply that IRAS 18293â0941 is capable of accelerating particles to VHE and potentially UHE, in line with recent studies linking microquasars to Galactic PeVatrons," the authors write. VHE is very high energy, meaning the particles have tera-electronvolt (TeV) levels. UHE is ultra-high energy, meaning the particles have peta-electronvolt (PeV) energy levels.

Detectors have sensed PeV level particles for years, but their source has remained unclear. Tracing them to IRAS 18293-0941 is an important development. It confirms the existence of microblazars and microquasars, and the discovery helps build a better understanding of the range of astrophysical objects in the Universe, especially high-energy ones.

"Our reported identification not only helps fill a gap in Galactic taxonomy, it also potentially strengthens the role of the microblazar and microquasar families in our understanding of the most energetic Milky Way phenomena," the authors write.

There's more to discover about this object, and the researchers intend to study it more to tease out more details. Astrophysical jets alter their surroundings, especially the interstellar medium they slam into, and that is certain to affect star formation.

This illustration shows the complex environment around IRAS 18293â0941. "1). A dense circumbinary dusty shell surrounds the system (2) and is distorted by the approaching (blue) jet (3), which eventually breaks out and expands into the lower density ambient medium, inflating a cocoon. The receding (red) jet (4) propagates toward a dense molecular cloud (5), where it produces a radio hotspot and injects accelerated cosmic rays into the cloud, giving rise to high-energy emission through hadronic processes," the authors write. Image Credit: MartÃ­ et al. 2026. A&A

The receding jet from the black hole smashes into a molecular cloud, creating what astrophsyicists call a "non-thermal hotspot." That means it's not created by a star, but by high-energy particles spriralling through magnetic fields, called synchrotron radiation, or by particle collisions. This creates high-energy radiation, and in this case, the radiation lines up with a known hot spot or source. The hot spot is the key to this work.

This artists impression shows the new microblazar (centre) creating two powerful jets, one directed at Earth (left) and the other hitting a molecular interstellar cloud (right). This is the first confirmed microblazar, and the discovery fills a hole in our understanding of the hierarchy of astrophysical objects. The receding jet slams into a molecular cloud, creating an opportunity to study high-energy particles in more detail. Image Credit: B. Marcote (JIVE/ASTRON)/MartÃ­ et al. 2026

Since the source of the jets and the hot spot the receding jet creates are so far apartâtens of parsecs away from each otherâit creates a kind of natural laboratory where astrophysicists can study how galactic particles can be accelerated to such high energies.

âWe are planning more observations on the area of the hotspot where the jet hits the interstellar medium," lead author Marcote said in a press release. âBetter characterizing this region and how the material gets heated and ionized would have strong implications for the galactic formation of stars, that happens in molecular clouds. It can also teach us how microblazars impact the structure and evolution of galaxies like the Milky Way.â

âThis discovery highlights the power of studying the Universe with different kind of telescopes at the same time, because none of the individual telescopes could have told the entire story," said study co-author Jakob van den Eijnden, from the University of Amsterdam. âIt is a great showcase of the international team efforts that are at the core of modern astronomy.â

Pa 30, linked to a supernova seen in 1181, reveals chains of tiny gas knots in a new image from the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where it is: 7,500 light-years away, in the constellation Cassiopeia

A mysterious "guest star" recorded by medieval astronomers nearly 850 years ago has revealed new secrets after scientists obtained the clearest images yet of its explosive aftermath.

New observations of Pa 30, thought to be the leftovers of a historic supernova called SN 1181, show that its spectacular firework-like filaments are not smooth streams of material. Instead, they consist of chains of tiny gas knots.

SN 1181 is so called because astronomers in China and Japan recorded its brief appearance in the year 1181, when they saw it as a naked-eye object in the constellation Cassiopeia. Eight surviving texts date its appearance to between Aug. 4 and 6 of that year. The mysterious object remained visible for 185 days.

"It's rare to get this level of detail on a supernova we can date to a specific week in history," Timothy Cunningham, an assistant professor of astronomy and astrophysics at the University of Warwick who led an international team of researchers to study the object, said in a statement.

SN 1181 is one of only five supernovas in the Milky Way galaxy known to have been witnessed from Earth before the invention of the telescope. (Those optical instruments first appeared in the Netherlands in 1608.) Now, advanced ground-based telescopes can produce wonderfully detailed images of those historic remnants. This latest image is from the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii and reveals about 10 times more filamentary structures in Pa 30 than have been seen before. This extraordinary detail gives astronomers fresh clues about the unusual explosion and the environment surrounding the star.

"These images give us the clearest picture yet of Pa 30's structure, and it's not what we expected," said Cunningham, whose team published their findings in The Astrophysical Journal. "The filaments are made of chains of tiny knots rather than smooth streaks, providing new constraints on the nature of the space around the star before it exploded and the physical processes that have shaped the expanding ejecta."

The knot-like structures may have resulted from variations in temperature or density in material surrounding the star as debris from the explosion expanded.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Pa 30 contains another unusual feature: a surviving star that sits almost exactly at the center of the remnant. That's highly unusual, because a supernova explosion typically sends stars away from their original positions. It suggests that the original explosion was highly symmetrical, the researchers said.

Furthermore, Pa 30 is thought to be a Type Iax supernova. Unlike standard Type Ia supernovas, which destroy their stars, a Type Iax event is a lower-energy, incomplete explosion of a white dwarf star that can leave behind a remnant known as a "zombie star." It's the only Type Iax supernova ever found.

He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.

The popularity of the giant-impact hypothesis can be attributed to the multiple lines of evidence supporting the impact scenario.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For as long as humans have watched the night sky, we have wondered about the moon, pondering everything from its alien appearance to its influence over phenomena on Earth such as ocean tides, climate stability, and even the natural rhythms of many organisms.

Among the many questions we have about Earth's lone natural satellite, one remains preeminent: what are the moon's origins, and how long has it orbited Earth?

Today, the leading theory among astronomers is that deep in our planet's past — perhaps within roughly the first 100 million years of solar system history — Earth collided with a planet-sized object, creating the moon within a period that may have been as short as just a few hours. Known as the giant-impact hypothesis, this proposed event involves a hypothetical Mars-sized protoplanet astronomers call Theia. The material ejected into orbit by the powerful impact in question would have accumulated afterward, forming the moon that we observe today.

The evolution of this striking solution to one of the moon's most enduring mysteries goes back to 1946, when geologist Reginald Aldworth Daly was among the first to suggest that an impact event might explain the formation of the moon.

Before Daly, scientists had been leaning toward theories that involved Earth's rapid spin billions of years ago, when each day may have at one time lasted as little as 2 or 3 hours. Decades later in the 1970s, researchers William Hartmann and Donald Davis developed their own models involving collisions of large bodies left over from planetary formation, which could collide with younger planets.

Building on such ideas, other researchers went on to propose similar scenarios between the early Earth and a Mars-sized object. Early in the following decade, the concept eventually claimed its place as the leading lunar-formation process during a landmark conference held in Kona, Hawaii, in 1984.

The popularity of the giant-impact hypothesis can be attributed to the multiple lines of evidence supporting the impact scenario. For instance, researchers have long recognized the similar stable-isotope ratios between both moon rocks and those from Earth, strongly suggesting a link between their origins.

Additionally, the unusually high angular momentum (or spin) of the Earth-moon system, when compared to observations of other rocky planets, also could be explained as one of the effects of a massive collision.

Further clues can be found in the moon's composition, which reveals a relatively small iron core and lower density. This is significant to astronomers, since a hypothetical giant impact would have seen the suspected Theia protoplanet's metallic core merging with the young Earth's interior — meanwhile, lighter mantle and crust material from both worlds would have become dislodged and blasted into orbit, eventually helping form the moon.

Another important piece of evidence involves the relative depletion of volatile substances (a chemical that easily turns into gas or vapor at room temperatures) in lunar material, which again suggests that it might have been lost during an extremely energetic event, an idea further supported by evidence that the early moon once possessed a substantial magma ocean.

Still, several significant questions remain, including what precise conditions led to the impact, and how the resulting planetary material evolved into the moon as it appears today.

Recently, a new study by Adeene Denton of Southwest Research Institute and colleagues at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory put a new spin on the Theia hypothesis, suggesting that the suspected ancient impact may have been significantly influenced by the heat and physical strength of the two colliding bodies.

The team's findings challenge some long-held views about the giant-impact hypothesis, while lending new support to others. For instance, the team's simulations revealed that while some impacts lead to the creation of a disk of debris that later coalesces into a moon, under other conditions, simulations support the idea that the moon could have been formed in a remarkably short period of time — perhaps within around five hours.

However, one of the primary issues with determining the exact conditions of the giant-impact hypothesis involves the ongoing debate over the moon's age.

"There is a large controversy regarding the age of the moon," said Dr. Erik Asphaug, a planetary science professor at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and one of the new study's co-authors.

In an email to Space, Asphaug explained some of the issues arising from this, since current estimates place the timing of the moon's formation anywhere from around 40 to 120 million years after the formation of the solar system. Therein lies part of the issue, according to Asphaug, who says this timing could have significant implications for models of the Theia impact.

If it had been an earlier collision, Asphaug says this would have involved a hotter Theia due to the greater degree of radiogenic heating; by contrast, a later impact would have meant a cooler and stronger Theia.

"I don't think we know enough yet to say the moon (and by corollary, the Earth) formed this way or that way," Asphaug told Space. "But knowing how temperature affects the result opens up a new dimension for viewing the problem, and that is always helpful because it shifts our frame of reference, like getting out of the car to have a walk around."

For researchers like Asphaug, understanding the moon's formation requires looking at it as more than just an event in space, but also as one in time. Doing so allows comparisons between three different metrics: isotopic decay, temperature-dependent material strength, and the geological record of debris striking other planets — a process through which he believes tighter constraints could be placed on precisely when the moon-forming impact might have occurred.

Adeene Denton, the study's lead author, also emphasized the introduction of the time component her team's research brings to the table, telling Space in an email that the outcome of the moon-forming impact could have depended significantly on the timing of the collision.

"Before, scientists have generally assumed that the outcome of the collision will be the same regardless of when it takes place," Denton wrote. "But now we know that temperature's effect on material properties, which is dictated by how old and/or cold the proto-Earth and Theia might be, alters things substantially."

By connecting impact simulations to data related to the moon's geochemical record, as well as models of early solar system formation, Denton thinks her team's work could help scientists better constrain precisely how and when the moon formed.

For now, in terms of which possible scenario — an earlier or later collision event — emerges as being the most likely, Denton says it's still difficult to say.

"It depends on which scenarios for solar system formation you favor," Denton told Space.

"I am generally in favor of an earlier formation of the moon, consistent with a rapid planet-building phase in our solar system," Denton said, "but we can't neglect the possibility that the moon formed late."

While much work remains to be done, Denton and Asphaug believe their findings help significantly advance present efforts to resolve some of the questions about the giant-impact hypothesis — a few of which have lingered now for many years.

For Asphaug, however, such lingering questions may simply be part of the scientific process.

"Science has a way of wandering around for a long time until finally it all comes to focus," Asphaug said.

"I believe that will happen, in part thanks to this work, in the coming decade."

#132. Something strange is happening beneath a volcano near 2 million people

A volcano famous for its glowing lava lake is hiding a surprisingly complex system of magma deep underground. Scientists at Penn State have uncovered evidence of two previously unrecognized magma sources beneath Nicaragua's active Masaya volcano, raising new questions about how molten rock moves beneath the surface.

The discovery is particularly important because approximately 2 million people live within 13 miles of the volcano, which is also a popular tourist destination. Understanding its underground activity could help scientists recognize warning signs of future eruptions and better protect nearby communities.

Using six years of satellite observations, researchers tracked subtle changes in the ground around Masaya. They discovered that one part of the volcano initially sank before beginning to rise, possibly indicating that fresh magma was entering a deep reservoir. Meanwhile, the ground around its active Santiago crater and lava lake continued to sink, suggesting that a separate, shallower magma reservoir was behaving differently.

The findings, published in Geophysical Research Letters, reveal that the volcano's underground magma system may be considerably more complicated than previously understood.

"These observations help scientists better understand how magma moves beneath Masaya and may improve monitoring and eruption forecasting in the future," said lead author Lizzie Johnson, who earned her bachelor's degree in geosciences from Penn State in May.

Located near Managua, Nicaragua's capital, Masaya is a geologically complex volcano featuring multiple overlapping craters and calderas. Calderas are large depressions that generally form when the ground collapses after magma is removed from an underground chamber.

Although scientists have studied Masaya for years, the movement of magma through its underground reservoirs and passageways remains poorly understood. These systems can change over time, making it difficult to determine exactly what is happening beneath the volcano.

"Having a thorough understanding of Masaya's volcanic activity and its related hazards is critical as around 2 million people live near Masaya and the caldera is a national park and popular tourist destination," Johnson said. "Although Masaya last produced a major lava flow in 1772, its persistent degassing often produces dangerously high concentrations of sulfur dioxide volcanic gas."

Sulfur dioxide is a potentially harmful volcanic gas released as magma approaches or remains near the surface. Even without a major eruption, elevated concentrations can create dangerous conditions for visitors and surrounding communities.

Young Cheol Kim, who completed his doctorate in geosciences at Penn State this summer, explained that monitoring the volcano continuously is essential for distinguishing normal activity from changes that might signal increasing volcanic hazards.

"Doing continuous monitoring allows us to understand the baseline activity and identify see if things are changing," he said, explaining that certain shifts in volcanic behavior could indicate a period of heightened activity or a possible eruption. "And then if there is a need to warn people, we can do that in a timely manner."

Satellites Reveal Hidden Movements Beneath the Volcano

To investigate Masaya's underground activity, the researchers analyzed measurements collected by the Sentinel-1 satellite, which observes the volcano approximately once every 12 days.

The team used a technique called interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR), which can detect extremely small changes in the elevation of Earth's surface. By comparing satellite measurements taken at different times, scientists can identify areas where the ground is rising or sinking.

The technique combines two important capabilities. Synthetic aperture radar sends microwave signals toward Earth's surface, allowing satellites to collect measurements even when clouds obscure the ground. Interferometry compares the returning radar signals to detect changes in distance between the satellite and the surface.

This is especially valuable in tropical regions, where frequent cloud cover can make conventional satellite imagery less reliable.

"Cloud penetration is important for volcanoes because many of them, like Masaya, are in tropical areas where there is often cloud cover," Kim explained. "And when we look at all the different satellite images across multiple years, we can see how the distance between the satellite and the ground changes, where it is uplifting or subsiding."

By examining these subtle movements over time, researchers can investigate processes happening far below the surface without directly observing the magma itself.

Two Magma Reservoirs Behaving in Different Ways

The satellite measurements revealed an intriguing pattern between 2018 and 2024. During the first part of the study, the ground within Masaya's caldera gradually subsided, meaning it moved downward. Later, the same general area began to rise.

Scientists believe this transition could reflect changes in the amount of magma stored underground. When magma drains away from a reservoir, the overlying ground can sink. When additional magma enters and increases pressure within a reservoir, the surface may rise.

The most surprising finding was that the area surrounding Santiago crater did not follow the same pattern. Instead, it continued to sink throughout the six-year study, even as the broader caldera began rising.

"When it's subsiding, that means that there's probably magma draining away from the volcano, but once the ground starts uplifting again, that can mean that there's potentially new magma moving in," Johnson said. "At the same time, the area directly around the active Santiago crater deflated over the entire study period independently of the transition to inflation of the main reservoir. This indicates that the plumbing system is more complex and could be due to decreasing magma in a second, shallower reservoir."

Together, these observations suggest that Masaya may have at least two distinct parts of its magma storage system undergoing different changes. A deeper source could be supplying additional magma to the main reservoir, while a shallower reservoir near Santiago crater may be losing magma.

This would help explain why different sections of the same volcano moved in opposite directions.

What the Discovery Means for Future Eruptions

Understanding these underground movements is important because changes in the ground can provide clues about where magma is accumulating, where it is moving, and how it might eventually reach the surface.

The researchers emphasized that their observations did not reveal any immediate danger to communities surrounding Masaya. However, identifying the volcano's normal behavior and understanding its magma supply system could make it easier to recognize unusual changes in the future.

Continued satellite observations, combined with more detailed computer models, could also help scientists better understand the connections between underground magma reservoirs and volcanic activity at the surface.

"Further long-term geodetic and modeling studies will provide a more thorough understanding and allow for effective hazard monitoring and mitigation at Masaya and other lava-lake hosting basaltic volcanoes," Johnson said.

The findings may therefore have implications beyond Nicaragua, particularly for other active volcanoes that contain persistent lava lakes and complex underground magma systems.

From Undergraduate Research to Volcano Science

Johnson became involved in the project after attending a presentation by Christelle Wauthier, a Penn State professor of geosciences and computational sciences hub director at the university's Institute for Computational and Data Sciences.

She completed the research as part of her Schreyer's Honors College thesis, working alongside graduate researchers, including Kim, to analyze satellite measurements and develop her scientific skills.

"I appreciated learning how a research group works," said Johnson, who has recently started a doctoral program in Earth sciences at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, where she will continue studying volcanoes using seismic waves to image below the surface of Kilauea volcano. "I had never had any experience with research, so it was great to be able to join in the group meetings and get to hear about everybody's work. And learning coding was also useful as I continue with my Ph.D."
