#134. NASA’s Curiosity Rover Unveils a Spectacular New View of Mars at Dawn

Curiosity’s latest panorama sharpens the view of a Martian rock layer that looks out of place and may have formed from ancient volcanic ash.

A band of wind-carved cliffs stretches roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp on Mars, and NASA’s Curiosity rover is climbing toward it. A newly released panorama offers the most detailed view yet of these formations, known as yardangs, which mission scientists have long wanted to examine up close.

“The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.”

Curiosity has been ascending the 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain since 2014. Each layer records a different period in Mars’ history, allowing scientists to reconstruct a time billions of years ago when lakes and streams covered this region. As the water dried up, it left salty minerals behind. Once new material stopped accumulating on the mountain, wind may have stripped some of it away to create the yardangs.

The panorama captures the distant cliffs in bright morning light, with blue hues across the foreground. Curiosity’s Mastcam took the six images that make up the scene at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time on Aug. 11, the mission’s 4,982nd Martian day, or sol.

The images were transmitted to Earth and stitched together. Unlike most Mastcam imagery, the panorama was processed without the color adjustment known as white balancing, preserving its early morning appearance.

The rover recently reached another milestone in its ascent, gaining 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) in elevation, the most ever climbed on Mars. It is now in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which began with an exploration of spiderweb-like formations called boxwork ridges. For most of the next year or so, Curiosity will drive through layers enriched with sulfates and carbonates, both signs of ancient drying at the surface.

Scientists expect increasingly detailed images as the rover approaches the cliffs. They hope to reach the base of the yardangs sometime in 2027, where Curiosity will be able to use its robotic arm to collect unique data about the formations and investigate how they came to be.

#135. New Research Reveals How Long Stays in Space Affects the Human Genome

Since its inception in 1990, the Human Genome Project has led to breakthroughs in our understanding of genetics. In April 2003, the project was declared complete after scientists determined the sequence of the 3 billion chemical base pairs that make up human DNA. Alas, many questions remain about the physical rules governing a genome's organization. Among them is the question of how gravity influences life on Earth, right down to the mitochondrial level.

A new study led by researchers at the Center for Soft Matter Research at New York University (NYU) seeks to address this question to help mitigate the effects of spaceflight. Behind their work is an innovative technique for creating a microgravity environment to reveal gravity's impact on human cells. This research has two goals: to isolate gravity's impact on human genes and to show how the genome functions in zero gravity.

Thanks to decades of expeditions to the International Space Station (ISS), scientists have learned that prolonged time in space can significantly affect human physiology. These include muscle atrophy, bone density loss, vision problems, and effects on the cardiovascular and central nervous systems. NASA's famous Twins Study also revealed that microgravity affects astronauts on the genetic level. The full extent of these effects is not yet known, raising the need for more research.

Identical twin astronauts, Scott and Mark Kelly, are subjects of NASA's Twins Study. Scott (right) spent a year in space while Mark (left) stayed on Earth as a control subject. Researchers looked at the effects of space travel on the human body. Credit: NASA

Despite the significance of the human genome, we still don't fully understand the physical principles governing its organization. What is known is that its structure is highly complex, consisting of a one-dimensional sequence encoded in two meters of DNA molecules packed inside a tiny cell nucleus barely 10 micrometers in size. It is also known that its structure is directly related to its function, and deviations can lead to diseases like cancer and developmental disabilities.

As Alexandra Zidovska, an associate professor in New York University's Department of Physics, explained:

On Earth, the role of gravity is intriguingâit is a constant mechanical stress on everything. We wanted to know what gravity's role is in the genome's organization and function here on Earth. To uncover it, you have to remove gravity as a force, so we simulated zero gravity in our experiments. Beyond Earth, the question of lack of gravity is also compelling: How will the human genome be affected when in outer space? We think our findings can be useful in better understanding how space travel affects us.

For their experiment, the NYU researchers designed and built a Random Positioning Machine (RPM) similar to the ones astronauts use for training. The machine was paired with dishes of living cell cultures, which were rotated along two different axes, following a three-dimensional path. This allowed the team to image the genes within the cell cultures and note how they responded to microgravity.

The researchers also developed 3D algorithms to simulate microgravity and minimize fluid flow, which typically arises during 3D rotation experiments on Earth but is absent in microgravity. They also developed algorithms to investigate how these flows would affect the cells. These innovations led to a reduction in both flows and the formation of cell aggregates, which obscured the effects of microgravity in previous studies.

After 24 hours of exposure to simulated microgravity or fluid flows, the scientists used advanced imaging techniques to observe the cells under each condition. They then recorded streams of images to conduct a detailed analysis, noting changes in the cells and their nuclei, as well as changes in the genome's organization, dynamics, and possible DNA damage induced by simulated microgravity.

European Space Agency astronaut Samantha Cristoforetti works with the Microgravity Science Glovebox aboard the International Space Station in 2014. Credits: NASA

Overall, the results showed that microgravity increases the volume of the cell nucleus, indicating that gravity diminishes it. They also indicated that exposure to flows elongated the cells. Despite these changes, the thickness and structure of the cells' nuclear envelope remained unchanged, suggesting gravity has minimal impact on these traits. The genome inside the cell nucleus maintained its physical organization and motions after 24-hour exposure.

Overall, the team found that a day-long exposure to simulated microgravity led to rather subtle changes, but note that these could amplify over time. The researchers also showed that microgravity does not cause DNA damage, but damage did occur when the cells were exposed to flows. Said Zidovska:

Our data show that the genome, its organization, and dynamics are incredibly robust and seem unaffected by gravity, or lack thereof, after 24 hours. Similarly, these results suggest that the physical organization of the human genome may change little in outer space over comparable timeframes. However, such changes could occur during longer exposures and due to DNA damage occurring in space.

This study offers fundamental insights into genome organization and highlights gravity's role in regulating life on Earth. The results are encouraging, showing that our genome is highly robust against mechanical stress and could withstand exposure to microgravity without serious changes. Nevertheless, this experiment is the tip of the iceberg when it comes to researching the long-term effects of microgravity. Understanding the range of effects is essential for future long-duration missions to places like the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

The paper describing the researchers' findings was published in Science Advances.

Further Reading: New York University, Science Advances

Editor's note: Japan launched its bold MMX sample-return mission to the Mars moon Phobos on Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT). Watch a replay of the liftoff and read our launch story here.

Japan will launch an epic mission to Mars today (Oct. 19), and you can watch the action live.

The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is scheduled to lift off atop an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center today at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. on Oct. 20 local Japan time).

You can watch it live via the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Coverage will begin at 2:45 p.m. EDT (1845 GMT).

As its full name suggests, MMX will focus on Mars' two moons, Phobos and Deimos. They're both tiny compared to Earth's own moon; Phobos is just 14 miles (22 kilometers) wide, and Deimos is even smaller, with a diameter of about 8 miles (13 km).

They're also quite mysterious. While astronomers have a pretty clear understanding of our own moon's birth — it coalesced from material blasted into space when a Mars-sized planet slammed into Earth long ago — there's no consensus about Phobos and Deimos' origin story.

The duo "may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars' gravity billions of years ago," Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters, said in an Oct. 15 statement. (NASA is a partner on the mission, providing a scientific instrument, a technology demonstration, communication support and funding for American scientists on the MMX team.)

"Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds," Statler added.

MMX will help provide that answer, if all goes according to plan.

The spacecraft will arrive in the Mars system in August 2027, then slip into orbit around Phobos a month later. It will study that moon and Deimos from a distance for about 18 months, then deploy the French-German Idefix rover onto Phobos' surface in early 2029.

The 55-pound (25 kilograms) Idefix "has two main tasks: providing information to prepare for the landing of the main spacecraft to collect samples, and analyzing the composition and texture of Phobos' surface," European Space Agency officials wrote in an MMX mission description.

"The gravity on Phobos is so low that Idefix will only weigh the equivalent of 15 grams [0.5 ounces] on its surface!" they added.

The MMX mothership's Phobos landing will occur in 2030. The spacecraft will grab at least 10 grams (0.4 ounces) of samples from the moon, then head back toward Earth with this extraterrestrial bounty. MMX's return capsule will land here in 2031, after which scientists around the world will scrutinize the Phobos sample for clues about the history and evolution of Mars and our solar system more broadly.

MMX was originally supposed to launch in 2024, but issues with the H3 rocket prevented it from doing so. Mars and Earth align properly for interplanetary launches just once every 26 months, so MMX had to wait a while for its next chance.

Japan already has an impressive sample-return track record. The country's Hayabusa mission brought home pieces of the asteroid Itokawa in 2010, for example, and Hayabusa2 did the same with material from the space rock Ryugu a decade later.

#138. Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for controlling brain cells with light

Scientists who worked out how to control brain cells with light have won this year’s Nobel prize in physiology or medicine. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were honored for their research into “light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.”

Peter Hegemann, at Humboldt University of Berlin, and Georg Nagel, at the University of Würzburg, wanted to understand how a tiny, single-celled alga called Chlamydomonas senses light. Light-sensing is not unique to animals with eyes: organisms throughout the living world use light to detect their surroundings and respond to changes in their environment. Even single-cell organisms have proteins that respond to light. These proteins are used to move towards or away from light, to generate energy and to respond to the various demands of a 24-hour day.

Hegemann and Nagel discovered that Chlamydomonas has a beautifully ingenious mechanism of light detection that relies on a single protein called channelrhodopsin.

Channelrhodopsin is built into the outer membrane of the algal cell. Part of the protein faces the water outside the cell and part faces the inside. The protein also contains a small molecule called retinaldehyde, which is able to absorb light.

When light hits the retinaldehyde inside channelrhodopsin, it changes shape. This makes the channelrhodopsin protein change shape too. That change opens a tiny passage through the cell membrane. Positively charged particles, including sodium, can then flow from the water outside the alga into the cell. This movement of charged particles sends a signal inside the alga that helps it swim.

How fantastic to have solved such an interesting biological question, but why the Nobel prize in physiology or medicine? The answer lies in the way nerve cells work. Nerve cells use the movement of charged particles (called “ions”) across their membranes to control their activity. When positively charged particles flow into a nerve cell, they can make it more active.

The researchers realized that if they could put channelrhodopsin into nerve cells, they might be able to switch those cells on simply by shining a light on them. That is exactly what Hegemann, Nagel and the third Nobel-prize winner, Karl Deisseroth, a psychiatrist and bioengineer at Stanford University in California, went on to do.

The ability to control nerve cells with light is called optogenetics. It has become a powerful research tool because scientists can use it to switch specific groups of nerve cells on and off and see what happens.

First, scientists deliver the gene for channelrhodopsin to the nerve cells they want to study. The gene is usually carried into the cells by a virus that has been altered so that it cannot cause disease. The cells then make the channelrhodopsin protein, which makes them respond to light.

In animals such as mice, scientists can shine light into the brain through a thin optical fibre. When the light reaches the cells, channelrhodopsin opens and the cells become active. Nearby nerve cells that do not contain the protein are unaffected.

Light can be aimed at a very small part of the brain and switched on and off extremely quickly. This makes optogenetics a powerful way to investigate how the brain works. For example, if scientists want to know whether a particular group of nerve cells is involved in memory, sleep, sensation or movement, say, they can switch those cells on with light and see what happens.

In one experiment in 2012, a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology gave mice a mild electric shock in a particular cage. They used optogenetics to tag the nerve cells in the brain’s memory center that were active during that the fear-conditioning experiment. Days later, in a different cage, they switched those cells on with light. The mice froze in fear, as if they remembered the shock.

Mice that were not shocked did not freeze, which showed that the light was reactivating a specific memory. Deisseroth was one of the study’s authors.

Optogenetics has transformed scientists’ ability to investigate how the brain and nervous system work. It may also have a future as a treatment. Optogenetics is already in early-stage clinical trials for people with retinal degeneration. In these trials, researchers introduce light-sensitive proteins into nerve cells that remain in the retina after the cells that normally detect light – called rods and cones – have been lost. This can make surviving cells respond to light and restore some vision.

Researchers are also investigating whether optogenetics could eventually be used to treat neurological conditions, including Parkinson’s and epilepsy.

This year’s Nobel prize celebrates work that started with a question that may sound esoteric: how do Chlamydomonas swim toward light? This question has no obvious practical importance. It doesn’t address an urgent need in human health, nor is it a clear route to riches. The success of optogenetics is an illustration of the importance of continuing to ask questions simply to understand the world around us because it’s impossible to predict where knowledge will take us.

#139. Scientists Create “Super Ice” That’s 10 Times Stronger and Rivals Concrete in Strength

A new form of reinforced ice could offer an unconventional building material for extreme polar environments, although questions about its long-term durability remain.

Scientists have developed a new form of ice that approaches the compressive strength of conventional concrete while resisting the sudden fractures that make ordinary ice so brittle. Known as BioPykrete, the material is about 10 times stronger under compression than pure ice and can absorb roughly 70 times more energy before breaking.

Instead of shattering when cracks spread through it, the reinforced ice can deform and fracture more gradually. The research, led by Prof. Ido Braslavsky of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem’s Robert H. Smith Faculty of Agriculture, Food and Environment, was published in Colloids and Surfaces B: Biointerfaces.

The material gets its unusual properties from cellulose nanocrystals, tiny, rigid particles derived from the natural substance that helps give plants their structure. As the material freezes, these particles form a three-dimensional network surrounding microscopic regions of ice.

To strengthen the connection between the two materials, the researchers designed a protein with separate regions that attach to ice and cellulose. This molecular bridge anchors the reinforcing network to the ice, creating a more tightly connected structure. Adding the protein doubled both the strength and energy absorption compared with a similar mixture containing cellulose but no engineered protein.

“We wanted to go beyond simply mixing fibers into ice and instead control how the different materials connect at the molecular level,” Braslavsky said. “The result changes not only how strong the ice is, but also how it breaks. Instead of suddenly shattering, it can absorb much more energy and deform gradually.”

Ordinary ice can fail suddenly because small cracks propagate rapidly through its crystalline structure. In BioPykrete, the cellulose network creates obstacles that can interrupt or redirect advancing cracks. The researchers propose that the protein connections make this network harder to deform or tear, increasing the energy required for fractures to spread.

The concept builds on an unusual experiment from World War II. Scientists developed Pykrete, a mixture of ice and wood pulp that was stronger and slower to melt than untreated ice. BioPykrete takes the same general approach but replaces conventional wood fibers with nanoscale reinforcement and molecular connections designed to improve mechanical performance.

Researchers see potential applications in Arctic and Antarctic environments, where transporting conventional construction materials such as concrete and steel can be costly and logistically difficult. Because BioPykrete consists largely of ice and plant-derived cellulose, it could eventually provide a biodegradable alternative with a smaller carbon footprint for certain structures in extremely cold regions.

However, the material remains an experimental proof of concept. Its impressive laboratory performance does not establish whether it can withstand years of structural use. Researchers still need to investigate its response to repeated freezing and thawing, prolonged loading, and gradual deformation under sustained pressure.

Future experiments will examine how fractures develop within the reinforced structure and whether different proteins or freezing techniques can further improve its properties. These tests will help determine whether BioPykrete can move beyond laboratory samples toward practical construction applications.

Reference: “Biomimetic engineering of a fortified ice composite with enhanced mechanical properties” by Chen Adar, Yulia Baron, Baruch Rofman, Maya Bar Dolev, Liat Bahari, Victor Yashunsky, Vera Sirotinskaya, Oded Shoseyov and Ido Braslavsky, 2 August 2026, Colloids and Surfaces B: Biointerfaces. DOI: 10.1016/j.colsurfb.2026.116037

#141. Stop Treating Your Pen Like an Afterthought—It’s an Essential EDC Tool

Take analog notes on these everyday writing utensils.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

While pocket knives and multitools are an integral part of EDC, an oft-forgotten piece—also neglected in our digital world—is the pen. They’re in junk drawers, prominently placed on desks, and were always in my dad’s shirt pocket when I was growing up. We take them from hotel rooms by accident or forget to return one at the doctor’s office because we like how smooth it is.

With the notes app on smartphones and tablets, asking someone if they have a pen is almost as rare as asking someone for the time (call me old-fashioned, but I miss these small, passing moments). Luckily, pens are a bit more of a necessity for me. I type 39 words a minute (just so you know, that’s really bad), so I prefer to use pen and paper wherever and whenever possible. I write my work notes and grocery lists on paper. Quick math (I’m bad at that, too) is easiest, scratching down on physical paper with a physical writing instrument.

I prefer a retractable pen with black ink. Felt tips always bleed through for me, but maybe I’m just heavy-handed. Ultra-fine pens are not my favorite because, at some point, I end up tearing the paper. So, you might think I’d loathe a fountain pen, right? Wrong! I just got this Kolo pen and have been thoroughly enjoying it. It’s not the most practical for fast notes, but gift it to someone and I bet they’d be stoked.

These are the pens I use the most for the day-to-day that aren’t an afterthought. It’s not a definitive list of must-have writing utensils, but it is what someone who wholeheartedly believes the pen is mightier than the (key)board uses regularly.

Craighill makes everyday objects but puts years’ worth of thought into the design and materials. The brand first caught my attention with a brass keychain, but held it with the Kepler pen. I acquired it when I first started my current job, and it has been going for over three years now.

The brass casing is heavy, a knock for some, but I thoroughly enjoy the weight. It still maintains a balanced feel when I’m writing, and I appreciate the durable build. Its nib sits a little deeper in the pen than those of others I use, which adds to the overall sleek look. The absence of a pocket clip also keeps it slim, but I do miss it at times. Since Revenge of the Nerds, having a pen peeking out of a shirt pocket has gotten a bad wrap— but I think it shows preparedness and purpose.

It produces a medium line as you’d expect from a ballpoint pen that glides on top of paper instead of digging into it. Refill it with the Schmidt 635 cartridges in the color of your choice, although I always opt for black.

Recently, I’ve been loving the Rite In The Rain Ballpoint. It’s weatherproof which didn’t seem all that practical for myself, but if you work outdoors it’s a great option. My best case use has been in the kitchen or grilling. I like to make notes in cookbooks and jot down tidbits when I’m grilling or smoking. Spills happen and it’s nice to know this pen can brave them.

I really appreciated my time as a buyer for a men’s store. It was a local business that generated 90 percent of its sales in person, and we had barely established an online presence at the time. Protocol and procedures were printed on clipboards, and a go-to method of communication was using words on Post-it notes.

The pen of choice was the Pilot G2. My boss had a cup of them at his desk and one behind his ear at all times, but not in the performative way. He was a graphic designer, so he was constantly jotting down ideas and doodling design concepts in a Leuchtturm 1917 notebook. The opaque black ink is perfect for drawing, as well as writing notes that you need to be dark and legible. Its rubber grip makes it comfortable to hold while furiously writing as well. This is also the pen most of us like in my current office, and is a step above the box of pens we order in bulk.

I’m usually averse to translucent plastic on a pen (mechanical pencils fly), but don’t mind it on the G2 Pilot. Perhaps it's because the silicone paste above the black ink—which prevents the ink from drying out or running back up the tube—reminds one of the mosquito in amber at the beginning of Jurassic Park. Whatever it is, it doesn’t bug me; the G2 is still an everyday pen that looks like one a person intentionally has, and not one they just picked up along the way.

The James Brand is a mouthful of a name, but they make a clean design. I’ve had the brand’s Elko knife on my keys since 2018, so I was excited to see it delve into pens. The initial ones they rolled out were a bit too EDC-friendly because they were pocket-sized, but the Burwell was what I wanted.

The stainless steel construction is both durable and lightweight. Its clip is ultra slim and slips onto a shirt pocket with ease. The overall diameter is also slimmer than that of any other nice pen; it feels a bit smaller than the BIC Roundstick, which isn’t the nicest pen, yet I have four in my junk drawer, and none of them work. I really like the clicker action and find it more satisfying than any other retractable pen I’ve used. It uses the same refill cartridges as the G2, so they’re easy to find.

Even if you are a capable typist, analog writing is something that won't go away. On a sentimental level, nothing beats a handwritten note to say thank you or acknowledge a life milestone; For the more practical-minded, a pen won’t lose its charge, is smaller than a laptop, and can be taken anywhere. They're uncomplicated yet distinctive, and don't have to be expensive. Work notes, journaling, or weekend planning—next time, close the laptop and pick up the pen.

#142. To turn invisible, we need to tweak the path light travels

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Some animals have real-life ways to be see-through

How many invisible people and creatures can you spot?

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It’s pretty hard to fight an opponent you can’t see. That’s what makes Invisible Woman an invaluable member of the Fantastic Four. She can disappear in the blink of an eye and take out entire factions of enemies, all while her adversaries kick and punch empty air.

Characters with invisibility powers — Marvel Comics’ Invisible Woman (aka Sue Storm), H.G. Wells’ Invisible Man and The Incredibles’ Violet Parr — can do all sorts of cool things. Escape embarrassing situations. Snoop on other people. Go places where they’re not allowed.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Short of a theoretical invisibility cloak, that kind of lurking is impossible for us. But some animals can hide in plain sight by turning nearly transparent.

Invisibility is useful for animals that spend a lot of time in places with no good hiding spots, such as the air or open ocean, says Kate Feller, a visual ecologist at Union College in Schenectady, N.Y.

The secret to invisibility is all about light. “The way we see things is when light is reflected back off of an object onto our eyes,” Feller says. The more light that can pass through something undisturbed, the harder it is to see that thing.

Light can’t easily pass through most animals, but those with nearly invisible body parts have tricks to get around this hurdle.

Animals get their colors from pigments, compounds that appear as different colors depending on which wavelengths of light they absorb and which they reflect. Green pigments, for instance, reflect green light and absorb all other colors. Invisibility requires getting rid of these colorful compounds.

Most baby fish lack pigments at first, helping them hide from predators. Some species stay see-through their whole lives. One is the ghost catfish (Kryptopterus vitreolus). With a body that’s fully transparent from gills to tail, it looks like a floating head from afar.

It’s hard to hide every body part, though. Eyes need light-absorbing pigments to see. And even clear stomachs will show up if animals eat colorful food. A ghost catfish eats only small bits of food and its long, thin, tubelike stomach stretches out a meal, helping the organ stay hidden, says Qibin Zhao, a physicist and materials scientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China. Blood can’t be transparent either due to the iron-rich hemoglobin molecules that carry oxygen. So up close, the ghost catfish’s blood vessels are still visible.

But even pigment-free objects are not entirely invisible. Light travels at different speeds through different materials so will bend or bounce when it goes from one material to another. That can create a shine, like sun reflecting off a puddle.

That’s not a big problem for a glasswing butterfly (Greta oto): Its wings have fewer reflective scales than other butterflies’ wings. The wings are also covered in tiny wax bumps that make light’s transition from air to tissue more gradual, so light passes through the wings mostly undisturbed.

Invisible Woman uses a completely different vanishing trick than real-life transparent animals. Instead of letting light pass through her, she bends lights rays to completely avoid her body. The rays never even touch her, so they are not reflected or absorbed, making her invisible to any onlookers.

In 2006, scientists proposed that this same logic could be used to create an invisibility cloak. But in practice, a material that perfectly bends light rays is expensive, hard to make and can divert only a narrow band of light at a time. That’s just enough to make a single-colored object disappear but not an entire human.

And there’s another problem: With no light getting into the cloak, a person inside can’t see out. Luckily, Sue Storm has the ability to use cosmic rays to see while she’s invisible, allowing her to protect the world from supervillains like Doctor Doom.

#143. Enigmatic Mercury Will Remain A Puzzle Until Someone Sends A Lander

Mercury remains one of our solar systemâs most elusive and difficult planets to study. It's easier to send probes to the icy moons of Saturn or Jupiter, or even Pluto, than to land on our innermost planet of Mercury.

Ground-based optical observatories donât risk turning their sights on Mercury, without potentially damaging their optics under the very nearby glare of the bright Sun. Thus, of the planets in our inner solar system, Mercury arguably remains both the least explored and most misunderstood.

NASAâs Mariner 10 performed three fly-bys of Mercury between 1974 and 1975. This was followed by a 2011 orbital insertion by NASAâs MESSENGER mission to Mercury which successfully orbited the planet for some four years.

But despite the European Space Agency's and the Japanese Space Agencyâs long-anticipated joint BepiColombo mission to Mercury, we aren't likely to solve this strange little world's conundrums until someone figures out a way to send a lander. That is, one that can safely land and function for long enough to return data that would give us a much clearer indication of the surface of Mercury's surface composition, and its interior.

BepiColombo, which sees orbital insertion late next month, is currently our only chance to acquire new data about the planet. However, itâs not expected to start taking science data until April of 2027.

After BepiColombo, there's nothing on the drawing board, Paul Byrne, a planetary scientist at Washington University in St. Louis, told me via email. But a lander is the next natural step in the exploration of Mercury, even if it's a technically challenging and expensive proposition, Byrne told me.

Without a lander mission Mercuryâs main science puzzles will remain.

--- The planetâs disproportionately large iron-rich core which is thought to make up some 85 percent of the planetâs radius.

We're beginning to find evidence for much larger, more massive rocky exoplanets that seem to have giant iron cores, says Byrne. So, he wonders if Mercury is a one-off freak, or a planetary outcome that's more common than we might think?

Two major hypotheses have been formulated to explain the presence of a large metallic core.

The first one posits that Mercury accreted from metal-rich building blocks; compared to other planets, such as the Earth, Anne Pommier, staff scientist and high-pressure experimentalist at the Carnegie Laboratory in Washington, D.C., told me via email. The second considers that Mercury was initially larger than today, with a crust and mantle core-ratio closer to that of Earth, Pommier told me.

Yet Pommier, who is a co-Investigator of the magnetometer instrument on BepiColombo, told me that large impacts likely stripped off a massive part of Mercuryâs rocky mantle thus leaving with an anomalously large iron core.

But the presence of a large metallic core remains difficult to explain; Mercury challenges our understanding of planetary formation, says Pommier.

--- Aside from Earth, Mercury is the only other rocky planet in our solar system that has a global magnetic field.

Compared to Earth, Mercury has a weak magnetic field, and it is thought that the field is generated in the liquid portion of the core, says Pommier. This continuous motion creates electric currents, which in turn create a magnetic field dynamo that can be sustained for billions of years, she says.

Mercury currently generates a global magnetic field that is dominantly dipolar at the surface, approximately 100 times weaker than Earth's surface field, the authors of a 2024 paper appearing in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters note. Remanent crustal magnetization with an inferred age of 3.7 to 3.9 billion years suggests the dynamo operated in Mercury's early history, the authors note.

Mercury does have a tenuous exosphere composed of very limited amounts of oxygen, hydrogen, sodium and helium.

But if Mercury has even a weak magnetic field, why canât it hold onto a real atmosphere?

It's not enough to have a magnetic field: you need to be big enough to replenish an atmosphere and far enough away from your star to not have your atmosphere blown off, says Byrne. Mercury is relatively close to the Sun, which means it takes a pounding from the solar wind, he says.

There is also evidence at the surface that the planet has been shrinking, says Pommier. This process is possibly due to core cooling but is not well understood, she says.

--- Finally, Mercury has some sort of enigmatic low reflectance material covering large areas of its surface.

This material possibly contains endogenic carbon, like graphite.

In some craters, it is expected to be hidden under layers of other deposits, so its presence is both at the surface and in the subsurface, says Pommier. One hypothesis regarding its origin is that it formed as part of the crystallization of a magma ocean, early in Mercury's history, she says.

NASAâs MESSENGER (MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging) spacecraft captured the image at left, an approximation of Mercuryâs true color as might be seen by the human eye, on Oct. 6, 2008. The exaggerated color view at right uses all 11 filters in the visible and near-infrared, to highlight subtle color differences and aid geologists in mapping regions of different composition. The nature of color boundaries, color trends, and brightness values help MESSENGER geologists understand the discrete regions (or âunitsâ) on the surface. Credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Carnegie Institution of Washington

This graphite might be the remains of a once-widespread and probably thin carbon-rich flotation crust which was likely all over the planet, says Byrne. Over time, with successive impacts churning up and redistributing crustal materials, as well as surface volcanism, most of this graphite-rich crust was buried, reworked, or removed into space, he says.

Are there any known Mercury meteorites here on Earth?

There are currently no officially confirmed meteorites from Mercury on Earth, despite several studies suggesting that some meteorites (such as enstatite chondrites) could come from Mercury, says Pommier.

But this is one reason why landing on the planet is so crucial.

Landing on Mercury and carrying out chemical analyses in situ would give us a much better idea of what to look for in the world's current meteorite collections, says Byrne. It's certainly possible that we already have unrecognized pieces of Mercury in these collections, he says.

The challenge is the time en route, the energy needed to slow the spacecraft down to do a successful orbital insertion and the landing. Dropping deep into the Sun's gravity well requires a massive change in velocity (or delta-V), even outstripping the amount of energy needed to send a probe to Pluto.

A 2020 NASA planetary mission concept study notes that a lander mission would have a ten-year cruise phase before touching down about 30 hours before Mercury sunset. The idea is for the lander to be fully operational during Mercuryâs night, which spans some 88 Earth days. The lander would use LED lights to photograph Mercuryâs surface and might even be aided by a diffuse glow from the planetâs sodium exosphere.

A lander must first softly touch down on the surface of Mercury.

With no atmosphere, a lander can only rely on retrorockets; we have experience doing that for the Moon, but gravity on Mercury is about twice as high, says Byrne. So, the challenge is greaterâand would necessarily happen after a much longer cruise phase than to the Moon or even Mars, he says.

Cuttlefish use rapid color-change while hunting. The question is, does it actually hypnotize their prey?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Like their cephalopod cousins the octopuses, cuttlefish are masters of disguise.

As they hunt, these marine predators send waves of color across their skin. The rainbow display stops prey in their tracks, granting the cuttlefish just enough time to shoot out two specialized hunting tentacles at lightning speed and snatch them into range of their deadly beaks.

But can cuttlefish actually mesmerize prey with their colorful skin changes? Or is something fishier at play?

Experts told Live Science that cuttlefish are ingenious hunters, but that there's likely an even more mysterious process than hunter to prey hypnosis going down on the seafloor.

Cuttlefish are visual hunters, using their large, complex eyes to locate and track potential meals. In general, their strategy involves a slow, stealthy approach, said Bret Grasse, the manager of cephalopod operations at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole Massachusetts.

"The cuttlefish will slowly approach the prey so as to not alert the unsuspecting shrimp, fish or crab," Grasse told Live Science in an email.

During their approach, cuttlefish often put on a showy display, producing moving bands across their body. These displays are produced by a combination of light-reflecting pigment cells known as iridophores, leucophores and chromatophores. These cell types contract and expand to produce specific colors and patterns, all within milliseconds.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Some may wonder whether this trick can mesmerize prey, but scientists don't think that's the case.

Hypnosis, defined as a mental state of increased relaxation and altered awareness, is thought to be a uniquely human psychological state. There is very little research on whether fish can be hypnotized, but a 2005 study found that pushing a steady stream of water through the snapper (Chrysophrys auratus) put them in an immobile state similar to being hypnotized. Another study looked at sedative hypnotic drugs like benzodiazepines and barbiturates and their effects on zebrafish, finding that the fish had molecular receptors for these drugs, which helped render them immobile. However, whether fish can be visually put into a state like hypnosis has yet to be directly studied.

And while some animals, such as chickens, can be induced into trance-like conditions of tonic immobility, an involuntary, temporary state of unresponsiveness that happens when humans or animals experience extreme trauma, it's unlikely that the cuttlefish's color changes "hypnotize" their prey, Connor Gibbons, the cephalopod facility manager at Columbia University told Live Science. Instead, some researchers believe that the color show serves as an ingenious disguise.

As waves of different colors ripple down the cuttlefish's body, the shape of the animal becomes less obvious to its prey, so they may not see the cuttlefish as a threat to flee from, Gibbons said.

"It's only part of something looming at them, which they're like, 'I don't know if you are a predator? Are you just passing waves? What are you?'" Gibbons said. "And then by that time, it's too late."

A cuttlefish uses its tentacles to capture a shrimp

Once they get close enough, the cuttlefish shoots their two long, specialized feeding tentacles from small hidden pouches near the animal's mouth at their prey.

"The closest thing I can compare it to is the tongue of a chameleon extending out to grab an unsuspecting insect," Grasse said. "Cuttlefish feeding tentacles will fire out in the blink of an eye before the prey can react and escape."

Then, the prey is pulled toward the cuttlefish's mouth, pierced by its sharp, chitinous beak and injected with venom. The use of the venom helps the cuttlefish reduce their energy usage when hunting "as the cuttlefish does not want to use unnecessary energy and struggle against the prey while it's trying to eat," Grasse said.

However, the notion that cuttlefish flash colors to hide their body shape is only one idea of why cuttlefish perform these strobing color displays. Other researchers, including Grasse, describe them as a way to distract their prey.

"Essentially, they are trying their best not to alarm the prey to their presence," he said. By breaking up the size of their bodies, cuttlefish can convince their prey they're not as large or alarming as they may seem.

Whether the light shows are for disguise or distraction still needs parsing out, Gibbons said, and scientists also need a better understanding of how the cuttlefish controls its deadly dermal display. "The jury is still out on exactly what is happening," he said.

MMX could be the first spacecraft to ever return from orbit around the Red Planet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: Japan launched its bold MMX sample-return mission to the Mars moon Phobos on Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT). Watch a replay of the liftoff and read our launch story here.

Japan's mission to Mars is one of the most ambitious in spaceflight history. It aims to become the first spacecraft to return to Earth from Mars orbit, carrying with it the first-ever samples from the Red Planet system.

The mission, known as Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), is a first-of-its-kind endeavor to study the origin of Mars' moons Phobos and Deimos. The robust undertaking includes a landing on Phobos to collect the samples — which will likely be the first from the Mars system to return to Earth — and a search for evidence that could shed light on events during the formation of the solar system billions of years ago.

MMX launched on an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center on Monday (Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan, Oct. 20). After a 10-month journey to reach Mars, the spacecraft will spend about three years studying Phobos, deploying a rover and landing to collect its samples. The mission will then shift its focus to Deimos for a series of flybys before departing for Earth in November 2030. If all goes according to plan, the MMX sample-return capsule is scheduled to land in Australia in 2031.

The MMX spacecraft is comprised of three main parts, as well as a small rover. After release from its H3 launch vehicle, a propulsion module will provide the boost to put MMX on course for Mars. MMX's main exploration module carries the microwave-size IDEFIX rover and most of the mission's scientific instruments, while the return module houses the sample-return capsule.

Japan's Mitsubishi Electric built MMX's three main modules, with the French space agency CNES (Centre National d'Études Spatiales) and Germany's DLR (Deutsches Zentrum für Luft-und Raumfahrt) jointly developing IDEFIX. The little rover is named for a dog in the 1960s French comic "Asterix," in a nod to the country's first satellite, Astérix, which launched in 1965.

IDEFIX carries a suite of cameras, as well as the Raman Spectrometer for MMX (RAX) and miniaturized radiometer (miniRAD) instruments to analyze Phobos' surface composition and temperature.

Most of MMX's scientific instruments are housed on the exploration module, like NASA's Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE, pronounced "meh-gah-nay") device, a gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL), and France's MIRS (MMX InfraRed Spectrometer) instrument.

The exploration module also houses the Japanese-built TENGOO (TElescopic Nadir imager for GeOmOrphology) tight-zoom camera, wide-angle OROCHI (Optical RadiOmeter composed of CHromatic Imagers) multispectral camera, laser altimeter (LIDAR) and Mass Spectrum Analyzer (MSA). The return module, meanwhile, carries Japan's Circum-Martian Dust Monitor (CMDM) and Interplanetary Radiation Environment Monitor (IREM).

MMX will arrive in orbit around Mars in August 2027, at which point it will shed its propulsion module and transition into a quasi-satellite orbit (QSO) around Phobos that allows the probe to fly in a sort of formation with the small, asteroid-sized moon as they both circle the Red Planet.

The spacecraft will spend its first few months in the Martian system observing Phobos from different altitudes, using its TENGOO and OROCHI cameras, LIDAR and MSA to map the moon's surface, study its composition and select potential landing sites.

IDEFIX will be released in late 2028 or early 2029, during the first of two MMX landing rehearsals, at about 130 feet (40 meters) above Phobos. Due to the 14-mile-wide (22 kilometers) moon's extremely low gravity, the rover will be able free-fall to the surface damage-free (hopefully), right itself after a few bounces and begin exploring to gather data on the terrain and surface conditions.

MMX sample collection could begin as early as December 2028, the acting director of NASA's Planetary Science Division, Lindsay Hays, said during a mission briefing on Oct. 15. The spacecraft will attempt two collection landings, with its exploration and return modules descending and returning to orbit as one vehicle.

On Phobos' surface, two different sampling mechanisms — the Corer Sampling Mechanism (C-sampler) and Pneumatic Sampling Mechanism (P-sampler) — will extract and collect at least 10 grams (0.35 ounces) of material for stowage inside the spacecraft's return capsule before MMX lifts off again for orbit. After its first touchdown and sample collection, MMX will return to QSO near Phobos before descending to a second landing site for a similar attempt and subsequent return to orbit.

MMX will end its observations of Phobos after about three years focused on the Martian moon, and will transition into a higher, resonant orbit around Mars in 2030. That course will repeatedly intersect Deimos' path for a series of flybys to collect and compare data with those from Phobos observations as scientists aim to investigate the moons' origins.

Near the end of 2030, the exploration module will separate, leaving the return module to fire its engine out of Mars' gravitational influence and begin an eight-month journey back to Earth with the collected samples. As MMX closes the last stretch of void during its approach to Earth in 2031, the sample-return capsule will separate and enter the atmosphere for a targeted parachute landing in Australia's Woomera region, where its contents will be recovered for laboratory analysis by Japan and its mission partners.

Those samples, and the data collected by MMX, could tell scientists a lot — about the moons' composition, geography and, perhaps most importantly, how they came to exist in the first place. There are two leading theories for Phobos and Deimos' origins, both of which point to very different versions of ancient Martian history.

"Phobos and Deimos are interesting, but not just in their own right. Their presence is a key piece of the larger story of the Mars system," said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and scientist in NASA's Planetary Science Division, during the Oct. 15 mission briefing. "By uncovering the moons' origin, we'll gain new insights into the history of both Mars and Earth, especially those events that shaped both planets billions of years ago and helped create the worlds we see today."

Both Phobos and Deimos are relatively small and irregularly shaped, and bear several resemblances and spectral characteristics to primitive D-type asteroids — ancient bodies thought to preserve material dating back to the solar system's formation about 4.6 billion years ago. Those similarities suggest Phobos and Deimos may have formed elsewhere in the solar system and were later captured by Mars' gravity.

Their near-circular, equatorially-aligned orbits around the Red Planet, however, somewhat complicate that theory. For example, a captured asteroid would be much more likely to have entered an elongated and tilted orbit akin to the direction and velocity of its original approach, scientists say. A competing hypothesis, therefore, offers a much more violent, but somewhat familiar, narrative for the moons' origins.

An enormous collision with ancient Mars could have blasted material into orbit to form a debris disk from which the two moons eventually coalesced. Such a process, which would be similar to the formation of Earth's moon, could explain their circular, equatorial orbits.

The contradicting geological and orbital observations for Phobos and Deimos collected to date have prevented scientists from definitively establishing one hypothesis over the other. MMX aims to provide an answer.

"It's two totally different lines of evidence that point in two different directions. That's what makes it an interesting puzzle," Statler said. Several theories have also been presented for hybrid scenarios combining the two, he added.

"There's all kinds of different ways, all kinds of different combinations of those two basic scenarios," Statler explained. "But that's the puzzle from the start, the two seemingly contradictory lines of evidence that are pointing us to what … the real history was, but we don't know what it is yet."

Each theory for where Mars' moons came from predicts different chemical characteristics for their surfaces. Presumably, captured asteroids would preserve chemical signatures of material originating elsewhere in the solar system, potentially rich in volatile elements like hydrogen. Moons formed through a planetary impact, however, would contain a mixture of Mars and impact material, altered by the intense heat of such a violent collision.

Determining which scenario is more likely could reveal whether Mars experienced a massive moon-forming collision or acquired its moons from elsewhere in the early solar system. Either answer could offer new insights into the planet's evolution and the events that shaped the terrestrial planets like Earth billions of years ago, mission team members say.

"At this point, we know nothing about the composition of Phobos," David Lawrence, MEGANE principal investigator at APL, said during the Oct. 15 briefing. "We have information about mineralogy, but no elemental composition. And so, elements are really a key way to get at some of these foundational questions."

MMX's scientific suite has been carefully calibrated to make those determinations. The cameras and sensors on the MMX exploration module's TENGOO, OROCHI and LIDAR instruments will map Phobos' terrain, geological features and variations in surface materials from orbit, to provide clues about the moon's formation and evolution. Complementing those measurements, MIRS is designed to detect and classify Phobos' surface minerals and search for organic compounds to further differentiate its possible origin as an asteroid or ancient chunk of Mars.

The RAX spectrometer and miniRAD instrument aboard IDEFIX will add localized context to those observations by examining surface mineralogy and their thermal properties up close.

Back in orbit, NASA's MEGANE instrument will measure Phobos' elemental composition through gamma-ray and neutron spectroscopy that can scan tens of centimeters beneath the moon's surface for signs of volatile elements. Higher abundances of hydrogen, chlorine, sodium and potassium, for instance, would favor the asteroid-capture hypothesis, while lower abundances of those compounds could point to the heat and chemical deterioration associated with a planetary impact.

"In Japanese, 'megane' means eyeglasses," Lawrence said. "So we like to think of MEGANE as being an instrument that will look at Phobos with gamma ray and neutron glasses."

When compared to the samples MMX will return to Earth, MEGANE's findings could help scientists determine if volatile depletion found on Phobos reflects the intense heat of a post-impact formation or billions of years of subsequent erosion from the natural effects of space exposure.

MSA, meanwhile, will measure charged particles around Phobos, searching for evidence of subsurface ice and investigating how solar wind exposure has altered the moon's surface. It will also study atmospheric particles escaping from Mars. CMDM will measure dust around Mars, including particles potentially ejected from its moons by impacts.

Comparative observations of Deimos after MMX's final departure from Phobos will help establish whether the moons share similar compositions and, potentially, a common origin.

Once safely returned to Earth, laboratory analysis of the Phobos samples will allow scientists to examine chemical composition and mineralogy with a precision beyond that of MMX's onboard instruments. Tests like isotopic analyses — measuring subtle differences in the atomic makeup of elements — can help identify the samples' origins by comparing their chemical fingerprints with those of Martian rocks and asteroid material.

JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) scientists think some returned material could even originate from Mars itself, deposited on Phobos after ancient asteroid impacts blasted rocks off the Red Planet's surface, potentially holding evidence of its geological past.

The JAXA-led mission represents interagency partnerships with NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA), which are providing hardware and communications support through the Deep Space and Estrack networks.

NASA's contributions to MMX also include MEGANE, the Honeybee Robotics-built P-sampler, and an approximately $87 million investment through the end of the mission. NASA is funding the United States scientists on the MMX team, who will, alongside NASA's astromaterials experts, "be fully involved in the examination and scientific analysis of the Phobos samples when they are delivered to Earth," Hays said during the mission briefing. "We get all of the value and all of the scientific participation at a lower cost total [than funding the entire mission]."

For its role, NASA will receive at least 15% of the returned samples, with materials to be maintained at the agency's Johnson Space Center in Houston for analysis and long-term preservation. To that end, MMX's scientific impact could extend far beyond the mission's conclusion.

"The Phobos samples will be historic," Statler said, with the potential "for future research to answer the questions we don't even know yet how to ask."

#146. Scientists Turn Ordinary Plastic Into Billions of Tiny Diamonds Using Powerful Lasers

Diamonds recovered from plastic contain roughly 3,000 atoms each and could be modified with other elements for future use in medical imaging.

Powerful lasers can turn plastic into tiny diamonds, but recovering the crystals means catching them as they shoot out at speeds comparable to a meteorite impact. Researchers at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) and the University of Rostock have now collected those diamonds intact, showing that they survive the return from extreme pressure and temperature to ordinary conditions.

The recovered particles averaged three nanometers across, or three billionths of a meter, with roughly 3,000 carbon atoms in each diamond. The laser technique produces a combination of high purity, exceptionally small size, and closely matched particle sizes that conventional methods, including explosions, cannot achieve.

The work began with experiments designed to simulate conditions inside planets such as Neptune and Uranus, where temperatures reach several thousand degrees Celsius and pressures are millions of times higher than Earth’s atmospheric pressure. Firing high-power lasers at plastics created conditions in which carbon formed diamonds, although the researchers could initially detect the crystals only briefly while those extreme conditions lasted.

“We did expect nanodiamonds to form under these conditions. What surprised us, however, was how quickly it happened, which immediately sparked the idea of a potential technical application,” says Dominik Kraus, founding director of the new HEDI Institute of High Energy Density Physics at HZDR and a professor at the University of Rostock.

To recover particles for closer study, the team worked at the Extreme Light Infrastructure (ELI) south of Prague, a laser facility that combines very high pulse energies with a high repetition rate. At its L4n-P3 facility, a high-power laser fired three times per minute at a PET plastic film just 100 micrometers thick, about 0.004 inches. As the beam scanned across the film, each pulse generated a shock wave that compressed the plastic, formed nanodiamonds, and sent them toward a collection cylinder.

“When the compression wave reaches the end of the sample, it abruptly enters a vacuum, accelerating the nanodiamonds to speeds of more than ten kilometers per second – comparable to a meteorite impact. To prevent the diamonds from immediate destruction upon impact with the collection cylinder, we need to use a very soft collection medium,” Kraus says.

To cushion particles arriving at more than 22,000 miles per hour, the team chose a water-soluble ionic gel that could function in a vacuum. The diamonds could then be extracted from the gel and purified for examination.

Even with approximately ten trillion diamonds produced per laser shot, the team needed around 100 shots to collect a few hundred micrograms of material. That was enough to identify and characterize the particles using the ELMI-MV electron microscope at the University of Rostock’s Department Life, Light, & Matter.

“After extracting the nanodiamonds from the catcher material and purifying them, we were able to see them for the first time directly using the ELMI-MV. That was a special moment we had been working towards for years. With this instrument, we can even resolve individual atoms,” says Ben Heuser of HZDR, the study’s primary author, who conducted the experiments as part of his doctoral thesis at the University of Rostock.

Hard, stable, and resistant to heat, nanodiamonds are already used in grinding and polishing agents. Producing smaller, cleaner particles with more consistent sizes could expand their applications in medicine, new materials, and energy technology. Potential uses include highly sensitive quantum sensors, which exploit quantum effects to make measurements, and medical contrast agents that make features inside the body easier to see in scans.

Smaller diamonds also provide more combined surface area for a given amount of material, offering more space for chemical reactions. That could improve their efficiency as catalysts, which accelerate reactions, in processes such as splitting CO₂ with sunlight. Starting with plastic also makes it easier to incorporate atoms of other elements into the diamonds, a process called doping. These additions could tailor the particles for particular tasks, including improving contrast agents for medical MRI examinations.

Fusion research is driving the development of more energy-efficient lasers capable of delivering powerful pulses more frequently. Applying those advances to nanodiamond production could increase output by allowing more shots in less time, potentially making the process scalable and supporting cleaner, more sustainable manufacturing. Through further experiments in their laboratories at the University of Rostock and at large-scale research facilities, the researchers aim to bring production into the milligram range, a quantity comparable to conventional production processes.

The team also wants to use laser compression to make BC8, a form of carbon that has so far only been predicted theoretically. It is expected to be denser than diamond, similarly hard, and less brittle. The conditions needed to form it do not occur naturally on Earth, so the researchers hope to create it directly from plastic by applying still higher pressures with powerful lasers in an initial experiment planned for November.

Reference: “Recovery of ultrasmall nanodiamonds from plastics shock-compressed to pressures around 100 GPa” by B. Heuser, P. Böhringer, K. Oldenburg, F.P. Condamine, G. Fauvel, M.-L. Herbert, J. Kuhkle, T. Laštovička, P. Luckmann, J. Lütgert, P.T. May, D. Ranjan, S. Schumacher, R.L. Singh, M. Stevenson, S. Weber and D. Kraus, 25 August 2026, Diamond and Related Materials. DOI: 10.1016/j.diamond.2026.114091

#148. Scientists discover why some people still can’t taste food after COVID-19

Scientists have uncovered changes inside taste buds that may help explain why some people struggle to taste food more than a year after recovering from COVID-19. The findings point to disruptions in the molecular signals responsible for detecting certain flavors, along with physical abnormalities in the structure of taste buds.

The study, published in Chemical Senses, offers the first direct biological evidence connecting persistent taste problems reported by patients to measurable changes within their taste cells.

Why Does Taste Loss Linger After COVID-19?

To investigate the lasting effects of COVID-19 on taste, scientists from the University of Colorado Anschutz and two Swedish universities examined 28 people who had experienced taste disturbances for more than a year following infection. None of the participants had been hospitalized for COVID-19.

Testing revealed that eight of the 28 participants had clearly abnormal taste scores. Eleven reported difficulty detecting specific flavors, particularly sweet, bitter, and umami, the savory taste associated with foods such as mushrooms and broth. In contrast, their ability to detect salty and sour flavors remained largely unaffected.

Seeking an explanation for this unusual pattern, the researchers collected small tissue samples from the taste buds of 20 participants and examined them for biological abnormalities.

Scientists Identify a Molecular Defect in Taste Cells

The research team, organized by Göran Hellekant, PhD, of the University of Wisconsin and the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, identified reduced amounts of messenger RNA (mRNA) involved in producing a protein known as PLCβ2.

This protein plays an essential role in how taste receptor cells communicate with the brain. Specifically, it amplifies the signals generated when the tongue detects sweet, bitter, and umami flavors. Without sufficient levels of the protein, those signals may become too weak to register normally.

"PLCβ2 acts like a molecular amplifier inside taste cells," said Thomas Finger, PhD, professor of cell and developmental biology at the University of Colorado Anschutz and corresponding author of the study. "It strengthens the signal before it's transmitted to the brain. When levels are reduced, the taste signal weakens."

The discovery may also explain why some flavors are affected more than others. Cells responsible for detecting salty and sour tastes use different signaling mechanisms that do not depend on PLCβ2, potentially allowing those sensations to remain intact even when other taste signals are disrupted.

Hidden Structural Changes Inside Taste Buds

The researchers also discovered that the abnormalities were not limited to molecular signaling. When they examined taste bud tissue under a microscope, they found that some participants had changes in the physical arrangement of their taste cells.

"Some subjects had normal-looking taste buds, while others showed structural disorganization," Finger said. "This suggests that both molecular and architectural changes may contribute to persistent taste dysfunction."

Together, these findings suggest that lingering taste problems after COVID-19 may involve multiple biological disruptions, affecting both the way taste cells are organized and how effectively they transmit information.

Why Can COVID-19 Taste Loss Last More Than a Year?

One of the most intriguing aspects of persistent taste loss is how long it can continue despite the body's natural ability to replace taste cells.

Under normal circumstances, cells in the taste buds are renewed approximately every two to four weeks. Yet the researchers found signs that the molecular processes needed for normal taste signaling may remain disrupted for much longer in some people.

Most individuals who experience taste changes during COVID-19 regain their normal sense of taste within weeks or months. However, a small group continues to experience symptoms long after the infection has resolved. The new findings provide measurable biological evidence that could help explain why recovery takes so much longer for these patients.

"Our findings offer measurable evidence of long-term taste disruption in some post-COVID patients long after the virus has been cleared," the authors write.

Although the discovery sheds light on a previously unexplained symptom, important questions remain. Scientists still need to determine whether these molecular abnormalities can eventually return to normal and whether treatments designed to restore healthy taste signaling could help people recover their sense of taste.

Materials provided by University of Colorado Anschutz. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#149. In the Search for Exoplanets, Some Failures Are A Success

In the near future, powerful new telescopes will power a big leap in exoplanet science. Telescopes like the Extremely Large Telescope, the Giant Magellan Telescope, and the Habitable Worlds Observatory will take us beyond exoplanet detection. They'll allow direct imaging of exoplanets, atmospheric spectroscopy, and more precise radial velocity. Beyond that, they may very well detect biosignatures on rocky planets, especially around nearby M dwarfs, if there are any.

But observing time on these powerful instruments will be in extremely high demand. Astronomers who request observing time for their research have to make a strong case. Part of that case is knowing what to target. That requires detailed advance preparation.

New research led by astronomers from the University of Michigan is part of that advance work. They used radial velocity to target a nearby binary star system and searched for terrestrial planets that would be ideal targets for more observations with more powerful upcoming telescopes. This work is especially relevant since so many stars in the Milky Way are binary stars. The transit detection method can struggle to detect exoplanets around binary stars. The radial velocity method is stronger in these systems.

Their results are published in The Astrophysical Journal in a paper titled "A Century of Radial-velocity and Astrometric Monitoring of 70 Oph AB: New PFS Data and Constraints on Possible Planetary Companions." The lead author is Yiting Li, a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Astronomy at the University of Michigan.

Both stars in 70 Oph AB are main sequence stars about 6.2 billion years old. 70 Oph A has about 0.89 solar masses and 70 Oph B has about 0.73 solar masses. They're not quite Sun-like stars because they're less massive and cooler. Of the two, 70 Oph A is more Sun-like.

"At a distance of 5.1 pc, the 70 Oph AB binary star system is one of the most favorable targets for future direct imaging and astrometry missions surveying mature, terrestrial planets," the authors write. The researchers used the 6.5 m Magellan II Clay Telescope in Chile and its Planet Finder Spectrograph (PFS) to capture new radial velocity data from the stars in 70 Oph AB. During 2025, they collected 499 measurements of 70 Oph A and 334 measurements of 70 Oph B. They combined these new RV measurements with archival RV data and spectrometry that spanned decades. 27 years of RV baseline data for Oph A was especially important.

Despite finding variable radial velocity measurements in the stars, they ruled exoplanets out as the cause.

"We find that the long-term RV variability of both components is consistent with stellar activity modulated by rotation periods, and we detect no coherent planetary signals in either component," they write.

While it's disappointing to find no planets there, this result is still scientifically valuable. A null result like this is still data, and the more data points there are, the more exoplanet science can advance.

âItâs a mix of disappointment and excitement,â lead author Li said in a press release. âWeâre finding out that there isnât a Jupiter-sized planet, but weâre also opening the latest chapter on this historic system.â

This work also means that 70 Oph A and B's orbits are now some of the most well-understood in the sky. The researchers achieved a new degree of sensitivity in their search, which showed that wobbles in the system are due to stellar activity, not orbiting planets. The research was aimed at massive, Jupiter-size planets, and the results place limits on the size of any exoplanets in the system, and ruled them out, within certain limits. "We place upper limits on any planets orbit in the plane of the binary," the authors explain.

For 70 Oph A, the results exclude Jupiter-mass exoplanets inside about 5 au. For 70 Oph B, exoplanets with ~0.25-0.3 Jupiter masses are excluded inside 0.5 au.

But the data does allow for Saturn-mass planets or smaller to follow stable orbits around 70 Oph A out to about 2.5 au.

âThe new limit enables us to design optimum search strategies in the future,â said Michael Meyer, a senior co-author and chair of the U-M astronomy department. âIn fact, the University of Michigan is part of a team studying a space mission called SHERA that will focus on binaries, where this system is one of a handful of targets. 70 Oph AB will certainly be a target of flagship missions, such as NASAâs Habitable World Observatory.â

âYiting assembled an absolutely huge amount of data from all over the world and carefully explored all possibilities,â Meyer said. âItâs a cautionary tale about how stellar activity can mimic planet signals using the radial velocity.â

This work has implications for habitability studies. Using more than a century of RV and astrometry data, the orbits of 70 Oph A and 70 B are now very tightly constrained. Their dynamical masses are now known very precisely. This means that 70 Oph AB is now one the best-characterized nearby solar-type binaries.

"This is especially valuable for habitability studies in binary stars, where even modest changes in eccentricity or periastron distance can substantially modify the extent of long-term stable zones," the authors write. "70 Oph AB presents a unique opportunity for the search and characterization of habitable planets in binary systems." They add that "70 Oph is one of the nearest binaries where the HZ can be spatially resolved."

It would be unusual to find no planets in the 70 Oph AB system, given what we now know about exoplanet numbers. So even though none were found, the results may only intensify the effort to find the ones that are likely there. The results show that an Earth-sized exoplanet could still reside there.

âThe study sets an upper limit, not a ban, on planets,â Li said. âGiven how prevalent planets are in our universe and in the Milky Way, I would wager that weâll find there are other planets there.â

"If stellar binaries can host Earth-like planets, 70 Oph is one of the best places to look," the authors conclude.
