#150. The 8 Best Laser Levels for Tiling and Mounting Projects

Give your projects precise, aesthetically pleasing lines with the most accurate and reliable options out there.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve ever tried to install cabinets or mount a mirror, you know how quickly things can drift out of alignment. Traditional levels are fine for quick checks, but when accuracy really matters—and when you need both hands free—you really need a laser level on hand.

Laser levels project bright, highly visible reference lines across walls, floors, and ceilings, making layout work faster and more precise. Recent upgrades like brand-dedicated batteries, USB-C charging, longer runtimes, and app connectivity have made modern laser levels more capable than ever, whether you’re tackling weekend projects or full-scale renovations.

Before you buy, it’s worth understanding how different types of laser levels work and which features actually matter in real-world use. Below, you’ll find practical suggestions on what to look for, along with our picks for the best laser levels we’ve tested and researched.

When considering products for this list, original author Alex Rennie used his experience as a residential and commercial carpenter—a job that relied heavily on precision leveling at all times—to choose models and brands he knew and trusted. He then tested several options that he wasn’t as familiar with specifically for this article.

To update this article, Paul Smith looked back on many years as both a homeowner (in a very crooked, old house) and a residential contractor. In both roles, he has used many of the brands listed here to help with projects.

This Bosch laser level is a great all-around option for those who need a reliable, high-quality tool and don’t want to spend much over $100. The controls are extremely simple to use: Simply push the control slider to the “on” position, and the crosshairs pop up on your wall—no other switches, buttons, or indicator lights to worry about.

The tool's magnetic mount, combined with its self-leveling mechanism and optional tripod threads, helps you easily position the beam exactly where you want it. The soft-sided storage pouch attaches to your tool belt using a velcro loop, and the internal pendulum lock reduces the chances of damage to its components in transit.

The laser doesn't display in all directions, but it's the only quibble associated with this excellent level. I’ve been using Bosch tools for years, and this one demonstrates the brand's commitment to precision and overall build quality.

Using an internal rechargeable lithium battery and micro-USB charging port, this laser level eliminates the need for inconvenient and expensive-to-replace batteries. And for a higher-end, 360-degree option, it's pretty affordable.

The level's red beam maintains visibility up to 65 feet away, which covers the majority of residential rooms. If you're working on a large home project, this model will save you the trouble of constantly repositioning it.

To add even more bang for your buck, the level comes with its own adjustable tripod, a feature that you won’t typically find in similar products.

This Huepar level provides 360-degree coverage—one horizontal beam and two vertical—at an impressively low price.

In addition to the self-leveling feature, this level also gives you the ability to lock the laser in any orientation you like, which is useful for working with slopes and angles, like installing handrails on staircases.

The level mounts conveniently to metal objects in your workspace thanks to its L-shaped magnetic bracket and also attaches via built-in mounting threads to tripods or pole attachments. The internal rechargeable Li-ion battery has an impressive 6,600 milliampere-hour (mAh) capacity.

It's a bulky device that isn't always the easiest to carry or transport, but the foam-lined storage case has compartments for organizing each of the components, reducing the chances of misplacing any pieces.

Designed with maximum durability in mind, this robust laser level from DeWalt stands up well to frequent, heavy-duty use. The laser sits behind a protective rubber housing, which not only protects it from drops and falls, but also prevents accidental scratches or scuffs during normal use.

In addition to the IP54 designation that protects the level from some dust and water damage, this model also has a one-meter drop rating. DeWalt’s three-year limited warranty has you covered if any issues arise. For even more protection, the entire unit fits inside a hard-sided case for safe transport and storage.

While it's on the heavier side for a laser level, it's still very easy to use, and the self-leveling laser beam flashes until it’s in a level position. For even more mounting functionality, the unit pivots freely when mounted to a metal stud thanks to its magnetic base.

If you’re looking for an affordable, easy-to-use laser level for indoor, preferably single-room use, you can’t go wrong with this Bosch option. It’s accurate within 5/16 inches as long as you’re within 30 feet, which should be more than enough for most residential, close-quarters projects.

You’re also getting magnetic and threaded mounting options (although you’ll need to supply your own tripod), and the 2xAA battery power source should be pretty convenient for anyone to have on hand.

The protective design is also rated IP55, which means the level’s internal components are protected from water and dust, and the 12.3-ounce weight makes it one of the lighter options on our list.

Unlike typical laser levels that provide a continuous line across the surface being measured, this Bosch model projects single dots on five points of reference.

This design accurately determines precise level and plumb points across a space—as opposed to general vertical or horizontal alignment. This level of accuracy is essential for tasks that require you to mark exact spots, like transferring points from wall to wall or ceiling to floor, and pinpointing 90 degrees.

It also has a rotating magnetic mount, which makes it a good choice if you're working in an environment with a lot of metal surfaces, such as metal framing studs, structural columns, or even metal fence posts.

The GLL330 from Bosch is solid and compact, giving it a great deal of stability and maneuverability. The standout feature here is the 18V battery upgrade for longer run time. Standard batteries are generally fine, but they tend to go bad during long periods of tool inactivity (or worse, they die out in the middle of a project). Integrating this laser into the Bosch 18V battery platform goes a long way toward preventing potential headaches.

Another noteworthy feature is the lateral adjustment knob, which helps dial in the stability of the laser. Some customer reviews noted that the line grew thicker the further the laser was placed from a given work area, but that was not my experience using this level.

If it has any faults, it’s simply that it might be more than some users might need. This laser is a significant upgrade from the two-directional units the average DIY enthusiast is probably familiar with, so it may take some getting used to.

If you’re looking for a complete laser level system to rival those geared toward commercial applications, DeWalt’s latest upgrade is a game-changer. While it is a bit on the heavier side in terms of both weight and price, it’s a feature-rich tool that is surprisingly easy to operate.

The laser throws beams in three different ways, each of which is easy to access at the push of a button. Alternatively, all three beams can run simultaneously, and each spans 360 degrees. Its average continuous run time on a 2aH battery is around 9 hours.

But the best feature of note here is the mounting system that works in tandem with the unit’s remote control. The magnetic mount houses a motorized tracking system, so you can make adjustments both vertically and horizontally from afar.

Cross-Line: Standard cross-line models are the most common type of laser level, projecting one vertical and one horizontal, forward-facing beam. For the majority of basic tasks—like mounting cabinetry, hanging a painting, or laying tile—a cross-line laser accomplishes everything you need. The Bosch Green Beam Self-Leveling Laser excels in this category, offering precise alignment and Bosch's high-quality construction.

Floor Line: These are specifically designed for tile work and sit on the floor or mount to the wall to create the required 90- or 45-degree angles.

360-Degree: For projects that span an entire room or space, like installing a chair rail or wainscoting, go with a 360-degree laser level. These models project their horizontal beam (and sometimes a vertical beam as well) 360 degrees around the room, instead of limiting the beam to the area in front of the unit. While these are typically more expensive than other types of levels, more budget-friendly options, like the Huepar 3D Green Beam Self-Leveling Laser, are also available.

Dot Lasers: Rather than continuous lines, dot lasers project single points, ideal for point-to-point transfer applications like installing lights and marking exact locations. Their vertical dots essentially replace traditional plumb bobs that serve the same purpose and offer increased visibility. It's typically easier to see a dot than a thin line.

Most laser levels are self-leveling, using an internal pendulum and magnet mechanism to indicate when the beam is completely level (and blinks to indicate it's not level yet). The accuracy of these mechanisms varies from one laser to another, especially as you increase the distance between it and the measuring surface. Because of this variance, keep your measuring distance in mind when choosing a level.

Laser levels have either green or red lasers. While red lasers are the most common—and the most affordable—green lasers provide superior visibility—especially outside in the sunlight—which helps with long-range and exterior use. Green lasers are more expensive to manufacture because they require additional components and more energy than red lasers in order to generate their green color.

The range of the beam also affects a laser level’s overall visibility, and all laser levels provide a maximum distance at which the beam is still effective. In my experience, these estimates should be taken with a grain of salt—personal eyesight, light exposure, and surface material also affect visibility. If you’re on the fence about two products, and plan on working in a large space, consider the range metric a useful tiebreaker.

If you'll use your level outside or in a dusty work area, choose one with an ingress protection (IP) rating. These ratings use a number system to specify the amount of protection against dust (the first digit) and water (the second digit). The maximum for each digit is six and nine, respectively. For example, according to the IP rating chart, an IP54 rating means that your laser level is “dust protected” and can resist “splashing water” from any direction without any harmful effects.

Features like protective rubber corners and hard-sided storage cases also help to keep your laser intact in the event of a drop. The DeWalt Line Laser Level, our choice for “Most Durable” model, is well-suited to this category as well, with a thick rubber exterior and IP54 rating.

It's important to keep your laser level stable and secure during use, so look for options that also offer useful mounting accessories. Some come with a small tripod (compatible levels like the Skil Self-Leveling Cross-Line Laser have a threaded mount to screw right into) or a clamp for attaching to the edge of a table or ladder. Larger, more heavy-duty levels, like the DeWalt Line Laser Level, are commonly designed with an attached magnet that conveniently mounts to metal studs when framing.

When temperatures rise, California redwoods slow down their rate of photosynthesis, a discovery that could have implications for the long-term survival of the iconic species.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When temperatures spike, California redwoods slow down photosynthesis, new research has found. This finding has serious implications for the long-term survival of the iconic trees in a warming world, and their role in storing carbon from the atmosphere.

California redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) forests are among the largest aboveground carbon stores on the planet. These towering trees are native to central and northern California, and evolved to take advantage of the region's historically mild weather. In recent decades, their range has contracted significantly. But climate change is threatening the health and function of these forests.

The region has seen significant warming in recent decades, and faces more frequent extreme heat days, with temperatures spiking above 100 degrees Fahrenheit (37 degrees Celsius). Now, in a new study, published Sept. 22 in the journal JGR Biogeosciences, a team of researchers has shown that California's renowned redwoods are struggling to photosynthesize in the heat.

Photosynthesis is the process used by plants, algae and some bacteria to turn sunlight into energy. It chemically converts carbon dioxide and water into sugars and oxygen.

"These trees adapted to grow in really temperate environments, so no one had really looked at the impact of heat on photosynthesis," study first author Lily Klinek, a doctoral candidate in the Plant Optics Lab at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science.

From 2022 to 2024, Klinek and colleagues measured how the leaves of redwoods in Garcia River Forest in Mendocino County responded to the heat. Once or twice a month, the researchers took three different California redwood leaf samples and measured their fluorescence and temperature.

A plant's molecules can use absorbed light in three ways: for photosynthesis, dissipated as heat, or reflected as light (florescence). Fluorescence is a proxy measurement to understand photosynthesis in the plant, Klinek said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers wrapped a fourth leaf in tinfoil for 20 minutes to put it in a state of "rest" before taking the same measurements. "When they're in a state of rest, we expose them to a pulse of light that’s in the wavelength they would use for photosynthesis to see what would be their maximum photosynthetic rate," Klinek said.

They found that on hot days, the leaves exposed to sunlight were up to 18 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius) hotter than the air temperature. "That's a huge difference and indicates that the leaves are stressed to the point where they can't thermoregulate effectively," Klinek said.

Many plants' leaves manage their temperature and photosynthesis by opening or closing their stomata, which are tiny pores on their surface. These stomata (from the Greek word for mouth) regulate the amount of carbon dioxide entering the plant, and how much oxygen and water vapor it releases. Lower carbon dioxide intake leads to reduced photosynthesis, meaning the plant has less energy.

The large differences between air and redwood leaf temperatures suggest that the leaves had closed their stomata to avoid losing water from evaporation during hot conditions and consequently overheated, Klinek said.

To further investigate the impact of heat on leaf physiology, the researchers took California redwood leaf samples back to the laboratory and exposed them to a range of temperatures while they were in water. Despite their access to water, the leaves still photosynthesized less as they got hotter, even though their stomata were open, Klinek said.

This shows that heat imposes direct limitations on redwood photosynthetical capacity, rather than indirectly decreasing that capacity by causing stomatal closure, the researchers wrote. The finding indicates that redwoods' ability to photosynthesise and store carbon will decrease as temperatures rise.

​​"It is not only stomatal closure that is causing reduced photosynthesis," Lucy Rowland, an ecologist at the University of Exeter in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email. "These trees are already suffering from the direct effects of heat on their photosynthetic systems."

The finding has serious implications for the future of redwoods and similar plants. "The points at which this damage becomes irreversible remains really poorly understood, but is something which is really essential to understand if we want to predict how our future climate is going to impact plants," she said.

The next step in Klinek's research is to move beyond leaf physiology to understand these thresholds on the trees and their ecosystems as a whole.

"We're not sure to what extent the effect that we saw is a reversible stress response and if they are sustaining damage from this constant stress," she said. Researchers need more data to "really get a better sense, beyond the leaf scale, how these ecosystems are responding to heat and drought," she added.

Klinek, L., Au, J., Rodriguez‐Caton, M., Rao, M. P., Fety, L., Koch, G. W., & Magney, T. S. (2026). Summer heat stress downregulates photochemistry in Coast Redwoods. Journal of Geophysical Research Biogeosciences, 131(9). https://doi.org/10.1029/2026jg010052

#153. Scientists Turn a Cancer-Fueling Protein Into a Powerful New Weapon Against Tumors

A protein that helps cancer grow could become an unlikely ally in treating it, with laboratory and mouse experiments showing that activating it in engineered immune cells curbs tumor growth.

Colorectal cancer has become the leading cause of cancer-related death in people under 50, and chemotherapy and newer immunotherapy drugs can fall short against its most common forms. That toll among younger people led researchers at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL) to investigate whether changing how immune cells burn fuel could help them fight the disease.

In a study published in Nature Immunology, the team found that activating a protein involved in fat burning helped engineered immune cells slow or stop tumor growth in laboratory and mouse experiments. The protein, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta (PPARD), helps control how human cells use fat. The researchers activated it in CAR T cells, engineered immune cells already used in some cancer immunotherapies.

To test whether the altered CAR T cells could attack human colorectal cancer, the team used organoids, miniature tumors grown from patient tissue samples. They also tested the cells against human cancer cells in a dish and human cancer cells implanted in mice, finding that tumor growth slowed or stopped in each setting. The researchers also validated their findings in other tumor types, including breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and melanoma.

PPARD is a transcription factor, a protein that helps control gene activity, and it usually promotes cancer growth. Investigating whether it could also help immune cells drew on a broader idea about fitness. Doctors have long recognized fitness as one of the strongest determinants of patient outcomes. For CSHL Assistant Professor Semir Beyaz, that concept extends beyond a patient’s physique to the capabilities of individual cells.

“We hypothesized that the fitness determinants of cancer and our immune cells may not be so different,” he said. “They’re in the same universe. They’re constrained by the same chemical and physical rules. So, it’s not surprising they’d end up evolving the same way.”

Before testing the approach in CAR T cells, Beyaz’s lab investigated PPARD in a mouse model of colorectal cancer. Although the cancer cells had their own PPARD, activating it in immune cells shifted the environment around the tumor from supporting cancer to opposing it. “It’s all about cell fitness,” Beyaz explains. “What cells eat affects who they are. When immune cells burn more fat, they become more fit for fighting cancer.”

Beyaz likens PPARD’s opposing roles to “the force” from Star Wars. It can promote disease like Darth Vader carrying out the Emperor’s will, or turn against disease like Anakin Skywalker seeing the light. “It’s the classic fight between good and evil,” Beyaz says. “How can good ultimately prevail? Activating PPARD in immune cells could be the way.”

The findings remain experimental, but Beyaz sees them as the “tip of the iceberg” for making cancer immunotherapy more effective. His lab is now applying the approach to endometriosis, a chronic inflammatory disease affecting one in 10 women for which more effective treatments are needed.

“Boosting immune cell fitness may also help with other conditions where the immune system fails to clear diseased cells,” Beyaz says.

Reference: “Compartment-specific PPARδ activity controls the outcome of cancer–immune cell competition and immunotherapy efficacy” by Paul Bunk, Ilgin Ergin, Timothy Maher, Vyom Shah, Julia R. Hamilton showed that, no matter how daunting the obstacles, there are few problems we can't solve.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dean Robbins is a journalist and children's author. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights.

The pioneering computer scientist Margaret Hamilton, who died on Sept. 30 at age 90, played a key role in putting astronauts on the moon. She was a problem-solver extraordinaire, and it all started in early childhood.

Considering the name "daddy longlegs" unfair to female arachnids, young Margaret decided to call half of them "mommy longlegs." Wondering why the neighborhood baseball players were all boys, she determined to join the team herself.

As she grew up in the 1940s and '50s, Margaret noticed a similar problem with various professions. Why were doctors, judges and scientists almost always men? The solution: she would study hard in school and prepare herself for any job she might care to do.

It's no surprise that a born problem-solver would gravitate to computers. In the late 1950s, the new technology offered mind-bending possibilities, and this college math major saw a chance to put her skills to use on a cosmic scale.

Hamilton had long been a stargazer, thanks to a philosophical father who taught her to love the night sky. In 1965, after stints in meteorology and satellite tracking, she became interested in a Massachusetts Institute of Technology project that designed in-flight computers for NASA's moon mission.

The team, of course, consisted solely of men. But, just as with her neighborhood baseball team, Hamilton refused to accept limitations for herself or anybody else. She kicked open the door and quickly rose to director of software engineering.

With her knack for devising novel solutions to seemingly insoluble problems, no one was better suited for the job. Working with the era's primitive technology, Margaret thought through the various mishaps that could occur on a spaceflight and designed the software to handle every contingency.

The epochal Apollo 11 moon mission of 1969 put her planning to the test. As astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin neared the moon's surface in their lunar module, an error overloaded the onboard computer's processing unit. Mission Control faced the prospect of aborting the landing, but Margaret's ingenious programming allowed the system to prioritize essential tasks while canceling the inessential ones. The lunar module touched down without a hitch, and Armstrong and Aldrin became famous.

Sadly, Margaret Hamilton did not. She continued to work behind the scenes, contributing to the five additional lunar landings as well as Skylab and the space shuttle. In 1976, she struck off on her own to start a software company. She might have lived the rest of her life in obscurity if not for a fateful black-and-white photograph from 1969.

This image began to attract attention on the internet in the 2010s. It showed Margaret wedged between a coatrack and a blackboard at MIT, standing beside a towering stack of her printed code from the Apollo missions. Bespectacled and smiling, she radiates the confidence of a scientist who had stormed the boys' club and conquered the universe.

I was one of those fascinated by the photograph, and I contacted Margaret about the possibility of profiling her in a children's book. She initially resisted, uncomfortable with being the center of attention. But she came to see the appeal of a book about herself that she could read to her great-grandchildren, so that they might be inspired to break barriers themselves one day. She warmed to the task of telling her life story and even sent me examples of her Apollo code, which Lucy Knisley incorporated in the illustrations for "Margaret and the Moon: How Margaret Hamilton Saved the First Lunar Landing."

With the 2016 book and movie "Hidden Figures" calling attention to women's overlooked contributions to the space program, Hamilton soon had to get used to being the center of attention. She received a Presidential Medal of Freedom and achieved LEGO immortality in the "Women of NASA" set. In 2019, to mark the 50th anniversary of the first moon landing, Google used reflected moonlight to create a massive portrait of Margaret in the Mojave Desert. Rarely has so humble a soul received so grand a tribute.

The world will miss Margaret Hamilton, but, just like her great-grandchildren, we will always have her example to inspire us. She showed that, no matter how daunting the obstacles, there are few problems we can't solve.

#156. Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea

Physicists have uncovered a strange new form of quantum behavior in which particles organize themselves in ways that challenge established theories. Even more surprising, the particles maintain a remarkable hidden order despite being driven into an extremely energetic state.

In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers from the group led by Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, working with theoretical physicist Alvise Bastianello of the CNRS and Université Paris-Dauphine, describe how to engineer an exotic quantum state known as a "fractional Fermi sea."

The breakthrough involves pushing ultracold cesium atoms far beyond their normal conditions by repeatedly changing how strongly they attract or repel one another. Rather than simply becoming disordered, the particles rearrange themselves into an unusual configuration that behaves differently from the quantum systems scientists have traditionally studied.

The theoretical findings provide the foundation for recent experimental research conducted by Nägerl's team at the Department of Experimental Physics.

Pushing Quantum Particles Beyond Their Normal Limits

Under ordinary conditions, quantum particles follow well-established rules that determine how they arrange themselves, particularly at extremely low temperatures.

One important example involves fermions, a category of particles that includes electrons. These particles cannot all occupy the same quantum state, so they fill available energy levels according to specific restrictions. At very low temperatures, this arrangement produces what physicists call a Fermi sea.

But what happens when researchers deliberately disrupt the conditions that normally govern how particles behave?

As Alvise Bastianello explains: "Fermions, for instance, stack neatly into the available energy states to form the so-called 'Fermi sea'. But what happens if one forces interacting atoms to continuously cycle through extreme conditions, smoothly shifting them from strongly repelling each other to strongly attracting each other?"

To investigate this possibility, the researchers studied ultracold cesium atoms confined to a one-dimensional system. This means the atoms are restricted to moving along a single direction, creating an environment in which their quantum interactions can be studied with exceptional control.

The team examined what happens when the interactions between these atoms are repeatedly adjusted, cycling between powerful repulsion and attraction.

Their calculations revealed something unexpected. Starting from the ground state, the lowest energy configuration available to the system, the atoms could be driven into a highly excited state without losing their underlying organization.

The researchers call this unusual arrangement a fractional Fermi sea because its particles appear to obey a modified rule governing how quantum states are occupied.

"Instead of simply heating the system, the interaction cycle reorganizes the atoms into a new many-body state," says Yi Zeng, the leading author of this study. "This gives us a controlled way to explore quantum matter beyond the usual equilibrium paradigms."

A Strange New Quantum State With Hidden Order

One of the most intriguing features of the fractional Fermi sea is that its particles remain organized even though the system has been pushed far from equilibrium.

In physics, equilibrium describes a condition in which a system's overall properties have settled into a stable balance. Systems driven far from equilibrium can behave in complicated and unexpected ways, making them particularly challenging to understand.

Yet the fractional Fermi sea is not simply a collection of excited particles behaving randomly. Instead, it contains distinctive mathematical patterns that reveal a deeper structure.

Among these patterns are pronounced ripples called Friedel oscillations. These are wave-like variations associated with the way quantum particles influence one another. The researchers also identified unusual patterns in how correlations between particles weaken with increasing distance, even when the repulsive interactions are relatively weak.

These signatures are important because they differ from predictions associated with Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory, a long-established framework for describing how interacting quantum particles behave in one-dimensional systems.

The findings therefore point toward a previously unexplored type of quantum behavior that cannot be fully described using this familiar theoretical picture.

"This state is highly excited, but it is not random," says Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, the group leader. "It has a hidden order that becomes visible in its correlations."

The strange behavior also raises questions about the effective particles that emerge within the system. Physicists call these collective excitations quasiparticles because they can behave like individual particles even though they arise from the coordinated motion of many interacting particles.

Nägerl suggests that the unusual excitations might eventually deserve a name of their own.

"We are not yet sure how we should name these new quasiparticles. Perhaps 'super-Fermions'?"

Opening a New Frontier in Quantum Physics

The discovery suggests that fractional Fermi seas represent an exotic critical phase of quantum matter, with characteristic patterns of particle correlations that extend beyond existing descriptions of one-dimensional quantum systems.

It also demonstrates the growing power of quantum simulation, a technique that allows scientists to use carefully controlled quantum systems to investigate physical behavior that would otherwise be difficult to reproduce or study.

Ultracold atoms are particularly useful for this purpose because researchers can precisely adjust their interactions and observe how the resulting quantum states change.

Rather than limiting these experiments to recreating phenomena already understood through established theories, scientists can now explore deliberately engineered states that reveal entirely new possibilities.

As Hanns-Christoph Nägerl says: "The discovery of fractional Fermi seas shows how far we can push quantum simulation: not only reproducing known models, but creating and probing states that go beyond established paradigms."

The current publication establishes the theoretical framework for fractional Fermi seas. A companion study describing their experimental realization through quantum simulation is undergoing peer review.

Together, the research points toward new ways of investigating the fundamental behavior of quantum matter, including unusual collective excitations and hidden forms of order that emerge only when particles are pushed far outside their normal conditions.

#157. A duo goes against the tide to explain an origin of human endurance

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Perhaps it was diving, not just chasing prey on the African savanna, that made us marathoners

To stay deep, a Sama-Bajau woman hunting for fish exhales. Two researchers suggest that such diving by human predecessors led to modern-day stamina.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Two researchers may have opened floodgates on the debate over why humans can run marathons, swim the English Channel or dive a hundred meters and back on a single breath and their ape cousins can’t.

Humans evolved endurance for feats like these not just by running down prey on the African savanna, but also by diving for food in lakes or coastal waters, the duo propose September 17 in PaleoAnthropology. The hypothesis adds complexity to a decades-old theory that puts the drivers for evolution exclusively on land. But it coexists with a history of pushback for any water-related ideas.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The work is causing ripples among anthropologists. “I could not work out [at first] if this was groundbreaking or dumb,” says Christian Tryon, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.

In 1960,  researchers came up with what’s been called the aquatic ape or waterside hypothesis, which suggested that our ancestors evolved longer legs and other adaptations from swimming for their suppers in watery habitats. Popularized in media accounts but not adequately vetted in peer-reviewed journals, the idea was shunned by the scientific community as additional fossils pointed away from a life in water.  More recently,  the dominant theory has been that it was landlocked human ancestors who gradually developed our remarkable endurance. “There’s been this reluctance to really think about anything sort of water-related as important in human evolution,” Tryon says.

Yet evolutionary anthropologist Josephine Joordens, a self-professed “water person” who trained as a marine biologist, had long wondered whether coastal life was vital to the evolutionary process, because it provides easy access to both water and land resources. Joordens combined forces with Erika Schagatay, a physiologist at Mid-Sweden University in Östersund, to formulate what they call the “dive first, run later” hypothesis.

Schagatay — herself a freediver — has spent decades observing and monitoring modern sea foraging people such as the Ama in Japan and the Sama-Bajau in Southeast Asia. Joordens studied fossil evidence and combed the literature about aquatic activities. Our evolution “was likely a very complex and very dynamic process,” says Joordens, of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany.

They propose some Homo species wound up shallow-water diving repeatedly about 2 million to 3 million years ago, much the way the Sama-Bajau do today. These people spend four to six hours per day repeatedly diving several meters deep to catch fish and collect shellfish and other food.  They evolved bigger spleens than their non-diving counterparts and, it seems, enhanced respiratory and cardiovascular capacity. They have the ability to “pace” breathing periods and breath-holding to avoid fatigue.  In our ancestors, that could have paved the way for the cardiorespiratory stamina needed in modern endurance running, Schagatay says.

These Homo divers evolved heavy bones to help stay underwater and downward facing noses to keep water out, the two suggest. They eventually passed those endurance-boosting traits on to other populations with lighter bones and a more terrestrial lifestyle.

The study “shows there is a lot of evidence” for forage diving as an early evolutionary driver, says Leslea Hlusko, a paleobiologist at the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana in Burgos, Spain.

This idea is not a retread of the aquatic ape theory, says Christopher Ruff, a biological anthropologist at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. “Occasional aquatic foraging is quite a different proposal“ from the discredited theory’s primarily aquatic existence and should be taken seriously, Ruff says.Not everyone thinks the dive first idea holds water.

Multiple factors work against the idea that diving could have helped humans become better endurance runners, says Daniel Lieberman, a paleoanthropologist at Harvard University.  He argues that endurance diving does not require an enhanced aerobic capacity: It slows the heart rate, whereas running speeds it up. He disputes how and why heavy bones arose; they could have developed in people who used their bodies for heavy work and not because such bones helped divers with buoyancy issues. Nor is the downward pointed nose meaningful given that many diving mammals have forward facing noses. Other reasons, such as keeping the air in nostrils moist, were probably more important in selecting for this feature, he says.

What’s more, many people around the world have long relied on running down game for food, says archaeologist Eugène Morin of Trent University in Peterborough, Canada.  “Diving is costly and the [caloric] returns are low,” so early humans would not choose to dive if other foraging opportunities existed, he argues.

Critiques aside, “the simple ‘ape walked out from forest to savanna’ story clearly does not cut it anymore,” says Pascal Gagneux, a biological anthropologist at the University of California, San Diego. Coastal routes around Africa, along Africa’s lakeshores and out of Africa “must have played a huge role” in human evolution, Gagneux says.

The pair knows they risk the ire of their peers in presenting this “dive first”  hypothesis, but Joordens says, “we are both in our early 60s and we both have beautiful careers, so we thought ‘whatever happens, happens.’”And Tryon ultimately found the paper worth the read. “If nothing else, it gets people thinking and it gets people looking.”

#158. The Flavor of Neutrinos Could Determine How a Large Star Dies

A core-collapse supernova occurs when a massive star reaches the end of its life. After running out of hydrogen and other light elements to burn, the star makes a last ditch effort to counter gravity, fusing ever heavier elements at an ever faster pace. Eventually it reaches the point where heavy fusion extracts energy from the core rather than adds it. The core rapidly contracts, then recoils. The resulting explosion rips the star apart and briefly outshines an entire galaxy. But not all giant stars end with a bang. Some of them experience a core collapse so quick and dense that the core squeezes itself into a black hole. These stars end with a whimper rather than a bang.

So what exactly causes this difference? Why do some stars explode and others not? What key features distinguish between the two? The answer could lie in an aspect of neutrinos known as flavor.

Neutrinos are the chargeless, low-mass cousins to charged leptons such as the electron. The electron is the lightest charged lepton, with the muon and tauon as the heavier versions. For each of these leptons there is a corresponding neutrino. So there's the electron, muon, and tauon neutrino, each known as a neutrino flavor. For a long time physicists thought neutrinos were massless, which meant that the flavor of a neutrino was unique. But we later found that neutrinos have a tiny mass that allows neutrinos to flip from one flavor to another.

When a massive star undergoes a core collapse, a tremendous amount of neutrinos are produced. Since neutrinos don't interact strongly with other matter, most of the neutrinos escape the core with little effort. In fact, one way to know a star's core is collapsing would be to observe a spike of neutrinos just before the star explodes.

Most simulations of a star's core collapse don't worry about these neutrinos. They don't have a great deal of mass, and since they flee the scene early on, you wouldn't expect them to play a major role. But different flavors of neutrinos have different mass, so flavor changing states might mean the difference between having enough mass to collapse directly into a black hole. This is the focus of a new study.

Simulations show how different flavor thresholds determine a collapse state. Credit: Gogilashvili & Tamborra

Flavor changing is a complex process, so the team used a simplified approach to include them in model simulations. Rather than worrying about the details, they assumed different levels of flavor changes. This way they could determine how the level of flavor change might affect the outcome. The authors then ran simulations of stellar core collapse for 195 progenitor stars with masses ranging from 9 solar masses to 120 solar masses. Each of these was run with different flavor-changing ratios to determine whether the core exploded or fully collapsed.

What they found was that even a small amount of flavor changing can flip the outcome for a star. The effect is strongest for stars in the 16-30 solar mass range, meaning that most stars in this mass range collapse directly into black holes. Smaller stars and the largest stars become supernovae unless the neutrino flavor changing is particularly strong. This result suggests that neutrinos play a critical role in the outcome of a dying star. This could also help explain why we seem to observe fewer supernovae than we expect given the rate of star formation in galaxies.

Now that we know neutrino flavor changing can be the difference between a star becoming a supernova or black hole, the next challenge will be to determine if they are the key player. One way to do this is to observe more stellar progenitors of supernovae. As large sky surveys come online, we will capture images of stars before they explode and even while they are in the critical transition stage.

One of the great mysteries of stellar evolution could just be solved by the elementary particles with the smallest mass.

Reference: Gogilashvili, Mariam, and Irene Tamborra. "Neutrino flavor conversion shapes the rate of failed core-collapse supernovae." Physical Review D 114.6 (2026): L061304.

#159. A Failed Drone Attack Unmasked Russia’s Secret Army of Accidental Spies

Russia built a gig economy for sabotage, and the cover is to make every attack look like a random crime.

It began with a drone on a tarmac in Germany.

The drone’s mission was to destroy a Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Had it succeeded, the “severe structural damage” it was intended to cause might have been attributed to a lone wolf—either as an act of domestic terrorism or just a random act of unhinged violence.

But, as a joint investigation by The Telegraph and the Welt am Sonntag points out, because the plot failed, authorities in Germany were able to recover the drone completely intact, along with the tin full of explosives that it was carrying. Investigators discovered that the explosive device wasn’t some amateurish improvised bomb made by a madman. Instead, it “closely resembled bombs in Russian plots elsewhere across Europe.” That resemblance allowed them to trace the plot not just to the “disposable agent” recruited to carry it out, but to the motorcycle-riding Russian intermediary German intelligence believes managed him, and to the man in Moscow suspected of giving that biker his marching orders on behalf of Russia’s military intelligence—the GRU.

At the center of this operation, the reporting suggests, is Oleg Levushkin, a motorcycle enthusiast who ran an import business in tea, coffee and spices. German intelligence says his job was “preparing the means of committing the crime before its actual execution,” after which he handed the attack itself to Belarusian proxy agent Andrei Karshakou. Further up the chain, at the far end of this “political leaders to pipe bombs” pipeline, sits Denis Smolyaninov, “an alleged chief planner of bomb attacks across Europe for Russia.”

A December 2025 Lithuanian intelligence report identified Smolyaninov as leading the Ukraine department of the GRU (GRU is the acronym of the department’s previous name during the Soviet period, Главное разведывательное управление—Main Intelligence Directorate). The report notes that Smolyaninov “specialised in psychological operations, and was associated with covert sabotage campaigns organized in Europe using the messaging app Telegram.”

That final sentence in their assessment is the key to understanding what many find so troubling about this new frontier of agent recruitment. Subversive groups and foreign powers no longer need to seek out “fellow travelers” (a euphemism for Communist agents/sympathizers adapted from Anatoly Lunacharsky’s term “попутчик”) at union meetings or intellectual gatherings. Now, even otherwise unassuming or even apolitical individuals can be converted into “disposable agents” with an app you can download on your phone.

Some of these gig agents are still acting on ideological grounds, certainly. But others are simply doing it for the money: $5 for putting up an anti-NATO poster, $400 if you install a spy camera, and so on. Payments are made via cryptocurrency; the gig agents’ GRU handlers don’t even need to set foot outside of Moscow.

Many of these unwitting agents are just ordinary people trying to get by. They’re the underemployed, or immigrants seeking gig work that pays under the table. They grab one of these seemingly innocuous jobs just as they would a rideshare or food delivery assignment, sometimes even in the same day, with no thought to the danger—or the geopolitical implications.

Even when an assignment does involve something undeniably destructive or otherwise illegal, like burning down a warehouse, the “disposable agent” is oftentimes more inclined to conclude it’s part of some street-level gangland rivalry rather than a global conflict between powerful nations. They assume their cryptocurrency payment is being furnished by a crime boss rather than the Kremlin.

The Guardian even found a case where these gig workers were completely unaware that they were fighting against their own side. “Last May,” the paper reports, “Polish authorities arrested a Pole and two Belarusians on suspicion of planning sabotage acts for the Russians inside Poland. All three men had previously fought in Ukraine on the side of Kyiv.”

This app-based à la carte infiltration represents an unsettling new chapter in the long history of cloak-and-dagger activity, one the International Institute for Strategic Studies has dubbed the “intelligence-operative gig economy.” It’s the evolution, and maybe even the perfection, of a principle of spycraft first established centuries before the USSR was even a twinkle in Vladimir Lenin’s eye.

The blueprint, it turns out, is roughly 2,400 years old. In the Arthashastra—a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft attributed to the Brahmin Chanakya—an early chapter lays out an entire taxonomy of sancháráh, or “wandering spies.” The roles these spies perform can vary, from the satri, the classmate spies, who stir up the educated populace with provocation, to the tikshna, the firebrands, who face and deal in deadly force for money, and to the parivrajika, the woman ascetic, who can infiltrate the homes of prime ministers and high society.

“The immediate officers of the institutes of espionage shall by making use of signs or writing set their own spies in motion,” the text notes. But it cautions that, crucially, “Neither the institutes of espionage nor they (the wandering spies) shall know each other.”

The Cold War-era KGB understood this, so it relied on layers upon layers of intermediaries and “cutouts” between state officials and the operatives actually getting their hands dirty in the cloak-and-dagger field. It made their spy network much harder for their targets to untangle, and kept the Soviet government at a safe distance, with plenty of plausible deniability should a mission be exposed or have unintended consequences.

According to a report from the International Centre for Defense and Security, modern-day Russia appears to be using contemporary technology to practice the same obfuscation techniques:

The ICDS’s criminal-enterprise comparison turns out to be apt in more ways than one. Trying to unravel the purposefully obscured chain of command can call to mind the old mafia movies, with cops pinning blurry photographs to a bulletin board, linked by bits of yarn. Yet the KGB knew this kind of obscuring wasn’t just a shield—it could also be a weapon in itself.

The KGB often relied on the doctrine of “маскировка,” literally meaning masking or disguising. The idea originated during WWII, when the Soviet army deceived Axis planners by utilizing fake tank turrets and implied troop movements to create uncertainty and deplete enemy reserves. This form of deception was a component of such pivotal battles as Stalingrad, Kursk, and 1944’s Operation Bagration.

During the Cold War, the Soviet intelligence apparatus relied on маскировка as a form of psychological warfare against its ideological opponents (and, in some senses, to keep its own citizenry in line as well). For example, one might think the goal in arranging an act of arson against an enemy structure is to, in mob parlance, “make it look like an accident.” But there’s a benefit to making it look only almost like an accident. If that fire could have been KGB sabotage, then so could the next one, and the one after that. Once you’ve created that sliver of ambiguity in your espionage activity, every real accident can also be attributed to your nefarious actions by your duly paranoid opponent.

Recent reports suggest that modern Russia operates on much the same principle, and that the advent of the “disposable agent” has made the method easier to deploy than ever. Consider the drone at Leipzig/Halle. Had it detonated on the wing of that Antonov, the planning behind the attack might never have surfaced. In that case, even if investigators identified the operator, they couldn’t easily say whether he was a foreign agent or a lone wolf radicalized online. And if the people carrying out these attacks don’t even know they’re serving Moscow, who can say with confidence which act of violence, or which small act of disruption, is the work of a lone wolf—and which is the work of a disposable agent?

Beyond the mind games, the strategy carries a simpler cost for its targets: every cheap attack forces an expensive defense. It might seem strange that so many of these “disposable agents” are being deployed for one-off attacks on small scale targets. The ICDS’ report speaks of agents being recruited online for tasks like warehouse fires, truck and railway explosions, and even a vandalism campaign against a Jewish memorial in Paris “reminiscent of the KGB’s swastika campaign of 1959.” At first blush, these civilian targets might have little strategic value. But in the big picture, that’s exactly why it benefits Russia to attack them. A $5 arsonist can oblige a government to spend millions guarding everything he might burn next.

A 1948 study for the United States Army’s Center for Military History, “Rear Area Security in Russia,” highlighted a strategy deployed by the Soviet Army that differed from conventional military wisdom. This “Soviet Second Front Behind the German Lines” used Russian partisans to attack individual bridges, trains, supply depots, and other small targets deep inside German territory to force the Nazis to divert much-needed security forces away from the front. The attacks would stress Nazi supply lines and make defending occupied areas in the rear far more costly and complicated.

The KGB’s Division V, which specialized in foreign assassinations and sabotage, adopted a similar strategy during the Cold War. And now, the GRU’s unit 29155 is essentially doing the same thing. By attacking small infrastructure targets with easily deployable disposable agents, they’re forcing their opponents to defend every little potential target in their territory. That doesn’t just cost money and manpower, it also means less attention can be paid to the larger targets that need defending, weakening the entire security apparatus.

Covert warfare is evolving before our eyes in the 21st century. Cultivating a fellow traveler once took years; now an agent can be hired in minutes, unaware of who he’s fighting for, or even that he’s fighting at all. Moscow is redeploying Soviet tradecraft against people desperate enough to take the work, and the espionage gig economy it’s built threatens to destabilize far more than Ukraine. There is a flaw in the design, though. It isn’t that recruits are too skeptical to be fooled. It’s that people chasing easy money are rarely interested in doing the job well.

Consider the Belarusian woman who was convicted with her boyfriend for papering her city with anti-NATO flyers she says neither of them believed in. As The Guardian reported, “Her boyfriend, she claimed, would often put up a poster, take a photo to provide proof, and then immediately pull it down.”

So the next time you see somebody half-heartedly taking a gig from an app, cutting corners and generally phoning it in to milk as much cryptocurrency as possible for the least amount of effort, be grateful. That laziness might be helping to curb a national security threat.

A recent study may reshape our understanding of brain evolution and open new avenues for studying neurological diseases.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Recent research challenges a long-standing idea about how the brain develops: Rather than arising from a single source, the brain may emerge from two distinct populations of cells, the study finds.

"The brain appears as one organ," said study co-author Kyle Loh, an associate professor of developmental biology at Stanford University. "However, we discovered that the front part of the brain and the back part of the brain come from different sources, which are pushed together to create the appearance of a single organ," Loh told Live Science in an email.

The findings, published in September in the journal Nature Neuroscience, not only challenge established models of how the brain forms but may also explain why researchers have struggled to grow certain types of brain cells in the laboratory. The scientists say the work could offer new ways to investigate diseases that affect the brainstem, the "stalk" that connects the brain to the spinal cord.

The human brain is divided into three main regions — called the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain — that perform different but interconnected functions.

The forebrain, which includes the cerebral hemispheres, is involved in higher-level cognitive processes, such as language, planning and abstract thinking. The midbrain, the uppermost part of the brainstem, connects the forebrain and the hindbrain and acts as a key relay center for sensory information and movement control. The hindbrain — which includes the bottom of the brainstem, along with other structures — also helps to coordinate movement, as well as regulate essential functions such as breathing, sleep and heart rate.

Historically, the hindbrain has been difficult to study. One reason is that scientists have faced persistent challenges in generating functional hindbrain neurons in laboratory conditions.

To help understand why, Loh and his team looked at the early stages of embryonic development in lab mice. They focused on gastrulation, the point when cells begin to organize into structures that will later form different organs. The researchers identified two distinct populations of immature cells that would go on to give rise to nervous system tissue, including the brain.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

One cell population expressed a gene called Otx2, which helps to direct the early development of the forebrain and midbrain. The second group of cells expressed the gene Gbx2, which is involved in the development of the midbrain and hindbrain.

This photograph shows a 9.5-day-old mouse embryo and depicts the two separate developmental origins of the brain. The forebrain and part of the midbrain (blue) express the Otx2 gene, while the hindbrain and the rest of the midbrain (red) express Gbx2. The red cell population also extends into the spinal cord.

The functions of these genes were already known, but their distinct expression in these two groups of cells was revealed by the new research. The cell populations remained distinct as they developed into full-fledged nervous tissue, rather than overlapping.

The team also examined chromatin, the molecular structure that packages DNA tightly inside the nucleus and helps regulate which genes a cell can use. The two cell populations show different chromatin configurations, the team found, which further supports the idea that they follow separate developmental pathways.

That may help to explain why scientists' attempts to grow hindbrain neurons have been largely unsuccessful.

"Previous attempts to make hindbrain neurons likely tried to coax forebrain and midbrain progenitors into hindbrain cells, which our study shows is not possible," study co-author Rayyan Jokhai, a graduate student in Loh's lab, said in a statement.

Using the information uncovered in their experiments, the researchers successfully guided human stem cells to transform into functional hindbrain motor neurons, which are involved in controlling movement. Specifically, these cells produced proteins characteristic of the hard-to-grow hindbrain regions that help control muscles of the face and those involved in swallowing.

In several neurological diseases, including spinal muscular atrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, motor neurons deteriorate and affected patients can lose their ability to swallow, speak and breathe independently.

"We cannot sample living motor neurons from a patient's hindbrain to watch how these diseases attack these neurons," Loh said. "Growing these hindbrain motor neurons in a dish gives us a way to investigate these diseases." Looking forward, the team aims to use their findings to study these diseases and pinpoint new treatments.

The new findings could also reveal something fundamental about the evolution of vertebrate animals.

The study authors investigated whether the two developmental pathways were unique to humans or reflected a much older evolutionary arrangement. They turned to previously published data on other species — including macaques (Macaca), zebrafish (Danio rerio) and chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus) — and again found two distinct cell populations expressing the two key genes.

And even in acorn worms — a marine invertebrate whose evolution diverged from vertebrates about 550 million years ago — they again found these two distinct groups of cells.

"The Stanford discovery establishes that the deep ancestry of the vertebrate brain is fundamentally modular," said Anna Di Cosmo, a professor of biology at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy who wasn't involved with the study. "The developmental separation between the anterior lineage (forebrain/midbrain) and the posterior lineage (hindbrain) is traceably ancient," Cosmo told Live Science in an email.

Loh's team speculates that these developmental trajectories seen in the womb may suggest that the two cell populations once belonged to two separate nervous systems. "Later in evolution, these two nervous systems may have been pushed together to give rise to the appearance of one integrated brain," Loh said.

However, the study doesn't reveal exactly when the two pathways arose or establish how they integrated. "It is important to emphasize that this is only an idea, and it might change as scientists learn more," Loh said.

A., Greenfeld, H., Wong, A., Qu, Y., Petkovic, A. S., Miao, Y., Garcia, K. C., . . . Loh, K. M. (2026). Two parallel neural ectoderm progenitors contribute to the developing brain. #161. New Triple-Action Drug Helps People With Diabetes Lose Up to 15% of Their Body Weight

An experimental drug that targets three metabolic pathways has shown promising results in people with type 2 diabetes.

An experimental drug that targets three metabolic pathways has produced substantial improvements in blood sugar control and weight loss in people with type 2 diabetes. In a phase 3 clinical trial published in The Lancet, participants receiving the once-weekly injection lost an average of up to 15.3% of their body weight over 40 weeks, alongside significant reductions in long-term blood sugar levels.

The drug, called retatrutide, belongs to an emerging generation of treatments designed to influence several hormones involved in metabolism. Unlike existing medications that activate one or two hormone receptors, retatrutide acts on three, potentially offering a different approach to treating diabetes and obesity.

The trial found that retatrutide reduced HbA1c, a measure of average blood sugar over approximately three months, by 1.69 to 1.94 percentage points, depending on the dose. Participants receiving a placebo experienced a smaller reduction of 0.81 percentage points.

Weight loss also increased with the dose. Participants receiving 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg of retatrutide lost an average of 11.5%, 13.9%, and 15.3% of their body weight, respectively. Those given a placebo lost an average of 2.6%.

Retatrutide activates three hormone receptors involved in regulating blood sugar, appetite, and energy metabolism: GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon. By comparison, Ozempic targets GLP-1, while Mounjaro activates both GLP-1 and GIP.

The addition of glucagon receptor activity could help explain retatrutide’s effects on body weight. Although glucagon normally helps raise blood sugar, it also influences how the body uses and expends energy. Combining its activity with GLP-1 and GIP signaling may support weight loss while maintaining improved glucose control. However, the trial did not directly establish how much each pathway contributed to the observed benefits.

Researchers conducted the 40-week trial at 48 sites across the United States, Mexico, and India. Of 930 adults screened, 537 were randomly assigned to receive one of three retatrutide doses or a placebo. All participants had type 2 diabetes that was inadequately controlled through diet and exercise alone and were not taking diabetes medications.

The most common side effects were gastrointestinal problems, generally mild to moderate, that tended to improve over time. Between 2% and 5% of participants receiving retatrutide discontinued treatment because of adverse events. No severe hypoglycemia was reported. Two participants died during the study, but both deaths were assessed as unrelated to the treatment.

Although the results support retatrutide’s potential as a diabetes treatment, the study did not compare it directly with currently available drugs such as Ozempic or Mounjaro. Additional clinical trials and longer-term follow-up are needed to determine whether its benefits persist and to better establish its safety profile.

Reference: “Efficacy and safety of retatrutide, a GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptor agonist, in people with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycaemic control with diet and exercise (TRANSCEND-T2D-1): a double-blind, randomised, phase 3 trial” by Harpreet S Bajaj, Michelle Welch, Parag Shah, Eduardo Luna, Fatima-Zahra Jaouimaa, Bing Liu, Rong Liu, Yanyun Chen, Hiren Patel and Amy Bartee, 6 June 2026, The Lancet. DOI: 10.1016/S0140-6736(26)00967-0

#163. A Radio Phoenix Beyond the Zone of Avoidance

We've gotta give credit to space scientists. They come up with great names for things, probably because so many of them like science fiction. One of these delicious names is given to the region of the sky that's blocked from our view by the Milky Way: the Zone of Avoidance.

The Zone of Avoidance (ZoA) covers about 20% of the sky and is opaque to optical light. The ZoA isn't completely impenetrable; astronomers can still observe the region beyond it in x-rays, infrared and radio. But observations in each of those bands have their limitations.

NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory isn't the best observatory for surveying beyond the ZoA, but is does excel in one way. Its strength is its angular resolution, and that makes it useful for pinpointing individual sources. It's useful for detecting things like active galactic nuclei and galaxy clusters.

There's a strange formation of radio waves beyond the ZoA nicknamed the Treble Clef (VLSSJ0318.9+5755), so-named because it looks kind of like the musical notation symbol. New research published in Astronomy and Astrophysics used the Chandra and SRG/eROSITA to determine what the Treble Clef is and to trace its history. It's titled "The Treble Clef radio phoenix and its old nonthermal filaments," and the lead author is Andrea Botteon of the National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF) in Italy.

"This source, also detected in previous radio observations, was originally believed to be a pulsar, but was later suggested to lie in a heavily obscured galaxy cluster behind the Galactic plane," the authors write. "In this paper, we characterize the main properties of the host cluster (redshift, mass, temperature, X-ray luminosity, and dynamical status) for the first time, using X-ray observations from Chandra and SRG/eROSITA."

Chandra and eROSITA detected extremely hot diffuse gas in the region. The gas is super-heated to millions of degrees and emits x-rays. The researchers also used radio observations from the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), a network of radio telescopes in Europe, to observe the Treble Clef.

This is a LOFAR image of the Treble Clef. Its main filament and other features are labelled. Image Credit: Shimwell et al. 2026.

Along with infrared data from the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope, the researchers created a composite, multispectral image of the Treble Clef. In the composite image below, x-ray data is blue, white is infrared, and radio is red.

The composite image of the Treble Clef is made of x-ray, infrared, and radio data. Image Credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/INAF-IRA/A. Botteon et al.; Infrared: UKIDSS-GPS ; Radio: ASTRON/LOFAR; Image processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/N. Wolk

This work also confirmed, for the first time, that galaxy clusters were involved in the creation of the Treble Clef. Initial observations of the Treble Clef region go back years, and in those surveys, researchers struggled to understand what they were seeing. Thanks to Chandra and eROSITA, galaxy clusters have been identified. A critical part of identifying a galaxy cluster or clusters is finding the Brightest cluster galaxy (BCG). A BCG is defined as the brightest individual galaxy in a cluster, and they're some of the most massive galaxies in the entire Universe. BCGs generally coincide with the peak x-ray emissions from their clusters.

X-ray images from eROSITA (left) and Chandra (right). In both images, a red star marks the location of the brightest cluster galaxy (BCG). Image Credit: Botteon et al. 2026. A&A.

According to the authors, the Treble Clef has a simpler explanation than other proposed explanations, yet its history is still long and dramatic. "We propose a simplified formation scenario in which the radio phoenix originates from an aged relativistic plasma, which was initially ejected by the BCG and subsequently revived by the cluster merger," they write. The Treble Clef is called a radio phoenix, due to it's re-energized brightness, like a phoenix rising from the ashes.

It started with a supermassive black hole (SMBH) outburst in the center of the BCG. The outburst sent massive clouds of charged particles outwards, along with magnetic fields, at relativistic speeds. Initially, this created a burst of x-ray light that gradually faded as the travelling particles lost energy.

Next, two galaxy clusters suffered a collision. This compressed them, and the compression re-energized the cloud of charged particles. They brightened again, but couldn't regain their prior energy level. Instead of emitting x-rays, they emitted radio waves. The colliding galaxy groups may have also generated shock waves that added to the re-energized crescendo.

The initial merger likely occurred several hundred million years ago, and the clusters are now moving in separate directions.

This schematic illustrates the formation scenario presented in the paper. It shows "two stages of a head-on collision between two clusters, A and B, in which the already aged (or âdeadâ) nonthermal plasma was injected by the BCG of cluster A prior to core passage. Following core passage, corresponding to the phase in which we currently observe the system (possibly within a few 10^8 yr after first passage, based on the disturbed X-ray morphology and the age of the radio plasma), clusters A and B move away from each other in opposite directions," the authors write. Swept off material is left behind, and in the space between A and B, the gas is stretched and compressed, creating the elongated shape observed in radio. The ICM in the region is turbulent from all this activity, and it creates the complex morphology and Treble Clef shape. Image Credit: Botteon et al. 2026. A&A.

"We conclude that this source is a radio phoenix belonging to a massive, merging galaxy cluster in the zone of avoidance," the authors write. "We speculate that its complex morphology is shaped by gas motions generated in the intracluster medium during the ongoing merger, which are also likely responsible for the candidate radio halo tentatively observed in the cluster center."

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."
