#164. "Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques

Scientists have discovered an unexpected reason why Alzheimer's disease disrupts sleep, and their findings suggest that the problem may be reversible. In experiments involving mice with Alzheimer's-like brain changes, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day without removing the amyloid plaques associated with the disease.

The surprising discovery points to an overlooked culprit: the brain's own immune cells. Rather than simply protecting the brain from damage, these cells can trigger inflammation that interferes with healthy sleep.

Researchers at the University of Kentucky found that temporarily eliminating most of these immune cells allowed the mice to sleep longer and spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep. The results suggest a potential new approach to treating one of the most disruptive symptoms of Alzheimer's disease.

The findings, published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, were reported by a team led by Shannon L. Macauley, Ph.D., an associate professor of physiology at the University of Kentucky College of Medicine, and first author Nicholas J. Constantino, Ph.D., a recent doctoral graduate.

Macauley described the discovery as "paradigm-shifting" because it challenges the prevailing understanding of why people with Alzheimer's often experience severe sleep problems.

How the Brain's Immune System Can Disrupt Sleep

To understand what the researchers uncovered, imagine a small fire breaking out in a kitchen. Instead of containing the flames, the building's sprinkler system activates everywhere, flooding the entire house and causing widespread damage.

Something similar may happen in the brain during Alzheimer's disease.

Amyloid plaques are deposits of sticky protein fragments that accumulate between nerve cells. They are one of the characteristic features of Alzheimer's and have long been investigated for their role in the disease.

The brain also contains specialized immune cells known as microglia. These cells normally protect the nervous system by removing debris, responding to injuries, and helping maintain a healthy environment for neurons.

However, when microglia detect amyloid plaques, their defensive response can become excessive. Instead of simply addressing the threat, they release inflammatory signals that may interfere with normal brain activity.

Scientists have traditionally linked sleep problems in Alzheimer's primarily to damaged neurons or the accumulation of amyloid plaques. The new findings suggest that the immune system's reaction to those plaques plays a major role.

"Basically, we showed that it is not the plaques themselves, or solely dysfunctional neurons, that cause sleep loss but actually microglia," said Macauley. "Microglia are immune cells that, when they respond to plaques, kick off this elaborate cascade of inflammation, as if the microglia are partying all night, and keeping the brain awake."

In other words, the brain's response to Alzheimer's pathology may create additional problems beyond those caused by the plaques themselves. The researchers compared this widespread reaction to a "whole house response," in which a defense mechanism ends up causing more disruption than expected.

Tracking Alzheimer's Sleep Changes Inside the Brain

To investigate the connection between microglia and sleep, the scientists studied two groups of mice. One group was genetically predisposed to develop amyloid plaques, while the other consisted of normal "wild-type" mice that experienced typical aging.

The researchers examined the animals at two ages: six months, when plaques first appeared in the genetically modified mice, and 18 months, when the disease model showed more advanced pathology.

Comparing these groups helped the scientists distinguish changes associated with Alzheimer's pathology from those that naturally occur as the brain ages.

The team used several advanced technologies to measure sleep and examine what was happening inside the brain.

Each mouse was fitted with a small device that recorded electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG).

EEG measures the brain's electrical activity, including the patterns and rhythms produced when networks of neurons communicate. These electrical signals change depending on whether the brain is awake, dreaming or experiencing deep sleep.

EMG measures electrical activity in muscles. Combining the two techniques allowed researchers to identify different sleep stages and determine how long the animals remained in each one.

The scientists also wanted to visualize the relationship between amyloid plaques and immune cells throughout the brain.

For this, they used light-sheet microscopy, an imaging technique that makes biological tissue transparent and illuminates it with a thin layer of laser light. The resulting images can be assembled into detailed three-dimensional maps, allowing scientists to examine structures that would otherwise be difficult to see.

This approach revealed the distribution of plaques and microglia across the brain, helping researchers understand where immune cells were responding to Alzheimer's pathology.

Scientists Temporarily Remove 87% of Brain Immune Cells

To determine whether microglia were actually responsible for disrupted sleep, the team conducted an experiment designed to temporarily eliminate most of these cells.

The researchers administered a drug called Pexidartinib (PLX3397), which was originally developed for cancer research. It blocks a cellular signal that microglia depend on for survival.

After the mice received the medication in their food for 14 days, approximately 87% of their microglia had been depleted.

This allowed the scientists to test whether sleep would improve when the cells driving the inflammatory response were largely absent.

The researchers also performed a detailed analysis of the animals' brain activity using a mathematical method called Fitting Oscillations and One Over Frequency (FOOOF).

This technique separates electrical signals into periodic activity (the rhythmic waves we usually think of as brain waves) and aperiodic activity (the background electrical noise).

By examining these different components, the team could identify changes in how the brain was functioning, including whether it remained unusually active during periods when it should have been resting.

The process is somewhat like monitoring a car engine to determine whether it continues running at high speed even when the vehicle is supposed to be idle.

A Surprising Discovery About Alzheimer's Brain Plaques

Macauley called the results "mind-blowing and unexpected."

One of the most surprising findings was that sleep problems did not continue worsening as amyloid plaques accumulated.

The researchers initially expected that increasing plaque buildup would lead to progressively more severe sleep disturbances. Instead, the mice developed substantial sleep problems relatively early, and those problems remained largely unchanged even as plaque levels increased dramatically.

"I expected that as plaque burden became more severe, sleep disruption would also worsen," said Constantino. "The disruptions in sleep and cortical EEG activity that occur at 6 months, when plaques first emerge, did not worsen by 18 months, despite more than double the amount of plaque burden."

The team described this pattern as a ceiling effect. Essentially, sleep disruption appeared to reach a certain level early in the disease process rather than increasing in direct proportion to the amount of amyloid in the brain.

This suggests that the initial inflammatory response triggered by plaques may be particularly important. Once microglia become activated and disrupt sleep, additional plaque accumulation may not necessarily produce an equivalent increase in sleep loss.

The discovery offers an important clue as to why sleep disturbances can emerge relatively early in Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Disrupts a Different Type of Sleep Than Normal Aging

The study also revealed a notable difference between sleep changes caused by normal aging and those associated with Alzheimer's pathology.

Sleep is not a single, uniform state. Throughout the night, the brain moves through several stages that perform different functions.

Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is strongly associated with vivid dreaming and plays an important role in processing memories. The researchers found that normal aging primarily reduced this type of sleep.

Alzheimer's pathology, however, had a different effect. It selectively disrupted non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, which includes the deepest and most physically restorative stages of sleep.

During NREM sleep, the brain performs essential maintenance functions that support learning, memory, and recovery. Deep sleep is also associated with processes that help clear metabolic waste products from the brain.

"That restorative sleep is super important for physical repair, learning and memory and washing out the toxins of the day," Macauley said.

Losing this important stage of sleep could have consequences beyond daytime fatigue.

Because healthy sleep helps maintain the brain's internal environment, disruptions may interfere with processes that normally remove potentially harmful waste. Researchers suspect this could contribute to a self-reinforcing cycle in which Alzheimer's pathology disturbs sleep, and inadequate sleep may further aggravate the disease.

Breaking that cycle could therefore become an important treatment strategy.

More Than Two Hours of Sleep Restored Without Removing Plaques

The most striking result emerged after the researchers temporarily removed most of the microglia from the brains of mice with Alzheimer's-like pathology.

The animals gained more than two hours of sleep per day.

They also experienced longer periods of restorative NREM sleep, giving them more opportunities to transition naturally into REM sleep, which is important for memory formation.

Even more surprisingly, these improvements occurred without any reduction in amyloid plaque levels.

The plaques were still present, but the mice were sleeping substantially better.

This finding provides evidence that the inflammatory response driven by microglia contributes directly to sleep disruption and that suppressing this response can reverse at least some of the associated sleep problems.

It also suggests that researchers may not need to eliminate amyloid plaques to improve sleep in Alzheimer's disease.

Although these findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and the same benefits have not yet been demonstrated in people. Temporarily removing most of the brain's immune cells is also not an established or practical treatment for Alzheimer's patients.

The researchers are now interested in whether the beneficial effects can be reproduced by adjusting microglial activity rather than eliminating the cells themselves.

If such an approach eventually proves successful in humans, it could provide a way to improve sleep and potentially reduce some of the additional stress that poor sleep places on the brain.

The work was conducted in Macauley's laboratory in the Department of Physiology at the University of Kentucky's Sanders-Brown Center on Aging.

Macauley credits the achievement to a "beautiful partnership" with students and researchers who were willing to challenge established ideas about Alzheimer's disease.

"I love people who take initiative, find their passion, are curious, and keep pushing to find an answer," Macauley said.

She encourages members of her laboratory to be "calculated risk-takers," emphasizing that meaningful discoveries often require scientists to investigate possibilities that may initially seem unlikely.

A quote from hockey legend Wayne Gretzky hangs in her office: "You miss 100% of the shots you don't take."

Constantino, who recently completed his doctorate at the university, said the laboratory's collaborative environment encouraged him to pursue questions that crossed traditional scientific disciplines.

"Dr. Macauley has also taught me to embrace uncertainty and failure as part of the scientific process," Constantino said. "Some of the most interesting studies I have been a part of emerged because our original hypothesis was wrong."

Macauley reinforces this mindset with a simple instruction to her team: "Follow the data, ask better questions, and figure out what is actually happening."

That approach helped the researchers move beyond the traditional emphasis on neurons and amyloid plaques to examine the broader role of the brain's immune system.

Could Existing Medications Help Restore Sleep in Alzheimer's?

The research team is now exploring ways to translate these findings into treatments and diagnostic tools that could eventually benefit people with Alzheimer's disease.

One promising direction involves calming overactive microglia without removing them.

Because microglia perform essential protective functions, eliminating them is not an ideal long-term strategy. Instead, the researchers hope to modify how these immune cells respond to amyloid plaques and regulate inflammation.

The laboratory is investigating existing medications, including the diabetes drug Metformin and the anti-seizure medication Stiripentol.

These drugs are being studied for their potential to alter how microglia produce and use energy, a process known as cellular metabolism. Changing that energy use could potentially reduce excessive immune activation and its harmful effects on sleep.

The hope is to prevent the brain's inflammatory response from becoming so intense that it disrupts normal sleep activity.

Researchers are particularly interested in whether intervention during the earlier stages of Alzheimer's could improve sleep and quality of life before substantial memory loss develops.

"If we can target that process, it might help with quality of life, attention, cognition and confusion," Macauley said.

The proposed drug strategies remain experimental for this purpose, and additional research will be necessary to determine whether they can safely produce similar benefits in humans.

A Simpler Way to Detect Early Alzheimer's Changes

Beyond identifying a potential treatment target, the study uncovered electrical activity patterns that may help distinguish Alzheimer's pathology from normal brain aging.

The researchers believe these patterns could eventually make EEG a useful tool for detecting and monitoring changes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Unlike more expensive imaging procedures, EEG records electrical signals through electrodes placed on the scalp. It is relatively affordable, does not require surgery, and can be repeated to follow changes over time.

The team envisions EEG becoming a "readily accessible, affordable and longitudinal biomarker of Alzheimer's disease."

A biomarker is a measurable biological sign that provides information about a person's health or a particular disease. A longitudinal biomarker can be tracked repeatedly to monitor how a condition develops or changes.

"Portable EEG systems could allow us to monitor people in their home environments and potentially screen for changes associated with an Alzheimer's disease, without the initial need for expensive or invasive tests," Macauley said.

If future human studies confirm the usefulness of these electrical signatures, portable EEG devices might eventually help doctors identify people who need additional testing.

This could be particularly valuable in rural communities across Kentucky, where patients sometimes must travel long distances to reach specialized medical centers.

Instead of requiring every potentially at-risk patient to undergo advanced testing immediately, local clinics might use simpler monitoring tools to identify individuals who would benefit from further evaluation.

Although this application still requires validation, it offers a possible path toward more accessible Alzheimer's screening and monitoring.

Ultimately, the study suggests that treating Alzheimer's may require looking beyond the plaques themselves and examining how the brain responds to them.

By identifying the immune cells responsible for much of the sleep disruption in their mouse models, the University of Kentucky researchers have uncovered a potential way to restore an essential brain function without first removing the underlying amyloid deposits.

The next challenge is determining whether calming these cells can deliver similar benefits in people, potentially improving sleep, cognition and quality of life long before the most severe symptoms of Alzheimer's develop.

#165. Your Fruits and Veggies Are Losing Their Nutrients—Here’s Why

The Green Revolution did wonders to increase calories to feed a growing population, but the nutritional value of those crops didn’t experience the same boom.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

• The “green revolution” increased crop yields following World War II to feed an ever-increasing global population, but the nutritional value of those foods steadily declined over the decades.

• A new report warns of a possible “tipping point” where a food system stressed by climate change could imperil populations already on the brink of nutritional deficiency.

• Some methods, such as biofortification, can help raise the nutrition levels of fruits, vegetables, and grains, but scientists warn that it’s far from a perfect fix.

One of the first rules of healthy eating that most of us learn as children, often drilled into us by exasperated parents, is to “eat your fruits and vegetables.” But decades of evidence suggest these dietary staples are losing their nutritional punch.

Back in 2004, a shocking study analyzing 43 garden crops and poring over USDA food composition data from 1950 and 1999 found worrisome deficiencies across the board. Calcium declined by 16 percent, iron by 15 percent, and phosphorus by 9 percent. In some cases, crops had up to 38 percent less nutritional value than they did in the 1950s and 60s. So, what exactly happened?

As the BBC points out, wartime food shortages and a fast-growing global population drove the development and adoption of high-yield crop varieties. Farmers also adopted synthetic nitrogen fertilizers on a massive scale, along with a rapidly expanding arsenal of chemical pesticides. Known today as the “green revolution,” the gamble worked—at least on paper. Cereal yields, for example, saw a whopping 215 percent increase per hectare while only expanding land use by 15 percent, according to a new report by London-based Deep Science Ventures. But as the 2004 study discovered, the nutritional value of foods, whether iron, calcium, zinc, vitamin A and others, didn’t keep pace.

“Over the past two decades, there have been a series of isolated reports that have shown nutritional density may have declined by over 40 percent since the green revolution in specific crops and contexts,” the new report says. “Such a decline in nutritional density would mean you have to consume 67 percent more calories to reach the same nutritional outcomes—a response that is simply not viable because of the vital importance of a healthy weight and hence strict matching of calories to energy needs.”

This leads to a phenomenon known as “hidden hunger,” where someone feels sated on empty calories but isn’t getting enough nutrients. A 2024 study in the journal Foods reported that more than two billion people suffer from nutrient insufficiency and highlighted multiple reasons for this slipping decline in food quality. One of the main causes is the agriculture industry’s emphasis on high-yield crops, which often trade nutritional quality for sheer volume. Other studies have found that increased carbon dioxide levels due to climate change can also negatively impact crops. One such study in 2018 found that increased carbon dioxide levels reduces protein, iron, and zinc in rice crops.

Other causes for the nutritional decline include the continued use of insecticides, fungicides, and herbicides; the rise of processed foods; and the declining availability of nutrient-rich soils to farm in the first place.

“This creates a plausible tipping-point risk—degrading nutritional density while stripping away the masking effect of excess calories, with impacts that would be especially acute for people already near the margin of deficiency, including children, women of reproductive age, older adults and populations dependent on staple cereals,” the new report concludes.

Humanity has a few methods that could help boost nutritional values, though. Chief among them is “biofortification,” a series of technologies and techniques that put nutrients directly into plants to help ease hidden hunger. Biofortification can include making genetic modifications to the plants, developing nutrient-rich fertilizers, or selectively breeding whole new plants. The World Health Organization reports early successes with iron-biofortified rice, which was shown to improve iron levels in women and children in the Philippines and India, while vitamin A-biofortified sweet potatoes eased deficiencies in countries throughout Africa. However, some scientists have argued that biofortification is far from a perfect solution, since it can harm crop yields while promoting genetic uniformity, which can lead to devastating plant disease outbreaks.

Today, the old maxim still holds true—it’s still healthy to eat your fruits and vegetables. But it’s worth keeping in mind that, at least nutritionally speaking, these aren’t your grandparents’ veggies.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

So there’s all these kind of basic properties of a person that are indexed in a voice.

Sanders: Voices can carry emotions too. A smile, for example, has subtle sound cues.

Bryant: There’s a slight increase in pitch when you smile and then you change what are called formants. The formants are structures in the speech signal underlying what your perception of vowels is. They’re energy bands that are associated with resonating chambers in your throat and in your mouth. And so when you are moving your tongue around and changing your lips and doing other things going, ahowowowow, you’re changing the formants. That’s the resonating bands of energy in the voice. So when you smile, then the formants change a little bit. And it’s detectable. It’s subtle, but you can hear it for sure.

Sanders: See if you can detect it here. It’s Jules introducing an episode of their podcast in 2020.

[podcast] So my wife comes to me today, and she says, babe, I have diarrhea.

Sanders: So setting aside the content he chose to share, which was a bold choice, you can hear the grin in his voice.

[podcast] Before we get into that, though, I also want to say one quick thing. Happy birthday, my love.

Sanders: That’s because his smile pulled his lips slightly upward and changed the shape of the air coming out, thereby changing the sound of his voice. All of these signals in the voice exist because voices are made by bodies. Bodies that move, smile, change, grow older, get sick. Our voices are actually a stunningly sophisticated bit of biology.

Jessica Pietrowski: You think about how, you know, we’re just talking, we’re just voicing, we’re barely even thinking about what we’re doing, but actually upwards close to a hundred muscles are being used.Sanders: That’s speech-language pathologist and scientist Jessica Pietrowski of UC Davis. Pietrowski: When we go to voice, we have to take a breath. Breath comes up, the diaphragm is contracting to get that breath. Breath comes up below the vocal folds, these tissues here, vibrates the vocal folds, creates a tone. That tone comes up through the oral cavity and other spaces, and resonates. And then you have to articulate it, and, and make the sounds clear and sharp. And then you have speech. And so really, you know, we’re not thinking about this as we’re doing it, but it’s incredibly complex and intricate and really an incredible human feat.

Sanders: Right now, as I say these words to you, I’m pushing air out of my body and using my muscles to move my diaphragm, face, throat, and mouth to make tiny ripples of sound shaped with a precision far below the level of my conscious perception. This mechanical, biological, physical feat is what allows me to shape air into sounds that then move to your ears.

Sergey Stavisky: So this is a very engineering-y perspective, but one thing about voices, it is our fastest means to communicate what we’re thinking.

Sanders: Sergey Stavisky co-directs the UC Davis Neuroprosthetics Lab, focused on using technology to replace or repair parts of the damaged nervous system.

Stavisky: So it’s actually, if you step back, kind of magical. So you have some idea in your mind, and your brain is able to take that idea, form it into language. So that’s already a complicated step. And then it’s able to move almost a hundred muscles in your tongue, in your jaw, and in your larynx to vibrate air in this exquisitely precise way.

Sanders: But then, even more magic happens when those vibrations move into someone else’s ear.

Stavisky: Those vibrations are going to fly through the air and they’re going to hit someone else’s eardrum and it’s going to vibrate that, and it’s going to vibrate the hair cells. And it’s going to send a bunch of nerve signals to their brain and they’re going to first make sense of the sounds you’re making amidst all of the other sounds, whether there’s background conversation or a train rumbling by or a dog barking. But then beyond that, they’re going to not just hear the words you just said, but remember all the previous words, put them together and like get the same idea in their brain. I mean, it’s telepathy through mechanical means.

Sanders: Telepathy through mechanical means. When you step back and think about it, it’s an absolute marvel. So here I am floating these ripples out toward my microphone. And then through more technology, they are reaching you, where your own amazing machinery senses those ripples and turns them into meaning. So with these ripples, I’m putting something into your mind.

Stavisky: We have this like shared scaffolding of understanding where I can pretty much visualize anything I want and with enough words, make someone else put that into their mind. And I think that’s a really remarkable ability. And that’s like the basis of civilization and learning and science and connection.

Sanders: But there’s something happening before all of this muscle moving and air rippling, and it’s something that Stavisky just mentioned. My words first started taking shape somewhere else. They started in my brain. Certain clusters of my synapses fired as I thought about what to say. This intricate path from brain to muscles to sculpted air is behind every word we say.

Casey Harrell: Hello there and thanks for being patient with me as I was running a bit late.Sanders: When I met Casey Harrell on Zoom, I asked him to tell me a little bit about himself.Casey: That is both the easiest and the hardest question to answer, right? So my name is Casey Harrell, and I am 47 years old. I grew up in the Atlanta area and have lived in the Bay Area for the past 23 years, most of them with my wife, Levana, and our seven-year-old daughter, who is going on 17. I spent most of my professional career as a climate campaigner and have went all over the globe, fighting companies who are destroying the earth and trying to bring some justice to our planet and the people who inhabit it.

Sanders: Like Jules, Casey has ALS. The disease has taken a lot from him. He can no longer move most of his body. That includes speech muscles.Casey: I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020.

Sanders: With time, he could no longer talk clearly enough to be understood. Casey: Then it became a slow-motion car crash of multiple years before almost no one would be able to understand me. A few other friends who were around often would be able to understand some of what I was saying. I relied upon my assistant and my wife to basically serve as my translators to other people. I did not go anywhere, even a video call without them, either one or both.Sanders: Casey’s life in the Bay Area was changing in difficult, almost impossible ways. Like Jules, Casey had received an ALS diagnosis in 2020. Like Jules, he had a kid, a partner, a career, a big, full life. And then wham, life threw them one of the biggest curveballs you can imagine. These two men, separated by 3,000 miles, Jules in Miami, Casey in Oakland, were both facing big losses. And one of the biggest of all was their ability to talk.

Speech-language pathologist Kate Nilson walks me through some of the standard approaches that she uses when she’s working with people who face similar futures. There’s a process called voice banking.

Nilson: So voice banking is the idea of recording specific sentences that you might not actually say in real life, but predetermined sentences that you record that give the software the combinations of sounds that it needs to make a computer voice that sounds like you.

Sanders: That process has actually improved quite a bit in recent years.

Nilson: When I started doing this, it was 1600 sentences. Now it can be an app on your phone that you do at home. It can be a website that you go to. The software that I use most of the time is 50 sentences. It can be done in like 15 minutes. It’s really come a long way and the voices are pretty darn amazing in how how true to the person they are. But they are still a computerized voice, right? They’re they’re they’re taking combinations of sounds and splicing them together. So it sounds computerized.

Sanders: Voice banking has the benefit of being flexible. This voice can say anything a person wants, but it sounds off. There’s another approach. This one’s called message banking.Nilson: So the idea of message banking is we just record an entire message. So instead of using that computer voice to say, “Good night, honey, I love you,” we can just record someone saying, “Good night, honey, I love you,” with their voice, like, with their true inflection and meaning.

Sanders: The beauty of these messages is that they capture the quirks of a person’s voice.

Nilson: You know, I live in Minnesota, and so there’s a lot of ooftas and doncha knows, and those kinds of things that do not come out right when you type them into a computer.

Sanders: Nilson encounters these sorts of sounds when she’s helping people save recordings of their voice for the future.

Nilson: You gotta get all those right sayings with the right, you know, “o’s” in them.

Sanders: These recorded messages are often things like an inside joke with the exact right timing or a favorite little nickname for someone special.

Nilson: It can be really emotional. And that’s, when you’re recording the sentences that are predetermined and they’re not sentences that you would normally say, that can be easy. But when your family has written down a list of meaningful words that they want to hear in your voice and you know that you’re recording it because you might lose your voice, that can be really emotional. And it can be hard. And I fully understand that, but we can also have fun with it.Sanders: Pre-recorded jokes come up pretty often when people are choosing what messages to preserve for later use. And swear words come up surprisingly often too, Nilson tells me.

Nilson: I had someone come in just the other day, and they had an entire category of recorded cuss words. So that’s important. Well, right? I mean, you don’t want them to be monotone when you’re frustrated. You want the right emphasis to come out on that.

Sanders: It takes the sails out of it for sure if it’s monotone. Nilson: Yeah, exactly. I mean, that’s communication, right? That’s important communication. So I guess it doesn’t really surprise me anymore, but it’s fun nonetheless.

Sanders: She says some people come to her with entire folders of swears, folders that she refused to share with me for the story, by the way.Nilson: The best part is it was a swear folder with all these different swear words and like different sayings and whatever. And then just one of them had a call-out to a specific person. And I was like, what did that person do to you that he’s the only one that has a specific? And then he laughed and he typed out, “If you knew him, you’d understand.”

Sanders: All of these quirks, the swears, the smiles in the voice, the familiar jokes, all of these things make a particular voice special. Jules created a banked voice. He didn’t love the result.

Jules: What I learned from banking my voice was that it really wasn’t my voice. It was more like a robot trying to emulate my voice. It had no emotion or tone behind it.

Sanders: This was a problem because it got in the way of something Jules wanted to do. The turmoil of ALS forced some clarity for him about what he wanted out of life, what he wanted to spend his time doing. And one of those answers, it turns out, was comedy. After his diagnosis, while he still had his voice, he performed stand-up a few times.

Sanders: But as his voice got harder to use, things changed. Jules could still talk, but it took a lot of work, especially since he was often using a mask for extra oxygen.

MA: He was wearing the mask pretty much the entire time. So his voice was very labored, because you have to take the breath in to utter anything. So it was very choppy. But he did have a voice.

Sanders: With time, a live performance with his original voice became impossible. The next option was to use a banked voice, but that wasn’t good enough for a comedy performance.

MA: So then he started to lose his voice and he was like, I don’t, you know, I can’t pull this off with a banked voice because it’s so robotic. It’s monotone. You can’t really do it.

Sanders: Jules couldn’t pull off a comedy show. But could there be a different way, a different voice?

I’m going to step back here and give you more context about Jules and about ALS. ALS is progressive and relentless, which means over time, more and more of the motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord are affected, and symptoms get worse.

And though this progression varies quite a bit from person to person, the median survival time after an ALS diagnosis is about 30 months. Time is short here. This diagnosis forces big choices about how to live and what a person wants their remaining time to include, for them and for their family. In the middle of everything else going on, Jules was facing a choice that many people in his situation must confront, whether or not he would get a tracheostomy.

That’s a procedure in which doctors place a tube in the throat. This tube is then connected to a ventilator that breathes for a person.

The procedure can leave a person unable to speak again, with whatever residual voice they might have left. Now, we have spent this episode on what it feels like to lose your voice. Jules was losing his. So it might seem like this part of the decision wouldn’t matter all that much. But to a person who’s losing their voice, and to their family, this moment marks an end point. It’s a hard stop.

MA: He was someone who didn’t want to do a tracheostomy. He was opting for, once I’m done, that’s it. And that was our plan.

Sanders: As Jules and MA confront this decision, could a different sort of voice change the story?

Jules: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice.

Sanders: This is The Deep End. Talk to me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot.

Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org. The Deep End is a production of Science News. It’s based on original reporting by me, Laura Sanders. #167. Not Getting Enough Daylight Could Be Linked to a Higher Risk of Dementia

Researchers found that insufficient exposure to bright daytime light may be a stronger predictor of dementia than several established risk factors.

Greater exposure to bright light during the day may be associated with a lower risk of developing dementia, according to research involving nearly 88,000 adults. Participants whose average daytime light exposure exceeded 1,000 lux had a 16% lower dementia risk than those exposed to dimmer conditions.

The study, published in General Psychiatry, analyzed light exposure in 87,577 adults who wore wrist devices equipped with light sensors for seven days. Over a median follow-up of 8.1 years, 741 participants developed dementia. The association between brighter daytime light and lower dementia risk remained significant after researchers accounted for numerous health, lifestyle, and environmental factors.

Both light intensity and exposure duration were associated with dementia risk. Participants who experienced at least 42 minutes of bright daytime light at 5,000 lux or higher had a 17% lower risk than those with less exposure. For comparison, 1,000 lux is roughly equivalent to the brightness of an overcast day outdoors, considerably brighter than typical indoor lighting.

In a separate analysis, receiving fewer than 42 minutes of bright daytime light ranked as a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors, including obesity, alcohol consumption, and traumatic brain injury. By contrast, nighttime light exposure showed no statistically significant association with dementia risk.

Daytime light helps regulate circadian rhythms, the body’s internal timing system that influences sleep, daily activity, and cognitive function. Additional analyses suggested that differences in these rhythms and certain brain structures might partly explain the relationship. The association was particularly pronounced among evening chronotypes, people carrying the APOE ε4 genetic variant, and those exposed to higher levels of nighttime light.

However, the observational findings do not establish that increasing daytime light exposure prevents dementia. Light exposure was measured for only one week, and wrist sensors cannot precisely capture the amount of light reaching the eyes. Further research is needed to determine whether changing light exposure can directly influence dementia risk.

“Daytime light exposure may serve as a novel indicator of dementia risk,” said corresponding author Hongliang Feng, PhD, of Guangzhou Medical University, in China.

Reference: “Associations between wearable-device-measured daytime and nighttime light exposures and dementia risk: A prospective cohort study” by Nana Zheng, Wei Wang, Biao Li, Xionge Mei, Yue Liu, Jing Du, Ngan Yin Chan, Joey W. Y. Chan, Xiaoman Xing, Xiao Tan, Christian Benedict, Yun Kwok Wing, Jihui Zhang and Hongliang Feng, 24 June 2026, General Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1002/gps3.70039

Petal, the world's first petabit transoceanic fiber cable, could theoretically support simultaneous music streaming for 75% of the world's population.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new 4,300-mile (7,000-kilometer) undersea fiber cable will shuttle data between the U.S. and France at breakneck speeds of up to 1 million gigabits per second (Gbps) — enough to move around 125 terabytes of data every second, or roughly 25,000 HD movies, each 5 gigabytes large. The cable, called Petal, will be funded and operated by Facebook and Instagram parent company Meta.

When it comes online in 2029, the ocean-spanning cable will be the first to deliver petabit capacity — double the capacity of existing subsea cables of this length — across transoceanic distances, Meta representatives said in a statement. That's enough to allow 75% of the world's population to stream music at once.

Petal will also be the first commercial subsea cable system to use multi-core fiber technology, according to the statement. Whereas conventional fiber strands typically contain a single core, each of Petal's fiber strands will contain two cores that carry optical signals in opposite directions, allowing a single strand to provide the capacity that would conventionally require a pair of single-core fibers.

Each fiber strand is roughly as thick as a human hair, measuring just 125 micrometers in diameter. Petal will contain 24 pairs of dual-core fibers, giving it 96 individual fiber cores in total and enabling it to carry as much data as 48 conventional fiber pairs, Meta engineers said.

Japanese technology company NEC will be responsible for the overall design and construction of Petal, while Sumitomo Electric will provide the fiber itself.

"Achieving petabit-per-second capacity across a transoceanic submarine system represents a major technological milestone in the history of global telecommunications," Eduardo Mateo, chief strategy officer of the Submarine Networks Division at NEC, said in the statement.

Subsea cables are among the most critical layers of internet infrastructure, carrying around 99% of the world's internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, the United Nations ​agency for digital technologies.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Installing thousands of miles of fragile glass cable on the ocean floor is an engineering feat in itself. Equally challenging is ensuring that these cables can carry the tiny pulses of infrared light that transport fiber-optic data across such huge distances without impacting performance.

This is typically achieved through repeaters — amplifiers installed at regular intervals along the cable that use lasers to boost the optical signals.

A 4,300-mile subsea cable typically needs about 100 of these repeaters to amplify the signals along its length, Meta representatives said.

Petal will incorporate something called "fan-in/fan-out" technology. As each two-core fiber strand enters a repeater, an optical interface routes the signal from each core into a separate single-core fiber strand so that each can be amplified independently. The amplified signals are then routed back into the two cores of the dual-core fiber before continuing along the cable.

Combined with its dual-core fiber, this feat of signal engineering will enable Petal to double its data-carrying capacity without requiring a proportional increase in power, Meta representatives said.

Petal is one of many subsea cable investments by Meta in recent years, including Marea in 2018, Amitie in 2023 and Anjana in 2025. Marea, the company's first transatlantic fiber instalment, supports 192 Tbps, meaning Petal will offer more than five times that capacity.

Owen Hughes is a freelance writer and editor specializing in data and digital technologies. Previously a senior editor at ZDNET, Owen has been writing about tech for more than a decade, during which time he has covered everything from AI, cybersecurity and supercomputers to programming languages and public sector IT. Owen is particularly interested in the intersection of technology, life and work ­– in his previous roles at ZDNET and TechRepublic, he wrote extensively about business leadership, digital transformation and the evolving dynamics of remote work.

Gopal Murali is at the Center for Ecological Sciences, Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru 560012, India.

“The importance of stillness as an aid to concealment can hardly be overestimated,” wrote zoologist Hugh Cott1. Yet prey cannot always remain still. Movement is among the most powerful cues that animals use to detect and track objects, creating a fundamental problem: even the best camouflage can fail once an animal moves2. Certain high-contrast patterns in prey, such as a zebra’s stripes, have long been proposed1,3 as an alternative defensive strategy during motion, but gaining supporting evidence has proved surprisingly difficult4. Writing in Nature, Hancock et al.5 put this century-old idea to a new test in butterflies.

On Oct. 18, 1963, a cat went to space! Félicette was a French "catstronaut" who became the first and only feline to fly to space. Here's why it mattered.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Oct. 18, 1963, a cat went to space! Félicette was a French "catstronaut" who became the first and only feline to fly to space.

While the U.S. and Soviet Union were busy launching primates, dogs and humans, the French decided to join the space race by launching a cat. Félicette, a stray tuxedo cat from the streets of Paris, was a substitute for another cat named Felix, who somehow escaped on launch day.

So Félicette went where no cat had ever gone before. She boarded a French Véronique AG1 rocket and soared 130 miles above the Earth before safely parachuting back down.

Luckily Félicette made it home alive and well, unlike many of the other animal astronauts that flew during the space race.

Félicette survived spaceflight, but was short of this world. She was euthanized two months after her recovery so scientists could study her brain.

A second cat was launched by the French on Oct. 24, but its flight did not go so well, veering off course. When the cat was found a day later, it was discovered it have died as a result of the journey. From there on, CERMA (Centre d'Enseignement et de Recherches de Médecine Aéronautique) changed its research to flying monkeys.

Félicette may have become a footnote to history had it not been for a crowdfunded effort to raise a statue in her memory nearly 60 years later. The sculpture was unveiled in 2019 at the International Space University in Strasbourg, France. European astronauts Helen Sharman, Paolo Nespoli and Reinhold Ewald were on hand for its reveal.

To this day, Félicette and her less-fortunate astro-cat classmate remain the only felines to fly on a rocket.

In 2013, reports surfaced that Iran was planning to send a cat into space as soon as the following year. By all accounts, though, that never happened.

In addition to the memorial statue, Félicette has been memorialized on postage stamps issued by Chad and Comoros, both former French colonies.Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

#172. A Distant Supercluster of Galaxies Points To Self-Interacting Dark Matter

Seven billion light-years from Earth, there is an unexpected cluster of galaxies. It has two regions in the process of colliding with each other with a combined mass of more than two quadrillion solar masses. Given its mass, the distant cluster has been nicknamed El Gordo, the Fat One. What makes it unusual is that it's extraordinarily large for that period of the Universe. How did such a large supercluster form so early? El Gordo is so surprising that some astronomers hold it as a counter-example to the standard model of cosmology. It's difficult to explain how cold dark matter in an inflationary universe could generate a large supercluster so quickly. A new study looks at how self-interacting dark matter could explain it all.

Dark matter makes up the bulk of mass in the cosmos. It doesn't interact strongly with light, if at all, hence the name. This also means that dark matter doesn't interact strongly with regular matter, since most matter interactions are electromagnetic in nature. One of the key questions, however, is whether dark matter can interact strongly with itself.

The most popular view is that dark matter isn't self-interacting. This is because observations show dark matter is mostly cold, meaning that dark matter particles don't have a lot of kinetic energy. If dark matter particles could collide with each other, then they would stay warm, just as regular matter can heat up when it collides. Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) could create an early supercluster like El Gordo, but it would also produce plenty of warm dark matter.

To overcome this problem, this new study proposes a two-state dark matter interaction. Regular matter mostly interacts through elastic collisions. For example, the air molecules in your room tend to bounce off each other without losing much energy. This is why your room can stay a constant temperature. If the collisions were inelastic, losing energy with each bounce, then your room would rapidly freeze. Most SIDM models assume a similar elastic interaction. Tweak the interaction just so, and you can accelerate galactic clustering while not overly warming dark matter. The results of this approach have been mixed.

The author considers a dark matter model that has a ground state and an excited state. With this two-state model, most interactions would be elastic, just like regular matter. But with the right energy, a collision could kick a dark matter particle into an excited state, thus removing kinetic energy from the collision. Dark matter particles can then cluster together and cool down at the same time.

Based on N-body simulations of the colliding regions of El Gordo, a two-state SIDM model with both elastic and inelastic collisions is the best fit to what we observe. It provides a better fit than both non-interacting and elastic only interactions. The catch is that there is still quite a bit of uncertainty as to the exact mass of El Gordo and the speed at which the two regions are colliding. If the supercluster is on the low end of this range, then the two-state model wouldn't fit the data. So this is a possible solution, not a definite one.

Until we directly observe dark matter particles, all sorts of possibilities are on the table. As this study shows, dark matter might be more complex than we've thought.

Reference: Valdarnini, R. "Hydrodynamical simulations of the merging cluster El Gordo in a two-state self-interacting dark matter scenario." The Astrophysical Journal 1008.1 (2026): 105.

Brian Koberlein is an astrophysicist and author of the books Astrophysics Through Computation and Radio Sky: 40 Years of the Very Large Array. You can find more of his work on his website.

#173. The Plan to Dim the Sun Could Actually Work—and That May Be the Most Dangerous Part of All

Experts simulated a rush to deploy solar geoengineering against global warming. The science was the least of their problems.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

The world is warming—there’s no question about that. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) reported that the period from June to August 2026 was the hottest on record in the contiguous U.S. in recorded history. Sweltering conditions throughout Europe caused the continent’s iconic rivers to run dry. A devastating flash flood triggered by rising temperatures stunned the world and killed nearly 1,500 people in Nepal. And an overheated Pacific Ocean is unleashing the most powerful El Niño in a millennium while many scientists declare that the future they’ve spent decades warning the world about has finally arrived.

“We are witnessing the rapid destabilization of the Earth’s climate system. This is no longer a warning for the future; it is a diagnosis of the present,” reads the opening lines of a 2026 State of the Climate report, released earlier this week in the journal BioScience. “Earth’s life-support systems are being pushed beyond stable limits, with changes unfolding faster than our ability to respond.”

As the popular saying goes, desperate times call for desperate measures, and one of these “desperate measures” is solar geoengineering, a series of complicated schemes aimed at intentionally reflecting the sun’s rays back into space to cool the planet. One such method to crank down Earth’s thermostat is a type of a solar radiation modification, or SRM, known as stratospheric aerosol injection. This idea is already backed by science, given that volcanoes regularly inject reflective sulfur dioxide particles into the atmosphere, thereby cooling the Earth. In 1991, for example, the eruption of Mount Pinatubo cooled the planet by one degree Fahrenheit and other eruptions throughout history have had even more profound climate impacts.

So, the thinking goes, why not just do that intentionally: pump the stratosphere with sulfur dioxide, reflect incoming solar radiation, and solve the climate crisis? Well, if that sounds too good to be true, that’s because it is. While sulfur dioxide would certainly cool the planet, it could also have many unforeseen consequences, including impacts on human health. The Solar Geoengineering Non-Use Initiative also notes that such a solution could push governments and industries to avoid addressing the root cause of climate change—fossil fuel emissions.

“It is also seen as raising profound questions of justice, legality, and political power, with many critics arguing that it could never be governed in a fair, inclusive, and effective manner over the long timescales deployment would require,” one blog post on the initiative’s website reads.

This fact was made painfully clear by a recent initiative, funded by the U.K. government, to simulate the political fallout of governments, industries, and startups rushing to develop geoengineering technologies to alleviate the worst outcomes of climate change. The project, called Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, asked scientists, former government officials, and military experts to gather at Queen Mary University of London to play competing nations and interests and see what, if anything, they could agree on.

The results weren’t pretty. One of the participants, who spoke with Wired after the simulations, said that the political situation quickly devolved into a “geoengineering arms race” with superpowers, such as the U.S. and China, jockeying to be in control of this literally world-changing technology. Within the simulation, the fossil fuel industry masqueraded as NGOs—one called itself the Climate Futures Cooperative—to sell geoengineering as an alternative to cutting emissions. Meanwhile, simulated threats of secret geoengineering experiments added fuel to the geopolitical fire. Almost immediately, climate concerns were overshadowed by strategic competition and state sovereignty issues.

“Multiple types of uncertainty hampered progress towards agreement,” the final report of the simulation exercise reads. “The most persistent and important of these uncertainties were: how to assess and trust information in a fraught political context; how to gauge the intentions of actors engaging with SRM; and how the continued emergence of SRM would influence existing relationships and dynamics between different actors, particularly states.”

So even if SRMs worked wonders (and somehow had no serious environmental or health impacts), the chances of implementing such a strategy on a global scale appears vanishingly thin. For now, cutting fossil fuel emissions remains the only proven way to slow the warming.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#174. Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago

What if the human brain works in ways that Sigmund Freud began describing more than 130 years ago? A new scientific analysis suggests that some of his ideas about the mind share surprising similarities with one of the most influential theories in modern neuroscience.

Published in the scientific journal Entropy, the paper explores connections between Freud's original theories, later developments in psychoanalysis, and a modern approach to brain research known as the prediction paradigm.

This approach describes the brain as a prediction machine. Rather than simply responding to information from the outside world, the brain is constantly anticipating what will happen next. It then compares those expectations with incoming information from the senses and works to reduce any differences between what it predicted and what actually occurred.

Scientists believe this ongoing process plays a central role in how people perceive their surroundings, make decisions, behave, and regulate emotions.

Researchers Erik Stänicke, Bendik Hovet, and Line Indrevoll Stänicke, together with colleagues, argue that this modern understanding of brain function has important parallels with ideas that psychoanalysts have been developing for more than a century.

"For over 130 years, psychoanalysis has developed psychological theories about how predictions take place at a subjective level, which cognitive neuropsychology is now studying at a physiological level."

How Freud's Ideas Connect to the Predictive Brain

Although neuroscience and psychoanalysis approach the mind differently, the researchers suggest that both may be describing related processes.

Neuroscience examines the physical mechanisms behind thought and behavior, often using mathematical models to explain how the brain processes information. Psychoanalysis, which grew out of Freud's work, focuses more on unconscious mental processes, emotional experiences, and the ways past relationships influence present behavior.

In other words, one field investigates what happens inside the brain, while the other explores how those processes are experienced by the individual.

A particularly interesting connection involves the psychoanalytic concept of projection and the neuroscientific concept of prediction.

In psychoanalysis, projection involves attributing feelings, intentions, or qualities to someone else. The researchers suggest that this resembles how the brain uses previously learned expectations to interpret new experiences.

"When we attribute qualities, intentions or feelings to other people, our brain shapes our experience of the world in line with established expectations," says Stänicke.

For instance, someone who has repeatedly experienced rejection may become especially sensitive to signs that other people are rejecting them. Even an ambiguous remark or facial expression might be interpreted negatively because past experiences have shaped what the person expects.

Over time, these expectations can influence how someone approaches unfamiliar situations and forms new relationships.

"This corresponds to the neuroscientific distinction between changing one's own predictions, perceptual inference, and the attempt to make the world conform to them, namely active inference."

Perceptual inference refers to the way the brain interprets sensory information and updates its expectations in response. Active inference, by contrast, involves taking actions that help bring experiences into line with predictions or reduce uncertainty.

Together, these concepts help explain why people do not always experience the world as it objectively is. Their expectations can influence what they notice, how they interpret events, and how they respond.

Why the Brain Holds On to Negative Expectations

The researchers believe the similarities between Freud's ideas and modern neuroscience could offer valuable insights into mental health disorders, particularly those involving deeply established patterns of thinking and behavior.

Both approaches portray the mind as constantly seeking stability and predictability. This tendency is related to homeostasis, the process through which a system maintains a relatively stable internal state.

In the predictive brain model, reducing uncertainty is an important part of maintaining that stability. The brain relies on familiar expectations to make the world easier to understand, even when those expectations are inaccurate or no longer helpful.

"Psychoanalysts refer to the tendency in the mind to recreate familiar relational patterns, even when these are poorly adapted," says Stänicke.

This could help explain why people sometimes repeat harmful patterns in relationships or continue interpreting situations negatively despite evidence that challenges their assumptions.

"Rigid and persistent symptoms, such as paranoid ideas or an internalized critical voice, may be stable but not very flexible prediction models," says Stänicke.

"For example, there may be people who automatically expect criticism, rejection or hostility from others, and therefore interpret situations through this filter despite the fact that reality does not warrant it."

Such expectations can become deeply entrenched because they make experiences feel familiar and predictable. Even when the resulting interpretation is distorted, maintaining an established mental model may feel less uncertain than changing it.

According to Stänicke, this offers a possible explanation for why some psychological symptoms can persist for years and why changing longstanding patterns of thought and behavior often requires considerable time.

The connection is particularly interesting because it suggests that some mental health difficulties may involve more than consciously held beliefs. They may also reflect deeply learned expectations that automatically shape emotional responses and interactions with others.

How Psychotherapy Could Help Change Deeply Rooted Patterns

The researchers also highlight an important distinction between what people consciously believe and what they have learned through experience.

"In addition, both models give us insight into how parts of our expectations of the outside world are not only anchored cognitively, but in procedural memory that is expressed in relational ways of being," he says.

Procedural memory is a type of long-term memory involved in learned habits and skills. It allows people to perform familiar actions without consciously thinking through every step.

In the context of relationships, the researchers suggest that a similar form of learning may help explain why certain emotional reactions and patterns of interaction become automatic.

Someone might intellectually understand that other people are not necessarily hostile or critical, for example, yet still instinctively respond as though rejection is inevitable.

These expectations are not simply thoughts that can be changed through reasoning. They can also be embedded in habitual ways of reacting to people and navigating relationships.

This distinction may help explain why psychotherapy sometimes needs to address personal relationships and emotional experiences rather than focusing only on conscious thoughts.

"Therefore, psychotherapy sometimes has to work relationally. For example, new experiences in the relationship between therapist and patient can gradually help to change entrenched relational patterns."

Through repeated experiences that challenge familiar expectations, patients may gradually develop different ways of interpreting situations and relating to other people.

Bringing Freud's Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience Together

The researchers argue that connecting psychoanalysis with modern predictive brain theory could benefit both fields.

Neuroscience may provide a biological framework for understanding processes that psychoanalysts have long described through subjective experience. At the same time, psychoanalytic theories may offer more detailed explanations of how expectations are experienced emotionally, interpreted personally, and expressed through relationships.

The proposed similarities do not establish that Freud's broader theories were correct. Instead, they suggest that two very different traditions of studying the mind may offer complementary ways of understanding some of the same psychological processes.

By examining both the brain's physical mechanisms and the individual's inner experience, researchers hope to develop a more complete understanding of human behavior and mental health.

"Bringing these two fields together can open up for a more holistic psychology, in which both neurological mechanisms and subjective experience are included. In this way, we can understand subjectivity in a more scientific manner."

#175. Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The gene variant may alter cells that support the brain’s blood vessels

APOE4 raises Alzheimer’s risk, but how it makes the brain vulnerable to disease remains unclear. A new study points to scarring around small blood vessels as one possible piece of the puzzle.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The gene APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. But it’s still something of a mystery to researchers.

Now, new work suggests one way the gene variant does its dirty work. It influences the production of scar tissue throughout vital vascular connections carrying blood to and from the brain, researchers report September 24 in Cell. This process may also contribute to the buildup of the protein amyloid-beta, which is thought to be one of the first signs of Alzheimer’s disease in the brain.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

APOE4 is an allele, one of three slightly different, common forms of the APOE gene, which makes a protein that helps carry fats in the bloodstream. The variant is common among people who have Alzheimer’s disease. “If you had a room of 10 people with Alzheimer’s disease, and you asked how many of those people have the APOE4 allele, six of them would,” says neuroscientist Joel Blanchard of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Yet many people who carry APOE4 never develop the dementia-causing disease, leaving researchers trying to understand what the gene variant actually does to make the brain more vulnerable.

One clue came from people who seemed unusually resilient to that risk. In 2024, researchers examined more than 3,500 people, including some who carried two copies of APOE4 but had not developed Alzheimer’s. Genetic analysis showed that they had a mutation in their DNA that meant their blood vessels had far lower levels of a protein called fibronectin, a kind of cellular superglue that assists wound healing. The reserachers suggested that too much fibronectin could make it harder for the brain to clear amyloid-beta from the brain. A buildup of those plaques is a hallmark of the disease.

That result pushed Blanchard and his colleagues to look more closely at blood vessels. “The prevailing thought in the field is basically that the Alzheimer’s disease is so bad that the blood vessels break down,” Blanchard says. ”But we wanted to ask the question: Is it the other way around?”

Blanchard and his colleagues built an atlas that mapped gene expression — how DNA is read and converted into proteins — across the human brain vasculature at a cellular level. Stitching together data from three existing brainwide maps, their atlas represented 66,000 cells from 220 people. They team examined how this map differed in people with two copies of APOE4 compared with those with less harmful gene variants.

APOE4 carriers had fewer pericytes, starfish-shaped cells that wrap around and stabilize blood vessels. They also had higher numbers of myofibroblasts, cells normally formed during tissue injury that pump out fibronectin, the team found.

The map offered a snapshot, but it couldn’t show whether the missing pericytes were actually transforming into myofibroblasts. The researchers turned to 3-D models of human brain tissue grown from stem cells. In models carrying two copies of APOE4, pericytes began taking on the characteristics of scar-producing myofibroblasts. The transformation also offered a possible explanation for the earlier clue from resilient APOE4 carriers: Myofibroblasts produce large amounts of fibronectin. And when the researchers prevented cells in their models from producing fibronectin, amyloid accumulation dropped.

The researchers also found a possible trigger for the cellular switch. In the APOE4 models, signaling through the immune molecule TGF-beta helped drive pericytes toward the scar-producing state. Blocking that signaling in cell models and aged mice restored the proportion of blood vessels wrapped up by pericytes.

The TGF-beta data are “particularly interesting,” because inhibiting the protein reversed some of APOE4’s effects on pericytes, says Abdel Ali Belaidi, a neuroscientist at the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health in Parkville, Australia. But TGF-beta performs many jobs throughout the body, he says, making it a difficult molecule to target safely with a drug.

And damage to the brain’s blood vessels is only one of the many ways APOE4 has been linked to Alzheimer’s. Other studies have shown that the gene variant alters inflammation and interacts with another Alzheimer’s-linked protein, tau. How all these changes lock together to link APOE4 so strongly to Alzheimer’s disease is a greater mystery than one study can solve. ”As a field, we’re all progressing toward an answer,” Blanchard says.

#176. Researchers Unleash Record-Breaking X-Ray Flashes in Just 300 Attoseconds

Researchers used the European XFEL to produce ultrashort X-ray flashes that reached record intensity for this type of pulse.

To understand chemical reactions and perhaps one day control the electrons involved, scientists need a detailed picture of how electrons behave inside atoms and molecules. X-rays offer a way to probe that behavior, but the flashes can also change the sample they are meant to examine. Researchers therefore need enough light to gather useful information before those changes become substantial.

At the European XFEL, a team has now concentrated X-ray flashes onto an area roughly 100,000 times smaller than the cross-section of a typical human hair. The pulses lasted an estimated 300 attoseconds, with each attosecond equal to a billionth of a billionth of a second.

The experiment used hard X-rays, light with particularly short wavelengths, and took place in April 2026 at the facility’s MID instrument. The results are published in Optica.

“A few years ago, we demonstrated terawatt-scale hard X-ray attosecond pulses at the European XFEL,” says DESY scientist Jiawei Yan, one of the corresponding authors of the study. “But generating powerful pulses is only the first step. For experiments, what really matters is what we can deliver to the sample. With this advance, we can now use attosecond X-rays to explore highly nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter.”

To concentrate that energy, the researchers used an advanced Kirkpatrick–Baez, or AKB, optical system brought from Japan. Each flash underwent four reflections in total, with one of the system’s two extremely precise mirrors focusing the light vertically and the other horizontally. Together, they concentrated the X-rays into a spot measuring just 180 × 330 nanometers. A nanometer is a billionth of a meter.

From the pulse energy, estimated duration, and focal-spot size, the team calculated a peak intensity of more than 10²⁰ watts per square centimeter. “This is a world record in intensity and fluence for a hard-X-ray attosecond pulse,” says Ichiro Inoue from the University of Tokyo, first author of the publication. Fluence measures the energy delivered to a given area, while intensity also accounts for how quickly that energy arrives.

To test that calculation, the researchers shone the pulses onto copper foil. The X-rays knocked electrons out of deep inner shells within the copper atoms, leaving gaps that other electrons could fill. As electrons moved into those gaps, they released X-ray light. At sufficiently high intensities, that light can stimulate other excited copper atoms to emit additional X-rays in the same direction, amplifying the signal through a process called amplified spontaneous emission, or ASE.

“It is almost magical to see this happening,” says Anders Madsen, group leader at the MID instrument. “Normal fluorescence goes in all directions, regardless of the direction of the incoming beam. But when the ASE threshold is crossed, you see the light cone starting to condense into the forward direction.”

The ASE signal initially rose rapidly as the pulse energy increased, then leveled off at higher energies. This saturation, expected only at extremely high X-ray intensities, provided independent confirmation of the team’s calculation.

European XFEL expects to receive its own AKB system in early 2027. Once installed and commissioned, the system is intended to give researchers from around the world using the MID instrument access to similarly brief, intense X-ray flashes.

Reference: “Generation of high-fluence and high-intensity hard X-ray attosecond pulses at the European XFEL” by 19 October 2026, Optica. DOI: 10.1364/OPTICA.613284

The new system is funded through a collaboration with the University of Hamburg and support from the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR)

Mount Everest may be the king of the planet today, but has Earth ever thrust a larger mountain from its surface?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sometimes, it takes a great struggle to build towering peaks. And what more thunderous event is there than the clashing of continental plates?

Geological pileups have birthed some of the largest and tallest mountains on the planet, including Mount Everest and its Himalayan neighbors. But has there ever been a peak taller than Mount Everest, which stands 29,032 feet (8,849 meters) above sea level?

The answer is still a mystery, but there are some geological clues about where the tallest peaks would have been in the ancient past, experts told Live Science.

Geologists don't have the level of detail required to pinpoint an exact highest peak hundreds of millions of years ago. "We're never going to get that granularity, unfortunately," Alan Collins, a professor of geology at Adelaide University in Australia, told Live Science.

However, clues in residual sediments lodged inside Earth's crust hint at the lost grandeur of primordial snowcaps and summits. Scientists study these crusts to understand how deep they went, which can reveal how tall ancient mountains might have been.

Mountains are really just parts of the continental crust that have been thrust upward as tectonic plates slowly crash together. This crust is very heavy, and there is much more to it than what you see on the surface; even the most spectacularly tall peaks, like Everest, are anchored in deep crust. Just as crust gets thrust up to form mountain peaks, it also gets pushed deep under the surface. Both Collins and Ziyi Zhu, a geochemist at Curtin University in Australia, compared mountains to icebergs, in the sense that only a bit pokes above the surface.

"We can argue or speculate that [the biggest mountain] was in a place where there were deep roots in the crust," Zhu told Live Science.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Geologists estimate that the Himalayas, for example, have a crustal column that goes down as far as 50 miles (80 kilometers). Compare that to Everest's elevation of about 29,000 feet (9,000 m), and the world's tallest mountain at most represents only 14% of the rock slab it's part of. That means there's a limit to how tall mountains can get before they collapse under their own weight.

The Himalayas began forming between 50 million and 40 million years ago from the collision between the Indian Eurasian continental plates. As far as mountains go, they are relatively young. And that's partly why they are still so tall. Tall, jagged mountains erode quickly over time, though the Himalayas are still growing as the two plates continue to collide.

Such continental collisions have happened countless times before, though. For example, the Transgondwanan Supermountain, an ancient range in what is now East Africa, began emerging some 650 million years ago when Africa and South America crashed into Arabia, India, Australia and Antarctica to form the supercontinent Gondwana.

Gondwana split up again, but evidence of these mountains in places like southern India, Sri Lanka, Tanzania and Kenya point to them being three times the length of the Himalayas. "If you walk around there now, you can see rocks that were at the bottom of this mountain belt," Collins told Live Science. On average, the crust is deeper than the crust of the Himalayas. "We think this is at least the scale of the Himalayas if not more," Collins said.

The crusts found in these areas also hint at how tall the mountains were, with sections that descend up to 18 miles (30 km) deep, despite half a billion years of erosion. "At some point, they were likely halfway down a crustal column that was 60 kilometers [37 miles deep]," Collins said. This means that the mountains above this base could have been as tall as Everest.

In the Himalayas, the tallest mountains sit around the rim of the Tibetan Plateau, which has the highest elevation on the planet, at about 3.7 miles (6 km) above sea level, on average. The Transgondwanan range may have had a similar plateau around southern Madagascar, meaning its rim would have been in eastern Madagascar, southern India and eastern Antarctica, Collins said.

Another candidate for the tallest mountains was the Grenville orogeny, which popped up with the formation of the supercontinent Rodinia starting about 1.3 billion years ago. Its remains can be seen around southeastern Ontario and northwestern Vermont. But less is known about this extinct range, Collins said, with some scholars arguing that it wouldn't have been as tall as the Transgondwanan range or the Himalayas.

Further back, some 2 billion years ago, the formation of the supercontinent Nuna (also called Columbia) also left evidence of truly giant mountains. Zhu's paper found evidence of this supermountain by examining the composition of zircon crystals left in the crust underneath this vanished range.

Look any further back, however, and the picture gets murkier. When Earth was hotter, mountains likely couldn't get as high because warmer crusts can support less weight, Collins said. Stable continental plates and rocks didn't start to form until about 4 billion years ago, and it took hundreds of millions of additional years for large continents to form.

For Zhu, the Nuna, Transgondwana and Himalaya ranges are currently the best candidates for holding the tallest mountains that ever existed. But it's likely impossible to pinpoint the highest specific peak, at least with current scientific methods. "It's an open question," Zhu said.
