#179. Scientists Detect Rare Type of Wood Alcohol in Space

Today, the question of where life's building blocks come from is largely settled. Thanks to numerous discoveries in recent decades, scientists have confirmed that the organic molecules are found in space. In addition, recent research has also confirmed that amino acids can be found in Near-Earth Asteroids (NEAs) and proteins can form entirely on their own. Alas, some pieces of the puzzle are still missing, which are crucial to finding how these building blocks come together.

This includes Methanol (CH3OH), also known as wood alcohol, an organic molecule that plays an essential role in the formation of complex organic molecules in space. However, new research from the ALMA COMPASS Large program has detected fully deuterated methanol (aka. "heavy methanol") (CD3OD) around the protostar IRAS4A2. The abundance of this molecule around this very young star challenges current chemical models, which cannot reproduce the amount observed.

The study was led by Arnaud Belloche at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy (MPIfR). He was joined by researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE), the Institut de Recherche en Astrophysique et PlanÃ©tologie (IRAP), the Niels Bohr Institute, the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO), the European Southern Observatory (ESO), the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute, and many other universities and institutes. The results are published in the current issue of Astronomy & Astrophysics.

The chemical structure of complex organic molecules detected in a protoplanetary disc. Â© Credit: ESO/L. CalÃ§ada/T. MÃ¼ller (MPIA/HdA)

Scientists have already detected evidence of other complex molecules (like isopropanol, or "rubbing alcohol") around very young star systems. Experiments suggest they likely form on the surface of icy dust grains in cold nebular clouds, reacting slowly with carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, and other atoms to form increasingly complex molecules long before a new star forms. Once the protostar begins to shine and warm its surroundings, these compounds are released as gases.

At that point, only instruments like the Atacama Large Millimeter-submillimeter Array (ALMA), located in Chile, are able to detect them. This latest study is one of many conducted through the ALMA Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys (COMPASS) program, which relied on ALMA to examine 11 nearby Sun-like protostars that are known to host complex organic molecules.

One such system was IRAS4A2, a protostar located 1,000 light-years away in the Perseus molecular cloud. Here, scientists unambiguously detected fully deuterated methanol for the first time, a form of methanol in which hydrogen atoms are replaced by deuterium (D, or "heavy hydrogen"). It was also the first time a quadruply deuterated molecule was detected in interstellar space. Said Silvia Spezzano, the research group leader at the MPE and co-author of the study:

Deuteration enables us to trace the chemical evolution of molecules during the formation of stars and planets. This helps us understand their chemistry and, ultimately, how molecular complexity is transferred from interstellar clouds to planetary systems.

Artist's impression of the water snowline around the young star V883 Orionis, as detected with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) in 2016. Credit: A. Angelich (NRAO/AUI/NSF)/ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO)

In addition to detecting CD3OD, the ALMA data also allowed the team to determine the chemical abundances of various methanol variants around the protostar. Their results showed that the CD3OD variant is about 100 times more abundant than chemical models predict. This suggests an unknown process is driving the formation of fully deuterated methanol, one that current models miss.

The team also detected several spectral lines they can't yet identify. But given the detection of fully deuterated methanol, they suspect these could come from multiply deuterated forms of methanol, such as mono-deuterated methyl deuterated alcohol (CH2DOD) and dideuteriomethyl deuteroxide (CHD2OD). The team is currently working to secure the laboratory data needed to confirm this. Said Spezzano:

At the Center for Astrochemical Studies at MPE, we are conducting a systematic laboratory program to study the spectroscopy of deuterated complex organic molecules, including CH2DOD and CHD2OD. These molecules allow us to study isotopic substitutions across different functional groups, which serve as chemical 'tags' to trace the growth of molecular complexity.

In addition to the team's paper, six other studies from the COMPASS project are being published. Together, they shed light on the diversity of complex organic molecules in space.

Further Reading: Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics

"With potentially thousands of new discoveries, we need all the help we can get."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Astronomers estimate that our home galaxy, the Milky Way, has churned out more than 10 million black holes over its 13-billion-year history. Yet so far, they have found only 70.

Now, a group of astronomers in the U.K. is trying to close that vast gap by enlisting the public. Their project, called Black Hole Hunters, is looking for volunteers with a computer and a few spare minutes to sift through troves of data gathered by a NASA space telescope. By flagging recognizable patterns that could point to a "missing" black hole, volunteers can help fast-track a search that would otherwise take years, the team says.

"You'll be narrowing down precisely where we need to point our telescopes next," project co-lead Adam McMaster, an astronomer at the University of Southampton in the U.K., said in a statement, "and you might be the one to discover a black hole."

Black holes form when massive stars roughly 20 times heavier than our sun run out of fuel and collapse, leaving behind an abyss with gravity so immense that even light cannot escape. While invisible themselves, these cosmic behemoths reveal their presence by bending the light of nearby objects, and the Black Hole Hunters project is searching for one specific manifestation of this effect.

It happens thanks to the fact that massive stars often form in pairs, and a star can sometimes survive the violent supernova explosion that turns its companion into a black hole. When that happens, the two bodies continue to orbit each other. If such a duo aligns just right with Earth, the black hole will periodically pass directly between its companion star and our planet. And when it does, the black hole's gravity acts like a cosmic magnifying glass, bending and magnifying the star's light, causing it to briefly appear brighter to watchful telescopes.

To find these hidden giants, the project relies on data from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, or TESS. Although the satellite's primary mission is to hunt for planets beyond our solar system, its method of data collection — tracking tiny, continuous changes in a star's brightness over time — is ideally suited for identifying black hole magnification events, the project description notes.

"It's a simple task with no expertise required," McMaster said in the statement. "We will show volunteers examples of what to look for so all they have to do is recognise the right patterns."

Automated algorithms conduct a preliminary sweep of the TESS data, screening millions of potential stars for the most obvious black hole candidate locations, according to the project description. But, the researchers say, artificial intelligence struggles with the messy realities of the cosmos, such as stellar flares and the natural pulsations of stars that can trick the algorithms into false positives.

That makes human volunteers a key part of the search. To keep errors in check, each graph is shown to multiple volunteers, and their answers are combined so that individual mistakes average out, according to the project's website.

"I can search for black holes on my laptop from my bedroom — and could make a real impact on real space science," Grace Clarke, an undergraduate student of physics and astronomy at the University of Southampton who's involved with the project, said in the same statement. "The data's easy to understand — it's just pattern recognition — and you don't need a degree in astronomy to read it."

The crowdsourced shortlist of promising signals lets astronomers aim follow-up observations at specific stars, such as precise measurements of whether a star is being tugged at by an unseen companion. Those measurements take time and are expensive, so a good shortlist helps researchers spend scarce telescope time wisely, the team says.

Since launching on the Zooniverse platform in October 2021, the project has attracted nearly 23,000 volunteers, who have completed more than 12 million classifications, according to its website.

Before turning to TESS, the team ran a similar search using data from SuperWASP, a ground-based survey that, like TESS, monitored stars for signs of planets from 2004 to 2016. Those results are still being analyzed and are expected to be published soon.

The team also plans to widen its search with observations from other instruments, including the European Space Agency's Euclid mission and NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

"With potentially thousands of new discoveries, we need all the help we can get," McMaster said in the statement.

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

#181. The 8 Best Shop Vacs for Tackling Tough Messes

From sucking up water to blowing sawdust off your tools, these powerful models have what it takes to get the job done. These are the models we’ve used and recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You can’t make an omelet without breaking a few eggs, and you can’t complete a project at home or in your workshop without making a mess. These are the laws of the universe. I don’t write them; I just obey them.

But because of this, I also know the importance of a reliable shop vac. Unlike the vacuum you use to clean the floors in your home, a shop vac gobbles up large, chunky messes, including sawdust, screws, bits of wood, and other debris (not to mention spills and other wet messes). So if you’re using woodworking tools like sanders, miter saws, and table saws on a regular basis, you need to have one close by.

When it comes to choosing the right shop vac for your home, there’s a lot to consider. Shop vacs come in both cordless and corded electric models and range in size from small, 1.6-gallon portable vacuums for cleaning out cars to large, 12-gallon shop vacs capable of keeping your entire garage sawdust-free.

All of the products written about below were tested by members of the Popular Mechanics team, including myself (Tony Carrick) and Test Editor Brad Ford.

In an effort to evaluate the performance of the shop vacs on this list, we put them through tests that involved collecting both dry materials and liquid. We conducted three timed tests using only each vacuum’s hose, no attachments. The first test involved vacuuming up 12 cups of sawdust to determine how quickly each vac could collect dry material. We then used each vac to drain 2 gallons of water from a bucket. Lastly, we tested suction power by attempting to use each vac to suck up wood screws and metal bolts.

Along with grading each shop vac’s vacuuming capabilities, we also evaluated how easy each model was to use, based on factors like weight, size, capacity, and cord and hose length. Since every person’s shop vac needs may vary, the list below includes a broad range of sizes.

In the latest update of this guide, we tested and added two new shop vacs. The Vacmaster Professional Beast Series FLT+ is a shop vac with next-level features you won’t find on any other shop vacs. Not only does it connect to the exhaust ports of the large sawdust-producing power tools in your workshop, table saws, miter saws, and the like, but it also syncs with them via a wireless remote. With a vacuum cleaner–like dust collection bag and top-mounted HEPA filter, it’s ideally equipped for collecting sawdust.

The Craftsman CMXEVBE17595 Wet-Dry Shop Vac is our largest pick (with its 16-gallon tank) and also one of our most powerful. With a max airflow of 185 cubic feet per minute (cfm), it sucks up material faster than any other shop vac we tested. It’s also powerful enough to pull in heavier objects, including bolts and small chunks of wood.

The Vacmaster’s impressive power and compact design make it the perfect all-around shop vac. One of our editors owns the previous iteration of this model and has found it to be the ideal shop vac for home use. Its 5.5-hp motor is much more powerful than what you’ll find with most other 5-gallon shop vacs. It also has a small, 18.6-by-13.4-inch footprint, so it’s easy to carry and store, though its smaller capacity may not be enough for busier workshops.

With an 18-foot power cord and 7-foot hose, you won’t need an extension cord to clean up a large two-car garage or reach a car in the driveway. Plus, the newest version of the Vacmaster adds wheels that make it even easier to move around. There are also four attachments, which offer enough versatility to handle different jobs, and all of the Vacmaster’s attachments fit neatly into a storage compartment on the vacuum.

Full Vacmaster Beast Series 5-Gallon Shop Vacuum Review

Stanley’s 6-gallon wet-dry vac is a fraction of the cost of other shop vacs, yet it still packs enough power and capacity to handle most cleanups. Though it lagged behind the top performers we tested, it still completed our sawdust test in a respectable 21 seconds, and it swallowed up 2 gallons of water in just 11 seconds. And with its smaller-diameter hose, it produced enough suction to pick up both screws and bolts.

It’s not too bulky, so it won’t crowd your workshop floor, nor is it so compact that it requires emptying too frequently. It sits on swiveling casters and is relatively light, which made it easy to wheel around our tester’s garage. We also liked its accessories, which include two extensions and three nozzles for both floor and spill cleanup. The crevice tool was particularly impressive in that it reached easily into the tight spaces between the seats of one of our cars.

We did find ourselves wishing the power cord was longer than 10 feet so we could reach all corners of the workshop without having to use an extension cord. Still, with its low price and ample capacity, this Stanley vac is a great value option for any home workshop.

Ridgid's shop vac is powerful and affordable enough to fit most budgets, making it an ideal companion for those bigger and messier home improvement projects.

During testing, it collected a pile of sawdust in just over 16 seconds before proceeding to drain a bucket of water in about 6 seconds. While we liked how quickly it picked up light debris, the Ridgid left a little to be desired with lift power. Its large-diameter hose made quick work of lighter material, but it struggled to pick up larger bolts (though we should note that this was an issue with most other vacs with large 2-1/2-inch-diameter hoses).

The Ridgid also has a sturdy feel to it. The hose resisted cracking or denting, even after mistakenly stepping on it, and the tub is made of thick plastic. There’s also a locking system on the hose, which prevents attachments from falling off when the vacuum is in use.

The vacuum’s long, 7-foot hose made it easy to clean a work area without having to repeatedly reposition the base. Attachments include two extension wands, along with a crevice tool and floor tool, all of which fit onto the shop vac for storage. An included wet filter would make this shop vac a real no-brainer purchase, but it’s not far off from that even without one.

Full Ridgid 12-Gallon 5.0 Peak HP NXT Shop Vacuum Review

The speed and capacity the DeWalt Stealthsonic displayed during my tests makes it a great choice for cleaning up wet messes.

It produced some of the most impressive vacuuming results during our tests. Backed by its 5.5-hp motor and 2.5-inch-diameter hose (about the same size as a fire hose), the Stealthsonic gobbled up our pile of sawdust in just 16 seconds and drained our bucket of water in just 5 seconds, which was among the fastest of any shop vac we tested.

It was also one of the largest of the shop vacs we tested, with a 12-gallon capacity. Thanks to its 20-foot-long cord, it covers an entire two-car garage without the need for an extension cord, and it sits on heavy-duty rubber casters that make it easy to wheel around.

While its larger-diameter hose worked well for the quick collection of lighter materials, it’s not ideal for heavier objects. The Stealthsonic struggled to produce enough lift to suck up wood screws and was unable to collect larger bolts like some shop vacs with smaller-diameter hoses could. It also is a bit too bulky to get into tighter spots, such as the small gaps in and around the seats in a car. But if you’re looking for something that quickly cleans up larger spills and messes at the job site or in a workshop, this vacuum is it.

Milwaukee’s M18 Fuel wet-dry vacuum, which runs off an 18-volt lithium-ion battery, is one of the most powerful shop vac options when there’s no electrical outlet in range. The vac impressed during testing, even matching some of the corded shop vacs we tested. It consumed our sawdust pile in 20 seconds flat and a bucket of water in just 11 seconds, which is saying something given that it has a long, 9-foot hose.

We also loved the design of this wet-dry vac. The accessories, which include a floor utility nozzle and crevice tool, fit nicely inside a compartment on the top of the shop vac, and the tray holds both extensions. The extra-long hose and the small profile of the crevice tool were particularly valuable when we used the M18 Fuel wet-dry vacuum to clean out a car.

The M18 6-gallon vacuum is also easy to maneuver. It sits in a sturdy tray with four casters with rubber wheels that rolled easily over our tester’s garage floor and driveway. The M18’s run time was also impressive. When loaded with a 12.0-ampere-hour (Ah) battery, we got 31 minutes of run time when set to high and a whopping 48 minutes on its lower power setting.

This was the priciest wet-dry vacuum we tested, but it’s worth the investment if you want to cut the cord without compromising power.

If the primary demand for your shop vac is to collect the mountains of sawdust left behind following a carpentry project, then look no further than the recently launched Vacmaster Professional Beast Series FLT+. Not only will this shop vac attach to your power tools’ exhaust ports, but it also synchronizes with them. It comes with a Synchro key remote, which you attach to a power tool via a neoprene strap. The key communicates wirelessly with the shop vac. When it senses the vibration of the tool turning on, the key sends a signal that turns on the vacuum, eliminating the need to walk across the room to turn it on manually. I used it with a table saw, and it worked well, reliably turning on as soon as I fired up the table saw and dutifully sucking up dust as I cut, then turning off when I shut down the saw.

The Vacmaster is designed for collecting dust particles, and it did that extremely well. It sucked up 12 cups of sawdust in under 20 seconds, which is impressive given that it comes equipped with a smaller 1-7/8-inch-diameter hose. The Vacmaster Beast FLT+ also comes with a dust bag similar to a vacuum cleaner and a HEPA filter, making it ideal for trapping fine dust particles.

While most shop vacs have a filter located inside the collection tank, the Vacmaster’s is on top. This frees up space inside the tank for more debris collection while also preventing the filter from becoming inundated with dust. Other notable features you won’t find on most shop vacs include an LED display that shows the vacuum's airflow percentage, so you know when it’s time to clean the filter, and a self-cleaning filter. It’s an excellent workshop shop vac for those who don’t mind springing for it.

With its cordless design, light weight, and compact, box-shaped design, Milwaukee’s M12 Fuel shop vac is made for the road. At just 15 inches long, 13 inches wide, and 12 inches high, and with a weight of just under 10 pounds, Milwaukee’s M12 Fuel shop vac was by far the easiest to carry around of the wet-dry vacuums we tested. Its shape also made it ideal for sitting in the trunk of a car or storing on a set of garage shelves.

Per its name, the M12 Fuel shop vac uses a smaller power source—a 12-volt battery—so it doesn’t have the power of the corded and 18-volt cordless models we tested. Still, it took a respectable 35 seconds for it to complete our sawdust test and was capable of sucking down both bolts and wood screws. Its 1.6-gallon capacity and a max runtime of 26 minutes on low and 14 minutes on high limit it to small cleanup jobs, however.

While it lacks the power of larger shop vacs, it’s hard to overstate how convenient it is to use. We appreciated its compact size and cordless design when we toted it into the car for some detailing, then later up to a second-floor bonus room to clean up drywall dust after mounting a TV.

The M12 Fuel is pricey when you factor in the cost of a battery and charger, but its convenience is unmatched, especially if you’ve already bought into Milwaukee’s 12-volt power tool universe and have a 12-volt Fuel battery to load into it.

Full Milwaukee M12 Fuel 1.6-Gallon Shop Vac Review

The Craftsman 16-gallon wet-dry shop vac was built to clean up large masses fast with a max airflow of 185 cfm, well above the 100 cfm I see on most shop vacs. It vacuumed up 12 cups of sawdust faster than any other shop vac I tested and gulped down 2 gallons of water in 5 seconds flat. Most of the shop vacs I tested with a larger 2-1/2-inch-diameter hose struggled to generate enough lift to pick up heavier debris. That wasn’t the case with the Craftsman, which effortlessly vacuumed up a pile of screws, washers, and large bolts.

The Craftsman sits on four sturdy casters that made it easy to maneuver around when I was using it to clean up my large two-car garage, which I was able to do thanks to its 20-foot-long power cord and 7-foot hose.

With its 16-gallon size, the Craftsman was also the largest shop vac I tested, which made it handy for cleaning up big messes and large open areas. It was less effective for cleaning out a car. The crevice tool and its bulkier hose made it difficult to maneuver around a car interior, and there are no crevice tools for cleaning the gaps between seats and other tight spaces.

While its large size makes the Craftsman capable of cleaning up large messes, it also makes it a bit of a space hog in a garage or shed. You also won’t be carrying it inside the house to clean up messes in the home. But if you’re after a shop vac with the muscle and capacity to handle large postproject messes, this is the one.

The drum capacity of a shop vac determines how much material you can vacuum without having to empty it out. While sizes range from 1.6 to 16 gallons, smaller-capacity shop vacs, like the Milwaukee M12 Fuel 1.6-Gallon Wet-Dry Vacuum, provide more versatility to the average user through easier transport and storage. If you’re short on space, a smaller unit that you have to empty more frequently could be more convenient than a larger-capacity machine cluttering up your garage. Keep in mind that the stated gallon capacity doesn't factor in the space taken up by the filter, so don’t expect a 6-gallon model to suck up exactly 6 gallons of material.

While the majority of shop vacs use corded power, cordless models are becoming more common. These battery-powered options offer more mobility—especially useful for car, boat, or RV cleaning—but they lack the runtime for extended projects. If you prefer the mobility of cordless models (especially if you’re interested in a larger-capacity model that requires a lot of power), choose one from the same brand as your existing power tools. This enables you to extend runtime by using additional batteries you already have on hand.

If you decide to go with a corded model, pay attention to the length of the cord. Models with a longer cord, such as the DeWalt Stealthsonic Wet-Dry Shop Vacuum, give you the freedom to cover larger workshops or reach to your driveway without having to get out an extension cord.

A shop vac’s airflow—measured in cubic feet per minute (cfm)—represents the amount of air a vacuum pulls through its nozzle. Roughly speaking, a shop vac with a higher cfm sucks up material faster than one with a lower cfm, though keep in mind this doesn’t include other factors like nozzle design, motor size, and suction power. As we found during testing, shop vacs with smaller-diameter hoses, such as the Milwaukee M18 Fuel 6-Gallon Wet-Dry Vacuum, often produce greater suction power. So while a larger shop vac with a larger-diameter hose will remove lightweight material, such as sawdust, more quickly than a shop vac with a narrower hose, that smaller vac is better able to pick up heavier objects, such as bolts and coins.

While most shop vacs include several nozzle attachments for the hose, some models offer a more useful variety of accessories. Think about the type and scope of your cleaning tasks, and look for a vacuum with applicable accessories. For example, we’ve found a brush-tip nozzle to be essential for automotive interior cleaning, allowing us to quickly clean dust and pet hair from the dashboard and display screen—areas easily scratched by a hard plastic nozzle. Or, if you want to suck up the cobwebs in the corner of your garage or sawdust deep under your workbench, look for vacs with multiple extension wands to extend the nozzle reach.

#182. NASA’s James Webb Telescope Reveals a Giant Alien Planet That’s Not Quite Round

Weather maps of distant planets are a step closer after the James Webb Space Telescope distinguished hotter and cooler regions around the giant exoplanet WASP-17b.

One side of WASP-17b’s atmosphere extends farther into space than the other, giving this intensely hot giant planet an uneven outline. Astronomers have now mapped that distortion with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), finding a pattern consistent with predictions of how heat and powerful winds shape a world with permanent day and night sides.

WASP-17b is a hot Jupiter, a giant planet that orbits close to its star, about 1,300 light-years from Earth. The study, co-led by Cornell University in the United States and the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom, was published in Nature Astronomy. It marks the first application of a method called transmission strings, developed at Bristol by astrophysicists Dr. David Grant and Dr. Hannah Wakeford.

“Having this very robust mathematical model that we can apply to this state-of-the-art data is incredibly exciting. The results are a really beautiful demonstration of the dynamics that are going on in these multidimensional and multifaceted worlds,” said Wakeford, a study co-author and associate professor of astrophysics at the University of Bristol.

JWST, the largest telescope in space, has already enabled researchers to use a technique called eclipse mapping, which measures changes in light as a planet passes behind its host star. Transmission strings, also called transit mapping, follows the planet as it crosses in front of the star. It analyzes the light passing through different parts of the atmosphere’s edge, or limb, to distinguish conditions around that boundary. Traditional modeling instead extracts a single spectrum, a measurement of light across different wavelengths, averaged over the entire limb.

Lead author Dr. Lili Alderson, a Klarman Postdoctoral Fellow at Cornell, began the investigation at the University of Bristol, where she earned her doctorate in physics.

“Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet,” Alderson said. “We’re able to go around the edge. So, we’ve gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak.”

On WASP-17b, the mapped bulge lies on the evening side of the equator. There, jets of wind carry heat from the permanently illuminated day side toward the permanently shadowed night side, inflating the atmosphere relative to the equator’s cooler morning side. The location matches what theory and previous modeling had indicated.

“Theory predicts that the morning and the evening sides should have a strong temperature difference, and WASP-17b fits really nicely in that trend – pretty much bang-on what we thought it would be,” Alderson said.

The study’s findings on atmospheric chemical composition and temperature differences, both from equator to poles and between the day and night sides, also agree with theoretical predictions and other modeling techniques.

“Planets are temperamental, their atmospheres complex and chaotic. The fact that all of these numbers came together and showed us this very structured, dynamical picture of this giant world over 1,000 light-years away was just really exciting,” Wakeford said.

Together, the findings provide one of the most comprehensive three-dimensional views of an exoplanet’s atmosphere. They also establish a benchmark for comparison with the more than 6,000 other exoplanets confirmed to date.

“This is proof of concept that planets are in fact 3D objects, and that consistently, as they go around their star, what we predict should be happening is happening. To move beyond computational exercises and see it for real is a different matter,” Alderson said.

The successful demonstration on WASP-17b opens the way to applying transmission strings to many more planets. The method is beginning to distinguish conditions across different latitudes, extending atmospheric maps beyond the contrast between day and night. That is a first step toward mapping weather-scale patterns in exoplanet climates.

Reference: “A spatial map of the atmospheric limb of a hot Jupiter” by Lili Alderson, Hannah R. Wakeford, David Grant, Nikole K. Lewis, Avinash Verma, Jayesh Goyal, Mark Hammond, Daniel Valentine, Natalie H. Allen, Ana Glidden, Amélie Gressier, Jingcheng Huang, Maura Lally, Dana R. Louie, Jacob Lustig-Yaeger, Cathal Maguire, Elijah Mullens, Kristin S. Sotzen, Jeff A. Valenti, Roeland P. van der Marel and Tiffany Kataria, 14 October 2026, Nature Astronomy. #183. Magic mushroom ingredient takes the fight out of aggressive fish

Psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in more than 200 species of mushrooms, appears to have an unexpected effect on aggressive fish. Most mushrooms containing this compound belong to the gilled mushroom genus Psilocybe. In mammals, psilocybin interacts with serotonin receptors in the brain, influencing emotions and behaviors such as mood, appetite, and aggression. However, scientists still know relatively little about how the substance affects social interactions among animals.

To investigate this question, researchers in Canada examined the effects of psilocybin on the amphibious mangrove rivulus fish (Kryptolebias marmoratus). Their findings, published in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience, suggest that even a brief exposure to a low dose can significantly reduce aggressive behavior without disrupting normal social interactions.

"We show that an acute, low dose of psilocybin significantly reduces activity and aggressive attack behavior during social interactions in adult mangrove rivulus fish, a species that is naturally highly aggressive," said first author Dayna Forsyth, a research associate and former MSc student at Acadia University in Nova Scotia.

"These findings provide the first evidence that psilocybin can selectively reduce escalated aggression in a vertebrate model without suppressing social interaction," added senior author Dr. Suzie Currie, a biologist at The University of British Columbia.

Why Scientists Studied Aggressive Mangrove Rivulus Fish

Mangrove rivulus fish are naturally combative, particularly when they encounter another member of their species. Their aggressive responses are easy to recognize and measure, allowing researchers to detect even small changes in behavior.

These fish also have an unusual reproductive ability. They can fertilize themselves, producing offspring that are genetically identical. This makes them especially useful for experiments because scientists can minimize genetic variation and more confidently attribute behavioral differences to psilocybin rather than inherited traits.

For the experiment, the researchers worked with three genetically distinct lines of fish bred in the laboratory. One group received psilocybin, another provided the fish used to provoke social interactions, and the third helped researchers measure how much psilocybin entered and accumulated in the animals' bodies.

The researchers first established a baseline for each fish's behavior. They placed a fish into a tank already occupied by another fish, with the two separated by a fiberglass mesh barrier and an opaque cover. The mesh prevented physical contact while allowing the fish to see and smell each other once the cover was removed.

After allowing five minutes for the fish to adjust to their shared environment, the team removed the opaque cover and recorded their interactions.

The following day, 24 hours after the initial observation, the researchers placed the same fish in water containing dissolved psilocybin. Following 20 minutes of exposure, they returned it to the tank with the same fish it had encountered previously. The opaque cover was then removed again so the researchers could observe any changes in behavior.

Magic Mushroom Compound Reduces Aggressive Attacks

The results revealed a striking change. Fish exposed to psilocybin moved around less and displayed fewer bursts of aggressive swimming than fish that had not received the substance.

To assess these changes, the scientists measured overall activity (time spent moving) and several signs of aggression (including swimming bursts). These rapid bursts are particularly important because they indicate that an encounter is escalating toward an attack, even when the fish cannot make physical contact.

"Swimming bursts are high-energy attack behaviors that represent an escalation of aggression towards the stimulus fish without making physical contact," explained Currie. "Other types of aggressive behaviors, like head-on displays, are more about communication and social assessment and require very little energy."

Interestingly, psilocybin did not suppress every form of aggressive or social behavior. While the fish became less likely to engage in intense, energy-demanding attacks, their less physically demanding social displays remained largely unchanged.

"Psilocybin's calming effect appears to selectively reduce energetically costly, escalated behaviors while lower-energy social display behaviors remained largely unchanged," said Forsyth. "This suggests that this compound can selectively dampen escalated social conflict rather than shutting down behavior altogether."

The compound also reduced general activity. When placed alongside another member of their species, fish treated with psilocybin spent less time swimming than untreated controls.

Together, these findings suggest that psilocybin may influence specific aspects of aggressive behavior rather than simply making animals less responsive to their surroundings.

What the Findings Could Mean for Psychedelic Research

The researchers believe animal studies like this one could eventually help scientists better understand how psychedelic compounds influence behavior and identify possible directions for therapeutic research.

By examining which social responses are most sensitive to psilocybin, researchers may be able to uncover biological mechanisms that are difficult to investigate directly in people. Such insights could ultimately inform studies of potential clinical applications.

However, the team emphasized that the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of a treatment for aggression in humans. The experiment involved fish, did not evaluate any clinical intervention, and cannot establish whether similar effects would occur in people.

There are also important questions about how long the calming effect lasts. The researchers examined only single doses and short exposure periods. They did not investigate repeated treatments, long-term behavioral changes, or whether the fish might adapt to the substance over time.

Additional experiments will be necessary to determine whether psilocybin's ability to reduce aggressive attacks can persist beyond the brief period examined in this study.

"Future studies can build on this work to explore how psilocybin alters neural signaling, which serotonin pathways are involved, and why some aspects of social behavior are affected while others are not," concluded Currie. "These are questions that are difficult or impossible to answer directly in humans."

#184. When climate change brings the heat, what happens to a mighty redwood?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Coast redwoods slow photosynthesis when heat waves get too hot to handle

Light filters through coast redwoods at the University of California, Davis Arboretum. A new study found the tree's needles can cut their net photosynthesis roughly in half when temperatures spike.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Towering coast redwoods are known for their resiliency, withstanding fire, fungus and rot to survive for centuries. But these ancient trees now may be vulnerable to a relatively recent foe: heat waves.

As temperatures climb, photosynthesis slows in these iconic trees, researchers report September 22 in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences. Lab experiments show the rate of the sunlight-driven food making process in its needles roughly halves when temperatures rise from 30° to 40° Celsius.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Such a change usually indicates “severe levels of stress,” says Lily Klinek, an ecophysiologist at the University of California, Davis. That vulnerability can cause tree deaths that may jeopardize one of California’s largest stores of carbon, a shield against climate change.

Coast redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens) live only in a narrow strip of coastal habitat from central California to southern Oregon, where temperatures are mild and fog is abundant. But recent heat waves have spiked temperatures in parts of their range to over 40° C.

The impact of heat waves on photosynthesis has been studied in other tree species, with some faring better than others. But this is the first study to investigate how coast redwoods respond to the heat, says Troy Magney, an ecophysiologist at the University of Montana in Missoula.

From July 2022 to October 2024, Klinek, Magney and colleagues repeatedly measured the performance of needles from redwoods in California’s Mendocino County. That period included two heat waves.

Typically, trees stay cool when small porelike openings called stomata allow water to evaporate, taking heat with it, similar to how sweat cools humans. But when conditions get too hot and dry, stomata close, retaining a plant’s moisture. Under extreme heat, the team found that needles reached up to 10 degrees C hotter than the surrounding air due to the dark needles absorbing ample sunlight. That suggests that the stomata were at least partially closed.

Those same pores are crucial for photosynthesis; it’s where the trees take in carbon dioxide — used to make food — and release oxygen. “They could essentially starve if they don’t have access to enough carbon,” Klinek says.

It’s hard to investigate the impact of heat on photosynthesis in the field, though. That would take building a “heat chamber around a real-life branch or wait[ing] for a heat event to happen,” Klinek says. Instead, she climbed onto the roof of her car with a pole pruner and collected samples from about five meters high, in the lower canopy.

In the lab, the researchers subjected the samples to increasing heat to match the heat waves seen in recent summers and measured the resulting photosynthesis rates. Even though the samples were submerged in water, so had their stomata open and had full access to the ingredients for photosynthesis, the rate still declined. “They weren’t slowing their photosynthesis because of carbon starvation,” Klinek says.

For practical reasons, the study focused on younger coast redwoods, not the old growth giants. It’s difficult to reach even the lowest branches on trees more than 100 meters tall. “There are just fundamental limitations on what you can sample if you don’t have a jetpack,” says Christopher Still, an ecophysiologist at Oregon State University in Corvallis who was not associated with the study. Even so, the team’s results show that coast redwoods are “really temperature sensitive. You don’t see this as much with other species necessarily,” Still says.

In the field, Klinek observed trees closing their stomata to preserve water. This suggests that in more realistic conditions, where a heat wave and drought hit simultaneously, lack of heat and water could make the slowdown “even more intense.” But more work needs to be done, she notes. “We still don’t know what the threshold is for irreversible damage.”

Archaeologists have discovered an ancient base camp in Alaska that has evidence of the oldest dwelling and possibly the earliest domesticated dogs in the Americas.

Archaeologists digging at a 13,800-year-old site in interior Alaska have unearthed thousands of artifacts and fossils, including what may be the bones of the earliest domesticated dogs in the Americas, the earliest needles and dwellings in the Western Hemisphere, and stone tools that reveal cultural connections across the Bering Land Bridge.

At a site called Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ (which means "They Were There" in the Alaska Native Athabascan language), about 34 miles (55 kilometers) southeast of Fairbanks, archaeologists have excavated an encampment that some of the first people to settle in North America used off and on for a millennium.

Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ is located in eastern Beringia, the geographical region that connected northeast Asia and northwest North America during the last ice age. The most recent archaeological and genetic studies suggest that the ancestors of today's Indigenous Americans entered the continent around 21,000 years ago. But since Beringian sites are often the remains of small seasonal hunting camps and are scattered across a large geographic area, much is still unknown about the earliest people who called the Western Hemisphere home.

"I expected we'd find hunting tools and knapping [stone tool making] debris surrounding a hearth or two, but I had no idea that we'd stumble into a base camp with tens of thousands of artifacts," study first author Kelly Graf, an archaeologist at the University of Kansas, told Live Science in an email. "It was a total surprise!"

In a study published Wednesday (Oct. 14) in the journal Science Advances, Graf and co-authors detailed their discoveries at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ, focusing on the earliest occupation, which occurred around 13,800 years ago, as evidence of people "settling in" to their new territory.

The researchers found a hearth, a small pit, and a dirt stain where a wooden post had once stood, likely the remains of a lean-to or early tent house. Additionally, the archaeologists unearthed stone tools, bone needles and a pendant made from an antler. Nearby, they found an earth oven, which was full of charcoal and animal bones and was likely used to slow-cook meat for a large family group.

"The complex feature at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ represents the earliest potential case of a habitation structure in North America," the researchers wrote in the study. "Early Alaskans knew their surroundings well."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The archaeologists were also surprised by the stone tools recovered at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ because they are distinctively shaped and unique to central Alaska. Known as diamond-shaped hafted bifaces, the tools were crafted from rhyolite and basalt and are similar to those typically found much farther west in Beringia, in modern-day northern Siberia. Additionally, obsidian artifacts discovered at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ reveal that people brought the volcanic rock to the site from a geological source hundreds of miles to the northwest.

Bones from more than a dozen wolf-like animals suggest a further connection to Asia, according to the researchers. An analysis of the jaw of one of the animals showed that it was not from a dire wolf (Aenocyon dirus) or from a Pleistocene Beringian or gray wolf (Canis lupus sp.) but rather a population of wolf-like animals unique to central Alaska. Current genetic evidence suggests that early domesticated dogs in North America came from Siberian wolves. The timing and geographical location of Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ provides circumstantial evidence that the people may have been dog owners.

"Like humans, potentially, the canids of Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ and other early Alaskan sites were recent immigrants from Asian Beringia," the researchers wrote.

Although Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ reveals a relationship with sites in Asia, there is also evidence of connections with early American sites south of the Canadian ice sheets, according to the study.

One clue to these connections is the presence of bone artifacts in a sewing kit. The archaeologists found eight bone needle fragments at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ. Previously, the only recovered eyed needles had come from Paleoindian sites in temperate North America. Therefore, the needles from Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ are the oldest needles ever discovered in the Western Hemisphere, and they reveal connections with sites farther south, according to the study.

Another clue is the pendant, which was crafted from antler. The pendant had a hole drilled at one end and was fashioned into a point at the other end. This piece of ancient jewelry is similar to personal adornment items found farther south in North America.

"The co-occurrence of these cultural features at the single site of Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ is truly notable," the researchers wrote, and they "highlight the strong cultural connection between early Beringians and Americans."

It is still unclear whether the people at Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ were traveling to make these connections. "It would be hard to pin down whether or not they were moving back and forth during a lifetime, but at least we can say there is a connection," Graf said.

Archaeologists recovered bison bone and a hearth, among other things, at the Beringian site.

Future excavations in Beringia could help archaeologists learn more about the earliest people in the Americas, according to Graf. "Alaska is a big place and so remote, so there are really just a few small areas that have been intensively investigated," she said.

Spencer Pelton, an archaeologist at the University of Wyoming who was not involved in the research, wrote in an accompanying perspective published in the journal Science Advances that early Indigenous sites in Beringia are key to understanding the peopling of the Americas.

"Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ is remarkable because it is the oldest site in the Americas containing a large and rich assemblage of features, artifacts, and faunal refuse indicative of prolonged residential occupation, providing an unprecedented glimpse into the lives of North America's first residents," Pelton wrote.

Graf is already planning future archaeological excavations in the area. "We're hoping to bring some younger Alaska Native folks out with us in the coming summers," she said, as incorporating local knowledge is important to the project. "Two of our co-authors are elders from Alaska Native corporations nearest to the site," she said. Elders named the Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ site and have visited it to discuss where to excavate and what the archaeologists might find.

There is much left to learn about what was happening in Beringia 14,000 years ago, the researchers wrote, particularly since there are currently only two archaeological sites — including the 24,000-year-old Bluefish Caves site in the Yukon — that suggest humans were settling in Beringia considerably earlier.

(2026). Highlights from an early base camp in Beringia 13,800 years ago: Shégˊ Xdaltthˊíˊ and the Late Pleistocene peopling of Alaska. #187. Will this sleep-disorder drug be the next big blockbuster?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Amanda Heidt is a freelance journalist in southeast Utah.

When US regulators approved a treatment for narcolepsy in August, some researchers immediately predicted a bright future for the class of compounds it belongs to, known as orexin agonists. Much like blockbuster GLP-1 drugs, such as Ozempic, which were initially approved to treat diabetes but have since taken off as treatments for other conditions, these new drugs seem capable of much more than treating sleep disorders.

First-of-its-kind narcolepsy drug opens door to new therapies for the brain

First-of-its-kind narcolepsy drug opens door to new therapies for the brain

“Diabetes was the tip of the iceberg for GLP-1s, and I’m convinced the same story will play out for orexin,” says Andrew Plump, president of research and development at Takeda, the Tokyo-based pharmaceutical company that developed the newly approved drug, called Orzeyful (oveporexton). “Our goal now is to unravel the science and understand what’s below the surface.”

This excitement comes on the heels of decades of research about orexins — peptides that are produced by the brain and that have a role in modulating metabolism, mood, appetite, memory and, most notably, sleep and wakefulness cycles. Now, scientists are racing to work out how best to apply what they have found in the clinic, exploring the use of orexin agonists in the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and other conditions in which attention and alertness are dysregulated.

“Anyone who has gotten a poor night of sleep can tell you that it impacts nearly every aspect of their life,” says Luis de Lecea, a psychiatrist at Stanford University in California, who was among the first to identify orexins. “It is very rewarding to have a hand in something that has led to a drug that helps people.”

De Lecea was a budding scientist with a new laboratory at the Scripps Research Institute in San Diego, California, when, in the mid-1990s, he took on a daunting project: identifying proteins produced only in certain parts of the human brain. Groups at the institute were divvying up brain regions to study, and de Lecea chose the hypothalamus, an almond-sized region deep in the brain’s interior.

The team generated a list of hypothalamus-specific messenger RNAs — small chunks of genetic material that carry the instructions for making proteins. Sifting through the list, the scientists identified a pair of neuropeptides that they named hypocretin 1 and 21. Unbeknown to de Lecea, researchers in Texas had, around the same time, isolated the equivalent peptides in rats, dubbing them orexin A and B2.

Neuroscientist Takeshi Sakurai was working in the lab of Masashi Yanagisawa, a molecular biologist then at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, when the group first identified the orexins. The researchers suspected that the peptides regulated feeding in rodents — the name comes from the Greek word orexis, meaning appetite — but when they artificially blocked orexin signalling, they found something unexpected.

Narcolepsy confirmed as autoimmune disease

Narcolepsy confirmed as autoimmune disease

“The animals sometimes abruptly collapsed,” says Sakurai, now at the University of Tsukuba in Japan. The behaviour bore a striking resemblance to a hallmark of narcolepsy type 1 in humans: a sudden, temporary loss of muscle control known as cataplexy. After further work, the team landed on a more complete understanding of the role of orexins. “Orexin does not simply wake us up, it keeps wakefulness stable,” he says.

Back in California, researchers were making more discoveries. Emmanuel Mignot, a sleep-medicine specialist at Stanford, and his colleagues were the first to identify a mutation in the gene that encodes orexin receptor 2 as the cause of canine narcolepsy3. In a study of people with narcolepsy type 1 who had died, Jerome Siegel, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles, and his colleagues found that the brains of these people nearly always had a massive loss of the neurons that produce orexins4.

It’s a small population — just 70,000 cells among the hundreds of thousands in the hypothalamus — yet they seem to be crucial.

“Once those neurons are gone, the brain isn’t able to find a workaround,” Siegel says.

From the moment they first noted the link between orexins and sleep, Sakurai says he and his team recognized the therapeutic potential. In a few years, so did pharmaceutical companies.

The first investigations at Takeda began in the late 2000s as a pet project. One of the technicians there had a friend with narcolepsy type 1, and he began looking for a molecule that could bind to orexin receptors and restore a normal sleep–wake cycle.

When the technician scanned Takeda’s libraries for a molecule that met the criteria, only a single candidate, called TAK-925, came back. Going forward with it would be a risk, says Plump. “No chemist in their right mind would start a drug-discovery programme with a single hit.”

First orexin agonists address root cause of narcolepsy

First orexin agonists address root cause of narcolepsy

Nevertheless, Takeda researchers gave it a try and the molecule performed well in animals. When the company launched the first human trial in 2017, the technician drove his friend to the study centre so that she could participate. He contacted Plump right away, saying that the drug seemed to work for her. “He could tell just from speaking with her,” Plump says.

Orzeyful, which has now received approval in three countries, builds on the foundation that TAK-925 and other early candidates set. The drug is a marked improvement on existing therapies that only mask symptoms of the disease and often come with severe side effects.

Mignot, who led Takeda’s late-stage trials says that people report that “after they take this drug, suddenly they really know what it is to be awake”.

With the approval of Orzeyful, competitors are now racing to tap into a global market for narcolepsy drugs that analysts predict could top US$6.4 billion by 2031. Narcolepsy — both type 1 and type 2, which is not associated with a die-off of orexin-producing neurons — affects roughly three million people worldwide, and estimates suggest that many more cases go unreported or misdiagnosed.

#188. Host Stars Shape Their Planetary Systems Into Two Families

The age of exoplanet science took shape with the Kepler mission, and gained more momentum with the TESS mission. The initial goal had a simple definition: use the transit method to find planets orbiting other stars. Beyond that, scientists have worked hard and used multiple tools at their disposal to determine exoplanet compositions and other characterstics.

Now exoplanet science is advancing beyond these initial stages. Planetary scientists want to understand not only the wide diversity in the exoplanet population; they also want to understand the different types of solar systems they're detecting.

In the 1990s, astronomers thought that our Solar System was a kind of template, where massive planets were further from their stars, while less massive ones were closer. That idea has fallen out of favour as exoplanet observations show us that it's not true.

Other ideas about solar system architecture came along. One idea was that giant planets on eccentric orbits are attributed to planet-planet scattering, and another was the idea that the occurrence of giant planets rose with stellar metallicity. The important 'peas-in-a-pod' idea was presented in a 2018 paper.

But a 2020 paper was particularly important, because it presented a way to compare how violent the dynamical histories of different solar systems is. It introduced the concept of the normalized angular momentum deficit (NAMD). NAMD compares a system's combined orbital angular momentum with the angular momentum of a hypothetical system with the same planet masses and orbital characteristics. Since inclined or eccentric orbits carry less angular momentum, a larger NAMD means a hotter system, or one with a more violent history of interactions.

The lead author of that important paper is also a co-lead author of new research that uses NAMD to establish a link between host star and solar system architecture.

The new research in Nature Astronomy builds on underlying ideas about host stars and how they shape their solar systems. It's titled "Two families of multi-planet systems with distinct architectures and stellar hosts," and has two co-first authors. One is Diego Turrini, an astrophysicist and planetologist at the Istituto Nazionale di Astrofisica (INAF) in Italy. The other is Camilla Danielski, a researcher at the University of Valencia and former INAF postdoctoral fellow.

âThe fundamental question we started from was: what determines the characteristics of planetary systems as we see them today?" - Diego Turrini, INAF.

"The rapidly growing census of exoplanets now includes over a thousand multi-planet systems, revealing architectures that span more than four orders of magnitude in mass and five in orbital scale," the authors write. "Explaining the origin of this striking diversity remains a central challenge for planet formation theory, compounded by observational biases that limit access to Solar System-like regimes."

Astronomers know of more than 1,000 multi-exoplanet systems in the Milky Way, and in this work, the researchers focused on 300 of them. These 300 are the most well-understood and best characterized of the 1,000. The researchers found that they can be divided into two distinct families of solar systems, and that the host star shapes the system in multiple ways.

"We identify a clear bimodality in system masses, dividing known architectures into two distinct families," the authors write. One family they describe as the lower-mass family, and they're hosted by stars with masses equal to or lower than the Sun. These systems exhibit "tightly packed configurations with mass distributions consistent with the âpeas-in-a-podâ pattern," the authors write. This means that neighbouring planets have similar sizes and masses. These systems also have "modal dynamical excitation comparable with that of the Solar System," according to the authors. This means how eccentric and inclined the orbits are, and that it's similar to in our Solar System, where orbital eccentricity is low and most planetary orbits aren't highly inclined. This points to systems with less violent, dynamical histories, which are termed 'cold' systems.

The second family features planets on wider orbits, and with combined masses that range from two times to ten times that of our Solar System.

"By contrast, the high-mass family forms in metal-rich environments around solar-to-supersolar stars, displays gravitationally compact architectures and is an order of magnitude dynamically hotter than both the Solar System and the lower-mass counterparts," the authors write. In this context, "hotter" means that the exoplanets have more inclined and more eccentric orbits. "Their high level of dynamical excitation points to violent evolutionary pathways driven by global instabilities and planetâplanet scattering," the researchers explain. These systems are termed 'hot'.

This figure shows a system's normalized angular momentum deficit (NAMD), its normalized system mass (NSM), and the orbital period of its outer planets (Pout). The horizontal grey dotted line represents our Solar System. "High-mass systems are always about an order of magnitude more excited than both lower-mass ones and the Solar System, suggesting violent dynamical histories shaped by instabilities and planetâplanet scattering," the authors write. Image Credit: Turrini, Danielski et al. 2026. NatAstr.

âThe main difficulty during the data analysis was determining whether the two families of planetary systems were real or just an illusion created by the technological limits of current observational techniques,â added Danielski. âAt the end of the path, it became clear that selection effects acted as the tip of the iceberg, revealing the existence of much deeper structural diversities between these systems.â

The researchers uncovered a clear link between the stars in each type of system and the planets in each type of system.

"The distinct architectural properties of the high- and lower-mass families of multi-planet systems can be explained by the interplay between planet formation and the different characteristics of their stellar hosts," the authors write.

"Lower-mass systems emerge from Solar System-like planet-forming environments," and are especially reliant on the host star's metallicity and mass.

"High-mass system are, instead, born from planet-forming environments that are, on average, three times richer in gas and solids," the authors write, and this creates a situation where planetary growth is a more efficient process than planetary migration.

âThe scenarios that best reproduce the dynamical properties of the family of wide and massive systems are those in which the systems are unstable from birth,â emphasises co-author Danae Polychroni, an INAF researcher. âThe greater abundance of material from which planets form around their host stars causes them to be born too large, preventing the system from remaining stable.â

Interestingly, both families share common properties that are different from our Solar System. The architectures of both families of system are less compact than our outer Solar System, and more compact than in our inner Solar System.

In the early stages of exoplanet science, researchers assumed that our Solar System was a template for all systems. Since we hadn't observed any others, this was a more or less sensible statement. But now, thanks to plenty of research, including this effort, we know that was an error. This research replaces that idea with a new template based on the links between the host star and the system's architecture.

"The distinct architectural properties of the high- and lower-mass families of multi-planet systems and their connections to different stellar properties show the importance of accounting for the starâplanet genetic link instead of adopting the Sun and the Solar System as universal templates," the researchers write in their conclusion.

âThe fundamental question we started from was: what determines the characteristics of planetary systems as we see them today? Are they established at birth or sculpted by evolution over time? The truth, in the end, turned out to lie somewhere in the middle,â Turrini explained in a press release. âOur results show that there is a genetic link between planetary systems and their stars, and that, depending on the star around which they are born, this link also determines their fate.â

#189. A Man Took a Hidden Prayer to Jesus to His Grave—It Could Rewrite Christianity’s Origin Story

A silver scroll buried near Rome’s frontier hints at a faith with surprisingly blurry boundaries.

Nearly 1,800 years ago in Nida, a Roman town in what’s now Frankfurt, Germany, a man was buried with a small silver capsule around his neck. Inside it was a rolled silver sheet containing a text that asked “Jesus Christ, Son of God” to protect him from attacks and illness.

In 2018, that man’s skeleton and amulet were discovered by archaeologists in an ancient Roman cemetery in Frankfurt’s Praunheim district. Six years later, in 2024, CT scans allowed researchers to read the brittle silver scroll without unrolling it. The inscription provided rare proof that the Christian faith had reached this part of Roman Germany by the third century C.E., decades before the other surviving evidence of Christianity’s arrival in the region.

But Santiago Guijarro, an early Christianity scholar at the Universidad Pontificia de Salamanca, thinks the man’s relationship with those words deserves more attention. What if he trusted Jesus to protect him while also taking part in the sacrifices Rome demanded?

The question matters because the amulet points to a kind of believer the written record was never designed to capture: someone who used Christian prayers while living in ways church leaders condemned. Our picture of the early church comes largely from bishops, who counted believers only when they conformed. How many people vanished from a history that recognized Christians only when they followed the rules?

Around 250 C.E., Emperor Decius imposed an empire-wide requirement to sacrifice to the Roman gods. For someone loosely connected to a Christian community, Guijarro says, “It is not obvious that such a person would have understood compliance with the imperial order as a betrayal of anything.”

Frankfurt’s Archaeological Museum dates the grave to 230–260 C.E. based on the age of a clay jug and incense burner buried with the man. He could have died before Decius issued his order, or lived through the persecution that followed. There’s no way to tell whether he was ever asked to sacrifice—but other Christians demonstrably faced that choice during the same period, which is why Guijarro considers the scenario plausible.

The proof is documentary. Papyri found in Egypt preserve statements signed by officials confirming that they’d witnessed sacrifices. Some Christians went through with the ritual despite their beliefs, while others found ways to obtain the paperwork without sacrificing at all.

Sacrifice was part of religious life in the man’s own town, too. Goethe University’s January 2026 announcement of funding to study Nida’s large sanctuary describes animal and plant remains interpreted as offerings and ritual meals, along with a dedication to a god dated 246 C.E. The complex served worshippers of several deities, including Jupiter and Apollo.

What happened afterward shows how unsettled the question was. Some Christians who sacrificed later wanted to return to their congregations, and bishops were forced to decide if and how to take them back. Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage, argued that these lapsi, or “lapsed” Christians, shouldn’t all be treated alike. In his letters, he asked whether a person had sacrificed willingly or given in under pressure, and he distinguished between performing the sacrifice and obtaining a certificate without really doing it. Guijarro points to those disputes as evidence that Christian belief and public compliance could coexist.

The amulet extends that possibility past the edges of any congregation. Someone only loosely attached to a community might have worn Christ’s name while making the required sacrifice, never sharing a bishop’s understanding of what that act meant.

“In the third century, the boundaries of what we call Christianity were considerably more porous than later ecclesiastical literature suggests,” Guijarro says.

The inscription itself seems, at first, to argue against that reading. Its 18 lines name Jesus, repeat “holy, holy, holy,” and draw on Philippians 2:10–11, where every knee bows before Jesus. And unlike many ancient protective texts, it contains no identifiable appeal to pagan gods alongside the Christian language.

But the person who wrote that prayer may have believed things its wearer didn’t, Guijarro contends. “The content tells us about the person who composed or wrote the text; it tells us rather less about the person who wore it,” he says. The man might have belonged to a Christian community, or he might have received the object as a gift from a Christian without being one himself.

That distinction could change how archaeologists read future discoveries. A Christian inscription establishes that Christian words reached a place; it takes separate evidence to establish that the person holding them thought of himself as Christian. Guijarro’s argument is that the second question has too often been answered by assuming the first.

Guijarro wrote about the amulet in a 2025 paper in Isidorianum. He observes that no older object or manuscript preserved these verses from Paul’s Letter to the Philippians in Latin. The remarkable part, he says, is where the text turned up: “not in a scriptorium or a library but rolled inside a capsule worn around the neck of a man buried on the frontier of the empire.”

One detail still resists explanation. The opening words of the inscription have been read as a reference to Saint Titus, one of Paul’s collaborators—a reading Guijarro calls “frankly, puzzling,” because the known traditions honoring Titus as a saint come much later. He hasn’t found a better explanation, so he’s leaving the question open until the inscription gets a closer look.

Even the choice of metal carried meaning. In the ancient world, silver was used for protection, while curses were typically written on lead. Whoever made this object understood what it was for: people across the empire wore amulets hoping to be shielded from illness and danger.

Church authorities eventually tried to stop them. A late antique canon attributed to the Council of Laodicea prohibited clergy from making amulets and ordered the exclusion of anyone who wore one. That the ban targeted clergy rather than outsiders tells Guijarro the practice had already taken hold inside the church—though the canon comes more than a century after the Frankfurt man’s burial, which leaves the question of who supplied his amulet unanswered.

It also suggests where people like him learned their prayers. Some may have picked up Christian language from whoever made their amulets, perhaps even a priest. If they were sick, they may have wanted something to help them get better without asking what else the church expected of them.

That is the gap more discoveries could close. If other third-century examples emerge, their inscriptions could reveal which prayers people shared and how they altered them, and their burial contexts could suggest who received them—showing how Christian practices spread among people who left no written account of what they believed.

For the Frankfurt man, we have only the words he wore. His amulet asks Christ for protection, but he might never have thought that praying to Jesus ruled out sacrificing to Rome’s gods. Whether he ever had to choose is lost. Guijarro’s point is that someone who did both still deserves a place in that history.

“Recovering that plurality does not weaken our understanding of early Christianity,” he says. “It makes it more honest.”

#190. What Kills Schrödinger’s Cat? Scientists Just Ruled Out a 60-Year-Old Theory

Gravity has been proposed as a reason quantum superpositions become difficult to observe in everyday objects. A new experiment challenges one longstanding model of this process.

A detector buried deep beneath an Italian mountain has challenged a decades-old theory about why quantum behavior disappears from the world we experience. After 62 days of measurements, researchers found no trace of the faint radiation predicted by a model in which gravity disrupts quantum states. The result rules out this particular explanation while leaving open the possibility that gravity contributes to quantum decoherence.

Decoherence helps explain why particles can display unusual quantum behavior, such as existing in superpositions of different states, while everyday objects appear to follow classical physics. “One of the deepest questions in modern physics is why the strange quantum behavior that governs atoms and elementary particles seems to disappear in the macroscopic world we experience every day,” says Catalina Curceanu, director of research and spokesperson for the VIP Collaboration at the National Laboratory of Frascati of the National Institute for Nuclear Physics (INFN-LNF) in Italy.

In the 1960s, Hungarian physicist Frigyes Károlyházy proposed that spacetime undergoes constant, extremely small fluctuations. According to his model, these disturbances gradually destroy quantum superpositions, preventing large objects from displaying effects such as those illustrated by Schrödinger’s famous thought experiment involving a cat that is both alive and dead.

The proposal connects quantum mechanics with Einstein’s general theory of relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. Although Károlyházy’s original idea dates back decades, it has continued to attract attention. FQxI researcher Angelo Bassi and his colleagues recently reformulated the model, allowing its predictions to be examined experimentally.

The hypothesized fluctuations cannot be measured directly, but they should have a detectable consequence. They would cause electrically charged particles to undergo tiny random accelerations, producing extremely weak electromagnetic radiation. Detecting that radiation, or establishing its absence, provides a way to test the theory.

The FQxI-funded experiment took place at the INFN Gran Sasso National Laboratory (INFN-LNGS), the world’s largest underground laboratory dedicated to fundamental physics research. Located beneath 1.4 kilometers (0.87 miles) of rock, the facility is shielded from much of the cosmic radiation that could otherwise overwhelm such a weak signal.

“The natural shielding provided by the rock creates one of the quietest environments on Earth for detecting extremely rare physical phenomena,” says Curceanu.

The researchers used a high-purity germanium crystal roughly the size of a coffee mug, enclosed within layers of copper and lead shielding. After collecting measurements for 62 days, they accounted for the expected background radiation and searched the remaining data for the signature predicted by Károlyházy’s model. They found no matching signal. The findings were published in the New Journal of Physics.

“This absence of a signal is itself a major scientific result,” says Curceanu. The measurements exclude the tested version of Károlyházy’s model, placing new constraints on explanations that attribute quantum decoherence to fluctuations in spacetime.

The findings do not establish that gravity has no role in decoherence. Other gravitational mechanisms remain possible, and the broader relationship between quantum mechanics and general relativity is unresolved. “By ruling out one of the oldest and most natural gravity-induced decoherence models, this work narrows the search for the theory describing the interplay between gravity and quantum mechanics, bringing us one step closer to understanding one of the deepest mysteries in fundamental physics,” says Curceanu.

Károlyházy’s proposal is based on the idea that nature imposes a fundamental limit on how precisely distances and positions can be measured. Related concepts appear in modern efforts to reconcile gravity with quantum mechanics, including string theory and loop quantum gravity. In these approaches, the familiar picture of perfectly measurable spacetime may break down at extremely small scales.

“Every quantum gravity approach ends up with predicting the existence of a minimal length connected to the uncertainty in the measurement of spacetime,” says Kristian Piscicchia, a quantum physicist at the Enrico Fermi Research Center/INFN/VIP in Italy and the experimental lead on the study. The new measurements do not establish whether such a minimum length exists, but they constrain one proposed physical consequence of spacetime uncertainty.

“Precision experiments are now reaching a level of sensitivity where they can test ideas that, until recently, belonged almost exclusively to the realm of theoretical speculation,” says Curceanu. “As sensitivity improves, the boundary between theory and measurement continues to move, opening new possibilities for discovering the fundamental principles that govern our universe.”

Reference: “Experimental exclusion of a generalized Károlyházy gravity-induced decoherence model” by Nicola Bortolotti, Kristian Piscicchia, Alessio Porcelli, Matthias Laubenstein, Simone Manti, Antonino Marcianò, Federico Nola and Catalina Curceanu, 19 June 2026, New Journal of Physics. DOI: 10.1088/1367-2630/ae774c

The research was supported by the Foundational Questions Institute, FQxI, through the Consciousness in the Physical World program.
