From the Costa del Sol to whitewashed mountain villages, here are 10 of the best places in southern Spain to experience the Aug. 2, 2027 total solar eclipse.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spain is one of the easiest places in the world to experience the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027. The so-called "eclipse of the century" first makes landfall in Andalucía, where totality will last up to 4 minutes and 40 seconds during mid-morning, with the sun comfortably high at around 38-42 degrees above the horizon in the eastern sky. Excellent roads, plentiful accommodation and Málaga's international airport make this an obvious alternative to North Africa and the Middle East.

However, choosing where to watch requires some thought. Southern Spain's narrowing shape funnels the path toward the Strait of Gibraltar, potentially concentrating huge numbers of eclipse chasers around Tarifa, the Costa del Sol and the British Overseas Territory of Gibraltar during the peak summer holiday season.

From busy Mediterranean beaches to mountain villages, here's where to see the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027 in southern Spain. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.

Start of totality and duration: 10:45 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 40 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

At the southernmost tip of mainland Europe, where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Mediterranean Sea, Tarifa is likely to be one of the country's busiest eclipse-watching locations because it will experience the longest totality in mainland Spain. Just 9 miles (14 km) across the Strait of Gibraltar from Morocco, the historic port town is known for its whitewashed old town, the medieval Castle of Guzmán el Bueno and its long, sandy beaches. Los Lances and Valdevaqueros offer wide horizons and plenty of open space.

Location: Málaga province, Andalucía, Spain

Start of totality and duration: 10:46 a.m. CEST; 3 minutes, 13 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

For eclipse chasers who would rather head into the mountains than join the crowds on the Costa del Sol, Gaucín is an intriguing alternative. One of Andalucía's classic pueblos blancos, the whitewashed village occupies a spectacular position in the mountains above the coast, crowned by the ruins of Castillo del Águila. Its elevated setting offers sweeping views across the surrounding countryside towards Gibraltar and, on clear days, the mountains of North Africa. Crucially, heading inland doesn't sacrifice too much totality.

Start of totality and duration: 10:45 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 29 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

Few places in Europe could provide a more dramatic setting for totality than Gibraltar, the tiny British Overseas Territory dominated by its famous 1,398-foot (426-meter) limestone Rock. However, eclipse chasers will need to view either from The Rock or its east coast, where elevated viewpoints and beaches face the Mediterranean and the eclipsed sun. However, Gibraltar has a potential complication — the easterly Levanter wind can create a distinctive cap of cloud over the Rock even when surrounding skies are clear. Another issue is accommodation, which is already at a premium. See Gibraltar Eclipse 2027.

Start of totality and duration: 10:45 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 24 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

Immediately north of Gibraltar, La Línea de la Concepción occupies the sandy isthmus between the Bay of Gibraltar and the Mediterranean Sea. Its location creates one of Spain's most distinctive possibilities for eclipse photography. On the Mediterranean side, Playa de Santa Bárbara is a wide sandy beach north of the border, with the immense Rock of Gibraltar rising to the south — a potentially spectacular foreground. The city has around 9 miles (14 kilometers) of coastline, providing plenty of alternatives for eclipse viewing.

Start of totality and duration: 10:46 a.m. CEST; 3 minutes, 41 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

About an hour's drive southwest of Málaga Airport, Estepona is one of the Costa del Sol's most attractive resort towns, with a pedestrianized old quarter of whitewashed streets, colorful flowerpots and squares centered on Plaza de las Flores. For eclipse day, the mile-long Playa de la Rada is the obvious gathering place, with its broad Mediterranean horizon and proximity to the town center. Other attractions include Estepona Marina and the Sierra Bermeja mountains rising behind the coast.

Start of totality and duration: 10:45 a.m. CEST; 2 minutes, 56 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 37 degrees above east

Historic Cádiz occupies a narrow peninsula jutting into the Atlantic and is packed with reminders of its long maritime past, including the Cádiz Cathedral, the Roman Theatre and Torre Tavira, one of more than 100 watchtowers once used to spot approaching ships. For eclipse day, the long, sandy Playa de la Victoria offers plenty of open space, while La Caleta provides a more historic setting between two coastal castles.

Start of totality and duration: 10:48 a.m. CEST; 2 minutes

Altitude of the sun: 39 degrees above east

Málaga may lose some duration compared with locations farther west, but it makes up for it with excellent transport links, plentiful accommodation and all the attractions of a major Mediterranean city. It combines the hilltop Gibralfaro Castle and Moorish Alcazaba with a Roman theatre, cathedral, museums and a lively historic center. For eclipse day, the obvious option is the coast. La Malagueta beach is within walking distance of the city center, while numerous beaches extend east and west along the Costa del Sol.

Start of totality and duration: 10:47 a.m. CEST; 2 minutes, 46 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 39 degrees above east

One of the best-known resorts on Spain's Costa del Sol, Torremolinos combines a long Mediterranean beachfront with easy access to Málaga and its international airport. Its 4-mile (6-kilometer) promenade links broad sandy beaches, including Playa del Bajondillo and Playa de la Carihuela, offering plenty of potential eclipse-watching spots with views toward the eastern sky. For a higher vantage point, nearby Mount Calamorro rises almost 2,600 feet (800 meters) above Benalmádena, with panoramic views across the Costa del Sol and, on clear days, towards Gibraltar and North Africa.

Start of totality and duration: 10:46 a.m. CEST; 3 minutes, 21 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 38 degrees above east

Marbella has around 17 miles (27 kilometers) of Mediterranean coastline, so eclipse chasers will have dozens of beaches to choose from, from San Pedro de Alcántara in the west to Cabopino in the east. Options include the sandy beaches and dunes around Cabopino, Las Chapas, Puerto Banús and San Pedro de Alcántara, all with open views across the Mediterranean. Away from the beach, Marbella offers a whitewashed old town centered on Plaza de los Naranjos, while the Sierra Blanca mountains provide a dramatic backdrop to the resort.

Location: Costa Tropical, Granada province

Start of totality and duration: 10:49 a.m. CEST; 1 minute, 57 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 39 degrees above east

Close to the northern edge of the path of totality, Motril gets a shorter eclipse than destinations farther west, but could be among the quieter places on Spain's Mediterranean coast from which to experience it. The largest town on Granada's Costa Tropical sits between the Mediterranean and the foothills of the Sierra de Lújar, with the Sierra Nevada rising beyond. Nearby Playa Granada and Playa Poniente offer broad coastal views.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#192. Scientists who discovered a third form of magnetism win major physics prize

Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown form of magnetism, overturning an understanding of magnetic behavior that had stood for more than a century. The discovery, known as altermagnetism, has revealed a third fundamental category of collinear magnetism and opened new possibilities for quantum materials, advanced electronics, and future computing technologies.

Three physicists responsible for the breakthrough have been named recipients of the 2026 Europhysics Prize, one of Europe's most prestigious honors in condensed matter physics. The European Physical Society (EPS) Condensed Matter Division selected Professor Jairo Sinova of Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU), Dr. Libor Šmejkal, and Professor Tomas Jungwirth for their work establishing altermagnetism as a distinct form of magnetic order alongside ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.

"This award recognizes a fundamental discovery that challenged one of the most established paradigms in condensed matter physics," said Professor Jairo Sinova, Director of the Spin Phenomena Interdisciplinary Center (SPICE) at Mainz University. "Discovering that an entirely new magnetic phase had remained hidden for more than one hundred years demonstrates that even the most mature scientific fields can still hold fundamental surprises."

The breakthrough emerged from years of collaboration between Sinova's research group at Mainz University and Jungwirth's team at the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague. Šmejkal, who also maintained an affiliation in Prague, spent eight years at Mainz between 2016 and 2024, first pursuing doctoral research and later working as a postdoctoral scientist in Sinova's group.

During that period, Šmejkal played a leading role in developing the theoretical framework behind altermagnetism. By combining advanced mathematical approaches to symmetry with spintronics, which studies how electron spin can be used in electronic devices, the researchers identified a previously unrecognized pattern of magnetic behavior.

Their predictions soon attracted experimental teams around the world. Measurements of electronic properties and electrical transport in multiple materials provided evidence supporting the new magnetic classification. Altermagnetism has since grown into one of the most active areas of condensed matter physics, with research efforts expanding across Europe, North America, and Asia.

A Third Form of Magnetism Rewrites Physics

For more than 100 years, physicists generally divided collinear magnets into two fundamental categories: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets.

Ferromagnets have an overall magnetic alignment that produces a net magnetization. These materials are essential to many magnetic memory technologies used today. In conventional antiferromagnets, opposing magnetic moments cancel one another, leaving no overall magnetization and producing electronic behavior very different from that of ferromagnets.

Altermagnetism introduces a surprising third possibility.

Like antiferromagnets, altermagnets have magnetic moments that cancel out, resulting in no net magnetization. However, their electrons can exhibit properties previously associated with ferromagnets.

This unusual combination allows altermagnets to support electrical currents with strongly polarized electron spins while also displaying extremely rapid magnetic dynamics. Those characteristics could make them valuable for a new generation of spintronic devices, potentially advancing the speed and capabilities of future information technologies.

The significance extends well beyond electronics. Altermagnetism represents a previously unrecognized symmetry class of matter and has revealed unexpected connections to several major areas of modern physics, including topological phenomena, unconventional superconductivity, and quantum materials with strong interactions between electrons.

The path toward this discovery began with theoretical investigations into unusual ways that electricity moves through magnetic materials. Among the early advances was the prediction of the crystal anomalous Hall effect, a phenomenon involving electrical transport in certain crystal structures.

Initially, these unexpected behaviors might have appeared to be unusual features of individual materials. However, the researchers eventually recognized that they were connected by a broader principle involving symmetries of electron spins.

Rather than representing isolated exceptions to established magnetic behavior, these materials belonged to an entirely different magnetic category.

A major milestone came in 2022, when the team published a comprehensive symmetry classification of altermagnetism and identified hundreds of materials that could potentially exhibit it.

Experimental physicists subsequently tested these predictions using several complementary methods. These included angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), which reveals how electrons behave inside materials, along with measurements of electrical transport.

The results confirmed altermagnetic behavior in several materials, helping establish the new classification experimentally.

Interest in the discovery has expanded rapidly. Hundreds of scientific papers have appeared within just a few years, and altermagnetism has become a prominent subject at international physics conferences. The growing research community is now investigating both its fundamental properties and its potential technological applications.

Discovery Earns Prestigious 2026 Europhysics Prize

The Europhysics Prize recognizes major advances in condensed matter physics, a field concerned with the physical properties and behavior of materials. Established in 1975, the award honors discoveries that have significantly advanced scientific understanding, with a substantial share of the recognized research conducted in Europe.

The 2026 prize recognizes the theoretical and experimental advances that established altermagnetism as a new fundamental form of collinear magnetic order.

The award ceremony was scheduled for September 2026 at the 32nd General Conference of the European Physical Society Condensed Matter Division (CMD32) in Graz, Austria.

Professor Jairo Sinova is a physics professor at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz in Germany and director of the university's Spin Phenomena Interdisciplinary Center. His research investigates magnetism, spintronics, and quantum materials.

Dr. Libor Šmejkal conducted much of the crucial theoretical work that led to the identification of altermagnetism while working at Mainz University from 2016 to 2024. His current affiliations include the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems, the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids, and the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences.

Professor Tomas Jungwirth is affiliated with the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences and the University of Nottingham. He has collaborated extensively with Sinova's Mainz research team and played a central role in establishing the theoretical foundations of altermagnetism.

Together, their work has revealed a fundamental property of magnetic matter that escaped recognition for more than a century, opening an entirely new direction for research into quantum physics and future electronic technologies.

Materials provided by Johannes Gutenberg Universitaet Mainz. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Atoms confined to a single line can bind into clusters called Bethe strings. A new experiment points to a mix of many such clusters, though the evidence is still indirect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Necklaces" of ultracold atoms have provided new evidence to support a nearly 100-year-old quantum theory.

In 1931, physicists were trying to use quantum mechanics to explain why some materials are magnetic. Then, a young physicist named Hans Bethe looked at a single row of electrons. Each electron's spin can point up or down. Bethe worked out the math for how such a row behaves and found that if a few spins in the row flip, they can stick together and travel down the row as a single unit.

Decades later, physicists found that Bethe's method also works for larger particles moving along a line, such as atoms. If those particles attract each other, the math predicts they will bind into clusters called Bethe strings.

Now, physicists have found evidence of these clusters in a line of ultracold atoms. The findings were published Aug. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The discovery may not create new gadgets, but it addresses a fundamental mystery in physics. Everything around us, from magnets to phone chips, consists of countless interacting particles. This makes their behavior difficult to predict. Ultracold atoms serve as a clear and adjustable way to study these complex systems.

Researchers have spotted small Bethe strings before, in magnetic crystals and superconducting quantum circuits ‪— but those experiments captured strings one at a time.

Theory predicts that crowds of strings, in many sizes, can change how an entire system behaves, and studying that idea requires making many strings at once. That has been hard to do with atoms. Atoms that attract each other usually collapse into a clump. But this time, the team appears to have made many strings of different sizes at once, including some with more than six atoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To make the "necklace" the researchers had to create a Bose-Einstein condensate, a special phase of matter.

It's tricky to get atoms to attract each other. In three dimensions, a gas made of attracting atoms tends to collapse as the atoms clump together and form molecules. That process releases energy that kicks atoms out of the experiment, so the gas quickly collapses and disappears. But when they're in a single line, the atoms behave differently.

"They are really a bit like pearls on a string, right? Like on a necklace, they cannot go past," study co-author Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, an experimental physicist at the University of Innsbruck, told Live Science. "In 3D, everything would collapse. But in 1D, it does not collapse."

To build their "necklaces," the team started with tens of thousands of cesium atoms cooled into a Bose-Einstein condensate ‪— a state of matter in which atoms chilled to near absolute zero share a single quantum state. Laser beams then divided the condensate into thousands of thin tubes, each of which held up to a few dozen atoms in a line.

At first, the atoms repelled each other. The researchers used a magnetic field to gradually turn that repulsion down to zero, and then turned it into attraction.

The team couldn't see the strings directly. Instead, they let the atoms go and measured how fast the cloud spread. When the atoms could expand only along their tubes, any strings stayed intact. When the atoms were freed in all three dimensions, the strings broke apart and released their binding energy as motion. The researchers found that the 3D clouds spread with about three times as much energy as the one-dimensional ones did.

From that difference, the team estimated how tightly the atoms had been bound. The answer pointed to strings of at least six atoms. The measurements also closely matched predictions from a theory called generalized hydrodynamics, which describes a gas like this one as a fluid made of many kinds of particles, including strings of different sizes. It also tracks how each kind flows over time rather than following every atom.

Nägerl was careful not to call this proof. "That some theory fits to your data is not a proof that something exists," he said; it's just more evidence to support it.

The strings likely don't survive long. Up close, the atoms still feel the three-dimensional world, and the strings eventually decay into ordinary cesium molecules. In the coldest runs, the team lost about 40% of the atoms.

"Transiently you create these Bethe string states," Nägerl said. "But I don't think they are long-lived."

He has an idea for future experiments. Physicists recently learned to shield ultracold molecules with microwaves, which keeps the molecules from colliding at close range. Strings made from shielded molecules might last long enough to be studied directly. But Nägerl stressed that the idea is untested. "I've had nobody do a theory check on my claims now, but I think intuitively this should work," he said.

Another option is quantum gas microscopy, which images atoms one at a time and could offer more direct evidence of individual strings.

For Nägerl, Bethe strings are one step in understanding how quantum systems with many particles behave and settle down over time. His long-term goal is an experiment in which physicists control both how every particle moves and how its spin flips, letting them assemble model materials piece by piece, "like a LEGO type," he said. His team has begun the next step: using lasers to control the spins of the atoms in its one-dimensional gas. He described Bethe strings as "a little diversion." But because the strings form whenever the atoms attract, they can't be ignored.

#195. How the Grand Canyon could have lost 1 billion years of geologic history

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The rise and fall of a massive cliff could help solve the mystery, a new study suggests

A rainbow arcs over this view of the Grand Canyon from Hopi Point. A new study proposes that the basement rocks — the oldest, lowermost units exposed in the canyon — were brought to the surface by erosion along an ancient mega-escarpment.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In the Grand Canyon, rock layers preserve a relatively continuous record of Earth’s geologic history going back about 2 billion years. But between 520 million and 1.8 billion years, the record is noticeably empty. It’s as if someone broke into a museum and made off with almost an entire wing’s worth of rocks, and sorting out “whodunnit” is one of the coldest cases in all geology.

Now, scientists studying the Grand Canyon’s rocks say that a gigantic Earth-spanning cliff  —with a global glaciation as its accomplice — could be to blame for the heist.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The giant cliff started forming about 800 million years ago as an ancient supercontinent called Rodinia split apart, Thomas Gernon, an earth scientist at the University of Southampton in England, and colleagues report August 17 in Geology. Forces like rain and ice weathered and eroded the rock and, like waves at the beach steadily erasing one layer of sand after another, deleted a billion years of Earth’s history.

The group used computer models to simulate how ancient Earth evolved over hundreds of millions of years. They watched as the cliff — known as an escarpment — formed around the time in Earth’s history when rocks in the region vanished.

The escarpment most likely extended across much of a continent called Laurentia, the ancient precursor to North America. It stretched from what was to become Alaska all the way to Arizona and would have been about one to two kilometers high.

Some 65 million years ago, the Great Escarpment of Laurentia would have stretched across much of North America, including the spot that would one day become the Grand Canyon and the site of an enduring geologic mystery. The escarpment itself is thought to have formed around 800 million years ago.

“No study has previously suggested the existence of a continental-scale escarpment in the Grand Canyon region. Our study shows it’s a plausible, straightforward explanation for the immense erosion that took place in the Grand Canyon,” Gernon says. Such an immense cliff created steep slopes that were ideal places for the elements to loosen and make off with exposed rock.

And the escarpment had a lot of help when it came to its disappearing act: ice, lots and lots of ice. The theft of the rocks coincided with an extreme period of glaciation called Snowball Earth. Massive ice sheets formed and may have extended all the way from the poles to equatorial latitudes. As the ice expanded, it would have eroded great quantities of rock, helping create the gap in the record.

And the escarpment, due to its high elevation, would have created ideal conditions for Snowball Earth glaciers and ice sheets to form. In a separate study published in Science, Gernon and a team explained how an escarpment created by tectonic activity was responsible for the formation of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet starting some 34 million years ago. “The exposed rocky peaks of the escarpment would have acted as glacier factories,” Gernon says.

It remains unclear, however, whether the erosion that erased the rocks occurred before, during or after the Snowball Earth glaciations. “That’s the real hole that needs filling: pinning down the erosion history in space and time, continent by continent, precisely enough,” Gernon says.

Linking the disappearance of the rocks to verified events in Earth’s history such as the breakup of Rodinia bolsters the case, says Alan Collins, a geologist at Adelaide University in Australia who was not involved in the new study. Not only that, but Gernon’s team points to modern-day examples where similar erosive processes are at work, including a similar escarpment in Antarctica as well as one in South Africa.

Maybe not quite case closed yet, but “I find this very convincing,” Collins says.

#196. Orionid, Taurid Meteors Haunt October Skies

Two annual meteor streams offer good cause to watch the sky in October.

Fall meteor season has begun. Late October not only sees dusk falling ever earlier as ghouls and goblins walk the Earth on Halloween, but it also sees the peak of two fine annual meteor showers kicking off Halloween season: the Orionid and Taurid meteor showers.

The Orionids always make the top of the dozen or so annual meteor showers worth watching for. The source of the Orionids is that most famous of all periodic comets, 1P/Halley. On a 75 year orbit, Halley just reached aphelion over 35 Astronomical Units from the Sun out beyond the orbit of Neptune on December 9th, 2023. Halleyâs Comet is actually the source of a second annual meteor shower, the springtime Eta Aquariids. Halleyâs Comet now begins its long plunge sunward towards its next perihelion apparition in 2061.

Halley's Comet, imaged from Arequipa Observatory in Peru in 1910. Credit: Public Domain.

In 2026, the Orionids are expected to top out at a Zenithal Hourly Rate (ZHR) of 20 meteors per hour. Jupiter seems to play a role in modifying the Orionid meteor stream, and we tend to see an enhanced uptick from the shower about mid-decade or so, as last occurred in 2006. The expected peak for the shower arrives around October 21st, but the shower is also active for most of the last half of October.

The orbit of Halley's Comet, plus its position in 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL

If you can trace a meteor back to the club of Orion the Hunter and its junction with Gemini the Twins, then youâve probably caught sight of an Orionid.

The Orionid, Taurid and antihelion source radiants in the sky. Credit: Stellarium

In 2026, the Moon is waxing gibbous at the Orionids' peak, just 5 days prior to the Full Hunterâs Moon on October 26th.

âOctober-November is my favorite time for meteor observing,â astrophotographer Eliot Herman told Universe Today. âWhile the Geminids can be great for one night (and) the Orionids and Taurids are not as prolific, the Orionids are scattered over days and the Taurids continue for weeks, often with bright fireballs. In addition, there are several other meteor showers occurring in the same time frame (the November Leonids and the Draconids). While none of these are major showers, together, this period brings together many opportunities to see meteors of differing colors, brightness, and sources.â

Next up, the Taurid meteor stream is active in late October into November. These are the notorious âHalloween Fireballsâ which often light up social media as late Fall nights draw pedestrian skywatchers out after hours. The source of the Taurids is the second periodic comet on the tally, 2P/Encke. This comet also has the distinction of having the shortest known orbit of just 3.3 years.

Clearly, thereâs something intriguing about the complex debris stream from Comet Encke. While the Taurids barely top a ZHR of 5 on most years barely above the background sporadic rate, they are also a prodigious producer of fireballs. Taurids are also slow movers, approaching the Earth from behind and frequently leaving long, stately trains across the sky.

The morphology of a 2022 Taurid fireball. Credit: Frankie Lucena

2P/Encke reaches perihelion in just a few months on February 10th 2027, so we could be due for an enhanced showing from the northern and southern Taurids this year. Note that in late October, the antihelion source where many sporadics hail from is nearby along the ecliptic plane in the constellation Aries the Ram, while the Northern Taurid radiant drifts from Taurus into Aries, and the Southern Taurid point source lies nearby in Cetus the Whale.

Meteor watching requires nothing more than a set of working 'Mk-1 eyeballs' and patience. A camera with a wide-angle lens equipped with an intervalometer can automate the meteor capturing process, leaving you free to watch the sky.

Itâs great to see these ghostly remnants of Halleyâs and other forgotten comets of yore silently piercing the night. Be sure to watch for October meteors, and ponder the returns of two historic comets.

#197. Quantum Computing Breakthrough Opens a New Path to Larger, More Powerful Processors

Keeping silicon quantum bits accurate while they work together could help turn established chipmaking technology into larger quantum computers capable of tackling increasingly complex problems.

The manufacturing technology behind everyday computer chips could help build larger quantum computers. Silicon spin qubits offer that possibility, but the precision they achieve on their own can slip when several are controlled at once.

Researchers from the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now demonstrated a way to preserve much of that precision during simultaneous operation. Working with five silicon qubits controlled through a single shared microwave line, they identified a major source of control errors and developed a calibration protocol to compensate for it. Their study was published in Nature Physics.

Quantum bits, or qubits, represent combinations of the conventional binary states 0 and 1. In silicon spin qubits, information is encoded in the spin of an electron trapped in a silicon substrate. Microwave signals manipulate those spins to carry out quantum operations. A useful quantum computer must perform many such operations simultaneously, making reliable parallel control essential.

The team’s optimized device design and carefully calibrated microwave pulses produced single-qubit gate fidelities well above 99.99% on each of the five qubits when tested individually, with the best approaching 99.999%. Fidelity measures how accurately a quantum operation is performed. With the new protocol, fidelities stayed above 99.99% when up to three qubits operated at the same time.

“This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors,” says Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments.

When all five qubits operated simultaneously, fidelities remained at approximately 99.9%, close to the practical requirements of fault-tolerant quantum computing, which is designed to keep computations reliable despite errors.

“Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal,” says Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST’s Moonshot Goal 6.

The researchers traced a major source of the accuracy loss during parallel operation to the AC Stark shift, an effect induced by the microwave control signals. It changes a qubit’s effective energy levels and shifts the phase of its quantum state. Phase describes how the wave-like components of that state line up with one another. These unwanted shifts interfere with the control needed to perform the intended operation.

Correcting those shifts required a calibration method that could accommodate more qubits without separately testing every possible combination. Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author, who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research, explains how the team approached that challenge. “Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts.”

“By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration,” says Camenzind, “our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon’s compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations.”

The remaining loss of accuracy was attributed to drive-induced decoherence caused by the increased microwave power needed for simultaneous operation. This involves a loss of quantum coherence, distinct from the phase shifts addressed by the calibration protocol. “This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error,” says Camenzind.

Reference: “Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array” by Yi-Hsien Wu, Leon C. Camenzind, Patrick Bütler, Ik Kyeong Jin, Akito Noiri, Kenta Takeda, Takashi Nakajima, Takashi Kobayashi, Giordano Scappucci, Hsi-Sheng Goan and Seigo Tarucha, 15 October 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03466-2

Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.Follow us on Google and Google News.

While the research team at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science, in collaboration with National Taiwan University, ETH Zurich, and TU Delft (Nature Physics, Wu, Camenzind et al.), makes valuable strides in mathematically compensating for AC-Stark shifts using pairwise phase calibrations along a shared microwave line, the underlying bottleneck remains structural: driving spin states with transverse microwave pulses inherently induces drive-induced decoherence and field bleed.

Rather than relying on software calibration to constantly correct the software artifacts of an interfering electromagnetic grid, a physical hardware alternative lies in straight-line directional propagation coupled with localized strain tuning. By routing incoming and outbound information along a uniserial waveguide and modulating individual qubit resonance through piezoelectrically tuned mechanical stress (tension, torque, or compression), physical stress replaces orthogonal field crossings.

Combining the strain-tuning hardware insights from piezoelectric quantum-control groups with the multi-qubit silicon platforms developed across RIKEN, NTU, ETH Zurich, and TU Delft could help eliminate drive-induced decoherence entirely at the hardware layer—offering a clean pathway toward scalable, low-power silicon spin architectures. #198. Kodak Ran a Secret Nuclear Device in Its Basement for Decades. It Was a Scientific Marvel.

In the middle of the Cold War, the film company found a surprising way to harness weapons-grade uranium.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

In a secured Rochester, New York, office basement, a nuclear device the size of a fridge spent three decades quietly firing off neutrons for Eastman Kodak without a fuss. But after it was shut down and shipped away, an employee mentioned it to a reporter. Word spread, alarms rang in newsrooms, and even CNN jumped in to cover the story: Kodak had been using weapons-grade uranium in the bowels of its labyrinthine research labs.

But the truth about the reactor was stranger, and tamer, than the headlines suggested.

In 1975, Kodak powered up the country’s first californium neutron flux multiplier (CFX). Though it couldn’t live up to the sci-fi-tinged promise of its name, it leveraged a neat trick of nuclear engineering to provide Kodak R&D with an ample stream of neutrons for materials analysis.

The CFX served two purposes: neutron activation analysis and neutron radiography. The former allowed Kodak to test chemicals for impurities. By bombarding a sample with neutrons, its elements formed radioactive isotopes emitting gamma rays. Researchers could measure the energy levels of the gamma rays to identify exactly what constituted the sample.

The analysis was convenient to have on hand, but the neutron radiography was a superpower for a private company. Though it operates similarly to an X-ray, neutrons interact with nuclei and X-rays interact with electrons. That means while X-rays are powerful tools for examining heavy elements with an abundance of electrons, lighter elements and compounds, like water or film, get washed out in images. Not so with neutrons. If an X-ray shows you the crack in a pipe, neutrons will show you the leak.

The truly impressive part was how Kodak’s machine achieved its stream of neutrons. It harnessed the spontaneous fission of californium-252 (CF-252). The lab-made isotope sheds neutrons like a husky shakes off fur in July. However, this fountain of neutrons was too expensive to be the sole source (today it goes for about $30,000 per milligram). So the CFX’s designers looked to a fission standard: highly enriched uranium (HEU).

Neutrons would trickle out of the tiny CF-252 source—about 3.1 milligrams in the device’s core—and pass through 52 plates of highly enriched uranium. Behind lead shielding, the neutrons slammed into the HEU atoms to produce unstable nuclei. These often, but not always, broke apart into lighter fragments while also releasing two or three more neutrons. By the time the stream reached the sample port, the flux was up to 30 times greater than from the CF-252 alone.

This might appear alarmingly similar to a nuclear reactor at first glance: uranium fuel plates, fission neutrons, heavy shielding. The crucial difference is that the CFX was deliberately engineered to remain subcritical so that each fission produced fewer neutrons than needed to sustain a chain reaction. Without the CF-252 feeding it, the process peters out.

From 1975 to 2006, the CFX chugged along within its two-foot-thick walls and government-approved security protocols. Roughly every seven years, the CF-252 source was replenished. And aside from a license renewal snafu in 1980, the device made no waves until its existence was shared with the local newspaper—it wasn’t a secret, just unpublicized.

Unsurprisingly, when news of Kodak’s CFX went nationwide in 2012, most outlets focused on the dangers of HEU instead of its prowess for generating neutron flux. Indeed, it’s difficult to imagine trusting private corporations with the stuff atomic bombs are made of today. But the CFX was installed at a time of nuclear optimism where it was standard for top-tier universities to run reactors and ambitious companies sought to harness nuclear power.

Within its bunker, the CFX was a tightly-regulated non-threat according to Kodak and officials. The greatest danger came in the 2007 decommissioning. An old CFX is the industrial lab equivalent of an asbestos-wrapped pipe in your basement. It’s perfectly safe until you decide to remove it.

While the CF-252 component weighed about the same as a snowflake, the HEU was a more substantial 3.5 pounds. And though it takes roughly 100 pounds of it to build an atomic bomb, the fear is that bad actors would wrangle up enough small lots to create a weapon. Under the scrutiny of the Department of Energy, the plates were carefully transported to a government facility. As a testament to the security involved, no public records state who exactly moved the plates, or how they moved them beyond the safety protocols using tongs and shields made of plexiglass—which is surprisingly adept at slowing neutrons and HEU’s alpha radiation.

The real story of Kodak’s flux multiplier is less a conspiracy than a technical curiosity. It was an ingenious bit of Cold War-era engineering subject to stringent government oversight tucked under a corporate campus. The building has since been sold off by Kodak and the room long ago declared safe despite a few isotopes activated in the concrete. But it’s a reminder that the bleeding edge of technology once was radioactive.

#199. Scientists discover a natural compound that could protect the brain from too much salt

Consuming too much salt can affect more than blood pressure. Growing evidence suggests that excessive salt intake may also interfere with memory, thinking, and emotional well-being. High salt (HS) consumption is already a major public health concern because of its connection to hypertension, but its potential effects on the brain make finding ways to reduce the damage even more important.

Researchers in Japan have identified a promising possibility in LPC70, a compound derived from soy. Previous research found that this ingredient could reduce high blood pressure and cognitive problems associated with a high-salt diet (HSD) in mice. The latest study takes a closer look at how it works, revealing that the compound influences important chemical signals in the brain and kidneys.

How a Soy Compound May Counter the Effects of Excess Salt

The research centers on prostaglandins (PGs), signaling molecules made from a fatty acid called arachidonic acid (AA). These substances act much like local hormones, helping regulate essential functions throughout the body.

In the cardiovascular system, prostaglandins help control blood pressure by balancing the widening and narrowing of blood vessels. Their effects in the brain are more complicated. Depending on which receptors they activate, they can trigger signals that either protect nerve cells or contribute to harmful processes, potentially affecting memory, thinking, and emotional responses.

LPC70 is a form of soy lysolecithin in which lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) accounts for more than 70% of the phospholipids. Although earlier experiments showed that LPC70 could ease salt-related hypertension and cognitive difficulties, scientists had not fully understood the mechanisms responsible, particularly its influence on prostaglandin signaling.

To investigate, a research team led by Professor Akihiro Mouri and Dr. Hisayoshi Kubota, working with Dr. Kazuhiro Kagotani, examined how LPC70 affected these signaling pathways in mice consuming a high-salt diet.

Dr. Kubota, the study's first author, played a central role in the experiments. He assessed blood pressure, monitored behavioral changes, and analyzed molecular activity associated with prostaglandins. His work helped clarify how LPC70 produces different effects in the organs involved in salt-related cardiovascular and cognitive problems.

Prof. Mouri and Dr. Kubota are affiliated with the Department of Regulatory Science for Evaluation and Development of Pharmaceuticals & Devices at Fujita Health University Graduate School of Medical Science, as well as the International Center for Brain Science (ICBS) at Fujita Health University in Japan. Dr. Kagotani is affiliated with Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd, in Japan and the Tsuji Health and Beauty Science Laboratory at Mie University, Japan.

The findings were released online on May 14, 2026, and published in Volume 197 of Neurochemistry International on July 1, 2026.

"We wanted to understand the role of LPC70 in coordinating changes in PG signaling across organ systems," mentioned Prof. Mouri. "Our study originated from a collaborative research project with Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd, a company that develops naturally derived food ingredients," he added.

Soy Compound Improves Blood Pressure and Memory in Mice

As expected, mice that consumed a high-salt diet developed elevated blood pressure. However, the consequences extended beyond their cardiovascular health.

The animals also became less socially interactive and had difficulty recognizing objects they had encountered before, indicating problems with memory. Interestingly, their general movement and anxiety-like behavior showed no substantial changes. This pattern suggests that excessive salt selectively disrupted more complex cognitive and social functions rather than causing widespread behavioral impairment.

When researchers supplemented the animals' diets with LPC70, several of these effects were reduced. Blood pressure improved, and the mice performed better on tests of social interaction and object recognition memory.

These improvements prompted the researchers to examine what was happening inside the animals' kidneys and brains.

Different Protective Effects in the Kidneys and Brain

In the kidneys, a high-salt diet increased the expression of two components involved in prostaglandin signaling: cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) and the PGE2 receptor EP3. Both may contribute to the development of high blood pressure associated with excessive salt consumption.

LPC70 reduced these salt-related increases, suggesting that the compound helps correct changes in kidney signaling that can interfere with normal blood pressure regulation.

The researchers found a different response in the prefrontal cortex, a brain region essential for thinking, memory, and social behavior.

Excess salt reduced the expression of the PGD2 receptor DP1, which plays a role in protective and anti-inflammatory signaling in the brain. LPC70 restored expression of this receptor without changing DP2, another receptor associated with potentially harmful effects on nerve cells.

This distinction is important because it suggests that LPC70 does not simply increase or suppress all prostaglandin activity. Instead, it may selectively favor signaling pathways that help protect the brain, potentially explaining the improvements in memory and social behavior observed in the mice.

A Surprising Change in Chemical Signaling

The team also discovered an unexpected change involving arachidonic acid, the fatty acid the body uses to produce prostaglandins.

Mice consuming excess salt had lower levels of circulating arachidonic acid. Yet when they received LPC70, levels of prostaglandins derived from this fatty acid, including PGE2 and PGD2, increased.

This seemingly contradictory result suggests that LPC70 may help the body use available arachidonic acid more efficiently to produce prostaglandins under high-salt conditions.

Taken together, the findings reveal a coordinated but highly selective response. In the kidneys, LPC70 appears to suppress signaling changes associated with hypertension. In the brain, it restores signaling linked to protection against inflammation and damage.

The compound's effects therefore depend on both the organ involved and the specific prostaglandin receptors being regulated.

Could Soy-Based Ingredients Help Protect Against Excess Salt?

The results suggest that LPC70 could eventually become a useful functional food ingredient for reducing some of the health consequences of excessive salt intake.

Its ability to improve blood pressure and cognitive performance in mice raises the possibility that it could support cardiovascular and brain health, particularly among people whose diets contain high amounts of salt.

However, the findings come from animal experiments, and further clinical studies are needed to determine whether the same benefits occur in humans.

"Our study elucidates LPC70's role in PG signaling, laying the groundwork for future clinical research and dietary interventions aimed at reducing hypertension-related cognitive decline and promoting healthy aging globally," concluded Prof. Mouri.

The research provides a clearer picture of how a soy-derived compound can influence the body's response to excessive salt, opening new possibilities for nutritional approaches to protecting long-term health.

The study received support through Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research from the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS: 20K07931, 22K07606, 22K11891, and 23H02843).

Additional support came from the Fujita Mind-Brain Research & Innovation Center for Drug Generation (Fujita Mind-BRIDGe) through Japan's Peak Research Universities (J-PEAKS) Program (JPJS00420240019), along with the Japan Science and Technology Agency FOREST Program (JPMJFR215H).

Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd. provided funding for the research. Grants and other support were also supplied by the Education and Research Facility of Animal Models for Human Diseases at Fujita Health University, the Smoking Research Foundation, and the Takeda Science Foundation.

TENERIFE, CANARY ISLANDS — The Artemis II astronauts may have traveled hundreds of thousands of miles away from Earth to the moon, but they made sure the rest of us didn't miss out on the adventure.

Now, their efforts to bring the wonders of space exploration back down to Earth have earned them one of science communication's most prestigious honors: the Stephen Hawking Medal.

NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Victor Glover, alongside Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, accepted the award on Saturday (Oct. 17), during the opening ceremony of the Starmus VIII festival. The honor recognizes all four crew members, including NASA astronaut Christina Koch, who wasn't in attendance.

For Wiseman, the experience of seeing our home planet from the vicinity of the moon carried a powerful message.

"If we could take each of you 250,000 miles away from this planet, 400,000 kilometers away from planet Earth, and you would see Earth the size of your thumb. It's tiny," Wiseman told the audience.

"When you're there looking through the moon, back at this tiny Earth, the only thing you feel is love, peace, hope, unity", he continued. "Those aren't the right words, but that is all you feel."

During their historic Artemis II mission, the astronauts did far more than put NASA's Orion spacecraft through its paces. Through live communications, interviews and glimpses into life aboard the spacecraft, not to mention the jaw-dropping photos that just keep on coming, they helped turn an extraordinarily complex mission into something people worldwide could experience and connect with.

And that's exactly what the Stephen Hawking Medal is designed to celebrate.

Established in 2016 by physicist Stephen Hawking and Starmus, the award honors those who have gone above and beyond to make science accessible, engaging and inspiring.

The Artemis II crew joins some pretty impressive company. Previous recipients include Apollo 11 moonwalker Buzz Aldrin, naturalist David Attenborough, primatologist Jane Goodall and astrophysicist Neil DeGrasse Tyson.

This year's ceremony marks the medal's 10th anniversary, with filmmaker Ridley Scott also among the 2026 honourees.

"It's a special thrill for us at Starmus to be able to honor the intrepid Artemis II crew members in the same way that we honored the Apollo astronauts who paved the way to the moon over 50 years ago," Starmus co-founder and Queen guitarist Brian May said in a statement ahead of the ceremony.

Wiseman left the audience with one final thought.

"When you come home to this beautiful planet, you realise that it's in every single one of us to choose to make tomorrow better," he said. "So let's all choose to make tomorrow better".

Starmus VIII runs from Oct. 17-22 across Tenerife and La Palma in the Canary Islands. This year's festival, themed "The Search for Truth", brings together leading scientists, astronauts, musicians and artists to celebrate scientific discovery and explore the importance of evidence and scientific thinking.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

The newly identified Invictibellatrix amberina lived about 120 million years ago and represents the first megaraptoran dinosaur found in Europe, according to a new study.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A fossil that sat in a museum collection for over a century is a previously unknown species of predatory dinosaur, researchers have found. The discovery could help scientists solve a longstanding mystery about how some of the Cretaceous period's most formidable hunters spread around the globe.

The dinosaur lived on what is now the Isle of Wight in southern England about 120 million years ago. It belonged to a group of two-legged carnivores called megaraptors, which are related to tyrannosaurs. But unlike tyrannousars, megaraptors are thought to have relied on their powerful arms and large curved claws to attack prey and defend themselves.

The newly identified species was described in an Oct. 14 study in the journal Royal Society Open Science. It is the first megaraptor identified in Europe, filling an important gap in the fossil record of a group whose evolutionary history remains poorly understood.

"It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years," study first author Cassius Morrison, a researcher in the Department of Earth Sciences at University College London (UCL) said in a statement. "Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight — who knows what else is waiting to be discovered."

The discovery of the megaraptor began in 1924, when an amateur fossil collector discovered a dinosaur skull fragment on the Isle of Wight. The specimen eventually entered the collections of London's Natural History Museum, but it was largely forgotten.

Recently, researchers revisited the fossil as part of a study on dinosaur braincases. To identify the animal, the researchers used micro-CT scanning to examine the fossil's internal structure and build detailed 3D digital models of the space that once held the dinosaur's brain.

The researchers then compared the animal's anatomy with that of other meat-eating dinosaurs, including tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs and other theropods (the group of two-legged, mostly meat-eating dinosaurs). Several features differentiated the unknown specimen, including an almost oval opening where the spinal cord entered the skull and an unusual, hourglass-shaped ridge at the back of the braincase.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The skull of the newly identified theropod dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina. The hole is where the brain would have sat.

Computer-based evolutionary analyses placed the fossils within the Megaraptora family tree, supporting the idea that the skull represented a never-before-seen species. The researchers named the dinosaur Invictibellatrix amberina, combining the Latin words "unconquered" and "female warrior" for the genus name, while amberina refers to amber found in the rocks associated with the fossil.

Megaraptors lived between roughly 125 million and 66 million years ago and varied considerably in size. While early members were relatively small, some later species became enormous predators. Maip macrothorax, discovered in Argentina, may have reached up to 33 feet (10 meters) long and weighed as much as an elephant. Based on comparisons with related dinosaurs, I. amberina was much smaller, likely around 10 to 13 feet (3 to 4 m) long and standing roughly 5 feet (1.5 m) tall. The researchers estimated it weighed around 440 to 660 pounds (200 to 300 kilograms), making it one of the smallest known megaraptors.

"It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex," Morrison said. "We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us."

Although the newly described fossil doesn't preserve the animal's arms or claws, its closest relative suggests that its claws may have measured around 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) long. The researchers also suggested I. amberina may have been feathered, though that feature can't be determined directly from the specimen.

Scientists have long suspected that megaraptors originated in Asia before spreading to other parts of the world, eventually becoming the dominant predators across the southern supercontinent Gondwana, which included present-day Africa, South America and Antarctica. But a lack of European fossils left an important gap in verifying this migration route.

The new study's evolutionary models suggest that I. amberina descended from Asian megaraptors that dispersed into Europe around 130 million years ago. From there, members of the group may have moved through what is now Africa and further into Gondwana via temporary landbridges and temporary land connections across the shallow Tethys Ocean.

"This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south," study co-author Charlie Scherer, a doctoral student at UCL Earth Sciences, said in the statement.

However, the specific route these animals took over millions of years is still unknown. The researchers also cannot yet explain why megaraptors disappeared from northern areas, but changes in climate or competition with other predatory dinosaurs may have contributed. More research on other megaraptor fossils like I. amberina could help uncover more clues.

"Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made," study co-author Paul Barrett, a researcher of dinosaur evolution at the Natural History Museum in London, said in the statement.

Morrison, Cassius., Scherer, Charlie R., Mannion, Philip., Porro, Laura B., Clark, Brett., Folkes, Daniel D, Barrett, Paul M.; A new megaraptoran dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous Wessex Formation, UK, and its implications for theropod evolution and biogeography. R. Soc. Open Sci. 1 October 2026; 13 (10): 260937. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.260937

#203. Scientists Discover Metals That Refuse To Crack at an Astonishing -424°F

Two experimental alloys resisted cracking at −424°F by forming new crystal defects, offering a possible route to tougher metals for extreme cold.

Most metals become stronger as they cool, but some also become more vulnerable to breaking. Iron, tungsten, and chromium belong to a class called body-centered cubic metals, whose atomic arrangement can make them increasingly brittle as temperatures fall. A crack that the metal might otherwise accommodate by bending or stretching can instead cause a fracture.

That ability to deform depends heavily on the movement of dislocations, line-like defects in the metal’s crystal structure. At low temperatures, these defects become harder to move, limiting how much the material can deform to relieve the forces building up around a crack.

Two experimental niobium-titanium-based alloys avoided this problem even at 20 kelvin, about −253°C (−424°F), by changing how they deform. An international team led by the University of California, Berkeley, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the University of Oxford found that the alloys remained remarkably resistant to cracking, with no measurable transition to brittle behavior at the lowest temperature tested. Their findings, published in Nature, reveal how the alloys create new opportunities for deformation when the usual mechanism becomes difficult.

To test the alloys under these conditions, the researchers used the Engin-X instrument at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source in Oxfordshire. They cooled samples with gaseous helium to around −253°C, then exposed them to a neutron beam while a testing machine pulled them from both ends. The tests precisely measured how much force the samples could withstand and how far they stretched before breaking.

Electron microscopes allowed the team to examine structural changes around cracks and inside the tested metal. The researchers observed nanoscale twinning, a process in which tiny regions of the crystal reorganize into mirror-image orientations, coupled with a local transformation of the crystal structure. They also used atom-probe analysis to map the distribution of individual elements and computer modeling to investigate how the different mechanisms worked together to prevent brittle failure.

When the newly formed structures reached boundaries between neighboring crystals, they created concentrated points of stress that triggered new dislocations. These fresh defects allowed the material to keep deforming and absorb the forces around a crack. Even as existing dislocations became harder to move, the alloys could generate new ones at these boundaries.

Lead author Dr. David Cook, who was at the University of California, Berkeley, during the study and is now at the University of Cambridge, said: “Our results suggest we should change how we think about what governs the transition to brittleness for these metals. Traditionally, the focus was on how readily existing dislocations can move through a metal, but now it appears that the ability to create new dislocations at interfaces may also be critical. Using these insights, we may be able to design underlying microstructural conditions that allow a material to create its own routes to remain ductile at extreme temperatures.”

Potential applications include components exposed to exceptionally cold conditions in the energy, transportation, and aerospace sectors.

Oxford corresponding author Professor Dong Liu, of the University of Oxford’s Department of Engineering Science, said: “For decades, the ductile-to-brittle transition has been viewed as a fundamental limitation of body-centered cubic metals. What surprised us is that these alloys remain remarkably damage tolerant even at 20 kelvin. By uncovering how twinning and phase transformation work together to generate plasticity before conventional dislocation motion, we identified a new pathway for designing structural body-centered cubic metals that can operate in extreme cryogenic environments. This class of materials will be extremely useful for components experiencing extreme hot and cold temperatures in one application.”

Reference: “Competing mechanisms toughen bcc binary and medium-entropy alloys at 20 K” by David H. Cook, Xiaoyu Chen, Michael O’Leary, Satish Rao, Wenqing Wang, Calvin H. Belcher, Madelyn Payne, Pedro Borges, Tung Lik Lee, Arun Devaraj, Mark Asta, Enrique J. Lavernia, Diran Apelian, Andrew M. Minor, Dong Liu, Punit Kumar and Robert O. Ritchie, 14 October 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11065-7

The research was principally supported by the US Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences, Materials Sciences and Engineering Division, through the Damage-Tolerance in Structural Materials program (KC-13) at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) under contract DE-AC02-CH11231.

#204. Here’s a look at the Nobel Prizes for science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Catching neutrinos, controlling brain cells and the mystery of mirror image molecules won

The discovery of a mysterious subatomic particle from beyond our solar system, achieved by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole (seen here), was recognized by this year’s Nobel Prize in physics.

Read another version of this article at Science News Explores

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It’s Nobels season — that time of the year when we find out which groundbreaking, paradigm-shifting, world-changing achievements beat out the rest to win what is arguably the most prestigious award on Earth.

From a light switch for the brain to the discovery of an ultra-elusive subatomic particle hailing from beyond our solar system to a solution to one of the most enduring puzzles in all of organic chemistry, the researchers behind this year’s scientific prizes each revolutionized the ways that scientists understand the world around them.

Take a look at the science behind each of this year’s awards.

A galaxy of nearly 90 billion neurons exists within a single human brain. But unlike stars in the void, neurons communicate with one another via some 100 trillion connections, allowing the human mind to learn, adapt and interact with its surroundings.

For scientists to understand how individual actions arise from such complexity, they needed a tool to directly link neural circuits to specific behaviors, said Abdel El Manira, a neuroscientist at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm. “Neuroscientists dreamed of a neuronal switch, a tool to turn specific neurons on or off with great precision,” El Manira said during the Oct. 5 announcement of this year’s prize in physiology or medicine by the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute.

Enter the bright idea that won. It’s a technology called optogenetics, which involves using light to precisely activate specific cells, like neurons, and watch how behavior changes. For their foundational contributions to optogenetics, biophysicists Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University in Berlin and Georg Nagel, of the Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg in Germany, and neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University shared this year’s prize.

The prize winners’ story starts in an unlikely place: the eye spot of a single celled green alga called Chlamydomonas. In the early 2000s, Hegemann, then at the Max Planck Institute for Biochemistry in Martinsreid, Germany, and Nagel, at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics in Frankfurt, discovered a unique protein in the alga’s eye spot. When illuminated, the protein generated an electrical impulse, enabling the organism to move. Further research revealed that when the protein, called channelrhodopsin, was exposed to light, it opened like a pore, allowing positively charged ions to flow into a cell, generating the electrical impulse. “They had just discovered the switch neuroscientists had long dreamed of,” El Manira said.

Building on the Hegemann and Nagel’s work, Deisseroth began testing whether channelrhodopsin could be used to activate brain cells. He and his colleagues first inserted the gene for channelrhodopsin into cultures of rat nerve cells and found that the cells reacted to light instantaneously. They then introduced the gene into nerve cells in the brains of living mice, along with optical fibers fed through the rodents’ skulls. By beaming blue light through the fibers, the researchers were able to control the movements of the rodents’ whiskers. This technology gave researchers the ability to test the links between certain brain circuits and behaviors.

“The technology, which soon became known as optogenetics, transformed neuroscience,” El Manira said. In addition to exposing the inner workings of healthy brains, he noted, “it has also helped reveal how brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression and dementia.”

For example, the technology has been used improve vision in some patients with retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that degrades light-sensing cells in the retina. It’s also helping researchers investigate the role that a person’s heart plays in how they experience and interact with their surroundings.

At the South Pole, there exists a block of ice unlike any other on Earth. Buried deep beneath the surface of the Antarctic ice sheet, a cubic kilometer of ice is threaded with thousands of beadlike sensors. Known as the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, this immense instrument enables researchers to detect the most elusive particle in the universe — the neutrino.

Detecting neutrinos from beyond our solar system had been a goal of scientists for decades, as that could help understand where and how the universe accelerates particles to extraordinary energies.

The researcher who led the creation of the Antarctic observatory, physicist Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin–Madison, received this year’s Nobel Prize in physics. Halzen was awarded “for his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” Mark Pearce, a physicist and chair of the Nobel committee for physics, during the Oct. 6 announcement by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

Neutrinos are subatomic particles that are chargeless, incredibly small and so ethereal that they often pass through objects without interacting. In fact, billions of neutrinos pass through each of us every second, most of which are formed by nuclear fusion reactions in the sun. But some of these ghostly particles were thought to have originated much farther away, in high-energy particle collisions so distant as to lie beyond the limits of observations. Because neutrinos are not deflected by magnetic fields and rarely interact with matter, the detection of a high-energy neutrino’s trajectory could enable the identification of its distant source. An instrument capable of that task could therefore open a new window into the cosmos.

In the 1980s, Halzen realized that the South Pole was an ideal location for detecting the rare flashes of light that are generated when neutrinos collide with atomic nuclei. Ice deep inside the Antarctic ice sheet presented a large, transparent medium plunged in darkness, in a spot free from earthquakes and biological interference. It was the perfect stage for a neutrino lightshow.

Halzen’s vision was realized in 2011, when IceCube completed construction. “The biggest risk we took is that nobody knew whether a kilometer-field detector was actually large enough to discover neutrinos beyond our atmosphere from the universe,” Halzen said in a phone call during the announcement ceremony. “It only took us two years to detect them.”

And the discoveries didn’t end there. In 2018, researchers using IceCube data reported that they had traced a neutrino back to the brilliant core of a distant galaxy, called a blazar, thereby identifying a source for the energetic particles for the first time. And in 2023, researchers used a decade of IceCube data to produce the first map of the Milky Way using anything besides light, simultaneously reporting the first evidence of high-energy neutrinos hailing from within the galaxy.

Plans for a global network of neutrino detectors are now in motion. So scientists will soon be even better equipped to pinpoint and demystify the distant cosmic accelerators that launch the mysterious particles across the vast reaches of space.

In nature, the building blocks of life exhibit a striking pattern. Many can exist in two versions that are mirrored images of one another, much like your right and left hand. Such molecules are said to be chiral. However, they overwhelmingly occur as just one of these chiral forms — for instance, amino acids are nearly always left-handed.

This uniformity, known as homochirality, had long puzzled scientists. When chemists first attempted to produce chiral molecules in the lab, they ended up with even proportions of right- and left-handed molecules, or enantiomers.

“It is this puzzle that this year’s laureates have solved,” Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry said during the Oct. 7 Nobel Prize in chemistry announcement by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

Henri Kagan, of the Université Paris-Saclay, and Kenso Soai, of the Tokyo University of Science, split the prize for discoveries leading “to a chemical reaction that spontaneously, without the involvement of other chiral molecules, creates only one mirror image,” said Linke, a physicist at Lund University in Sweden. “This is the first time this had happened since the processes that led to the chirality of life billions of years ago.”

Putting aside the laureates’ impact on one of organic chemistry’s greatest mysteries, their research has immensely benefitted the development of pharmaceuticals. So many active drug molecules are chiral, and one enantiomer of a drug might have the desired therapeutic effect while its other might have no effect or even be harmful, Linke said.

A notorious example of such harm occurred in the 1950s, when thousands of babies with severe birth defects were born to women who had taken a sedative called thalidomide. It was later revealed that one of thalidomide’s enantiomers was the source of the birth defects. Even making the drug with only the “safe” orientation didn’t solve the problem: It could switch handedness in the body.

In 1986, Kagan and his colleagues became the first to report chemical reactions that produced specific enantiomers in proportions far exceeding what chemists previously assumed was possible using catalysts.

Nine years later, Soai and his colleagues reported that they had figured out how to make a chiral catalyst that could, in turn, be used to form itself. That allowed them to perform reactions that resulted in products made almost entirely of one enantiomer. “This is not the final answer,” Soai said of his groundbreaking work on chirality, while calling into the ceremony from Japan. Speaking to future generations, he said “the study of chirality should be more and more developed.”

Even so, as Nobel committee member Peter Somfai, a chemist at Lund University in Sweden, said during the ceremony: “This is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry.”

#205. SPHEREx Just Took the Fingerprints of Failed Stars Across Our Cosmic Neighborhood

Brown dwarfs are the black (or brown?) sheep of astronomy. Theyâre too big to be considered a traditional gas planet, but they are too small to have started nuclear fusion and made the full transition to star-hood. They also change dramatically over time, cooling, shrinking, and spinning faster as they age. Or at least we think they do - our models of the atmospheres of these celestial objects arenât the best, according to a new paper in The Astrophysical Journal Letters by a team led by Zafar Rustamkulov at Caltech and NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Given that they arenât bright like stars, brown dwarfs are relatively hard to find, but light does filter out from their hot interior. As it passes through its upper atmosphere, the molecules there absorb specific wavelengths. This allows astronomers to perform spectroscopy on it, analyzing the dips and peaks of brightness at different wavelengths that represent the telltale signs of methane, water vapor, or carbon monoxide.

In the past, astronomers used the broadband filters on survey telescopes like 2MASS and WISE. While they did give a picture, it wasnât a complete one - their resolution was too low. You could make out the general color palette, but the individual brushstrokes were lost.

Fraser talks about dark matter in brown dwarfs

Luckily, the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx), which entered service in May 2025, is a game changer for exactly this kind of study. It maps the entire sky in 102 continuous wavelength channels, ranging from wavelengths of 0.75 microns up to 5 microns, which covers 80% of the heat energy released by brown dwarfs as infrared light.

Rustamkulov and his team used that SPHEREx data to compile a high-fidelity sequence of 33 nearby brown dwarfs between 7 and 100 light years away from Earth. They cover the three coolest spectral classes of these objects - L dwarfs, which hover around 2,200â, T dwarfs, which lie between 700 and 1,000â, and Y dwarfs, which can dip down to a frigid -20â. They also accounted for brown dwarfs with low gravity and low metallicity, in an effort to capture as many different combinations of features as they could.

With the SPHEREx spectra in hand, they then compared its findings to five leading theoretical brown dwarf atmosphere models: Sonora Diamondback, Sonora Elf Owl, BT-Settl, ATMO2020, and ATMO2020++. Each makes different assumptions about how the atmospheres would behave. None of them seemed to be correct.

Fraser talks about low mass, low energy stars.

Notably, they struggled to match a series of near-infrared flux peaks between 1 and 2.5 microns, and missed a critical âopacity windowâ at around 4.0 microns where light can easily escape the atmosphere. They also predicted sizes for these failed stars that were completely physically unrealistic, and sometimes off by as much as 20-50%. And they appeared to do so simply to make up for the modelâs poor understanding of the underlying chemistry.

They did get some things right, though. The researchers originally developed a series of custom spectral indices that focused on how carbon shifts in the atmosphere between carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and methane. In the data, there was a very clear trajectory - as brown dwarfs cool below 1,000 K, the amount of carbon monoxide drops off sharply and methane begins to take over. This match one of the models - Sonora Elf Owl - well, when it used weak vertical mixing. If that is what happens on brown dwarfs, it would contrast with giant planets like Jupiter, where strong churning of its atmosphere is an everyday feature.

Though brown dwarfs themselves might be isolated, the results of this work isnât only about them. Actually, the fact that they are isolated make them excellent test beds for what happens to large objects that isnât caused by a host star. But until we improve our models to better match the observed spectra of these objects, it will be difficult to apply that improved understanding to other, more traditional exoplanets.

SPHEREx is just getting started, though, and its cataloging thousands of additional brown dwarfs during its two year all-sky survey. That should provide modelers with the empirical roadmaps they need to refine their code and fix their physics. Keep an eye out for dramatically improved models of these sub-stellar wanderers in the near future.
