#206. The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Quickly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These models deliver fast cleanup with minimal effort when there isn't enough accumulation to take out the snowblower. Here are our recommendations.

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association says it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart issues, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Understanding that snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models capable of clearing up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter-weight electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver around smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

If you don’t mind its hefty build, this electric shovel from Greenworks Pro runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

With a large 80-volt 2.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor, you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. Clearing a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blowing it 20 feet away, this snow shovel is ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was quickly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small tool head, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multi-tool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel, rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#207. China picks first researchers for 15-year mega grants

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Scientists say long-term funding makes it easier to pursue high-risk research. Credit: Weiquan Lin/Getty

China has selected its first group of young researchers to receive funding for up to 15 years, in one of the longest research grants on offer to scientists globally.

Most research funding is awarded in grants that last for five years or less, says Nicole White, a statistician at Queensland University of Technology in Brisbane, Australia. But short funding cycles favour projects that are able to deliver results quickly, which can disadvantage high-risk but potentially ground-breaking research and cut promising work short before its impact is fully realized, she says. “Some of the most impactful scientific discoveries have taken decades, not years, to achieve,” White adds.

China boosts prestigious grants for young scientists — will it ease competition?

China boosts prestigious grants for young scientists — will it ease competition?

Dou Xiankang, president of the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), described the agency’s latest initiative at aforum held by the New Cornerstone Science Foundation in Shenzhen on 19 September. He said that 44 researchers under the age of 35 (women under 38) had been chosen, including 9 from outside China, as part of the National Distinguished Young Scientists Fund. Their names and projects have not been released.

At the forum, Dou said the 15-year grants would work in a “five-plus-five-plus-five arrangement”. That means, recipients whose initial five-year grants were about to end could be considered for a second five years and after ten years, another portion would be selected for a third five years of funding.

“During those 15 years, we will not conduct any short-cycle, short-term target assessments. We will assess only one thing: whether you are there in the laboratory,” Dou told the forum.

The NSFC first announced plans to create 15-year grants in 2023, stating that initial five-year grants would be worth 4 million yuan (US $596,000), they would then double to 8 million yuan for the second five years, and then double again to 16 million yuan for the final five years.

The NSFC has been ramping up funding for young researchers. Earlier this year, it pledged to increase the number of grants it provides for early-career scientists by 50%, adding 12,000 projects through its Young Scientists Fund.

#208. Scientists link a strange sugar in red meat to a 63% higher diabetes risk

A sugar naturally present in red meat may help explain why eating these foods has been associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. Preliminary findings from a large observational study suggest that people who consume the most of this sugar face a substantially greater risk of developing the disease, potentially because of its effects on the immune system and chronic inflammation.

The sugar, known as N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), is particularly common in beef and lamb. Researchers found that participants with the highest intake of meat-derived Neu5Gc had a 63% higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2D) compared with those who consumed the least.

The association remained statistically significant after researchers accounted for several established diabetes risk factors, including physical activity, overall diet, smoking, and existing health conditions. It became weaker after body mass index (BMI) was also considered, but remained significant.

The findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of The European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy.

“Our findings support chronic inflammation as a specific mechanism linking red meat consumption with T2D, partly beyond the amount of red meat a person eats and partly independent of body fat,” said lead author Dr. Leopold Fezeu from the Université Sorbonne Paris Nord, Bobigny, France.

The researchers also observed that diabetes risk generally increased with greater consumption of meat-derived Neu5Gc, particularly among those with the highest exposure.

“Although we do not know exactly what levels of Neu5Gc trigger an immune response, our data suggest that higher intakes of meat-derived Neu5Gc are associated with a progressively higher risk of T2D.”

Neu5Gc is produced naturally by most mammals, but humans lost the ability to make it following an ancient mutation in the CMAH gene. Despite this evolutionary change, the sugar can still enter the human body through food.

It occurs in red meat (particularly beef and lamb), with smaller amounts also found in dairy products.

After Neu5Gc is consumed, the body absorbs it and can incorporate it into human tissues. Because humans do not naturally produce the molecule, the immune system may recognize it as foreign. Scientists classify it as a xeno-autoantigen, a foreign substance that becomes incorporated into the body's own tissues and can provoke an immune reaction.

In response, the immune system produces antibodies against Neu5Gc. The resulting prolonged immune activity, called xenosialitis (xenosialitis), has previously been associated with cardiovascular disease and cancer.

Researchers suspect that this persistent inflammatory response could also contribute to type 2 diabetes. However, before this investigation, no large prospective study had examined whether dietary Neu5Gc might promote diabetes through chronic inflammation.

To investigate the possible connection, the scientists analyzed dietary and health information from 89,953 adults participating in NutriNet-Santé, a large French observational study that follows people over time to examine how nutrition and lifestyle influence health.

Participants were 42 years old on average, and 79% were women. None had type 2 diabetes or cancer when they entered the study.

Each person completed three 24-hour dietary records. The research team then used a validated food database to calculate how much Neu5Gc participants were likely consuming based on the measured amounts of the sugar in different foods.

The analysis included a broad range of red meats, such as beef, lamb, pork, rabbit, goat, and game. Processed meats (such as bacon, sausages and cured meats) were evaluated as a separate category, while dairy products were analyzed independently.

Using the dietary information, the researchers estimated total Neu5Gc intake from all reported foods. They then ranked participants separately by sex according to their intake of meat-derived Neu5Gc and divided them into five equally sized groups (quintiles).

Diabetes risk was compared across these groups, using those with the lowest intake as the reference.

During a median follow-up period of 7.2 years, researchers recorded 966 new cases of type 2 diabetes.

The results showed a significant relationship between meat-derived Neu5Gc consumption and the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes. The association became particularly pronounced among participants with the highest estimated intake.

Compared with the lowest intake group, individuals in the highest group had a 63% greater risk of developing the disease. Those in the second-highest group had a 41% greater risk (men and women combined).

These estimates accounted for potentially influential factors, including age, sex, exercise habits, overall dietary quality, smoking, and existing medical conditions.

The researchers also examined how much meat participants typically consumed.

Among men in the highest Neu5Gc intake group, median red meat consumption was 97 grams daily (136 g including processed meat). For women, the corresponding amount was 73 grams (96 g).

By comparison, men in the lowest intake group consumed a median of just 5 grams of red meat per day (21 g), while women consumed 0 grams (9 g).

The relationship between Neu5Gc and diabetes was observed in both sexes, with no statistically significant evidence that it differed between men and women (see tables in notes to editors).

The findings were also consistent when differences in total calorie intake were considered.

Researchers noticed that the increase in diabetes risk was especially steep at higher levels of Neu5Gc exposure. One possible explanation is that the immune system begins to respond more strongly after enough of the foreign sugar has accumulated in body tissues, although this proposed threshold mechanism has not been confirmed.

Importantly, when the analysis additionally accounted for the total amount of red meat consumed, the relationship between Neu5Gc and diabetes weakened and was no longer statistically significant. The direction of the association remained the same, however.

This means the researchers cannot determine whether Neu5Gc itself (rather than other components of red meat) is responsible for the increased risk. The findings suggest it could contribute to the relationship, but they do not establish that the sugar acts independently of red meat consumption.

Another notable finding was that obesity appeared to explain only a relatively small portion of the association.

According to the researchers' estimates, obesity accounted for approximately 13% of the relationship between meat-derived Neu5Gc consumption and type 2 diabetes.

This suggests that factors unrelated to excess body weight may contribute substantially to the observed connection.

One possibility is that immune reactions to Neu5Gc produce chronic inflammation that interferes with insulin-producing cells or tissues that normally respond to insulin. Such effects could potentially increase the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes even without substantial weight gain.

However, additional studies are necessary to establish whether these inflammatory processes actually explain the association.

Although Neu5Gc occurs in both red meat and dairy products, the researchers found an important difference between these dietary sources.

Higher consumption of Neu5Gc from dairy products was not associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes.

This finding may reflect the relatively small amounts of Neu5Gc in cow's milk compared with red meats such as beef and lamb. The typically smaller amounts of Neu5Gc consumed through dairy servings may also contribute to the difference.

When the scientists considered Neu5Gc intake from all dietary sources combined, participants in the highest intake group had a 37% greater risk of developing type 2 diabetes compared with those in the lowest group.

That association appeared to be driven primarily by Neu5Gc obtained from red meat.

“Together, these findings suggest that the association between Neu5Gc and T2D may depend on its dietary source, with meat-derived Neu5Gc showing a stronger association with T2D risk than total dietary Neu5Gc,” said Dr. Fezeu. “There may be differences between sources, or other components of red meat may contribute.”

The findings raise the possibility that reducing dietary exposure to meat-derived Neu5Gc could eventually become one approach to lowering diabetes risk.

However, researchers emphasize that studies are still needed to determine whether replacing foods rich in Neu5Gc with other protein sources would actually produce measurable health benefits.

“Given how common red meat is in Western diets, the strong association between meat-derived Neu5Gc and T2D risk is an important finding. Future research should explore whether reducing exposure to meat-derived Neu5Gc, for example by favoring poultry or plant-based proteins over beef and lamb, which have the highest Neu5Gc content, could help prevent T2D. Studies directly measuring anti-Neu5Gc antibodies in large cohorts would also help to directly test the xenosialitis mechanism in humans.”

The research team plans to investigate how Neu5Gc interacts with other substances found in red meat, including heme iron (a form of dietary iron), and how these components may collectively relate to diabetes risk.

They also intend to measure antibodies against Neu5Gc directly. Doing so could help determine whether the proposed immune response is an important biological mechanism connecting red meat consumption with type 2 diabetes.

The researchers caution that their findings are preliminary and have not yet been validated. The reported estimates could change once the final analysis is completed.

Because the study was observational, it cannot establish that Neu5Gc causes type 2 diabetes or identify precisely which factors are responsible for the higher risk.

Although the analysis accounted for several established diabetes risk factors, unmeasured lifestyle and social influences could still have affected the results.

There were also limitations in how dietary exposure was assessed. Neu5Gc consumption was estimated using participants' food records rather than measured directly, and the researchers did not account for possible dietary changes during the follow-up period. Both factors could have introduced errors into the exposure estimates.

The findings therefore offer a potential new explanation for the established connection between red meat consumption and diabetes, but further investigation is needed to determine whether Neu5Gc directly contributes to the disease.

The table shows typical daily meat consumption in each of the five groups, ranked according to estimated intake of meat-derived Neu5Gc.

Participants were assigned to these groups based on their estimated Neu5Gc intake, calculated from all reported foods and their measured Neu5Gc content.

The meat consumption figures represent the typical amounts eaten by participants in each group. They do not establish a specific risk threshold or indicate how much meat can be considered safe.

Results for men and women combined, using the fully adjusted statistical model.

The results suggest a similar association in men and women, without a statistically significant difference between the sexes.

However, relatively few diabetes cases occurred within each sex-specific intake group, making the separate estimates less precise. For this reason, the researchers presented their principal findings using the combined data.

Stellar remnants called white dwarfs ‪appear to come in a rainbow of colors, according to a new study.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Stellar cores called white dwarfs come in an astonishing array of colors, including what scientists say is the first known green star and the reddest star ever found, new research reveals.

A white dwarf star is the dense, cooling core that remains after a low- to medium-mass star runs out of fuel. The new study, published Thursday (Oct. 15) in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments, shows that white dwarfs come in far more colors than their name suggests.

White dwarf stars got their moniker because the first known examples glowed in either white or pale blue. The new study, however, suggests that "white" dwarfs also emit visible-light colors like pink, green, cyan, purple and yellow.

"Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like 'perfect radiators,' so their colour is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs," Mark Hollands, an astronomer at the University of Warwick in the U.K. and first author of the study, said in a statement. "It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colours nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me."

The variety of colors is possible due to white dwarfs' densities compared with main-sequence stars, the study suggests. Cooler white dwarfs have a density of about 1 gram per cubic centimeter, much like flowing water on Earth. The density of these white dwarfs is also millions of times denser than the sun's visible surface, or photosphere, leading to unusual conditions.

"Any trace elements that may be present, such as carbon, calcium and sodium, interact with the surrounding dense helium plasma and absorb light across a wider range of colours than they would at lower densities," the researchers said in a statement. "This shifts a star's colour away from the orange, white and blue [typical] of a perfect radiator."

Color-accurate simulated images of white dwarfs. The varying amounts/compositions of accreted material and white dwarf temperatures allow for a diverse array of colors, including green.

White dwarfs are far away and small, making it difficult to verify their color. So, in the new study, astronomers inferred the colors using spectra, the distinctive chemical fingerprints produced by stars' light. The team analyzed the spectra within a model of color vision that the human eye can see, making the color pop out.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Scientists found that carbon-rich white dwarfs tend to be purple or pink, while those that contain debris from asteroids or comets are usually yellower. Cyan or pale-blue white dwarfs occur when hydrogen and helium molecules strike each other in very dense atmospheres.

The team also discovered WD J1330+6435 — a green star that contains rocky material. The green comes from the additional elements of calcium, lithium and sodium in the star's atmosphere, creating a unique "chartreuse green appearance" that would be visible to the human eye, if we could see it up close.

"The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow," Hollands explained, adding that the one-of-a-kind green star "feels like something out of science fiction." The team also discovered what is likely the reddest star ever found. This white dwarf, called WD J1011+2845, is located roughly 48 light-years from our planet. It has carbon closer to its surface — because the element is being lifted from the interior, due to strong convection currents — that is bending the star's light. This process is making a "deep salmon-pink glow" because the carbon molecules are obstructing the star's other wavelengths.

Overall, in the sample of stars studied — 151 white dwarfs within 65 light-years of Earth — about 1 in 30 white dwarfs glowed in a color other than white. This could mean there are far more colorful stellar remnants littering the universe than anyone anticipated.

Hollands, Mark A., Gänsick, Boris T., Tremblay, Pier-Emmanuel., Koester, Detlev. Any colour you like: the diverse chromaticities of white dwarfs, RAS Techniques and Instruments, Volume 5, 2026, rzag069, https://doi.org/10.1093/rasti/rzag069

#210. Chernobyl’s Radioactive Debris Is Defying Scientists’ Expectations 40 Years Later

Some of Chernobyl’s radioactive debris is more resilient than scientists expected, offering clues to when the material trapped inside could escape into the environment.

Radioactive dust still contaminates the soil around Chernobyl four decades after explosions scattered debris from the nuclear reactor in Ukraine in 1986. The fragments measure just 8 to 50 micrometers across and remain highly radioactive. Assessing their risks requires understanding how quickly they break down and release radioactive substances, yet scientists still cannot fully explain why these “hot particles” weather at different rates.

An analysis of six fragments by researchers at Leibniz University Hannover and the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) found that the nuclear fuel’s crystal structure has remained largely intact. The examined particles are chemically more stable than previously assumed, retaining fission products, substances created when atomic nuclei split. That could limit the release of radioactive material into surrounding soil and water, while helping researchers refine assessments of the risks these particles pose.

Examining the fragments required complex synchrotron X-ray diffraction experiments, which reveal a material’s internal structure through the way it scatters X-rays. HZDR researcher and crystallographer Dr. Christoph Hennig carried out the first successful structural investigation of this kind at the Rossendorf Beamline in Grenoble, working with Tobias Weissenborn, a physicist and doctoral candidate at Leibniz University Hannover.

“The colleagues from Hanover and I used various methods to isolate the particles from Ukrainian soil samples and attach them to tungsten electrodes,” Weissenborn explains. The team secured the samples within several confinement layers before shipping them to Grenoble for examination by Hennig’s team.

“First, we had to figure out how to examine the particle structure,” Hennig explains. “Ultimately, we fully rotated the particles in an X-ray beam focused down to 100 micrometers—about the thickness of a human hair. We measured each particle from 2,000 different angles to seamlessly capture all the reflections.”

Those measurements allowed the researchers to identify different oxide phases, or distinct crystalline forms, within the samples. This phase analysis can help estimate how quickly the fragments release radioactive substances as they deteriorate and form different uranium oxides.

The particles’ structures reflect the different conditions the fuel experienced during the disaster. “There are three classes of these particles,” Weissenborn explains. “First, there are particles that are chemically and physically still very similar to the nuclear fuel uranium dioxide. Then, there are particles that are partially or fully encased in, or completely fused with, their zirconium layer.”

Particles containing fused fuel and zirconium formed when temperatures inside the reactor rose dramatically. The heat melted the fuel and bonded it to its surrounding protective layer of zirconium, a highly resistant metal.

“The third type of particle was created when the graphite-moderator caught fire,” Weissenborn adds. The graphite normally slowed fast neutrons to help sustain the nuclear chain reaction. During the accident, it burned for ten days.

“In the process, the fuel oxidized into various uranium oxides,” Weissenborn explains. These included U₃O₈, a mechanically unstable compound that readily breaks into microscopic particles that wind can carry away. Inhaling such radioactive dust poses severe health risks. Protective suits are still required to enter the affected areas.

The stability observed in the six examined fragments cannot yet be assumed to extend across the contaminated region. “However, every single particle has a different structure,” warns Weissenborn, “and our experiment only studied six such particles from two different locations.” Establishing broader patterns would require examining many more particles collected from far more locations.

“And even if we obtained some averages at some point, we still wouldn’t be able to make universal statements about health risks in the region,” Weissenborn cautions. “Because even if the particles decay in a largely uniform pattern, there will always be outliers, more persistent particles, that will release radionuclides at a later point in time.”

The findings therefore offer no basis for lifting restrictions on the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone anytime soon. Weissenborn and Hennig are already conducting follow-up experiments on the debris’s highly radioactive transuranic phases, which contain elements with atomic numbers higher than uranium’s.

Reference: “X-ray diffraction phase analysis of single hot particles from Chornobyl” by Tobias Weissenborn, Christoph Hennig, Laura Leifermann, Paul Hanemann, Eleanor Lawrence Bright, Florian Meurer, Aaron Lehnert, Kristina Kvashnina and Clemens Walther, 18 February 2026, Journal of Hazardous Materials. DOI: 10.1016/j.jhazmat.2026.141533

This work was supported by the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR, Germany) within the scope of the SOLARIS project (2020+ 02NUK075A).

#211. The Perseverance Rover Reaches Another Milestone

After five-and-a-half years on Mars, NASA's Perseverance Rover has set a distance record for travel on another world. Since landing in Mars' Jezero Crater, an ancient paleolake, on February 18, 2021, Perseverance has travelled 45.22 km, or 28.10 miles. That puts it slightly ahead of NASA's Opportunity rover, which travelled 45.16 kilometers (28.06 miles) during its mission. It must be noted, however, that Perseverance took only 5.5 years to travel this far, while Opportunity required almost 15 years.

Comparing the plutonium-powered Perseverance to the solar-powered Opportunity is unfair. But in any case, Perseverance deserves recognition for this milestone.

âThe original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. Weâve blown well past that..." - Steven Lee, Perseverance and Curiosity project manager, JPL/NASA.

Perseverance is currently in a region named âLac de Charmes,â which is off the western end of Jezero Crater. It reached its new milestone while heading toward a feature named "Idubi," a scientific target notable for its ancient rocks. On Earth, there are no rocks as old as these because they've all been destroyed by plate tectonics.

Perseverance has found igneous rocks, a surprising result considering that scientists expected to find mostly sedimentary rocks. In fact, a primary reason Jezero Crater was chosen as the mission's landing site is because sedimentary rocks are good at preserving evidence of ancient life. While the rover found plenty of sedimentary rocks, it found igneous rocks, along with fluorite, which forms when rock interacts with heated water. This is evidence of hydrothermal activity, and scientists are hoping Perseverance will find more traces of ancient hydrothermal systems at Idubi.

Perseverance captured this backward-looking image on the day it set its new distance-travelled record. The date was Oct. 11th 2026, or on the 2006th Martian sol of its mission. Image Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

Perseverance's skill at travelling long distances rests on more than just its power source. It also has an autonomous navigation system called AutoNav. AutoNav continuously takes images of the terrain and creates a 3D map of hazards. It uses this information to plot its own course. It can do this while travelling close to its top speed, and as a result, it can travel up to 412 meters (1,351 feet) in one Martian day.

Spirit and Opportunity were the first rovers to use AutoNav, though theirs wasn't as sophisticated. Those twin rovers used their first-generation AutoNav to travel about 5% of their total distance, while Perseverance has relied on it for about 90% of its travelled distance. (Sojourner used a limited form of hazard detection, but nothing as sophisticated as AutoNav.)

Steven Lee is the project manager for Curiosity and Perseverance at NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. âIt is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine,â Lee said in a press release. âThe original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. Weâve blown well past that, and with all mobility systems fully operational and favorable extended-ground-life test results, we expect Perseverance to keep adding to this record for many years to come.â

Perseverance is on its extended mission now, which began this month. The mission will have the rover exploring the rim of Jezero Crater until about the end of 2028. Throughout its primary mission, software updates have given its AutoNav increasing sophistication, and that should continue through its extended mission.

âThe rover that broke this record did so by making its own decisions about the path," said Mark Maimone, the deputy team chief of Perseverance's robotic operation. "Given the autonomy to just go, Perseverance is a better driver than the one that landed, and weâre not done. Our newest software teaches Perseverance to steer less and roll more, and to check its own position against orbital maps mid-drive."

The glare from the Sun is the next obstacle to be overcome with the rover's AutoNav system. The Sun's glare places limits on the rover's operations, and by overcoming that, the rover's daily maximum distance travelled will grow.

"The next frontier is sunlight itself," Maimone said. "Glare in the navigation cameras is why we park by mid-afternoon if weâre driving toward the Sun, and if we can teach the rover to see past those artifacts, every rover that follows gets a longer working day.â

The distance records themselves are remarkable, and they illustrate NASA's growing prowess in robotic exploration. But the real payoff is the increased science operations. The further it can travel in less time, the more geologic targets Perseverance can explore. And after all, Perseverance studies Martian geology in order to meet the objectives of its astrobiological mission.

This infographic shows how far various rovers have travelled on the surface of Earthâs Moon and Mars. Only Perseverance and Curiosity are still operational and moving across the surface; the figures shown for those two are distances driven as of Oct. 11, 2026. Image Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

Among the mission's highlights, which are partly attributed to its AutoNav capabilities, Perseverance has discovered potential biosignatures, and may yet discover ancient hydrothermal systems. Hydrothermal systems are like a 'Holy Grail' in astrobiology because they provide water, heat, and chemistry important for life. Hydrothermal systems may also contain fossilized evidence of ancient, simple life, in the form of microscopic structures, organic molecules, and even microbial mats.

The only sad part of Perseverance's mission concerns the samples it's gathered. Perseverance has cached 29 samples of Martian rock and regolith as part of a future Mars Sample Return mission. That mission was to be a cooperative endeavour between NASA and the ESA, but as of now, there's no firm commitment to the mission. It's currently deemed to expensive, and there are many unanswered questions about its potential success.

While Perserverance's AutoNav represents an impressive feat beyond the capabilities of previous rovers, the system also inspires an even more capable future. It's easy to imagine a future mission using AutoNav and AI to coordinate multiple rovers and even UAVs to coordinate the study of specific, hard-to-reach yet scientifically important targets on Mars and elsewhere. Think caves, elevated outcrops, and other challenging terrain.

But for now, we can enjoy Perseverance's accomplishments, which bring us closer to potentially, hopefully, finding conclusive evidence of ancient life on Mars.

#213. Stihl’s New Chainsaw Cuts Like It Runs on Gas—and Its Battery Life Outlasted Every Saw I Tested

This electric chainsaw is as good as or better than similar sized gas saws.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Stihl’s new battery-powered MSA 260 C-O tops the list of my favorite chainsaws tested this year. The two main reasons why? Runtime and constant, consistent power. Coincidentally, these are the two most common concerns or complaints I hear from people when it comes to electric saws. The MSA 260 C-O made significantly more cuts on one battery charge than any other saw I tested. That’s only partly attributable to the saw—it’s also due to Stihl’s new AllPro 300.0 battery. Working in concert, the battery and saw deliver power at a constant level, maintaining a chain speed through most of the saw’s runtime.

Aside from runtime and consistent power delivery, the MSA 260 C-O has the ability to chew through big, tough logs. I should point out that the MSA 260 C-O is positioned “for professional applications” so the performance does come at a cost: $770 for the 18-inch model we tested, plus another $350 for the battery. While that might seem like a lot, it’s in line with other pro battery and gas saws. So if you’re a frequent chainsaw user, the investment is going to be worth it.

Pulling the MSA 260’s trigger and holding it down for cut after cut through the logs, I kept waiting for the chain to start slowing and the battery to start dying—but it didn’t until the charge indicator on the battery got down below about 25 percent. That’s pretty remarkable, as many saws will start slowing a little as high as 75 percent.

When batteries are discharged rapidly, they can heat up, and heat is wasted energy. Stihl does a great job managing heat with its new AllPro battery line. The battery packs are made with tabless cells, which allows for the whole end of the cell to transfer energy, rather than through a small tab as most batteries do.

Stihl also spaced the cells out, to allow airflow between them, so the heat from one cell has less impact on those around it. On the MSA 260 itself, Stihl has a steel mesh air filter to prevent debris from packing up around the electric motor, keeping it cool.

The MSA 260 C-O has a display above the handle that I found simple and helpful when using the saw. It has three icons, one for the chain brake, one to indicate the saw is on, and one to let you know when the bar oil is low. A single orange button turns the saw on, indicated on the display with a green arrow. If you don’t pull the trigger to start cutting, the saw automatically turns off in a few seconds. This is an important safety feature because if you set it down, it shuts off and no one can pick it up and accidentally pull the trigger to activate the chain.

Of course, you should set the chain brake if you put the saw down. With a gas saw, if you set it down running, the engine idling alerts you that it’s on and active. A silent saw doesn’t do that, so the auto-off feature helps ensure everyone’s safety.

The chain brake icon lights up when the brake is set. So, if you turn the saw on, it will be lit up if the brake was on when it shut down. I found myself checking the screen when I turned the saw on to confirm the brake status. The last icon, for low bar oil, can help save your chain. I’ve had times when I went through bar oil faster than I anticipated, and just a minute or two running the saw with no bar oil can smoke a chain—so I appreciated the warning.

The MSA 260 C-O is a professional-grade saw that is every bit as good and powerful as a gas saw—in some ways, arguably better. I found its ability to cut through tough logs and its consistent power through most of the battery’s charge impressive. The cost may not be warranted for everyone, but if you use a chainsaw regularly, its capabilities and performance warrant the expense.

#214. Eating blueberries every day may have a surprising effect on your mood

A small pilot study suggests that eating blueberries every day may influence gut bacteria and potentially affect mood in older adults. Participants who consumed blueberries regularly experienced a greater and more consistent reduction in depressive symptoms, along with subtle changes in genes associated with gut microbial enzymes.

However, the improvements in depressive symptoms were not statistically significant when compared with the placebo group. Although the findings do not establish that blueberries can relieve depression, they offer preliminary clues about a possible connection between blueberry consumption, the gut microbiome, and mental health.

"Fiber and anthocyanins in blueberries have potential to modify the gut microbiome and metabolites that are relevant to depression in older adults," said lead author Courtney L. Millar, PhD, assistant scientist II at Hebrew SeniorLife's Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research and assistant professor of medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School. "Our objective was to preliminarily determine the effect of blueberry consumption on the gut microbiome, metabolites, and depressive symptoms."

Testing the Effects of Daily Blueberry Consumption

To investigate the potential connection, researchers recruited adults aged 65 and older who were physically inactive and experiencing mild depressive symptoms. The pilot study used a randomized, double-blind, parallel-arm, placebo-controlled design to evaluate whether consuming blueberries could influence gut microbes and mood.

Over three months, participants consumed either 48 grams of blueberry powder each day (approximately two cups of fresh berries) or a matching placebo powder.

Researchers examined the participants' gut microbiomes using metagenomic sequencing, which allowed them to measure the abundance of different microbial species and genes. They also used liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry to analyze gut-derived fecal short-chain fatty acids, compounds produced through microbial activity. Depressive symptoms were assessed using validated questionnaires administered before and after the three-month intervention.

Blueberries Linked to Subtle Changes in Gut Microbial Activity

A total of 18 participants completed the study. Most were women, and the group was predominantly white (placebo group, n = 8; mean age: 75 ± 6; blueberry group, n = 10; mean age: 71 ± 4).

Despite the encouraging pattern in depressive symptoms among participants consuming blueberries, the researchers found no statistically significant difference in mood improvements between the blueberry and placebo groups.

The gut microbiome results also revealed a mixed picture. The overall abundance of microbial species, MetaCyc metabolic pathways, and short-chain fatty acid metabolites remained unchanged.

However, researchers identified statistically significant changes within the blueberry group in the abundance of genes associated with several gut microbial enzymes. One of these was EC 3.6.3.31 Polyamine Transporting ATPase, which is involved in the production of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a neurotransmitter that plays a role in brain signaling.

These findings suggest that blueberries may influence specific aspects of gut microbial function even without producing measurable changes in the overall composition of the microbiome. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these changes are connected to meaningful improvements in mood or depressive symptoms.

The study, "A pilot study of daily blueberry intake modulates the gut microbiota enzyme commissions in older, sedentary adults with mild depressive symptoms," was published in the Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging.

Other contributors included Mohit P. Chopra, MD, of the Deanna and Sidney Wolk Center for Memory Health at Hebrew SeniorLife and the Department of Psychiatry at UMass Chan Medical School; Xochitl Morgan, PhD, and Emily A. Green, PhD, of the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; Alex Wolfe of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife; Kerry A. Pierce of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; and Lidan Gao, PhD, and Christopher N. Blesso, PhD, of the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the University of Connecticut.

Additional contributors were Alyssa B. Dufour, PhD, of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife and the Department of Medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School; Douglas P. #215. The World May Be Much Closer to a Major Conservation Goal Than Scientists Thought

The world may be closer to its 30% land conservation goal, but gaps in grassland and shrubland protection show why acreage alone cannot safeguard wildlife.

Some areas that support wildlife appear in national conservation records but are missing from the global tally. Including them could bring the share of land in some form of conservation to 26.8%, or nearly 27%, well above the officially reported 18.5%.

That difference changes the picture for an international commitment to protect nature. Almost every country has agreed to conserve 30% of land and sea by 2030 to help halt and reverse the biodiversity crisis, yet official figures suggest that progress on land has stalled.

“With four years to go, the terrestrial component of the 30% target seems out of reach. Our analysis suggests that much more of the land is in some type of conservation area than currently recognized,” says lead author Helen O’Neill, a postdoctoral research associate at the Institute of Zoology in London.

To build the broader estimate, an international team of conservation experts combined global measures of protection with national data on conservation areas. The study, published in Nature, was led by the Durrell Institute of Conservation and Ecology at the University of Kent in the United Kingdom.

“We need much more effort to officially recognize the existing conservation areas that are currently only recorded in national datasets.” That is the call from the study’s lead investigator, Bob Smith, director of the Durrell Institute of Conservation and Ecology at the University of Kent in Canterbury. The university is part of the London and Southeast University Group.

Grasslands and shrublands, home to uniquely adapted wildlife, still have limited protection even within this larger conservation network. These gaps mean that expanding the total area alone cannot ensure that the full range of habitats receives protection.

Co-author Heather Bingham, who leads the Protected Planet Initiative at the United Nations Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre in Cambridge, stresses that “conserving 30% of lands and seas is not sufficient on its own. The target also calls for these areas to be managed effectively for positive biodiversity outcomes, and to be placed where they will have the greatest impact for biodiversity.”

Meeting those requirements means connecting conservation areas, including diverse ecosystems, and managing sites fairly for local people. Smith adds, “We also need to focus much more on improving the effectiveness of all conservation areas, as increasing the area of land under conservation will do little unless these sites are effectively and fairly managed.”

Reference: “Global conservation area coverage substantially exceeds current estimates” by Helen M. K. O’Neill, Joe Beeken, Heather C. Bingham, Rachel E. Golden Kroner, Yifan He, Jessica L. The remains of two Ramesses II statues — one of which would have originally stood around 28 feet tall — were found by a villager in Egypt.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While working on his land in a village in northern Egypt, a man made an astonishing discovery: the remains of two massive statues of Ramesses II.

The man, Khaled el-Shahat, immediately notified the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, which sent a team to the village of Behbeit El Hagar to excavate and study the statues, the ministry said in a translated statement.

Ramesses II had one of the longest reigns in Egypt's history, ruling from around 1279 to 1213 B.C. During his 66 years in power, Egypt controlled an empire that stretched as far northeast as modern-day Syria. He initiated many building projects throughout the empire, and numerous Ramesses II statues have been found throughout Egypt.

Archaeologists had previously found architectural fragments bearing the name of Ramesses II at Behbeit El Hagar, which is known for its temple dedicated to Isis, a goddess associated with healing and magic, said Mahmoud Emam, an Egyptologist at Cairo University who has worked on remains from the site but was not involved with the recent excavation. He noted that the newly found statues were unearthed on the western side of the temple complex.

Both of the newfound statues were once larger than life, with the bigger one likely standing nearly 28 feet (8.5 meters) tall when it was originally built. However, most of what remains is its head, which is 5.2 feet (1.6 m) tall and depicts the pharaoh wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt.

Part of this large statue's back pillar has a hieroglyphic inscription that gives the pharaoh's "Horus" name: Hor-Ka-Nakht-Mery-Maat. This name means "Strong Bull, Beloved of Right, Truth," Joyce Tyldesley, a professor emeritus of Egyptology at the University of Manchester in the U.K., wrote in her book "Ramesses: Egypt's Greatest Pharaoh" (Penguin Books, 2001). In Egypt, it was common for pharaohs to have several alternate names with a Horus name, given in honor of the sky god Horus.

The second statue, which stands about 7.9 feet (2.4 m), also likely depicts Ramesses II, the statement said. The king is shown wearing the "Nemes" headdress, a type of striped headcloth that pharaohs wore, the Egypt Exploration Society notes on its website.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Near this statue is a block of pink granite with two hieroglyphic inscriptions that name Ramesses II and describe him as "King of Upper and Lower Egypt" and the "Son of Ra," an ancient Egyptian sun god, the statement said.

Hieroglyphs have been found on the statue remains. Some of them describe Ramesses II as the "son of Ra," a sun god in ancient Egypt.

The new finds add more evidence that Ramesses II was heavily invested in the site.

Previous discoveries include two architectural fragments bearing the name of Ramesses II near the Isis temple at Behbeit El Hagar, Emam and his colleagues reported in a 2017 paper. One is believed to be from the upper part of a statue, and another seems to originate from the upper part of a wall.

"We concluded that Ramesses II had undertaken major building works at the temple and recommended further archaeological investigations to shed more light on the early history of the site," Emam said. He noted that the site is threatened by urban growth and that excavation work should be carried out at the temple.

Live Science reached out to the team but did not hear back by the time of publication.

#217. Astronomers Observe The Limb Darkening Effect On Nearby Stars

The Sun is so intensely bright we can't safely look at it directly. We need a filter to block much of its light. And when we do, we can start to see some interesting features. Sunspots are one of these features, and the ebb and flow of their numbers has been studied for centuries. But a more subtle feature is that the edge of the Sun appears less bright than its central region. It's an effect known as limb darkening.

The limb darkening of the Sun was first measured by Pierre Bouguer in the 1700s. It is an effect of the Sun's atmosphere. When you look at the center of the Sun you see light that passed straight through the solar atmosphere. Not much of the Sun's light is absorbed or scattered. When you look at the edge of the Sun, that light had to take a shallow path through much more of the atmosphere to reach you. More of the light is scattered or absorbed, so less light reaches you. Thus, the edge appears dimmer.

With careful measurements of limb darkening, we can get a measure of the solar atmosphere. We have a good idea of its thickness and how its density and temperature vary. Since other stars should have the same limb darkening effect, we could use it to study the atmospheres of other stars. Unfortunately this is difficult to do. We have directly observed limb darkening of a few large stars such as Betelgeuse, and astronomers have looked at the light curves of transiting exoplanets to measure the limb darkening of a few stars, but stellar limb darkening is difficult to observe.

Limb-darkened model images for the sample of 31 stars observed with the CHARA Array in the near infrared. Credit: Center for High Angular Resolution Astronomy

Recently the Center for High Angular Resolution Astronomy (CHARA) Array has observed limb darkening in 31 nearby stars, and the results are published in The Astronomical Journal. The team measured the brightness of these stars along a line going from center to edge, similar to the way Bouguer first measured the effect in the Sun. But rather than observing in visible light, the team used two near-infrared wavelengths, 1.6 microns and 2.2 microns. This allowed them to compare how limb darkening varies with wavelength.

As expected, the limb darkening of these stars is less at the 2.2 micron wavelength than the 1.6 micron wavelength. Longer wavelengths are less scattered and absorbed by an atmosphere. This is why, for example, sunsets appear red. What was surprising is that the longer wavelength was about 38% weaker than the shorter one. Stellar atmosphere models predict about a 20% difference. This means that our understanding of stellar atmospheres is a bit off.

The study demonstrates that we now can observe stellar limb darkening directly. As future studies observe these stars at visible wavelengths and more infrared wavelengths, it will give us a clearer view of their atmospheres. But it's pretty astonishing that we can now see in stars an effect that for centuries we could only see in the Sun.

Reference: Anugu, Narsireddy, et al. "Empirical H-and K-band Limb Darkening for 31 CHARA Stars: A Near-infrared Benchmark for Stellar-Atmosphere Models." The Astronomical Journal 172.4 (2026): 214.

Brian Koberlein is an astrophysicist and author of the books Astrophysics Through Computation and Radio Sky: 40 Years of the Very Large Array. You can find more of his work on his website.

The successful Antares launch restored U.S. cargo ship redundancy for NASA space station crews.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Oct. 17, 2016, Orbital ATK (now Northrop Grumman Space Systems) returned to flight, successfully launching a cargo shipment to the International Space Station (ISS) after its previous cargo mission failed to launch.

The private spaceflight company was contracted by NASA to fly cargo to the ISS, and stakes were high for this launch. Orbital ATK's last attempt nearly two years earlier ended in a catastrophic explosion a few seconds after liftoff.

Despite some delays, the newly upgraded Antares rocket flawlessly blasted off into the night sky from NASA's Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia. Six days later, the Cygnus cargo spacecraft arrived at the ISS to deliver food, supplies and science experiments to the crew.

For the International Space Station to be able to sustain a continuous human occupancy, periodic cargo deliveries are needed. Russia fulfills part of this requirement with its Progress spacecraft, and both ESA (European Space Agency) and JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) have contributed with their Automated Transfer Vehicle (ATV) and H-II Transfer Vehicle (HTV), respectively.For its part, NASA contracted with Orbital (today, Northrop Grumman) and SpaceX to fly commercial resupply service missions. Both were needed to keep the U.S. operating segment of the station well supplied and with the science and research materials needed for the crew's work.

Though adjustments can be made to go without one or more of these vehicles for a short period of time, the Progress, Cygnus and Dragon are key components of the ISS's continuous operation. So returning a vehicle to flight after a catastrophic exploration is important to well-being of the International Space Station program.

As it happened, Antares would fly another 12 times before having to stand down again to be redesigned, but that is for a different This Day in Space entry.
