#220. The 8 Best Air Purifiers for Your Home

Whether you’re dealing with smoke or pet dander, these are the most effective (and affordable) models we stand behind based on testing and research.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Clean indoor air has become more important than ever. While allergens like dust, dander, mold, and bacteria are all teaming up to infiltrate the air you breathe, the widespread wildfire smoke affecting much of the U.S. right now is also proving just how quickly outdoor pollution can make its way inside. According to the EPA, Americans spend about 90 percent of their time indoors, where pollutant concentrations can sometimes be even higher than they are outside. An air purifier protects your airways from airborne irritants while providing clean, fresh air indoors (which is why we think everyone should invest in an air purifier).

We got our hands on air purifiers from brands like Coway, Levoit, and GermGuardian and put them to the test. Filtration was our main concern, so we could determine the air purifiers’ efficiency. Then we moved along to other factors such as noise while running, how well they work in a given room, and convenience features. After our in-home testing, these are the air purifiers that came out on top.

We tried out several air purifiers with a range of filtration systems, noise levels, and features. We tested these models in multiple different apartments, placing them in various rooms of the home to measure their efficiency. We considered the different uses of an air purifier, like if you’re an allergy sufferer or have a home filled with furry friends, and tested special features like light-up displays and automatic shutoff to determine their ease of use and effectiveness. We considered the amount of time it took to set up the different purifiers and install their filter systems.

For units that we haven’t tested, we combed through dozens of potential products and their specifications, reviews, and user complaints to identify what we thought were the best air purifiers. We settled on the following list, which includes options that are budget-friendly, sleekly designed, and high-performing.

The Airmega Mighty2 is the latest version of our previous Best Overall pick, the Coway AP-1512HH. The newest model combines power, quality filters, and robust controls to help you breathe easier.

The Mighty2 uses a three-stage filtration system to capture 99.7 percent of airborne particles, and cleans spaces up to 1,800 square feet in 60 minutes. It has three standard fan speeds, but there’s a turbo mode that will kick on if there’s a big uptick of matter in the air.

The original version just used an indicator light system that let you know basic air quality levels, but this updated model has a built-in air quality index sensor that measures and displays particulate matter counts in real time.

Our tester tried the air purifier in his New York apartment, putting it up against pet odors, litterbox dust, and other household allergens. “Results after about a day were already noticeable. The air in the room seemed clearer and there was less dust on the ground in the area immediately around the litterbox. Not enough that I’m going to have to sweep up any less, mind you, but there was a material difference that I wasn’t getting from using a smaller purifier.”

Full Coway Airmega Mighty2 Air Purifier Review

This air purifier from Clorox uses a three-stage filtration system to trap allergens, pollutants, and VOCs, and it successfully cleared strong scents and odors from the apartment we tested in.

It was quiet enough that you hardly hear it activate, especially if it kicks on automatically while you’re cooking to clear the kitchen of smoke. But on higher settings, you do tend to notice its noise a bit more. The 360-degree, cylindrical shape of the filter offers purification from all directions, and the unit covers 1,000 square feet so you don't have to be as strategic about placement.

We also liked that it has a color-coded indicator light on the front that tells you how hazardous the air is in the room where it's located (though it will add insult to injury when it turns purple while you’re trying your best to sear a steak.)

If you’re a pet owner, specifically with cats, then you know that the litter box smell lingers long after your little fur ball has left the lavatory. The Vital 200S-P from Levoit is a great way to combat the odors that candles and air fresheners just can’t cover up. I set the air purifier up in my living room and noticed a clear improvement in scent after running for the day.

This unit has a traditional air inlet, along with a unique U-shaped inlet that is ideal for trapping pet hair without clogging up the filters. If you pair your air purifier with the app and select Pet Mode, it automatically alternates between fan speeds, too. The pre-filter is easy to remove and wash, so you don't have to purchase replacements as often.

Since we tested the Vital 200S-P in a smaller apartment, it was a bit obtrusive. But the air purifier covers up to 1,875 square feet, so if you live in a townhouse or single-family home, this unit will accommodate.

Full Levoit Vital 200S-P Air Purifier Review

The Airmega 100 is the first cylindrical unit in the Coway line, which is a nice switch-up from the rectangular model that we tested in the past. It tucked nicely into the corner of the living room, and you can change the light between blue, orange, and off, which is ideal if you’re using the purifier in a bedroom.

I tried the fan on various settings, and the lowest mode could barely be heard over the TV playing at an average volume, which aligns with its claimed 20-decibel noise level. You can manually adjust everything on the control panel, or let the purifier do its thing and adapt accordingly as it monitors the air quality of the room.

Setup of the unit was simple; you essentially just need to click the filter into place. This model uses a 3-in-1 filtration system, with a HEPA filter sandwiched between a vacuumable pre-filter and deodorizing filter. The deodorizer layer is especially useful if you have pets, love to cook, or live in an apartment or complex with odors.

Full Coway Airmega 100 Air Purifier Review

For smaller rooms or office spaces, the smart Blueair 511i Max offers much of the same performance and features as larger, more capable models. It only purifies areas of up to 465 square feet, but does so within just 30 minutes on the highest setting. The three-layer filtration system captures up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles, too.

We appreciate that the air quality level is clearly displayed on the front in a five-color scale, and that the display has auto-brightness controls if you're running it overnight while you're sleeping. Advanced features are available through the app, including scheduling and air quality reports.

This unit has a four-stage filtration system, along with Blueair's proprietary HEPASilent filter that uses a combination of electrostatic charge and mechanical filtration to capture 99.97 percent of airborne pollutants and contaminants. This type of filtration technology is less dense than other filter options, so it's designed to run quieter and use less energy.

The value offered by such a small air purifier is unmatched, considering it targets both allergens and odors—all with relatively quiet operation.

If you have a large space or even an entire apartment that needs air purification, the Coway Airmega 400 is the smart model you need. It's designed to cover up to 1,560 square feet in 30 minutes, and has a variety of smart features and sleep settings, all packed into a compact yet capable unit. While this is the most expensive option we recommend, it's relatively affordable considering its capacity, and you shouldn’t have to supplement with an additional air purifier.

It’s surprisingly quiet given its size, reaching only 22 decibels on its lowest setting. We like that it uses multi-stage purification methods, combining a pre-filter, an activated carbon filter, and a True HEPA filter to capture the tiniest of particles. The pre-filter is washable, but the air filter indicator light will let you know when it actually needs to be replaced.

The Airmega 400 has a three-setting smart mode that adapts to its environment, with a fan speed that automatically adjusts based on air quality or lighting conditions. We also appreciate the option to use eco mode, which turns the fan on and off when the room has remained purified for 30 minutes, and there’s also a timer and pollution sensor.

The GermGuardian isn’t a flashy design with robust features, but it aids in keeping the air in my apartment free of pet odors, dust, and smoke.

I have a self-cleaning litter box, which significantly cuts down on smells and dust associated with cat waste, but it doesn’t solve every problem. I let the purifier run during one of the Litter Robot’s cleaning cycles, and thanks to the GermGuardian’s built-in air quality index (AQI) sensor and display screen, I was able to see the particulate matter count in the air reach triple digits in seconds. The automatic fan speed varied as needed, and it wasn’t long before air quality was back to a healthy level.

I put the GermGuardian up against incense smoke, too, and it went to work quickly. The fan had to run at high speed for longer, but by the end, my living room was clear of any lingering haze and odor.

In addition to a HEPA filter and activated carbon, this model also has a UVC light, which is claimed to disinfect bacteria, viruses, and mold. While I did give this feature a try, I didn’t keep it on for long because it’s hard to prove whether these lights are actually useful in an air purifier.

Read Full GermGuardian AC4880B Air Purifier Review

The Sans HEPA 13 air purifier offers quiet operation, whole-home purification, and smart features. This unit runs at only 25 decibels on the lowest fan setting, and I could hardly tell that it was on, even when standing next to the unit.

The air purifier is best used for whole-home use, as it purifies spaces up to 1,854 square feet. The internal sensors monitor and show you the air quality index in real time, and the reading is visible on the touch display. I’m able to view PM2.5, which is particles that are 2.5 microns or smaller, such as dust, smoke, pollen, and pet dander, as well as PM10, which are slightly larger particles up to 10 microns, like coarser dust and mold spores.

This unit pairs a medical-grade HEPA 13 filter with a pre-filter, activated carbon filter, and UV-C light to capture 99.9 percent of particles. This might be overkill for general household use, but I’ve appreciated the multi-stage approach. The only downside I’ve come across is that overall cost will likely be higher, considering the Sans recommends replacing the filter every three months.

There is no shortage of air purifiers on the market, and many of them use a lot of the same tech to achieve better air quality. We’re often testing many different models to find the top recommendations. Ahead are some that haven’t made it to this roundup, but are still worth considering.

Rabbit Air A3 Air Purifier: This air purifier uses a six-stage filtration system to rid your home of smoke, dander, odors, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and germs. The lowest fan setting clocks in around 20 decibels, which is extremely quiet, so you can run this model daily without being disturbed. The build is relatively bulky so it’s not the easiest to tuck into a corner and out of the way, and the $760 price tag is pretty steep.

GermGuardian AirSafe+ XL: This model is shaped like our best portable pick above, and comes with a lot of the same features as the other GermGuardian we recommend, and it has a companion app for tracking air quality metrics. That said, the app doesn’t specify what type or size particulate matter the sensor is measuring, so it’s hard to tell what common allergens are actually floating around your home.

Air purifiers vary in filtration range, so it's important to first consider your room size before buying. To find a model that accommodates your space, the EPA recommends that you first multiply the length and width of the area where you intend to operate the air purifier to calculate the square footage.

Most air purifiers have a maximum coverage area listed, so just compare to your calculations to find an air purifier that is the best fit for your home.

If you have an open floor plan or high ceilings, opt for an air purifier with more coverage. You should also place the air purifier in the room you use most regularly, and make sure it’s in an area where the airflow isn’t obstructed.

The filter system of your air purifier might differ depending on the model and issue you're trying to target such as allergy relief, odor elimination, or germ protection. You’ll often see three-stage filtration (or four-, five-, or six-stage), which includes all three of the filter types detailed below.

Pre-filters are typically the first line of defense in an air purifier and trap larger particles like dust, hair, and fur, which helps extend the lifespan of the main filter and improves the overall efficiency of the unit.

All of our selections on this list involve a multi-step filtration system to target a majority of common pollutants and allergens in your household.

Purvi Parikh, MD, an allergist and immunologist with NYU Langone Health, recommends selecting an air purifier that comes with a HEPA filter. “Make sure it's a HEPA air purifier since these filter down to 0.3 microns and have a robust amount of studies done showing their efficacy.” HEPA filters remove at least 99.97 percent of airborne particles like dust, bacteria, and pollen, and are the gold standard for air purification.

Activated carbon filters are more porous and help get rid of gases and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are commonly found in household items like surface cleaners and candles. These filters absorb molecules onto carbon and are best used in environments with strong odors or smoke.

With laundry machines, dishwashers, and fans all emitting their own noise, adding another loud appliance into the mix could be overkill, especially since air purifiers are meant to run the entire day.

Look for models that range from 10 to 30 decibels. A whisper is around 30 decibels, so expect air purifiers in this noise range to be almost virtually silent.

“Air purifiers need to be kept clean, and filters should be changed every six months,” Parikh says. Since air purifier filters are designed to collect and trap different-sized particles, contaminants, and hair, they get gunky pretty easily. This buildup could even reduce the efficiency and the air quality of the purifier if not cleaned often enough. Most air purifiers come with reusable filters, so just rinse them off in between replacements.

App compatibility, savvy control panels, remotes, check filter indicators, and variable settings are beneficial features that make it easier to use your air purifier. If you want to monitor the air quality levels in your home or keep tabs on filter life, look for an air purifier that pairs with an app. If you’re easily overstimulated by loud noises, consider an air purifier that has different modes for adjusting the speed of the internal fan.

Air purifiers use a fan to draw air into the unit, then pass it through a series of filters to remove particles and contaminants. Said filters vary in effectiveness and normally target a specific concern like odors, smoke, and viruses. Once the air has passed through the fan and all of the appropriate filters, it is recirculated back into the room for a cleaner and healthier environment.

“Air purifiers filter out pollutants, improve air quality, remove infectious agents and pollen,” says Parikh. “They limit your level of exposure and reduce lung damage and flare-ups of underlying chronic conditions such as asthma attacks, COPD exacerbations, and heart issues.”

“It can affect everyone’s health by causing inflammation and lung damage over time that may be either reversible or irreversible,” Parikh says. “It is especially dangerous for those with underlying heart disease, lung disease, pregnant women, children, and immunocompromised individuals.”

#221. A 1,000-Year-Old DNA Mystery Links Hawaii and Easter Island and Reveals Hidden Genetic Dangers

The DNA that traces Hawaii’s settlement also points to overlooked disease risks, with some globally rare variants common enough among Eastern Polynesians to warrant screening.

Hawaii and Easter Island lie about 7,000 kilometers (4,350 miles) apart, roughly the distance from San Francisco to Lima, Peru. New genetic evidence suggests that ancient sailors from the Easter Island region crossed that vast stretch of the Pacific to settle Hawaii. No written record describes their journey, but traces of it remain in the DNA of people living on the islands today.

Stanford Medicine researchers and collaborators uncovered the connection by analyzing genomes from more than 1,000 people throughout Polynesia. Their study, published Oct. 8 in Science, extends a settlement route that researchers previously thought had ended at Easter Island.

“What we uncover in this paper is where the native people of Hawaii had come from,” said Alexander Ioannidis, PhD, assistant professor of genetics and of biomedical data science at Stanford Medicine and co-senior author of the study. “Hawaii is the only Polynesian island in the Northern Hemisphere, so it’s a long way from everything.”

The study’s other co-senior author is Keolu Fox, PhD, an associate professor of anthropology at the University of California, San Diego, and a Native Hawaiian.

Across Polynesia, more than 1,000 islands occupy an expanse of ocean roughly equal to the combined areas of North and South America. Reconstructing connections among those islands, from tropical Hawaii to temperate Easter Island in the far South Pacific, requires evidence that can reach back through centuries of migration.

“People on the islands today have encoded in their genomes essentially the genealogy of all of their ancestors,” Ioannidis said.

To follow that ancestry, the researchers isolated genome segments of Polynesian origin, excluding more recent contributions from populations such as Europeans and Asians. They then compared stretches of DNA shared by people from different islands. These stretches, called identity-by-descent segments, come from a common ancestor. Longer shared segments generally indicate that two people shared an ancestor more recently.

Among the populations compared, Native Hawaiians shared the most Polynesian ancestry with people on Easter Island, followed by people on Mangareva, nearly 3,000 kilometers (1,860 miles) from Easter Island. Ioannidis interprets that pattern as consistent with a culture capable of exceptionally long voyages. Seafarers who could reach Easter Island from Mangareva would also have had the capabilities needed to travel onward to Hawaii.

Double-hulled catamarans carried provisions such as taro, sweet potatoes, and bananas, which could supply food for weeks at sea and crops for a new settlement. An earlier study by the researchers found that members of the same long-distance voyaging population also reached South America and made contact with Native Americans.

The team’s previous genetic reconstruction had traced Polynesian settlement from Samoa to Fiji and Tonga, then gradually eastward through the Cook Islands, the Society Islands, which include Tahiti, and Mangareva. It placed settlement of Easter Island around 1210. The new findings suggest that this was another stop along an expanding migration route.

Genetic evidence also allowed the researchers to investigate how many people founded an island population and what happened afterward. Tahiti offered the largest collection of genomes in their dataset, making it the focus of a more detailed analysis. By comparing identity-by-descent segments among people from the island, the team estimated that its founding generation consisted of approximately 800 people who arrived about 34 generations ago, around 1070.

That estimate covers a single generation of people of reproductive age. It does not include children or elders who may have accompanied them.

“Archaeologists and others have long wondered how many people founded these islands. That’s not something that you can determine definitively from archaeology, but we can determine it from genetics,” Ioannidis said.

The analysis reconstructed rapid population growth on Tahiti after settlement, followed by a substantial population crash in the 1700s after European colonial contact. Similar reconstructions are underway for Easter Island and Hawaii, but they will require additional genomes.

Each island settlement also shaped the genetic inheritance of later generations. When a small group separates from a larger population to establish a new one, it carries only part of the original population’s genetic diversity. This bottleneck, known as a founder effect, can make an otherwise rare variant more common among descendants, including variants associated with disease. Across Polynesia, small groups, perhaps only a few hundred people at a time, founded successive island populations over several centuries.

“We thought Easter Island was the end when we were first doing that study, but now it looks like it was part of this path to Hawaii, which is really incredible,” Ioannidis said. “By the time you’ve gotten all the way to Hawaii, you’re at the end of a series of founder effects, so it’s really intense.”

Founder effects have been extensively studied in populations of European descent, including the Amish, Ashkenazi Jews, and Finns. That research has led to standard screening for certain inherited conditions. The new analysis indicates that the scale of these effects among Eastern Polynesians has been overlooked.

“What we discovered is in the Eastern Polynesians, such as Native Hawaiians, the founder effects are more than an order of magnitude, so more than 10 times, larger than what we have in the populations of European descent we’ve studied so well,” Ioannidis said.

To examine the medical implications, the researchers analyzed three genetic variants recently linked to autosomal recessive conditions among Eastern Polynesians. These conditions generally develop when a person inherits a disease-causing version of the relevant gene from each parent. The variants occur in ADAMTSL4, associated with dislocation of the eye’s lens, PDE6B, associated with progressive vision loss, and FAN1, associated with kidney failure.

Although these variants are exceedingly rare worldwide and barely represented in international genome databases, the researchers found carrier rates of 2% to 3% among the Eastern Polynesians studied. Those rates meet standard thresholds for recommending genetic screening. Larger genomic studies could identify additional clinically relevant variants that are unusually common in Polynesian populations and help guide precision medicine.

“We should be doing more sequencing and trying to characterize more of these conditions among Native Hawaiians,” said Ioannidis, noting that the Native Hawaiian population is nearly twice the size of the Amish population. “We don’t have recommendations for genetic testing, and there’s no reimbursement from insurance because these are conditions we don’t even know about.”

“This is a population that should be getting research resources and attention from geneticists even more urgently.”

Reference: “Message in a bottleneck: Nested founder effects from French Polynesia to Rapa Nui and Hawaiʻi” by Cole Shanks, Edward C. Huang, Christophe Thomassin, Anne-Katrin Emde, Vahinetua Rodière, Mauricio Moraga, Karla Sandoval, Tony Merriman, Tristan Pascart, Andrés Moreno-Estrada, Stephane E. #222. Nepal’s disaster is an urgent wake-up call

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Christian Huggel is a professor in the Department of Geography, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland.

Simon K. Allen is a senior scientist in the Department of Geography, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland, and at the Institute for Environmental Sciences, University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland.

Emily Mark is a senior geological engineer at BGC Engineering, Vancouver, Canada.

Dan H. Shugar is an associate professor in the Water, Sediment, Hazards, and Earth-surface Dynamics (waterSHED) Lab, Department of Earth, Energy, and Environment, University of Calgary, Calgary, Canada.

Jakob Steiner is a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Geography and Regional Science, University of Graz, Graz, Austria, and a senior engineer at Hydrosolutions, Zurich, Switzerland.

Kavita Upadhyay is an independent journalist and researcher in Nainital, India.

Many houses were submerged or washed away by the August flash floods in Nepal. Credit: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP via Getty

On 26 August, an avalanche and massive flood swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa district. Thousands of lives were lost, homes were destroyed, roads and energy infrastructure were washed away, and trade and tourism were disrupted.

Disaster early-warning systems can succeed — but collective action is needed

Disaster early-warning systems can succeed — but collective action is needed

This catastrophe should not be treated as just another disaster. It is the latest — and worst — in a series of exceptionally massive deluges of rock, ice and debris from mountains. The unprecedented scale of the damage shows that current approaches of assessing and managing these risks have failed. Moreover, with global warming accelerating, further disasters of this magnitude are expected.

How scientists analyse and officials manage environmental risks in mountainous regions must urgently be restructured. Here we outline how such hazards are changing and propose how researchers can assess coupled, cascading risks to protect communities and save lives.

The Rasuwa disaster is not a freak event. Over the past few years, the world has seen several similar massive rock and ice collapses with ensuing floods (see ‘Cascading risks’).

Sources: M. C. Matthew et al. Landslides 21, 2307–2326 (2024); D. Schneider et al. Earth Surf. Process. Landf. 36, 1948–1966 (2011); Y. Zhong et al. Landslides 22, 989–1001 (2025); J. A. Coe et al. Landslides 15, 393–407 (2018); A. Kääb et al. Cryosphere 15, 1751–1785 (2021); Alaska Volcano Observatory yearly reports (https://avo.alaska.edu)

In February 2021 in India, an avalanche from Ronti peak led to a huge flood in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand. The flow of water and debris devastated the Ronti Gad valley, killing more than 200 people and destroying hydropower structures1.

Just a few months later, in June 2021 in Nepal, a small glacial lake burst its banks, sending flood waters surging into the Melamchi River. This triggered a cascade of hazards that washed away more than 50 million cubic metres of sediment and altered river-bed levels by roughly 20 metres in some places2. Around 600 people were displaced and at least 20 died. The region’s freshly established drinking-water infrastructure was severely damaged and vast areas of agricultural land were lost.

Losing your way of life to climate change matters — and we need a way to measure it

Losing your way of life to climate change matters — and we need a way to measure it

Similarly, in October 2023 in Sikkim, India, a massive slide of glacial sediment into South Lhonak glacier lake initiated another outburst and flood. The waters swept an incredible 270 million m3 of sediment down the Teesta River. More than 100 people died, around 26,000 buildings were damaged and hydropower structures were destroyed. The impacts, including infrastructure damage, affected Bangladesh, too3.

Furthermore, in May 2025, the village of Blatten in the Swiss Alps was buried under an avalanche that released nearly 10 million m3 of rock and ice after a glacier collapsed. The glacier was weakened by a series of rock slides that deposited material onto it4. The village was destroyed and there was one fatality, but the other residents were evacuated before it was inundated.

And, in Alaska, less than three months later, an extraordinary landslide (roughly 64 million m3) crashed onto South Sawyer Glacier and into Tracy Arm Fjord5, generating a tsunami with heights of close to 500 m. Fortunately, this happened a few hours before cruise ships would have been travelling through the fjord, avoiding what might have been a maritime disaster.

Roads, bridges and other infrastructure were swept away by the water after the August avalanche in Nepal.Credit: Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto via Getty

The Rasuwa disaster exceeds these events. On the northern slopes of Langtang Lirung mountain, a failure in the bedrock caused a massive rock avalanche that took the overlying glacier with it. The resulting avalanche (around 125 million m3 of rock and ice) is one of the largest on record worldwide.

As the ice, debris and water rushed down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river valleys, the ice melted and extra sediment and water were incorporated into the flow. Damage extended over 100 kilometres from the source. More than 1,400 people have died, more than 5,000 are missing and tens of thousands have been displaced. Settlements, roads and bridges were washed away and around 10% of Nepal’s hydropower production was knocked out. Reconstruction costs have been put at around US$5 billion.

And on 11 October, the Himalaya region of central Nepal was hit by floods in the upper Budhi Gandaki river valley that were triggered by another large rock and ice avalanche from a steep mountain slope. The avalanche was around half the size of the August collapse. The floods damaged settlements, roads, bridges and hydropower structures.

These events resulted from a combination of interacting and cascading processes: collapses of steep rock or glacier slopes, failures of banks of sediment, outburst floods from lakes and further entrainment of water, debris and sediment by the flood as it raced downstream.

The scientific community knows this and has repeatedly signalled the need for an improved understanding of these cascading hazards and for them to be incorporated into risk analyses6,7. But, so far, little has changed in how such hazards and risks are considered in practice.

The likelihood of one-off events is typically gauged on the basis of the historical record. But events at the scale that we are now seeing are rare or missing from those archives. That makes it hard to predict how frequently massive avalanche-triggered floods might occur in future — the number seen over the past few years is too small to determine long-term trends. But one thing is certain: the world is warming, meaning further rock-slope failures and glacier collapses are likely to occur in coming decades. What has happened historically will not be a good model for what is to come.

Expanding development in mountainous areas is also increasing the exposure of people, settlements and infrastructure to hazards. For example, hydropower development in the Trishuli basin in Rasuwa has expanded since 2010, as has development along the road to the Rasuwagadhi–Kerung border between China and Nepal.

Scientists and decision makers must rethink how they analyse hazards and risks in mountainous regions. Rather than a single method, we propose a complementary set of approaches that can be combined as needed depending on the context.

First, define the purpose and scope of the assessment. For instance, a risk analysis can inform land-use planning, guide funding allocations, identify protection gaps, calculate potential economic losses or establish priorities for risk management at scales ranging from a single hydropower plant to large populated areas. Together, governments and local communities need to decide what level of risk they are willing to tolerate and consider how to protect the most-vulnerable groups and infrastructure.

Second, we suggest applying a combination of several risk-evaluation methodologies. Each approach covers a specific risk aspect and is complemented by the others. Disasters such as the one in Rasuwa underline the importance of using several tools to capture the multifaceted impacts comprehensively.

Probabilistic risk analysis can be used to compute the distribution of asset losses for events of various sizes and frequencies8. For example, for a hydropower plant, such an analysis might provide a statistical representation of the extent of damage in relation to different event probabilities.

AI to the rescue: how to enhance disaster early warnings with tech tools

AI to the rescue: how to enhance disaster early warnings with tech tools

However, performing a probabilistic analysis is challenging when assessing future events that have few or no precedents. In such cases, we suggest that analysts consider using models of credible, physically plausible scenarios. These can be built from likelihoods and judgements based on existing knowledge9 and by extending the analysis to a wide range of possible events.

For this, the geological record can sometimes provide clues. For example, in Rasuwa, large boulders lying well beyond the current river bed are testimonies of similar floods some 5,000 years ago10. A plausibility analysis would then check whether such an event is plausible under current or near-future conditions.

Storyline approaches that consider a range of far-reaching possibilities in both qualitative and quantitative ways should be applied to explore cascading effects beyond current populations and structures11. For instance, the Rasuwa disaster destroyed important trade and transport routes between Nepal and China with consequences for Nepal’s economy. The destruction of hydropower sites also affects neighbouring countries that depend on energy imports, including Bangladesh.

Risk-network analysis can be used to address gaps in risk assessments, such as the lack of inclusion of the consequences for disadvantaged populations. Such methods evaluate, for example, connections between flooded houses and their inhabitants, lost local businesses and livelihoods, and disruptions to social networks and education and health-care services.

#223. A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks

For the first time, researchers have demonstrated that severely bleached corals can fully recover after spending just a few days in contact with healthy, genetically identical corals.

In laboratory experiments, corals that had turned white and were close to dying regained their health within seven weeks. According to a study published on October 14 in Science Advances, this represents the fastest documented recovery from coral bleaching. The discovery could lead to new techniques for restoring coral reefs, which some estimates suggest could disappear within decades as climate change fuels increasingly severe and frequent marine heat waves.

Coral bleaching occurs when rising ocean temperatures cause corals to lose the beneficial algae living inside their tissues. These algae supply much of the energy corals depend on for growth and survival. Without them, corals lose their vibrant colors, struggle to obtain enough nourishment, and become more susceptible to harmful algae. Even when they survive, regaining their health can take months or years.

"While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet," said lead author Danny Collins, an oceans PhD student at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. "The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?"

An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a Way to Rescue Dying Corals

Although they may resemble plants or rocks, corals are animals. In most coral species, individual animals reproduce by creating genetically identical copies of themselves. These clones grow together into large colonies that form the foundation of coral reefs.

The idea for the study emerged from an unexpected observation in 2025. Steve Palumbi, a study coauthor and the Jane and Marshall Steel, Jr. Professor in Marine Sciences, noticed something unusual in his laboratory. Two fragments taken from the same coral colony, one healthy and the other bleached, had fallen against each other in an aquarium.

Where the fragments touched, the bleached coral began regaining its color. The change suggested that beneficial algae were returning to its tissues.

At roughly the same time, Collins was investigating how coral diseases develop and spread. He was particularly interested in bacteria carried by plastic debris that lands on corals and can introduce harmful microorganisms through direct contact.

"Harmful bacteria enter corals through physical contact," said Collins, who is also a Knight-Hennessy Scholar. "We were curious about what would happen if we used contact to reintroduce something good - the beneficial algae from healthy corals."

To investigate, Collins designed an experiment using 10 pairs of coral fragments. Each pair consisted of one healthy fragment and one bleached fragment originating from the same coral animal.

Five pairs were positioned so that the fragments physically touched. The other five pairs were separated by gaps measuring only a few millimeters.

The results revealed a dramatic difference. Every bleached fragment that touched its healthy counterpart recovered completely within seven weeks. In contrast, the bleached fragments that were kept apart died.

How a Simple Touch Triggers Rapid Coral Recovery

The researchers discovered that the remarkable recovery depends on a special ability of genetically identical corals to connect their tissues.

"Genetically identical corals recognize one another when they come into contact," said Palumbi, who is a professor of oceans in the Doerr School of Sustainability and of biology in the School of Humanities and Sciences. "Their tissues fuse if they are from the same clone. We see something similar in humans. Organ transplants are often successful if the donor is your identical twin."

Using a powerful microscope, Collins and his colleagues examined what happened when the coral fragments touched. They found that tiny channels within their tissues quickly lined up, forming connections that allowed materials to move between the two fragments.

Through these connections, beneficial algae and the nutrients they produce could pass from the healthy coral into the bleached one. Within just three days, researchers observed algae transferring into the damaged fragments.

The team then investigated how long the corals actually needed to remain connected. By separating pairs after different periods of contact, they discovered that a single week was enough to transfer the algae required for complete recovery. In some cases, just five days of contact produced the same result.

Remarkably, the separated corals still returned to full health within seven weeks, the same amount of time required by corals that remained connected throughout the experiment.

This finding revealed that the rapid recovery was not primarily driven by a continuing supply of algae from the healthy coral. Instead, once enough algae entered the bleached fragment, they reproduced rapidly inside their new host and restored its energy supply.

"Once beneficial algae enter bleached corals, they don't just spread out," said Palumbi. "They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals."

During the second week of contact, the beneficial algae living inside the bleached fragments doubled in number approximately every four days. That growth rate was about ten times faster than what researchers have observed in wild corals.

A Promising Breakthrough for Coral Reef Restoration

Scientists have spent decades searching for ways to protect coral reefs from rising ocean temperatures, disease, increasingly acidic seawater, and other environmental pressures.

Their efforts have included selectively breeding corals that can withstand higher temperatures, raising young corals in nurseries to rebuild damaged reefs, and transferring communities of microorganisms between corals to improve their resilience.

The new findings suggest another possibility: helping bleached corals recover quickly enough to survive the dangerous period following a marine heat wave.

"Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all," said Fiorenza Micheli, the David and Lucile Packard Professor in Marine Science and a faculty advisor of Collins. "We hope this new research will inspire solutions that keep corals healthy long enough to enable full recovery after heat waves through slower processes such as growth, reproduction, and recruitment of new colonies."

However, the researchers emphasize that their experimental approach cannot yet be used to restore reefs on a large scale. For the technique to work as demonstrated, every bleached coral would need access to a healthy, genetically identical counterpart. Finding and supplying those matches across entire reefs would be impractical.

Important questions also remain about how the recovery mechanism could be adapted for broader use.

Over the coming months, the team intends to investigate other ways to introduce beneficial algae into bleached corals without requiring them to remain physically connected to healthy fragments.

One possibility involves collecting beneficial algae from healthy corals well before marine heat waves occur. Researchers could then deliver large quantities of these algae to damaged corals after bleaching events, potentially allowing them to recover much faster.

"These new insights into how corals can naturally recover give us hope for the future," said Micheli, who also co-directs the Stanford Center for Ocean Solutions. "They open the door to what's possible and may lead to the breakthrough we need to accelerate reef restoration."

Micheli also serves as a professor of oceans and (by courtesy) of biology. Both Micheli and Palumbi are senior fellows at the Woods Institute for the Environment, which is part of the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.

Additional Stanford researchers who contributed to the study include Jana Sipkova, Nathaniel Mollica, Tom Rolander, Courtney Klepac, Gabriel Calistro, and Vanessa Barone.

Mollica is a research scientist in Stanford's Oceans Department, where Calistro works as a research assistant. Rolander is a research engineer in the Fabrication Lab at the Harold A. Miller Library at Hopkins Marine Station, which belongs to the Doerr School of Sustainability.

Sipkova is a postdoctoral scholar, while Klepac is a research scientist. Barone is an assistant professor in the Biology Department of Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences and is affiliated with Bio-X and the Maternal & Child Health Research Institute.

The Molecular and Cellular Biodiversity Imaging Center, operated by Stanford's Biology Department at Hopkins Marine Station, conducted the coral image analyses.

Financial support came from the National Science Foundation and Stanford University, including seed funding through the Big Ideas for Oceans grant program. The program is organized by the Oceans Department and the Woods Institute for the Environment within the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.

#224. Astronomers Uncover More Intriguing Detail in an Ancient Supernova Remnant

In 1181, astronomers, poets, and diary keepers in China and Japan recorded a 'guest star' in Cassiopeia. The luminous transient lit up the sky for 6 months. Those ancient astronomers didn't know it was an exploding starâa supernovaâbut we do.

Today, astronomers are almost certain that they've found the SN's remnant. It's named Pa 30, or IRAS 00500+6713. Researchers think that this SN wasn't a core-collapse supernova, a massive star exploding at the end of its life, but the result of two white dwarfs merging and creating a Type Iax SN.

The remnant, Pa30 is a heavily-studied astronomical object. It provides an opportunity to study the aftermath of SN explosions, their nebulae, and how material from the explosion is spread out into space, where it can eventually be taken up in new star formation. As the only known supernovae remnant (SR) in the Milky Way, Pa30 is elevated to the top of many astronomers' list of observing targets.

In new research, astronomers used the Gemini North Telescope and its Gemini Multi-Object Spectrographs (GMOS) instrument to uncover new details in the SN remnant. It's titled "Detection of Knots in the Type Iax Supernova Remnant Pa 30," and the lead author is Tim Cunningham. Cunningham is an assistant professor in the Department of Physics at the University of Warwick, and is also associated with the Center for AstrophysicsâHarvard & Smithsonian.

"We present deep, narrowband Gemini North/GMOS images of the Pa 30 nebula that reveal rich small-scale structure in the ejecta filaments," the authors write. Their observations revealed an order of magnitude more filaments than previous observations. "The imaging further reveals that the filaments are not smooth radial streaks, but instead are composed of cascades of knots or clumps," the researchers explain.

âWe can see this much detail because of Pa 30âs proximity to Earth,â study co-author Ilaria Caiazzo from the Institute of Science and Technology Austria said in a press release. âThis proximity makes Pa 30 uniquely valuable for study.â

These new observations rely on the GMOS' ability to observe different chemical elements. In this case, emission lines from [S ii], or singly-ionized sulfur, play a leading role. [S ii] is an important emission line in astronomy that lets astronomers study ionized gas clouds.

These images of Pa30 were captured with the Gemini North Telescope and its [S ii] filter. It reveals far more filaments than previous images, and shows that the filaments are cascades of knots. Image Credit: Tim Cunningham et al 2026 ApJ 1010 28

The new images show that the filaments are not smooth streaks of gas, but rather continuous chains of knots. This is evidence of variations in density and temperature in the circumstellar medium that material from the SN explosion slammed into. These variations shaped the SN ejecta as it expanded outward.

The greater level of detail in the [S ii] images contrasts with previous [O iii] or doubly-ionized oxygen images of Pa30.

These panels compare [S ii] images of Pa30 with [O iii] images. [S ii] is on the top and [O iii] is on the bottom, and top and bottom panels are aligned. Clearly, the [S ii] images reveal much more detail. Image Credit: Tim Cunningham et al 2026 ApJ 1010 28

The Pa30 SNR is more than just an expanding cloud of ejecta. There's also a stellar component, a white dwarf. It may be an exceptional white dwarf called a super-Chandrasekhar white dwarf. This means the white dwarf exceeds the normal mass limit of white dwarfs, which is about 1.4 solar masses. Pa30's white dwarf may have about 1.5 solar masses. The white dwarf also has an extremely high temperature, about 200,000 C, and stellar winds with a record-breaking high velocity of about 16,000 km/second.

SNe remnant white dwarfs typically recieve a kick from the SN explosion that moves them from the nebula's center. Not only is the existence of Pa30's white dwarf unusual, since it's a Type Ia(x), but so is its position in the very center of the nebula.

"A unique characteristic of the Pa 30 nebula as a historical SN of Type Ia(x) is the presence of a central stellar remnant," the researchers write. "Because the explosion in many Type Iax models proceeds as a failed detonation or an off-center partial deflagration of the white dwarf, the surviving remnant can receive a substantial recoil kick."

"We measure a nebula center consistent with the position of the central star, indicating that the remnant has not received a large transverse kick," the authors write. This is extremely unusual, since nebulae are messy and their central stars are usually offset, and noticeably so.

This figure shows the center of the Pa30 nebula in two epochs, 1181 and 2025. The blue shows the nebula center in 1, 2, and 3 sigma uncertainty contours. Compared to other nebula, the stellar remnant is in the center of the nebula. Image Credit: Tim Cunningham et al 2026 ApJ 1010 28

The authors explain that Pa30's unusual knotty filaments place useful constraints on models that can explain its morphology. A better understanding of the recoil kick it received can also help astronomers understand its progenitor better. Progress on those fronts awaits better observations.

"Further observations exploiting the exquisite angular resolution of the Hubble Space Telescope would greatly enhance this analysis," the researchers write.

There are likely other Type Ia(x) SNR in the Milky Way awaiting discovery. Human beings have only been recording their observations of the heavens for a very short period of time, compared to the age of the Milky Way.

âReliable historical records of stellar explosions extend back only about a thousand years. For all we know, there might well be similar remnants still lurking in the dark in our own galaxy,â Cunningham said. âToday, we are lucky to study an intriguing object we know was observed by astronomers who made three independent historical records of the event centuries before the invention of the telescope.â

âWe will likely identify more similar objects as new telescopes continue to inspect the depths of our night sky,â

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

Space-based solar power has the potential to meet Earth's energy needs many times over. Will it see the light of day?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The year is 2050, and as the sun sets, the night's first constellations emerge in perfect rows. But these amber-glowing arrays aren't stars at all; they're satellite clusters, harvesting the day's last rays before beaming their power back to Earth.

If it reads like science fiction, that's because it started that way. Called space-based solar power (SBSP), the concept featured prominently in the techno-utopian imaginations of 20th-century visionaries and writers. But for decades, it was dismissed — a pie in the sky proposal.

Now, as a new space race heats up, governments and private companies in China, the U.S., the U.K. and Japan are developing several projects to reassess the idea's feasibility. These include China's ZhuRi ("Chase the Sun") program, Japan's OHISAMA project, the U.K.'s Space Solar, and power-beaming experiments by Caltech and the Air Force Research Laboratory in the U.S., all of which are targeting test launches in the next five years.

Proponents say the technology has the potential to meet Earth's energy needs many times over while causing minimal harm to the environment. But first it needs to get off the ground: In the eyes of critics, space-based solar power is exorbitantly expensive, riddled with untested assumptions, and far too complex to be deployed in time for an urgent green-energy transition.

The challenges include getting the massive solar-panel-covered satellites into space; assembling them; getting those solar panels to constantly face our star; and then finding ways to convert, concentrate and transmit their collected power back to Earth.

Despite these hurdles, researchers keep returning to the idea. Perhaps because the most crucial step — generating energy in the first place — is already being done by the sun. Every second, our star fuses hydrogen atoms to expel the same energy as nine trillion atomic bombs. All that's left to do is catch it.

"We're not a competitor to fusion. We are fusion," Peter Garretson, the U.S. Air Force's former chief of future technology and an SBSP expert, told Live Science.

The first glimmers of SBSP as a concept came from the Russian rocket scientist and astronautics pioneer Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, who, in 1923, suggested deploying space-based mirrors that could concentrate sunlight to Earth with enough intensity to boil 10 cups of coffee.

Konstantin Tsiolkovsky inside his workshop in Kaluga, Russia. Long before he became globally celebrated for his pioneering formulas on rocket design and space travel, Tsiolkovsky spent decades obsessively working on designs for a steerable, all-metal cargo airship.

Tsiolkovsky's fanciful proposal soon entered science fiction, appearing in the British writer Olaf Stapledon's 1937 novel "Star Maker" as a "gauze of light traps" that an advanced alien civilization used to focus "the escaping solar energy for intelligent use" — an idea later formalized by theoretical physicist Freeman Dyson as a Dyson sphere.

Then, in 1941, Isaac Asimov made the clearest, most famous early sketch of SBSP in his short story "Reason," in which a robot colony toils aboard a power station that collects solar energy and fires it back to Earth in the form of microwaves. Asimov provided few details on the fictional station's engineering, instead focusing on the robots' religious worship of the vessel.

But the transformation from science fiction to a concrete proposal didn't take long. In 1968, aerospace engineer Peter Glaser, a consultant and project manager for the Apollo 11 mission's distance-measuring laser reflectors, drew up an engineering design for a "solar power satellite" consisting of three key elements: a ray-collecting device, a converter and a transmitter.

Glaser's collector was a disk of photovoltaic panels that would be lifted some 22,400 miles (36,000 kilometers) off the ground. Locked in a geostationary orbit above Earth and bathed in near-constant sunlight, the satellite would harvest solar rays before converting them into microwaves to be beamed, largely unimpeded through the atmosphere, to receiving antennae on the ground. Once there, the microwaves would be converted into electricity and distributed across the grid.

A 1976 artist's illustration of a solar power satellite based upon Peter Glaser's original design.The image shows the assembly of the satellite's microwave transmission antenna.

NASA awarded Glaser a contract to study the concept further, with both domestic and international energy crises (such as the 1973 oil crisis and the 1979 Three-Mile Island nuclear accident) adding wind to his solar sails.

But Glaser's design hit technical and financial roadblocks, the most forbidding being the project's sheer size. By 1981, when the U.S. Department of Energy's four-year study of space-based solar power was released, it estimated that a "meaningful" contribution of 300 gigawatts (sufficient to power hundreds of millions of homes) would require 60 satellites, each spanning 21 square miles (55 square kilometers) and weighing 50,000 tons (45,000 metric tons). The plan was deemed unaffordable.

Later reassessments, such as a 1997 report by NASA physicist John Mankins, pointed to advances such as improved solar cells that made the concept more realistic. Yet the overall consensus remained hostile. A 2015 report released by the Strategic Studies Institute (SSI) of the U.S. Army War College stated that while SBSP systems are "technically feasible," there was "no compelling evidence that such systems will be economically competitive" with terrestrial power systems. It concluded that "the reality is that such systems always seem to be seen as just 10 years away by their advocates."

But a lot can change in a decade, including the cost of firing rockets. Since the SSI report, SpaceX's reusable Falcon 9 rocket has sent launch costs plummeting to around 30 times less than those of NASA's Space Shuttle, with satellites also getting cheaper due to mass production and advances to the clean rooms where they're made. And SpaceX's even bigger Starship rocket promises to more than quintuple Falcon's payload capacity, lowering prices further.

SpaceX's Starship Flight 14 launches from Boca Chica Beach, Texas on September 28 as part of its first orbital test flight.

"What you have is a cadre of people in the space community that have grown up before Starlink and SpaceX," Garretson said. "They literally could not believe that, as your launch rate goes up and you amortize your costs, [the launch cost] approaches the cost of fuel." Some took notice. A 2021 assessment commissioned by the U.K. government estimated that a 2-gigawatt, mile-wide space-based solar power array would cost 17.3 billion British pounds ($23.4 billion) and generate energy at 50 British pounds ($68) per megawatt hour over its century lifetime.

That's the equivalent output of a large power station in the U.K., with the initial costs being 39% to 49% cheaper than biomass, nuclear or the most efficient gas energy sources, according to the assessment. And while it's still 14% to 52% more expensive than current terrestrial wind and solar energy, the technology could be beamed anywhere, even to remote locations.

Based on these findings, in 2023, the U.K. government awarded 4.3 million British pounds ($5.8 million) in seed funding to a handful of companies and universities to develop SBSP further.

The U.K. report chose one satellite design as its reference architecture: CASSIOPeiA. Belonging to the U.K. SBSP company Space Solar, the satellite's design is an attempt to crack a significant challenge faced by early solar satellite blueprints: how to keep solar panels constantly aligned with the sun to maximize radiation collection.

Unlike other satellite designs, such as China's Multi-Rotary Joint Solar Power Satellite or Mankins' SPS-ALPHA, which rotate the panels or use a system of mirrors to constantly redirect sunlight onto them, CASSIOPeiA is shaped like a gigantic DNA strand.

This design, alongside a sun-synchronous orbit and a slow spin, enables CASSIOPeiA to constantly receive and transmit solar energy without any heavy or failure-prone moving parts. Space Solar claims that a single CASSIOPeiA satellite, which would be about 1 mile (1.6 km) in diameter, could microwave-beam as much as 2 gigawatts of constant power to a fixed point on the ground — enough to supply a city of 2 million people.

Space Solar says that once the satellite is in space, it will be far more efficient and economical than gathering sunlight on the ground could ever be. That's because the light hitting the space-based power station isn't deflected or attenuated by the atmosphere.

"You use a lot less materials compared with terrestrial solar, and you utilize them more," Sam Adlen, co-founder and co-CEO of Space Solar, one of the funding recipients, told Live Science. "So it's 100% utilized in space rather than 10% if you're on the ground — and you've got 13 times more instant energy, so you're getting much more out of the materials."

However, the next step — beaming gigawatts of energy down and across tens of miles of atmosphere and through potential cloud cover — remains a major technical hurdle.

Proposed power-beaming methods are currently split between two types: lasers and microwaves. California-based startup Aetherflux, which has plans to beam power from satellites in low Earth orbit, has developed an infrared laser transmission system that it will test using a demonstration satellite launched on October 1. The microwave energy will be transmitted at around one kilowatt (enough to supply the basic electrical demands of a household).

Meanwhile, Caltech and Overview Energy, another U.S. startup, have both demonstrated respective microwave and laser-power beaming from orbit and from a plane, respectively, albeit in negligible amounts ( less than a kilowatt).

Despite their efficiency and proven ability to travel vast distances, optical beams in the infrared and near-infrared ranges are easily scattered by water droplets in the atmosphere, preventing power from being transferred on cloudy days. Persisting efficiency issues with optical power transmission also worsen at gigawatt power levels, meaning lasers are less feasible for use at the utility scale.

Microwaves, on the other hand, can be beamed at frequencies with much higher power and suffer relatively little atmospheric attenuation. That's why Space Solar, Japan's OHISAMA project and China's ZhuRi program all plan to use microwave-beaming systems. Nonetheless, microwaves have comparatively longer wavelengths, so their beams diffract more widely across longer distances. This means that even if beams are sent by transmitters hundreds of meters wide, they would need Earth-based receivers spanning dozens of square miles.

An aerial view of China's Five hundred meter Aperture Spherical Telescope, the world's largest single dish. With current technology, transmitters of this scale would need to be constructed in space in order to successfully beam microwaves to magnitudes bigger receivers.

These limitations mean that "it's going to take many years" before gigawatt-scale power beaming is achieved, Remo Proietti Zaccaria, head of the DELTA Lab at the Italian Institute of Technology, told Live Science.

Improvements in power-beaming efficiency will bring their own challenges. Even battery-powered laser pointers can blind or burn, so prototypes by laser-beaming SBSP companies like Aetherflux must be designed with that possibility in mind. They promise safety mechanisms that switch off their lasers if anything flies between the transmitter and the receiver.

"Definitely for the weapon side, this technology now can be used efficiently," Proietti Zaccaria said.

If you're imagining an orbital weapon devised by a Bond villain, you may be disappointed — even fully developed power-beaming lasers and microwaves would take a while to cook an egg, or boil Tsiolkovsky's coffees. But beaming technology could still have potent military use: Scrambling communications systems on Earth to create havoc with relatively little effort.

"If you throw even that amount of intensity of power to our antennas, you're going to freeze the electronics; that's for sure," Proietti Zaccaria said. "It's not necessary to destroy them. As long as you freeze the electronics, you've done the job."

The challenges associated with power beaming have pushed some engineers to simpler concepts. One (going full circle back to Tsiolkovsky's original proposal) envisions the deployment of space-based mirrors that reflect sunlight back to Earth after sunset, with a single reflector extending the daylight delivered onto solar panels by around 20 minutes.

This may not seem like much on its own, "but then you can increase this with multiple reflectors," Onur Celik, a researcher in space technology at the University of Glasgow, told Live Science. "If you have 10 or more of them, you can arrange them in space in such a way that you can extend this to up to two hours or so at that altitude."

"The sunlight that you deliver, if it all turns into electricity, could power thousands of homes," he concluded.

The trillion-dollar question is whether that power will be cheaper and more efficient than that generated on the ground. The median cost of the electricity generated by SBSP as estimated by the U.K. government is 50 British pounds per megawatt hour ($68), putting it roughly in line with the costs of offshore wind and terrestrial solar power.

However, this estimate is orders of magnitude too sunny for the 2024 NASA cost report, with its projections suggesting SBSP's baseline electricity costs fall between $610 and $1,590 per megawatt hour, depending on the array design. NASA concluded that the U.K.'s median estimate was achievable only after drastic future reductions in launch and manufacturing costs.

Independent studies are also divided over feasibility. One assessment suggests that SBSP could reduce Europe's need for land-based renewable energy by up to 80%, while another counters that the costs could be 12 to 80 times more expensive than those for terrestrial alternatives. This variability exists within the studies themselves, with research published in the journal Acta Astronautica estimating that SBSP could contribute to meeting anywhere from 3% to 31% of global electricity demand, depending on possible constraints in how many satellites can safely fit into an orbit, the receiver size, and where power is beamed to.

"For the numbers we found, I don't believe that this technology could actually be employed to generate energy for Earth," said Proietti Zaccaria, a co-author of the Acta Astronautica study. If humanity had used up all available space for solar panels on Earth, "then I will tell you it would make sense, because at that point, 3%, 5%, 10% could make a difference."

Proietti Zaccaria does see use cases for SBSP schemes for future moon or Mars missions, but otherwise, "the cost for building technology of this kind is really very, very high," he said. "Vice versa, the cost nowadays of buying and installing a solar panel on the roof of any building has become extremely cheap."

Among the challenges would be ferrying the raw materials for the systems into space and then assembling them. Such a feat would make the construction of the International Space Station — currently the most complex structure built in orbit — seem like child's play. Maintaining arrays and preventing them from crashing into other satellites in Earth's increasingly crowded orbits would also take significant international coordination.

Exposures taken over just 30 minutes on a night in June 2024 show the growing crowdedness of Earth's skies.There are now roughly 20,000 active and inoperational artificial satellites in Earth's orbit, with the number expected to reach around 60,000 by 2030.

Then there are the unweighed environmental costs. All modern rockets use methane, a potent greenhouse gas, to propel them into space, and they release much of it into Earth's upper atmosphere, where its effects are the strongest.

"And so clearly, there is a question there on how launching 100,000 of these superheavy vehicles into the atmosphere will actually impact the atmosphere itself, as opposed to the benefit that we get in the next 20 years or so from having solar power from space," Matteo Ceriotti, a senior lecturer in space systems engineering at the University of Glasgow, told Live Science. "It's not entirely clear."

Ceriotti said the likeliest route for overcoming all of these difficulties come from smaller companies running, and then streamlining, proof-of-concept tests in space.

"Obviously, it's not something that we have ever done," he said. "So clearly, we need to start somewhere, and we need to start small."

The hopes of SBSP proponents remain unclouded by gloomy estimates. They cite several technologies, from personal computers to reusable rockets, that were once thought to be impossibly expensive, even fictitious, that are now ubiquitous and cheap. Their eyes remain fixed on demonstration missions to be launched over the next four years by the likes of Space Solar, Reflect Orbital, Aetherflux and Virtus Solis. If these missions succeed, another once-impossible idea could appear much brighter.

"The private sector is good at this, because it has to be," Sanjay Vijendran, an SBSP consultant who led the European Space Agency's now-shuttered SOLARIS project to test the feasibility of SBSP, told Live Science. "It can break the problem down to quite a small level and start to do things with today's technology and today's way of doing things, and start to show that this can be valuable."

Ben Turner is a U.K. based writer and editor at Live Science. He covers physics and astronomy, tech and climate change. He graduated from University College London with a degree in particle physics before training as a journalist. When he's not writing, Ben enjoys reading literature, playing the guitar and embarrassing himself with chess.
