#226. The 8 Best Space Heaters to Keep the Chill Out of Your Home and Office

We compared different models’ heating levels, timer functions, safety features, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Take the edge off those chilly winter nights without ballooning your energy bill. Space heaters offer immediate warmth for cozy nights in the bedroom and for brisk days in a drafty office. The small radius of heat also makes them ideal for improving the temperature in your immediate surroundings without wasting energy turning up the thermostat and heating the entire house. Some even double as fans during the summer.

The top space heaters run quietly and efficiently, offer multiple heating levels, and come with safety features like automatic shut-off for accidental tipping. We researched and tested the most promising models from brands like Vornado, Lasko, and Dreo. Below, you’ll find our selections for the most efficient, durable, and safest space heaters out there.

We tested space heaters by first evaluating each model based on important factors like safety, setting variety, and size. We paid attention to how well the appliances were able to warm up a space by using them around our homes and offices. We also took note of the number of heat settings each unit had and the temperature range they offered.

To evaluate the unit’s heat capabilities, we took into account its temperature range and wattage, and prioritized heaters that offered a broad range with good control and output of at least 1,200 watts or more. We’ve made a point to include options that operate via remote-controlled desktops and smart picks that come with a companion app as well.

For heaters that we haven’t had the chance to try in person, we heavily vetted specs and assessed each space heater based on the same factors we used during testing.

Lasko calls the CW100 bladeless because it doesn’t technically have a fan, per se. Instead, it uses a multi-vane impeller. That design contributes to the appliance’s quiet operation because it pulls in air through its base and into the tower. It comes with a cleanable air filter, which is accessible via a tool-free hatch at the back of the heater—no tools required.

We appreciate the slick touchpad on the front for adjusting the wattage for the heating element, tower oscillation, and the eight-hour timer. The space heater only has two actual heat settings—high and low—but there is a manual thermostat for controlling temperatures, which helps make up for the lack of power options.

The wide window of airflow and consistent heat distribution helps bring a room up to temp faster than most space heaters on this list, and this unit covers up to 300 square feet. One gripe: The battery hatch cover on the remote is tricky to remove. There is a holster for that remote control, though, making for one tidy package.

Full Lasko Oscillating Bladeless Ceramic Tower Space Heater Review

For a low-cost option, the Vornado MVH Vortex Heater heats a surprisingly large area—up to 256 square feet—with minimal noise. This unit worked well in a bedroom that has exterior walls on five sides, even during cold overnight temperatures. We like how simple, compact, and lightweight this unit is, and the appliance case stays cool to the touch, so you can move it around safely without concern.

The unit’s controls are a miss for us, though. While we liked the simple on/off button and the three-position toggle for heat levels, the thermostat dial is vague. The numbers on this dial range from 1 to 7, which don’t really show how warm each setting is.

As a result, we had to experiment with different settings until we figured out what worked best for us (you’ll likely have to do the same). Despite this drawback, the thermostat feature is helpful for when temperatures dip or get too high, as it manages the unit’s auto shutoff/on feature.

Full Vornado MVH Vortex Space Heater Review

It’s rare to come across a space heater that oscillates both horizontally and vertically, and that’s the feature we liked the most while testing the Dreo Whole Room Heater. It rotates 60 degrees up and down and 90 degrees from side to side for noticeably more coverage. Better yet, you can use both oscillation modes at the same time.

This space heater also has three heat and fan settings, and we appreciated being able to control the fan speed separately, even if we were running on high heat. Temperatures range from 41 to 95 degrees Fahrenheit, so we were able to truly customize the output. We kept our space heater at 73°F a majority of the time, and we never felt overheated or chilly.

The space heater comes with a remote, but there’s also a control panel on the base of the unit. The main thing we don’t like is that the remote was a little confusing to navigate at first. You have to use one button to access the fan speeds, heat levels, and temperatures, so we found ourselves clicking through a few times to get to the setting we wanted.

If your office is generally cold, then a heater small enough to sit on your desk might be the perfect solution for dealing with the frigid temperatures of your building. At only 12 inches tall, the Ellipse ceramic heater from Lasko is truly a compact model— discreet enough to tuck into the corner or underneath a workspace.

The highest settings pump out powerful heat in seconds, but there are medium and low settings if you want toned-down warmth. Temperatures are adjustable through the touch panel on the space heater.

We appreciate that even though this is a smaller design, it comes with its own remote. You can make the space heater oscillate and conveniently set a timer with the press of a couple buttons, and everything is viewable from the LED panel on the front.

The only thing we didn’t particularly like is that the Ellipse turns on at the highest setting automatically, so you’ll have to make adjustments almost immediately to find the ideal temperature and power.

A tech-facing space heater certainly has its benefits. The Lasko Therma-Smart tower heater has WiFi connectivity and pairs with the Aria home app for a virtual remote.

Connecting the heater was fairly easy: simply hold the WiFi button on the space heater for five seconds so it enters “pairing mode,” and then connect the device to the app. You can see wattage use and heat levels, and there’s a temperature dial in the center of the page to adjust to your liking. The Therma-Smart heater also pairs with Google and Alexa if you prefer to use voice commands.

Otherwise, the space heater has similar settings to other Lasko models that we recommend, like touch-sense controls and a digital window for viewing purposes. There are low, medium, and high heat settings, a max heat output of 1,500 watts, and a 12-hour timer function for running most of the day. One thing we noticed is that the oscillating feature seems to move very slowly, so you still might get hit with targeted heat if you’re sitting directly in front of the heater before it starts the rotation again.

The Lasko 751320 Ceramic Tower Heater is a reliable, mid-range option for homes and offices. Tester and Popular Mechanics editor Tom Price loves this model for its versatility. “The tower design and mid-sized build mean you can comfortably place it on a coffee table in the living room without it taking over the space. At the same time, it isn’t so small that I don’t feel the heat in larger spaces.”

The space heater has programmable controls that will turn the unit off and on after a certain period of time (or once the room has reached the desired temperature). It’s also equipped with an oscillating mode and comes with a multi-functioning remote control, too.

Although the gate on the front of the heater is designed to be cool to the touch, one aspect to keep in mind is that this unit does not come with an auto shutoff feature in case it gets tipped over.

A cold bathroom early in the morning feels like punishment, but a space heater on the floor near a bathtub or shower isn’t exactly a safe alternative. This fixed, wall-mounted unit from Dreo is a more reliable alternative. It’s IP24 waterproof-rated, so it’s protected against splashes from every direction, and has the same kind of ALCI plug you typically find on hair tools.

The bathroom heater accommodates spaces up to 200 square feet. With smart functionality, the companion app allows you to schedule timers, adjust temperatures, and change heat levels remotely.

Though this model has a child lock and a cool-touch exterior, we recommend mounting it out of reach of littles because the exhaust vent gets pretty warm.

If noise is one of your biggest concerns while shopping for a space heater, then an oil-filled radiator heater might be the right option. The Pelonis heater doesn’t use an internal fan, and offers the quietest noise operation on our list, maxing out right around five decibels.

It offers just about the same features as the ceramic heaters we recommend, with three different heating modes, tip-over security, and overheat protection. The heater has 360-degree warmth circulation, so you’re covered from every angle.

The radiator sits on four casters so it easily moves from room to room. It has a carrying handle, but it’s relatively small compared to the overall size of the unit and may overheat, so we recommend moving to your desired space before turning it on.

Simple, affordable, and versatile, these use electrical resistance to warm your space. A ceramic block or element is electrically conductive and heats up, and that heat is transferred to the air with an internal fan. The majority of the heaters on our list fall into this category.

Ideal use: These are great for general household use, shared offices, or wherever quiet heat is needed. Their simplicity makes them quite rugged; they have fewer parts to wear out or break.

This style of space heater emits infrared radiation rays that heat objects and individuals rather than the air, and it’s one of the more straightforward designs. They provide warmth almost instantly and aren’t loud while running, but they do have limited range.

Ideal use: Spot heating or small areas that need to be warmed up in a short amount of time.

These appliances burn propane or kerosene to warm an infrared emitter that projects the energy to heat your space. They’re considered convection heaters because they transfer thermal energy through a fluid, either by gas or oil.

They elevate the temperature of the air in certain spaces and are most suitable for delivering warmth in an area where you might walk around, like the surroundings of your desk or workshop.

Ideal use: Construction sites, garages, or work areas are the best places to use these heaters, since you want to place one at a comfortable distance and keep the work area unobstructed. Gas or liquid-fuel heaters direct the heat wherever you’re working.

Most residential space heaters use about 1,500 watts of power. If you’re using one of these devices as a primary heat source, it’s recommended to choose a model that offers 10 watts of heat output per square foot of space. 150 square feet is the common standard for coverage. You may consider investing in more than one unit if you’re trying to warm a larger space, or finding a design that has the right power combined with a fan or oscillating mode to disperse heat more evenly.

If you have pets or young children, then choosing a space heater with safety features is especially important for avoiding accidental burns and fires. The majority of the heaters on our list come with an automatic shut-off feature if it tips over. A good portion of our recommended heaters also include a timer to prevent the device from running for the entire day if you forget to shut it off.

During our testing and research journey, we learned some other valuable safety tips along the way such as the “three feet rule” (keeping the space heater at a distance from anything flammable) and not using these appliances in moist areas. But most importantly, you should never plug a space heater into an extension cord, power cord, or power strip. They’re not equipped for the electrical load that these devices require, and can be a potential fire hazard.

The short answer is it depends. Whether it’s “a lot” depends mainly on how long you run the heater and your local electricity rate. In the U.S., residential electricity prices typically range from $0.12 to $0.20 per kWh, with the average being around $0.17 per kWh as of December 2025.

Because most space heaters operate at 1,500 watts, they can cost between $0.18 and $0.30 per hour at average electricity rates. To find a more accurate estimate, divide the heater’s wattage by 1,000 to convert to kilowatts, then multiply that number by the number of hours the heater is running, and multiply that result by your electricity rate per kilowatt-hour (kWh).

These appliances aren’t intended to replace your home’s central heating system, so it’s better to use them supplementally if you don’t want to pay more on your electric bill.

You should turn them off when sleeping or left unattended. Common overnight hazards like a unit tipping over, bedding sitting too close to the heater, or an outlet overheating pose significant risks that you might not notice until you wake up. While most space heaters have preventative safety features like automatic shutoff or built-in thermostats, and may even be rated for continuous use, it’s best to resist the temptation of 24-hour warmth for safer operation.

#227. Something Unexpected Is Happening to Antarctica’s Collapsing Ice Cliffs

Satellite observations show Antarctic ice cliffs stabilizing after unexpectedly rapid collapse, challenging assumptions about runaway ice loss and its contribution to rising seas.

Antarctica’s ice shelves help hold back the ice sheet behind them, but rising temperatures are causing these supports to melt and break apart at record rates. As sheer ice cliffs are left exposed, scientists have worried that a collapse could reveal a taller cliff farther inland, setting off a chain of failures that eats into the ice sheet and raises seas worldwide.

In a four-year satellite survey of more than 15,000 Antarctic ice cliffs, researchers at MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) found that the tallest cliffs they examined closely did collapse, and the ice sheet in those regions retreated faster than models predicted. “But that retreat was short-lived,” says Caroline Needell, a graduate student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program.

Needell conducted the study, published in Science, with Catherine Walker, an assistant scientist at WHOI, and Jeremy Bassis, an associate professor at the University of Michigan.

The observations came from NASA’s Ice, Cloud, and Land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2), which passes over Earth’s polar regions. Its laser altimeter measures the height of ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice, as well as ocean levels in and around Antarctica. The team analyzed measurements collected every three months from 2019 to 2023 to determine how tall the cliffs were and how they changed over time.

Those measurements offered a much broader test of a proposed process called marine ice cliff instability, or MICI. In this scenario, a cliff exceeding a critical height collapses under its own weight. If that exposes a taller cliff, the failures continue inland. Previous studies had investigated this process by modeling ice’s physical properties, scaling those relationships up to entire cliffs, and combining the predictions with a few observations from Antarctica.

“Predictive ice-sheet models that have been used so far to represent ice cliff instability just take into account cliff height,” Needell notes. “That’s the only variable that matters. And once the cliff height reaches the critical threshold, usually 100 meters, it should initiate this runaway effect of ice sheet retreat.”

Across the satellite survey, the average ice cliff stood about 30 meters (98 feet) tall, well below that proposed threshold. A few rare cliffs exceeded 100 meters (328 feet), roughly the height of the Statue of Liberty, giving the researchers an opportunity to examine what happened near and above the predicted danger point.

“After we did that global analysis, we thought, ok, let’s zoom in on the tallest cliffs and see how they’re behaving,” Needell says.

The team focused on four cliffs in four regions around the Antarctic ice sheet. These cliffs were roughly 100 meters tall, with the tallest reaching 127 meters (417 feet). Tracking them through the same four years of measurements revealed that their rapid collapse and retreat did not continue unchecked. The ice eventually spread back out toward the ocean.

“It’s this rapid retreat, punctuated by periods of stabilization,” Needell says. “That was puzzling to us. Then, we thought: We need to look at all the things that affect cliff height.”

The researchers first examined the shape of the land beneath the ice. Over relatively flat ground, changes in the ice surface’s elevation reflect changes in the thickness of the ice itself. Where the ground rises, however, some of that elevation comes from the land underneath, leaving a thinner layer of ice above it. Such a rise could act as a speed bump for retreat by making the overlying ice less prone to collapse. When the team checked Antarctic topographic measurements, they found that cliffs stabilized around places where the underlying land rose.

Taller cliffs also “thin out” faster, the researchers found. As they collapse, they settle into shorter, more stable cliffs, limiting further collapse.

“Now we know what to look for,” Needell says. “We really need to know the bed topography, and we need to know the ice thinning rate, in order to get ice cliff instability right, because this value really matters in the context of projecting sea level rise.”

Conditions in front of the cliffs offered additional clues. In the broader survey, cliffs that stayed roughly in place had thicker mélange, the slushy mixture of broken icebergs and sea ice that collects against a cliff’s ocean-facing edge.

“We measured mélange height and found taller cliffs have thicker mélange, which could be a built-in stabilizing effect,” Needell explains.

The satellite data also indicated that deeper surrounding water could help keep a cliff standing. The water buoys the ice and pushes back against it, providing support that can make collapse less likely.

“We found that when the cliffs were retreating, they were doing so faster than what has been modeled, which would mean more ice loss and higher contributions of sea level rise,” Needell says. “But because we found that the retreat was short-lived, and all the glaciers eventually stabilized, that would suggest that things won’t be so bad. We don’t see this runaway effect.”

Reference: “Empirical constraints on ice cliff calving” by Caroline Needell, Catherine C. Walker and Jeremy N. Bassis, 15 October 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aee0658

This research was supported, in part, by NASA, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the DOMINOS project, a component of the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration.

I don’t see any incontrovertible evidence that the cause and effect are firmly established. That is to say, it seems plausible to me that ice calving isn’t responsible for an acceleration of the ice stream. A correlation has been established for calving and surging, but causation is still in play. It may well be that surging (acceleration) results in instability in the ice mass and therefore calving increases. Generally speaking, effects should lag the cause. I don’t see any temporal evidence presented that would resolve the question of cause and effect.

A rare discovery reveals that 75,000 years ago, a Neanderthal from Shanidar Cave in Iraq died a grisly death, likely from a wooden spear.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Neanderthal who was buried 75,000 years ago in Shanidar Cave in Iraq died from a wooden spear straight through the chest, archaeologists have revealed.

While it's impossible to know exactly what happened, the violence may have been a targeted hit.

"The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal's body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart," study first author Emma Pomeroy, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Cambridge, said in a statement.

In a study published Thursday (Oct. 15) in the journal Scientific Reports, Pomeroy and co-authors analyzed the bones of Shanidar A, a Neanderthal who died violently at about age 45 and was then buried in Shanidar Cave.

The archaeological site at Shanidar is famous for its evidence of purposeful burial, which experts once thought was only done by modern humans. Although the Neanderthal "flower burial" at Shanidar has since been debunked, the cave holds other evidence of repeated Neanderthal burials, which shows that these extinct humans placed specific meaning on that location, the authors wrote in the study.

The skeleton of Shanidar A was incomplete when it was discovered in 2019, consisting of a mostly complete right hand, three ribs, six teeth and a left scapula or shoulder blade, which meant they could not figure out the sex of the Neanderthal.

Near the edge of the shoulder blade, archaeologists noticed a round hole about 0.6 inches (1.5 centimeters) in diameter and a round piece of bone that had been punched out of the shoulder blade. The researchers ruled out post-mortem damage to the bone, including animal gnawing and insect burrowing.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

An example of a Paleolithic thrusting spear found in Germany. This may have been the kind of weapon that killed the Shanidar A Neanderthal.

"The perforation is best explained as resulting from perimortem [around the time of death] penetrating trauma, such as that caused by a projectile or a thrusting implement such as a spear," the researchers wrote in the study. Specifically, the Neanderthal was killed by a spear that entered their chest from the front at a high velocity and pierced their shoulder blade.

The shape of the wound in the shoulder blade appears to match experimental evidence of injuries made by wooden spears rather than stone-tipped weapons, the researchers wrote in the study. Neanderthals would have used wooden spears for both thrusting and throwing. But it is unclear if this individual died because of a violent interaction with another Neanderthal or by accident, such as a hunting incident.

"All we can ever know about the end of this Neanderthal's life is that it was violent, and came at the end of a wooden spear," study co-author Graeme Barker, an archaeologist at the University of Cambridge, said in the statement.

Even though this Neanderthal had an untimely demise, evidence on the teeth suggested that the individual was cared for during life.

The six teeth from Shanidar A were heavily worn-down in an unusual manner, the researchers wrote. One of them — a front tooth with a large quantity of tartar on it — had been split in half during the Neanderthal's life, and the individual continued to use the damaged tooth for a considerable amount of time. The collection of teeth suggests the Neanderthal sustained a major trauma to the face that fractured the lower front tooth and may have caused additional injuries to the jaw.

The Neanderthal's lower front tooth was fractured during life.

"There’s no doubt that Shanidar A would have had difficulty communicating and been in absolute agony for a long period of time," Pomeroy said in the statement. "Surviving a blow that splits a tooth in this fashion, then continuing to live and eat for a period of at least a year and maybe more, would have required care and support from other Neanderthals."

Rebecca Wragg Sykes, an archaeologist and author of "Kindred: Neanderthal Life, Love, Death and Art" (Bloomsbury, 2020) who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email that the apparently fatal chest injury is an important addition to our understanding of Neanderthals. While it is plausible the Neanderthal was stabbed by a wooden spear, Wragg Sykes said, "it would be interesting to also compare whether a wild goat horn, the most intensely hunted species at Shanidar, might have been responsible."

Shanidar A is not the first mortally wounded Neanderthal to be found at the site. In 2009, researchers analyzed the skeleton of Shanidar 3, an older adult male who died 50,000 years ago, and found a deep slice in one of his ribs. The researchers suggested that the Neanderthal may have been killed by a stone-tipped spear possibly thrown by a modern human. Although modern humans first reached Europe around 54,000 years ago, experts aren't sure exactly how they interacted with Neanderthals.

Pomeroy told Live Science in an email that the discovery at Shanidar of two stabbed Neanderthals 25,000 years apart is interesting but possibly just a coincidence.

"We know from the archaeology that Neanderthals were repeatedly coming back to Shanidar and using it for short periods at a time, both around 75,000 years ago and around 45-50,000 years ago, as well as leaving their dead there," Pomeroy said.

The traumatic injuries, purposeful burial and indirect evidence of wooden spears all show that 75,000 years ago, Neanderthal life — and death — were complex, the researchers wrote in the study.

Pomeroy, E., Hunt, C.O., López-Polín, L., Sala, N., Pantoja-Pérez, A., Holman, J., Twyman, J., Bennett, P., Reynolds, T., Lane, R., Pirrie, D., Barker, G. (2026). Evidence for funerary behaviour and lethal trauma in a new Neanderthal individual from Shanidar Cave. Scientific Reports. http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-69193-z

#229. Chandrasekhar Placed A Limit On White Dwarfs, But A New Study Finds This Limit Is Not Absolute

In the 1930s, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar placed a limit on stars. Using our understanding of relativity and quantum theory, Chandrasekhar demonstrated that white dwarfs could never have a mass greater than 1.44 suns. It didn't matter how they formed or whether they were mostly hydrogen or carbon. The very laws of physics forbid a greater mass.

White dwarfs are the remains of smaller stars such as the Sun. When such a star runs out of fusable hydrogen, it swells to a red giant in a mad race to burn heavier elements. But without enough mass to achieve that reliably, the star soon collapses into a nuclear shell. Gravity wins the day, and the star can burn no more. Without nuclear pressure, the core collapses under its own weight until the quantum pressure of electrons can push back. The stable balance between gravity and electrons is what keeps the star from collapsing into a neutron star. Chandrasekhar was the first to prove that relativistic electron pressure can only counter gravity up to 1.44 solar masses. It became known as the Chandrasekhar limit.

For decades this limit was thought to be rock solid. Theorists, forever bothered by limits, imagined ways a white dwarf might overcome this limit, but the observational evidence supported Chandrasekhar. This is part of the reason we can use Type Ia supernovae as a standard candle, since they are triggered by the collision of two white dwarfs. But then in 2003, the Supernova Legacy Survey observed a supernova that seemed to defy the Chandrasekhar limit. Perhaps the progenitor was rotating rapidly or hadn't fully collapsed when it exploded. As similar limit-defying supernovae were observed, the evidence began to chip away at Chandrasekhar's rock-solid prediction.

But how could a super-Chandrasekhar white dwarf possibly form? This is the question explored by a recent publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The study focuses on one way white dwarfs can break the limit: magnetic fields. If a white dwarf were to be highly magnetized, then the electrons would interact with the magnetic field in a way that gives them an extra boost. The magnetic field prevents them from settling down, meaning that they can push back more easily against gravity. In theory, such a white dwarf could be nearly 3 solar masses before collapsing. We know that neutron stars can be highly magnetized as magnetars, but they are formed from much larger stars. The key question is whether a Sun-like star could have such a strong magnetic field and still collapse into a white dwarf.

To answer this question, the team ran simulations using a modified version of STARS, which is used by many researchers to study stellar evolution. They added the effect of magnetic fields into the mix and modeled how a magnetic star evolves from the main sequence to a white dwarf. What they found is that a sun-like star doesn't need to be highly magnetized from the get-go. Even though a dying star casts off much of its outer layers as it swells to a red giant, the magnetic field remains with the star. As the core collapses to a white dwarf, the magnetic field is concentrated with the core. This means a highly magnetic white dwarf can form from a fairly typical star.

The study shows that magnetized white dwarfs may be more common than we thought. This study could help explain why some white dwarfs appear to be larger than their mass would predict, since magnetic fields would swell the star measurably. This could also explain events such as the 2003 super-Chandrasekhar supernova.

Sometimes when you test the limits of astrophysics, you learn something new about the Universe.

Reference: Zuraiq, Zenia, et al. "Super-Chandrasekhar White Dwarfs by the Evolution of Magnetized Main-sequence Stars: New Mass Limits from STARS Simulation." The Astrophysical Journal Letters 1010.1 (2026): L8.

Brian Koberlein is an astrophysicist and author of the books Astrophysics Through Computation and Radio Sky: 40 Years of the Very Large Array. You can find more of his work on his website.

#230. Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse

A massive volcanic eruption that struck Japan about 7,300 years ago had a devastating impact on prehistoric communities, but its aftermath was far more complicated than scientists once believed. While some populations declined or disappeared from affected areas, others continued to grow despite the destruction.

An international research team led by Lund University investigated how the Kikai-Akahoya eruption changed population patterns across Japan. Their findings challenge the idea that the disaster either completely wiped out nearby communities or left them largely unaffected. Instead, the researchers uncovered a surprising mix of population decline, migration, adaptation, and growth.

A Catastrophic Volcanic Eruption in Ancient Japan

When the Kikai-Akahoya volcano erupted beneath the sea approximately 7,300 years ago, Japan was home to Jomon communities that depended on hunting and gathering for survival.

"This eruption must have been devastating, exploding out of the seabed with little warning. It battered the Japanese islands with powerful earthquakes and enormous tsunamis, and then blanketed the landscape with meters of volcanic ash," explains senior author Peter Jordan, professor in archaeology at Lund University.

For decades, archaeologists have disagreed about what happened to the people living near the eruption. One theory describes an almost complete apocalypse, with human populations abruptly disappearing from areas closest to the eruption. Another suggests that some communities managed to survive even relatively close to the disaster.

The new findings indicate that neither explanation fully captures what happened. The eruption severely damaged ecosystems, forced people from their homes, and made some regions uninhabitable. Yet evidence also points to remarkable adaptability among survivors, with certain populations actually increasing after the catastrophe.

"The disaster caused major loss of life. However, survivors migrated, forged new social relations, innovated new kinds of economy, and appear to have found creative ways to exist and later thrive in the new post-disaster conditions," says lead author Enrico Crema, professor at Cambridge University.

How the Volcanic Disaster Reshaped Japan's Population

The researchers identified striking differences in how communities across Japan responded to the eruption.

In southern Kyushu, Jomon populations had already been shrinking long before the volcano erupted. By the time the disaster occurred, relatively few people remained in the region, which was primarily visited by highly mobile groups of foragers.

Northern Kyushu followed a very different pattern. Its population had been increasing before the eruption, and that growth continued through the catastrophe and afterward, even though the surrounding ecosystems experienced extensive and lasting damage. The researchers suggest that people fleeing the most severely affected regions may have contributed to this unexpected population growth.

Evidence also indicates that survivors who had lived inland relocated toward the northern coast. Marine ecosystems in these areas recovered relatively quickly, providing valuable food resources. By developing new ways to take advantage of the sea's abundance, these communities may have supported further population growth.

Perhaps even more surprising, the researchers identified population changes in parts of Japan much farther from the eruption.

These distant regions had experienced population growth before the catastrophe, but afterward, that growth stalled or even reversed. Such widespread demographic consequences had not previously been recognized.

Several possible explanations could account for these changes. The eruption may have caused temporary climate disruptions that affected communities across Japan. Another possibility involves severe tooth wear among deer and wild boar, two important food sources for the Jomon (possibly a consequence of the animals grazing in ash-covered landscapes). Other volcanic effects on human health and living conditions may also have contributed.

Together, these findings suggest that the consequences of a massive natural disaster can extend well beyond the areas experiencing the most immediate destruction.

According to Jordan, the results demonstrate that the effects of catastrophes are rarely straightforward. Even when faced with overwhelming destruction, human communities can respond in different ways, depending on their circumstances and the choices available to them.

"This study helps in creating a deeper understanding of the contingent ways in which cultures and societies cope with sudden shocks and catastrophes. Even in the most impossible situations, survivors and communities have choices, however limited: they need to act and make decisions; they need to adjust, collaborate, and find new connections and social networks," he concludes.

Materials provided by Lund University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#231. Scientists Solve a Quantum Mystery Hidden Inside Crystals

Tiny flaws in crystals could become building blocks for quantum sensors, and scientists can now better predict how these imperfections lose energy.

A laser can excite electrons at a tiny flaw in diamond or silicon carbide, but the energy does not always return as light. As the defect relaxes toward its lowest-energy, or ground, state, it can emit a photon, move between states with different electron spins, or release energy as vibrations of the surrounding atoms.

These spin defects could serve as stable, readable qubits, the units that hold information in quantum technologies, with potential uses in quantum sensing. Developing them requires understanding that entire cycle of excitation and relaxation. Physicists have used the fundamental equations of quantum mechanics to describe light emission and transitions between different spin states, but predicting energy loss through atomic vibrations, called internal conversion, has been harder.

Researchers at the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME) have now developed a computational framework that captures the full optical cycle, including internal conversion. Their study, published in Physical Review Letters, shows how accounting for this process can resolve a long-standing mismatch between predictions and experiments.

That discrepancy concerned a divacancy in silicon carbide, a defect formed by two neighboring missing atoms. The team’s calculations showed that internal conversion makes a substantial, previously overlooked contribution to the lifetime of its triplet excited state. Including that contribution brought the predictions into agreement with experiments, potentially informing efforts to develop this type of defect as a qubit.

“We were expecting to see an effect, but of a smaller magnitude,” said Giulia Galli, the Liew Family Professor of Electronic Structure and Simulations in UChicago PME and the Department of Chemistry and the study’s senior author. “What we found is that this internal conversion process turns out to be more important than we thought.”

For a nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond, where a nitrogen atom sits beside a missing carbon atom, the framework’s predictions matched recent spectroscopy measurements. Internal conversion contributed little to energy loss when triplet states were involved, but dominated energy loss from singlet states. These categories describe different arrangements of the electrons’ combined spin, and both results were consistent with previous assumptions.

“We provided the missing piece of the puzzle needed to completely describe the optical cycle of spin defects,” Galli said.

The obstacle to calculating internal conversion had been computational rather than a lack of fundamental equations. “Although the equations are known, it’s hard to describe the process accurately because of computational difficulties,” said Stefano Villani, a UChicago PME postdoctoral researcher and the study’s first author. “You need to account for complex interactions between the electrons and surrounding atoms, and that’s challenging in realistic solids represented by models with hundreds or thousands of atoms.”

Galli and Villani worked with Yu Jin, a former graduate student in Galli’s group who is now a postdoctoral scholar at the Flatiron Institute in New York, to combine several methods previously developed in the group. They described the defect’s excited states using many-body wavefunctions, mathematical descriptions that account for interacting electrons. Exact mathematical derivations then allowed them to calculate how strongly each excited state couples to atomic motion. The resulting formulation could account for the coupling between each defect state and all the vibrational configurations of hundreds of nearby atoms, rather than calculating those configurations one at a time.

“In the past, a clear mathematical derivation and efficient algorithms were not available,” Jin explained. “The new derivation came together after years of work on the optical cycle of spin defects.”

The team implemented the framework in WEST, an open-source simulation code optimized for graphics processing units, or GPUs. Galli’s group has developed WEST over the past decade within the Midwest Integrated Center for Computational Materials (MICCoM), which has received funding from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Basic Energy Sciences since 2015. With the framework already incorporated into the code, other laboratories can begin using it.

“Our work can now be used to make more accurate predictions about many materials of interest for quantum technologies,” Jin said.

“This internal conversion process is not only relevant to spin defects—it’s also related to processes of interest to energy technologies,” Galli said. “That’s one of the reasons this work is so exciting.”

Access to the code does not eliminate the computational demands, however. Galli cautioned that the framework still requires substantial resources. “We are working on ways to integrate machine learning into excited states calculations to further improve the efficiency of our method,” Villani said.

Alongside efforts to lower those costs, the team is extending the framework to spin defects in silicon and to a different class of materials used in renewable energy conversion and storage, where internal conversion plays an important role.

Reference: “First-Principles Calculations of Internal Conversion Processes in Spin Defects” by Stefano Paolo Villani, Yu Jin and Giulia Galli, 14 October 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/y6z6-h16k

#232. The Best Outdoor Pizza Ovens That Deliver Delicious Homemade Pies

We tested the Ooni Karu 2, Ninja Artisan, Gozney Tread, and others to find out which models are worth the dough.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Just like tending to the grill and gathering around a fire pit are inherently enjoyable, enjoying a fresh, piping-hot pizza is similarly rewarding, and it’s just a bit more special when it’s homemade. Baking a pie in the oven can yield good results, but there’s nothing like the crunchy crust and smoky flavor of a pizza made in a proper hearth. If you’re hoping to replicate your favorite restaurant’s pie, an outdoor pizza oven can take your homemade slices from decent to genuinely artisan.

Stand-alone and countertop outdoor pizza ovens reach much higher temperatures than regular ovens, and in less time. That high heat is exactly what you need for a perfectly cooked pizza crust—and several of the models we tested can cook up a pie in as little as 60 seconds.

Plus, many of the best outdoor pizza ovens we write about are suited for cooking other tasty foods, just like a real hearth. You can make fish, meat, roasted vegetables, and even bread in these wood-fired and gas-fueled models.

To find the best pizza ovens, we looked at models with good features and designs and called in a handful to try out for ourselves. We selected pizza ovens that use a variety of fuels, including gas, charcoal, and wood. Outdoor pizza ovens all pretty much come with a learning curve, but we identified models best suited to beginners and pizza aficionados alike to offer a range that caters to different skill levels.

For testing, we heated each oven for 30 minutes to season them and burn off any oils or contaminants from manufacturing, then let them cool completely. Fifteen minutes after firing up each oven on high using propane burners, we measured the temperatures on the pizza stones with an infrared thermometer.

Then, we made pizza, using the same dough each time, with propane and oak firewood as our fuel. During cooking, we noted how well each oven performed, different features, and their ease of use. Finally—and most enjoyably—we assessed (a.k.a. ate) the pizza. We recommend the following pizza ovens based on our hands-on experience, their specs, and quality.

Over a decade ago, Ooni built its first portable pizza oven with a design that many have mimicked. Our previous pick for the best pizza oven, the Karu 16, has been replaced by the Karu 2 Pro. It’s the exact same as the Karu 16 with three new features: an air vent, Bluetooth-connected thermometer, and an even larger window on the oven door.

Like the Karu 16, the Karu 2 Pro makes 16-inch pizzas fired either with propane or wood. In testing, we liked the locking door with a glass window, which helped maintain a consistent temperature and allowed us to keep an eye on our pizza while it cooked.

Ooni also added a digital thermometer to this model that monitors air temperature in the oven via a wired probe. That info is sent to your phone so you can be in the kitchen prepping more pies or enjoying company instead of babysitting the oven.

Using the propane burner is easy and gets the job done, but we appreciate the large firebox for wood, which provides a lot more flame across the top of the oven. The large capacity also had us refilling it less frequently than smaller wood-fired ovens.

The Karu 2 Pro also doubles as a capable charcoal grill if you want to cook meat or veggies. While we like a dedicated grill for burgers and steaks, the Karu 2 is a do-it-all outdoor kitchen if you have limited outdoor space. The addition of the new air vent even gets it down to a consistent 200 degrees Fahrenheit for low-and-slow cooking.

Full Ooni Karu 2 Multi-Fuel Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

The Ninja Artisan is the only electric outdoor pizza oven we've come across that's worth a double take. It needs to be covered if left outside because of the electrical components, but the body is made of weather-resistant steel.

There's no hassling with pellets or propane—simply plug it in, preheat, and start cooking. It has a max temp of 700 degrees Fahrenheitahrenheit, which is less than most gas and wood-fired ovens, but it's not necessarily a bad thing.

While a 1,000-degree oven that makes pizza in 90 seconds sounds easy, there's a lot more to it. Shredded mozzarella starts melting in seconds, the dough crust needs a minute to bake, and toppings may require a different cooking time. Electric temperature controls and a lower max heat offer more runway before taking off on your pizza-making journey. Another plus of an electric outdoor pizza oven is even cooking because there's no need to turn the pizza when it's in the oven.

The Ninja has built-in preset pizza modes to cook different styles of 'za: Neapolitan, New York, thin crust, and pan. It preheats to respective target temps for each and then prompts you to add the pizza. Hit start and it starts counting down for a perfectly timed cook.

We tried the thin crust setting, which cooked our pizza at 550 degrees Fahrenheit for four minutes. When the timer went off, out came an evenly cooked pepperoni pizza.

The Neapolitan setting worked great as well. It cooked the pizza at 700 degrees F for two and a half minutes yielding an impressively crisped crust with some leopard spotting.

Full Ninja Artisan Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

A lot of outdoor pizza ovens are portable enough to pick up and move, but they aren't designed with transportation in mind. Fair—most of us park them in the backyard. Gozney put more thought into portability than its competitors with the Tread pizza oven.

It weighs 30 pounds, has two handles on top, and has a manageable square shape. It can go from home to tailgate with ease. We tested the Tread with the collapsible Venture Stand, which gives you a cooking space wherever you take it.

Getting the Tread fired up only takes a few seconds when using the control dial on the side. The flames instantly extended across the roof of the pizza oven, and we wanted things to get hot, so we preheated for about 20 minutes. Once it reached an optimal temperature, we were ready to pitch the first pizza.

The compact size can fit up to 12-inch pies, which is plenty big for personal pizzas. In testing, we found that the oven has great heat retention, so you can cook them one after another. We also found the opening offered enough wiggle room to rotate the pie with a pizza peel for even cooking.

The Tread comes with a built-in thermometer on the side, but we still used an infrared heater to measure the temperature of the pizza stone itself. The quick-release gas hose and regulator make for quick setup, too. For those that plan to take the Tread on-the-go, Gozney also has a handy carrying case.

Full Gozney Tread Portable Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

You'd be hard-pressed to find an electric pizza oven that gets the job done like the original Ooni Volt, but the Ooni Volt 2 is an honorable step up. This model has a smaller carbon footprint than its predecessor, and it's even easier to use.

Messing with temperatures can get complicated quickly, but the Volt 2 has three presets for cooking Neapolitan, New York, and Chicago Deep Dish-style pizzas to perfection. We usually use an infrared thermometer to gauge the temperature of pizza stones, but we trusted the presets and weren't disappointed.

While this electric pizza oven doesn't exactly mimic a wood-fired or propane-fueled model, it has its place in the kitchen. The Volt 2 can be used all year long, is capable of cooking plenty of your favorites, and is much easier to manage. Even if you already have an outdoor model, we'd go so far as to say that you might need this indoor version, too.

Full Ooni Volt 2 Electric Pizza Oven Review

The brand best known for stainless-steel cookware has made an impressive outdoor pizza oven. The design is familiar with one addition—an automatic rotating pizza stone.

Typically rotating pizza stones are a gimmick you find on budget pizza ovens to make up for a low temperature range. All-Clad's pizza oven, however, has both firepower and an effective rotating stone that runs on four AA batteries and only requires a push of a button to start. The stone rotates at a slow, consistent speed to ensure even cooking.

All-Clad includes other niceties, like a built-in analog thermometer, matchstick holder in case the igniter fails, and an oven floor that's easy to clean. The pizza stone takes up the majority of the interior, so after cooking is done, it can be removed with little to no burnt remnants collecting at the bottom.

The directions are simple and straightforward to follow, though we wish there was a little extra in terms of cooking tips. As with all the other models on this list, we set aside some time to preheat the oven during testing. The All-Clad reached 900 degrees Fahrenheit in just over 10 minutes.

While we love the automatic rotating stone—as with anything—the more moving parts, the more potential for those parts to break. Overall, All-Clad's oven has great build quality, including the electrical box that houses the batteries. We expect it to last as long as the pizza oven is kept covered.

Full All-Clad Rotating Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

The Gozney Dome Gen2 is definitely a luxury pizza oven, but it's chock-full of features that could potentially make it a worthy investment for those who are dedicated to perfecting their pizza and baking crafts.

A 14-inch flue sits atop the roof of the oven, and this was helpful for maintaining airflow and flames. The Dome Gen2 comes with a standard propane burner, and the wood kit is optional. This helps simplify the process for newer pizza-makers, since wood-fired takes some time to master.

One of the highlights we appreciate the most is the size of the oven itself. After preheating, we had no problem cooking two midsize pizzas side-by-side, and we could move the pies around if we needed to slow the cook time.

It takes a little longer for the oven to heat up when using wood, but luckily, changing the fuel mode doesn't make the burner obsolete. We were able to fire up the oven with the burner first, then switched to wood when it reached the right temperature and turned off the propane.

We tested the Dome Gen2 on a somewhat windy day, and the propane burner blew out a few times. To offset this, we kept the temperature a little higher than usual and burned charcoal on the wood tray for better control.

The digital display is a very convenient feature. Instead of using an infrared thermometer, we could monitor levels in real time right on the pizza oven without worrying about accuracy.

Full Gozney Dome Gen2 Dual Fuel Pizza Oven Review

A pizza oven from the smokeless fire pit folks? Sign us up. The ease of cooking with a propane burner is tough to beat.

It took us about 20 minutes to heat up the oven using propane, though you should expect a bit more time when it’s relatively cool out and less when it’s hot. In testing, the average cook time was about 90 seconds and required turning the pie every 20 seconds or so.

The Pi Prime’s manual not only had thorough assembly instructions, but a lot of helpful notes and tips to get started, including suggested target temperatures for different styles of pizza.

We found that managing oven and stone temperatures didn’t take too much time, although like other ovens without a door, breezy or windy days could make it more challenging. The oven opening on the Pi is 13 inches wide, so 12-inch pies are about as big as this oven can handle.

Similar to Solo Stove fire pits, ventilation holes line the bottom of the pizza oven for plenty of airflow. The Pi Prime is also constructed with durable 304 stainless steel to withstand high temps and different weather conditions.

Full Solo Stove Pi Prime Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

The Arc Lite is about as analog as it gets, equipped with only a pizza stone, ignition knob, and stainless steel insulated housing to bake your favorite pies. While this model is smaller and less features-heavy than the Dome Gen2 we’ve tested, that doesn’t mean it’s any less effective.

It didn’t take long for us to get the Arc Lite up and running. We just connected the hose to the propane tank then pressed and turned the knob to ignite. It took about 20 minutes for the pizza oven to warm up on a cooler spring day, and we maintained an internal temperature of 800 degrees Fahrenheit. The Arc Lite reaches 950, but that high heat requires more attention so you don’t overcook your pie.

The pizza we made was ready in about 90 seconds, and had the crunchy crust and bubbly cheese we desired, and the only downside we really came across during testing is that the Arc Lite is limited on size and can only cook up to 12-inch pizzas. Great for everyday bites, but not ideal if you’re looking to host and make multiple pies at once.

Full Gozney Arc Lite Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

Outdoor pizza ovens use gas or wood to create flames across the top that radiate intense heat downward, warming the pizza stone—like preheating an oven in your house. However, unlike your home oven, outdoor pizza ovens can reach up to 950 degrees Fahrenheit.

Once the outdoor pizza oven hits cooking temperature and your pizza is placed inside, it only takes a couple of minutes to cook. The pizza stone or oven floor gets to the same temperature as the roof so the pizza cooks fast and evenly. While it cooks, those flames up top produce a golden crust that’s crispy on the outside and soft and airy on the inside. Because the pizza only takes a minute or so to cook, you can make a few with different toppings one after another.

Wood is the traditional fuel of choice for pizza ovens, favored for the smoky flavor it imparts in the crust and toppings. However, wood (or charcoal) fires take longer to heat up and require more attention to maintain the right temperature. That may not be an issue if you’re only making a couple of pies, but it can become a hassle if you’re cooking multiple pies for a large group, or entertaining a party while you cook.

Propane fuel can heat a pizza oven up rather quickly. Since it only takes around 15 to 20 minutes to preheat, it's hard to deny the convenience of being able to cook a pie in a relatively short time frame. Plus, cleanup is easy when there’s no ashy firebox to empty. Just keep in mind that a propane oven won't give you that unique, wood-fired flavor.

Luckily, you don't have to sacrifice one for the other: A few of the brands we recommend offer extra accessories you can buy to accommodate a different fuel type. There are even some options with combined fuel, so you can heat up your oven fast with the propane and imbue the pizza with wood-fired flavor, too.

The oven’s size determines the maximum temperature output the unit can reach, as well as the size of pie you can cook. Most outdoor pizza ovens are designed for 12- or 14-inch pies. Our Best Overall pick, though, can accommodate pizzas up to 16 inches for oversized, restaurant-like slices.

Pizzas are typically cooked between 450 and 600 degrees Fahrenheit. Classic Neapolitan pizza requires temperatures around 900 degrees—these are the ones with golden crusts, mottled with dark leopard spots. High-end models top out at around 950 degrees Fahrenheit.

The pizza ovens we recommend have max temperatures that far exceed 500 degrees, but note that an oven with a relatively low maximum temperature still gives you a delicious, cooked-through pie—it just may not look quite as picture-perfect.

In short, yes. Outdoor pizza ovens are incredibly versatile. Beyond pies, you can cook meats like steak and chicken, roast veggies, bake bread (like sourdough or focaccia), prep seafood, make cast-iron dishes, and bake desserts. Since it's essentially a super-hot wood-fired oven, you can use plenty of different methods to whip up your favorite foods.

Accessories aren't necessarily a requirement for operating your pizza oven, but they can make the process a lot smoother and safer. We recommend using tools such as a pizza peel to move and adjust your pie, an infrared thermometer to check stone temp accurately, heat-resistant gloves, and a brush or scraper for cleaning the stone.

Outdoor pizza ovens are generally easy to clean and don't require a ton of maintenance since their high temperatures naturally burn off a majority of food residue. Usually, you can just brush off ash and debris after the oven has cooled down. You can also occasionally run it at high heat to get rid of any extra stubborn bits, and wipe down the exterior as needed. Avoid using water or soap on the pizza stone to prevent cracking.

Women are using testosterone in the hope that it will treat their menopause symptoms, but little evidence supports the approach, experts say.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're approaching menopause, you are likely being bombarded by online ads for treatments promising relief for everything from hot flashes to brain fog. Some of these therapies have been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and have strong evidence to support them — but one hormone-based treatment that's gaining in popularity has much less science to back its use for menopause.

More doctors are writing their menopausal patients prescriptions for testosterone therapy. A 2026 study conducted in the U.S. recorded over 90,000 off-label prescriptions for testosterone to women in 2025, mainly among women ages 45 to 64 and those with diagnoses of menopause. This marked a 58.7% increase from 2024.

These prescriptions are "off-label" because the FDA has not yet approved testosterone as a treatment for menopause, perimenopause (the transition into menopause) or postmenopause (the time period afterward).

So, does scientific evidence support the use of testosterone to alleviate menopause symptoms? Or is it too soon to say?

While testosterone treatment for menopause has gained popularity, there's limited evidence to back up its use, experts say.

Although often called a "male" hormone, testosterone is also produced by females, albeit at lower levels than in males, on average.

There's a common misconception that females experience "androgen deficiency" — a marked decline in testosterone and related hormones — leading up to menopause, said Susan Davis, a professor of endocrinology and the head of the Women's Health Research Program at Monash University in Australia. This is not the case.

Rather, in females, testosterone levels tend to drop slowly between ages 20 and 60, and there's a slight rebound from age 60 onward. Menopause, which generally occurs around age 51 to 52, is not linked to a marked decline in testosterone. Estrogen and progesterone fluctuate during perimenopause and then decline sharply, and these changes clearly contribute to the telltale symptoms of perimenopause and menopause.

Placebo-controlled trials have not been able to show that testosterone treatment helps to alleviate brain fog or improve well-being, mood, bone density or muscle function in menopausal patients, said Davis, who has conducted a number of these trials herself.

"Telling women that fatigue, low mood, brain fog are symptoms of androgen deficiency is completely untrue," she emphasized.

On Sept. 17, the FDA held a public workshop to evaluate the evidence for testosterone therapy for menopause, concluding that more evidence is needed to fully assess the use of the hormone as a menopause treatment.

There is some evidence to suggest that testosterone might help to treat a condition called hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) in postmenopausal women. HSDD describes when a person has little to no sex drive and it causes them distress. Men and women of many ages experience it, so the condition is not unique to menopause. But it can sometimes develop in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women.

A review of 36 randomized trials involving 8,480 participants found that testosterone treatment delivered with skin patches was associated with 0.85 additional satisfying sexual events per month in postmenopausal women, compared to a placebo. This observed effect is not huge, Dr. Nanette Santoro, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, told Live Science in an email.

Of all the studies done to date, if there was a screaming benefit, you think you would have seen it.

Lately, anecdotal accounts of postmenopausal women having "fantastic sexual awakenings" after taking testosterone have been floating around, Santoro said. But these anecdotes haven't been backed by hard data yet. "Patients are being bombarded with a tsunami of information providing them with the most sky-high expectations imaginable," she said.

Notably, testosterone is not FDA approved as a treatment for HSDD in menopause yet. A drug called flibanserin, which affects serotonin in the brain, is approved to treat HSDD for pre- and postmenopausal women under age 65.

The placebo effect — when patients perceive an improvement in their health or well-being despite receiving a treatment with no active ingredient — can also complicate testosterone trials.

Davis said that in her patient groups, it's common for about 1 in 3 trial participants to report an improvement of their symptoms even though they are taking a placebo. Other trials have reported similar findings in their placebo groups, with about 30% to 40% experiencing some improvement in sexual desire and satisfaction, for example.

"I wouldn't say that there is definitely not a benefit," Davis said. "It's just that a benefit has not been shown."

One study trying to address this gap is the U.K. National Institute for Health and Care Research's ESTEEM trial. This large-scale, gold-standard trial aims to recruit hundreds of menopausal women and test whether using testosterone cream can reliably improve their quality of life. The cream will deliver testosterone through the skin and be applied to the lower abdomen and thighs. (Doctors often advise women to apply the creams in this way because those body parts are easy to hide if the treatment causes localized hair growth that the patients would prefer to conceal.)

The trial runners will track participants' symptoms linked to menopause, looking at sleep quality, memory performance, feelings of anxiousness, migraines, body mass, and overall well-being. The results of that trial are currently expected by 2028.

In the meantime, though, there isn't strong evidence that testosterone directly improves symptoms of menopause beyond HSDD. "Of all the studies done to date, if there was a screaming benefit, you think you would have seen it," Davis said.

Females' testosterone levels generally decline throughout adulthood, with a slight increase after age 60. However, there isn't a sharp dip in testosterone around the time of menopause.

Testosterone treatments available in most countries are not necessarily dosed for use in female patients. Only four countries — Australia, South Africa, New Zealand and the United Kingdom — have authorized a testosterone cream that's specifically formulated and dosed for women. These products differ from testosterone therapies for men in that they contain lower doses of the hormone. They are available to postmenopausal women with HSDD, specifically.

In other countries, such as the U.S., doctors are left trying to adapt medication dosed for males for their female patients, which can lead to a wide variation in dosing. And the effects of these different dosing regimens are poorly understood for female patients. "It is not necessarily unsafe to use male preparations for women, it's just that much, much less must be used," Santoro said.

Excessive doses raise concern about unwanted masculinizing effects, such as clitoral enlargement, voice deepening, hair thinning, baldness, and rapid growth of facial and body hair, Santoro said. (These masculinizing effects might be sought after in the context of gender-affirming care for transgender men and transmasculine people, but would often be undesirable for cisgender women.)

Additionally, the potential impacts of extra testosterone on cardiovascular health and breast cancer risk are poorly understood, Santoro noted. At lower doses, testosterone can cause mild acne, oily skin, and some increase in facial and body hair growth in postmenopausal women, trials have found; if these symptoms remain mild, they are generally considered acceptable.

Testosterone is being used off-label in the U.S., which means the "safety, efficacy and appropriate dosing for that use have not been evaluated and approved by the FDA," a spokesperson for the agency told Live Science in an email. The dosages and formulations approved for males "may differ substantially from what might be appropriate for women, whose testosterone levels and metabolic profiles are clinically distinct," the spokesperson said.

Anecdotally, Santoro encountered one female patient who had received very high levels of testosterone through an implant placed under the skin, which had been prescribed to her by a different doctor. She started losing her hair and seeing sizable growth in her clitoris, while her breasts started "shrinking away."

"Women are being prescribed some very big doses in North America, and no one studied the safety of these," Santoro said.

At the end of the day, Davis argues that women deserve to be given accurate information, given that navigating menopause can already feel like "swimming through wet cement." Good menopause care not only involves discussing potential pharmacological treatments, but also evaluating a patient's lifestyle, such as diet and exercise, and discussing societal pressures that often affect menopausal people. For instance, they may face pressure to maintain an active sex life and younger-looking physique.

When it comes to hyped therapies like testosterone, she said, "just be cautious about people who tell you they've got the answer that no one else has got."

#234. Scientists Simulated the Universe – And Discovered the Milky Way May Be One of the Best Places for Life

Galaxy simulations suggest the Milky Way offers some of the universe’s best conditions for life, while smaller, more crowded galaxies remain less forgiving.

Earth seems like a troubled place right now, but at least our cosmic surroundings appear peaceful. But this is not universally true, as explosions, collisions, and other dangers lurk in other places and times.

In our new research, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, we scoured simulated universes to find the friendliest locations for life.

We discovered something reassuring: the Sun, sitting here in the outskirts of the Milky Way galaxy, is about as good as it gets.

Regions of the universe that would be friendly towards life are known as habitable or Goldilocks zones – they’re just right.

Whether life is actually there is another question. As astronomers and biologists explore how life could form on exoplanets (planets outside the Solar System), astrophysicists follow the structure and evolution of the universe to identify the nicest places, as well as those where life could be snuffed out in an instant.

For example, there is a Goldilocks zone in the immediate neighborhood of stars. Too hot or too cold will not do. This “circumstellar habitable zone” is just right for liquid water instead of steam or ice.

Zooming out, we can look for the nicest places and times to live in our own Milky Way galaxy. A young star that’s too close to the galactic center will suffer in the hustle and bustle of all the nearby stars, whilst stars that are too far away will be in a sterile environment, devoid of the chemicals essential for life.

Just as Earth is in the Sun’s circumstellar habitable zone, the Sun is in the Milky Way’s “galactic habitable zone.”

Let’s zoom out even more. What about other galaxies?

We followed synthetic galaxy evolution using the EAGLE (Evolution and Assembly of GaLaxies and their Environments) project – one of the most realistic simulations of the observed universe.

They track the expansion of space, gravity’s pull, and the physics of gas, stars, and black holes, and provide us with a detailed map of what the universe looks like across hundreds of millions of light-years.

With such a map, we asked: where might life be most welcome?

With no observations of alien life, we must make assumptions. The hydrogen and helium produced in the Big Bang are too simple to make organisms, so we focus on generations of stars that have seeded the cosmos with heavier elements essential for life.

Exoplanet observations reveal that Earth-like rocky planets require a certain concentration of those heavier elements. However, too much could produce a hot Jupiter, a gas giant that sweeps through the planetary system, eating rocky planets on the way. This is best avoided.

Our breakthrough involves detailed modeling of those things that are bad news for life. Big stars blow up, sterilizing their local environment. Bigger explosions, such as gamma-ray bursts, can fry a much larger volume. Paleontologists think that the Ordovician mass extinction 450 million years ago might have resulted from a nearby explosion.

There are other dangers to avoid. We wouldn’t want another star to wander through our Solar System and disrupt Earth’s nicely circular orbit. So, steer clear of crowded galactic neighborhoods.

Then there are the black holes. Most of these are small and don’t pose any danger, but in the hearts of galaxies lurk monsters. Weighing more than a million suns, these can roar into life as they swallow matter that gets too close. So, stay away as this can result in intense radiation that can strip the atmosphere off your planet.

While we don’t know if life would form in these nice spots, they are the ones that offer the best conditions.

And the results tell us another thing: the Milky Way is rather nice.

This isn’t just a fondness for our own neighborhood. We could have found that life should exist in earlier galaxies, smaller ones, or farther from galaxy centers.

We find that our universe has created plenty of opportunities for habitation, though it seems to be slowing down as the rate of catastrophes catch up with the creation of new planets. Our Milky Way seems typical in the galaxies that have been efficient in turning the raw materials of the cosmos into life-friendly environments.

Similarly, the Milky Way, and its kindred, have put their energetic and dangerous days behind them and settled into a relaxed retirement. These days, even in a billion years of wandering around our Milky Way, less than one star in a thousand would experience an extreme, life-annihilating extinction event.

The story is different for smaller galaxies, which are far more numerous than the Milky Way, as they are too crowded and too energetic.

So, rest easy. And if you get the chance, buying a property in the Milky Way is probably a secure investment, astronomically speaking.

Reference: “Life in the cosmic neighbourhood: galactic habitable zones in the eagle simulations” by Luke A Barnes, Geraint F Lewis, Jaime Salcido, Pascal J Elahi, Miroslav D Filipovic and Richard G Bower, 5 October 2026, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. DOI: 10.1093/mnras/stag1750
