#235. Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief

Scientists at Mount Sinai have identified three important brain connections associated with long-term improvement in patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) for severe depression that has not responded to conventional treatments. The discovery could help researchers make this experimental therapy more precise and effective.

Published October 1 in the American Journal of Psychiatry, the research examined the largest group of patients assembled across multiple independent cohorts to date who had received subcallosal cingulate deep brain stimulation (SCC DBS) for treatment-resistant depression.

The researchers found that lasting improvements were consistently associated with electrical stimulation reaching three specific white matter pathways: the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.

These findings strengthen the case for using detailed maps of the brain's connections to determine exactly where electrodes should be implanted, rather than choosing their positions based primarily on anatomical landmarks. Known as connectome-based targeting, this strategy has already helped shape the ongoing Abbott TRANSCEND clinical trial, a randomized, controlled study that uses individualized brain connectivity maps to guide SCC DBS treatment.

"This study underscores the importance of individualized surgical targeting for achieving optimal outcomes with deep brain stimulation for depression," said Helen Mayberg, MD, Mount Sinai Professor in Neurotherapeutics and founding Director of the Nash Family Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. "In any randomized controlled trial of a neuromodulation treatment, precise lead placement and confirmation that the intended brain target has been engaged are essential first steps. We still have much to learn about which patients are most likely to benefit from stimulation of this particular target, but developing imaging-based signatures that can match patients to their optimal treatment remains a central goal of our research."

How Deep Brain Stimulation Targets Severe Depression

For people with treatment-resistant depression, standard therapies have failed to provide adequate relief. Researchers are investigating deep brain stimulation as a possible treatment for individuals living with severe, persistent symptoms.

The procedure involves surgically placing electrodes inside the brain to deliver controlled electrical signals to circuits involved in depression. However, positioning the electrodes correctly remains one of the greatest challenges.

Electrical stimulation does not simply affect the brain tissue closest to an implanted electrode. It can also influence larger networks through the white matter pathways that connect different brain regions. As a result, two patients with electrodes implanted in nearly identical locations may experience very different outcomes depending on which connections are actually stimulated.

Earlier research from Mount Sinai and Emory University helped establish the importance of these networks. In studies published between 2014 and 2023 in Biological Psychiatry, Molecular Psychiatry, and Nature, the teams identified white matter pathways associated with successful SCC DBS treatment and developed a method for planning electrode placement using brain connectivity maps.

The latest investigation sought to determine whether those connections were also important in patients treated at other research centers. Scientists also wanted to understand whether differences in the pathways reached by stimulation could help account for patients who did not benefit.

Three Brain Connections Linked to Lasting Improvement

To investigate, the researchers examined information from several clinical studies, including the BROADEN trial and a patient cohort at the University of Toronto, where SCC DBS was originally developed.

They used computer models of the electrical fields generated by implanted electrodes alongside maps of brain connectivity. This allowed them to estimate which pathways received stimulation and compare those patterns across different patient groups.

The results showed a consistent relationship between sustained improvement and stimulation of the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.

One finding was especially notable. Across the study sites, patients who had not responded to treatment after two years showed a lack of stimulation engagement with the left cingulum bundle.

The researchers did not investigate whether moving electrodes to reach this pathway would improve those patients' symptoms. Nevertheless, the pattern offers a possible explanation for why apparently similar electrode placements can produce different results. An electrode might be positioned in the correct general region but still fail to activate all the connections associated with lasting improvement.

"This study addresses an important question in DBS: not simply which area of the brain to stimulate, but which connections within that area need to be engaged," said Brian Kopell, MD, Director of the Center for Neuromodulation at Mount Sinai. "For a network disorder such as depression, millimeters can determine whether stimulation reaches the pathways we intend to modulate. Identifying and reproducibly engaging those pathways gives us a more precise surgical target and a framework for understanding why otherwise similar electrode placements may produce different clinical outcomes."

Toward More Personalized Depression Treatments

Although reaching these three pathways appears important, the researchers emphasize that electrode placement alone is unlikely to determine whether a patient improves.

The investigation concentrated on identifying the brain connections that should receive stimulation. Additional studies are needed to determine which individuals are most likely to benefit from SCC DBS and how electrical stimulation should be adjusted as treatment continues.

There were also limitations to the brain imaging data. Individual diffusion MRI scans, which can provide information about a person's white matter connections, were not available for every participant. Consequently, much of the analysis used generalized maps of brain connectivity rather than maps created specifically for each patient.

For the Emory patient group, the researchers were able to compare results obtained from generalized connectivity maps with those based on individual diffusion imaging. Both approaches produced consistent findings, providing further support for the importance of the identified pathways. However, more research is needed to establish the value of patient-specific imaging.

Future investigations will explore whether additional brain imaging measurements, including white matter integrity and functional connectivity, can help identify suitable patients, improve electrode placement, and guide treatment settings.

"Our findings show precisely engaging these white matter pathways is a critical first step toward sustained response," said Ki Sueng Choi, PhD, Associate Professor, Imaging Core Leader at the Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at Mount Sinai, and corresponding author of the study. "The next step is to characterize abnormal functional and structural brain states along these pathways to build more detailed models for setting patient-specific stimulation parameters, including amplitude, frequency, and pulse width, for precision medicine."

By combining increasingly detailed brain maps with personalized stimulation settings, scientists hope to better understand why some people experience lasting relief while others do not. The findings represent another step toward developing more targeted treatments for severe depression, although further clinical research is necessary to establish how much these approaches can improve outcomes.

The research received support from the National Institutes of Health BRAIN Initiative through grant UH3NS103550, the Hope for Depression Research Foundation, and the DANA Foundation.

Abbott's Neuromodulation business supplied data from the BROADEN clinical trial but did not participate in designing or analyzing the current study.

#237. The 8 Best Electric Scooters Built for the Daily Commute—And Beyond

These reliable models give you a comfortable, safe commute and offer good range, top speeds, and anti-theft features.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Instead of driving for every short trip to the store or commute to work, hop on an electric scooter and zoom through your neighborhood. Electric scooters are easier to ride than electric skateboards and more portable than electric bikes, so they’re a great alternative for city-dwellers who don’t have the space for a car or would prefer a smaller mode of transportation for short distances.

These days, there are plenty of affordable and durable electric scooters available. Options range from electric scooters built for just a few miles of daily commuting to ones designed to handle uneven trails, high speeds, and long distances. We tried out electric scooters on our own commutes to find the best.

What Are the Laws for Riding E-Scooters?In many areas, electric scooters aren’t allowed on sidewalks, so check whether you need to ride in bike lanes before you jet around. Some areas have speed limits on small electric vehicles like scooters and e-bikes. For instance, in Florida, e-scooters with seats must be registered and have a title and license plate, so check your local laws before you opt for one of our seated options. Similarly, there are some restrictions based on battery size and type.

If you’re looking for a scooter that can do just about everything well—with a long range to boot—check out the Segway Ninebot Kickscooter Max. It can go up to 40 miles on a single charge, handle slopes up to 22 degrees, and carry riders up to 265 pounds.

Its 10-inch pneumatic tires are great at absorbing bumps in the road, and it folds easily for storage. The tires are “self-sealing,” meaning an interior liner will automatically fill in punctures for a short-term patch. It’s not a permanent solution, but even if you roll over a nail or sharp rock, you’ll be able to continue driving without stopping for an immediate replacement. At just over 40 pounds, this Ninebot is heavier than some commuter scooters. But some of that comes from the bigger battery for extended range.

While 40 miles won’t take you on long-range adventures, it should last for multiple weeks of scootering around town. The Ninebot is the second most expensive of the scooters we recommend. But considering how well-rounded this e-scooter is, it’s the best for most people.

The GoTrax XR Elite needs to be on your radar if you’re looking for an electric scooter that doesn’t take a bite out of your wallet. At just 32 pounds, it’s one of the lightest and easiest to carry among the scooters here. This is further amplified by the foldable design and slender frame.

This scooter has an estimated range of 16 miles, a top speed of about 15 miles per hour, and a max incline of 15 degrees. What really sets it apart from the others is the affordable price given the quality performance. This costs about $400 less than the Segway Ninebot Kickscooter Max.

While the XR Elite isn’t built for long distances or top speeds, it’s a perfect choice for puttering around town. Moreover, its battery charges in just four hours, allowing you to get around sooner if need be.

Very few electric scooters offer the balance of affordability and performance that the Gotrax G3 Max does. With a maximum range of 37 miles, the scooter is ideal for daily commuting back and forth to work without the constant need to recharge.

Beyond this, the scooter is equipped with a number of features that caught our eye, including the integrated number lock on the body that dissuades thieves by preventing them from actually being able to unfold and ride the scooter without the right code.

The G3 Max also comes with an LED display showing your speed, speed modes, mileage, and battery life. There’s an LED headlight for riding at night too.

Full Gotrax G3 Max Electric Scooter Review

Don’t confuse this electric scooter with a bike or moped. Built with a seat and basket, the Flex Ultra from Gotrax is more than just a quick commuter.

When testing this scooter, I took it from Central Park all the way back to my apartment in Brooklyn. I had my backpack, which weighed over 20 pounds, in the basket, and I sat on the seat for the majority of the trip.

What I noticed immediately was the zip of the motor as I got close to 20 miles per hour on straightaways and churned up the incline of the Queensboro Bridge without losing momentum. I also have to admit that I loved the seat. Instead of standing for over 30 minutes on the ride back, I could rest a bit more while still making better time than I would on the subway.

The throttle is responsive, and the larger 14-inch wheels stood up well to the potholes on the streets and cracks on the pavement. While its size prevents it from being an easy storage item in a closet—even though it folds—this electric scooter comes with the power, comfort, and convenience for quick grocery trips and long city commutes alike.

With a 34-mile range and a top speed of 20 miles per hour, the Ninebot E3 Pro is an ideal commuter scooter balancing speed and range. It’s also quite durable, with an alloy frame boasting an IPX5 water resistance for riding through puddles, rain, and even mud.

Furthermore, the electric scooter is a relatively quick charge, going from zero to fully charged in 7 hours. This means you can plug it in overnight and ride out in the morning on a full charge with no worry. Alongside an LED headlight, the scooter comes with lighting underneath the board so you’ll have full visibility at night.

The headlight and under-board lighting are paired with real turn signals as well, so you don’t have to take your hands of the handles to let drivers around you know which direction you’re headed.

Full Segway E3 Pro Electric Scooter Review

This lightweight and affordable scooter won’t take you everywhere with just a 16 mile range, but you can take it anywhere you please. The scooter is small enough to fold up and carry without feeling like it’s dragging on your arm after a few minutes.

While it won’t exactly disappear under a desk, it’s probably one of the few that will fit with ease in a storage closet or under the bed at home. At the same time, you can toss it in the back of your trunk and take it out whenever you go to the park.

The hollow tires also mean you’ll never run flat and don’t need to worry about inflating them after a few winter months out of use.

Have you ever wanted to take a load off while riding but don’t want a permanent seat? The Gotrax Eclipse offers the best of both worlds. The electric scooter comes with a detachable seat so you can plop down if you know you have a long ride ahead, but can take it off and leave it at home when portability and foldability take priority.

The scooter is more than just the seat as well. With a top speed of 25 miles per hour and a max range of 38 miles, this is a performance-focused option that is great for longer commutes and open streets.

At the same time, the electric scooter has a small rear shelf that can be used to securely tie down small packages and backpacks so you can actually use it for carrying more than just yourself.

Reaching speeds of over 30 miles per hour and boasting a range of 45, this electric scooter from Segway is aptly named the SuperScooter GT3. This heavy-duty option is designed with performance as the end all, be all priority. In fact, in combination with its 11-inch self-sealing tires, the SuperScooter GT3 is one of the few electric scooters that is legitimately well-equipped to handle gravel, dirt, and general off-road adventures.

Beyond pure power and battery, the electric scooter comes with one of the most useful displays that we’ve found. The full color screen comes with smart technology that connects to your phone so you can receive notifications and access navigation routes in real time.

That said, before you click buy, make sure it’s actually legal to ride in your city. Electric scooters of this speed and size are often highly regulated and illegal to ride in densely populated cities across the United States.

An electric scooter’s range is based on battery and motor size and is impacted by a number of factors, including rider weight, weather conditions, surface type, and incline of the roads you travel on. The ranges we include are based on the manufacturers’ claims, and your real-world use will vary.

Many scooters get up to 10 miles, while some can last for up to 40 miles or more on a single charge. Some have various drive settings that help you get the most juice out of your battery based on the type of ride you’re on. For instance, if you’re trying to conserve power for a longer trip, many options have a low-power or eco mode, which reduces top speed or acceleration for the sake of saving the battery. Furthermore, if you want to extend your scooter range as much as possible, consider routing yourself on smooth flat roads with little incline that don't require lots of stopping and starting.

Most of the e-scooters we recommend top out between 15 and 20 mph. That should be fast enough to zip along city streets and paths without feeling like you’re falling behind.

The only exception to this speed range is the Navee XT5 electric scooter, which reaches a top speed of 31 mph. However, if you’re seeking a quicker commute or more of a thrill, there are other e-scooters that reach speeds up to 60 mph. We didn’t recommend any of those because many states and cities have banned them or require you to gain an additional license to use them.

Electric scooters often have motors with a power rating between 250 and 350 watts. This is enough for most daily city commuting. If you’re a heavier person or expected to ride up steep inclines, you may want to opt for a scooter with a larger, more powerful motor. High wattage motors offer significantly more torque and acceleration but typically come at a premium. Their size also makes them heavier than lower wattage motors, which can make the scooter more cumbersome to carry or transport when not in use.

Almost all electric scooters have rubber tires, whether they’re solid, tubeless, or tires with inner tubes. Solid rubber tires are the longest-lasting and are ideal for those making shorter rides on smooth streets, but they also absorb less shock than their tubeless counterparts.

Tires with inner tubes were more common in the past, but we’re starting to see more tubeless and tube-ready tires today. Both tubeless and tube-ready tires can suffer punctures, but offer more cushioning during a ride than solid rubber models.

If you plan on riding a scooter in the early morning or night, look for a scooter with good front and rear lights. It’s also a good idea to look for a scooter with a horn or bell to warn bikers, pedestrians, and other scooter riders that you’re approaching. Some high end scooters also come with board lights and turn signals for additional visibility in the dark.

All scooters should have good brakes as well. Some only have them on one wheel, but more powerful scooters that need to decelerate quickly should have front and back brakes, and possibly a motor brake so you don’t go flying down a hill faster than intended. Motor brakes can also provide some regenerative braking, extending the scooter’s range slightly as you ride.

Some other extras to look for on electric scooters are items like seats or baskets. These are great to have if you prefer a seated ride and/or if you plan on using the scooter for errands, like grocery shopping.

In selecting these electric scooters, we rode multiple options. We used the scooters in daily work commutes to test their power, speed, range, and comfort over distance. This included trips over long bridges, on steep inclines, and many times, on streets without bike lanes. We also gauged how the acceleration and brakes felt in our hands, and how smooth the scooter stayed when riding over bumps or uneven asphalt.

For scooters we haven’t tested yet, we based our picks on research, evaluating the opinions and ratings of professional reviewers, as well as checking out customer reviews and rankings, and evaluating each model’s most important specs like wattage, range, and safety features. We chose reputable brands, selecting electric scooters that are not only the highest-performing models on the market, but also the easiest to find in stock.

Tom Price is a reviews editor for Popular Mechanics while also contributing to Runner's World, Best Products, and Bicycling. Here at Popular Mechanics, Tom loves testing out home appliances, smart tech, gear for city life and outdoor adventures, small gadgets like watches and multitools, and anything else you can find piled up at his hoarder's nest of a desk.

Prior to working here, Tom attended NYU, graduating with a degree in English and a minor in creative writing. He also wrote for Best Reviews, The Daily Beast, and other publications covering tech, fitness gear, gadgets, and lifestyle products. Furthermore, he covered startup news, pop culture, and even professional wrestling. To follow more of his work, check back here for new stories.

Rachel is the Deputy Editor of Reviews for Hearst's Enthusiast and Wellness Group where she supports Popular Mechanics, Runner's World, and Best Products. Her background is in service journalism and earlier in her career she worked as a daily newspaper reporter and book editor. She spent more than a decade as a staff editor and writer at TripAdvisor and Penguin Random House and her byline has appeared in Time Out New York, the New York Daily News, and New York Magazine. Outside of work, Rachel can be found planning her next trip, visiting museums and galleries, and walking her wirehaired dachshund in Central Park.

Movement-induced flares in chronic back pain activate brain regions involved in self-reflection, suggesting chronic pain may be processed differently than acute pain.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For people with chronic back pain, everyday movements like bending down to tie their shoes or picking up a grocery bag can trigger painful flare-ups. Now, scientists have made a surprising discovery: These episodes may activate a brain network that's associated with our sense of self.

In a new study, the researchers found that movement-induced chronic back pain was tied to increased activity in the brain's default mode network, a group of connected brain regions that lights up during self-reflection and mind wandering. This finding was unexpected because the network typically becomes less active during acute pain, such as transient pain triggered from touching a hot stove or banging your knee on a table.

The new study, published Oct. 5 in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, suggests that chronic-pain flare-ups may involve brain processes beyond those responsible for detecting painful sensations.

Chronic lower back pain, defined as lasting at least three months, is a leading cause of disability worldwide. It's thought that when chronic pain first begins, a network of regions in the brain called the "pain neuromatrix" becomes sensitized so that the pain persists even after the painful stimulus is gone. Although scientists know that chronic pain is associated with changes in brain activity, they don't fully understand what happens when movements trigger sudden increases in that ongoing pain.

To investigate, researchers recruited 114 adults with chronic lower back pain and used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine their brain activity. fMRI measures changes in blood flow, which acts as an indirect measure of brain activity.

After an initial scan, a researcher helped lift each participant's leg until their back pain increased, held it in position for 10 seconds, and then lowered it. The researchers scanned the participants' brains immediately after this pain-inducing leg movement and compared the results with scans collected beforehand. On average, the test increased the participants' reported pain intensity by 23%.

As expected, during the leg movement, the researchers observed increased blood flow in brain regions involved in processing pain and movement. But they also detected increased activity in key regions of the default mode network, which typically becomes more active when a person is thinking about themselves or their autobiographical memories or just letting their mind wander.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

We expected it to be deactivated to the point that we had to triple-check our work to make sure that the results were legit.

Acute pain lowers activity in the default mode network, studies show, presumably because it induces an awareness of something separate from yourself.

"When we saw just the first round of analysis, we're like, 'Did we do it right?'" study co-author Morgan Gianola, a postdoctoral scholar at the University of California, San Diego, told Live Science.

"We did not expect [the default mode network] to be involved at all," said study co-author Fadel Zeidan, a neuroscientist at UC San Diego, told Live Science. "We expected it to be deactivated to the point that we had to triple-check our work to make sure that the results were legit."

The researchers also exposed participants' calves to painful heat ‪—‬ a common method of studying brain activity during acute pain. Unlike the movement-induced back pain, the heat was associated with reduced activity in part of the default mode network, suggesting a different mechanism was at play.

Participants who reported more severe chronic back pain had stronger connectivity between the default mode network and brain regions that process sensations from the back. This suggests that chronic pain may become intertwined with how people perceive themselves and their bodies, the study authors concluded.

"This pain flare has almost become a part of who they are from an egocentric perspective," Zeidan said.

Katherine Martucci, a neuroscientist at Duke University who wasn't involved in the study, praised the experimental design, noting that researchers typically avoid movement during brain scans because it can interfere with the clarity of the scan. This study "nicely gets around" that problem by taking scans before and after the painful motion, Martucci told Live Science in an email.

However, she noted that the observed brain activity could also reflect lingering pain or anxiety following the painful leg raise. In addition, the study couldn't determine whether the altered brain activity observed contributes to chronic pain or develops in response to it.

Nonetheless, Zeidan and colleagues think the findings could eventually inform future treatments for chronic pain. The therapies might address how people relate to their pain, rather than solely targeting the painful sensations themselves. Zeidan, who coincidentally developed chronic back pain while conducting the study, believes that people's past experiences and memories with chronic pain have influenced their brain processes to a point where the pain itself becomes part of who they are.

Zeidan's team is now investigating whether existing approaches, such as mindfulness meditation or cognitive behavioral therapy, can influence the default mode network and help relieve chronic pain. (Cognitive behavior therapy for chronic pain, or CBT-CP, is already a well-established treatment option.)

Martucci cautioned that it's too early to draw conclusions about how these results might be applied in clinical practice. But she said the current findings provide important evidence of how the brain responds to chronic pain flare-ups.

"They do provide solid data on how people with chronic low back pain show important changes in their brain responses after a condition provoking their pain," she said. "The brain imaging data validate their [the participants'] experience of pain in an important and very visible way."

#239. Scientists discover that male and female skin play by different rules

Female mice heal skin wounds faster than males, and scientists have uncovered a surprising biological difference that may help explain why. By watching skin stem cells in living mice for five months, researchers found that female cells work together in a more coordinated way, while male cells tend to behave more independently. These differences are regulated by sex hormones and could eventually help scientists develop more personalized treatments for wound healing and skin diseases.

The discovery comes from researchers at the Université libre de Bruxelles (ULB), working with scientists at the University of Cambridge. Their findings suggest that biological sex influences how skin renews and repairs itself, even though the skin is not part of the reproductive system.

Historically, much of the research into biological differences between males and females has focused on reproductive organs. However, sex can also influence other tissues and organs throughout the body. Understanding these differences could be important for improving the prevention and treatment of inflammatory diseases and cancer, yet researchers have often overlooked their significance.

Published in Nature, the study was led by Prof. Cédric Blanpain, MD/PhD, an investigator at the WEL Research Institute, director of the Laboratory of Stem Cells and Cancer, and professor at the Université libre de Bruxelles. The research was conducted in collaboration with Prof. Benjamin Simons and his team at the University of Cambridge, along with scientists from several other institutions.

Using an advanced microscopy technique, the researchers were able to record individual cells through the skin of living mice. This allowed them to follow the same stem cells and their descendants for five months, an unprecedented period of observation. Although their original goal was to understand the mechanisms behind skin renewal, the team unexpectedly discovered striking differences between females and males. Further experiments revealed that sex hormones were responsible.

The skin's outermost layer is constantly replacing itself. This process begins with stem cells located at the bottom of the layer, where they divide to produce new cells. Some of the resulting "daughter" cells retain their ability to function as stem cells, while others begin developing into specialized cells.

These specialized cells form the protective barrier that shields the body from its surroundings. As they mature, they lose the ability to divide (a process called differentiation), gradually move toward the surface, and are eventually shed.

Scientists have debated the precise organization of this renewal process for decades. By repeatedly observing the same areas of skin over five months, the researchers found that stem cells do not immediately become fully mature skin cells.

Instead, they pass through an intermediate stage in which they can divide only a limited number of times before completing their development into specialized cells. This finding helps clarify a long-standing question about how the skin maintains itself.

Female Skin Cells Work in Surprising Synchronization

One of the most unexpected findings involved the behavior of newly formed cells.

In female mice, two "sister" cells produced by the division of a single parent cell frequently make the same developmental decision at the same time. Both may divide again, or both may begin specializing into mature skin cells.

Their behavior resembles two rowers moving their oars in unison. In male mice, however, sister cells are less closely synchronized and tend to follow more independent patterns.

"We initially set out to understand how the skin renews itself, and whether there is a hierarchy with stem cells at the top. We were surprised to discover strong differences in the way stem cells renew the skin in females and males," explains Doctor Dan Engelman, the first author of the study.

Sex Hormones Control How Skin Cells Behave

To determine what caused these differences, the scientists investigated the influence of male and female sex hormones.

They first examined what happened when male mice were castrated, removing the primary source of testosterone. Without this hormone, their skin cells began behaving more like those in females. When the researchers administered dihydrotestosterone (DHT), an active form of testosterone, the cells returned to their typical male pattern.

These experiments showed that male sex hormones help regulate how rapidly skin cells mature and move out of the stem cell layer.

The team also investigated the role of female sex hormones. Removing the ovaries (ovariectomy) reduced the rate at which stem cells multiplied and almost completely eliminated the characteristic synchronization between sister cells.

Treatment with estradiol, a form of estrogen, reversed the reduction in stem cell proliferation.

Together, these findings revealed that testosterone, which is generally more abundant in males, influences the speed of skin cell maturation. Estrogens, which are generally more abundant in females, promote stem cell proliferation and help coordinate the behavior of newly produced cells.

The researchers also tested testosterone on human skin reconstructed in the laboratory. They found that the hormone accelerated stem cell differentiation, suggesting that at least part of the mechanism observed in mice may also operate in humans.

Why Skin Wounds Heal Faster in Female Mice

The differences in stem cell behavior were accompanied by another important finding: female mice recovered more quickly from skin injuries.

When researchers examined wounds on the animals' backs, they found that wounds closed substantially faster in females, particularly during the first few days after injury.

This early advantage was partly associated with skin stem cells becoming active sooner and working in a more coordinated manner. As healing progressed, the difference between males and females gradually became smaller.

The results suggest that the hormonal regulation of stem cells may help explain why skin repair differs between the sexes.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Wound Healing and Skin Cancer

Doctors have long recognized differences between men and women in wound healing, the severity of certain inflammatory conditions, and the frequency of some skin cancers. However, the underlying biological explanations have remained incomplete.

By identifying how sex hormones influence stem cell activity, the new research provides a possible explanation for some of these observations.

The findings could eventually contribute to medical treatments that account for a patient's sex. Potential applications include improving recovery from burns and surgery, as well as treating chronic wounds in people with diabetes, a problem affecting millions worldwide.

Understanding these differences may also help researchers develop new approaches to preventing skin cancer, one of the most common forms of cancer.

For now, faster wound healing and coordinated stem cell behavior were demonstrated in mice. Additional research will be needed to determine how closely these processes match those in human skin and whether they can be used to improve medical care.

Beyond their potential clinical importance, the findings also provide new insight into the fundamental process of skin renewal, helping address a question that has challenged scientists for decades.

"This study is a technological tour de force, and the discovery of differences between male and female skin stem cells is fascinating and entirely unexpected. It sheds light on a series of clinical observations that previously lacked a biological explanation. It opens up a wide range of new questions, spanning from fundamental stem cell biology to clinical issues such as wound healing, cancer development, and autoimmune diseases. Sex is a parameter too often overlooked in biology and medicine. We will now investigate the differences between males and females during the formation and progression of skin cancers, as well as the molecular mechanisms responsible for these differences," says Prof. Cédric Blanpain, who led the study.

The project brought together Prof. Blanpain's team (ULB, Belgium) and Prof. Simons' group (University of Cambridge, UK), along with research teams led by Michele De Luca (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, Italia), Yulia Shwartz (Broad CIRM Center, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, US) and Esther Hoste (VIB-Ghent University, Belgium).

Funding was provided by the FNRS (including FRIA fellowships), TELEVIE, the WEL Research Institute, the Fondation contre le Cancer, the Fondation ULB, the Fonds Erasme, the Fondation Julie et Françoise Drion, the Fonds Yvonne Boël, the joint FNRS/FWO EOS (Excellence of Science) program and the European Research Council (ERC).

A study of DNA from early colonial-era skeletons in a Montreal cemetery has revealed that none of them had any Indigenous ancestry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ancient DNA from skeletons buried in a historic cemetery in Quebec is changing people's understanding of their Indigenous ancestry. Contrary to popular belief, there may be little truth to stories of intermarriage between Indigenous and French people during the early days of colonization, according to a new archaeology study published Oct. 5 in the journal PNAS.

"Family stories of an Indigenous ancestor are very common" in Quebec, study first author Diane Martin-Moya, a biological anthropologist at the University of Quebec in Trois-Rivières in Canada, told Live Science in an email, and "commercial genealogy and DNA tests have amplified this." But distant or claimed Indigenous identities can actually undermine the rights, resources and recognition of Indigenous nations, she said.

To learn more about the founders of Quebec, Martin-Moya and co-authors investigated Notre-Dame Cemetery, which was established in Montreal in 1683 and used for Catholic burials until 1796. Based on previous studies of the skeletons in the cemetery, experts disagreed on whether people of Indigenous, European, African or mixed ancestry were buried there. To settle the question, Martin-Moya and her colleagues sequenced DNA from 45 people buried in the cemetery and compared it with the genomes of people from Europe, West Africa and Indigenous groups in the Americas.

"The ancient DNA showed that all 45 individuals we analyzed had French European ancestry, with no sign of recent Indigenous or African admixture," Martin-Moya said of the research, which she conducted while at the University of Montreal.

These findings suggest that people descended from Indigenous and African populations may have been marginalized in early Montreal, challenging the popular narrative of cooperation and intermarriage, she said.

"Our sample is small and comes from a single cemetery, so this does not show that such unions never happened," Martin-Moya cautioned. "It is, however, consistent with genealogical and genetic studies suggesting that Indigenous ancestry among present-day French Canadians is very limited."

The apparent lack of genetic mixing among European, African and Indigenous populations in this cemetery group "provides a perspective on population relationships during the colonial period, one where perhaps nongenetic interactions were present but no biological relationships were found," Raquel Fleskes, a molecular anthropologist at Dartmouth College who was not involved in the research, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The DNA helped the researchers find several genetic lineages of people that spanned multiple generations. But the graves were scattered across multiple areas of the cemetery, suggesting that burials were not organized into family plots. This finding suggests that, in the 17th century, people in Montreal may have been burying their dead in a way that was not defined by strict biological kinship ties, Fleskes said.

Martin-Moya stressed that the results of the new study do not necessarily apply to all of colonial Montreal.

"Not identifying recent Indigenous or African admixture in this sample does not imply that Indigenous or African-descended people were absent from the city," Martin-Moya said.

In addition, "biological ancestry cannot by itself establish Indigenous belonging," as it "is rooted in kinship, community and relationships with land, not in blood or DNA," she added.

Changes in the use of the cemetery over time also may have influenced the findings, as reburials and later urban development disturbed or destroyed earlier graves.

"Those buried inside the church, mostly clergy and wealthier residents, were more likely to be exhumed and moved," Martin-Moya explained, while the city's poorer residents were buried outside the church and further buried beneath the expanding city. This means that the skeletons in the study may have been the remains of lower-class French colonists.

Archival records show that some Indigenous people were buried in Catholic cemeteries in Montreal as early as the 17th century, Martin-Moya said. "Over time, though, Indigenous communities were increasingly separated from the colonial town through land dispossession and the relocation of missions away from urban centers," she explained. "Their dead would most likely have been buried in those communities. Enslaved people, both Indigenous and African, were often buried on their enslaver's property or in cemeteries for the poor."

The results of the study don't mean that Québécois have no Indigenous ancestors or that relations between French settlers and Indigenous peoples were only hostile, Martin-Moya said. Those relationships were complex and included alliances, trade, conflict and, sometimes, family ties.

"What our results suggest is that when such ancestry exists, it needs to be put in context," Martin-Moya said. "A single ancestor who lived more than 300 years ago does not say the same thing about a person today as being raised within an Indigenous family, community or nation."

Martin-Moya, D., Grenier, J.-C., Lanigan, L.T., Pelletier, J., Irving Pease, E.K., Racimo, F., Bhérer, C., Schroeder, H., Hussin, J., Milot, E., Ribot, I. (2026). Ancient DNA challenges to admixture narratives: Insights from Notre-Dame cemetery (1683-1796) in colonial Montreal, Canada. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2523026123

#241. I Liked the Shark PowerDetect Stick Vacuum’s Smarts and Power. Not So Much Its Weight and Recharge Time.

Spending more money can seem counterintuitive as a value play, but I recommend the bundle that comes with a dock for easier emptying and storage for $100 more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The main benefit of cordless stick vacuums is ease of use. They’re lighter and more maneuverable than upright vacuums, and they make more sense for hitting single rooms or if you have a smaller home.

Shark stick vacs, though, seem to skew large, with run times on the higher end compared with competitors like the Dyson V15 Detect (the one our resident vacuum expert Amber Joglar recommends as the best overall). The PowerDetect I tested recently fits that mold. It’s big and heavy for this kind of vacuum, but it comes with plenty of features that didn’t require much managing or interpreting from me.

In the end, this vacuum hits a pleasant middle ground. It’s certainly not cheap ($450 without the dock when it isn’t discounted), but it also doesn’t come at the premium price the Dyson name and engineering command. It’s also more powerful and helpful than the Bissell PowerClean FurFinder—the current best value cordless stick vacuum on the market. This is one to consider if you’re not on too strict of a budget. Read on for my full thoughts after testing.

I don’t know when this trend started, but I’m a fan of vacuum companies printing quick-start guides on the inside of their box lids. (Tapo did the same for a robot vacuum of theirs I reviewed earlier this year.) I didn’t feel like I had to pore over the startup pamphlet—though it was still included—to get an idea of what the PowerDetect could do and how I could best use it.

Inside the lid was a list of parts; primers on how to read the vacuum’s digital display and the different types of detection it’s capable of; and a QR code to download the owner’s guide, among other things.

Beyond that, setup was intuitive. Shark also placed stickers on the vacuum as pointers. One flagged that the battery comes partially charged and advised I plug the PowerDetect in for a top-off before I started vacuuming.

The PowerDetect was, well, powerful, pulling up crumbs, cat litter, and shredded bits my cat had ripped off his scratching post. It didn’t pick up a slightly larger chunk of cat tree, but if you’re trying to vacuum anything much bigger than dirt or litter, you’ll probably want an upright vac anyway.

I did appreciate that the airspeed didn’t push debris away before the rollers could pull it in. I never felt like I was chasing crumbs across the floor or had to carefully roll over them to avoid sending them skittering into a corner.

The PowerDetect has three modes: Eco, Detect, and Boost. It defaulted to Detect when I turned the vacuum on, and this was the mode I kept it in for most of my testing. It’s a helpful catchall, since the vacuum will sense when it’s on hardwood or tile and when it’s on rugs or carpet—and adjust the power accordingly.

I could hear the vacuum kick into high power when I rolled onto a rug. It’s nice to not have to press a button every time I change surfaces. The automatic suction only works in Detect mode. Eco mode keeps the rollers moving at a low speed for the sake of squeezing out battery life. Boost mode speeds them up if all you need is oomph.

I did have one hiccup with the vacuum automatically changing power on me. As I was moving from the hardwood in the kitchen to a thin area rug in the living room, the PowerDetect sensed the change and upped the power before it was fully on the rug. And it pulled the edge of the rug into the rollers in the process. So moving quickly or picking the vacuum head up when moving between surfaces couldn’t hurt.

I like the display on the back of the vacuum too. It’s simple, showing which mode you’re in and remaining battery life. One button starts the vacuum, and a trigger on the grip switches modes. It was easy to flip through them with one hand while I was testing.

The lights on the front and back of the roller head are nice touches. The front lights help with visibility, while the back ones that face you change color depending on how dirty the floor is. It was a helpful visual as I was vacuuming to see the back lights go from purple to white (showing that the floor was sufficiently clean) and to know I could move on.

It’s unclear, though, if the color shows the vacuum is detecting actual debris it can pick up or just spots on the floor. There were some muddy smudges by the door to the backyard that it seemed to be sensing but couldn’t pick up.

The PowerDetect also ramps up the suction if it senses it’s up against a wall or other surface. Say you’ve got the right side up against a cabinet; the right light will stay on while the left turns off, showing you that the vacuum is working harder.

This was a nice-to-have feature, fitting in with the PowerDetect telling you what it’s finding and doing. I wouldn’t call it necessary, though. Just note that these lights are only on in Detect mode. Eco mode shuts them off.

I appreciated the hinge on the stick too. As my fellow tester Tom Price noted in his review of the PowerDetect Speed, the feature is a boon to my lower back and knees. It took me a bit to get used to and remember that I didn’t have to stoop over to get under tables and between chairs. I’m tall but could stay almost upright with the hinge bent as I worked my way around the kitchen.

The 70-minute battery life (in Eco mode) is plenty for my home, which is around 1,500 square feet. I can easily hit every room with run time to spare while staying in Detect mode. This is better than the PowerDetect Speed and many other cordless stick vacuums we’ve tested, beaten only by the Tineco Pure One Station 5 Pro we recommend as the best with a docking station.

The battery pops out if you want to put it on a counter to recharge. (Shark includes a standard plug-in power cord.) And since the vacuum doesn’t have a dock or mount, taking the battery off means you don’t have to leave the whole vacuum standing out in the open next to an outlet if you want to leave it on the charger; you can tuck it in a closet while the battery refills.

But the recharge time is six hours! If the battery dies mid-job, you’re SOL unless you bought a spare. You’ll probably be better served by a plug-in upright if you have a big house.

The attachments—a crevice tool and a pet hair tool—are pretty standard. It’s a bummer there’s nowhere permanent to store or attach them other than stowing them in the included cloth bag.

The PowerDetect doesn’t have a self-emptying dock, so I had to clean out the dustbin manually. That’s not an issue, as the dustbin is big enough that I didn’t feel like I was having to make many trips back and forth to the trash. But the vacuum did feel a bit heavy in my hands. It’s on the high end of vacuums we recommend, weighing twice as much as the best for pets Levoit LVAC-300.

The vacuum does not stand up on its own. It’s too top-heavy. But another benefit of the hinge on the stick is that it allows the PowerDetect to fold all the way forward on itself. Folded like that, it does stay upright without having to lean against anything or taking up too much space.

I haven’t had the PowerDetect for long, so I can’t speak to its long-term durability. But I like how easy it is to remove the soft roller. Push forward on a bright green button on the side of the brush head and it pops out. Opening the dustbin and removing it from the vacuum entirely to access and change the HEPA filter were both easy.

So the question here becomes: Is the PowerDetect $450 worth of vacuum? I think so. Like I mentioned, it ain’t cheap. But it was intuitive enough and easy to use that it feels like an investment in easier cleaning and less of a workout for my knees and back.

That leaves us with another question though. Is $100 more too much to buy up for the bundle with the dock? I don’t think so. I did find myself wishing the PowerDetect had a dock so I wouldn’t have to take the battery off and tuck it away in a closet. But that’s a nice-to-have, not a disappointment.

If you don’t mind dedicating closet space for the PowerDetect (like you might already do for an upright vac) or just don’t want to spend more, I don’t think you’ll be disappointed either.

Shop the Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum

Will Egensteiner has been reviewing products for 10 years, testing and writing about everything from climbing gear to video game consoles to cars. #242. The 9 Best Multitools for Fixing Things in a Pinch

Cut, tighten, loosen, open, and twist your way through whatever challenges crop up.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

For situations where you don’t have your full tool kit by your side, jump into action like a real-life MacGyver using a multitool. These handy pocket-size companions have come a long way from the Swiss Army Knives of yesteryear, boasting major improvements not just in overall design, but in the quality of tools, materials, and the total number of features offered. Modern-day multitools are designed to be twisted, wrenched, and squeezed with just about the same force that any regular item in your toolbox endures.

A good multitool is typically made of all-stainless steel or equally durable metal with as many as 30 tools integrated into the frame. That said, the majority of them still fit comfortably in a pocket and weigh less than a half pound.

There are dozens of multitool manufacturers, so we got our hands on models from established, popular brands like Victorinox, Gerber, Leatherman, SOG, and more to find out which stood out from the pack. Following our tests and in-depth research, these are the multitools we pick up for fixing nearly anything in a pinch.

It’s hard to nail down one aspect of the Arc that I like best, because it does just about everything well. The opening and closing mechanism is responsive and every tool is accessible from the outside. Plus, the 20 listed functions all work well, as opposed to those on some other multitools that feel like afterthoughts for the sake of an eye-popping marketing claim. This effectiveness across the board is precisely why it is our new best overall pick.

In comparison to our former best overall pick, the Victorinox Spirit X, the Arc shines the brightest when looking at its blade. Unlike the Spirit X, which is made entirely of stainless steel, the knife on the Arc is made of MagnaCut. That means it’s more resistant to corrosion and rust and retains its edge longer.

Beyond this, the blade is simply wider, longer, and based on a pretty basic touch test, feels a lot sharper. In my hands, it made it easier to poke through boxes sealed with duct tape and slice off a chunk of an apple.

The Arc also comes with a larger set of scissors, a thicker saw, and a larger file. Furthermore, it’s equipped with a hip clip that slides directly onto your pants while the Spirit X requires a holster that must be looped through your belt to carry it on your person outside of a pocket.

While no multitool can replace a set of full-size hand tools, the Gerber Gear Center-Drive multitool is by far the closest that we’ve tested. The foldable center-axis provides a lot more length in comparison to the average multitool screwdriver, which gives you extra reach for tight spaces.

The blade on the Center-Drive is also the longest of any that we’ve tested. It feels large enough to take on real cutting responsibility like thick rope or small branches. The high-carbon steel also ensures long-term durability so you don’t have to worry about constantly sharpening the blade between uses.

The Center-Drive is bulkier than other options on this list, but the included nylon sheath is designed to slip onto your belt. Another plus is that there’s a full bit set included.

RoverTac’s 12-in-1 initially caught our eye because it has a good number of useful tools—and it’s affordable, too. While it might be bulky and heavy, we have to admit it’s a decent value. We don’t expect it to hold up to intense use, but in a “save your butt” kind of capacity, it’s certainly holds up to light use.

The long-nosed pliers, wire cutter, and wire stripper all worked reasonably well, as did the can and bottle openers and various screwdrivers. RoverTac claims the tool includes a saw blade, but it’s more like a serrated knife, which worked—just not very well.

The plain knife blade is sharper than it looks and easily cut through rope and twine during our tests. The 12-in-1 comes with a sewn nylon sheath to attach to your belt. Don’t expect this to be the pride of your tool collection, but when you need it most, it will be there.

Fresh out of the box, the Swiss Tool Spirit X impressed us with its design and finish. The tools are packed into the frame very closely, like scientific instrumentation. All the tools—save one—deploy from the outside of the frame, so you can access them without much hassle. The company claims 24 tools in this multitool, but we counted 23, including one that’s simply a hook for a lanyard.

While the needle-nose pliers, wire cutters, scissors, three standard screwdrivers, and can opener work well, it was the less common tools that really impressed us. This is the first multi we’ve seen with a metal saw, which is on the edge of the file. It cut through mild steel hardware surprisingly well, and the file did a nice job cleaning up the edges when we were done.

The Phillips screwdriver shank flares out at the end so that all four points on the head are the same size, making for very solid engagement. The Spirit X’s bottle opener is made from wide stainless steel stock, which keeps it flat on the bottle cap so it doesn’t slip or cut into the cap. The combination reamer-punch efficiently opens up holes in wood, leather, and soft metals, and it can drill holes through 3⁄4-inch pine board.

An all-around great pick, this multitool will get the job done, no matter what that job happens to be.

Full Victorinox Swiss Tool Spirit X Multitool Review

The next iteration in one of Leatherman’s most popular lines comes with a weighty price tag. But it’s justified, since we had a hard time finding fault with the Wave Alpha.

The multitool comes with a standard knife blade, a saw, a file, and a pair of scissors. The file worked well smoothing out nails, and the saw comfortably powered through small branches.

However, we were most pleasantly impressed with the scissors. They’re much larger than any other pair of scissors we've seen on a multitool (“the largest cutting surface ever on a pliers-based Leatherman,” according to the brand). Because of their size and the spring that pushes the handle back up after every snip, we were able to hold the bottom still in hand and easily use our thumb to press down on the blade to cut. This simplified cutting through large pieces of paper, even for those of us who are lefties (since nearly no scissors are designed for cutting with our dominant hand).

The classic pocket knife is made of MagnaCut steel, which is corrosion-resistant and has great edge retention. During testing, we focused on everyday items like twine, paper, cardboard, and zip ties and opening sealed packages. We never needed more than one stern pull of the blade to get through any of them.

The central tool of the Wave Alpha is the plier-wire cutter, which we found easy to use thanks to the biting grip of the ridges and the ergonomic handle.

Though Leatherman lists 16 tools, we counted closer to 12. For instance, the file is designated as two separate tools, with the traditional flat side counting as one and the diamond-coated edge counting as another. That’s a fairly common embellishment with multitool descriptions.

Full Leatherman Wave Alpha Multitool Review

With its svelte, minimalist frame featuring three main tools, this Gerber cuts down on the unnecessary junk and keeps its tools simple and effective.

As a pocket knife–based multitool, it features a full 3-inch, locking plain blade. Although it isn’t the sharpest right out of the box, it cut cleanly through paper, plastic, rope, twine, and steak, and was adequate for some light whittling.

The side opposite the blade features a hex bit driver and scissors. The driver has a reversible bit in a magnetic holder—we love this because you get legit flat and Phillips screwdrivers that just plain work.

The scissors are a bit larger than those found on other models and were easy to control when cutting out intricate shapes from paper to medium cardboard. Between the scissors and the driver is a sharp, narrow awl. We weren't able to use this to drill holes in wood and plastic, but it works well, as intended, to poke holes through leather and canvas.

Rounding out the eight functions is a nice bottle opener that pivots off the end of the tool frame. It doubles as a pry bar (the bottle opener flipped over) and a “hammer” (the wide base of the bottle opener). Is it less a hammer and more just a flat surface for hitting things? Sure. But when you need to finish tapping in a tent stake or small nail, it’ll do.

The plier-based Leatherman Signal comes with several standard items, including a stainless steel blade and a serrated saw. However, it impressed us most with its several outdoor-specific functions.

These include a detachable ferro rod that, in combination with the serrated saw, creates sparks for your campfire. The ferro rod also doubles as an emergency whistle. During testing, I was particularly pleased with the carabiner on the bottom of the multitool. While not a major feature, being able to clip it onto my hiking backpack and forget about it made it so much easier to carry with me than other options.

Perhaps the only major downside is the hammer tool. It functions more like a blunt, flat end you can use in a pinch.

Everyday life doesn’t always require a saw, hammer, or bulky pliers. The Leatherman Micra is a keychain tool, and it doesn’t pretend to be anything else. The Micra hosts a number of items that are still quite handy when small and, importantly, are often the most useful in day-to-day life.

The multitool is built around a pair of scissors, which are the perfect size for cutting tags and snipping loose threads. Tools on the body include tweezers, a nail file and cleaner, a small screwdriver, and a bottle opener, among others.

While carrying the Leatherman Micra around, I was genuinely astonished at how often I used it. I frequently pulled it out for small tasks like picking something out from under my nails, plucking a small hair out of place, or tightening the screws on my sunglasses’ hinges.

The Micra works so well because it knows what it is. The convenience and portability make it hard to go anywhere without it.

With its wide frame and large plier jaws, the Dual-Force is a beast of a multitool. You can open the pliers and slip the pivot to spread the dual-position jaws extra wide to grab large fasteners or objects. The jaws feature three separate gripping areas: two for large or small round objects and one for gripping flat things. We appreciated their versatility for holding well in a variety of situations.

One of our favorite things about the Dual-Force is that all the other tools are accessible when the pliers are closed. This multitool also features a bit holder with two Phillips and one plain screwdriver bit. We regard these among the most useful multitool screwdrivers available, although they are sometimes difficult to use in tight spaces.

The Dual-Force is rounded out with a large knife, a saw blade, and a three-sided file. The knife blade is reasonably sharp out of the box, and we easily cut through thick rope with it. We used the saw blade to cut both green and dried-out sticks and branches with relative ease. We were able to use the file on both wood and metal, although it was better suited for the metal.

While the number of tools and functionalities on your multitool isn’t the only measure of how helpful it’ll be, it does give you a sense of its versatility. The multitools we recommend have anywhere from five to 20 or more different functions.

Note that, in their descriptions, manufacturers often count different capabilities of a specific tool individually to arrive at a higher number of “tools.” Pliers, for example, may be counted three or four times if they can function as needle-nose pliers, regular pliers, wire cutters, and wire strippers.

It’s key to pay attention to the quality of each tool and, of course, how often you’ll use them. For instance, a multitool with a screwdriver attachment is great, but if that multitool’s grip doesn’t give you the leverage to twist off seized screws or only comes with one screwdriver bit, it’s far less effective in practice.

We recommend starting your search by listing three or four tools you use most. Then, opt for a multitool that performs well at those functions. A multitool that has a few tools you use frequently will end up being more valuable to you than one packed to the brim with tools you don’t use much at all.

One of the key reasons to own a multitool is for its portability and convenience compared with carrying a full set of tools. So, if you can’t fit it in a pocket or in the center console of your car, it’s probably too big. That said, size isn’t everything. Each item on a multitool needs enough space from the others to work effectively, and you need to make sure you have a good grip for leverage.

The weight of a multitool only becomes a problem if it is too heavy to comfortably clip onto a belt or slip into a pocket. The majority of the tools on our list are made of stainless steel, which is durable yet relatively lightweight.

Can a Multitool Replace a Tool Kit? In short, no. Multitools are useful in a pinch or when you just need them for a quick fix, but they cannot replace a full tool kit. The biggest utility of a multitool is its convenience. It can function well enough for small repairs or to get by when you’ve got nothing else nearby.

We designed our tests to utilize every tool and function of each model. We carved white pine boards and maple branches. We opened bottles, cans, and shipping packaging. We disassembled and reassembled an old British carburetor, an electrical junction box, and a standard three-prong outlet.

We cut rope, twine, lamp wire, 14-gauge indoor branch circuit wire, maple saplings, branches, paper, and plastic. We also stripped the wires we cut and crimped electrical connectors. With the pliers, we gripped, squeezed, twisted, and turned various bits of hardware. Finally, we filed wood, metal, and even our own fingernails.

During these tests, we paid close attention to the performance of the tool in the given task, the ease of use, how each multitool ergonomically fit in our hand as we worked, and how we expect each tool to last over a long period of time. After all that was said and done, we noted our impressions to compile our final list.

For testing across the board, we evaluated each tool in common situations. For instance, the saw isn’t likely going to cut through 2x4s, so we opted for small branches, twine, and cardboard boxes.

Tom Price is a reviews editor for Popular Mechanics while also contributing to Runner's World, Best Products, and Bicycling. Here at Popular Mechanics, Tom loves testing out home appliances, smart tech, gear for city life and outdoor adventures, small gadgets like watches and multitools, and anything else you can find piled up at his hoarder's nest of a desk.

Prior to working here, Tom attended NYU, graduating with a degree in English and a minor in creative writing. He also wrote for Best Reviews, The Daily Beast, and other publications covering tech, fitness gear, gadgets, and lifestyle products. Now that he's back, he leads product reviews for PopMech, as well as Runner's World, Best Products, and Biography. #243. Astronomers discover a ghostly green star unlike any known before

Astronomers at the University of Warwick have discovered that white dwarf stars can display a surprising variety of colors, including green, pink, purple, yellow, and cyan. Among their findings is the first known star that would appear genuinely green to the human eye.

For most stars, color is closely tied to temperature. Cooler stars appear orange, stars like our Sun look white, and the hottest stars shine pale blue. The relationship is similar to heating a piece of iron, which changes from red to orange and eventually white as its temperature rises.

White dwarfs, the extremely dense remains of stars similar to our Sun, were long believed to follow this same pattern. In fact, they received their name because the first examples discovered were unusually hot and appeared white or pale blue. However, scientists have now found that these stellar remnants can produce a much broader spectrum of colors.

The findings, published in RAS Techniques and Instruments (RASTI), suggest that some white dwarfs would look dramatically different from ordinary stars if they could be viewed from close enough.

"Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like 'perfect radiators,' so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs," said Dr. Mark Hollands, Warwick Prize Fellow in the Astronomy and Astrophysics Group, University of Warwick, who led the work. "It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colors nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me."

Why Some Dead Stars Glow in Unexpected Colors

The explanation lies in the extraordinary density of white dwarf atmospheres. In the coolest of these stars, atmospheric material can reach densities of approximately 1 gram per cubic centimeter, comparable to water and millions of times denser than the Sun's visible surface, known as the photosphere.

Under these extreme conditions, small amounts of elements such as carbon, calcium, and sodium interact with the surrounding helium plasma. These interactions allow the elements to absorb a much wider range of light wavelengths than they would in less dense environments.

As a result, the light escaping from a white dwarf can take on colors that would not normally be expected based on temperature alone. Instead of appearing orange, white, or blue, some of these stars develop entirely different hues.

Because no white dwarf is close enough for astronomers to directly distinguish its color with the human eye, the researchers used measurements of starlight to determine how each star would appear.

They analyzed stellar spectra, which are produced by separating light into its component wavelengths, much as a prism divides sunlight into the colors of a rainbow. Each spectrum acts as a distinctive fingerprint, revealing information about a star's temperature and chemical composition.

By processing these measurements through a model of human color vision, the team calculated the colors that people would actually perceive. This approach demonstrated that spectral data can reveal not only what a star contains and how hot it is, but also its true visual appearance.

Astronomers Identify the First Known Green Star

When the researchers examined white dwarfs throughout the sky, they found that the stars could be divided into several color groups based on the chemical makeup of their atmospheres.

White dwarfs containing large amounts of carbon often appear pink or purple. Others that have accumulated material from destroyed asteroids and comets, remnants of planetary systems that once surrounded them, tend to look yellow.

Cooler white dwarfs with atmospheres containing both hydrogen and helium can develop cyan or pale blue coloring. This effect occurs when hydrogen molecules collide with helium atoms under the immense pressures found in these stars.

Perhaps the most remarkable discovery was WD J1330+6435, a white dwarf with a temperature of approximately 4,000 degrees Celsius.

Over time, this star has drawn in rocky debris from its former planetary system, introducing calcium, lithium, and sodium into its atmosphere. According to the researchers' calculations, these elements give the star a distinctive chartreuse green appearance.

As far as the team knows, no other star, whether still undergoing nuclear fusion or already dead, has ever been credibly identified as genuinely green. This makes WD J1330+6435 the first known example of a green star in the Milky Way.

Dr. Hollands added: "The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow. Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star. It feels like something out of science fiction."

A Dead Star That May Be the Reddest Ever Found

At the other end of the color spectrum, the astronomers identified another extraordinary white dwarf that may be the reddest star ever documented.

Known as WD J1011+2845, this stellar remnant is located just 48 light-years from Earth. It has a deep convection zone that transports carbon from its interior to its surface.

Once there, carbon molecules dramatically alter the wavelengths of light escaping from the star. Nearly all of its light is shifted toward wavelengths longer than 600 nanometers, producing an unusually deep salmon-pink appearance.

The resulting color is unlike anything typically observed in ordinary stars and makes WD J1011+2845 another striking example of how the unusual chemistry of white dwarfs can reshape their appearance.

How Common Are These Unusually Colored Stars?

To determine whether these remarkable colors are rare exceptions or part of a larger pattern, the researchers also examined a representative sample of 151 white dwarfs located within 20 parsecs (about 65 light-years) of Earth.

Among these stars, five had unusual colors. Two appeared yellow, while three were pink.

Based on these results, the researchers estimate that approximately one in every 30 white dwarfs throughout the Universe could display an unexpected color. Although this represents a relatively small percentage, it suggests that enormous numbers of strangely colored stellar remnants exist across the cosmos.

The remaining 146 stars were examined using a measurement known as color temperature. This describes how the color of an object compares with that of an ideal radiator at a particular temperature. The same concept is commonly used to characterize household lighting, such as bulbs labeled ('warm white' at 3,000K, 'cool white' at 6,000K).

The researchers found that the median color temperature of these white dwarfs was approximately 6,800 Kelvin, corresponding to light that appears white to human eyes.

This finding also challenges the widespread impression that white dwarfs are usually blue. Hotter, bluer white dwarfs produce more light and remain visible across greater distances, making them disproportionately common in astronomical surveys that select stars based on brightness.

When astronomers instead examine a more representative nearby population, the typical white dwarf turns out to be white after all.

Professor Boris Gänsicke, Department of Physics, University of Warwick, said: "One in thirty might not sound like a huge fraction, but across the entire population of white dwarfs in the Universe, that is still a lot of oddly colored stars out there. Yet if we take the median across a representative population of white dwarfs, we found that the average white dwarf really is white."

Materials provided by University of Warwick. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
