#263. Scientists find a youth protein that helps aging brain cells act young again

A protein associated with youth may help aging brain cells regain some of their lost abilities. Scientists at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have discovered that TIMP2 plays an important role in keeping the brain's immune cells healthy, offering new clues about how the brain changes with age.

In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers found that removing TIMP2 caused brain immune cells, known as microglia, to develop characteristics linked to aging and neurodegenerative disease. When the scientists restored TIMP2 in the bloodstream of older mice, these cells became better at removing cellular debris and showed fewer molecular signs of inflammation and other potentially harmful changes.

The discovery suggests that proteins associated with youth may help preserve the brain's natural defenses as it ages. It also identifies TIMP2 as a potentially important factor in maintaining healthy immune activity in the brain.

Why the Brain's Immune Cells Become Less Effective With Age

Getting older is the greatest known risk factor for Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative disorders. However, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that make the aging brain increasingly vulnerable to these conditions.

One important piece of the puzzle involves microglia, specialized immune cells that serve as the brain's maintenance and defense system. They remove cellular waste, help maintain the networks through which neurons communicate, and respond when brain tissue is injured.

As the brain ages, these cells can lose some of their ability to perform these essential tasks. They may also shift into states that promote inflammation and interfere with normal brain function.

"TIMP2 facilitates healthy function for the brain's immune cells," said Joseph M. Castellano, PhD, Associate Professor of Neuroscience at the Ronald M. Loeb Center for Alzheimer's Disease and The Friedman Brain Institute at The Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, and corresponding author of the study. "By supporting the ability of microglia to clear debris and limit maladaptive responses, TIMP2 may help restore aspects of microglial function that become compromised with age. Since our previous work identified TIMP2 as a regulator of synaptic plasticity through the extracellular matrix, these findings suggest that this factor sits at the intersection of several processes that are critical for normal brain function."

Synaptic plasticity refers to the brain's ability to strengthen or weaken connections between neurons, a process essential for learning and memory. The extracellular matrix is a network of molecules surrounding cells that helps support and regulate their activity.

To investigate how TIMP2 affects brain immune cells, the research team studied several groups of mice representing different biological conditions.

The study included Brittany Hemmer, PhD, the first author, who was a graduate student in Castellano's laboratory during the research.

Some of the mice were genetically modified to lack TIMP2 throughout their bodies. In others, the researchers removed the protein specifically from either microglia or neurons. Comparing these models allowed the team to examine how TIMP2 influences immune cell behavior in both healthy and aging brains.

The scientists used several advanced techniques to study the changes. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing allowed them to examine patterns of gene activity in individual cell nuclei. They also used detailed imaging, functional tests, and a technique called in vivo microdialysis, which collects and measures substances from the fluid surrounding cells in living brain tissue.

The results revealed striking changes when TIMP2 was absent.

Microglia developed several features typically associated with aging and brain injury. Their cellular activation markers changed, their ability to remove debris declined, and they showed molecular signatures linked to cellular senescence, a biological state associated with aging and cellular stress.

The effects extended beyond the immune cells themselves. Using in vivo microdialysis, the researchers also detected higher levels of proteins associated with inflammation and stress in the extracellular environment surrounding brain cells.

Together, these findings indicated that TIMP2 helps prevent microglia from shifting toward potentially damaging states.

Restoring a Youth-Associated Protein Improves Aging Brain Cells

The researchers next explored whether supplying TIMP2 could counteract some of the changes observed with age.

They administered TIMP2 through injections to older mice, allowing the protein to circulate throughout the body. The treatment produced encouraging results.

Microglia became more effective at clearing cellular debris and showed a reduction in molecular markers associated with inflammatory states. In other words, restoring the youth-associated protein helped the aging immune cells recover some of the functions that normally deteriorate over time.

These improvements suggest that TIMP2 influences how microglia respond to conditions within the brain. By supporting their protective activities and limiting potentially harmful responses, the protein may help maintain a healthier environment for neurons.

The results also point to a possible biological connection between factors circulating in the body that are associated with youth and the activity of the brain's innate immune system. This system provides a first line of defense against injury and other threats.

A Potential New Direction for Brain Aging and Alzheimer's Research

The discovery adds to growing scientific interest in whether biological factors associated with youth can influence the aging process.

Because microglia help maintain brain health and can contribute to harmful inflammation when their behavior changes, finding ways to preserve their normal function could have important implications for understanding age-related neurological disorders.

"While additional studies are needed, this work provides new insight into how youth-associated factors influence pathways involved in brain aging and age-related neurological disorders that may ultimately inform therapeutic strategies," Dr. Castellano added.

However, the researchers caution that these findings come from experiments in mice. It remains unknown whether TIMP2 produces similar effects in humans or whether manipulating the protein could eventually become an effective treatment.

Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether TIMP2 itself, or the biological pathways it controls, can be targeted to reduce harmful changes associated with brain aging.

For now, the findings provide a promising new explanation for how a protein linked to youth helps maintain the brain's immune defenses, and how restoring it may recover some functions that weaken with age.

This work was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG061382 (JMC), RF1AG072300 (JMC), 1F31AG079604-01A1 (BMH), T32AG049688 (BMH, SMP), R01AG061382-02S1 (JMC, SMP), and Cure Alzheimer's Fund (JMC).

#264. The Edmund Fitzgerald Took 29 Men. In 1994, a Submersible Found One of Them.

The discovery of a sailor’s body outside the wreck offered a haunting new clue to the mystery—and complicated it even more.

It was late on a July night in 1994 when the Anglian Lady left the dock in Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan, carrying a tiny yellow submersible named Delta. Ric Mixter, a former television reporter and the author of Tattletale Sounds: The Edmund Fitzgerald Investigations, was aboard the tugboat, along with explorer Fred Shannon, Shannon’s wife, Betty, and a crew of 16 that included photographers, boat operators, and submersible pilots.

The Edmund Fitzgerald’s rapid disappearance—amid Lake Superior waves that likely exceeded 25 feet—raised questions from the very beginning. The ship had an experienced captain during a storm that was bad but not unusual by Great Lakes standards. The massive ship wasn’t the only vessel on the lake that stormy night in November of 1975. But it was the only one that sank, despite being built to withstand even worse conditions. It went down rapidly and without any survivors. According to Mixter, the National Enquirer ran a story after the accident claiming that the crew had been abducted by aliens. “That’s how weird this was that nobody came off this wreck,” Mixter says. He’s been researching its demise for decades, trying to figure out what happened in those final minutes.

Aboard The Lady, Mixter passed through the Soo Locks around midnight, finally reaching Whitefish Bay in Lake Superior at dawn. Shannon made the first dive a couple of hours later, on a day so gorgeous that Mixter, wearing a wetsuit, jumped into the water to cool off and get some video footage of Delta’s descent.

He joined the day’s third submersible dive, starting in the late afternoon. When the sub reached the bottom at 550 feet, Mixter was surprised that there was no sand—just mud and rocks. On the hull of the ship, he saw the word EDMUND, now faded and rusted over. As he filmed and tried to take everything in, he suddenly got spooked at the sight of water on the floor of the sub but then relaxed when the pilot told him it was just condensation from their breath. At around 6 p.m., after two mesmerizing hours underwater, Delta returned Mixter to the surface in time for one more dive, which carried the Lady’s owner and his 12-year-old son. They were the ones who spotted the crewman. He was lying face up outside the ship by an open door near the bow on the port side.

As a media frenzy ensued, the find sparked a slew of new questions. Had the sailor tried to escape through the door, or did he fall off the ship? Was his neck broken, as it appeared to Mixter? Had the crewman even been on the Fitz, or was the body there before the ship went down? These new mysteries compounded the bigger one: What happened here?

As the unknowns continue to linger decades later, technological advances have raised a tantalizing possibility: Maybe science could be the key to finding answers. By the time Mixter dived to the wreck, sonar had improved significantly, producing images with better resolution than what the first search crews had been able to get right after the crash. Since then, tools have become far more affordable and accessible, facilitating a new era of mystery solving for shipwreck hunters.

Remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), which could easily cost $100,000 a few decades ago, now go for about $2,000, Baillod says. Submarines, too, are cheaper than they were in the Fitz’s day. Sonar systems have gone DIY. Figuring out where to aim sonar is now easier with help from accurate GPS, electronic navigation, and Google Earth. Scientists are developing AI programs that incorporate data on known shipwrecks in order to locate new ones. Modern searchers also benefit from sonar-equipped autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and close-range cameras on ROVs. They can get help from magnetometers, autonomous boats that carry sonar, lidar for shallow water, and photogrammetry, a process of turning two-dimensional images into three-dimensional ones.

If it ever becomes possible to return to the site of the Fitz with the technologies available now, Mixter believes, there’s so much more researchers could uncover. Today’s sonar alone, he says, offers 50 percent better resolution. Without even diving, they could collect new information. “We could tow a sonar over the top and it would show us resolution right down to a two-inch rope,” he says. “We could easily see.”

#265. Archaeologists discover 1,200-year-old mummified hairless dog in Peru

Archaeologists working at an ancient burial complex in Peru have uncovered remarkable evidence of hairless dogs that lived more than 1,200 years ago, long before the rise of the Inca Empire. The discoveries include naturally mummified remains, unusual skeletal features, and clues about what the animals ate and how they were treated by the people around them.

Peruvian hairless dogs are a distinctive Indigenous breed known for their slender bodies, pointed ears, and lack of fur. They frequently appear in pottery created by ancient societies along the Andean coast. Today, a variation of the breed is recognized by the American Kennel Club as the Peruvian Inca Orchid. The dogs are also an important national symbol, having been officially designated part of Peru's cultural heritage in 2000.

A study published in the Journal of Anthropological Archaeology reports the first physical evidence of Peruvian hairless dogs at Castillo de Huarmey, the only known Wari Empire site discovered so far on Peru's northern coast.

Ancient Dog Remains Discovered at a Wari Empire Site

Located approximately 190 miles north of Lima, Castillo de Huarmey covers 110 acres and once served as an administrative and burial center for the Wari Empire. The complex was occupied between 600 and 1050 CE, roughly 400 years before the Inca rose to power.

The site has already produced several extraordinary archaeological discoveries. In 2012, researchers uncovered the first undisturbed elite Wari tomb, containing the remains of 58 high-status women, six human sacrifices, and approximately 1,300 artifacts. Another important discovery followed in 2022, when archaeologists identified nearby burials of elite craftspeople accompanied by gold, silver, and bronze tools. Together, these findings have helped researchers understand how the Wari Empire governed its territories.

The newly examined dog remains offer a different perspective on daily life at the site, particularly the complicated relationships between people and animals.

"Our findings indicate that humans and dogs coexisted at this Wari site, but reconstructing their bond is challenging, as past emotions are difficult to capture through archaeological methods," says first author Weronika Tomczyk, a research associate in Dartmouth's Department of Anthropology and a postdoctoral fellow in its Ecology, Evolution, Environment and Society Program.

"The goal of our study was to not only present data on Castillo de Huarmey's dog burials, but also emphasize that people in the past had often contradictory relationships with the animals, just as they do today: a pet for one group of people could at the same time be considered a pest by their closest neighbors."

Remarkably Preserved Dog Mummies Found in the Peruvian Desert

Castillo de Huarmey lies in an extremely dry region of Peru's Pacific coast. The desert's exceptionally arid conditions have helped preserve materials that would normally deteriorate over time, including hair, bones, clothing, leather, pigments, and decorated pottery.

Among the artifacts recovered from the site is an unusual ceramic vessel depicting a seated Peruvian hairless dog with humanlike features. The animal appears to be holding an object resembling a musical instrument.

Between 2010 and 2025, excavations also uncovered numerous remains of South American camelids, probably domesticated llamas and alpacas. Some may have been deposited as offerings during funerary ceremonies, while others appear to have been discarded as waste. Archaeologists also recovered the skeletal remains of dogs.

However, interpreting these discoveries has been complicated by extensive damage and looting. A powerful earthquake in 1970 caused part of Castillo de Huarmey to collapse, exposing burial chambers containing pottery and other valuable objects. Looters subsequently disturbed large sections of the complex.

The deeper archaeological layers remained untouched and retained their original Wari context. In contrast, the upper layers, where most of the animal remains were discovered, contained materials that had become mixed together.

During excavations in the northern section of the main ceremonial area, three sets of dog remains stood out.

One was a naturally mummified skull that still retained visible hairless skin and attached ears. The skull had also been colored with cinnabar, a bright red pigment commonly used in ancient Peruvian funerary traditions.

Researchers discovered a second, larger dog skull, along with the naturally mummified skeleton of a male dog buried in a shallow pit. The male skeleton was almost complete, missing only the lower portions of its front limbs.

At first, the researchers suspected that the mummified dog might have been buried relatively recently, perhaps around 50 years earlier during the period of looting. But Tomczyk noticed two important details: the animal was hairless, and all three dogs lacked their first premolars.

Missing Teeth Reveal the Dogs' Ancient Identity

The missing teeth provided an unexpected clue that helped researchers identify the animals.

"What I noticed is that some of the dog skeletons were missing teeth, and not that they lost them during their lifespan; some teeth, especially first premolars and sometimes last molars, had just never erupted," said Tomczyk. "And then I found in the literature that the same gene which is responsible for hairlessness in dogs is responsible for a reduced number of teeth, indicating that these were Peruvian hairless dogs."

In other words, the animals were not necessarily missing teeth because of injury, disease, or old age. Their reduced number of teeth was linked to the same genetic trait responsible for their hairlessness.

This distinctive biological connection offered evidence that the remains belonged to Peruvian hairless dogs rather than other ancient dog populations.

To investigate further, the researchers applied standard zooarchaeological techniques, which involve studying animal remains recovered from archaeological sites. These methods helped them estimate the ages of the dogs and examine their physical characteristics.

The team also analyzed chemical signatures preserved in the animals' bones and teeth. Known as isotopic analysis, this technique can reveal information about what an animal ate and drank, as well as where it may have lived.

The researchers examined isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and strontium. These are different forms of chemical elements that can preserve clues about diet and environmental conditions. Strontium is particularly useful because its composition varies with local geology and can help scientists trace an animal's geographic origins or movements.

The results were compared with similar measurements from human and camelid remains recovered at Castillo de Huarmey.

"Isotopic analyses of a dog's tooth give a signal of its life as a puppy because dog teeth erupt so fast, and the bone gives a signal of more or less the last year of its life," said Tomczyk. "Such sampling strategy aimed to provide signals from distinct stages of a dog's life."

Ancient Puppies Buried Alongside Elite Members of Society

Altogether, the excavations produced 341 dog bone specimens representing at least 19 individual dogs, in addition to the complete mummified male dog.

Some of the remains were found in particularly intriguing burial contexts.

For example, the bones of a puppy estimated to have been just 6 to 8 weeks old were discovered alongside an elite craftsperson nicknamed the "Master Basketmaker." Other finds included the bones of an adult dog buried within the site's palace and part of a puppy skeleton buried with a male individual identified as XY, who was probably sacrificed to serve as a tomb guardian.

Most of the dogs were adults at the time of burial. However, their remains suggest that the animals did not all receive the same treatment.

Some appear to have been deliberately buried, potentially reflecting a special role in Wari society. Others were found among discarded materials. Only a small number of bones displayed butchery marks, suggesting that dogs were not commonly consumed as food.

Radiocarbon dating provided another important discovery. The complete mummified male dog was determined to be at least 1,200 years old, making it the oldest radiocarbon-dated specimen recovered from Castillo de Huarmey so far.

This result has important implications for understanding the site's chronology because it provides an additional dating reference for the ancient complex.

Ancient Hairless Dogs May Have Eaten Like Humans

The isotopic evidence also revealed surprising similarities between the diets of dogs and people living at Castillo de Huarmey.

Most of the dogs had consumed at least some maize, or corn, which was a major food source throughout the pre-Hispanic Andes. Their diets therefore overlapped with those of the human population.

An especially interesting pattern emerged among the dogs believed to have been hairless.

When these animals were puppies, their diets appeared more similar to those of human children. As they grew older, however, their food sources became more varied.

The findings raise the possibility that some puppies received particular attention or were raised under controlled conditions, potentially as part of an organized breeding practice.

"We do not know if the dogs were intentionally fed maize or if perhaps, they were just eating leftovers or trash," said Tomczyk. "Yet, the distinct dietary patterns of hairless puppies provide insights into what may have been organized breeding."

The researchers emphasize that the archaeological evidence cannot establish whether these dogs were cherished pets, working animals, or animals with other roles in Wari society.

Nevertheless, the differences in burial practices, physical characteristics, and dietary patterns suggest that the hairless dogs held a distinctive place within the community.

"While we will never know if any of the three dogs were pets or how people treated them, it is evident they received different treatment than other dogs," said Tomczyk.

The discoveries provide a rare glimpse into the lives of dogs and humans more than a millennium ago, showing that relationships with animals could be just as varied and complicated in ancient societies as they are today.

The study's co-authors include Miłosz Giersz, Wiesław Więckowski, and Roberto Pimentel Nita of the University of Warsaw, along with Claire Ebert of the University of Pittsburgh.

John Stewart goes rogue in Sector 2814 and embraces fear hopefully leading into season 2

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

HBO and HBO Max's "Lanterns" served up its big cliffhanger finale on Oct. 4, 2026, and we’ve been slowly digesting thoughts on what the creative direction and ultimate legacy of this debut season were.

While by no means a perfect experiment in trying to shake up the aging superhero genre, there are enough worthy elements to consider this sci-fi mystery show an evolutionary step towards the next generation of comic-based storytelling.

After the emerald-tinted dust has settled, there are many lingering questions about where this acclaimed series from creators Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof, and Tom King might be headed and where the twists and turns might lead for a sophomore season should it be greenlit (get it?) for a triumphant return.

Warning: Major Spoilers For "Lanterns" Season 1 Ahead!

One of "Lanterns"' standout achievements is revealing the true costs of superheroism by deconstructing its DNA and examining the ugly guts of it all.

It dives into the fear, trauma, and seduction that drive humans to take up the serious business of protecting the universe and doling out justice against both Earth-bound evil and intergalactic threats. "Lanterns" also explores mental health issues and PTSD that are the inevitable byproducts of a life of unimaginable violence. The compelling series achieves a provocative dissection of it all with rare confidence without the overindulgence of distracting CGI tossed in for sheer spectacle.

It might not have been exactly the Green Lantern TV series fans wanted, but it was the show we got, and kinda the show we needed. Sure, for a series about a noble order of intergalactic space cops, we were treated to very little cosmic action, and instead we're given a grounded slow-burn police procedural à la "True Detective."

As I said before, it's not perfect, but we shouldn’t dismiss "Lanterns" for its mild shortcomings when it gets so much right. We're willing a second season into existence, and with an average of 20 million global viewers and solid reviews, HBO/HBO Max would be very wise to bring it back.

Whether a second season shifts into the heavens to rocket off on an outer space trajectory for a follow-up season is yet to be seen. For now, though, the Lanterns season one finale has left us with plenty of questions to ponder.

"Lanterns"' season finale revealed that Kerry, in an unhinged moment of maternal panic trying to protect her mutant son, Noah, had put a bullet in Hal's head. RIP to the original Green Lantern... or is it?

Kyle Chandler was a fantastic choice to play Hal Jordan, and he brought a charismatic gravitas and twisted sense of humor to the storied comic character. His sudden death in Rushville, frozen in the bleachers of the high school football stadium, certainly looked final, but this is the wild topsy-turvy universe of superheroes, so anything is possible.

And don’t forget that the newly-freed Thaal Sinestro (Ulrich Thomsen) told the AI “Halogram” and Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart on Antaan's dead planet that the magical green ring could be used to restore Hal’s life. But Sinestro is a sly, slippery foe and is never to be trusted!

Online speculation has proposed that Hal Jordan might be revived and enter the series as Parallax, the living embodiment of fear, but that’s not likely according to the series creators. What’s more probable is that we either see Chandler's Hal Jordan revived, or he'll just turn up in occasional flashbacks or Halogram pop-in scenes.

With his unsanctioned lantern battery now in hand to power his ring, Stewart has become an independent contractor protecting Earth for Guy Gardner’s (Nathan Fillion) Sector 2814.

Fortified with the Sinestro-forged yellow charging unit deemed illegal by the Guardians and the broader members of the Green Lantern Corps., this unattached Lantern is now free to make sure Noah doesn’t turn to the dark side and lean into his evil Manhunter programming.

Will Stewart be seduced into the path of corruption by using Sinestro’s emotionally tainted battery, or steel himself against ill influences and continue to blaze his own trail as Earth's sole protector for the time being?

As a gold-toothed Gardner tells Stewart, "When I take this bull**** up back to Oa, they’re gonna send an army to put you down." This sounds like the perfect setup for an eventful "Lanterns" season 2 where the Lantern Corps come to take Jordan in, dead or alive. It’ll be interesting to see which of the infamous space cops they eventually send. This ain't over!

Sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald) and the dorky Billy Macon’s (Jason Ritter) immaculately conceived son, Noah, is outed as a Human-Manhunter hybrid that came into being after Kerry’s initial encounter with Manhunter Zoe years ago.

He might be one helluva gunslinging high school quarterback now, but that pales in comparison to what he could become using his frightful shapeshifting Manhunter genes inherited from his grandmother.

With his new Nebraska collegiate ball cap and now headed off to university, the sleeper agent has some vital decisions to make way beyond declaring a major. His desire will be to wipe out the Green Lanterns and the Guardians, but Earthly domination might come first unless he pledges to subdue his instincts and lead a normal life. And is Noah really the last Manhunter, or are there legions more ready to activate?

Spazkaban (or Space Azkaban), the notorious cosmic penitentiary controlled by the Guardians, lost one of its most lethal inhabitants in the crimson-skinned Sinestro when Noah (Shea Pritchard), the nascent Manhunter, broke him out of jail to craft him a yellow fear-based lantern.

This persuasive villain was last seen wrapped in chains in the season finale, "Dirt and Stars," being dunked in the waters of madness by Stewart on the poison planet after a portal hop, before trying to coerce Halogram to deliver the prized ring for Jordan's resurrection.

Avid comic fans know Sinestro once commanded his own intergalactic corp that fed upon the addictive yellow glare of fear instead of the emerald light’s will-imposed power.

Will he unite with Noah to take down the manipulative Guardians of the Universe and their legion of space-bound enforcers, the Green Lanterns? Will Noah break bad or go good? And is it possible for Sinestro to forge another yellow lantern and a custom companion ring to escape captivity? As Sinestro explains, "If harnessed correctly, fear can be the most powerful force in the universe."

Shards of "Lanterns" will invariably bleed over into James Gunn's "Superman" sequel, "Man of Tomorrow," which soars to theaters on July 9, 2027, so there’s still a lot of life left in DC Studios' DCU.

All 8 episodes of "Lanterns" season 1 are available on HBO and HBO Max.

#267. The Airthings Renew Is Less Obtrusive and Quieter Than Any Other Air Purifier I’ve Tested

The understated air purifier fits quietly into the background of any room.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Air purifiers should excel at two key things: improving the air quality in your home and fading completely into the background. Nothing is worse than wasting precious floor space on a large, bulky device that is distractingly loud when running. Based on these criteria, I don’t think I’ve ever tested a more complete air purifier than the Airthings Renew. With a clean, minimalist design and quiet, yet effective, operation, it’s an air purifier I’m happy to have in my home.

What makes the Airthings Renew unique in comparison to most of the other air purifiers I’ve tested out is its shape. The device has a boxy, rectangular shape similar to an old desktop computer, which means it can slide tight next to furniture, fit easily under a desk, or blend in seamlessly with the rest of your room decor. At the same time, the air purifier has a four-stage filter system that removes everything from large particles to odors and chemicals from the air.

Despite not being the smallest air purifier by pure size, the Airthings Renew might be the easiest to store and hide away. Its rectangular shape is a lot easier to fit in tight places than the generally cylindrical air purifiers I’ve tested in the past. I was able to fit it easily under my desk without sacrificing any real legroom.

At the same time, the air purifier has a sort of modern look to it, and the dark gray color helps it basically blend into any living room. Even when I set it next to my trash can or by my white couch, it never looked out of place nor did it draw unwanted attention.

Even sitting in the middle of my living room, it didn’t look out of place. While it’s probably not how I’d keep it long term, I didn’t mind just plopping it up next to a wall and letting it sit by itself.

Quiet operation from an air purifier is always important, but that’s especially true in small spaces, like an apartment, where the ceilings are lower and every noise is amplified. Like our most portable pick, the Coway Airthings 100, the Airthings Renew can operate virtually silently. In fact, on Quiet mode, the air purifier runs at a noise level of just 23 decibels, only three more than the Coway, which is a much smaller model.

When using it in my bedroom, the sound was barely perceptible, even when no music was on and I was reading quietly. In fact, it was quiet enough to run while I fell asleep.

One of the best parts about the Airthings Renew is its four-stage filter. The two pre-filters stop large particles like hair, dust, and pollen while the HEPA filter removes all finer particles down to 0.3 microns in size. This is followed by an activated charcoal filter which captures gases, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and smells.

This makes it particularly valuable for when I’m cooking. In my apartment, the kitchen vent is not nearly powerful enough to prevent my living room from flooding with smoke, especially when cooking something greasy like bacon.

With the Airthings Renew set to Boost mode, I’m able to weather the storm and prevent my smoke detector from going off multiple times throughout the cooking process. Using the Airthings app, I’m able to monitor the air quality index (AQI) in real time and make manual adjustments to the power (or simply let the Auto mode take over).

At the same time, the charcoal filter is great for getting my cooking smells out of the apartment in a fraction of the time. No more lingering bacon smells for hours on end.

As far as air purifiers go, simplicity reigns supreme. If it works well, offers a few basic features, and blends into my room, I’m happy.

The Airthings Renew does the basics better than nearly any air purifier I’ve tested. It fits seamlessly in my living room, it operates quietly in my bedroom, and its filters and fans work powerfully in the kitchen.

While it isn’t quite large enough to handle big living rooms or spaces with tall ceilings and open layouts, it should be perfect for most enclosed spaces. If you don’t want to think twice about where to place your air purifier or worry about it distracting you, the Airthings Renew is an excellent option.

Tom Price is a reviews editor for Popular Mechanics while also contributing to Runner's World, Best Products, and Bicycling. A brand-by-brand guide to wildlife cameras, chosen for their autofocus capabilities, burst speed and animal tracking in real conditions, curated by our experts.

Wildlife photographers need a camera that is reliable and built to capture fast-moving action at a moment's notice. A fast burst rate, accurate autofocus and robust handling are vital when it comes to wildlife cameras, or you'll end up with sad, blurry photos of an empty tree stump.

We've curated a list of the best models from each of the top camera brands, so no matter which system you want to invest in, there will be something for you here.

Kimberley Lane, senior e-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, including a huge variety of cameras and lenses. With over 7 years of photography experience, her skills span across many different genres, including landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in numerous national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan.

Canon's highest-resolution mirrorless camera with a 45MP stacked sensor, the R5 II is for wildlife photographers who want a professional workflow and need to crop aggressively. It's flexible across multiple wildlife types and delivers pro-level output without going all the way up to the R1.

The new Canon EOS R6 III is an absolute triumph for wildlife photography, and it has solved all the niggles we had with the R6 II when we reviewed it. It has blackout-free 40FPS shooting and an improved 32.5MP sensor, with pre-continuous shooting and up to 7K video. This camera is hard to beat for enthusiasts and intermediate-level shooters.

A monster camera for professional wildlife and sport photographers who need unrivaled power and reliability and can afford to invest in their photography career. Even though it doesn't have the best resolution, the stacked sensor produces less noise and better image quality, and allows for a faster readout speed.

Read the full Canon EOS R1 review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

If you prefer a DSLR and are happy to stick with a hobbyist camera that won't receive any future updates.

A beginner-friendly wildlife option with a 1.6x crop factor to extend the reach of your lenses — effectively a cheat code for wildlife photography.

If you like the look of the R6 III but want to save a bit of money, its predecessor is definitely still worthy of your hard-earned cash.

It's an excellent starter camera for more general styles, but the buffer fills up quickly and there aren't enough buttons and controls on the body to make it efficient for wildlife photography.

A big and welcome upgrade from the previous generation, with a new partially stacked sensor, improved AI autofocus and finally, a higher burst rate than the rather feeble 10FPS of the previous generation. The Sony A7 V is a very attractive option for wildlife, as well as general photography and hybrid shooting, but its Achilles heel is the shallow buffer, which fills up fast and will very quickly get annoying if you regularly shoot in bursts.

We will be reviewing the A7 V soon, but until then, you can read the full review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

With Sony's highest resolution yet, the monstrous A7R VI is the newest and most expensive model in the R lineup. Sony has finally answered our prayers by boosting the burst rate from 10FPS in the previous model up to a massive 30FPS in this new one. For this price, that's more like it. Plus, with a massive 67MP, you'll get some serious cropping power, which comes in handy if you're shooting distant wildlife or birds.

We will be reviewing the A7R VI soon, but for now, you can read the full review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

Experienced users looking for a balance of resolution and speed need look no further than the Sony A1 II. It has a 50.1MP stacked sensor, 30FPS bursts and Sony's class-leading AI autofocus, so what's not to love? That said, it's overkill for beginners and amateurs — plus we'd only recommend it if you can also invest in some of Sony's more expensive glass.

Read the full Sony A1 II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

Stunning 61MP images, but with a much slower burst rate of 10FPS. It's long been our favorite Sony camera (until the new releases), and it's an excellent option if you don't shoot fast-moving animals or birds in flight. We've taken some beautiful wildlife images with it.

A more affordable option here, and it still has AI-powered autofocus, although the 33MP sensor isn't stacked like the new A7 V. Plus, like the previous generation R model, it only has a 10FPS burst rate. Still, its noise handling is excellent, and it is suitable for more general styles of photography.

If you don't need pre-capture, go for the original Sony A1. It's still a wildlife powerhouse with the same 50MP resolution and 30FPS bursts as the new Mark II.

An absolute speed demon, but let's be honest — does anyone actually need 120FPS? Probably not. However, the Sony A9 III is considered to be one of the best cameras for birds in flight (BIF), but it'll be overkill unless you only shoot sports or fast-action bird photography.

Sony's entry level and older cameras tend to be capped at around 10FPS burst rates, and the older models also don't have any AI-powered autofocus features, which make wildlife photography much more fruitful. It's a shame, as there's no real "beginner" Sony wildlife camera on the market that suits these criteria.

For wildlife photography (and most other styles, too, while we're at it), the obvious choice for most Nikon shooters is the Nikon Z8. Often dubbed a "baby Z9", it has all the brains and brawn of the flagship Z9 in a smaller and more affordable package.

If you saw the Z8 and thought, "Hey, I need something big and heavy", then the flagship R9 could be better for you. The integrated grip offers improved balance and weight distribution for longer lenses, although it's only compatible with CFexpress cards, making this model best suited for professionals.

Read the full Nikon Z9 review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

For anyone on a moderate budget looking for a capable wildlife camera, the Nikon Z6 III has a partially stacked sensor, 20FPS RAW shooting and dedicated animal and bird detection modes, all wrapped up in a compact and lightweight body — the only downside being the rather limited 24.5MP resolution.

Read the full Nikon Z6 III review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

A budget-friendly crop sensor (DX) model with flagship level autofocus and up to 30FPS bursts in a small, lightweight body. Plus, the 1.5x crop factor gives you extended reach when paired with full-frame lenses.

Known as one of the best DSLRs ever made, the Nikon D850 is an incredible choice if you don't need the bells and whistles of a mirrorless — but keep in mind that it won't receive any future updates.

If you need unparalleled zoom, the P1000 bridge camera has an insane 24-3,000mm zoom range. There are drawbacks, including the limited 16MP resolution and lack of weather sealing, but for beginners who want an all-in-one package for casual shooting, it's definitely worth a look.

An affordable, entry-level APS-C model with 10FPS bursts, sharp 20MP images and fierce autofocus.

Older DSLR models are typically much slower, have outdated autofocus and limited ISO performance for low-light work.

Wildlife photographers who want a powerful system in a small package should look at the OM-1 Mark II — it can shoot a blisteringly fast 50FPS with full AF/AE tracking (or 120FPS with locked focus), and even though the 20.4MP resolution sounds a little on the low side, we were pleasantly surprised by the image quality.

Read our full OM System OM-1 Mark II review

If you're just getting into wildlife photography and don't need the best of the best, the OM-5 Mark II is a great camera for people who want to photograph wildlife among other styles. It lacks dedicated bird/animal subject detection, but on the whole, OM System's autofocus is still pretty good.

Read the full OM-5 Mark II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

While MFT cameras are often favored for being small and lightweight, big lenses can often feel unbalanced. The OM-D E-M1X fixes this issue with its integrated vertical grip, and the speedy bursts and AI animal detection modes are ideal for fast action — we called it a "wildlife wonder."

If you want to save a few hundred bucks, get the original OM-5 instead of the OM-5 Mark II.

It's not the fastest for wildlife photography with only 5FPS with tracking, but it's a great camera for casual shooters.

With its speedy burst shooting, accurate autofocus and stacked sensor, the X-H2S is ideal for fast action shooting, birds in flight and hybrid photo/video shooters.

Read the full Fuji X-H2S review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

The Fuji X-T5 is a compact APS-C camera to suit traveling photographers perfectly, but the small buffer and hit-and-miss autofocus are better suited to photographing slow-moving, larger mammals as opposed to fast action and birds. Still, it's a versatile option that can shoot multiple styles and produces beautiful 40.2MP images.

Read the full Fuji X-T5 review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

The Fuji X-T50 is an attractive, compact option for beginner wildlife photographers who don't yet need an expensive model with all the bells and whistles. Still, the 40.2MP resolution is beautiful, and it can shoot 20FPS bursts, which is great for wildlife action.

Read the full Fuji X-T50 review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

Where the X-H2S offers speed, the X-H2 offers a higher 40.2MP resolution, which offers more room for cropping. However, the autofocus isn't as good as on the X-H2S, and there's more rolling-shutter due to the non-stacked sensor.

If you're a serious wildlife shooter, we'd recommend upgrading to a full-frame system from Sony, Canon or Nikon in order to get the best autofocus systems for your money.

The Lumix G9 II is particularly well suited to birds and fast-moving subjects thanks to its high-speed bursts, improved animal tracking and the extra reach advantage of Micro Four Thirds lenses. It sacrifices some low-light performance compared to full-frame models, but for wildlife, where reach and speed matter, it's the standout choice from Panasonic.

Read the full Panasonic Lumix G9 II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

The Lumix S5 II is for wildlife photographers who want full-frame image quality and strong modern autofocus, but don't want to pay Canon/Sony/Nikon flagship prices for their camera bodies and lenses.

Read the full Panasonic Lumix S5 II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

This premium wildlife workhorse has a partially-stacked 24.1MP sensor and 70FPS blackout-free burst rate. It features animal and bird detection, but although the autofocus is generally very good, it still trails behind the best-in-class autofocus from the likes of Sony, Canon and Nikon.

Read the full Panasonic Lumix S1 II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

The video-centric sibling of the S5 II. They're very similar in terms of stills performance, so this might be the better option if you also focus on wildlife videography.

Primarily optimized for video workflows and other benefits that don't necessarily benefit stills shooters. It's a hybrid powerhouse, but stills-focused shooters should opt for the G9 II.

The original G9 still performs well for general wildlife, with decent burst shooting and solid handling, but the contrast-based autofocus struggles to keep up with birds in flight and fast, unpredictable movement.

Dedicated wildlife photographers typically choose full-frame mirrorless cameras due to their larger sensor, better noise handling, accurate autofocus and rugged build. Many of these cameras also have fast burst rates, which is essential for capturing fast-moving wildlife or birds in flight.

Beginners and hobbyists can certainly get great shots with more portable models, but some compromises will have to be made in terms of speed and power.

This depends on what kind of wildlife you're photographing, and how fast they move. Generally speaking, the best wildlife cameras have a burst rate of at least 20FPS (frames per second) — but the faster the better. If you photograph large, slow-moving mammals or stationary subjects, your burst rate doesn't need to be rattling off 40FPS at a time. If, however, you photograph birds in flight or fast moving animals, you will need a faster burst rate in order to capture that killer shot.

There's no right or wrong answer here, but generally speaking, a higher resolution is preferred because it produces more detailed images, and you have more room to crop without losing image quality. However, more megapixels equals bigger file sizes, and you therefore need faster cards in order to keep up, especially when you're taking bursts.

That said, you can absolutely get some great shots with lower resolution cameras. We've been impressed by the quality of OM System cameras, and they typically only have around 20MP.

The most important aspect of a wildlife camera for beginners to prioritize is good autofocus. Provided your subject is in focus, you don't necessarily need the fastest burst rate, top of the line weather sealing or highest resolution.

For our money, Sony, Canon and Nikon offer the best autofocus on the market. We'd recommend the Sony A7C II, Canon EOS R7 or Nikon Zf for beginners.

You don't need to go overboard unless you're a professional wildlife photographer looking for the top of the range flagship models. You can get a really impressive wildlife camera for "most people" for anywhere between $2,000 and $3,000, but as many photographers will tell you, it's more beneficial to invest money in a better lens as opposed to splashing out on the very best camera.

#269. Fatty liver disease is actually five different conditions, scientists discover

A common liver disease affecting nearly 30% of adults worldwide is far more complex than previously understood. Researchers at Mayo Clinic have identified five biologically distinct forms of the condition, each associated with different risks of serious health complications, including heart disease, liver failure, cancer, and the need for a liver transplant.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, come from a collaboration between Mayo Clinic and Virginia Tech. Scientists discovered that metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, or MASLD, can develop through several different biological pathways. Some are closely connected to obesity and diabetes, while others appear to be driven by inherited genetic differences.

One of the most important findings involves the genetic forms of the disease. These subtypes are associated with a greater likelihood of progressing to advanced liver damage, even in people who do not have the metabolic risk factors typically linked to fatty liver disease.

By identifying these differences, doctors may eventually be able to recognize vulnerable patients sooner, improve screening, and select treatments based on the specific biological processes responsible for their illness.

"When clinical and genomic data are analyzed together at this scale, you begin to see patterns of disease progression that would otherwise remain hidden," says Shulan Tian, Ph.D., co-senior author and a bioinformatician at Mayo Clinic. "Once you separate these subtypes, you can start to match treatments to the biology that's actually driving the disease."

MASLD, previously known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, develops when excess fat accumulates in the liver. Many people experience no noticeable symptoms, allowing the condition to go undetected for years.

Although fatty liver disease does not always cause serious complications, it can progress to inflammation, scarring, and permanent liver damage. Over time, severe cases may develop into cirrhosis, a condition in which extensive scarring prevents the liver from functioning properly.

MASLD is a major contributor to cirrhosis, liver cancer, and liver transplantation worldwide. Understanding why some patients experience severe complications while others do not has therefore become an important goal for researchers.

Genetic Analysis Reveals Five Distinct Liver Disease Subtypes

To investigate these differences, the research team examined genetic sequencing results alongside extensive medical information from more than 4,600 patients diagnosed with MASLD.

Their analysis included liver enzyme measurements, body mass index, blood lipid levels, and other indicators of metabolic health. The researchers also considered additional medical conditions, including diabetes, depression, and sleep apnea.

Using advanced computer models, they searched for patterns connecting patients with similar genetic characteristics and clinical findings. This approach revealed five distinct groups, each with its own underlying biological features.

The results suggest that patients who receive the same fatty liver disease diagnosis may actually have substantially different forms of the condition, with different risks of developing serious complications.

"What's emerging here is a way to systematically identify meaningful subgroups within complex disease," says Eric Klee, Ph.D., co-senior author and the Everett J. and Jane M. Hauck Midwest Associate Director of Research and Innovation. "It helps us map complex disease with such precision that we can begin to anticipate its course and intervene before the most serious damage occurs."

How Large-Scale DNA Research Made the Discovery Possible

The researchers relied on Mayo Clinic's Research Data Atlas, a system designed to connect patients' genetic information with detailed medical records. By bringing these large collections of data together, scientists can detect relationships that might be difficult to recognize when studying individual patients.

Dr. Klee helped develop the platform, which draws on resources including the Tapestry Study.

That project has produced Mayo Clinic's largest collection of exome data, involving more than 100,000 participants. An exome is the portion of a person's DNA that contains instructions for making proteins, which carry out many of the body's essential functions. Studying this genetic information can reveal inherited differences that influence how diseases begin and progress.

The combination of genetic data and medical histories allows researchers to investigate diseases in much greater detail, potentially uncovering important differences that conventional diagnostic methods cannot detect.

"This is exactly the kind of insight large-scale genomic research was built to deliver," says Konstantinos Lazaridis, M.D., the Carlson and Nelson Endowed Executive Director for the Center for Individualized Medicine who led the Tapestry Study and is a co-author of the research. "When you connect genetic data with detailed clinical information across large populations, you can start to redefine diseases in ways that directly impact patient care."

Surprising Links to Depression, Sleep Apnea, and Migraines

The findings also suggest that the differences between fatty liver disease subtypes extend beyond the liver itself.

For the first time, researchers identified associations between particular MASLD subtypes and conditions such as depression, sleep apnea, and migraine.

These connections suggest that the biological processes underlying certain forms of fatty liver disease may be linked to health problems affecting multiple parts of the body.

Although the findings do not establish that fatty liver disease directly causes these conditions, they highlight how closely liver health may be connected to other biological systems.

Could Personalized Treatments Change Fatty Liver Disease Care?

The discovery could eventually change how doctors assess and treat MASLD. Rather than approaching every patient as though they have the same disease, clinicians may be able to use genetic and clinical information to determine which subtype is present and which complications are most likely to develop.

Such an approach could be particularly valuable for identifying patients with genetic forms associated with severe liver damage, including those who appear to have relatively few conventional risk factors.

The research team now plans to evaluate its findings in larger and more diverse patient populations. Scientists also want to determine whether different subtypes respond differently to available treatments, including GLP-1 receptor agonists, a class of medications used to treat conditions such as type 2 diabetes and obesity.

If future studies confirm these differences, the findings could help move fatty liver disease care toward more precise screening, earlier intervention, and treatments tailored to each patient's underlying biology.

#270. Microdosing LSD shows some cognitive benefits — but only for women

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

The human brain’s response to psychedelic drugs is intriguing.Credit: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis via Getty

In a small preliminary study, women who received 15 micrograms of the psychedelic drug LSD focused for longer periods and responded faster to a stimulus than did those who were given a placebo. This effect was not observed for male participants.

The study was presented on 12 October at a neuropsychology meeting, the ECNP Congress in Munich, Germany, by psychopharmacologist Iva Totomanova at Maastricht University in the Netherlands and her colleagues. The findings are “very cool”, says Conor Murray, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “This work is a notable addition to emerging evidence that low doses of LSD have cognitive benefits.” The data also suggest that some people might be more sensitive than others to small quantities of psychedelics, he adds.

‘Microdosing’ involves taking small doses of a psychedelic every few days, purportedly to improve mood and cognitive function. A typical microdose of LSD can be roughly one-tenth of the amount needed to produce a full psychedelic experience. Although proponents report experiencing a brighter mood and sharper focus, controlled studies on the effects of microdosing have shown mixed results1,2.

Previous research from some members of the team, in collaboration with others, suggests that women feel the drug’s influence more strongly than men do3. To find out whether this can be measured objectively, for example in tests of cognitive performance, Totomanova and her colleagues reanalysed data from a previous study that explored the effects of low doses of LSD on 53 healthy people4.

For the new analysis, the researchers focused on 48 participants. Half of the participants received 15 micrograms of LSD four times over two weeks; others received a placebo. The participants completed a set of cognitive tests assessing sustained attention, information processing and working memory at the beginning of the study, after the first and fourth doses and at a follow-up a week after the last dose. The study was double-anonymized: neither the participants nor the researchers knew who had received the drug.

During the 10-minute test of sustained attention, which involved responding to signals as they appeared on a screen, women who had taken a microdose of LSD reacted 8% faster than those who had been given a placebo. They also experienced fewer attention lapses (see ‘Microdose magic’). By contrast, a microdose of LSD didn’t have much effect on men's reaction time.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03265-y

An early bird with many dinosaur-like features discovered in China seems to have been a fast-running, land-based carnivore with killer claws.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Illustration of the flightless Jurassic bird Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, which had features of both birds and dinosaurs.

Paleontologists in China have discovered a small Jurassic bird that was likely a land-based predator — like a carnivorous pheasant with killer claws. It had some features of birds and others of dinosaurs, suggesting that the earliest birds had a greater diversity of lifestyles than previously recognized.

Jurassic birds first emerged 150 million to 148 million years ago, and fossils of them are rare, so experts are just starting to understand how early birds diversified and evolved the ability to fly.

The researchers discovered the newly identified Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis in 2024, in the fossil assemblage known as the Upper Jurassic Zhenghe Fauna in southeastern China. It lived 150 million to 148 million years ago, roughly when birds started to appear in the fossil record. The team published their findings Wednesday (Oct. 14) in the journal Nature.

Analysis of the fossilized skeleton revealed the animal was small and weighed about 1.8 pounds (0.8  kilograms). "It was probably as large as a crow," Min Wang, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science via email.

Y. yangyuanensis had a mix of features seen in birds and predatory Deinonychosauria dinosaurs, such as Velociraptor, which are known for their sickle-shaped toe claws. It had deinonychosaur-like hyperextensible toes, with forelimbs that were roughly one-third shorter than its hind limbs. This is odd because modern birds and many other Jurassic paravians — the group that includes bird-like dinosaurs, including the ancestors of birds as well as modern birds themselves — have long forelimbs, linked to giving wings more lift force for taking off.

Y. yangyuanensis also had slender cranial elements and sparsely spaced teeth. These features, alongside the curved claw-like toes that were capable of securing prey, suggest that the animal's diet included meat.

"Its key anatomical features are the combination of dinosaurs' and birds' features: for instance, its teeth, pectoral gird, and especially the hyperextensible, 'sickle-clawed' second pedal digit are similar to that of dinosaurs," Wang said. Meanwhile, he said its slender cranial bones and bird-like pelvis are comparable to early birds.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This combination of features suggests that "the morphological gap between birds and dinosaurs is much smaller than we thought," he added.

Comparisons with 377 living bird species showed that the limb proportions of Y. yangyuanensis were most similar to those of terrestrial birds.

Wang suggested that Y. yangyuanensis was a flightless bird, but not one specialized to live in trees or wade in the swamps in the region. It was a small carnivore, with similar proportions to a pheasant, that was well adapted for running. "I think there are no directly comparable modern birds," he said.

The mosaic of features hints that Y. yangyuanensis may have occupied an ecological niche that was rarely utilized by early birds, and that there wasn't a systematic progression toward flight optimization, Wang said.

Despite being flightless, Wang and his colleagues place Y. yangyuanensis closer in the evolutionary tree to modern birds than to Archaeopteryx, one of the world's first proto birds, which lived about 150 million years ago and is thought to have been able to fly.

This adds to evidence that "the ability to fly arose not once, but several times among disparate groups of carnivorous dinosaurs that are closely related to birds," wrote Fernando Novas, a paleontologist at the Felix de Azara Natural History Foundation in Buenos Aires, Argentina, who wasn’t involved in the study, in an accompanying article in Nature. This includes flight evolving in early birds and in scansoriopterygid dinosaurs, which had membranous folds like the wings of bats, and the four-winged microraptors. Y. yangyuanensis seems to have taken a different road, eschewing the flying ways of its relatives.

"It highlights the extraordinary breadth of ecological and morphological diversification that took place close to the origins of avialans," Wang said.

Liming Xu, Min Wang, Ganmin Lin, Liping Dong, Ke Deng, Xing Xu, Honggang Du, Min Lin, Runsheng Chen & Zhonghe Zhou. Nature 658, 690–697 (2026) https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10972-z

#272. This Eerie State of Consciousness Makes Your Brain Feel Broken—but It May Be Keeping You Alive

Suddenly everything becomes unfamiliar...

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

On a cloudy, nondescript day, Akira O’Connor was driving along the M1 motorway in England when, suddenly, the controls of his car became totally unfamiliar. He had to consciously think about how to control the car: moving his right hand up and left hand down on the wheel would move it counterclockwise, which in turn would make the car go left. Bewildered, O’Connor pulled over to get his bearings. Within a minute, everything felt normal again, and he was able to drive home safely.

O’Connor, PhD, a psychology professor at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, had experienced the psychological phenomenon known as jamais vu. Compared to its counterpart, déjà vu, very little is known about these fleeting feelings of unfamiliarity. But recent research has aimed to uncover its roots, leading to speculation that—despite the danger it put O’Connor in—jamais vu could be your brain protecting itself.

While déjà vu occurs when an experience that you know hasn’t happened before feels familiar, jamais vu is the inverse: a disconcerting feeling of unfamiliarity for something that should be known. What distinguishes the phenomenon from a simple memory malfunction is that, ultimately, all of the knowledge is still there. Take a musician who experiences jamais vu while playing a song. They still know how to play the instrument—it’s the sense of familiarity with the process that is lost, making it momentarily feel foreign.

Jamais vu doesn’t strictly occur with routine activities, such as driving or playing music. It can also take place when you encounter previously known faces, places, and even words. However, it appears that the glitch may be more likely to transpire alongside states that diminish your brain’s processing abilities. For instance, fatigue, stress, and certain neurological conditions (particularly temporal lobe epilepsy) all make the list.

But just because jamais vu occurs in a variety of settings doesn't mean it occurs often. Though exact figures vary, researchers agree that healthy individuals are far less likely to experience the phenomenon than déjà vu, which only occurs a couple of times a year itself. That infrequency—in addition to it being a subjective personal experience—makes jamais vu extremely difficult to study in a controlled setting.

However, O’Connor and other researchers solved part of that problem. Led by Chris Moulin, PhD, a cognitive neuropsychology professor at Grenoble Alpes University in France, the team used word alienation tasks to induce jamais vu–like feelings. In one part of the experiment, researchers instructed participants to copy the word “the” 120 times and pause at any point if the word felt peculiar. Fifty-five percent stopped before completing the task fully, reporting a variety of strange sensations the researchers defined as jamais vu.

The researchers also hypothesized that the rate of jamais vu–like feelings depended on the word’s frequency of use in everyday life—the idea being that common words are more likely to generate the disconnect present in jamais vu, as they already have familiarity established. The results supported their idea, as trials with high-familiarity words (like “door” and “money”) caused higher rates of jamais vu than those with low-familiarity words (like “sward” and “usury”).

In an article for The Conversation, Moulin and O’Connor explained how their findings support the idea that jamais vu signals when something has become too fluent, helping people snap out of that repetitive processing. “It makes sense that this has to happen,” they wrote. “Our cognitive systems must stay flexible, allowing us to direct our attention to wherever is needed rather than getting lost in repetitive tasks for too long.”

The researchers’ conclusion mirrors a popular theory that characterizes déjà vu as an evolutionary adaptation. With the dissonance between familiarity and actual experience, déjà vu helps the brain become aware that there’s a mismatch in memory, acting almost like a fact-checking process. Could detecting the inverse problem—that is, a known setting seeming unfamiliar—through jamais vu mean it’s a biological safety net as well?

O’Connor thinks it’s an intuitive conclusion to arrive at, especially in the context of doing something repeatedly: “In a kind of evolutionary sort of way, it does make sense to say that’s a stop mechanism in your brain.” However, he notes the use of the term “evolutionary” is intentionally provocative, and there’s currently no concrete evidence to support or refute the claim.

Moulin follows the same line of thought. “It could be a byproduct of how we’re hardwired,” he says. “[But] the fact that it doesn’t happen much makes me think that it might just be a meaningless glitch.”

Before researchers uncover the theoretical purpose of jamais vu, Moulin says they still need to accomplish the basics—like what jamais vu even looks like to begin with. “That would be the best thing—just simply that we can measure something that’s different in the brain of somebody who says they’re having jamais vu,” he says. “There’s a whole bunch of related phenomena, and it would be nice to know if they are all the same thing.”

Despite this uncertainty, there are already hints as to what regions of the brain might be involved with jamais vu. The phenomenon’s high occurrence in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy—a condition involving seizures in the brain’s temporal lobe, an area associated with memory processing—suggests its physiological roots lie in that region. And a study published in Nature Neuroscience in 2017 identified potential pathways within this area for these errors to occur. Researchers from the University of Massachusetts Medical School found evidence that the interpeduncular nucleus (IPN), a group of neurons in the midbrain, controls familiarity signaling—judgment of whether an experience is brand-new or familiar. Their experiments with mice found evidence the IPN balances its judgments based on input from two other areas within the midbrain: The ventral tegmental area signals whether or not an experience is novel, while the medial habenula relays information on its familiarity.

These independent, yet overlapping patterns could be key to explaining where the disconnect between novelty and familiarity occurs with jamais vu. But that requires further study—research that Moulin believes has great potential, regardless of outcome. “You can see the building blocks for lots of interesting metacognitive subjective experiences by studying that kind of thing,” he says. “Even if it is just a weird quirk, it’s a weird quirk that tells us something about how the mind operates.”

#273. Scientists predicted doomsday for November 13, 2026. Should we be worried?

In 1960, Science, one of the world’s leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026. It predicted that on this future date — less than a month from today — the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself.

The outlandishness of the claim landed the article widespread public attention. More surprisingly — because its underlying research and math seemed sound — it also received careful and sustained scientific attention.

The authors — Heinz von Foerster, an Austrian-American professor and cybernetics expert and two of his students, Patricia M. Mora and Lawrence W. Amiot — argued that human populations are exceptional and might grow beyond an exponential rate, at an ever-increasing one.

“Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve,” they argued. “They will be squeezed to death.”

The article was regularly cited, and its predictions appeared remarkably accurate — until around 1993, halfway to the predicted “doomsday,” when the global population began falling behind its forecasts.

Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half what it was in 1960. Hopefully, we will all wake up on Nov. 13 to an ordinary day. Nonetheless, this article remains exemplary for blending rigorous science with the art of stagecraft to staggering effect.

The mid-20th century saw increasing societal concern about global population growth and its potential to lead to resource scarcity and geopolitical conflict. Underlying much of this concern was implicit or explicit acceptance of the Malthusian idea that whereas population has the potential to grow exponentially, it is kept constantly under check by its capacity to feed itself.

In their article, however, von Foerster and his co-authors argued that as far as populations go, humans may be exceptional.

Given our capacity to communicate and form “coalitions” that help us resolve problems, rising population density might simply mean more opportunities for collaboration, so that our numbers might grow not only beyond an exponential rate but at an ever-increasing one.

They then used 24 estimates of the world population stretching across the past 2,000 years to show that human numbers have in fact continually outpaced expectations. All this was presented in calm, scientific prose and aided by dense mathematical equations.

Von Foerster and his co-authors then projected these historical figures into the future, calculating that thanks to ever-increasing growth, in the year 2026 our numbers would near infinity.

Thankfully, the same capacity for collaboration that assisted our species’ development throughout history could now avert this catastrophe. Since we are unlikely to want to reduce our life spans, they concluded, we should work together to reduce the global birth rate by half.

This publication caused an immediate stir. There were stories in Time and The New York Times. It became the subject of a series of Pogo comic strips and many commentators took the article as strictly a tongue-in-cheek comment on population fears.

Rather than the story dying out, a funny thing happened. When Science published letters to the editor from mathematicians and demographers attacking von Foerster and his colleagues’ work — calling it “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd” — the authors responded with spirited defenses that doubled down on the underlying math and its conclusions.

Throughout the 1960s through to the 1980s, the “doomsday” equation became regularly cited — usually at face value — in textbooks on genetics, ecology and demography.

It appeared in stranger places, too. In a 1963 Canadian Parliamentary committee, for example, a witness from the chemical industry prominently cited it as reason chemical pesticides were required: to feed the approaching population explosion. In a 1971 U.S. Supreme Court abortion case leading up to Roe v. Wade, it was cited as why there was no compelling reason for the government to favor increased population.

The doomsday idea persisted in part because its predictions for future populations turned out to be highly accurate — at least for a while. Its core equation yielded projections that were better than those of most demographers throughout the 1970s and 1980s.

Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter and the global population began falling behind the forecasts — because the world began to do what von Foerster and his colleagues recommended it do. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.

We will probably not all wake up on Friday, Nov. 13 “squeezed to death.” But before simply moving on — prepping for the next doomsday scenario — it is worth asking what we can learn from this one.

For me, the lesson is in how we present our beliefs to the world. Heinz von Foerster was, at one point in his life, a stage magician. Borrowing the classic language of stagecraft, an effective illusion relies on three parts: the setup, the extraordinary turn and the final reveal that returns the situation to normal.

Von Foerster and his co-authors’ article gained attention because it was an ordinary scientific article wrapped in an extraordinary title and conclusion. It retained significance because it was firmly grounded in research and argument.

To draw the world’s attention to a serious matter by way of absurdity — that’s a good trick.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Alan MacEachern, Professor, History, Western University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22, bringing a spectacular display of shooting stars to the autumn sky.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22, triggering a spectacular display of shooting stars as Earth plunges through the densest part of the debris trail shed by Halley's Comet. Here's what you need to know.

Orionid meteors are best spotted between the hours of midnight and dawn on Oct. 22, when 10-20 shooting stars may be seen brightening the night sky each hour under ideal dark-sky.

The glare cast by the 74%-lit waxing gibbous moon will hide fainter shooting stars for much of the night. Thankfully, the lunar disk will set a few hours after midnight, leaving a window of beautifully dark sky before dawn in which to enjoy the full majesty of the annual meteor shower. Remember to use a trusted website like Time and Date to discover the exact moment of moonset for your location.

Orionid shooting stars will appear to originate from a patch of sky, or radiant, located close to the red giant star Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion, which glistens above the southeastern horizon for stargazers in the U.S. during the early hours of Oct. 22.

For the best views look 40-90 degrees away from the radiant, where the glowing trains left in the wake of the fast-moving meteors will be at their longest. Be sure to head away from artificial lights and allow 20-30 minutes for your eyes to fully adapt to the dark for the best

The Orionid meteor shower is active each year as Earth passes through the stream of debris left behind by Comet 1P/Halley, which was observed by a fleet of spacecraft when it last visited the inner solar system in 1986.

Shooting stars become visible when particles of the ancient comet collide with our planet's atmosphere at 147,600 miles per hour (237,539 kilometers per hour), vaporizing in a spectacular display of natural fireworks.

Hoping to catch a shooting star for yourself? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing meteor showers, along with our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography.

Editor's Note: If you would like to share your Orionid photos with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.
