Analysis of tiny zircon crystals buried within the 10-mile-wide Ames crater in northwest Oklahoma suggests that the submerged structure dates back to 370 million years ago, during the Frasnian-Famennian mass extinction event.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of America's largest meteor craters is around 100 million years younger than scientists thought, which means the ancient impact coincided with — and potentially contributed to — one of the biggest global extinction events in Earth's history, according to a new study.

The underground impact structure, known as Ames crater, is located in northern Oklahoma and is named after a small town that sits above the submerged crater. At around 10 miles (16 kilometers) wide, it is the fourth-largest impact structure in the U.S.

Ames crater was created when an Eiffel Tower-size space rock slammed into our planet at more than 70,000 mph (110,000 km/h). At the time, the region was covered in a shallow ocean, and the crater was subsequently buried beneath layers of seafloor sediment. Therefore, there are no visible signs of the crater at the surface today. It was only discovered in 1991, when oil prospectors accidentally drilled into it.

Until now, researchers thought Ames crater dated to the Ordovician meteor event around 467 million years ago. During this period, an unusually high number of large space rocks smashed into Earth, likely due to the fragmentation of a single parent body somewhere in space. Scientists found fossils of marine animals in and around the crater that date to around the time of that event.

But in the new study, published July 7 in the journal Meteoritics and Planetary Science, researchers analyzed fracture patterns within tiny rocky fragments known as zircon crystals that were embedded in the underground crater. This revealed that the impact actually occurred 370 million years ago, around 97 million years after the Ordovician meteor event.

There are no visible signs of the Ames crater today. However, scientists have been able to map out its size and shape using ground-penetrating radar. This circle represents the rough outline of the the submerged structure.

"No matter what technique we used, it was coming back to this younger signal," study first author Elizabeth Catlos, a geologist and planetary scientist at the University of Texas at Austin, said in a statement.

Zircon crystals are tiny pieces of a superdurable mineral known as zirconium silicate. These crystals are scattered throughout most of Earth's rock formations, including most of the oldest known rocks on our planet. The near-industructible crystals are extremely useful to geologists because their internal structure preserves evidence of being exposed to extreme conditions, such as high temperatures and intense pressures.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Analyzing zircon crystals is now one of the primary methods of dating ancient meteor craters, and the technique has led to several other impact dates being revised. For example, in July, researchers in Australia revealed that the North Pole Dome crater was around 500 million years younger than initial studies predicted, and in 2025, experts found that the impact that birthed Scotland's Stac Fada Member structure happened around 200 million years later than earlier research estimated.

The crystals offer insight into what Earth may have looked like shortly after it formed and have recently been used to more accurately date the moon.

The internal structure of zircon crystals preserves evidence of being exposed to extreme conditions, such as high temperature and pressure, making them ideal for exploring ancient impacts. This photo, captured during a completely unrelated study, shows one such crystal under an electron microscope.

"These small crystals allow us to go back in time and learn about the major changes to Earth's ancient landscapes," study co-author Danny Stockli, a geologist and dean of the Jackson School of Geosciences at the University of Texas at Austin, said in the statement. "It would be great to do this for more of the meteor impact sites across the continent so we could get a more accurate timeline for these major events."

The crater's new age takes it firmly out of the Ordovician meteor event and places it into the Frasnian-Famennian mass extinction event, also known as the Kellwasser event or the Late Devonian mass extinction.

During the Frasnian-Famennian event, which began around 372 million years ago and lasted for several million years, as much as half of all marine life went extinct as Earth's oceans were depleted of oxygen. The die-off, which was most likely triggered by global cooling due to increased levels of volcanic activity, is often cited as one of the five major extinction events in Earth's history.

The researchers emphasized that the Ames impact was not the cause of the Frasnian-Famennian event. However, they noted that the fallout from the impact, which would have injected huge clouds of dust into the air, may have contributed to the atmospheric cooling effect in the region.

It is an important reminder that the ability to accurately date specific events like this can inform our understanding of wider global patterns and trends, the researchers wrote.

"With this research, we're basically taking a major pawn out of the Ordovician Meteor Event and dumping it into the Frasnian-Famennian event, and saying, 'This is where this impact belongs,'" Catlos said.

The new study was dedicated to co-authors Andrew Parisi and Michael Brookfield, who sadly died before it was published.

Catlos, E. J., Parisi, A. F., Brookfield, M. E., Erickson, T., Gulick, S. P., Schmitt, A. K., Stockli, D. F., Miggins, D. P., Ruchte, B., & Cloos, M. (2026). The Ames impact structure, Oklahoma: New radioisotopic constraints and implications for North American impact chronology. Meteoritics and Planetary Science, 61(8), 2103–2139. https://doi.org/10.1111/maps.70191

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. #276. Tesla Just Unveiled Its Flying Car. History Says It Might Not Work Out.

Tesla says its Air-Nozzle Roadster will be here in three years. But the flying car was just a decade away in 1957.

On December 17, 1903, the Wright Brothers made history with the first powered flight, at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. A little under 123 years later, and a little under 1,500 miles away, a SpaceX facility in McGregor, Texas livestreamed a demo of Tesla’s latest Roadster model.

This particular vehicle is able to go from zero to 60 mph in less than a second, but its distinguishing feature is something far more vertical.

As company founder Elon Musk said to an eager, whooping crowd, “We need an audience to prove that it’s not AI or SI.”

“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX engineers,” Musk continued, “working closely together to make something that you haven’t seen in any movie.”

Which is true, provided you’ve never seen Blade Runner. Or Back to the Future Part II. Or The Fifth Element. Or The Jetsons Movie. Or Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets. Or Total Recall. Or The Absent-Minded Professor. Or Chitty Chitty Bang Bang. Or the ninth Fast & Furious movie.

You get where this is going. They made a flying car.

The vehicle launched itself up a ramp until it was in the air, upside down. Then, as it appeared to fall, it instead righted itself in mid-air, and gently glided down to the ground on gusts of forced air like one of the landing vessels in 2001: A Space Odyssey. It was, undeniably, an impressive and elegant display.

Later, this new Roadster (operating without a driver “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” as Musk noted) did another demonstration, this time hurtling through the air in a daredevil jump over a row of Teslas, showing the vehicle’s future utility—if in the future, Bo and Luke Robo-Duke need to jump a ravine to get bootleg ketamine past Cyber-Boss Hogg.

Musk revealed that the propulsion comes courtesy of 10 nozzles attached to “ultra high-pressure air tanks,” and he told the eager audience that the car will be going into production in 2028.

So now, is this the point where Popular Mechanics puts their name on the line to tell you that you’ll be driving one of Tesla’s flying cars in 2028? Absolutely not.

This is far from the first time someone has claimed to have invented the flying car. There have actually been a myriad of flying cars supposedly right around the corner for the last half-century or more, and Popular Mechanics has been there to cover them. Before Elon Musk, there was an inventor by the name of Stanley Hiller Jr. who dreamed of letting the average man take flight from his own driveway.

So, you know, fool us once, shame on you. Fool us twice...

In July 1957, the cover of Popular Mechanics Magazine promised readers that the Hiller Helicopter Company’s Aerial Sedan was “your flying car for 1967.” The article’s author, Thomas E. Stimson Jr., even boasted to readers that they would “be able to order a four-door model, a sports job, or even a light truck configuration.”

Personal aerial automobiles were the dream of Stanley Hiller Jr, founder and namesake of the Hiller Helicopter Company. It’s no surprise Hiller believed it was possible; he’d invented the first coaxial helicopter at just 15 years old, and his XH-44 “Hiller-Copter” so impressed the U.S. Army that he got himself a draft deferment from WWII. But the post-war period saw Hiller make several attempts at some form of “flying car,” and he took Popular Mechanics along for the ride.

In our February 1951 issue, Hiller took Thomas E. Stimson, Jr. on a ride in a two-person helicopter “small enough to land on your lawn” called the Hiller Hornet. Priced under $5000 ($71k today), Hiller believed that the vehicle would already be on the market for consumers the following month, were it not for that darned Korean War. It’s true that manufacturing helicopters for the military during the then-ongoing Korean War commandeered most of Hiller's factory floor during that period, but the war wrapped up in July 1953, and the Hiller Hornet nevertheless did not, in fact, make its way to market that August.

Perhaps by then, Hiller’s focus was on the forthcoming Aerial Sedan. Looking like a cross between the iconic “Rocket 88” Oldsmobile of the 1950s and the Fantastic Four’s Fantasticar (still a few years away, debuting in 1961), the designs Hiller shared in our 1957 issue showcased both civilian and military applications for his flying vehicle. “How can engineers be so sure about something that hasn’t been flown yet?” our article asked. “For one thing, the flying fan is nothing more than four ducted fans that are held together by a framework that supports the engine and cabin.”

You can decide for yourself whether that seems safer or less safe than Tesla’s 10 nozzles and “ultra high-pressure air tanks.”

What likely doomed the Aerial Sedan actually appears a few paragraphs later:

During the late 1950s, the U.S. Army became very interested in developing a flying car. They actually funded the development of several different models from competing companies. Eventually, though, the project was scrapped, as often happens with experimental military initiatives. Once that line of business dried up, Hiller refocused his efforts on helicopters, before pivoting in the 1960s to being a “company turnaround specialist.” The Hiller flying car was not to be.

Others have tried; in 1994 we showcased Kenneth G. Wernicke’s Aircar, for example. But to date, none of them wound up on your local auto dealer’s showroom floor.

The dream keeps crashing into practicality. Not to lean on that Jurassic Park line about scientists “so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn’t stop to think if they should”—but just take a moment to think about everything that’s gone awry involving automobiles and airplanes in the last seventy years. Now imagine those two technologies were combined into one. Think of the reckless drivers who have nearly (or fully) crashed into your car, or even your house, and now you want to give them the gift of flight? Is that not like giving your cousin who blew his fingers off with a firecracker the key to the Raytheon warehouse?

Ultimately, only time will tell if Elon Musk makes good on his promise of a flying car in 2028. Perhaps he will achieve what Stanley Hiller couldn’t, for good or for ill.

All we can say for certain is, no, you didn’t get a flying car in 1967. But you did get the first Super Bowl, and Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, so ultimately, maybe you got the better deal back then.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

#277. How pregnancy reshapes the brain throughout life

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Liisa Galea is a neuroscientist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, University of Toronto, Canada.

Mental as well as physical health can be affected during gestation and beyond. Credit: Getty

A Mother’s Brain: The New Science of the Neuro-Maternal Revolution Susana Carmona MIT Press (2026)

When I acquired a copy of the book A Mother’s Brain by neuroscientist Susana Carmona, I thought: at last, a book about what happens to your brain during pregnancy. I recalled how I’d realized in 1997, when I was a young assistant professor, soon after giving birth to my first child, that books for expectant or new parents were light on what happens to the brain. As a neuroscientist, I was curious. What was going on with my brain?

Another observation that I had was how jarring it was to go from having so much attention being paid to me when I was pregnant — including intrusive attention about what I was consuming and unwanted hands on my belly — to the utter lack of attention on me after my baby was born. All of the attention went from pregnant me to the baby. Fair enough, babies can be cute, but what about the mum? What was happening to me? Clearly things in my brain were different, but there was little in the scientific literature to tell me what was happening — which is one of the big reasons I started to work in this area of neuroscience.

My first study on this topic (L. A. Galea et al. Horm. Behav. 37, 86–95; 2000), was about memory and changes in the volume of the hippocampus, a region of the brain, throughout pregnancy. Fast forward two years to me being pregnant with my second child, and I could not for the life of me find where I had parked my car at the end of the day. It was not unusual to find me crying in the stairwell of a ten-storey car park because I was about to be late to pick up kid number one from childcare.

In my experience, mums are often told that our bodies will ‘bounce back’ after pregnancy. But work from Carmona and others now suggests that pregnancy can leave lasting signatures on the brain and body. This will probably not shock any parent, particularly the one who gave birth.

A Mother’s Brain is, in many ways, an ode to the remarkable ‘plasticity’ or adaptability of the brain and body during and after pregnancy. Gestation requires adaptations across almost every physiological system, and Carmona describes these changes to the cardiovascular, immune and circulatory systems exceptionally well. The book also details the remarkable role of the placenta in orchestrating many of these adaptations. When considering this physiological transformation, it’s no surprise that pregnancy also leaves a signature on the brain.

Embryos share cells with the parent through the placenta.Credit: OMIKRON/SPL

Carmona conveys her palpable love of being a mother while recognizing that motherhood is not universally joyful. I agree strongly with Carmona’s contention that people need to be truthful with parents-to-be. The experience isn’t always positive. Some people will experience mental-health challenges during this period, possibly for the first time.

It is important that they seek — and receive — the support that they need. Care during pregnancy and in the postpartum period must attend to mental as well as physical health, and timely access to effective treatments, including talk therapy, should be standard. The repercussions of not receiving enough support can be tragic.

The book is at its best when Carmona conveys just how biologically extraordinary pregnancy is. For example, she describes how cells from a baby can linger in the bodies of people who have been pregnant, sometimes for decades, yet it is still not known how these cells contribute to long-term health. Carmona also takes the reader through the genesis of her own research questions and the paths they took from idea to publication, interspersing the science with anecdotes from her life and pregnancies.

What drugs are safe during pregnancy? There’s a shocking lack of data

What drugs are safe during pregnancy? There’s a shocking lack of data

Yet, I found myself wishing that Carmona had gone into more detail about another part of this story: how difficult it has been to convince the scientific community that pregnancy’s effects on the brain are worth studying. Carmona’s first landmark paper on this topic (E. Hoekzema et al. Nature Neurosci. 20, 287–296; 2017) did not have an easy path to publication. I know this first-hand. I was one of the reviewers who argued with the editors about the importance and novelty of the work.

There are many hidden obstacles to publishing research on women’s health, even though the paucity of existing research might suggest the opposite, given that new findings are paramount for getting your work accepted. Many researchers in the field need to justify that their findings are worth publishing. I would have welcomed more exploration of that resistance and why questions concerning pregnancy and the brain are often overlooked.

Discussion of what these pregnancy-related brain changes mean is also important. These are natural adaptations. For example, people often experience a reduction in brain volume during gestation. But this is not necessarily a bad thing, just as an increase is not necessarily good. Different brain regions and measures (such as volume and connectivity) change in various ways during pregnancy and in the postpartum period, and the overall effects can be confusing to piece together. But such distinctions are, as Carmona points out, important for a public audience for whom headlines about a ‘shrinking brain’ can sound alarming.

Consider the hippocampus. A Mother’s Brain describes this region but pays relatively little attention to the striking parallels between human findings and decades of work in other mammals. These studies have shown that rodents experience pregnancy-related and postpartum changes to cognition, to the structure of the hippocampus and to the creation of nerve cells in the brain. In rats, the production of neurons decreases during pregnancy and the early postpartum period, with subtle variations between first and second pregnancies. There are also later differences between foster mothers and birthing mothers in terms of brain-cell creation in the hippocampus and memory that remain to be explained.

In the long term, beyond the postpartum period, reproductive experience improves memory and the plasticity of the hippocampus because it results in changes to nerve-cell quantity and connections throughout life. That paradox — decreases in one measure alongside improved function in others — is why interpreting pregnancy-related brain changes requires more than asking whether a measure went up or down.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03312-8

#278. NASA’s SpaceX launch lights up the sky with a giant glowing jellyfish

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket transformed the early morning sky into a spectacular display of light on October 13, 2026. As the rocket climbed above Earth carrying a Dragon spacecraft, sunlight illuminated its expanding exhaust plumes, creating an enormous glowing shape that resembled a jellyfish.

This striking phenomenon, known as a "jellyfish," occurs when a rocket launches near sunrise or sunset. Sunlight reaches the exhaust high in the atmosphere, making the spreading plume shine brightly against the darker sky below.

SpaceX Launch Creates a Spectacular Sky Display

The mission lifted off at 6:33 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The illuminated exhaust plumes were visible across the eastern United States, giving observers a remarkable view of the rocket's journey into space.

The launch marked SpaceX's 35th commercial resupply mission for NASA, delivering scientific experiments, essential supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station.

New Space Station Upgrades and Medical Experiments

Among the cargo aboard Dragon is the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, known as IROSAs. These additional solar panels are scheduled for installation later this fall and will help provide electricity for the orbiting laboratory.

The spacecraft is also transporting equipment for several scientific investigations that could lead to important advances in medicine and materials science.

One experiment will explore manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity, where the near absence of gravity creates conditions that cannot easily be reproduced on Earth. The research could help develop technologies to restore vision in people with certain forms of vision loss.

Another investigation will use 3D heart tissue models to support the development of more efficient drug testing methods during future space missions.

Additional experiments will examine how a new type of glass forms in microgravity and investigate brain organoids, miniature models of brain tissue grown from cells. These models could help researchers identify new targets for treating neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis.

#279. The 8 Best Trail Cameras for Hunting, Wildlife Watching, and Even Home Security

These expert-tested trail cams help hunters and wildlife watchers capture what happens off-grid.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Fall is peak season for those who want to gather last-minute information on deer and other game animals ahead of hunting seasons. Even if you’re not heading into the woods to hunt, it’s one of the most interesting times of year for observing wild animals. Whitetail deer, elk, bears, and other animals are becoming much more active due to seasonal mating periods while waterfowl and other birds migrate for the winter.

The advantage of having a modern trail camera is the ability to capture the action you’d otherwise miss, whether it’s an elusive buck passing by your stand in the night or the raccoon creating backyard mayhem. If you’re considering a trail camera that uses a cellular network to send photos and videos directly to your smartphone, the good news is these have gotten even easier to use.

While the trail cam experience improves every year, the cost of many units is more than $100, and cellular models require recurring data plan charges, making it trickier to assess value. Images from game cameras are better than ever, even in budget models, and apps add software features often.

Sorting out what matters most to you and how you plan to use your trail cameras can be a challenge, so we explain what to look for along with sharing our top recommendations selected from year-round testing of dozens of cameras evaluated side-by-side.

The Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0 replaces the Reveal Pro 3.0 camera, our previous pick for Best Overall. Released this summer, the Pro 4.0 version keeps what made the 3.0 great and improves on it in two key areas: image quality and battery life. Reveal has one of the best apps in the space, with tons of settings and features to tweak your setup and manage your cameras and images. Updates to these basics are big usability improvements that demanding trail camera users will notice.

Cameras going dead in the field is a major gripe for users of these gadgets. You have to physically go and replace batteries, which adds hassle and cost to your experience. I tend to place cameras in early summer and let them run for several months until my hunting season starts. The problem is that active cameras can run through eight to 12 AA batteries in a month depending on the model and your camera settings.

Tactacam has tackled this issue in a few ways with the Pro 4.0 release. The brand told me it audited everything about camera operation that drained the battery and then made small tweaks to reduce power demands anywhere it could.

Tactacam has also developed sold separately R5 and R10 lithium battery packs that replace previous battery add-ons, which have the notable benefit of swapping into the same form factor as the AA battery tray, so they don’t add bulk to the camera.

Image quality in the Reveal cameras has always been solid, but the company took a unique approach to dealing with the challenge of getting both crisp day and night images by installing separate sensors for each. Photographers know that night images require different gear and settings than daylight shooting, so the split makes sense. The early returns from a month of testing confirm that the quality of both day and night is much improved.

The rest of this flagship Reveal camera is impressive, carrying over from the Pro 3.0 and now-discontinued Ultra camera. The Reveal lineup now has just two similar cameras: the Pro 4.0 and the X 4.0. The Reveal X 4.0 is basically the Pro 4.0 without a built-in display screen, which saves $30 and is a great option if you don’t value the screen for aiming and reviewing images at the device.

As mentioned, the robust app gives you remote control over everything including photo and video capture settings, transmission frequency, night image flash, trigger delays, and more. You’re also able to launch a live stream to follow up on interesting images, but there’s an additional subscription cost and it will drain the battery quickly. There’s also built-in GPS that shows the location of your camera on a map within the app—essential if you’ve forgotten where you placed it or if it’s stolen.

Cell-connected trail cameras are handy, but if you’re low on funds or trying to run a multitude of cameras, paying $150 and up per camera gets pricey fast. Spypoint’s Flex M2 trail camera keeps both the upfront purchase cost and recurring subscription fees reasonable. Spypoint even has a free data plan that gives you 100 images per month if you want to avoid subscription fees altogether. (The Flex M2 doesn’t have onboard memory, nor does it ship with an SD card, so you’ll have to spend at least another $20 per camera for a high-speed SD card.)

Despite the low price, the camera’s 32-megapixel photos and 1080p video are clear and well-exposed. The Flex M2 displays lower-resolution images in the app but you can request full-resolution images when you want more detail. This is beneficial because it keeps data demands low and shows up in the battery usage as well. After a month in the field, the eight AA batteries I was using displayed in the app at “High” strength.

Additionally, I appreciated that this camera is compact since I’m usually hauling my cameras several miles into the backcountry in a pack. If you want to run this camera year-round, I’d consider picking up the $60 five-watt solar panel add-on, which has a built-in battery and should allow you to leave the Flex M2 up indefinitely.

I was impressed with the overall experience with the Flex M2, but the highlight here is the cost to purchase and run this camera. Yes, you’ll need to pay up for video or a higher quota of images, but this is a great option if you want the excitement of getting trail camera images on your phone without the annoyance of yet another recurring subscription fee on your credit card.

The best way to cut down on battery costs for your trail cameras is running solar panels. While many cameras have the option to run on solar, it’s often an additional upfront cost. The new 2026 Moultrie Edge 4 Solar trail camera has it all smartly packaged together in an integrated unit that costs less than some standalone cameras.

Setting up solar often requires separate mounting as well as hauling out lots of separate pieces and cables to be connected. The Edge 4 Solar just straps to a tree as a single unit, ready to run indefinitely. The camera comes with a rechargeable lithium-ion battery powered by the panel, which enables you to place a camera and leave it running as long as you need. Having the solar panel integrated is convenient and compact, but you’ll need to choose spots wisely to ensure both good captures and sun exposure.

Beyond the solar power setup, the Edge 4 is a solid trail camera with crisp 40-megapixel photos and 1080p video. The app is polished and makes setup and use hassle-free even if you’re not particularly tech-savvy. The subscription plans are in line with the industry average, ranging from $8.99 to $22.99. The lowest-tier plan offers more than most other companies’ $5 plans (1,000 images and 10 videos) and the most expensive plan offers unlimited images and 50 videos and discounts steeply to $7.99 per month for each additional camera.

There are two significant recurring costs with a cellular trail camera: the data plan and batteries. Connected cameras can chew through batteries, which can add up, especially since you’ll want to use more expensive lithium batteries if you can. Sehmua’s 4G Solar Trail Camera comes with rechargeable batteries and a solar panel, which allows the camera to run indefinitely given adequate sun exposure.

The camera itself has a fast trigger and 2K photo and video that can be saved to an SD card, or to cloud storage for an additional cost. The app, which is a little clunky and can be confusing due to some quirky menus and word choices, works with images that show up quickly and reliably.

Notably, even though this is a 4G cellular-connected camera, you can still use the camera to record to the SD card if you decide not to pay for one of the data plans. This is another sneaky way this camera provides solid value for its low price point.

The convenience of cell-connected trail cameras is undeniable, but if you’re burned out on subscription charges and don’t mind checking your cameras manually, you can save a significant amount on your trail camera setup. The WOSPORTS Trail Camera is a budget option with impressive image quality and low one-time cost. The camera doesn’t ship with the required eight AA batteries, but it does come with an SD card.

This compact G600 records imagery to an SD card and lasts longer since it doesn’t use batteries communicating over cellular networks. You’ll have to walk into your hunting zone to swap cards, but the purchase price is a fraction of the lifetime cost of buying and operating a modern cell-connected setup.

The 56-megapixel images and 4K video aren’t Planet Earth–level quality, but I was still more than satisfied with the pictures and videos I got. I don’t put too much stock in megapixel numbers as a true measure of trail camera image quality because these numbers are mostly inflated with software enhancements. That said, the images and videos from the WOSPORTS camera were sharp enough for clear identification of details.

No matter how great your trail camera placement, it’s easy for cameras to miss animals. This is exacerbated in big open areas such as wetlands or crop fields where it can be hard to know precisely where animals might appear.

Muddy’s Trifecta 180 is built to minimize these misses. Three motion sensors and a rotating camera capture wide-angle 180-degree images. This is the perfect camera for the edge of large agricultural fields where animals could appear anywhere and often turn up in groups that can be hard to capture in a single image. You have the option for the camera to stitch together impressive panorama images (though they’re harder to appreciate on a phone screen) or the option to capture single-zone images like a regular trail camera would.

The downside of this impressive device is that it seemed to use more battery power than usual, likely attributable to the camera’s need to move and the usual drains of taking and transmitting images. If you’re planning on running it long-term, I’d consider picking up the solar panel accessory with integrated battery.

The Defend by Reveal 360 is not your traditional trail camera—it’s closer to a home security camera that’s designed to work anywhere. Ring and other doorbell cameras usually rely on WiFi for connectivity, which makes them impractical more than about 50 yards from your router. The Defend 360 uses cellular networks instead so you can place this camera anywhere with a decent cell signal.

In the field, the Defend 360’s biggest advantage is motion. Most trail cams are fixed in place, but this one adds remote pan-and-tilt control, allowing you to reposition the camera from your phone. Its 355-degree pan and 75-degree tilt effectively eliminate blind spots when combined with the wide-angle lens.

Like a regular trail camera, motion detection triggers photos only to conserve battery and data. A 1080p live view can be activated on demand when you need a closer live look. That approach makes sense for remote monitoring, though it feels different if you’re used to continuous video feeds from home security cameras.

A rechargeable battery and included solar panel allow for long-term deployment with minimal maintenance. Setup is straightforward via the app, and the camera automatically connects to the strongest available carrier via eSIM.

There are a few downsides. Night footage is serviceable but not amazing, and like most cellular cameras, it requires a subscription plan to unlock full functionality. Still, if your goal is reliable, wide-area monitoring in remote locations, the Defend 360 delivers better coverage and control than standard trail cameras.

A lifetime warranty usually isn’t reason enough alone to buy a product, but in the world of electronics generally and with trail cameras specifically, it’s unheard of and fairly compelling.

With Yellowstone.ai’s Y2 Camera and Solar Bundle, your upfront cost is on the higher side at $250, but the solar panel and rechargeable battery mean no recurring battery costs. You’ll also save on gas and time, since this is a cell-connected camera, and there’s no need to visit the camera unless you want to move it.

Compared to the big-name trail camera apps, the app is not quite as polished, but over several months of testing, I did not experience any of the quirks and bugs I’ve experienced with some trail cam apps from overseas companies (Yellowstone.ai is U.S.-based).

The image and video quality isn’t quite as sharp as the top tier of the cameras I’ve tested like the Reveal Pro 4.0 or Moultrie Edge 4 Solar, but it’s by no means unacceptable. I was impressed by features such as built-in GPS, automatic cell network selection, and remote settings adjustments.

The solar bundle comes with the panel, Y2 camera, and two rechargeable battery packs. If you want to keep the upfront cost down, the camera alone is half the price at $125.

I’ve assembled my choices in this guide based on years of firsthand testing, and I continue testing new trail cam options every season to keep up with the constant rollout of new features and improvements. For decades, I’ve been hanging trail cameras with professional hunters and friends to capture wallowing elk, nursing moose, and scavenging bears on camera.

Historically, I’ve preferred inexpensive, simple cameras that I monitor manually, which keeps my trail camera budget in check, but as connected cameras have gotten more reliable and affordable, I’ve shifted to using cell cams almost exclusively. I hunt in three different states as well as in spots several hours from my home in Colorado, which makes manually checking all my cameras nearly impossible. I still employ “manual” cameras around my property where pulling memory cards frequently isn’t a pain.

One of the main divisions in the trail camera market is whether your trail camera connects to a cellular network, which, if it does, is what allows you to wirelessly send images over great distances. Connected models are so common now that AT&T and Verizon offer monthly service plans that often come bundled with the camera.

This connectivity means that you don’t have to physically visit your camera to check out the imagery it has captured—a benefit that’s most tangible when cameras are placed in far-flung hunting spots, but less valuable if you’re using the camera closer to your house. The cellular connection also makes the cameras easier to operate since most cell-connected cameras can be controlled via your smartphone through apps. These allow you to use remote-control camera settings to switch between photo and video modes, adjust camera sensitivity, and check battery levels.

Networked cameras are addictive to use because they can provide instant, or at least frequent, gratification from your camera(s). However, there’s usually a recurring data plan cost in addition to setup complexity. Bottom line: Be sure you really need the connectivity. There also may be legal restrictions on wirelessly connected cameras that limit how you can use them. Be sure to double-check your state’s regulations before buying.

All trail cameras store images locally on the device, whether or not they have the ability to transmit them wirelessly. More often than not, that storage comes in the form of an SD or micro SD card, which you can remove to download your photos. Cameras with wireless support, however, now often feature an internal hard drive, which stores data more reliably, since you no longer need to physically “pull cards” to collect your footage.

If you’re planning to only use a networked camera, I recommend choosing a camera with internal memory. The No. 1 source of problems I’ve had over the years of testing dozens of different trail cameras and helping others set up many more is memory cards. These plastic chip-like cards are fragile, easy to lose, and can be formatted incorrectly. Even when there’s nothing wrong with a card, cheaper SD cards with slower transfer speeds can cause errors when processing larger images and videos.

The only advantage of having a camera with removable memory is if you want to use the camera without a data plan. This is required for the increasingly rare non-networked cameras, but even connected cameras can be used manually if they have physical cards. Some cameras with internal memory also have an optional SD card slot, such as the Reveal Pro 3.0, which gives you the option to expand storage capacity and use the camera without paying for a data plan.

This might seem like a minor detail, but given that many people want their trail camera to capture their subjects without alerting those subjects to the camera’s presence, the camera’s exterior color can be a critical factor. Since a majority of trail cameras are marketed to hunters and are intended to be used outdoors, these devices generally come in solid earth tones or camouflage patterns.

If you’re a hunter, you probably already have a good sense of what patterns are most appropriate for your area. If not, snap some photos of the trunks of the trees where you intend to mount the camera; then compare them to the patterns on the cameras you’re considering.

Cameron Shrum, avid bowhunter and co-owner of C&K Archery in Frisco, Colorado, says, “People will get a good deal on a camera and not realize how important it is to have [it] match [their] habitat. The goal is to get pictures of animals without them knowing they are being watched, and when something is out of place, game animals have a tendency to figure it out.”

As a professional photographer and videographer, the first thing you need to know about judging the quality of a camera is that there is no single metric that easily tells you which camera will record more clearly. At a glance, checking specs like the number of megapixels in a camera’s sensor gives you a decent clue as to what you can expect.

Ultimately, the best way to gauge the quality of a trail camera is with your eyes. Take a minute to look at sample photos posted by customers on retailers such as Amazon, which give you a practical way to evaluate images taken under natural conditions.

Trail cameras rarely take print-worthy shots, but that isn’t what they’re for. If you’re just patterning animals, image quality isn’t as crucial as simply detecting them. Trophy hunters trying to identify certain calibers of animals or monitor a specific animal across multiple cameras will want to be more picky about image quality and clarity.

Even if you don’t need great fidelity, a better image makes using trail cams more useful and rewarding. I’ve come to appreciate having modern trail cameras that deliver clear images and 4K videos over the crude, fuzzy work of older, lo-fi models.

I recommend using only lithium batteries in trail cameras. Especially with cheaper cameras, I’ve found that regular alkaline batteries don’t provide enough voltage for the IR flash, and many times a trail camera may not record video with underpowered batteries (alkaline batteries start decreasing in voltage as soon as you start using them). Lithium batteries deliver higher voltage consistently, and they work better in the cold.

If you’re setting up a cellular trail cam, make sure you check signal strength in the area. If you have a camera that offers an app or website (as many now do) that lets you view images on your smartphone, try triggering the camera and see if you receive the notification and image.

Since trail cameras are often left alone for days, weeks, or even months at a time, setting them up properly is important. Shrum recommends testing your trail camera before you walk away. “Have it snap a few pictures with you walking by and then review them. Sometimes you may not have the right angle; it may be too high or too low. Try to set the height and angle to capture the game in the center of the camera’s view.”

Trail cameras are usually strapped to a tree and most come packaged with a long strap for this purpose. If you’re placing a camera somewhere without convenient trees for the angle you want, look into a camera stand or even a tripod. Most trail cameras have a standard tripod plate mount (¼-20) and stands or stakes are available from most manufacturers.

A common spot to place cameras is along well-traveled game trails. A tip I picked up watching champion archer Levi Morgan put up cameras on one of his hunting leases: rather than pointing the camera down a trail where it’s likely to be in the line-of-sight of animals as they walk it, put the camera off-trail between 10 and 30 feet away perpendicular to the trail. This will usually give you broadside images of animals instead of head-on and puts the camera in their periphery.

Once you’ve tested your placement (and image transmission for connected cameras) by viewing a test photo on the app or the camera itself, scan the camera’s field of view for new-growth vegetation. Plants and tree branches can result in a near-constant stream of false triggers on a windy day. I like to place any plants or branches I cut behind the camera for a bit of concealment, making sure they can’t blow in front of the camera.

Since trail cams are motion-activated, a fast trigger seems important. You don’t want an animal to pass by the camera before you get a photo, right? In my experience, the real problem is taking the photo too quickly, which results in seeing just the nose of a slow-moving deer. Still, many brands tout their fast trigger speeds as if they solve an important problem.

“It’s kind of a BS spec, frankly,” Gregg Farrell, vice president of marketing for Tactacam Reveal, told me. “The goal is to capture the animal in the center of the frame and our cameras do that through the operating system working with the [motion] sensor.”

Most trail cameras have listed trigger speeds around a half second, which can work well, but are often too quick if implemented poorly. I almost always switch my cameras to shoot a multishot burst, if available, to give the camera more opportunities to grab a well-framed shot. Keep in mind, though, that this will double or triple the number of images you receive, so it may not be a solution if you’re using a cell-connected camera and trying to save with a limited-data plan.

Some cameras have detection delay settings that let you set a period of time after an image is captured before it’ll take another. This can cut down on look-alike images if an animal is hanging around in the detection area, especially if you’ve enabled a multishot mode.

Connected trail cameras make scouting convenient, but they come with hidden costs. Almost all cellular trail cameras require a monthly data plan to cover the cost of cloud storage and image transmission.

Many companies tack on extra fees for features such as live streaming, which eat up a lot of data and cost the companies money with their network provider partners. Like sitting at a blackjack table, it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of scouting and click your way to hundreds of dollars in recurring monthly charges. You can review the details of each company’s data plans before you buy and decide what features you want to use in advance. You can save money on a camera if you decide you don’t need all the latest features and avoid the temptation of activating those extra charges in the process.

Common game animals such as whitetail deer and elk tend to settle into routines during the summer months which often persist into early fall. The change of seasons and seasonal mating windows will help throw routine out the window in the fall, but if you can identify high-traffic areas in the spring and early summer, that will likely continue all summer.

The best practices for finding a good spot and setting up the camera properly are the same in any season. Spring in some ways makes it easier to identify animal travel patterns since the ground is often wet and recent activity is more obvious. Hike your zone and look for fresh signs to identify intersections, pinch points, and frequently visited locations. If you’re able to access your cameras easily and often, use the early season to experiment with different locations for a few weeks and try new spots you hadn’t considered before that show promise based on animal signs. Half the fun of placing these cameras is finding that perfect location and image framing that yields a ton of exciting wildlife images.

There are plenty of things that can trigger a trail camera other than the type(s) of animals you’re looking to capture, including squirrels, lights, and vegetation moving in the wind. “False triggers,” as we call them, are not only disappointing, but waste storage and burn through your data plan. It’s hard to eliminate them completely, but there are lots of ways to minimize them.

The most important is proper camera setup. Once you’ve got it framed up the way you want and have a successful test image, look for branches and weeds in the frame, primarily in the foreground. A single goldenrod stalk or pine bough can burn through a month’s data allotment on a windy day, so take your time to clear the immediate area in front of your camera.

You can’t always clear cut in front of a camera, so if you find you’re still getting more false triggers than you’d like, adjust the camera’s trigger sensitivity down. Many cameras only offer high or low, but if you have a more finely graded adjustment such as the 1 through 10 sensitivity settings on the Reveal Pro 3.0, adjust slowly down until you stop getting false triggers so you don’t overcorrect and miss animals.

Some cameras also use recognition software to reject images that appear to be empty. Moultrie’s Edge cameras allow you to only accept motion triggers in selected zones of an image, effectively blocking triggers from, for example, a corner of a detection zone with moving tree branches.

Most states have some sort of regulation with the use of trail cameras, especially when used on public land and as they relate to hunting activities. Arizona, where game animals tend to congregate around limited water sources, banned trail cameras for hunting statewide in 2021. Colorado, where I live, has few restrictions on trail camera use before your hunting season begins, but limits employing them while you’re actively hunting.

Using trail cameras on your own private property doesn’t usually involve too many restrictions, but be sure to check the regulations from your state’s wildlife management organization to confirm, as private land practices can still be regulated through the hunting codes since wildlife are considered a shared public resource.

There are so many options for security cameras dedicated to home use, and because of that, most of the time it makes more sense to just buy a security camera from a brand that specializes in that application, such as Ring or Google Nest.

These products generally have superior apps and software to hunt-focused trail cameras. Since they're designed for home use, they effortlessly connect to your home WiFi network, don’t require a data subscription, and will have features trail cameras won’t such as two-way communication.

That said, if you already own trail cameras and don’t need specific features, most trail cameras can serve a security purpose. The best trail cameras to employ for security are the newer “live” trail cameras that transmit imagery instantly via cell networks and notify you on your phone when the camera has been triggered.

Another option is WiFi-enabled trail cameras that can connect to your phone without a cellular network to transmit images. However, these cameras don’t usually transmit if you’re not within range of the camera (i.e., at home), so they’re limited to general monitoring rather than real-time notification when you’re away.

Jamie, Senior Reviews Editor, joined the Hearst Enthusiast Group in 2021. She has covered technology and consumer lifestyle gadgets since 1995—and shared her expertise in print, digital, and in broadcast originating the role of The Gizmo Girl for ESPN’s Cold Pizza. She has written about, tested, and reviewed everything from turkey fryers to high-definition TVs. Her byline has appeared in TWICE, Sound & Vision, Consumer Reports, and many others. In her free time, Jamie is in a yoga class, searching for the perfect matcha latte, or walking the boards.

Doctors ran many tests to uncover the cause of a teen girl's auditory and visual hallucinations.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 16-year-old girl in California

The symptoms: The teenager was referred to an emergency department because she was having hallucinations, including seeing a flying green dinosaur and hearing voices telling her to hurt others. She also had a sense that she was being followed.

In the emergency room, she was trembling and sweating and had a racing pulse and shallow, fast breathing. She did not have a fever, although she did have one at the hospital that had referred her.

During her conversations with ER clinicians, the teen reacted to the vision of the dinosaur as though the creature were present in the room. She reported that she had experienced these hallucinations since seventh grade,‬ so for about four years.

While her parents countered that she hadn’t exhibited psychotic symptoms until 48 hours before they arrived in the ER, they noted that her interest in school and extracurriculars had waned over the past month.

What happened next: Because of the patient's abnormal vital signs, the ER doctors suspected that her hallucinations might be secondary to some physical ailment, such as trauma to the brain, they wrote in a case report. However, a CT scan showed no signs of swelling or hemorrhage in her head. The doctors attempted a lumbar puncture (also called a spinal tap) but failed to collect any cerebrospinal fluid that they could test for irregularities.

The doctors judged the girl to be too medically unstable to be referred to the hospital's psychiatric ward, so she was admitted to the general pediatric department. Pediatric neurologists suggested an electroencephalogram (EEG), a test that measures electric signaling in the brain, but this revealed no further clues.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

On her second day in the hospital, the girl entered a complete catatonic state. Her specific symptoms were not described in the report, but in general, catatonia disrupts how a person processes and reacts to the world around them. Catatonic patients often stop moving and speaking. Doctors treated the patient with lorazepam, which slows down nervous-system signaling, and her catatonia subsided in days.

Meanwhile, interventional radiologists performed a successful second lumbar puncture, but the girl's cerebrospinal fluid appeared normal in the initial panels they ran.

After the patient had spent eight days in the hospital, psychiatrists recommended that the girl be transferred to their ward. However, this was not possible because she developed problems with feeding herself. Her continued psychotic symptoms were treated with the antipsychotic drug olanzapine.

The diagnosis: While initial tests of the girl's cerebrospinal fluid did not show signs of meningitis or other abnormalities, a later test came back positive for autoantibodies — immune proteins that target healthy tissues instead of foreign invaders. These antibodies targeted neuronal intermediate filament (NIF), a protein that helps give nerve cells structural support.

Based on this finding, the patient was diagnosed with autoimmune encephalitis, a condition in which the body produces antibodies that attack nervous tissue, leading to harmful inflammation that can cause psychiatric symptoms.

Autoimmune encephalitis is often triggered by a tumor; proteins produced by the growth can resemble proteins within nervous tissue, and the immune system develops a harmful response against the latter while attempting to fight the tumor. The doctors performed MRIs and a PET scan to look for tumors, but they did not find any.

The girl was diagnosed with autoimmune encephalitis, a condition in which antibodies attacked her own nervous tissue.

The treatment: The girl received intravenous infusions of a steroid to reduce inflammation, as well as immunoglobulin — antibodies from healthy donors that are often used to calm autoimmune reactions. She also got an infusion of rituximab, a drug that kills B lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell that makes antibodies like the ones attacking the girl's neurons.

In addition to these infusions, the girl underwent five sessions of plasmapheresis over the next month. In that procedure, blood is drawn from the body, a machine separates plasma (the liquid portion of blood) from blood cells, and the extracted plasma is substituted with a replacement fluid before that blood is returned to the patient. This treatment can help rid the body of autoantibodies.

The girl was discharged after having spent almost two months in the hospital. She was treated with ongoing prescriptions of olanzapine and lorazepam, as well as prednisone and monthly immunoglobulin treatments. As her symptoms improved over the following year, she stopped taking the psychiatric drugs but continued her immunotherapy.

What makes the case unique: Autoimmune encephalitis is rare. One study conducted in the U.K. suggests it affects only 5 to 8 out of every 100,000 people. Additionally, most data about the condition in pediatric patients comes from cases caused by autoantibodies that target NMDA receptors, which detect a key chemical messenger in the brain, rather than NIF.

The case report did not name a specific trigger for the girl's condition, but the authors noted that anti-NIF autoimmune encephalitis has been documented in adults following infections, including certain tick-borne bacterial infections, HIV and COVID-19. Cases associated with these infections are rarer than those linked to tumors.

The doctors did not attribute the teen's case to a specific infection, but her family did report that she'd had a cough three weeks before going to the emergency room. The family had visited the Philippines, and the girl and multiple relatives came down with the same illness.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#281. NASA discovers hidden fires burning beneath the Amazon rainforest

A dangerous wave of wildfires is spreading across the tropics, and the Amazon rainforest is now facing a growing crisis. Fueled by severe drought linked to El Niño, fires are sweeping through parts of Brazil, filling cities with smoke and threatening forests already damaged by previous fire seasons.

Unlike tornadoes or thunderstorms, which can cause widespread destruction in a matter of minutes, El Niño influences weather patterns over many months. The climate phenomenon can disrupt rainfall across vast regions, creating unusually dry conditions that allow fires to spread rapidly. Scientists warn that the Amazon may be entering the beginning of a prolonged and destructive fire season.

NASA Satellites Detect Surging Amazon Wildfires

Beginning in September 2026, satellite observations revealed a sharp increase in fires and smoke emissions across the central and eastern Amazon. The growing activity appeared in several monitoring systems, including NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), and NASA Worldview.

The affected area extends from the forests surrounding Manaus and Santarém, two major commercial and transportation hubs in Brazil, eastward toward the mouth of the Amazon River.

On October 12, 2026, the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) instrument aboard NASA's Aqua satellite captured an image showing enormous plumes of smoke rising from fires on both sides of the Amazon River.

At the time, thick smoke had engulfed Manaus, the capital of Brazil's Amazonas state. City officials reported dangerously polluted air, with concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exceeding 135 micrograms per cubic meter. These microscopic particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and pose serious health risks. The measurements placed the city's air quality in the second-worst category of a regional air quality index.

The smoke brought major disruptions to Manaus, which is home to more than 2 million people. Schools shut down, public events were canceled, and children's sports leagues suspended activities as authorities warned residents about hazardous conditions, according to news reports.

El Niño Is Triggering a Wildfire Domino Effect

According to Douglas Morton, an Earth system scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, the fires surrounding Manaus and Santarém are part of a much larger pattern.

Morton describes the phenomenon as a "cascade" of tropical fires driven by rainfall disruptions associated with El Niño. The sequence typically begins near the equator, where drought helps ignite peat fires in Indonesia. These fires burn through carbon-rich organic material in the soil. As dry conditions develop elsewhere, fire activity intensifies in the central and eastern Amazon.

This pattern is not new. Following the devastating 2015-2016 El Niño, Morton worked with scientists from the University of California, Irvine; Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam; and the University of Maryland to examine how tropical fires followed shifting rainfall patterns. Their findings were published in a 2017 study. Researchers observed a similar sequence in 2023.

Now, the 2026 El Niño appears to be producing the same progression.

Indonesia has already experienced months of drought, smoke, and destructive fires beginning in August. During October, wildfires destroyed hundreds of homes, while dense smoke covered entire islands on most days.

"Now, in the Amazon, we're seeing the second domino in the cascade fall," Morton said, referring to the increasing number of fires in the Brazilian states of Pará and Amazonas.

Scientists Warn More Fires Could Spread Into 2027

The current surge may be only one stage of a much longer fire season.

Morton and his colleagues anticipate that fire activity will expand northward during November and December 2026. The regions at risk include the Brazilian states of Roraima and Amapá, northern Pará, and portions of Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname.

The pattern is then expected to shift southward. By August and September 2027, drought conditions and wildfire danger could reach their highest levels in the southern Amazon regions of Brazil and Paraguay.

One particularly troubling aspect of the current crisis is that many of the threatened forests have burned before.

"It's so striking -- and frustrating -- that this is happening all over again," said Morton, noting that forests affected by the 2015 and 2023 El Niño events are once again catching fire.

Wildfires are especially destructive in tropical rainforests because most of the plants and animals living there have not evolved to withstand frequent burning. Unlike ecosystems where fire is a regular natural process, Amazon forests can suffer severe and lasting damage when flames move through them.

Previous fires have also left parts of the forest more vulnerable. Trees partially burned during earlier events may be weakened or damaged, making the remaining vegetation more susceptible to future fires. Morton warned that some of the current blazes could therefore burn more intensely than before.

He expects fires near Manaus and Santarém to persist until seasonal rains return, likely in December 2026 or January 2027.

However, communities in regions farther north and south still have an opportunity to reduce the danger before conditions deteriorate.

"Given the intensity of this El Niño, this really is the year for people to avoid burning at all costs," Morton said.

Extreme Drought Turns Human-Started Fires Into Wildfires

Although the Amazon is experiencing a severe fire emergency, lightning is rarely responsible for igniting fires in Brazil's rainforest.

The region is normally so wet that lightning causes less than 1 percent of fires, according to Morton. This means that nearly all of the fires currently spreading through the Brazilian Amazon originated from human activity.

What makes 2026 particularly dangerous is the severity of the drought.

Brazil's National Institute of Meteorology reported that rainfall in Manaus was 95 percent below normal in August and 60 percent below normal in September.

These extremely dry conditions have transformed fires that might otherwise have remained confined to managed areas into uncontrolled wildfires.

Morton explained that many of the larger blazes began as deliberately set fires used for land management, such as removing shrubs from grazing land or clearing crop residue from fields. Once the flames escaped, they spread into the rainforest's parched understory, the layer of vegetation growing beneath the taller trees.

Satellite analysis suggests that approximately 50 to 70 uncontrolled fires are currently burning in the Santarém area alone, according to Shane Coffield, an assistant research scientist at the University of Maryland who works at NASA Goddard.

NASA Uncovers Hidden Fires That Satellites Are Missing

The actual number of Amazon wildfires may be substantially higher than standard satellite monitoring systems indicate.

As part of a NASA Earth Action project, Coffield is studying observations collected by VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite), a satellite instrument capable of detecting heat signatures associated with active fires.

His goal is to identify fires that fail to meet the detection requirements used in official FIRMS data products.

These additional detections, known as "candidate fires," could help researchers develop a more complete picture of wildfire activity. Coffield plans to provide their locations to MapBiomas, a collaborative network of universities, nongovernmental organizations, and technology companies that tracks fires and changes in land use throughout the Amazon.

The initial findings suggest that conventional monitoring is overlooking a significant number of blazes.

"For the area around Santarém, we've identified about 40 percent more fires than you'll see in active fire counts from FIRMS," said Coffield.

Detecting fires beneath a rainforest canopy can be surprisingly difficult, even with sophisticated instruments in orbit. Satellite sensors identify wildfires by measuring infrared radiation, which reveals the heat generated by burning vegetation.

However, thick smoke, persistent cloud cover, and dense tree canopies can interfere with those measurements. Fires that burn slowly through the understory are particularly difficult to detect because the vegetation above them can conceal their heat signatures.

As a result, satellite fire counts may sometimes fall even when extensive burning continues on the ground.

"On some of the smokiest days, we have very few detections from MODIS and VIIRS, and we know that isn't right."

By identifying fires that existing monitoring systems overlook, NASA researchers hope to provide scientists and land managers with a more accurate understanding of the threats facing the Amazon as the El Niño-driven fire season unfolds.

#282. This Under-$100 Cabinet Finally Solved My Tiny-Bathroom Storage Problem

This $75 cabinet tripled my bathroom storage without drilling into tile.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Getting a Tushy was a huge upgrade to my tiny bathroom. It was one of those purchases that made me question how I ever lived without it. The same now goes for my over-the-toilet cabinet. It’s completely solved my storage problem. With only one small cabinet and a shallow drawer, my sink top was constantly in disarray. For under $100, this fixed that.

When I say I looked at dozens of over-the-toilet cabinets, I'm not exaggerating (and I may be underestimating). I looked at a lot. It’s an unglamorous product category with a plethora of ugly, poorly made options. I wish I could skip them entirely, but my bathroom walls are tile, and I rent, so drilling into them for shelving or other storage options isn’t an option.

Admittedly, the Yaheetech cabinet got me on its look. I liked the cobalt blue color and tempered glass doors, but expected little in terms of construction quality. To my pleasant surprise, this cabinet nailed both.

The cabinet is made from medium-density fiberboard, an engineered wood that’s more durable than particle board. It arrived with clearly labeled, separated hardware and even extra pieces. The instructions were thorough and clearly illustrated, so assembly was easy, though not quick. It’s not overbuilt, per se, but it has more pieces than I expected. I’d say this is a positive, though, because it adds to the overall build quality with secured hardware and fastened pieces. I worried it wouldn’t fit the toilet gap between my sink and shower, but I still had a couple of inches to spare on either side.

I wish I'd found this sooner; it’s tripled my storage space and keeps my toiletries organized, whereas before mornings were a mess of toppled contact solution bottles and me fighting to open my drawer halfway. Scientists are racing to explain why hundreds of southern right whale calves have died this year in Argentine Patagonia, and the first clues are starting to emerge.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Since June, more than 300 southern right whale (Eubalaena australis) calves have died in Argentine Patagonia, in what scientists describe as an "exceptional" die-off. The preliminary figure already far exceeds the previous annual record set in 2012, when 113 southern right whale calves died — the highest number ever documented for the species, both locally and globally.

Now, scientists are racing to figure out exactly what's causing the record-breaking die-off.

Laboratory analyses of specimens that died this year tested positive for the pathogenic bacterium Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, environmental authorities in Chubut province told Live Science. E. rhusiopathiae was first identified in southern right whale calves in 2013, but scientists don't know what might have changed this year to cause an infection-driven die-off of this magnitude.

Researchers say they need to quickly find the answer to better understand the changing threat this species faces, the risk to the wider ecosystem and humans, and what can be done to manage it.

"The battle between living organisms and pathogens is constant," said Carla Fiorito, a researcher at the Center for the Study of Marine Systems (CESIMAR) who previously identified the bacterium in right whales. "But for this to happen now, there must have been a shift in the balance between the agent, the host, and the environment," she told Live Science.

The first dead calves appeared on the beaches of Península Valdés in June, at the start of the breeding season, which runs through to December. Península Valdés is located in Chubut province, on the coast of northern Patagonia.

In a typical year, calf mortality reaches 20% to 30% of a cohort from various causes, including infections. But this year's losses have already far surpassed that.

In September, 409 calves were counted among a total of 1,375 southern right whales during a survey conducted by CESIMAR's Marine Mammal Laboratory. With more than 300 deaths already recorded, the die-off represents an exceptional proportion of these calves. The final figure will be released by the Southern Right Whale Health Monitoring Program in December.

Scientists have responded by expediting routine research to determine what's different this year to previous years.

"Samples were sent for analysis earlier than usual — typically, they are analyzed at the end of the year — because the higher-than-usual mortality is a cause for concern," said Víctor Fratto, the director of the Native Wildlife Rescue Program and a contributor with the whale monitoring program. "What those samples are showing is that the calves died from erysipelas," he told Live Science.

A person suffering from a case of facial erysipelas.

Erysipelas is a bacterial infection that affects the skin. In its most severe form, it can spread through the bloodstream and cause a systemic infection, damaging vital organs and sometimes leading to death. Animals that catch the disease, for example through a wound, may develop characteristic skin lesions, which are rhomboid or rectangular in shape, caused by alterations in the blood vessels.

The bacterium that causes erysipelas, E. rhusiopathiae, is not exclusive to whales. It can be found in marine environments and in a wide variety of animals, including fish, crustaceans and birds. Pigs are one of its natural reservoirs.

"It is a ubiquitous and opportunistic bacterium," Fiorito said. (The human illness of the same name is different and caused by Group A streptococcal bacteria, although humans can also catch the E. rhusiopathiae form of the illness.)

The presence of E. rhusiopathiae does not necessarily mean an animal is diseased. Yet many questions remain about E. rhusiopathiae in whales.

"We don't know much about the bacterium itself; we don't know which serotypes are present in the whales, or how common it is in healthy animals or other species," Fiorito said. "There is also no data on the environment."

Calves are especially vulnerable because their immune systems are still developing and they spend more time at the surface than adults do, exposing them to more attacks by gulls, which can transfer the disease.

"The working hypothesis is that the gull is the vector: Pecking causes wounds on the back, allowing the bacteria to enter," Fratto said. "The bacteria might already be present on the skin, or they could be carried on the beak of a gull that had previously pecked another whale suffering from erysipelas."

Attacks by kelp gulls (Larus dominicanus) on southern right whales were first recorded at Península Valdés in the 1970s. The behavior began with just a few individuals in Patagonia's San José Gulf and became increasingly frequent over time, Ricardo Bastida, a marine biologist and professor emeritus at the National University of Mar del Plata who has studied these cetaceans for more than four decades, told Live Science. The birds also began scavenging the carcasses of stranded whales, Bastida said

Gull populations have grown and new breeding colonies have emerged in the region thanks to increased food availability linked to fishing activities and discarded catch, he noted. However, the attacks alone do not explain the 2026 mortality event: They have been occurring for decades, and gulls are a regular part of the ecosystem.

The working hypothesis is that the gull is the vector: Pecking causes wounds on the back, allowing the bacteria to enter.

Fratto said that swabs will be taken from gulls to check for the presence of E. rhusiopathiae and assess whether the results could help develop a management strategy for the species.

Diego Rodríguez, a marine biologist at the National University of Mar del Plata, said that research must go beyond the dead calves and examine the ecosystem's fauna to determine where the bacterium is present and how it might be circulating. "It is far more likely that [the die-off event] is linked to cross-infection," Rodríguez told Live Science.

The major question for scientists is what might have changed this year to cause a bacterium already present in the ecosystem to trigger a die-off of this magnitude. Experts told Live Science they believe the phenomenon could be the result of several factors acting simultaneously.

"The bacterium was present, but this year it resulted in a widespread infection, making this event unusual," Mariano Coscarella, a researcher at the Marine Mammal Laboratory at CESIMAR, told Live Science. "It is a major step forward to have a fairly clear idea of what caused the disease, but we do not know what changed."

One factor could be the environment. Changes in water temperature, salinity, pH or rainfall could alter the conditions under which infection occurs. There could also be changes in food availability, affecting the mothers' body condition and the vulnerability of their calves. Another possibility is that the pathogen itself has changed — for instance, through the emergence or increased circulation of a more virulent strain or a different serotype, Fiorito said.

The El Niño phenomenon could also play a role by altering oceanographic conditions and food availability, although the researchers said there's insufficient evidence to link it to the die-off.

It is too early to determine what impact this die-off will have on the southern right whale population. Rodríguez suggested that losing such a large proportion of a season's calves could have demographic consequences. "It is very risky to predict what will happen in the future at this stage, but clearly, this year's cohort of live-born calves will essentially be absent from the adult records of future populations," he said.

Coscarella is more cautious. Southern right whales are extremely long-lived, and calves represent only a fraction of the population. Therefore, a single season of exceptionally high mortality does not necessarily mean the population will go into decline, he argued. "What would be concerning is if there were two, three or four episodes like this," he noted.

The event also has public health implications. Fiorito pointed out that erysipelas can infect humans, usually through skin wounds. The whales' carcasses could also pose a risk of exposure to anyone coming into contact with them, as could seawater for people swimming in the area.
