#284. NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is performing even better than scientists anticipated after engineers completed an extensive series of tests and precision adjustments. The work has brought the observatory's powerful instruments into exceptionally sharp focus, with its main camera system now delivering image quality nearly 30% better than predicted.

The achievement marks an important step toward the telescope's ambitious mission to investigate dark matter, dark energy, and other mysteries of the universe. Even the smallest improvements in optical precision could help Roman capture clearer images during its sweeping surveys of the cosmos.

"All of Roman's sweeping surveys will rely on the Wide Field Instrument," said Dave Hickey, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "Many of the mission's primary goals, like studying dark matter and dark energy, wouldn't be possible without it, so it's both exciting and a huge relief to see that it's working well!"

NASA Puts Roman's Powerful Camera System to the Test

Following the activation of the Wide Field Instrument in September, engineers began a comprehensive testing campaign to confirm that each component worked properly on its own and as part of the complete system.

Their first priority was examining the instrument's 18 detectors, each roughly the size of a sticky note, along with the electronics that operate them. The team then evaluated the element wheel, a rotating mechanism equipped with filters and other optical components. These allow selected wavelengths of light to reach the detectors and can separate incoming light into its individual colors.

Next came the instrument's internal calibration system. Engineers activated its light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, which function as adjustable light sources that can produce different colors and brightness levels under commands from Earth. By measuring how the detectors respond to these controlled signals, scientists can identify differences in sensitivity and make the corrections needed for accurate observations.

Engineers also tested the instrument's alignment mechanism and moved it from the deliberately unfocused position used during launch to the position expected to provide the sharpest images. They finished by checking the thermal control system, which maintains the temperatures required for the instrument's various components to function correctly.

"Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," said Maxime Rizzo, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA Goddard. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

A Space Telescope Already Close to Perfect Alignment

While one group concentrated on preparing the Wide Field Instrument, another worked to refine the telescope's overall optical alignment.

The results were encouraging from the beginning. Roman's mirrors and other optical components were already positioned with remarkable accuracy, meaning engineers needed to make only minor corrections.

"The telescope's performance was excellent even before we began adjusting the alignment of all the mirrors and other optics, thanks to exceptional preparatory work done on the ground prior to launch," said Matthew Bolcar, Roman's optical systems lead at NASA Goddard. "All of the testing and modeling work done at Goddard and by contractors at L3Harris and BAE Space and Mission Systems left only small corrections for us to make to bring everything into near-perfect alignment."

Achieving that level of precision is especially challenging for a spacecraft. The forces experienced during launch can cause tiny shifts in sensitive equipment, and conditions in orbit differ significantly from those on Earth. Roman launched on August 30, carrying optical systems that had been meticulously tested before leaving the ground.

"Our ground testing couldn't exactly reproduce the environment Roman would experience in space, such as the absence of gravity," Bolcar said. "And there are also slight differences in temperature variations and moisture content. Despite those challenges, the recent assessments showed that our ground testing was excellent, with both instruments either matching or exceeding the performance we had predicted."

A Mirror Adjustment Smaller Than a Human Hair

Roman relies on an intricate arrangement of mirrors and optical components to collect light from distant cosmic objects and direct it toward its two scientific instruments. For the resulting images to remain sharp, the light must follow an extremely precise path.

Even a microscopic misalignment can affect how accurately the telescope brings light into focus.

Fortunately, Roman's optical system was already so well aligned that only incredibly small movements were necessary to improve its performance.

"We moved the secondary mirror by about one-sixteenth of the diameter of a human hair," said Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer working on Roman at NASA Goddard. "This adjustment nudged the height of the secondary mirror above the primary. If we scale that height up to the height of the Empire State Building, the change in height is a little bit less than you would get by stacking a single U.S. penny on top of the tip of the tower."

Although nearly impossible to appreciate at a human scale, such a small adjustment can make an important difference when a telescope is designed to study objects across vast cosmic distances.

The team initially concentrated on Roman's Coronagraph Instrument, which had been producing images that were slightly out of focus. The problem was less severe than engineers had anticipated, making it relatively straightforward to correct.

The coronagraph now meets the team's demanding performance expectations. Engineers will continue refining its camera settings and determining the optimal configurations for its deformable mirrors, which can change shape to make extremely precise corrections to incoming light.

In the coming weeks, the team plans to test the coronagraph's ability to block unwanted light, an essential capability for observing faint objects near much brighter ones.

Once the coronagraph's focus had been optimized, engineers returned to the Wide Field Instrument for another round of adjustments.

Roman's Image Quality Exceeds Expectations by Nearly 30%

The final measurements revealed an especially impressive result. Roman's Wide Field Instrument achieved optical performance nearly 30% better than the team had predicted.

Before launch, engineers established an image quality requirement of approximately 90 nanometers RMS (Root Mean Square). This measurement describes the amount of optical error in the system, or how far the incoming light deviates from an ideal, perfectly focused wavefront.

To put that scale into perspective, 90 nanometers is roughly 1,000 times thinner than a human hair. At these tiny dimensions, even seemingly insignificant imperfections can influence the sharpness of astronomical images.

After the latest corrections, however, engineers measured an optical error of just 63 nanometers RMS, substantially better than the original requirement.

That improvement means Roman should be capable of producing even sharper images than its designers initially expected, strengthening its ability to carry out detailed observations across enormous regions of the sky.

"All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Jurling said. "It's a great outcome from years of careful modeling, precision metrology, and testing."

With both scientific instruments meeting or surpassing their expected performance, Roman has cleared another important milestone in its preparation for routine observations. The results highlight the extraordinary precision of the telescope's design and offer a promising outlook for its upcoming investigations into the hidden structure and evolution of the universe.

#285. I Tested the Loop Earplugs Day and Night—and They’re Absolutely Worth It

They helped me sleep, focus, and protect my hearing in loud places.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

I wake up to what seems like a nice, quiet morning. I stretch, then take the Loop earplugs out of my ears—and I’m instantly hit with a barrage of noises. Cars honking, people conversing, kids shrieking—and a cat meowing behind the bedroom door so much you’d think I'd been asleep for days and hadn’t fed him.

I’m cat-sitting in Park Slope, Brooklyn, near a busy avenue, an environment much louder than my home, facing an alleyway in Easton, Pennsylvania. I’m a ridiculously light sleeper, but my Loop earplugs let me sleep through the night, even in a city that never does.

As a matter of fact, I’ve been using various Loop earplugs in different situations for days, and they’ve definitely saved me a headache or seven—and, what’s more, they should protect my hearing.

Let’s start by defining when it’s too noisy for our ears’ good. “We use 85 decibels as our main point—anything at 85 decibels or louder can cause hearing loss,” says Alicia Kunkel, doctor of audiology based in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. “It’s safe for eight hours if it’s around 85 decibels; when you go above 90 decibels, it goes down to two hours; 100 is maybe 15 minutes.”

Noises such as a vacuum cleaner, a blender, a motorcycle, or heavy traffic hover around 85 dB. Even louder are concerts and venues like football or soccer games, which can reach above 100 dB. The ear ringing you experience after seeing a live show of your favorite band? That’s a temporary reduction in hearing sensitivity caused by loud noise exposure that you’ll likely recover from, but which Kunkel says can also slowly lead to a decline in hearing.

Wearing ear protection in those environments is essential. Kunkel keeps hearing protection in her bag at all times. “I carry one pair that is completely trying to block out hearing and one that is just taking the edge off, only about 12 decibels,” she says. And it’s never a bad idea to follow the experts.

One form of hearing protection is foam earplugs you can buy in bulk at nearly every store—and they work great as long as you use them correctly and each pair only once. “Foam is typically a safe material to use, but they can’t really be washed,” Kunkel says, adding that reusing them risks an outer ear infection. They typically block 25 to 30 decibels, depending on the brand, material density, and how you insert them.

I have a love-hate relationship with foam earplugs—the rolling, squishing, twisting, holding them in place, waiting for the foam to expand again, and, in the end, them somehow popping out of my ear canal anyway.

Which brings me to the other, easier-to-use AND reusable, environment-friendlier, washable option: Loop earplugs.

Use Intent: Social gathering, parenting, conversation

Use Intent: Concerts and festivals, live entertainment, sporting events

Material: Body: Hypoallergenic silicon; Tip: Foam-Silicone

Ear tip sizing: 8 tips - 2 different shapes (oval/round); 4 tips for each shape (XS/S/M/L)

Loop makes three different pairs for day use, each reducing noise by a different number of decibels. I didn’t test the Quiet 2, but I did receive a pair of the Experience 2 and Engage 2, one reducing noise by 8 and the other by 12 dB. Curious whether I could “hear” the difference, I took them out of the case without looking at which pair was which.

After testing them in various settings, I quickly developed a preference for which pair I reached for based on what I was doing. The Engage 2, with its 8 dB reduction, became my preferred pair for when I was trying to understand the conversation during a movie in a theater and just wanted to take the edge off the loudest noise, while the 12 dB reduction of the Experience 2 was what I went for when I wanted to tune out my surroundings in the office or in a coffee shop and really focus on work.

I keep both pairs attached to my keys. They’re so easy to insert into the ear canal. Neither pair tunes out the surroundings completely; I’m aware of what’s going on around me and can easily take them out when a coworker comes to talk to me.

FYI: Unlike workplace environments, movie theaters do not have strict legal limits or government regulations controlling how loud local operators can turn up the volume.

After trying most of the Dream earplug tips, I chose the round M size that fit my ear best, and before I laid down to sleep, I made sure I could still hear my morning alarm through the earplugs. I always fall asleep on my side, and as soon as my ear touched the pillow, I couldn’t feel them. They didn’t bother me at all, didn’t need readjusting, and didn’t move or suddenly pop out. I used them while traveling to unfamiliar places, in hotels, and in places louder than I’m used to, and I slept great through it all.

After a few nights in a row, my ears started to get a little itchy, which made me worry I might be overusing them, but a short break to let the ear canal air out should be all that’s needed. To further help fix the dryness they may cause, Kunkel recommends using a tiny bit of mineral oil. My itch went away on its own after I stopped putting anything in my ears (including headphones). Of course, if the itchiness doesn’t go away, see an ENT specialist.

The price of the Loop earplugs may seem steep compared to foam earplugs, but they’re worth it. They’re reusable, washable, and quick and easy to insert and remove. The day pairs come with a case you can attach to your keys, so you never forget to take them with you. I pop them in and out several times a day—when I’m trying to tune out coworkers’ conversations in our open office, or when I want to go easy on my ears during an action scene in a movie. The more accessible and easy such an accessory is, the more you’ll actually use it.

And, yes, because it’s always better to overuse hearing protection. ”Even if you think, ‘Oh, I’m only using this drill for five seconds, it’s better to be safe,” Kunkel says. “You don’t want to take your hearing for granted.”

#286. Climate scientists face deluge of public-records requests about fossil-fuel studies

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Protestors demonstrate outside the US Supreme Court on 5 October, as justices hear a case for which the outcome could determine whether fossil-fuel companies can be held responsible for global warming.Credit: Mehmet Eser/Anadolu via Getty

Last month, a climate scientist working in the University of California system received an unsettling message from her institution. University officials asked her to submit all correspondence related to a study she had published linking emissions from fossil fuels to environmental harms caused by climate change. The university had received a public-records request from a law firm representing the Patriots Foundation in Des Moines, Iowa, which describes itself on its website as a government watchdog.

It was the fifth such request connected to the organization that the scientist, who requested anonymity to avoid further demands, had received this year.

Heatwaves linked to carbon emissions from specific companies

Heatwaves linked to carbon emissions from specific companies

The requests seem to be part of an expanding effort by groups with ties to the energy industry to discredit findings in the burgeoning field of climate attribution science, which estimates the extent to which extreme weather events, such as floods and heatwaves, are due to climate change. The demands come at a time when attribution science’s role in lawsuits against major industrial emitters is growing.

An investigation by Nature has identified at least 30 requests for correspondence relating to climate attribution science that researchers in the United States say they have received since 2024. These requests, involving the Patriots Foundation and other groups, have gone to 13 public universities and involved the correspondence of dozens of climate scientists, legal scholars and attorneys. Last month, the news outlet Politico reported that it had identified more than 100 open-records requests made to researchers since 2021, related more broadly to lawsuits about damages caused by climate change, rather than just to climate attribution research. It’s unclear how many of these requests overlap.

Neither the Patriots Foundation nor the law firm representing it responded to Nature’s queries about the reason for the requests, or about researchers’ concerns over them. Another organization that has submitted requests — called Government Accountability and Oversight, based in Sheridan, Wyoming — directed Nature to blog posts saying that attribution researchers are activists opposing the fossil-fuel industry and that, if they have the right to do “this sort of lobbying”, “the rest of us have a right to see the receipts under state transparency laws”.

Climate science is supporting lawsuits that could help save the world

Climate science is supporting lawsuits that could help save the world

Recipients say that the timing of the requests and the information they ask for suggest that their purpose is to fish for conflicts of interest that could be used to discredit the scientists’ findings. A hypothetical example of such a conflict might be attorneys paying a climate scientist to conduct a particular study. The researchers think that the requests might also be attempts to collect information about collaborators and contacts who are not subject to public-records laws, such as scientists and attorneys at private institutions.

Requests of this kind are legal. And Nature spoke to several recipients who say they have nothing to hide. They emphasize that communicating with attorneys involved in climate litigation does not bias their work or represent a conflict of interest.

But some say that the volume of requests seems intended to dissuade work on climate attribution, and wastes time and public money. They also say that if scientists know that any e-mail discussion with a colleague might become the subject of an investigation or taken out of context, that could suppress open scientific debate. “It’s annoying. It’s harassment,” says the University of California climate scientist.

Studies linking climate change in general to certain weather events have been conducted since 20041. But only in the past several years have researchers begun to use their climate models to estimate how much the emissions from particular companies contributed to specific ‘damages’, such as deaths caused by a heatwave.

Dozens of climate-related lawsuits that are now working their way through the US courts could hinge on whether judges or juries agree that such ‘source attribution’ research is rigorous. That includes a case involving the US energy company Suncor and representatives of Boulder County in Colorado, heard by the US Supreme Court this month. The outcome could determine whether similar lawsuits proceed in state courts.

Climate attribution science estimates the extent to which extreme weather events, such as the wildfire in Boulder, Colorado, shown here, are due to climate change.Credit: Michael Ciaglo/Getty

Researchers say that the legal relevance of attribution science has made the field a political target. For instance, a Republican-led committee of the US Congress has investigated a chapter in a reference manual for federal judges that explains attribution science, alleging it represents an improper attempt by climate activists to influence judges. US President Donald Trump, a Republican who is friendly towards the fossil-fuel industry and has called climate change a hoax, weighed in, declaring the chapter “fraudulent, biased, and misleading” on social media.

“Climate attribution is under attack,” says Christopher Callahan, a climate scientist at Indiana University Bloomington. In May, he received a public-records request from Government Accountability and Oversight to review his correspondence with eight individuals involved in climate litigation.

The volume of requests for climate researchers has noticeably increased this year, says Lauren Kurtz at the Climate Science Legal Defense Fund in New York City, an organization that helps scientists to address legal issues in this field. “It’s totally a surge,” she adds.

Do climate lawsuits lead to action? Researchers assess their impact

Do climate lawsuits lead to action? Researchers assess their impact

A human sacrifice was found next to an elite warrior's 2,000-year-old burial in Russia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The warrior was buried with the remains of his weapons and his horse near the center of the ancient necropolis in the Kuban region near the Russian city of Krasnodar.

Archaeologists in southern Russia have unearthed the 2,000-year-old grave of an elite warrior who was buried with his weapons, horse — and a human sacrifice. The grave and sacrifices were found with other lavish goods, including two gold coins featuring Alexander the Great.

A team found the elite grave in Russia's Kuban region east of the Crimean Peninsula, in a necropolis of more than 150 ancient graves arranged around it. This central placement indicates the man had been a member of the social elite, according to the study, which was published in September in the journal Russian Archaeology.

The evidence of a human sacrifice comes from another burial assemblage beside the warrior's grave. This neighboring burial had the remains of three horses, two cattle, a pig, a dog and a fragment of a human pelvis that seems to have come from a sacrificed person, the researchers wrote.

The remains of three horses, two cattle, a dog and a pig were found in a separate burial complex nearby.

The two gold coins — one found on the warrior's skeleton and one found nearby — indicate that the burial took place in the early first century B.C., while the location and style of the burial indicated the warrior had been a noble of the Indigenous Maeotian people. At that time, the Maeotians were allied with the neighboring Mithridatic Empire, a Hellenistic-Persian kingdom and the enemy of the expanding Roman Republic.

The researchers think the two gold coins were prestige items, rather than ordinary currency for commerce. "It is likely not money in the conventional sense, but rather a means of storing wealth, akin to a … cryptocurrency," study first author Mikhail Abramzon of the Institute of Archaeology at Russia's Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email.

The two gold coins are key to the discovery. One was found in a ritual shaft near the burial in the center of the necropolis; the researchers think it was placed there as an offering to the gods.

The second was found beneath the jaw of the skeleton of the ancient warrior, which indicates it had been placed in the dead man's mouth before the burial and is an example of "Charon's obol" — the traditional ancient Greek payment for the mythical ferryman of the dead.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both coins are gold "staters" in the Greek style adopted by Alexander the Great (who lived from 356 to 323 B.C.) and show portraits of Alexander.

Two gold coins, in the style of ancient Greek "staters," were found nearby. One seems to have been an offering while the other was placed on the man's tongue.

Experts have determined that these coins were minted during the much later reign of Mithridates Eupator (lived 135 to 63 B.C.), also known as Mithridates the Great, who claimed descent from both Alexander and the Persian nobility and who initiated the three Mithridatic Wars with Rome. The Alexander portraits on the coins are designed to also look like Mithridates Eupator, the researchers wrote in the study.

According to the Greek geographer Strabo, writing in the first century A.D., the Maeotians were an Indigenous people integrated into the nearby Bosporan kingdom, a Greek and Scythian state founded on the north side of the Black Sea in the fifth century B.C. The Greek historian Appian, in the second century A.D., wrote that the Bosporan kingdom became part of the expanding Mithridatic Empire in the second century B.C. — and so the Maeotians were Mithridatic allies at the time of the burial in the first century B.C.

The warrior was buried with weapons — two iron spearheads and an iron arrowhead were found in his grave — as well as his riding gear and his horse, which had been sacrificed. The grave also held luxury items, including a rare glass "alabastron" — a small vessel for oil or perfumes, which had probably been imported from Cyprus or the Levant region of the eastern Mediterranean, the researchers wrote.

A two-handled clay cup, called a "kantharos" in ancient Greek, was also found in the grave. Its surface was engraved with a pentagram, a symbol of the sun, which the researchers think was considered spiritual protection against magical threats.

The researchers think the sacrifices in the nearby burial assemblages could have had different purposes. The cattle may have been offerings in the style of an ancient "hecatomb" — a mass slaughter of animals that would supposedly please a god. The horses were for riding in the afterlife, the pig was for eating in the afterlife, and the dog may have been intended to guide the dead warrior's spirit. The role of the human sacrificed with the animals is unknown, but it may have been to act as a servant for the warrior.

The researchers wrote that the coins and grave goods illustrate both the beliefs of the Maeotian people at this time, and the extent to which they had been influenced by the ancient Greek traditions of the neighboring Bosporon kingdom.

Abramzon, M. G. (2026). First-century BC Complexes with Gold Lysimachus Type Staters from the Maeotian Necropolis Of Vinogradny 1. Russian Archaeology. https://journals.rcsi.science/0869-6063/article/view/454250

Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#288. The 9 Best Carpet Cleaners to Lift Set-In Stains and Eliminate Odors

You could always rent a unit, but you'll save some cash in the long run using one of these reliable models.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Vacuums are great for everyday cleaning, but if you need something to go the extra mile, a carpet cleaner gets deep into fibers to lift dirt, pet hair, and tough stains through a mix of scrubbing power, suction, and cleaning solution. This freshens up the look of your carpet beyond what a regular vacuuming is capable of, and extends its life by removing debris that damages the fibers if left untreated.

While it’s possible to rent heavy-duty carpet cleaning machines from home improvement stores, in the long run it’s more convenient and economical to purchase your own and use it as needed. We typically recommend them for spot treatment of spills and stains, as well as for a deep clean of your carpets once every couple months depending on foot traffic. Most carpet cleaners are corded uprights (though there are a few canister-style models) and they typically include attachments for dealing with specific messes, like mud or pet stains.

Our favorite models come from trusted brands like Bissell and Hoover—and many cost roughly the same as regular vacuums. These are the best carpet cleaners we recommend, along with advice on how to pick the right model for your home and needs.

This list was compiled based on our extensive research and general familiarity with household cleaning gadgets. We focused first and foremost on brand reliability—prioritizing names like Bissell and Hoover that are known for producing high-quality models that hold up over time and get the job done. Furthermore, we also looked for brands that offer solid warranties and customer service lines in the case of any faulty products.

From there, we wanted to provide a range of options so all price points and room and home sizes were reflected in our choices. To do this, we pored over verified customer reviews and product specs to create a list that meets our standards.

We believe each carpet cleaner on this list fills a specific role or category better than other, similar models. So, regardless of whether you're looking for a quick spot treatment machine to store in a cupboard or an industrial strength option for a public venue, we've got you covered.

Beyond this, we recently tested out the Tineco Carpet ONE Cruiser in person. Our evaluation method involved basic cleaning and setup that you might use it for on a regular basis, as well as specific testing of individual special features. We also paid close attention to the actual ease of setup, cleanup, and storing the device as part of our overall assessment.

For our latest update, we evaluated newer carpet cleaner models with upgraded features to give home users more versatility. We also carefully reviewed the latest customer feedback to ensure our recommendations reflect the best machines currently on the market. Additionally, we drew on our own experience using a range of carpet cleaners in our busy (and often messy) homes.

This carpet cleaner stands out for more than its powerful cleaning ability. The steam and water cleaning combination in tandem with the two scrubbing rollers break down set-in dirt and stains easily and efficiently.

Best of all, even with this deep level of cleaning, your carpet dries in about 30 minutes if you use the quick-drying mode. Most other models at this price point don't have this feature, which is helpful for households with kids or pets that must be corralled away from wet carpets.

Other highlights of this full-size model include an attachable hose and two different cleaning heads for removing set-in stains and lifting pet hairs from furniture, respectively.

Bissell provides two sample cleaning solutions as well: one for general deep cleaning and one that’s formulated for removing pet urine.

Full Bissell Revolution HydroSteam Carpet Cleaner Review

This portable and affordable carpet cleaner fits comfortably on a shelf or in a cupboard. It's mainly designed for spot cleaning yet offers plenty of power, with a three-stage cleaning process that involves spraying cleaning fluid, scrubbing the affected area with a stain tool, and suctioning up the stain and remaining fluid.

Beyond the basics, the carpet cleaner comes with a self-cleaning attachment for circulating clean water through the hose and tanks to prevent gunk or mildew buildup over time.

While portability is the main draw, it has its disadvantages. The clean water tank only holds 16 ounces and the small head makes it tedious for cleaning larger areas.

Full Bissell Little Green Mini Portable Carpet and Upholstery Cleaner Review

If you want a carpet cleaner with a user-friendly cleaning and drying system, this Hoover model is the right choice. The carpet cleaner has a sensor for quick washing and drying that's operated by simply pushing the unit forward for washing and pulling it backward for drying.

This lets you clean a portion of your carpet and dry it in quick succession. Another feature we appreciate is the dry boost button that generates hot air for even more effective drying.

While the cleaning and drying mechanism is the standout feature, we also like the automatic solution dispenser. Simply snap in the solution container and the machine mixes the cleaning liquid with water for the correct ratio every time.

During our in-person testing of the Tineco carpet cleaner, two things became abundantly clear: the carpet in our office is horrifyingly dirty, and the power drying feature is a complete game changer.

We used the Tineco cleaning formula without any kind of spot treatment beforehand, deliberately rolling it back and forth in straight lines. The results were a tank full of the murkiest water, accumulated fibers, and dirt I have ever seen with my own two eyes, but we also experienced distinctly cleaner carpets.

I particularly liked the power-pushing design that lets you push and pull the device across the carpet while barely lifting a finger. This didn't play a huge role given the relatively small size of the carpet I cleaned, but it would certainly play a much larger factor in rooms where I would be pushing it back and forth for an extended period of time.

Beyond this, the drying feature completely changed how easy the whole process is. Instead of cleaning and then spending a massive chunk of time simply waiting for the carpet to dry, I was able to go over the carpet again using the PowerDry feature and it was literally dry to the touch seconds afterward. The only drawback is that the dirty water tank isn't the largest (0.45 gallons), so it did require us to empty it pretty frequently.

Many carpet cleaners are quite heavy, weighing upwards of 18 pounds. The Hoover PowerDash is one of the lightest full-size models available, weighing just over 12.5 pounds. It’s also much smaller than other full-size options so it's a smart choice for homes low on storage space.

The simple design has a 0.5-gallon water tank and a separate compartment for dirty water, and its antimicrobial brush roll helps lift pet hair out of rugs while protecting against odors. This carpet cleaner uses hot air to help rugs dry faster and comes with a nozzle clean-out tool to make maintenance a breeze.

While its weight is certainly a plus, it does shed it by removing extra features like an attachable hand tool for upholstery cleaning and spot stains.

If you have large carpeted rooms that are subject to spills and tracked dirt, opt for a commercial-grade carpet cleaner like the X3 from Rug Doctor. It boasts a 2.5 gallon clean water tank that covers a lot of ground without needing to be refilled midway through the clean.

Its powerful suction not only lifts up dirt and stains better than standard models, it also improves drying times. By pulling up more of the moisture left behind from the initial wash, drying times are lower than your standard full-size model.

The X3 also comes with an attachable hose and handheld tool for cleaning carpeted stairs and upholstery. It's likely more than most need, though you won't find a better option that delivers a professional cleaning job but is designed for home use.

If pet hair, muddy paw prints or mystery stains are a regular presence in your household, Bissell ProHeat 2X Revolution Pet Pro Plus is one of the most capable upright cleaners we’ve used. It uses dual DirtLifter brushes to agitate carpet fibers and pull out embedded dirt, while maintaining water temperature during cleaning for more efficient stain removal.

We especially love the CleanShot pretreatment feature, which lets you target stubborn spots before running the main cleaner over them. Express Clean Mode is another excellent feature for households with pets or kids, since it helps carpets dry in about 30 minutes and you don’t have to wait long before getting back to your normal routine. The only slight nuisance that our tester noticed was that this pick is slightly louder than other upright cleaners they’ve used in the past.

For homeowners who want near-professional results, and want a little more oomph compared to the Little Green option on our list, Bissell’s Big Green is one of the most powerful machines available for residential use. The large water tanks allow extended cleaning sessions without constant refilling, which we found especially useful for people tackling large carpeted areas.

It also has a dynamic extra-large brush with eight rows of bristles to remove even the most stubborn dirt embedded in carpet fibers. A nine-foot hose and six-inch tough stain tool allowed us to clean hard-to-reach areas, while an adjustable handle makes cleaning wall-to-wall carpet more comfortable. However, the trade-off is weight. This is a heavy machine that requires more storage space and effort to move.

Full Bissell Big Green Professional Carpet Cleaner Review

Our tester is a big fan of Shark, especially since many of their products are lightweight and fit in small spaces. Shark’s CarpetXpert is no exception, as it’s a nice middle ground between portable spot cleaners and bulky full-size machines. We like that it’s compact while still offering strong suction and integrated scrubbing brushes. This combination makes it effective at lifting stubborn dirt without feeling overly cumbersome to maneuver around furniture.

The built-in spot-cleaning tools are another bonus if you’re prone to stains on stairs or upholstery. Best of all, this machine fuses two formulas that simultaneously target both stains and odors so your carpet will not only look clean, but smell fresh as well. This feature makes it a smart choice for homes with pets or kids while staying compact. Just bear in mind that its smaller tanks will require you to refill it a little more frequently.

Full Shark CarpetXpert Upright Carpet Cleaner Review

Over the lifespan of this article, we’ve made several changes to the carpet cleaners that we’ve featured. Many carpet cleaners were considered and ultimately left off this list or removed over time. Here are a couple notable options that, while not quite making it on our list, are worth considering.

Bissell Little Green Multi-Purpose Carpet Cleaner: While we have the Bissell Little Green Mini on our list, the classic Little Green didn’t make the cut this time around. Both are better suited to small stains and upholstery, and we found the general cleaning power differences between the two not as compelling when evaluating them as overall carpet cleaners. So in this case, we leaned toward the less expensive choice.

Costway Multipurpose Steam Cleaner: The Costway steam cleaner is a great choice for folks looking to avoid long drying times and the use of excessive cleaning solutions and concentrates. The powerful steam is great to brighten carpets, upholstery, and break down dirt stains. While versatile, we ended up leaving it off due to the lack of scrubbing power.

Commercial-grade carpet cleaners feature the largest water tanks and the most powerful scrubbing or steaming features to dislodge dirt and remove stains. This allows them to cover much larger areas of carpet at a time before they require a refill with water or cleaning solution.

Similarly, because they are commercial grade, most of them last for years and rarely need a repair. The tradeoff, of course, is that they aren’t easy to store and cost more than smaller models do. For the most part, it's got more power and capacity than you'll actually need.

For most households, we recommend a full-size carpet cleaner. They take up about as much space as a standard upright vacuum and come with a gallon-size tank that allows them to run for approximately 15 to 20 minutes. This is typically enough to cover small rooms in one tank and larger rooms with a single refill.

If you have small rugs or sections of carpeting, a portable carpet cleaner is the way to go. They’re generally no bigger than a handheld vacuum and feature an attached hose and a handful of cleaning tools. These are best for spot cleaning and small stains on furniture items. Many full-size models come with attached hoses for spot treatment as well.

Most carpet cleaners work by shooting a mix of water and cleaning solution at the carpet and then vacuuming it back up once it removes the set-in dirt and grime. This baseline design is typically effective for pulling up moderate dirt and light stains, but it may not be enough for larger issues.

Many of the carpet cleaners we recommend offer more than just water and suction. Several full-size models have built-in roller brushes that scrub the carpet to dislodge dirt in tandem with the cleaning spray and suction functions.

Some models, like the Bissell Revolution HydroSteam, clean using heated water or steam to more effectively break down dirt and set-in grime, while others use hot air to dry carpets after a wash, which is particularly helpful in homes with kids and pets where you won't have the time to let the carpet dry naturally.

Some full-size models, like the Hoover PowerDash Pet Compact Carpet Cleaner, often come with special hoses and heads for upholstery cleaning or spot treatment on stains. Others come with tools designed for digging into carpets and lifting away pet hair and dander. These have scrubbing brushes on the end that pull up dander and hair more easily than models with traditional suction designs.

Most carpet cleaners on this list will provide sample cleaning solutions from their brand, which you can try out for yourself before committing to any one individual option. For the most part, the specialized options built for specific stains likely won't make a huge difference in day-to-day cleaning in comparison to generic ones. Concentrated formulas are well suited for lifting up serious dirt and stains similar to your laundry detergent, but may not be necessary for light refreshes in low foot traffic areas.

In fact, many people use vinegar solutions or substitute with a mix of laundry detergent, fabric softener, and water. While we don't necessarily recommend that, these homemade options should work fine in a pinch and will still be effective in cleaning your carpet.

Most households will find that an upright cleaner will provide the best balance of power and convenience, since these machines deep clean entire rooms efficiently.

“Upright is great if you’re cleaning whole rooms with wall to wall carpet,” says Ryan Knoll, owner of Tidy Casa, a professional cleaning company that services more than 600 homes a month. He also owned a carpet cleaning company for many years, learning firsthand (and often the hard way) what works and what doesn’t when it comes to upright versus portable carpet cleaners.

However, Knoll says portable carpet cleaners have rightfully earned their spot as well. “Portable carpet cleaners are great for spot cleaning and getting into smaller spaces,” he explains. “Think, pet accidents, upholstery, or cars.”

Some carpet cleaners include attachments designed for upholstery, car interiors, and stairs. These tools are great for cleansing fabric surfaces around the house, but most experts advise against using carpet cleaners on hardwood or tile floors since excess moisture can damage those materials.

“These carpet cleaners do one thing really well: they push moisture through the carpet and pull it back out,” Knoll says. “This is what catches all the muck and gets that deep clean. With that said, wood floors don't like moisture, so this is a no-fly zone for wood. Tile is the same.” Instead, Knoll recommends using a steam mop for tile or finished cement surfaces.

Cleaning professionals generally recommend deep-cleaning carpets once or twice a year. “For most homes, every 6 to 12 months will keep things super fresh,” Knoll says. “This works great for homes with 2 to 4 people, maybe a pet or two. For busier homes with lots of kids and pets, stepping it up to 3 to 4 months helps.”

#289. SpaceX just delivered some very strange cargo to the International Space Station

SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft arrived at the International Space Station at 10:27 a.m. EDT on October 15, docking at the space-facing port of the station's Harmony module. The spacecraft delivered more than 6,300 pounds of food, essential supplies, and scientific equipment for the Expedition 75 crew.

The arrival marks SpaceX's 35th commercial resupply mission to the orbiting laboratory under its contract with NASA. Along with everyday necessities for the astronauts, Dragon brought an unusual collection of scientific experiments that could help researchers develop new medical treatments and better understand how materials behave in space.

Artificial Retinas, Brain Research, and New Solar Arrays

Among the most important items aboard Dragon is the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, known as IROSAs. These solar panels are designed to expand the station's ability to generate electricity, providing additional power for its operations and scientific research. Installation is planned for later this fall.

The spacecraft also delivered equipment for manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity, the condition of near weightlessness experienced aboard the space station. Researchers hope that producing these structures in space could eventually lead to technologies that help restore vision for people on Earth.

Other experiments include 3D heart tissue models, which recreate important features of human heart tissue. Scientists plan to use these models to advance methods for testing large numbers of potential drugs during future space missions.

Dragon also transported materials for investigating how a new type of glass forms in microgravity. Studying the process without the usual influence of Earth's gravity could provide insights into how the material develops and behaves.

Another experiment involves brain organoids, tiny three-dimensional models of brain tissue grown from cells. These miniature models allow scientists to investigate aspects of brain biology that can be difficult to study directly in humans. Researchers hope the findings will reveal potential targets for treating neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis.

Dragon is expected to remain docked at the space station until mid-November. After completing its stay, the spacecraft will carry time-sensitive research materials and other cargo back to Earth, ending its journey with a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean off the California coast.

The mission began on October 13 at 6:33 a.m. EDT, when a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

#290. The Best Dehumidifiers for Keeping Basements, Bedrooms, and Bathrooms Dry

These top-rated dehumidifiers remove excess moisture and reduce musty odors.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Towels that don’t dry, a basement with a lingering musty smell, air that feels heavy no matter what temperature you set your smart thermostat to—if any of this sounds familiar, it may be time to invest in a dehumidifier.

Unlike an air conditioner, a dehumidifier’s primary job is removing excess moisture, rather than cooling the room itself. By pulling moisture from the air, dehumidifiers not only improve how your home smells, but they also help to prevent mold and improve overall air quality.

Dehumidifiers often come with a variety of features, like adjustable humidity settings, automatic shutoff, and energy-efficient operation. Some models have additional user-friendly features like continuous drain hookups and built-in Wi-Fi, while others stand out more for their power and reliability.

I researched models from trusted brands like Midea, Costway, and GE and incorporated insights from Popular Mechanics testers to help you find the best dehumidifier for your needs. Below, I also share tips and tricks to keep in mind when shopping for a dehumidifier.

For this guide, I researched dozens of dehumidifiers, reviewed expert and consumer feedback, and incorporated hands-on testing from Popular Mechanics reviews editor Tom Price. I’ll update this guide as more testing is completed. I also spoke with Michael Rubino, a mold and air quality expert and founder of HomeCleanse, for tips on what to look for in a dehumidifier and information on how these appliances can impact indoor air quality.

To test each model, we placed every dehumidifier in a room within its coverage and capacity range. It was difficult to maintain equal humidity for each option, given the wide range of rooms where testing occurred (including bathrooms, living rooms, and laundry rooms—all places where you really notice a change in humidity), so success was measured based on the dehumidifier’s ability to lower humidity levels over one hour, as well as the amount of water collected. The goal was to use each device in everyday settings where excess moisture and humidity tend to become most noticeable.

This dehumidifier from Homelabs has the best balance of features and usability that I came across in my research. Designed for spaces up to 4,500 square feet, it’s a flexible option for medium- to large-sized rooms or those living in humid climates. It's designed to remove 35 pints of water per day, with a listed maximum of 80 pints under ideal conditions.

It has a removable and washable air filter, auto shutoff when the tank is full, and turbo mode for optimal moisture removal. The dehumidifier is also Energy Star-rated, which means it meets the EPA’s energy-efficiency standard. It has a washable air filter and sits on rotating wheels so you can easily move it around your home.

Regardless of the room you’re in, you can monitor and control the dehumidifier's readings and settings via Wi-Fi. This appliance also has an auto-defrost feature and a filter quality indicator light that alerts you when it’s time to clean the filter.

The Costway 32-Pint Dehumidifier is an updated version of the Costway 30-Pint Dehumidifier, which Price previously tested. Based on his experience and my own research, I think Costway offers one of the most affordable dehumidifiers on the market, especially given its size and capacity.

What stands out most with this model is the variety of operating modes. There’s an auto mode that turns the device on or off based on your selected humidity level, a continuous dry mode for persistently damp spaces, and a sleep mode that dims the display lights and lowers operating noise to around 33 decibels.

The Costway also includes a 24-hour timer and two fan speeds for additional customization. Its relatively compact size makes it easy to move between rooms, though Price noted that you’ll probably want to keep it near a drain if possible. He also observed that the half-gallon tank fills surprisingly quickly in humid conditions, especially when running continuously.

For ultra-clammy crawl spaces or damp attics, the Alorair dehumidifier excels. It’s compact and portable, and the lack of an attached tank greatly reduces its size. It’s also quite powerful: This particular model is capable of removing up to 70 pints of moisture from the air over the course of a day.

Because it lacks a holding tank for all the moisture it collects, you’ll need to provide your own holding container or have a drain nearby. The Alorair has two draining options: gravity draining, or you can use the water pump. Gravity draining, as the name suggests, means that the dehumidifier can expel water through the attached tube, though this also means that the unit must be higher than the draining point. You’ll also want a bucket or other receptacle to catch all that water.

The water pump, on the other hand, pushes the collected water out and upward. This feature is especially useful for spaces with a window, sink, or drain that can collect that excess water. Once you’re done using the water pump cycle, the Alorair pushes any remaining water out of the unit in order to prevent any lingering moisture that could cause mold or mildew within the device itself.

Price was particularly impressed by the built-in pump, which he found made it much easier to drain water upward into a sink rather than relying on gravity. That, combined with its custom humidity settings and continuous operation capabilities, makes the Alorair a smart pick for attics and basements.

If you're looking for a dehumidifier with more precise controls, the Frigidaire is one of the more customizable options out there. You can adjust humidity settings directly on the unit, through Frigidaire’s app, or via compatible smart home devices. Once it reaches your selected humidity level, it automatically shuts off; this is especially useful if you live in a humid climate but don’t want your air to feel overly dry.

Another standout feature is the 1.7-gallon water bucket, which is fairly generous for a 35-pint model and allows it to run longer between emptying sessions. There’s also a continuous drainage option if you’d rather not deal with the tank at all. As an added bonus, the Frigidaire can double as an air purifier with the purchase of an attachable filter that helps capture dust and allergens.

Designed for much smaller spaces, this dehumidifier from Pro Breeze is best suited for bathrooms, closets, laundry rooms, or bedrooms up to around 250 square feet. During testing, Price was impressed by how simple and unobtrusive it felt. Unlike most larger dehumidifiers, it doesn’t use a compressor, so it runs very quietly, enough that he barely noticed it while getting ready or working nearby.

Its compact size makes it easy to tuck the Pro Breeze away on a shelf or a countertop. Price used it in his bathroom and found it helped to prevent his towels from feeling like “perpetually damp rags between showers.”

There isn’t a continuous drainage option, though, with its size, it’s relatively easy to empty it out. Once the 52-ounce reservoir is full, an indicator light turns on and the unit automatically shuts off to help prevent overflow. Just keep in mind that while this model works well for small-scale humidity issues, it doesn’t have the power needed for large rooms or damp basements.

If you’re dealing with a damp basement or large living space that always seems humid in the summer, the Midea Cube is one of the more practical high-capacity options we’ve found. The holding tank has an enormous capacity—4.2 gallons—and can pull up to 50 pints of moisture from the air within 24 hours. That extra-large tank also means less frequent emptying, which can be a huge plus if you often find yourself forgetting to check your dehumidifier (or just find constantly emptying a tank tedious and time-consuming). Of course, that large tank also means it can be quite heavy when full, which is something to consider before purchasing (though it does come with a hose for continuous draining).

For all its power, the Midea Cube 50-Pint is surprisingly energy-efficient; it’s Energy Star Certified, which is nice to know, especially if your dehumidifier tends to run frequently. It’s compatible with Alexa and allows remote humidity monitoring, which can be helpful if you’re stashing it in a room you don’t frequent very often. I also think its design is quite clever: The unit twists open for use and collapses into a more compact shape when it's time to store it for the season.

For smaller spaces, such as an apartment, bedroom, or laundry room, a 50-pint dehumidifier may be excessive. You need something smaller, quieter, and more compact, which is where I think the GE 22 Pint Portable Dehumidifier really shines. Its relatively petite size makes it easy to move from room to room, and it features a Smart Dry mode that automatically adjusts the fan speed based on room conditions. It’s also considered a fairly quiet option, which is a plus when working with a small space.

That said, its smaller footprint also means a smaller tank size; at only 8.5 pints, some report having to empty the GE every 12 hours. It’s also not powerful enough to dry out extremely damp spaces. However, if you need a small, unobtrusive dehumidifier, I think this is a solid pick.

If noise is a consideration (think bedrooms, shared spaces), then you’ll want to pay attention to a dehumidifier’s decibel level. Forty decibels is comparable to a library or a quiet suburban street; not silent, but not enough to be disruptive to most people. That’s what sets the Waykar CTH30A apart from other models; it runs at about 34 decibels, making it quiet enough for a bedroom or shared space, while still efficiently pulling unwanted moisture from the air.

Besides its exceptionally quiet operation, this model can cover approximately 2,000 square feet, has four operating modes (including a turbo mode for when you need to dehumidify a space quickly), and has a washable, reusable filter. The wheeled base makes it easy to move from room to room, and it comes with a 3.3-foot hose (which you can extend with a garden hose for better reach) for continuous drainage. This is important, as the 0.4-gallon holding tank fills quickly, especially in very damp areas; the continuous drain option will save you multiple trips to the sink.

“Choosing the right machine for the size of the space is massively important for reaping the benefits of using a dehumidifier,” Rubino explains. “If the dehumidifier’s capacity is insufficient for the square footage or moisture load, it may run constantly without ever effectively lowering humidity levels.” Conversely, a bigger model may be unnecessarily powerful and bulky for everyday use.

Capacity is something you’ll often see referenced when shopping for a dehumidifier, and this is measured by how many pints of moisture the unit can remove from the air over a 24-hour period. For mildly humid bedrooms, bathrooms, or laundry rooms, smaller 20- to 30-pint models are often enough. But if you’re dealing with a damp basement, stale air, condensation on windows, or towels that never seem to dry completely, it’s usually worth sizing up.

A room’s temperature also plays a factor. Warm air holds more moisture than cool air, so a dehumidifier will work more efficiently. As a result, cool but humid basements might require larger units.

You may also notice that newer dehumidifiers sometimes list lower pint capacities than older models with similar performance. That’s because the Department of Energy updated its testing standards in recent years to better reflect real-world home conditions, resulting in lower (but generally more realistic) capacity ratings.

You essentially have two options for disposing of all that collected moisture: manually emptying the tank or setting up continuous drainage with a hose.

Manual tanks have their advantages. For one, you have a lot more flexibility in where you place your dehumidifier: it can be set up anywhere there is an outlet, and you can let it run until the tank is full. The installation process is not complex and can be more cost-effective, as well. However, manually dumping a tank of water can get old, fast, especially if the bucket fills quickly.

“Continuous drainage is always a great option for rooms that are consistently humid,” Rubino says. “That way, the machine can run steadily without frequent monitoring or the need to constantly empty the reservoir.”

For basements, crawl spaces, or rooms with persistent moisture problems, continuous drainage is usually the more practical long-term solution. “This is also a great option for seasonal or vacation homes that aren’t lived in year-round,” Rubino adds. Many models include a hose adapter that allows water to drain automatically into a floor drain, utility sink, or nearby window. Some higher-end models (like our HomeLabs pick) also include built-in pumps, which allow water to travel upward instead of relying on gravity alone.

While your dehumidifier is hardly the noisiest appliance you own, noise levels can make a difference. Most compressor-style models produce a steady fan and compressor hum while running, which may not matter much in a basement but can become a lot more noticeable in bedrooms, home offices, or shared living spaces.

As a rule of thumb, larger-capacity models tend to be louder because they move more air and work harder to remove moisture quickly. Smaller thermoelectric units (like the Pro Breeze) are usually quieter, though they’re also significantly less powerful and best suited for very small spaces.

If you’re planning to run a dehumidifier overnight or in a room where you spend a lot of time, it’s worth paying attention to fan settings, sleep modes, and overall size. A louder, more powerful unit may dry the room faster, but it can also become annoying if it’s running constantly nearby.

Many dehumidifiers now include extra smart features like Wi-Fi connectivity, app controls, and voice assistant compatibility. While these aren’t strictly necessary, they can be useful in certain situations.

For example, remote monitoring allows you to check humidity levels or adjust settings without walking down to the basement every few hours. Scheduling features can also help reduce energy use by running the unit only during certain times of day, such as when you’re at work.

That said, not everyone needs app integration or smart-home compatibility. For many people, features like auto shutoff, automatic restart after power outages, and built-in humidistats (like the GE) are going to be far more useful than voice controls or smartphone notifications.

Energy efficiency is especially important because dehumidifiers often run for hours at a time. That means energy efficiency can make a noticeable difference over time, especially if you live in a particularly damp climate or plan to run the unit continuously in a basement.

Energy Star-certified models are generally worth prioritizing because they remove moisture more efficiently while using less electricity. In some cases, a slightly more expensive model may actually save money long-term if it runs more efficiently and doesn’t need to operate as often.

Choosing the right humidifier size for your needs really depends on two things: the square footage of the space, and the amount of moisture you’re trying to remove. We usually recommend 30- to 35-pint models for larger spaces like basements. Smaller units in the 20- to 30-pint range generally work well for bedrooms and offices.

Sometimes, but it all depends on your home’s layout. Your dehumidifier will work best in an open space where air can circulate freely, so if rooms are separated by closed doors or by hallways, a single unit may not work as effectively. For enclosed rooms or rooms on different floors, you’ll have more success by either using multiple dehumidifiers or moving your dehumidifier between spaces as needed.

Since humidifiers use both a fan and a compressor to remove moisture from the air, they all produce some level of noise. Most will produce an amount of noise similar to what you’d get from a window air conditioner or box fan. If noise is a concern, look for models that list decibel ratings or have a quiet mode for bedrooms or living areas.

Scientists have developed AI tools to measure a person's true "biological age." Live Science asked readers whether they would be comfortable using these tools.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists are harnessing the power of artificial intelligence (AI) to measure people's biological ages.

Unlike chronological age, or the number of years a person has been living, biological age should reflect how well a person's bodily systems are working. Someone with a higher biological age has a higher risk for age-related diseases, such as cancer or dementia, than a person with a younger biological age. While some AI clocks look at epigenetic markers, others focus on other features, like the pitch and pace of people's voices, to calculate a biological age.

We recently asked our readers if they would trust such AI tools to measure their biological age. Over 170 people responded, with 44% of voters choosing "Yes, I would take the results with a grain of salt, but it can still provide some helpful insights." The next-largest group, including 23% of voters, also chose a positive answer, clicking the "Yes, I think it would provide useful health information."

But readers' comments seemed to reflect the opposite trend, with one commenter writing, "NO!!! Unplug it !!! Heed the warnings!" Another reader posted a similar sentiment, saying: "A.I. is dangerous! It's often going beyond its programming and doing things it's not supposed to do! Trusting it with my life is something I will never do!"

Other commenters highlighted the need for more research to be conducted before using they'd use the tools, with one reader writing, "I might wait at least a few years before trying this, because the genetic research the AI is basing its results on is likely to expand quickly, so results are likely to be more accurate & meaningful."

Another reader commented on the idea of accuracy and truth when using these tools, saying, "I won't trust AI. Al on one hand gives amazing possibilities, but on another hand with AI we would never know what the real truth is."

What do you think? Let us know in the comments!

#292. This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch

A bird that migrates thousands of miles has revealed a surprising secret about how wings work. Scientists have discovered that European nightjars sacrifice flight efficiency for agility and use an unexpected wingbeat technique previously associated mainly with bats and insects.

The European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus) is a nighttime hunter that makes an extraordinary annual migration between Europe and southern Africa. Yet the wings that carry it across vast distances must also perform a very different task: helping the bird catch insects while flying slowly and making sharp turns.

Scientists at Lund University have discovered that these competing demands come with a surprising trade-off. Although the nightjar is built to handle long migrations, its wings are not perfectly optimized for efficient flight at higher speeds.

Why Nightjar Wings Sacrifice Efficiency for Agility

To investigate how nightjars fly, researchers studied the birds in a wind tunnel, recording their movements at different speeds and measuring the patterns of airflow left behind their wings.

The experiments revealed that the nightjar's broad wing tips, which likely help it maneuver during slow flight, become a disadvantage as the bird flies faster. At higher speeds, its wings generate lift less efficiently. Lift is the aerodynamic force that helps keep a bird airborne.

The findings challenge the assumption that birds traveling enormous distances must have wings optimized primarily for efficient long-distance flight.

"This runs counter to the intuitive image of a long-distance migrant as a perfectly optimized flying machine. Instead, the nightjar's wings appear to be a compromise between several different demands. The bird can fly slowly and maneuver while hunting, but the trade-off is reduced efficiency in lift generation at higher speeds," says Christoffer Johansson, associate professor at Lund University.

Scientists Discover an Unexpected Wingbeat Trick

The researchers also uncovered another surprising feature of the nightjar's flight. Even as the bird raises its wings during the upward portion of each wingbeat, it continues to generate thrust, the force that helps propel it forward.

This is unusual because such an active upward wing movement, known as an upstroke, has previously been linked mainly to the flight mechanics of bats and insects rather than birds.

The discovery suggests that animals with very different evolutionary histories may have developed similar aerodynamic solutions to the challenges of flying.

"What's interesting is that the same type of aerodynamic solution seems to appear in quite different animals. This suggests that the upstroke does not have to be merely a passive or lift generating part of the wingbeat. It can be actively used to generate thrust when the wings cannot be folded very much," says Christoffer Johansson.

What Bird Flight Reveals About Evolution and Flying Robots

The results offer a broader lesson about how evolution shapes animals that depend on the same body structures for different activities.

Rather than producing wings perfectly suited to one purpose, evolution can favor designs that balance several competing needs. For the nightjar, that means combining the ability to migrate across continents with the agility required to hunt insects at low speeds.

Understanding these compromises could also lead to improvements in aviation technology, particularly drones and other robotic aircraft that use flapping wings.

Like birds, these machines may face mechanical restrictions on how much their wings can fold during each wingbeat. Learning how nightjars generate thrust during the upstroke could help engineers develop more effective ways to move through the air.

Researchers now hope to determine whether this unusual flight mechanism is widespread among other birds and flying animals or whether it represents a more specialized adaptation.

"We now want to investigate how common this way of generating force is among other birds and flying animals. It could help us understand which aerodynamic principles are specific to the nightjar and which are more general. This knowledge may also inspire the development of new types of flapping aircraft," Christoffer Johansson concludes.

Materials provided by Lund University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

"It's not only so beautiful, but it's so precious. "

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station wish that we could all see Earth as they just did.

An orbital view reveals the immense beauty of our blue planet, the only world we know of that hosts life. But it also highlights how fragile that life is, tethered to our lonely Earth in the vast void of space, according to Crew-12 commander Jessica Meir of NASA.

"You see this very thin, tenuous band of an atmosphere, and you know that that is all that is supporting life, and we really need to do our best to protect it," Meir said on Thursday afternoon (Oct. 15), during a press conference that discussed the recently concluded Crew-12 mission.

"I wish that I could bring all the eyes of all the humans to look back at the Earth in this extraordinary way that we are so privileged to have," she added. "I think it really does change you philosophically and [in] how you see each other, how you see yourself, how you see the human race when you look on it down from the vantage point that we have from above — you know, [it] gives everybody this understanding that we need to protect our planet, that it's not only so beautiful, but it's so precious."

From the International Space Station (ISS), Meir said, it's clear that everything on Earth is connected — and that the borders we've laid down between states and nations are artificial constructs.

"You realize that we really are one human when you are in space," she said. "I wish I could share that perspective with all the eyes of all the humans. I think it would be a very healthy thing for everyone to understand.

Crew-12 mission specialist Andrey Fedyaev, of the Russian space agency Roscosmos, voiced similar sentiments, though he would turn an ISS visitor's eyes inward, to focus on the crew.

"I always say that the life of crewmembers on board the space station is the best example of how people need to live on Earth," Fedyaev said during Thursday's briefing (in Russian; in interpreter translated his words into English in real time)."

"We don't have borders. We are all friendly. We're just one crew, and the safety of the crew, the safety of the station, depends on the actions of the entire crew," he added. "So, if humankind does arrive at the same conclusion — that our Earth, our planet, is one and the same space vessel that flies through space — we need to take care of it and not to destroy it. So, that's what I would like to show to everyone on Earth."

Meir and Fedyaev are far from the only ones to have their perpsectives shifted by a space mission. Pretty much every astronaut experiences this phenomenon, which is known as the overview effect, a term coined in 1987 by space philosopher Frank White.

Crew-12 consisted of Meir, Fedyaev, NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway (the mission's pilot) and the European Space Agency's Sophie Adenot (mission specialist). It was the second spaceflight for Meir and Fedyaev and the first for Hathaway and Adenot.

The quartet launched toward the ISS on Feb. 13 atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Their Crew Dragon capsule, named Freedom, arrived at the orbiting lab a day later.

Crew-12 spent nearly eight months aboard the ISS, finally returning to Earth on Oct. 8. They conducted a wide range of scientific experiments and maintenance work during that time and set a few records as well.

For example, Adenot became the first French woman ever to perform a spacewalk, and she broke the mark for longest continuous spaceflight by a European at 237 days. The previous record, 201 days, was set by Luca Parmitano in 2019-2020.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.
