#294. The 4 Best Nugget Ice Makers to Get Soft, Chewable Ice at Home

We tried out the best versions that sit on your countertop and churn out several pounds of ice per day.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a fan of soft, crunchy, chewable ice, a countertop nugget ice maker can bring that sought-after texture right to your kitchen. Also known as pellet or “Sonic” ice, nugget ice is made of compacted flakes that are soft, airy, and easy to munch on and slow to melt. It’s especially good for soaking up the flavor of whatever you’re drinking, making it a favorite for everything from sodas and cocktails to iced coffee and just plain, old water.

Nugget ice makers have become increasingly popular home appliances, but the machines themselves can be relatively advanced. They require more complex internal components than basic ice makers, and thus tend to cost more—often starting around $400 for a high-quality design. Depending on the appliance, you’ll also find features like large ice baskets, water reservoirs, self-cleaning cycles, and high daily production.

To help you find the right machine for your kitchen and budget, we researched, tested, and reviewed the best nugget ice makers from manufacturers such as GE, Euhomy, and Gevi. Whether you’re entertaining friends or just ready to retire the built-in ice maker on your fridge, these are the models we recommend.

The selection of countertop nugget ice makers available from trusted and reliable brands is limited, so we dug to find and test the best options by considering product specs, capabilities, and prices. During testing, we ran cleaning cycles to get the systems ready to go. We then timed how long it took for each machine to produce one batch of ice, and again for how long it took to fill the ice basket completely.

Throughout our setup and testing, we evaluated each model’s ease of use, reliability, and the quality of the ice they made. We took note of any cool or unique features like app compatibility, storage options, and more.

Our home appliance writer, Nick Hilden, also spoke with Jessica Randhawa, founder and head chef at the Forked Spoon, and Yu Jiang Zhao, mixologist, about what to keep in mind when choosing a nugget ice maker.

This was the nugget ice maker that made our tester throw out their ice trays once and for all. It takes everything we liked about the previous version, GE Profile Opal 2.0, and boosts the ice production speed, upgrades a smattering of components and functions to make it easier to clean and enhance its lifespan, and includes an external water tank and ice scoop to boot.

We’ve found that it churns out ice at a rapid enough pace to keep round after round of cold beverages for a sizable gathering. It has an easy-to-use app that offers smart functions such as scheduling alerts for maintenance. Additionally, its sleek design has a timeless vibe that won’t look dated two years from now.

It’s got a footprint nearly that of two shoeboxes side by side, which is a bit big for a smaller kitchen. It can also get somewhat noisy when it’s actively producing ice—about the volume of a loud refrigerator—though it’s basically silent when it’s just keeping it cool. But if you’re looking for reliable, convenient ice on demand, there’s none better.

Full GE Profile Opal 2.0 Ultra Nugget Ice Maker Review

This little unit packs a surprising amount of ice production power, churning out as much or more than any of the larger models on our list (40 pounds per day). Additionally, its compact size makes it perfect when you have less countertop real estate to spare, or if you want portable ice production for a backyard barbecue or camping in an RV.

Our testing found that it churns out ice fast, with the first batch in under ten minutes. Its operation is as straightforward as they come, and its cleaning is easier than most other machines, with an automatic cleaning mode that requires little effort on your part besides draining out the water that runs through the system.

All told, it’s a great ice maker for anyone who wants a no-fuss model that will look nice in the kitchen without taking up too much space. It also offers similar performance to larger, more expensive models, minus the roomy storage capacity.

Full Euhomy Smart Countertop Nugget Ice Maker Review

The Gevi 2.0 is the kind of ice maker you won’t mind taking up prime countertop real estate, given its polished design. The bin holds almost five pounds of ice (the largest capacity on our list), and the machine has thick insulation on all sides to keep cubes frozen for longer.

One of our favorite features is the door on the ice maker that opens to a 90-degree angle. To achieve this, the Gevi ditches the viewing window that’s present on other models, but this design choice allows you to pull the ice basket forward. This made it very simple to scoop our pellet ice once the container was full.

The instruction manual says that it takes about 15 to 30 minutes for the first cubes to form, but I noticed a couple of pellets had dropped around the 9-minute and 20-second mark. They were fairly wet to start but began forming more compactly over time and were the perfect, crunchy texture. However, it takes a few hours to get a full basket, which is tricky if you need ice immediately.

The water reservoir is kind of awkward to access with the door style, but the Gevi also comes with a hose that hooks up to your tap if you want it to fill automatically.

Ice makers require regular cleaning to ensure both quality ice and a long lifespan for the unit, and we found that the Silonn Nugget Ice Maker makes it easier than the rest. Most notable is its self-cleaning function, which is as effortless as it gets: Push a button to start the clean cycle, and let it do its thing. This is unlike other models that require removing a lot of parts or going through a complex series of steps. We also like that you can just toss its removable water reservoir and ice bin in the dishwasher, with no hoses or bottles to clean.

In terms of operation, it delivers most everything you want from a solid ice maker. It produces a hefty 44 pounds of ice a day, and its 2.6-pound bin holds plenty of ice for several rounds of drinks. It’s straightforward and intuitive to use—all you need to do is fill it with water—and is somewhere in the middle in terms of countertop footprint.

It does produce more noise than other popular models. Most nugget ice makers crank the volume up when actually producing ice, but this one has a noticeable hum even when on standby. For reliable ice with no-hassle cleaning, however, it’s hard to beat.

One of the key benefits to a good nugget ice maker is that it can churn out upward of 30 or even 40 pounds a day, making it ideal for hosting large, thirsty groups. The best models can have the first cubes ready within about 10 minutes, and will have a full bin within an hour or so.

A countertop machine, of course, can’t store three dozen pounds of ice. Most ice bins hold 1 to 3 pounds, which will replenish as depleted. It’s rare to go through a full bin, so unless you expect to host a particularly large number of people, this may not be the most pressing concern.

The vast majority of home nugget ice makers are equipped with a built-in water reservoir. These are great for at-home use as they don’t require installation and are highly portable, making it easy to pack them away for storage.

The larger the tank, the more ice the machine will produce. However, this also means that it will require more counter space. Models with smaller water reservoirs eat up less room, but require you to refill them frequently.

You can plug some models directly into your home plumbing system, which eliminates the need to fill a tank as it will draw water continuously. These, however, may require expert installation depending on your DIY skills, and will usually end up in a cabinet or closet rather than on your countertop.

The bigger the ice maker, the more countertop space it uses, so consider how much room you have in your kitchen. Our top pick, the GE Opal 2.0, is a great ice maker, but it has a pretty big footprint for a kitchen with limited counter real estate. When measuring dimensions, don’t forget about the inch or two of clearance that you’ll need for the fan, which keeps the motor from overheating.

If you have the space for it, Randhawa recommends placing the model in the pantry. This not only keeps your countertops open, but can muffle the operating noise.

“With most nugget ice machines you should expect some sound when operating on standby, but they can get pretty noisy when producing ice,” says Randhawa. “That might not matter in the din and clatter of cocktail hour, but could be more bothersome when things quiet down.”

It’s difficult to determine how loud a particular model will be without actually hearing it as there is no standardized noise rating. Your best bet is to check reviews for what previous buyers or reviewers have to say.

Nugget ice makers use a large metal cylinder with an auger inside that freezes as the machine runs. Water then pours into the cylinder and starts to freeze along the walls, producing a thin sheet of ice that the auger scrapes and pushes through the machine as ice flakes.

The machine then squeezes the flakes to push out excess water and compacts them into small, airy pieces so that what you end up with is a soft, porous nugget of ice that (probably) won’t crack your teeth when you chew it. They’re ideal for beverages because they take on the flavor of the drink, and there’s really nothing quite like that taste and texture.

Unfortunately, nugget ice makers aren’t ready to use right out of the box. Once you’ve gotten your unit, it’s best to let it sit upright on a level surface for at least two hours before plugging it in. This helps the refrigerant settle. The time may vary depending on the model you have, so it’s best to refer to the manual for the specific time.

You should also run the self-cleaning or sanitizing cycle before getting started. A combination of equal parts water and vinegar can get the job done. By doing this, you’re clearing the machine of any lingering residue or grime that could affect the clarity and taste of the ice. After completing a cycle with the solution, you can run another one with just water for a full wash-down.

Nugget ice makers are not a set-it-and-forget-it machine—they require regular cleaning and additional upkeep. One of the main concerns with these appliances is calcium buildup, or limescale, which accumulates if you have hard tap water.

To prevent this, it’s a good rule of thumb to occasionally descale your ice maker. You can make a 1:1 solution of distilled white vinegar and water, put it in the reservoir, and run it through the machine for a few cycles. Another tip is to use filtered water.

Self-cleaning modes should be run at least once a month, but if you’re a frequent party host, every other week couldn’t hurt. If you’re using a nugget ice maker that hooks up to a water line, you would benefit from an inline filter. Vacuuming the fan and blowing out the condenser also prevents clogs from dust and debris that may cause overheating.

Nugget ice makers make anywhere from 24 to 44 pounds of ice in a 24-hour period. They start up relatively quickly (as little as 10 minutes) but may take up to an hour to fully fill the ice bin.

Models with large capacity bins are best for big groups, while smaller ones are good for home bars and entertaining a couple of friends. Some options have ice bins that are insulated to keep ice from melting, while others just have an acrylic bucket in which ice melts faster.

For those that regularly host large gatherings or just don’t want to run out of nugget ice, we suggest running your nugget ice maker the day before and storing nugget ice in the freezer. Alternatively, you could stockpile extra nugget ice just in case you’re burning through more than expected the day of your event.

Most nugget ice machines are countertop units, so special installation isn’t necessary. We’ve specifically recommended models that don’t require you to install them, as the vast majority of owners will want something user-friendly and easy to store when not in use. Typically speaking, ice makers that require installation are heavy-duty, professional-grade units for serving large groups of people.

According to Randhawa, “Most nugget ice machines just use a standard outlet and require space around it to vent per the instructions.” Without proper ventilation space, your unit could overheat and break down.

“[Nugget ice makers] run compressors constantly and consume more power than people think it should for a countertop appliance,” says Zhao. “If energy consumption is a concern to you, look for those with an Energy Star rating, and factor in that it will likely be running a good portion of the day.”

Newer models tend to need about 0.05 to 1 kilowatt-hour per day, depending on your ice use. The more ice you make, the more power you’ll need. That’s roughly the equivalent of an energy-efficient fridge, which increases electric bills by about $10 to $15 a month.

If you always want ice at the ready, then you’ll have to run your nugget ice maker at all times, but it’ll likely shut off once the bin is full. “This is a normal operating procedure,” says Zhao. “Turning it off and on [manually] every day reduces its life and means you are waiting 15 to 20 minutes for your first batch every day.”

However, these machines don’t technically need to run year-round if you’re worried about possibly running up your electric bill. “You can turn them off and put them away when you don’t plan on using them,” says Randhawa. “We put ours away during vacations and over the winter, after the temperature drops, which is generally when we don’t want ice in our drinks.”

Amber is a Reviews Editor with bylines on Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products sites. Specializing in kitchen gadgets, small appliances, lifestyle, and consumer tech, she brings hands-on testing and a detail-oriented approach to every review. In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.

Nick Hilden is a writer, globetrotter, and jack-of-many-talents who has written gear reviews for the likes of  Runner’s World, Popular Science, Men’s Health, Thrillist, the Daily Beast, the Los Angeles Times, Greatist, and the Manual, and his lifestyle, culture, and tech writing has also appeared in Scientific American, Afar, Salon, Vice, Healthline, and many others. Before entering journalism some 15 years ago, he worked as a bartender, brewery manager, sound engineer, recording and touring musician, cook, teacher, and in a variety of other trades. These days, he lives all over the world, performs music sporadically, and spends a lot of time thinking how to best improve his Honda Element conversion.

Xavier’s previous experience includes editing shopping, home, and lifestyle content at major outlets such as Real Simple, Better Homes & Gardens, Popsugar, and more. When he isn’t thinking about the best products for readers, Xavier is likely watching the latest flicks at a nearby AMC, or filling out his physical video game collection.

#295. ‘Fiercely stubborn’: the US scientists continuing their research amid funding cuts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Virginia Gewin is a freelance reporter in Portland, Oregon.

Government funding for Josh Plotnik’s elephant conservation work has been cut because it doesn’t match the priorities of the current US administration. Credit: June Zhang Stancil

Equity. Racial discrimination. Climate change. Gender. These are just a few of the 200 or so terms being used to flag federal grants that are under review to determine whether they align with the research priorities set by the administration of US President Donald Trump. The administration initially terminated US$3 billion in grants in 2025, and despite many reversals, roughly $1.4 billion in funding from the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the US National Science Foundation (NSF) remained frozen or cancelled earlier this year. In addition, roughly $25 billion for international aid and development — including for research on global health, infectious-disease surveillance and environmental conservation — was lost when the US Agency for International Development (USAID) was closed down last year.

During the first two years of Trump’s second term, amid funding cuts, agency and programme closures and lawsuits (see ‘Lost funding and shut-down science’), some researchers had to get creative to keep their research moving in a productive direction. Many have turned to private donations or crowdfunding; others tweaked their focus or explored interdisciplinary collaborations. Some have even been wildly successful at spinning their research animals into viral Internet eye candy to raise awareness and funds (see Nature https://doi.org/rsk4; 2026).

Selected major developments and policies from US President Donald Trump’s administration that have led to a loss of resources and funding.

20 January 2025: Executive Order 14169 initiates stop-work orders amid a government-wide 90-day review of all foreign development assistance, effectively halting grants for global-health projects funded by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s International Affairs grants for conservation research.

21 January 2025: Executive Order 14173 directs the dismantling of diversity, equity and inclusion policies, programmes, preferences and activities across the federal government.

January to March 2025: USAID funds are frozen; its website and most programmes are shut down, with the termination of 5,200 contracts and grants.

14 February 2025: The US Office of Personnel Management begins a mass reduction in the federal workforce; nearly 25,000 probationary federal workers were affected in the early stages.

28 February 2025: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) starts to terminate research grants.

18 April 2025: The National Science Foundation starts to terminate research grants.

April and May 2025: Individual researchers, the American Public Health Association, Health Professionals Advancing LGBTQ+ Equality and other organizations file lawsuits against the NIH over grant terminations.

June 2025: The Climate.gov website disappears.

1 August 2025: A US district court rules in the GLMA: Health Professionals Advancing LGBTQ+ Equality v. NIH case that the NIH cannot terminate grants related to research on the health of people from sexual and gender minorities and orders funding to be reinstated.

Nature’s careers team spoke to six researchers about how they kept their work going strong and their teams resilient despite the government scrutiny. Although some funders — the NIH, USAID, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the US Department of the Interior (DOI) — did not respond to Nature’s requests for responses to these accounts of lost funding, the NSF stated that the Trump administration’s current budget priorities and goals “reduce administrative burden on researchers, broaden access to funding opportunities, and better match the structure of awards to the character of the research being supported”. In addition, a White House spokesperson said in a statement to Nature: “The Trump administration remains committed to ensuring that taxpayer dollars fund research that actually can benefit everyday Americans and is not ideologically grounded.”

Elephant-cognition researcher at Hunter College, the City University of New York, New York.

My laboratory group studies Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) in Thailand. We research both the evolution of intelligence, to understand how different animals adapt to a rapidly changing world, and interventions to reduce human–elephant conflict. Two of my group’s grants were frozen when the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s International Affairs grants were suspended in February 2025. The cumulative impact on global wildlife conservation efforts was substantial.

Meeting the moment: how scientific philanthropies are expanding their reach

Meeting the moment: how scientific philanthropies are expanding their reach

We, like many researchers, turned to philanthropy and fundraisers. Hunter College in New York City held a fundraiser to support several research and education programmes. I also received a grant from the Templeton World Charity Foundation in Nassau, the Bahamas, and support for my staff in Thailand comes, in part, from the Golden Triangle Asian Elephant Foundation in Chiang Rai. But many researchers are chasing the same pots of philanthropic funding.

To secure US federal support, I’m currently exploring interdisciplinary research projects to study how cognition changes across an elephant’s lifetime and how those changes might compare with what occurs in humans. Elephants might offer a particularly valuable comparative model because of their long lifespans, complex social lives and sophisticated problem-solving abilities. I think ambitious multidisciplinary teams are key to the type of groundbreaking research that will secure NSF or NIH funding. Collaboration has always been important, but it’s even more so now. Why compete, if instead, you can collaborate and push the boundaries of science?

Eranga Galappaththi (left) has pivoted to US-based research on climate and food.Credit: Sithuni M. Jayasekara

Climate-adaptation researcher at Virginia Tech in Blacksburg.

My research team has spent the past decade building relationships with Indigenous peoples’ networks to co-produce research about how climate change is affecting, for example, hunting and gathering activities in the Canadian Arctic and Sri Lanka. Our original goal was to do a large-scale comparative analysis of fisheries systems and how they’ve been affected by climate change in the two regions. In April 2025, we lost more than $400,000 in NSF funds.

US science after a year of Trump: what has been lost and what remains

US science after a year of Trump: what has been lost and what remains

We had another pending grant from the Belmont Forum, an international partnership of funders focused on environmental sustainability. That funding helped us to maintain research relationships with our Indigenous community partners. In community-engaged Indigenous research, trust is built by showing up consistently, following through on commitments, returning results to communities and developing the research together rather than simply arriving to collect data and then leaving. When funding suddenly disappears, activities that communities were expecting might be delayed, reduced or cancelled — and community members might not realize the distinction between a research team changing its plans and a funding agency terminating support. So far, our partners have remained supportive and interested in continuing the collaborations. But maintaining those relationships becomes much more difficult without stable funding.

Now that the NSF has shifted its priorities away from knowledge-co-production with Indigenous communities, I’m reworking research proposals. The current NSF strategic plan emphasizes topics such as artificial intelligence and machine learning, biotechnology innovation and quantum-information science. And because funding for international research has dwindled, I need to establish a track record of US-focused research.

To that end, I’m doing some original analyses on food-system vulnerabilities and health outcomes using existing publicly available data sets. These data are related to climate, food systems, health, demographics and socio-economic conditions. We are also developing systematic-review and meta-analysis projects to identify broader patterns, effect sizes and sources of variation that might not be visible from individual studies. These approaches help my team to ask original research questions and produce scientific knowledge with fewer resources than would be required for field-based data collection. These approaches are adaptations to the current funding environment, not substitutes for community-engaged research. But I’ll also be doing the slow work of building collaborations with Alaska-based communities.

Rebecca Lindsey started an effort to keep US climate data online and accessible.

Project director for Climate.us, a public climate-information website affiliated with the non-profit organization Multiplier, based in San Francisco, California.

More than one million people were visiting the Climate.gov website every month until, after nearly 15 years, it disappeared in June 2025. At the time, the account had more than 500,000 followers on social-media platforms. It was run by NOAA and I thought of it as a climate-literacy warehouse in which users could view a dashboard of global climate-change and climate-variability data, see maps showing projected changes in US temperatures in coming decades and get scientist-vetted answers to questions about the causes and impacts of human-caused global warming.

Inside the new political screening that’s stalling NIH grants

Inside the new political screening that’s stalling NIH grants

In January 2025, I and other NOAA employees were told by the Trump administration to review Climate.gov and remove content deemed to be in violation of administration policies. For example, the climate-literacy guide used by educators had to be removed because it covered equity. In late February 2025, I was fired by the Department of Government Efficiency, four months before the website was removed. Users are now redirected to a NOAA climate landing page, which doesn’t include the comprehensive dashboards and offers a limited view of what science can tell us about the state of the climate.

In August 2025, I and two other former Climate.gov employees turned to crowdfunding to recreate the effort as the website Climate.us. The non-profit organization Multiplier hosted us, because starting our own non-profit organization would have taken valuable time. Relying mostly on word of mouth, we raised more than $630,000 from various funding platforms.

We also knew that launching a website would create demand for fresh content. We are updating articles, maps and graphics and adding new ones. On top of that, we are restoring the climate-literacy guide, which offered an educational tool to explain core concepts such as greenhouse gases, fossil fuels and ecosystem threats. But I no longer have the expertise of NOAA’s pool of scientists, who used to provide this as part of their jobs. We have about 80 volunteers — academics, non-profit researchers and retired federal scientists — but we certainly don’t have enough depth of expertise in subfields of climate research. We might have to consider paying researchers for that expertise. Going forwards, it would be ideal to host the site on a platform that could partner flexibly with the government at all levels — federal, state and tribal — and that would remain protected from political decisions.

Sharon Hillier turned to funds from private donors to salvage HIV clinical-trial samples from Africa.

Expert in reproductive infectious diseases at the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania.

My work focuses on how best to prevent sexually transmitted diseases. Over the past three years, my colleagues and I have been working on drug-based products to prevent HIV infection, focusing on three African countries. The nine-year project had a total cost of $205 million, and was funded by USAID in 2024. But on 27 February 2025, we received a termination letter that stated that our research award “is not aligned with Agency priorities”. As a result, we lost $138 million. At the time, I had hundreds of samples from three clinical-trial sites in Zimbabwe, Kenya and South Africa where we were testing combinations of antivirals and contraceptives. We had no way to cover our collaborators’ costs for either long-term storage of the samples or shipping them to the United States for analysis. I asked USAID for $20,000 to ship the samples to my lab. During a call, USAID staff asked me whether it would be cheaper to burn or to ship the samples; I responded “to burn them”.

‘Shattered’: US scientists speak out about how Trump policies disrupted their careers

‘Shattered’: US scientists speak out about how Trump policies disrupted their careers

Without those samples, we were on the verge of losing the results from the three clinical trials. I thought about calling it quits and retiring, but scientists are fiercely stubborn and driven to do good research. So, I started looking for ways to keep this research alive.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03315-5

New data reveals that flu season is off to an early start in several Western states. Live Science wants to know if you have already gotten the flu vaccine or plan to do so this year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Flu season in the U.S. typically starts around late October or early November and peaks between December and February. But new data reveals that the current flu season is starting slightly earlier than normal.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), around 3.4% of respiratory samples tested for flu came back positive for the week of Sept. 26. That's around seven times the rate compared with the same week in 2025.

The positive tests are coming mainly from Western states, including California, Washington and Arizona. Regardless of where you're located in the U.S., though, most people are recommended to get their annual flu shot in September or October, and the same goes for this flu season.

The annual flu shot is the best way to prevent hospitalization and death from seasonal influenza. Nearly everyone ages 6 months and older is recommended to get a flu vaccine, and older adults have several special options, including a high-dose shot, a vaccine containing an extra immune-stimulating ingredient called an adjuvant, and a brand-new mRNA vaccine.

Given that flu season is off to an earlier start this year, our latest poll asks whether you plan to get vaccinated or have gotten vaccinated already. Tell us your thoughts in the comments below.

#297. Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before

A new microscope developed at Stanford University allows scientists to watch the tiny structures inside living cells move and interact in real time, providing an exceptionally detailed view without the fluorescent labels typically used to make these structures visible.

Researchers at Stanford have created a powerful new imaging system that reveals the inner workings of living cells with remarkable clarity. By combining two advanced microscopy techniques, the instrument achieves a resolution of approximately 120 nanometers, an unprecedented level of detail for an approach that does not require fluorescent labels.

Known as Interferometric Image Scanning Microscopy (iISM), the technology makes it possible to observe multiple cellular structures simultaneously while they move, change, and respond to their surroundings. Scientists can also investigate what happens when cells encounter drugs or disease causing organisms, potentially uncovering biological processes that have been difficult to study.

The breakthrough, described in the Nature portfolio journal Light: Science and Applications, could lead to advances in cancer research, drug development, infectious disease studies, and investigations of how plants interact with microorganisms.

"This new microscope provides a fantastic new view into the cell, where you can see the tiny structures and machines in the cell moving, changing, and interacting without having to add fluorescence to observe them," said senior author W.E. Moerner, the Harry S. Mosher Professor of Chemistry in Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences. "It's a wonderful look into these complex little cellular boxes that drive our life."

Seeing Inside Living Cells Without Fluorescent Labels

One of the most important advantages of the new microscope is its ability to reveal cellular activity without relying on fluorescent markers.

Many existing microscopy techniques use fluorescent substances to highlight specific structures inside cells. Although these methods have transformed biological research, they come with limitations. Researchers can generally label only a small number of structures at once, making it difficult to observe how different components interact across an entire cell.

Fluorescent signals can also fade during observation through a process known as photobleaching. In addition, introducing the labels can be challenging, and some markers may alter the behavior of the very structures scientists want to study.

The Stanford system avoids these problems by imaging cells without fluorescent labels. This allows researchers to follow numerous cellular components over extended periods while observing their activity in a more natural setting.

Another advantage is that iISM requires substantially less illumination power than comparable label-free methods that produce high-contrast images. Lower light exposure reduces the possibility of photodamage, which occurs when the light used for imaging harms living cells or interferes with their normal functions.

Although other specialized microscopes can achieve finer resolution, the combination of detailed imaging, gentle illumination, and extended observation makes iISM particularly valuable for studying living biological systems.

The researchers emphasize that their technology is intended to complement fluorescence microscopy rather than replace it.

First author Michelle Kueppers, a postdoctoral scholar in Moerner's laboratory, explained that combining the strengths of different imaging approaches could help scientists answer previously inaccessible questions.

"Every method has its advantages and disadvantages, and we believe in a complementary implementation in the future," Kueppers said. "If we use the strengths of fluorescence for molecular specificity and the strength of iISM for label-free context and dynamics, we can really start tackling questions that have been difficult to address before."

How the New Microscope Achieves Unprecedented Detail

The breakthrough comes from bringing together two different microscopy technologies, each with its own advantages.

Moerner received the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his pioneering contributions to super-resolution fluorescence microscopy. He specifically recruited Kueppers to Stanford because of her doctoral research involving a technique called "interferometric scattering microscopy."

This method relies on a familiar property of light: scattering.

Light changes direction when it encounters tiny particles. The same basic phenomenon explains why the sky appears blue. As sunlight passes through Earth's atmosphere, molecules, dust, and water droplets scatter its different wavelengths. Shorter blue wavelengths scatter more strongly than longer red wavelengths, producing the blue color we see overhead.

Interferometric scattering microscopy takes advantage of this behavior on a much smaller scale.

A laser illuminates a cell, causing tiny structures inside it to scatter some of the incoming light. Because the scattered signal is extremely weak, a second laser beam is used to amplify it through interference, allowing the microscope to detect structures that would otherwise be difficult to observe.

The Stanford team improved this approach by combining it with technology adapted from advanced confocal microscopes.

Traditional confocal microscopes use a small opening called a pinhole and a single detector to isolate light from a selected area. More advanced versions replace that arrangement with camera-based detector arrays capable of collecting multiple views of the same region.

The researchers incorporated an array detector into their new microscope, allowing it to collect more light than a conventional system built around a pinhole and single detector.

Hundreds of Views Combined Into One Sharper Image

The advantage of collecting multiple perspectives is similar to the way human vision works.

Our two eyes observe the world from slightly different positions, helping the brain distinguish nearby objects from those farther away. The Stanford microscope uses a related principle, but instead of relying on just two perspectives, its detector array gathers tens to hundreds of views.

The researchers developed a computational method that combines these measurements to generate images with improved sharpness, contrast, depth information, and precision.

By merging the strengths of interferometric scattering microscopy and advanced detector arrays, the team created an instrument capable of resolving structures as small as approximately 120 nanometers.

For perspective, a nanometer is one billionth of a meter. At this scale, researchers can examine extremely small cellular structures and follow their movements and interactions.

Crucially, the microscope achieves this resolution without sacrificing imaging speed or requiring intense laser illumination. Scientists can therefore observe living cells for longer periods while minimizing the risk of disturbing or damaging them.

From Cancer Drugs to Malaria: New Possibilities for Research

Moerner and Kueppers are continuing to refine the instrument, with the goal of eventually making it accessible to scientists across many areas of biology.

Three collaborations with other Stanford research groups are already underway or in development, demonstrating the range of questions the technology could help investigate.

One project uses the microscope to observe interactions among plant cells, fungi, and bacteria as they happen. By watching these organisms interact in real time, researchers hope to gain a clearer understanding of the complex relationships between plants and microbes.

Another collaboration focuses on cancer treatment. Scientists are using iISM to investigate how a cancer drug enters a cell, potentially providing valuable information about how medications interact with their targets.

A third project, still in the planning stages, will examine how red blood cells change shape when exposed to malaria infection. Observing these physical changes could offer new insights into how the disease affects blood cells.

These applications illustrate why the researchers believe their microscope could become a useful tool across numerous scientific disciplines rather than serving only a narrow area of research.

"This is not a niche technique," Kueppers said. "It has broad applications, and we hope the life science community will be well served by it, leading to many new discoveries."

Materials provided by Stanford University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#298. If You’re a Serious Record Collector, You Need One of These Budget-Friendly Record Storage Options ASAP

These budget-friendly options keep your records safe and secure.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Audiophiles know vinyl offers the best listening experience. They also know it’s not the most space-saving hobby. A full record player setup—albums included—can be cumbersome, especially in confined spaces or apartments. Even if you do have more room to work with, serious collectors still need a way to store and preserve their precious records. Fortunately, there are plenty of options, and most of the best ones are available straight from Amazon (two-day shipping for the win).

Without proper storage, your chances of damaging your records virtually skyrocket. If you’re a vintage collector, it’s disastrous. But casual listeners don’t like a skipping record, either (or anyone, for that matter). We went through the top options for vinyl enthusiasts, from fireproof boxes to full-on record player stands. These options accommodate both small and large spaces, at very reasonable price points. Here are some of our favorites.

If your collection is ultra-precious, you might want something with a little more firepower—quite literally. DocuSafe designed this one, and it offers plenty of fireproof and water-resistant protection for your valuables. It holds over 100 records, features a combination lock, and offers high-quality, peace-of-mind storage without breaking the bank.

Victrola has been a mainstay in the record player space for decades, and it also makes some solid accessories. This storage case is one of the best-reviewed on Amazon; it’s portable, holds over 30 records, and comes in a few colors. It fits a variety of turntables, and if you have a small collection, this is the way to go.

These are your classic, run-of-the-mill record storage boxes. You’ve probably even seen them at a vintage record store or antique shop. They do the job well, especially for around $20. They’re compact, foldable, and can fit over 50 records. They stow away easily and represent your more traditional, bang-for-your-buck option.

If you need something space-conscious that still fits a full setup, this record player stand/storage cabinet is a great option. It’s a great value at just over $100 and holds over 250 records. The cabinet features a timeless midcentury modern design, a built-in power strip for easy plug-in, and a spacious top surface to house your entire audio setup.

These cubes let you customize your storage setup to fit your space. Each cube is individual and free-standing, so you can mix and match as you like. You can get them in packs of three or four, and setup takes about 15 minutes. The boxes feature a pretty unique design: iron mesh and composite wood for a rustic, almost vintage feel.

This is another full record player stand with built-in storage, but this one saves quite a bit of space. You’re getting the full setup here, only in a more compact design. The three-tier design accommodates your turntable, speakers, and up to 160 albums. It also includes a built-in power strip for fast, easy charging.

The Orionid meteor shower peaks next week, but a bright moon makes much of the night less than ideal. Sometimes the sensible observing decision is knowing when to stay in bed — and when to get up early.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I used to think being interested in the night sky meant I had to try every meteor shower. If a calendar said "peak," I interpreted that as an instruction. I'd set an alarm, find several layers of clothing and go outside at around 2:00 a.m. when even the neighborhood cats seemed surprised to see me. Then I'd spend an increasingly resentful 45 minutes staring upward, occasionally see one meteor and wonder whether I was somehow doing it all wrong. As I've grown into stargazing, I've become much more selective.

The Orionids peak next week, and normally I'd be tempted. These fast meteors come from debris from Halley's Comet, which is enough of a connection to make almost anyone want to go outside. However, another object is in the sky this year — a big, bright waxing gibbous moon that will brighten the night sky and make "shooting stars" very hard to see.

That doesn't make the Orionids unobservable. In fact, there is a narrow window when the night sky will be free from moonlight. But it does make me far less inclined to sacrifice an entire night for them, and I certainly won't be trying to spend the night camping under a dark sky in a remote rural location far from light pollution. I've discovered that knowing when not to observe is an underrated stargazing skill.

The Orionids are active from Oct. 2 through Nov. 7, with their 2026 maximum expected overnight on Oct. 21-22. They appear to radiate from a point near Orion, although the meteors themselves can streak across almost any part of the sky.

The shower happens because Earth crosses a stream of debris left behind by Halley's Comet, which was last in the inner solar system in 1986 and will return in 2061. Those tiny particles hit our atmosphere at roughly 41 miles (66 kilometers) per second, making Orionids particularly fast meteors.

Under ideal conditions, the International Meteor Organization gives the shower a zenithal hourly rate of 20 or more around maximum. But "zenithal hourly rate" is not the same as promising that I will personally see 20 meteors while standing in my backyard for an hour. It assumes an excellent dark sky, a well-placed radiant and unobstructed viewing. In reality, that's impossible — at the very least you'd have to have eyes in the back of your head. And on each side.

This year adds another complication. The moon reaches first quarter on Oct. 18 and continues waxing toward full on Oct. 26. On the peak night of the Orionids, an 80%-illuminated waxing gibbous moon will be in the night sky as it gets dark on Oct. 21 and sets around 03:00 a.m. local time across Europe and North America on Oct. 22. You can probably see the workaround. Sunrise is roughly 06:30 a.m. local time, which means astronomical darkness — when the sun is more than 18 degrees below the horizon, meaning complete darkness — lasts until around 05:00 a.m. local time (these times work as a ballpark, but you can (check the exact times of moonset and sunrise for your location on Time and Date).

So there is a dark window before dawn, and that is when I would try to see the shower if I were determined to see it. The Orionid radiant is also much better placed after midnight than it is in the evening.

Knowing exactly what's going to happen in the sky turns a casual meteor watch into a rather more calculated exercise.

My plan for the Orionids this year is the same as usual — after checking the moon phase and the moonset and sunrise times, there's one more variable. The weather forecast first.

If the forecast is excellent and I'm feeling enthusiastic, I'll target the period after moonset and before morning twilight on Oct. 22. If it's due to be cloudy, I'm staying in bed.

This sounds obvious, but I think beginners are sometimes given the impression that successful stargazing requires heroic commitment. It doesn't. A meteor shower is not a performance that disappears the moment the advertised "peak" passes. The Orionids have a relatively broad period of activity, so meteors can appear on nights either side of maximum, too.

If I do go outside at 3:00 a.m., I'll do so without two hugely valuable resources for meteor showers — a lawn chair and bags of patience.

The moon reaches first quarter on Oct. 18, making stargazing tricky this week. That means I'm changing what I observe rather than declaring the week a write-off. The moon itself becomes an excellent target in early evening around first quarter. Sunlight strikes the lunar landscape along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night — throwing mountains and crater rims into strong relief. A cheap pair of binoculars can reveal a surprising amount. With a telescope, you can spend hours getting lost in the Montes Apenninus mountain range and three nearby craters — Eratosthenes and Archimedes on either side, and Plato above. Saturn remains another easy evening target after its Oct. 4 opposition. Look toward the eastern and southeastern sky after dark for its steady yellowish light. Even a modest telescope pointed at Saturn's rings will astound.

Cassiopeia is one of the easiest constellations I know to find because its five main stars form a conspicuous W — or, right now, something that looks suspiciously more like an M. Look toward the northern sky in the evening. From mid-northern latitudes, Cassiopeia is high and prominent during autumn, on the opposite side of Polaris from the Big Dipper. That relationship is more useful to me than memorizing exactly which way the W should point. Cassiopeia circles Polaris as Earth rotates, so its orientation changes through the night. From sufficiently northerly locations, it's circumpolar, meaning it never sets below the horizon.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

A recent satellite photo shows a patchwork of tens of thousands of size-restricted farms tightly crammed into Taiwan's Yunlin County, which grows a majority of the island's food.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Yunlin County, Chianan Plain, Taiwan [23.78563273, 120.44373747]

What's in the photo? A multicolored 'mosaic' of small, tightly compacted farms

Which satellite took the photo? Landsat 9

This recent satellite snap shows off a multicolored "mosaic" of tightly packed mini farms covering part of Taiwan in the western Pacific Ocean. The sea of fields and shade nets demonstrates the scale of the agricultural challenges facing the densely populated island.

Taiwan is 14,000 square miles (36,000 square kilometers) — about the same size as Maryland — but has a population around four times as large, with approximately 23 million people living there, according to NASA's Earth Observatory. This places a heavy burden on the island's agricultural industry to provide enough food for everyone on the island, especially as large parts of the landmass are covered by mountains and rainforest.

Researchers estimate that there is only around 3,200 square feet (300 square meters) of Taiwanese farmland per citizen, which is around two-thirds the size of a basketball court, according to the Earth Observatory. This is around 10 times less than the equivalent for U.S. citizens.

The majority of the island's food is produced within Yunlin County, which is situated around halfway along the Chianan Plain, a lengthy strip of flat terrain that hugs Taiwan's west coast. Just under half of the county is visible in the satellite image, which spans roughly 15 miles (24 kilometers) across.

The flat ground in Yunlin County, as well as access to water from the island's largest river, the Zhuoshui (visible across the top of the image), makes it an ideal place to grow a variety of different crops, including "rice, sweet potatoes, peanuts, corn, sugarcane, garlic, scallions, coffee, fruit, and leafy greens," Earth Observatory representatives wrote.

The restricted size of Taiwanese farms means that vastly different crops can be grown alongside one another.

The average size of a farm in Yunlin County is under 100,000 square feet (10,000 square m), which is around 90 times smaller than the average U.S. farm. As a result, the region looks like a giant patchwork of tens of thousands of irregular cuboids when viewed from above.

The sizes of Taiwanese farms are restricted by longstanding legislation that limits the amount of land any individual can own, according to the Earth Observatory. Most of the farms are passed down from generation to generation.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

While Yunlin County's agricultural mosaic is fairly consistent across this image, two main areas stand out from the rest (see below).

The first outlying region is a swarm of blue and turquoise rectangles surrounding the town of Xiluo in the upper right of the image (just below the river). These farms are covered with plastic shade nets, which shelter them from harsh sunlight in the summer and monsoon-like rains in the wet season

Two specific areas of Yunlin County stand out when viewed from above.

The second and perhaps most noticeable anomaly is a cluster of much larger, lightly colored farms near the town of Baozhong (bottom left of the photo). These are sugarcane fields, left over from when Japan controlled Taiwan between 1895 and 1945.

A large portion of the Chianan Plain was used to grow sugarcane by the Japanese, who also constructed railway lines to move the crop across the island. However, most of these fields have since been repurposed, and all but one of the railway lines have fallen out of use.

In addition to growing crops, these small farms are used to rear livestock, including chickens, cattle and "millions of pigs," according to the Earth Observatory.

A 2016 astronaut photo mosaic highlights a "sunglint" phenomenon that transformed Lake Powell into a winding metallic "river." The artificial reservoir, which is the second largest in the country, is home to many visible and long-lost geological wonders.

A 2025 satellite photo shows the Caldas Novas dome, a 12-mile-long monolith that towers above the Brazilian state of Goiás. The structure acts as a giant sponge, soaking up water that helps fuel nearby hot springs.

A 2024 astronaut photo captured an unusual salt patch shining like snow on top of northern Chad's imposing Emi Koussi volcano, which is covered with ancient lava, hidden vents and shadowy waterways.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. #302. Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline

Brain cells that normally help protect the brain may play an unexpected role in cognitive decline as we grow older. Scientists have discovered that cells responsible for maintaining the protective coating around nerve fibers can become dysfunctional with age, potentially contributing to the gradual loss of memory and thinking abilities.

The research, published in Nature Medicine, challenges the long-held belief that these cells are always beneficial. By examining human brain tissue and conducting experiments in mice, researchers found evidence that problems with these normally supportive cells can damage nerve fibers and interfere with cognitive function.

The discovery also points to a possible new approach for protecting the aging brain. Drugs that act on the biological pathway involved are already being used to treat other neurological conditions, raising hopes that existing treatments could eventually be adapted to combat age-related cognitive decline.

Scientists Discover Changes in the Aging Brain

The study was led by researchers from the University of Edinburgh and the UK Dementia Research Institute, who investigated how changes in the brain relate to declining cognitive abilities later in life.

Their research focused on the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936, a group of people whose cognitive abilities have been tracked from childhood into old age. This unusually extensive record allowed scientists to investigate how thinking and memory changed over decades.

Between ages 70 and 82, participants underwent assessments measuring memory, the speed at which they processed information, and their ability to understand spatial relationships.

Of the 1,091 people enrolled in the cohort, 866 completed additional cognitive testing after age 70. Nearly everyone experienced at least some decline, but the rate varied considerably. These differences gave researchers an opportunity to investigate what might distinguish brains experiencing faster deterioration from those aging more gradually.

When scientists examined brain tissue collected after death from a subset of participants, they discovered a striking pattern. Individuals who had experienced greater cognitive decline tended to have fewer large nerve fibers, along with an abnormal buildup of unhealthy myelin.

Myelin is the protective coating that surrounds nerve fibers, helping electrical signals travel efficiently through the brain. Although this insulation is essential for normal brain function, the findings suggest that excessive or abnormal myelin may become part of the problem.

The changes were especially pronounced around the large nerve fibers that remained. Importantly, these abnormalities were associated with how quickly cognitive abilities declined, rather than how well someone performed on cognitive tests at a particular age.

A Protective Brain Cell May Have a Hidden Weakness

To understand what might be causing these changes, the researchers turned their attention to oligodendrocytes, specialized brain cells responsible for producing and maintaining myelin.

Oligodendrocytes have traditionally been regarded as beneficial because they help keep nerve fibers insulated and functioning properly. However, the new findings suggest that these cells can become dysfunctional during aging and may contribute to the very problems they normally help prevent.

The researchers discovered that people with more severe cognitive decline had lower levels of a protein called NRF2 inside their oligodendrocytes.

NRF2 plays an important protective role in cells by regulating hundreds of genes involved in defending against damage and maintaining normal cellular function. When its activity decreases, cells may become less capable of protecting themselves and performing their usual jobs.

To investigate whether this protein was directly involved in the brain changes, the team conducted experiments in mice.

When researchers specifically reduced NRF2 in oligodendrocytes, the animals developed excessive myelin and lost large nerve fibers, closely resembling the abnormalities observed in human brain tissue. The mice also showed reduced improvements in cognitive performance as they aged.

These experiments provided evidence that declining NRF2 activity can directly disrupt oligodendrocyte function, potentially triggering changes in myelin and nerve fibers that contribute to cognitive decline.

Existing Drugs Could Offer a New Treatment Strategy

The findings may have important implications for developing treatments that help preserve cognitive abilities in older adults.

One particularly promising aspect is that the NRF2 pathway is already a target of medications used for other conditions, including a drug prescribed to treat multiple sclerosis (MS).

Previous studies have found that increasing NRF2 activity can improve cognitive function in people with MS. That raises the possibility that medications acting on the same pathway might eventually be repurposed to address oligodendrocyte dysfunction and age-related cognitive decline.

Although further research is needed to determine whether such treatments would benefit older adults experiencing cognitive decline, the discovery identifies a potentially valuable therapeutic target.

Veronique Miron, MRC Senior Non-Clinical Fellow and UK Dementia Research Institute Group Leader at the University of Edinburgh and St. Michael's Hospital, part of Unity Health Toronto, said:

"As the prevalence of cognitive decline is rising with an aging population and no current treatments exist, we are excited about this work as it points to a potential strategy for new therapeutic strategies to preserve cognitive ability in aging."

Beyond its potential medical applications, the research changes how scientists understand the role of oligodendrocytes in the aging brain.

Rather than simply providing support for healthy nerve function throughout life, these cells appear capable of becoming dysfunctional and contributing to cognitive problems.

Georgina Craig, the study's first author and a Postdoctoral Fellow at St Michael's Hospital in Toronto and the UK Dementia Research Institute, said:

"This study has fundamentally shifted how we think about these brain cells in aging. We have always considered oligodendrocytes as purely beneficial, yet here we surprisingly find that they can become dysfunctional and contribute to cognitive impairment in aging."

The findings suggest that maintaining healthy oligodendrocyte function could become an important strategy for protecting memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.

Published in Nature Medicine, the study was funded by the UKRI Medical Research Council (MRC) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR). The research also involved scientists from the University of Edinburgh's Lothian Birth Cohort studies and Northwestern University.
