In this excerpt from "Neanderthals Among Us," author Peter Sahlins looks at the way Neanderthal extinction theories are often engrained with our own societal fears.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Since the discovery of their remains in the 19th century, Neanderthals have fascinated scientists and the general public alike. Although our understanding of these ancient hominins has been transformed tremendously since then, how we have viewed this other human lineage became deeply entrenched in how we see our own species, with geopolitical events shaping the rhetoric around our ancient relatives.

In his new book, "Neanderthals Among Us: The Making of a Prehistoric Human" (Oneworld Publications, 2026), historian and author Peter Sahlins examines our complicated view of Neanderthals, with this lost human lineage being viewed through the lens of cultural and political ideologies. In this excerpt, he looks at our theories for why they went extinct and the philosophical reckoning we've placed up on them.

Between violent extermination and peaceful absorption — with cultural exchange — prehistorians and others propose a wide range of theories to account for Neanderthals' extinction. Just as we've projected our concerns and anxieties about race and gender onto Neanderthals, so too do contemporary challenges shape how we imagine their extinction.

Sometimes it's the newspapers that translate a more neutral science into easily relatable headlines. "Immigrants Halt Neanderthal Era," announced the Glasgow Herald (29 July 2011), claiming that "Europe's earliest residents may have been crowded out by uncontrolled immigration 40,000 years ago." Glossing a highly technical study by Cambridge archaeologist Paul Mellars about the notable increase in population size during the Upper Palaeolithic, the news reports tweaked the science to speak to contemporary anxieties.

But often the science itself is framed or informed by current events. The pathogen thesis gained credence during and after the COVID-19 epidemic. A 2024 study of a 50,000-year-old case of herpes in a sequenced viral genome confirmed widespread speculation that Sapiens-borne pathogens were passed to a Neanderthal population without immunities. Jonathan Kennedy's popular world history "Pathogenesis" (Crown, 2023) argued that Homo sapiens would have been less vulnerable to Neanderthal diseases because they arrived in much larger numbers and had more evolved immune systems from their tropical environment.

Of growing importance over the last twenty years is the thesis that climate change, our own existential challenge of the Anthropocene, was the principal cause of Neanderthal extinction. The idea takes many shapes, beginning with an update of French geologist Georges Cuvier's "catastrophism," where species died off in cataclysmic geological events like earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Since 2007, researchers point to the Campanian Ignimbrite eruption near Naples (Italy), now dated to around 39,280 BP [before present] (+/- 110 years), fictionalised in the 2013 animated film The Croods.

Scientists argue that arriving Homo sapiens were not as affected, perhaps because there were fewer directly touched by the 120 cubic miles [500 cubic kilometers] of magma released, or perhaps because almost everyone died out — but waves of Sapiens arrived later. After all, while most of us share small parts of the Neanderthal genome, the lineages from which we 'directly' descend settled much later in Europe — long after the Ice Age. By far, the greatest portion of our genome comes from our Neolithic, not Palaeolithic, ancestors.

But perhaps "Climate Change Killed the Neanderthals," that is, the extreme climatic fluctuations during the Upper Pleistocene that National Geographic (9 February 2004) announced, following the work of an international team of thirty scientists who laboured for more than seven years on the study. The team identified a general climatic instability during the Middle Palaeolithic marked by a severe cooling event around 41,000 years ago, lasting six centuries — interstadials GIS 13 to 7 of the Greenland ice-core records, to be precise.

St. Michaels Cave in Gibraltar, which was used as a refuge for Neanderthals until around 40,000 years ago.

For the last twenty years, scientists have sought to specify the timing, magnitude and ecological impact of a "mini-Ice Age" — the prehistorical obverse of global warming — that reduced vegetation and herbivore food sources, forcing Neanderthals towards warmer climates, including southern Spain. Clive Finlayson, trained as a zoologist, was an early contributor to sophisticated ecological modeling of Neanderthal extinction. At Gibraltar, he argued, "the last Neanderthal" could be found as late as 29,000 years ago, but there's competition for the title: elsewhere in the southern climatic refugium, Zafarraya (Granada) yielded a skeleton dated to 30,000 BP, but there are skeptics, while other candidates come from the Mezmaiskaya Caves in the Caucasus.

The trope, we've seen, is a frequent one in Neanderthal fiction, including Claire Cameron's "The Last Neanderthal" (Little Brown & Co., 2017), a moving, feminist revision of "Neanderthal Woman." It's also been widely used in popular nonfiction, including in Ludovic Slimak's 2023 account of twenty-five years of research in the Mandrin Cave .

Some of the science blaming climate change for the demise of Neanderthals marks a retreat from the recent archaeological rehabilitation of Neanderthals as a type of human equal to Homo sapiens, as these theories need to account for Sapiens' survival in the same severe conditions. Some experts rewrite basic wisdom, arguing that Neanderthals were not a cold-adapted species, since their origins lay during a warm interglacial stage (MIS 11); or that they lacked the technologies for making complex (and warm) clothing; or perhaps that their preexisting biological cold adaptations delayed the development of such technologies — a story about their technological inertia and deep conservatism.

That Neanderthals died out because of their conservatism, while humans alone mastered innovation, and with it, conquered the world, is the principal claim in Philip Lieberman's "The Unpredictable Species: What Makes Humans Unique" (Princeton University Press, 2013), and it's a widely shared belief.

Aside from the fact that the high value placed on "innovation" corresponds to the ideological superstructure of contemporary neoliberalism and late-stage capitalism, it seems fitting that Neanderthals died out because, in this view, they were, well, truly Neanderthal. The rhetorical figure returns to haunt the science: Neanderthals were conservative, backward, clinging mindlessly to the past in a changing world.

Neanderthal conservatism — not rhetorically, but as an original character trait — has origins in nineteenth-century anthropological judgements about "primitive" peoples. Augustus Pitt Rivers, an early innovator in British archaeology, underscored "the form of a persistent conservatism" of indigenous peoples, and quoted approvingly his colleague E. B. Tylor's "Primitive Culture" (1871): "The savage is firmly, obstinately conservative. No man appeals with more unhesitating confidence to the great precedent-makers of the past; the wisdom of his ancestors can control against the most obvious evidence of his own opinions and actions."

Just as "savages" were once seen as descendants of Neanderthals, so too is their conservatism a cultural legacy, even when anthropologists, transcending an outdated comparative method, no longer deem them ancestral, or even savage.

NEANDERTHALS AMONG US: The Making of a Prehistoric Human by Peter Sahlins is published by Oneworld, hardback £28.

Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

In "Neanderthals Among Us," historian Peter Sahlins offers a sweeping interdisciplinary history of an obsession that has made Neanderthals into a distorting mirror of our claims to human uniqueness and our anxieties about human difference.

At their discovery, Neanderthals helped invent prehistory itself, saturated with racial science; initially cast as ugly, stupid, and hairy, they underwent a long and uneven rehabilitation, with science and popular culture moving at different speeds, and sometimes in opposite directions.

The reputation of “Neanderthal Man,” our Paleolithic double, has been in constant flux, remaining a site of endless fascination and debate about human uniqueness, race, gender, and the very look of the human.

Peter Sahlins is Professor of History Emeritus at University of California, Berkeley. The son of renowned anthropologist Marshall Sahlins, Peter studied early modern French and European history at Harvard and Princeton, then taught for thirty years at the University of California, Berkeley. He has written six books and scores of articles on a range of topics, most recently "1668: The Year of the Animal in France". He divides his time between Paris and Arcy-sur-Cure in Burgundy, where he also gives guided tours of its famous prehistoric caves.

#325. NASA captures strange waves high above Hurricane Simon

Despite remaining offshore, Hurricane Simon battered Mexico's Pacific coast with powerful winds and flooding. At the same time, NASA satellites captured an extraordinary sight high above the storm: enormous waves rippling through Earth's upper atmosphere.

Hurricane Simon was the latest in a series of powerful tropical cyclones to sweep across the Eastern Pacific during the 2026 hurricane season. On October 11, 2026, the Category 4 hurricane moved dangerously close to Mexico's coastline as it traveled north-northwest, with sustained winds reaching 250 kilometers (155 miles) per hour.

Hurricane Simon Batters Mexico's Pacific Coast

At approximately 2:30 p.m. local time (20:30 Universal Time) on October 11, the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) instrument aboard NASA's Suomi NPP satellite captured an image of the massive storm. At that moment, Simon's eye was located roughly 50 kilometers (30 miles) offshore, between the coastal cities of Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta.

According to the National Hurricane Center (NHC), sustained winds had weakened to approximately 210 kilometers (130 miles) per hour by the time the image was taken. However, the hurricane's powerful inner core was still moving close enough to threaten communities along the coast.

The Sierra Madre mountains appeared to help limit Simon's strength, with the rugged terrain reducing the storm's intensity and shrinking the area affected by its winds. Even so, the hurricane brought torrential rainfall and flooding to coastal communities, including the port city of Manzanillo. The heavy rain also increased the threat of dangerous mudslides in mountainous regions, according to news reports.

NASA Captures Strange Waves Above the Hurricane

While Simon churned across the Pacific, satellites detected something remarkable happening far above the clouds.

During the early morning of October 11, the storm generated rippling disturbances that traveled into Earth's upper atmosphere. A nighttime satellite image, captured by the VIIRS instrument aboard NOAA-21, revealed atmospheric gravity waves spreading outward from the hurricane.

These waves are created by intense activity within the storm. Near the hurricane's eyewall, the release of latent heat fuels powerful convection, causing warm, moist air to surge upward and form towering cumulonimbus clouds.

The strong updrafts inside these clouds can disturb the surrounding atmosphere, generating waves that travel upward into the stratosphere and mesosphere. Unlike ocean waves, which move through water, atmospheric gravity waves are disturbances that propagate through the air, with gravity acting as a restoring force.

Why the Rare Atmospheric Ripples Were Visible

Although powerful hurricanes can generate atmospheric gravity waves, satellites cannot always detect them. Strong winds at high altitudes can weaken or disperse the disturbances before they reach the mesosphere, where they may become visible through a phenomenon known as airglow.

Airglow is a faint, natural light produced by gases high in Earth's atmosphere. When atmospheric gravity waves pass through this glowing region, they create subtle variations in brightness that can reveal their distinctive ripple patterns.

The VIIRS instrument's day-night band is sensitive enough to detect this faint light. However, it also captures moonlight reflected from Earth's surface and atmosphere, which can make the much weaker airglow difficult to distinguish.

Fortunately, conditions were unusually favorable when the satellite observed Simon. With very little illumination from the Moon, the delicate atmospheric ripples stood out more clearly, allowing the satellite to capture the striking patterns.

Hurricane Simon's Unpredictable Path Raises Concerns

By the morning of October 13, meteorologists were still struggling to predict where Simon would go next and how strong it might become.

The National Hurricane Center described confidence in its intensity and track forecasts as "very low confidence," reflecting how the storm had repeatedly behaved differently than expected.

At the time, one possibility was that Simon could turn northward, enter the Gulf of California, and eventually make landfall.

Regardless of its exact path, large ocean swells generated by the hurricane were expected to create hazardous conditions along portions of Mexico's southwestern and west-central coastlines in the following days.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS).

#326. James Webb reveals a strange bulge in an alien planet's atmosphere

Astronomers have long depicted distant exoplanets with smooth, circular outlines. But new observations reveal that the atmospheres surrounding some of these scorching alien worlds can have surprisingly uneven shapes.

Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), researchers have discovered that the atmosphere of WASP-17b, a giant planet roughly 1,300 light-years from Earth, extends farther outward on one side than the other. Although its overall outline remains approximately circular, its atmosphere is noticeably asymmetrical. The distortion provides new evidence of how extreme temperatures and powerful winds reshape the atmospheres of distant planets.

The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, comes from a study jointly led by Cornell University in the United States and the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom. Researchers used an innovative technique called 'transmission strings', developed by Bristol astrophysicists Dr. David Grant and Dr. Hannah Wakeford, to investigate the planet's atmospheric structure in unprecedented detail.

James Webb Reveals the 3D Structure of an Alien Atmosphere

WASP-17b belongs to a class of planets known as 'hot Jupiters', enormous gas giants that orbit close to their host stars and experience intense heating. Its unusual atmospheric shape offers a new perspective on how heat moves around these extreme worlds.

Lead author Dr. Lili Alderson, a Klarman Postdoctoral Fellow at Cornell University, began the research while studying at the University of Bristol, where she earned her doctorate in physics.

"This is proof of concept that planets are in fact 3D objects, and that consistently, as they go around their star, what we predict should be happening is happening. To move beyond computational exercises and see it for real is a different matter."

The observations provide valuable information about WASP-17b's atmospheric chemistry and temperature variations, including differences between its equator and poles and between its permanently illuminated and dark hemispheres.

These results closely match earlier theoretical predictions and computer models. Together, they offer one of the most detailed three-dimensional pictures of an exoplanet's atmosphere yet produced, establishing a useful reference point for studying the more than 6,000 exoplanets confirmed so far.

Co-author Dr. Hannah Wakeford, Associate Professor in Astrophysics at the University of Bristol, said: "Planets are temperamental, their atmospheres complex and chaotic. The fact that all of these numbers came together and showed us this very structured, dynamical picture of this giant world over 1,000 light-years away was just really exciting."

A New Technique Uncovers Hidden Atmospheric Features

James Webb's extraordinary sensitivity has already enabled scientists to investigate alien atmospheres using a method called eclipse mapping. This approach examines subtle changes in light as a planet moves behind its parent star, helping researchers determine how conditions vary across the planet.

The new "transmission strings" technique, also called transit mapping, examines the opposite part of the planet's orbit. As an exoplanet passes in front of its star, some starlight travels through the outer edges of its atmosphere before reaching the telescope.

By analyzing that light from different angles, scientists can investigate the atmosphere's composition and determine how far it extends at different locations around the planet. This outer atmospheric boundary is known as the limb.

Traditional methods generally combine light measurements from the entire limb into a single average spectrum. The new approach instead separates information from different regions, allowing researchers to identify atmospheric variations that would otherwise be concealed.

"Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet," Dr. Alderson said. "We're able to go around the edge. So, we've gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak."

Powerful Winds Create a Lopsided Atmosphere

The new measurements revealed a particularly interesting feature near WASP-17b's equator, precisely where previous models predicted it would appear.

The distortion occurs on the planet's "evening" side, where powerful atmospheric winds carry heat away from the hemisphere that permanently faces its star and toward the hemisphere locked in darkness.

This movement of hot gas causes the atmosphere on the evening side to expand farther outward than it does on the cooler "morning" side. As a result, the planet's atmospheric outline is not perfectly symmetrical.

The findings confirm a major prediction about the temperature differences between these regions. The transit mapping measurements also supported other previously identified characteristics of WASP-17b.

Dr. Alderson added: "Theory predicts that the morning and the evening sides should have a strong temperature difference, and WASP-17b fits really nicely in that trend -- pretty much bang-on what we thought it would be."

A Breakthrough for Mapping Weather on Distant Planets

Successfully applying transmission strings to WASP-17b demonstrates that the technique could be used to study the atmospheres of many other exoplanets.

Until recently, much of what astronomers could determine about these distant atmospheres came from measurements averaged across large regions. The new method offers a way to distinguish conditions at different latitudes, as well as between the day and night sides of a planet.

Eventually, this approach could help scientists investigate atmospheric structures on smaller scales, bringing them closer to mapping weather patterns on worlds far beyond our solar system.

Dr. Wakeford said: "Having this very robust mathematical model that we can apply to this state-of-the-art data is incredibly exciting. The results are a really beautiful demonstration of the dynamics that are going on in these multidimensional and multifaceted worlds."

The study used observations gathered through JWST's Telescope Scientist Deep Reconnaissance of Exoplanet Atmospheres through Multi-instrument Spectroscopy (TST DREAMS) Guaranteed Time Observations program.

Funding was provided by NASA, the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), and the Klarman Fellowship.

The three-day celebration, from Oct. 23 to Oct. 25, will bridge the Apollo and Artemis eras.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Your invitation to revisit the Space Age has arrived.

Whether you miss the days when people got dressed up to fly or you wish your "other" ride was a rocket, Mission: 60s has a *space* reserved for you.

"This is a three-day celebration of Apollo, aviation, space exploration and 1960s culture," reads a promo for the Oct. 23 to 25 event in New York. "You will be fully immersed in the sights, sounds and spirit of the 1960s Space Age."

"The weekend features astronauts, Apollo flight directors, Mission Control engineers, Star Trek legends, space artists, a Saturday Spacefarer Soiree with live music (1960s attire encouraged!), and a Sunday NASA Artemis keynote."

Organized by Luna Replicas, a company specializing in vintage space gear, and Space for Humanity, a nonprofit that underwrites spaceflight experiences, Mission: 60s is aimed at being the bridge between the last time humanity reached for the moon and today's "second space race" to do it again — this time to stay.

Your journey back to the 60s begins when you check into the TWA Hotel at the John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in New York.

Once a functioning terminal for Trans World Airlines (as featured in the 2002 movie "Catch Me If You Can"), the TWA Flight Center has been reimagined as a hotel like no other.

"At the center of the hotel is Eero Saarinen's iconic TWA Flight Center, where restaurants, bars and retail outlets have taken flight. Two hotel wings, designed to reflect and defer to the landmark TWA Flight Center, sit behind the historic building and contain 512 guest rooms with views of JFK's runways and the TWA Flight Center," reads the hotel's website.

The TWA Hotel is only the first sight straight out of the past that guests will encounter. On Friday (Oct. 23), Mission: 60s begins with a guided tour of the 1964 World's Fair site in Flushing Meadows. Today the home to the New York Hall of Science, the outdoor exhibits includes the Rocket Park, where Gemini-Titan II and Mercury-Atlas D rockets and a Saturn V F-1 engine still stand.

"The space age was less than 10 years old when rockets like these powered incredible missions to outer space," reads the description on the museum's website. "Visitors will learn about the history of these vehicles as well as the United States' mission to reach the moon."

Also on view at the World's Fair site is the Unisphere, a spherical stainless steel representation of Earth, and the Astro-View Observation Towers (later reimagined as actual flying saucers in the 1997 movie "Men in Black").

The first day concludes with Space For Humanity's (separately-ticketed) "Celestial Soiree" and a Mission: 60's pool party on the hotel's rooftop.

Saturday and Sunday at Mission: 60s will bring together members of Mission Control (MCC), spaceflight experts (including ILC Dover, makers of the Apollo spacesuit) and representatives from the Hollywood community who brought about the 60s-era visions of space exploration (including Industrial Light & Magic [ILM]) for a series of engaging panel discussions.

Among the various topics scheduled for the two days of talks are:

Featured speakers and moderators include Apollo flight director Gerry Griffin, TIME Magazine science editor Jeffrey Kluger, former NASA astronauts Nicole Stott and Ron Garan, "Star Trek" actor Bob Picardo and researcher Frank White.

On Saturday evening, there will be a second gala, "The Spacefarer Soiree," featuring a limited meet and greet aboard a Lockheed Constellation airliner and music by Bonnie Gordon. Set in 1969, attendees are encouraged to come wearing their finest period clothing.

Then, on Sunday afternoon, Uplift Aerospace will host a shared "Overview" VR experience for up to 50 people participating together.

Both days will include a vendor and artists' hall, with guests signing autographs and their books, as well as companies such as NASA's official patch provider A-B Emblem, selling Apollo-themed souvenirs and memorabilia.

A weekend pass is $150 per person, with add-ons for VIP access, the galas and Friday's World Fair excursion. Single-day admission is $85.

#328. How to compare and strengthen research systems

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Lin Zhang is a professor of quantitative science studies at Wuhan University, China, and project coordinator of the China Fundamental Research Report (2026).

How does a country get the biggest bang for its buck when it comes to science? Comparing science systems between countries can be a good way to see what’s working well and what’s not. But it’s difficult to do.

Want to speed up scientific progress? First understand how science policy works

Want to speed up scientific progress? First understand how science policy works

Different countries analyse different things; relevant data can be hard to find or access; and the same concepts can be defined and measured in various ways.

Scientific outputs such as numbers of publications, citations and patents are easy to quantify. But they say little about what factors influenced them. Standardized statistics published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), for example on investments, allow for easy comparisons between countries. But these measurements are not enough to analyse the intertwined effects that different approaches to funding, running institutions and supporting researchers can have over time. Some metrics — such as how funding shapes researchers’ careers — are rarely measured systematically.

And even when countries report on similar measures, differences in data collection can make comparisons difficult. For example, one country reporting information about its fundamental research might publish detailed spending statistics by sector and funding source; another might report only aggregated spending that includes applied research. This makes it hard to form a coherent global picture.

To overcome these problems, a group that I lead has developed an approach to analysing national research systems — gathering data from a broad range of sources and developing measures for often-overlooked aspects of such systems. I hope that other researchers, funders and international organizations will use our framework, and find ways to improve it.

China’s shift towards ‘organized research’: how can coordination and innovation co-exist?

China’s shift towards ‘organized research’: how can coordination and innovation co-exist?

Our project, the China Fundamental Research Report, examines research systems in 25 countries and regions, including the European Union (www.cfrr.net). The chosen regions have systems of various sizes, structures and stages of development. In particular, China offers a useful case study because its scientific landscape has transformed over the past 40 years, through sustained investment in funding, institutions, talent and research infrastructure.

Our work was possible thanks to a rapid expansion in the amount of research information that is now openly available — from publication and funding databases to data repositories and more. This has made it much easier to compare many facets of research between countries. We used large-scale computational methods to analyse data sets that were previously difficult to study together.

One key part of our work was developing fresh indicators to capture areas of research that are not usually measured. For example, we used large language models to identify signals of novelty in research questions and methods — how far a study ventures beyond established knowledge. We also linked publications to patent citations to trace connections between fundamental research and technological development. And we combined funding and workforce data to trace how, in China, junior researchers make a substantial contribution to scientific output. This group, we found, was supported by a long-term expansion of funding for early-career researchers from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

#329. A protein that fuels cancer could also be the key to fighting it

A protein that helps cancer grow may also hold a surprising key to fighting it. Scientists at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL) have discovered that activating this protein in immune cells can make them more effective at attacking tumors, potentially opening a new path toward treating cancers that resist existing therapies.

The findings, published in Nature Immunology, could be especially important for colorectal cancer, which has become the leading cause of cancer-related death among people under 50. Many patients with difficult-to-treat forms of the disease have limited options, particularly when chemotherapy and newer immunotherapy treatments fail. The research suggests that a protein normally associated with cancer growth could instead become a powerful cancer-fighting "force" when activated in the right cells.

Turning a Cancer-Promoting Protein Into an Immune System Weapon

Scientists have long understood that a patient's physical fitness can influence their ability to withstand illness. But CSHL Assistant Professor Semir Beyaz is exploring a different kind of fitness: the metabolic health and performance of individual cells.

"We hypothesized that the fitness determinants of cancer and our immune cells may not be so different," he said. "They're in the same universe. They're constrained by the same chemical and physical rules. So, it's not surprising they'd end up evolving the same way."

At the center of the research is peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta (PPARD), a protein that helps regulate how cells burn fat for energy. PPARD is a transcription factor, meaning it controls the activity of genes involved in important cellular processes.

To understand its effects, Beyaz and his colleagues began by studying mice with colorectal cancer. They found that although cancer cells use PPARD to support their own activity, activating the same protein in immune cells had a dramatically different effect. Instead of helping tumors thrive, it shifted the surrounding environment toward one that favored the immune system's attack on cancer.

"It's all about cell fitness," Beyaz explains. "What cells eat affects who they are. When immune cells burn more fat, they become more fit for fighting cancer."

Supercharging Cancer-Fighting CAR T Cells

The researchers next wanted to determine whether boosting this fat-burning process could improve immune cells' ability to attack human colorectal cancer.

They turned to engineered immune cells known as CAR T cells. These cells are modified to recognize and attack cancer, and CAR T cell therapies are already used to treat certain cancers.

The team activated PPARD in the engineered cells and tested them against several experimental models of human colorectal cancer. These included organoids, which are miniature tumor models grown from patient tissue, as well as human cancer cells cultured in laboratory dishes and implanted into mice.

Across these experiments, the PPARD-activated CAR T cells slowed or stopped tumor growth. The results suggest that changing how immune cells process energy could make existing immunotherapy strategies more effective, although the approach has not yet been proven in patients.

A Potential Strategy Against Multiple Types of Cancer

Colorectal cancer was the researchers' initial focus because of its growing toll on younger adults. However, the team also confirmed promising results in other cancers, including breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and melanoma, a serious form of skin cancer.

These findings raise the possibility that improving immune cell fitness could become a broader strategy for treating tumors that are difficult to control with current therapies.

Beyaz believes the discoveries represent only the "tip of the iceberg" when it comes to finding new ways to strengthen cancer immunotherapy.

The potential applications may also extend beyond cancer.

"Boosting immune cell fitness may also help with other conditions where the immune system fails to clear diseased cells," Beyaz says.

His laboratory is now investigating whether the same approach could help treat endometriosis, a chronic inflammatory condition affecting approximately one in 10 women. Like difficult-to-treat colorectal cancer, endometriosis remains a major medical challenge, with existing treatments often unable to provide lasting relief.

The Surprising Good and Evil Sides of a Cancer Protein

Beyaz compares PPARD's opposing roles to "the force" in Star Wars. Depending on how it is used, the same underlying power can produce very different outcomes.

In cancer cells, PPARD can support disease progression, much like Darth Vader serving the Emperor. But when activated in immune cells, it can take on the opposite role, resembling Anakin Skywalker's return to the light and helping destroy the disease instead.

"It's the classic fight between good and evil," Beyaz says. "How can good ultimately prevail? Activating PPARD in immune cells could be the way."

You don't have to wait until dark to see the moon. Here's why it appears in broad daylight — and why this week is a particularly good time to spot it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I know perfectly well that the moon comes out during the day. I have known this for decades. Yet whenever I spot it in a blue afternoon sky, some primitive part of my brain still thinks it has turned up early.

I'm certainly not the only one. Many people don't understand how it could be visible in daylight. In their eyes, the moon is a nighttime object. Why? Because that's when they notice it — it appears brighter.

We tend to think of the sun as belonging to the day and the moon to the night because that's how they're usually presented to us as children. Astronomically, it makes little sense. The moon spends plenty of time above our horizon while the sun is also up — it spends half its time in the daytime sky, in fact.

If the moon, pale but unmistakable, looks slightly out of place against a blue sky, it's not — you are. This week is a great time to get used to seeing it there. Just past first quarter, the moon will spend each afternoon hanging in the daytime sky, becoming easier to spot as the sun sinks towards the horizon.

The moon reached first quarter on Sunday, Oct. 18, and is now waxing toward full moon, which occurs early on Monday, Oct. 26 (Oct. 25 in some time zones). That puts it in the right part of its orbit to be conspicuous during the late afternoon this weekend.

Here's the useful bit to remember. Around first quarter, the moon rises roughly around midday. As it waxes towards full, it rises progressively later in the afternoon. By full moon, it rises around sunset.

That makes the days immediately after first quarter an excellent time to get into the habit of finding the moon before sunset. On Monday, Oct. 19, look southeast in the afternoon for a moon just over half-lit. Each afternoon this week, it will become a little more illuminated, move farther east against the background stars, and appear progressively later in the day.

You don't need to wait until dusk. In fact, that's the point. Start looking during the afternoon, when the sun is still well above the horizon. Once you find the moon, it can be surprisingly conspicuous against the blue sky.

I'll start looking in the mid-to-late afternoon this week, when the waxing moon should already be high enough to find easily. You can check the exact moonrise time where you are, but there's no need to catch it as it rises. Look towards the east or southeast and scan the blue sky.

Once you've found the moon in daylight, keep checking on it as sunset approaches. The moon doesn't suddenly become brighter, of course. Instead, the surrounding sky darkens, increasing the contrast until the pale daytime moon seems to switch on at dusk and grow increasingly brilliant.

Binoculars will give you a superb view at dusk, particularly along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night. That's where low-angle sunlight throws mountains and crater rims into sharp relief. As the moon waxes this week, the terminator will move steadily across its surface, revealing a different landscape each afternoon.

That's another reason not to wait for the full moon. The full moon gets most of the attention, but the week beforehand is arguably a much better time to get to know our nearest celestial neighbor — and you don't even have to wait until dark.

This is a bright-moon week. Full moon arrives early on Monday, Oct. 26, so moonlight will wash out faint stars and make galaxies and nebulas much harder to see. So go for Saturn instead. It reached opposition earlier this month and remains very well placed in the evening sky. Better still, the nearly full moon passes near Saturn around Oct. 23-24, giving beginners a convenient landmark for locating the planet. The moon's glare will hide faint nearby stars, but Saturn itself is easily bright enough to cope. A good example will be Oct. 27, when the Pleiades is passed closely by a bright moon. The Seven Sisters therefore won't be at their best, so you'll need to use binoculars — if you do, you'll see them easily enough.

Auriga, "the Charioteer," is climbing in the northeastern and eastern sky during late October evenings. It's easiest to find if you start at Capella, one of the brightest stars in the entire night sky. It's just 43 light-years from the sun. From there, I look for the other stars that form Auriga's rough pentagon, including Menkalinan, Mahasim and Almaaz. The fifth corner is Elnath, although it officially belongs to neighboring Taurus.

Auriga gets even better with binoculars. The Milky Way runs straight through it, bringing with it three bright open star clusters — M36, M37 and M38. All three show up in binoculars under a reasonably dark sky, while a small telescope starts to resolve them into individual stars. There's always another layer to find in the night sky.

There's something special about stargazing during the blue hour — that brief transition when daylight drains from the sky and night's window begins to open. It's particularly beautiful a few days before full moon, when the near-full orb is already rising in the east as the sun sets in the west. Look below it, and you may also see the Belt of Venus, a pinkish band above the eastern horizon caused by reddened sunlight shining through Earth's atmosphere, with our planet's dark blue-gray shadow beneath. As the sky fades through ever-deeper shades of blue, the moon brightens, and the first stars emerge around it.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#331. USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells

Scientists at the University of Southern California (USC) have discovered a way to produce a potentially renewable supply of cancer-fighting immune cells, opening a promising new direction for cancer treatment. By working with immature cells that can develop into powerful immune defenders, the researchers have created a system capable of generating large numbers of genetically engineered cells that recognize tumors and help activate the body's natural defenses.

The breakthrough, described in a study published in Cell, could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles facing cancer immunotherapy, including the difficulty of manufacturing enough immune cells and keeping them active in the body. In experiments involving mice, the engineered cells established themselves in bone marrow, produced new immune cells, and slowed the progression of both blood cancers and solid tumors.

The USC Stem Cell-led team focused on a type of immature immune cell called granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs). These cells normally develop into macrophages and other immune cells that protect the body from infections and participate in immune responses. The researchers found that GMPs could be grown extensively in the laboratory while retaining their ability to develop into functioning immune cells. They could also be genetically modified to recognize specific cancer markers and strengthen broader immune responses.

"The study establishes a scalable and engineerable GMP platform for cellular immunotherapy and introduces concepts that we believe could have broad implications for both cancer immunotherapy and stem cell biology," said the paper's corresponding author Qi-Long Ying, MD, PhD, professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC.

Scientists Discover a Surprising Ability in Immune Cell Precursors

Beyond its potential applications in cancer treatment, the discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of how blood and immune cells develop.

Stem cells are known for their ability to self-renew, meaning they can repeatedly divide while maintaining their original properties. In the blood-forming system, this ability has traditionally been associated primarily with hematopoietic stem cells, which can produce all the major types of blood and immune cells.

Progenitor cells, by contrast, are further along in development and are already committed to producing a more limited range of cells. They are generally thought to have less capacity for long-term self-renewal.

The USC researchers demonstrated that GMPs can retain this ability under carefully controlled laboratory conditions. Rather than quickly maturing into other cell types, the progenitors continued multiplying while preserving their identity and their capacity to generate functional immune cells.

"The prevailing view has been that long-term self-renewal in the blood system is primarily a property of the hematopoietic stem cells that can generate any type of blood or immune cell," said Ying. "We found that, under the right conditions, GMPs can also self-renew, dividing extensively while keeping their identity and ability to produce functional immune cells. That gives us a scalable starting point for engineering cell therapies for cancer, infectious disease and potentially many other conditions."

This finding could be especially important for developing treatments that require large, reliable supplies of genetically engineered immune cells.

Why Macrophages Could Be Powerful Weapons Against Cancer

Macrophages are among the immune system's most versatile defenders. Their name comes from Greek words meaning "big eaters," reflecting their ability to surround and engulf bacteria, damaged cells, and other unwanted material.

They also help coordinate immune responses by sending signals that influence the behavior of other immune cells. Some macrophages can enter tumors and attack cancer cells, making them attractive candidates for cancer immunotherapy.

One particularly promising application involves solid tumors, which include cancers that form masses in organs and tissues. Existing therapies based on engineered T cells have achieved their greatest successes against certain blood cancers, but treating solid tumors has proven more difficult.

Macrophages offer a potentially different approach because they naturally migrate into tissues and can penetrate tumors. However, turning them into practical treatments presents several challenges.

Once macrophages have fully matured, they are difficult to multiply in large quantities outside the body. They are also challenging to modify genetically and can be damaged during freezing and storage, complicating the production and distribution of cell therapies.

Another problem occurs after administration. Mature macrophages often collect in organs such as the lungs and liver instead of spreading widely throughout the body. Their relatively rapid disappearance can also limit how long a treatment remains effective.

To work around these limitations, the scientists decided to begin at an earlier stage of immune cell development.

Creating a Renewable Supply of Cancer-Fighting Immune Cells

Rather than trying to manufacture large numbers of mature macrophages, first author Shi Yue, MD, of Ying's laboratory and his colleagues concentrated on GMPs, the progenitor cells that can produce macrophages.

The researchers developed a precisely defined mixture of chemicals that allowed GMPs to survive and multiply for extended periods in the laboratory. The mixture prevented the cells from prematurely developing into mature immune cells, preserving a renewable population of progenitors.

Even after extensive laboratory expansion, the GMPs maintained the molecular characteristics that defined them. Importantly, they also retained the ability to develop into functional macrophages and other related immune cells when needed.

This approach could make it possible to manufacture large numbers of engineered immune cells from a starting population that can be continually expanded, instead of repeatedly collecting and preparing mature cells.

To confirm that the method could be reproduced, collaborators in the laboratory of Ravi Majeti, MD, PhD, at Stanford University independently demonstrated that GMPs could be maintained for extended periods and genetically engineered. Their results provided additional support for the reliability of the technique and its potential use in future cell therapies.

Majeti, Director of the Institute for Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine at Stanford University, noted: "This method for the expansion and engineering of GMPs opens the door to numerous translational applications, much like T cell expansion and engineering. We have already demonstrated engineering of these cells to drive multiple potent functions, and there is a lot more to be explored."

Engineering Immune Cells to Recognize and Attack Tumors

The team next investigated whether these expandable progenitor cells could be programmed to fight cancer.

They genetically engineered GMPs to carry a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. This engineered receptor allows immune cells to identify a particular molecular marker on the surface of cancer cells, helping direct their activity toward tumors.

CAR technology is already an important part of cancer immunotherapy, particularly in treatments that modify a patient's T cells to recognize and attack cancer. The USC researchers explored whether a similar strategy could be applied to GMPs, allowing them to generate engineered macrophages and other immune cells.

The scientists also equipped some of the progenitor cells with an additional immune-activating signal. This modification was designed to recruit and stimulate nearby immune cells, including T cells, which can help mount a stronger attack against cancer.

The added signal offered another potentially important advantage. It remained effective even when the immune characteristics of donor cells did not match those of the recipient.

That finding raises the possibility of developing off-the-shelf treatments using cells manufactured in advance from donors. Unlike personalized cell therapies, which must be prepared separately using each patient's own cells, such products could potentially be produced in larger batches and made available to multiple patients.

Engineered Cells Slow Cancer Progression in Mice

After successfully expanding and engineering GMPs from both mice and humans, the researchers investigated their therapeutic potential in mouse experiments.

When administered to mice, the progenitor cells established themselves in the bone marrow and other locations responsible for blood cell production. These environments provided places where the GMPs could generate additional engineered macrophages and related immune cells.

This was an important difference from treatments using mature macrophages. Instead of relying solely on immune cells that may disappear relatively quickly, the progenitors could provide a continuing source of replacement cells from within the body.

The strategy may therefore help overcome the rapid clearance that has limited macrophage therapies, including approaches evaluated in recent clinical trials.

The researchers tested the engineered cells in mice with blood cancers and solid tumors. GMPs carrying CAR receptors slowed disease progression in both types of cancer.

The effects were even stronger when the progenitors carried both CAR receptors and the additional signal designed to activate other immune cells. This combination improved the treatment's ability to stimulate a broader antitumor response.

Although these findings are encouraging, the cancer-treatment results remain preclinical. Further research will be needed to establish whether engineered GMPs can be used safely and effectively in people, particularly if they are intended to persist and produce immune cells over extended periods.

Potential Applications Beyond Cancer Treatment

The scientists also explored whether their approach could help treat conditions involving defective immune defenses.

In a separate mouse experiment, they studied chronic granulomatous disease, an inherited disorder that interferes with the ability of certain immune cells to kill harmful microbes. People with this condition are particularly vulnerable to recurrent bacterial and fungal infections because their immune cells cannot eliminate some pathogens effectively.

When the researchers administered GMPs to mice with the disorder, the cells restored the animals' ability to fight bacterial infection.

This result suggests that renewable, genetically engineered immune cell progenitors might eventually have applications beyond cancer, including treatments for inherited immune deficiencies and potentially infectious diseases.

The broader lesson, according to the researchers, is that the developmental stage of an immune cell may be just as important as the genetic modifications used to turn it into a treatment.

By engineering cells before they fully mature, scientists may be able to create therapies that are easier to manufacture, more adaptable, and capable of maintaining a continuing supply of specialized immune defenders.

"Our study suggests that the future of immunotherapy may depend not only on designing better CAR receptors, but also on choosing the right developmental stage of the cell," said Ying.

The study, published in Cell, is titled "Expansion and CAR engineering of granulocyte-monocyte progenitors for cellular immunotherapy."

Along with Ying, Yue, and Majeti, the research team included Zheng Guo, Crystal Pan, Xueyuan A. Jing, Tai Nguyen, Jiaqi Tang, Yanpui Chan, Humberto Contreras-Trujillo, Du Jiang, Xue Yan, Hang Xiang, Xugeng Liu, Xiao Wang, Ziyuan Wang, Natalie Shu, Daniel B. McKim, Rong Lu, and Chao Zhang of USC; Litao Tao and Celia Bloom of Creighton University; Asiri Ediriwickrema and Sebastian Koschade of Stanford University School of Medicine; and Yingxiao Shi of Harvard Medical School and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

Financial support came from the Chen Yong Foundation of the Zhongmei Group, a sponsored research project from Myelogene Inc., the L.K. Whittier Foundation, the Eli and Edythe Broad Innovation Award, the Ming Hsieh Institute for Research on Engineering Medicine for Cancer Award, the USC SBIR/STTR Planning Award, the Xia Research Fund, and the Wu & Jiang Research Fund.

Majeti also reported support from the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research. Guo received funding through the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine Predoctoral Training Fellowship.

#332. Why failure is a taboo topic in science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Magdalena Skipper explains why failure needs to be talked about more in science.Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Experiments fail and careers plans can go awry, forcing us to pivot in a different direction. Organizations also make mistakes.

But failure, at both an individual and institutional level, can be a useful teacher.

In the first episode of a six-part podcast series about failure in science, Nature editor in chief Magdalena Skipper says: “I find it surprising that we don’t talk more about failure, that we’re not more honest about the role that it plays. Nobody wants to talk about it. Hence, it’s a taboo.”

In April, the journal partnered with Imperial College London on a one-day conference looking at the role of failure in science. Some of the themes from that event will be covered in future episodes, including how Silicon Valley celebrates “failing fast” as an important learning tool which academia can learn from, and the importance of risk-taking in research.

Launching the conference alongside Stephen Webster, who leads Imperial's Good Science project, a programme that examines research culture, Skipper said the best career decision she ever made was stepping away from active research.

She tells the podcast: “To some who are wedded to the idea that the only true path for a researcher is to continue in active research, that was a sign of my failure. I failed to be a successful academic researcher.” She ends by quoting British statesman Sir Winston Churchill, who said: “Success is the ability to go from one failure to another with no loss of enthusiasm.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03328-0

But I just want to welcome you, those of you who are external to Imperial.

Of course, those of you who are at Imperial, welcome too.

It’s not often we can get together as colleagues to discuss these kinds of things.

That’s me kicking off the opening session of the Failure in Science conference.

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture and what we don’t.

And of course, being a university, that means conferences.

And this one, Failure in Science, has really got a lot to do with Magdalena Skipper sitting here because she said to me this time last year, ”Should we have a conference on failure in science?”

And I just thought, Imperial College, Nature magazine, a conference about failure. You know, this is really too good to be true. Let’s work on this.

So, and so Magdalena Skipper, (she’s editor-in-chief of the journal Nature), and I got to work.

And in April 2026 at Imperial, we welcomed 150 delegates, all of them eager to talk about something not much talked about: failure in science.

We spent the day focused on stuff going wrong, mistakes being made, opportunities being missed, and good things just being neglected.

In this series of six podcasts, using the conference as a springboard, we’re exploring different aspects of failure.

That means much more than simply looking at failure as something personal, a spot of bad luck coming our way.

When it comes to science, is there institutional failure too? For example, should universities frame failure not as a problem, but as part of a creative process, as part of good science? How can institutions look more sympathetically at failure and see failure as a necessity when quick progress is so often the bottom line.

And we’ll also look at the impact of science more widely. What can go wrong when scientific knowledge leaves the lab and tries to make a difference in society?

But first, in episode one, over to Magdalena Skipper.

First of all, actually, I want to start by thanking you and Imperial for following up on what I honestly did not think you were going to follow up on.

Even though we know that failure is part of success, failure is one of the best teachers that we have, as long as we learn from those failures and don’t repeat those mistakes.

I’m Magdalena Skipper. I am editor-in-chief of Nature.

At the conference, I talked about the fact that failure is often a taboo. We don’t talk about it. We know that in science, failure is an everyday occurrence, and of course, failure itself is a very large umbrella term.

Most experiments fail. We learn from that failure, a great deal. Sometimes our plans in our career fail. We learn from that as well. We have to back up and pivot in another direction.

Considering how useful those lessons are, how contextualized they are, I find it surprising that we don’t talk more about failure, that we’re not more honest about the role that failure plays.

If you failed, you’re a loser, and that’s why nobody wants to talk about it.

Failure is part and parcel of our lives, be it professional or personal. We learn through failure. There isn’t a single individual who hasn’t failed at something.

The really crucial aspect of it is how much we learn from it. We learn it’s a matter of building resilience, but it’s a matter also of delving deep into the topic, into the situation in which we have failed, and understanding it much, much more deeply in a much more nuanced way.

So, on the one hand, it’s a natural process. There isn’t a person or a system that hasn’t failed at some point. And on the other hand, it’s such a useful teacher.

The conference was part of a wider project called the Good Science Project, and in the end, the day focused on a number of levels.

One was an individual level. How individuals fail themselves and how they feel about it, how they recover from it, what they learn from it.

We talked about what failing means at an institutional level, or an organizational level.

And of course, since science or research more broadly doesn’t just happen in an academic setting, we also talk about how failure is dealt with in other settings, in the private sector, in in society more broadly.

Much later on in my professional career, I made a decision to step away from scientific, active scientific research and become a scientific editor.

I did that after a PhD and after a postdoc. And now, for me, looking back over the years, I think that was, without a doubt, the best professional decision I ever made. But to some who are wedded to the idea that the only true path for a researcher is to continue in active research, that was a sign of my failure.

I failed to be a successful academic researcher.

And it’s really interesting because that one act, that one action that I took, for me, was a manifestation of success or successful decision, and a manifestation of failure for others.

So I have been referred to as a failed scientist. And of course I’m a failed many other things.

Once upon a time, I wanted to be a firefighter. I’m also a failed firefighter. That never came to pass.

I think the most important thing is that I don’t fail all the time at what I’m actually doing right now.

And perhaps the next thing to add is, in general, in failure, if you do fail, learning from that experience so you move on, and you move on as a richer individual, a richer professional, is really important.

If you are constantly petrified of failing, you are going to play safe all the time. You’re not going to take risks. You’re not going to place big bets, if you like.

Now, in science, that translates into addressing big questions, formulating risky hypotheses, deciding to dedicate funding to a risky, perhaps long-term project that is not fail-safe, is not something that, broadly speaking, we already understand, and you colouring in the boxes or filling in the blanks.

No, if you are not afraid of failure, you are more likely to take bigger risks. And of course, when you take bigger risks, yes, there is a risk of failure.

But there is a risk of there’s a possibility of of great of great gain. Now, our general aversion towards failure means that in our funding systems, we tend to we tend to prefer to fund projects that have quite a lot of foundation, that is safe already.

Many scientists have the experience when they apply for grants, that a large proportion of what it is they’re proposing in the grant they already know is going to work because they have demonstrated it at some smaller level to a smaller degree.

So the question then becomes: is our funding system really designed to push the boundaries of knowledge and make us take those risks and discover something completely unknown, take us in a new direction, maybe open a new avenue, maybe even create a new discipline, or uncover a new approach to probing some questions?

Or is it more designed to walk, take very small steps in some direction?

It’s fascinating to consider the different attitudes that different sectors, different industries have towards failure.

But my understanding is it’s a practice that is relatively widespread in technology companies, especially in Silicon Valley.

And the practice is as follows. In order not to stifle and prevent that risk-taking attitude, which may lead to failure, those companies actually reward their employees financially for failing.

But if they fail fast, imagine without this incentive, you have a situation where only the employees-and this is in the research setting within Google X, only the employees that come up with quote unquote ”positive results”, something that can be taken forward, are rewarded.

But those positive results may be less impactful, or less influential, or have fewer implications if all the employees are thinking: Oh, I will only get rewarded if I succeed. I therefore must not fail at all cost.

Now, of course, from a company’s perspective, there’s no point investing employees’ time or money in long-term pursuit of a project that fails. So what is being rewarded is fast failure. That is crucial.

That is failing fast. To me, it’s a really interesting way of incentivizing risk-taking.

Basically, ultimately, of course, everyone wants to succeed, but the road to that success often leads through failure, and maybe there isn’t another way. Maybe you have to go through failure in order to get to that success.

And contrasting that to an academic setting, where often a lot of time and money is invested in long-term projects, then there should have been a stop, no go decision made earlier on, but perhaps I’m sure there are a number of reasons why a similar approach is not adopted in academic setting.

But one of them I would suggest is that fear of failure? Once you have a project, it’s your project, it’s your baby. You’ve created it. You need to continue proceeding with it.

At the conference I mentioned one specific example of how failure can really energize and motivate researchers.

So the specific example, it’s an example of a paper, a scientific paper, describes a metascience study, so a science of science, where the researchers obtain data from a funder, a US funder, looking at a population of scientists around the cutoff bar for funding.

So they looked at a small, small sliver of this population just above that cutoff. So individuals who just scraped in and got the funding. And then those individuals who just didn’t make it, who just didn’t get the funding. They followed those researchers through time.

And the really interesting finding is that those who just failed to get the funding did better in terms of their career, establishing their career, and contribution to science, than those who just got the funding.

Now that was an observation in the paper. We can speculate why there might be, but I myself find it particularly compelling to think that it’s almost a demonstration of a saying: What doesn’t kill you make you makes you stronger.

That if you’re really convinced that you have a great idea, that you are committed to pursuing a scientific career, and you failed in gaining this support, financial support, then you will find another way.

And that induces that inventiveness and creates a greater motivation for you to persevere, because you are sure that you need to succeed.

So here, failure gives you a boost, if you like, is an additional motivator.

We all know, we have discussed already, that science progresses through self-correction, through a series of failures. These are learning opportunities.

Every graduate student, every scientist, working scientist in the lab, whether it’s the wet lab, or computational lab, or in the field, knows that a large proportion of experiments are going to fail, and that setup and expectations need to be adjusted.

Maybe the question needs to be modified. Maybe parameters need to be changed. Again, that learning process, that comes out of failure.

But we never talk about it. We never talk about that process, that iteration, that trial and error, (it’s not random. It’s intentional), but it’s there. We never talk about it when we talk about science to the general public.

Sometimes the rhetoric is more reminiscent of religious belief than actually a scientific fact that has been arrived at through that iterative process, stops and starts, and failures, and consolidation of ideas, and changing the hypothesis, etc. etc.

It’s not that the scientists don’t know what they’re doing, that they’re not following the scientific method, they are, but they’re not communicating that to the public.

I think the best example of that was during the pandemic, the COVID pandemic, when the general public, I have a sense the general public got a little bit confused and tired of scientists advising policymakers and then policymakers making decisions that appeared to flip flop.

You know, "now do this, now wear face masks, then maybe don’t wear face mask, maybe isolate, maybe don’t isolate.”

There were changes of recommendation and position. Now, to somebody who understands the scientific process, this is to be expected. We are in a completely new situation.

Nobody who’s alive today, who does research on the pandemic, has ever experienced a pandemic of this scale. So of course we’re learning as we go along.

It’s natural that it’s going to lead to failures, which then can be corrected.

And again, this is so crucial to emphasize it.

We learn from these failures, and the next decision, the next recommendation, is going to be better informed, better underpinned by facts.

And so taking a step back from this example, communicating that scientific process, which is all about failing, learning from failure, moving on, maybe failing again, taking a step back, taking two steps forward, maybe another step back, and and so on.

I think by missing that opportunity, we miss the opportunity to make science and scientific process more trustworthy, to show that it really is worthy of trust. We talk about trust in science a great deal, rightly so.

We are worried about the fact that trust in science is dropping.

Perhaps by embracing failure, we can reverse that trend.

We can be more transparent, more honest, and therefore bring more people along.

It’s an interesting point to consider whether a conference on failure should itself be a success or failure.

I think whatever we discuss here will be important, will be success.

And I will just end with a quote that I came across by complete coincidence in a bit of a trashy novel that I was reading on holidays recently.

I was very surprised. The quote comes from Winston Churchill, and apparently he said: "Success is the ability to go from one failure to another with no loss of enthusiasm.”

And I actually think that summarizes many of the endeavours that you all engage in, whatever you do.
