#362. PhD students who write dissertations with AI less likely to stay in academia

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

PhD students are increasingly using AI to help write their dissertations.Credit: Ginaellen/Getty

Roughly 30% of PhD dissertations in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) in the United States this year contained AI-generated text, according to a working paper1 that reviewed the abstracts submitted to an online database since 2019.

What’s more, the working paper, which has not been peer reviewed, found that PhD graduates who use artificial intelligence to help write their dissertations are more likely to work in industry and less likely to enter academia.

Various studies have shown a marked increase in the presence of text generated using AI in scientific literature over the past few years. Researchers at the US-based non-profit organization the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) wanted to understand how PhD students use AI, because insights into students’ training and capabilities will shape science over the next several decades.

“If our students are only doing half the work and they’re dishing the rest to AI, do they really have the depth of understanding” to be good scientists? asks co-author Daniel Gross, an economist at NBER who is based in Durham.

The working paper analysed dissertations from more than 226,000 STEM doctoral graduates completed between January 2019 and May 2026 at US universities. The team used the AI-detection service Pangram to assess the abstracts. For the study, the researchers categorized abstracts as either AI-written or not; they did not distinguish between text that was wholly or partly generated by AI. (Although Gross says that 90% of the flagged AI-generated abstracts were classified by Pangram as entirely AI-generated.)

The team found that AI-generated text in dissertation abstracts first appeared in 2023, and rose from 1.7% that year to 18.8% in 2025. For dissertations filed during the first five months of 2026, 29.4% of abstracts contained AI-generated text. AI use was highest in mathematical and computer sciences: 36% of the abstracts had been written using AI. About 41% of dissertations by graduates educated in non-English-speaking countries had AI-generated abstracts, compared with 23% of dissertations by those from English-speaking countries.

Ang Liu, an engineer at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, says that one issue with PhD students using generative AI tools to write their dissertations is that researchers are expected to explore areas in which the answers are not already known. AI can be extremely helpful when students are working in areas in which there is already a substantial body of knowledge, he says. However, the challenge comes when research moves into areas in which knowledge is incomplete or uncertain. “That is where rigorous research training becomes even more important,” he says.

The researchers also reviewed PhD graduates’ education and employment profiles on the social-media platform LinkedIn. Among PhD graduates who completed their undergraduate degrees in the United States, those with AI-generated abstracts were 17% less likely to be employed in academia than were graduates who did not use AI. However, using AI made those graduates 16% more likely to be employed in industry than those who did not use it. The authors found that the link between AI use and landing a job in academia was less pronounced for graduates who did their undergraduate studies outside the United States.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03253-2

Gross, D. P., Shvadron, D. & Zhang, H. NBER Working Paper 35859 (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2026).

"There is a genetic link between planetary systems and their stars, and that, depending on the star around which they are born, this link also determines their fate."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You can tell a lot about how a child will age by looking at their parents, and it turns out that this could be true for planetary systems, too. Scientists have performed cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems.

The study team, led by researchers at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), studied 300 of the best-understood multiplanet systems of the over 1,000 that astronomers have discovered in the Milky Way.

The team's research clarifies how the environments around infant stars directly affect planetary fates and, in turn, the survival of extrasolar planets, or exoplanets, that are potentially capable of hosting life. That could be crucial as astronomers search for life beyond the solar system, pointing them to systems with potentially habitable planets like Earth.

"The fundamental question we started from was: What determines the characteristics of planetary systems as we see them today? Are they established at birth or sculpted by evolution over time? The truth, in the end, turned out to lie somewhere in the middle," team member and INAF researcher Diego Turrini said in a statement sent to Space.com.

"Our results show that there is a genetic link between planetary systems and their stars, and that, depending on the star around which they are born, this link also determines their fate," Turrini added.

The first "family" the scientists identified consists of wide, massive systems, often with total masses between two and 10 times that of our own solar system. The planets in these systems orbit stars more massive than the sun with lower concentrations of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium (which astronomers somewhat confusingly call metals) than seen in our star.

The second family is more compact and lower-mass systems. The members of this family are composed of planets with comparable masses and sizes, a so-called "peas-in-a-pod" configuration. They orbit stars with mass and metallicity equal to or lower than those of the sun, with orbits that are usually much tighter than those of Mercury, the closest planet to the sun.

One of the "genes" Turrini and colleagues selected to sort planetary systems into families was the deviations that planets make from orbiting their star in the same circular plane. That, in turn, reveals a family history of violent gravitational instability caused by events like giant collisions and planetary ejections.

Violent events were common for the first family, but much less so for the second group of planetary systems, the researchers found. They determined that the number of these turbulent events a planetary system experiences can be linked to even modest variations in the environment in which planets form. These variations arise due to different properties of the parent star of those systems.Thus, the nature of the star in these systems doesn't just fundamentally change the formation of planets in their systems; it influences the system's future evolution, determining whether it will be characterized by phases of marked instability and giant impacts.

"The main difficulty during the data analysis was determining whether the two families of planetary systems were real or just an illusion created by the technological limits of current observational techniques," said team member Camilla Danielski, of the University of Valencia in Spain.

"At the end of the path, it became clear that selection effects acted as the tip of the iceberg, revealing the existence of much deeper structural diversities between these systems," Danielski said.

The scientists tested their conclusions by running simulations of planetary system evolution, all of which began with different conditions.

"The scenarios that best reproduce the dynamical properties of the family of wide and massive systems are those in which the systems are unstable from birth," said research supervisor and INAF researcher Danae Polychroni. "The greater abundance of material from which planets form around their host stars causes them to be born too large, preventing the system from remaining stable."

The team's research was published on Tuesday (Oct. 13) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall has officially arrived, and as autumn leaves blaze in vivid colors, there is no better time to plunge into the imaginative world of New York Times best-selling author Matt Dinniman's "Dungeon Crawler Carl", the wildly addictive science fantasy book series that's taking the world by storm.

Even if you haven't read them, you've probably seen folks carrying these books, emblazoned with their loud, neon-colored covers, at your neighborhood coffee house. You'll see it even more in the future, too, as a streaming adaptation of the novels is coming to Peacock, with Seth MacFarlane's Fuzzy Door and co-showrunners Eric Heisserer and Chris Yost at the helm.

The eighth book in the series, "A Parade of Horribles," dropped in May of 2026 and continues the story of Carl and his ex-girlfriend’s precocious pussy cat named Princess Donut as they try to navigate the dangerously daunting levels of a lethal doomsday dungeon for an intergalactic television show deciding the fate of humanity and the planet Earth.

Think Douglas Adams's "The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy" meets "The Running Man" and "Ready Player One" in the "Dungeons & Dragons" RPG realm, and you've got a pretty good idea of the stylistic narrative you'll soon discover when you dare to enter Dinniman's slightly demented literary world.

"The genesis is that I’ve been writing my whole life, and I have a thousand story ideas," Dinniman tells Space on the origins of his sci-fi sensation. "I’ve kept a running list of ideas since childhood, and this one had been on there for some time. The line in my list for this particular one was 'Alien' game show.'"

With over 14 million copies of the "Dungeon Crawler Carl" series sold to date, spooky season is the ideal jumping-on moment so you can share your favorite sadistic dungeon level kill next time you're at a cool cocktail party or fun family function!

"The success is a whole other question. I think I just happened to hit the right story at the right time," admits Dinniman. "It's about a man pushing back against impossible odds. The antagonist isn't just a single person or entity, but an entire system designed to crush any life out of him, all for the entertainment of the masses. That sort of story seems to really be resonating right now. Plus there's a talking cat in it."

Dinniman has described the most recently-released sequel as "the Carl and Donut version of Mariokart—only deadlier," with the cruel dungeon architects tightening their brutal grip. As the current king of LitRPG titles in circulation, "Dungeon Crawler Carl" is the next best thing to a living video game.

"Luckily I’m still in love with this story, and I am in love with writing it," he admits. "It hasn’t gotten old yet. The end is in sight, and I’m more sad than anything that it'll eventually be over."

An episodic series adaptation seems like a no-brainer, and Peacock has wisely tapped into the considerable talents of both Heisserer ("Arrival," "Bird Box") and Yost ("Thor: The Dark World," "Thor: Ragnarok") for this ambitious TV project.

"Both Chris and Eric have a great amount of experience in Hollywood, but more importantly, both have read the books and like them," Dinniman notes. "Chris is a mega fan, and Eric knows more about gaming than any adult probably should. That's a great combination."

Dinniman also confirmed to us that he's serving as co-executive producer on the show, and will be involved throughout the production.

"The most important thing to preserve, I think, is the tone, which will also be the most challenging," states Dinniman. "Thankfully, the team that's been assembled is up to the challenge, and I can't wait for the world to see how it turns out."

With eight books released so far (and another two to come), you've got plenty of reading to do before the Peacock show and/or the next book lands. You can find the Dungeon Crawler Carl book series in your local bookstores and on Amazon. It's also available via Kindle e-readers and as an audiobook.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#365. History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Enigma machines were used by the German armed forces to encrypt communications during the Second World War.Credit: Ullstein Bild via Getty

Carter Leffen couldn’t believe his eyes when the artificial-intelligence model GPT-6 Astra decoded a secret German army message that had been encrypted for 85 years. Leffen, who has no cryptography experience, asked the model to decipher the message, nudged it a few times to keep thinking and encouraged it to keep working when he went to bed. Sure enough, when he woke up in the morning, it had a solution.

Leffen is one of many non-experts who are now using large language models (LLMs) to break historical codes. Their efforts harness the LLMs’ ability to rapidly deploy decryption algorithms while also searching the Internet for extra historical documents or information that might help.

Cryptography specialists are thrilled at the surge in interest in codebreaking — but they are also being overwhelmed by a deluge of requests to validate AI solutions, which can often be incorrect. “There are so many false positives that are coming in from people who don’t really understand cryptanalysis,” says Elonka Dunin, a retired game developer in the Washington DC area who has written books on cryptography.

In September, Leffen, a product development coach at financial data and media company Bloomberg in New York City, asked GPT-6 Astra to scour Crypto Cellar Research, a website listing historical, unsolved ciphers that is run by independent cryptographer Frode Weierud in Oslo. Leffen tasked the LLM with selecting and then decoding a message encrypted by Enigma, a machine used by the German armed forces during the Second World War to hide military communications from enemies. Enigma’s rotors and plugs rerouted electrical signals to encrypt the letters of the alphabet in up to 103 sextillion possible ways.

AI is helping to decode animals’ speech. Will it also let us talk with them?

AI is helping to decode animals’ speech. Will it also let us talk with them?

GPT-6 Astra, developed by the firm OpenAI in San Francisco, California, chose a message sent on 10 July 1941, possibly because it was short — 82 characters — and was potentially related to another Enigma message sent on the same date that had been decoded in 2017. If that already-solved message contained some of the same words as the unsolved one, it could help to ease the decryption, providing what cryptographers call a crib. For instance, both messages might be addressed to “Obergruppenführer”, a high-level Nazi official.

GPT-6 Astra wrote code to simulate an Enigma machine and searched for the settings that would both reproduce the crib from the message solved in 2017 and render the unsolved message comprehensible. In ten hours, the LLM tested more than four billion settings. Leffen was “gobsmacked” by the solution it presented to him and sent it to Weierud for confirmation. It turned out that the message had been encrypted with Enigma settings different from those used on the already-deciphered message, even though they were sent on the same day — this is unusual and might explain why the code went unsolved for so long.

Days later, inspired by Leffen’s success, Carter Church, a staff engineer at cybersecurity company SentinelOne in Mountain View, California, decided to tackle an unsolved cipher sent by an Italian official to one of French emperor Napoleon’s generals in 1809. Church gave GPT-6 Astra a picture of the message, which had been listed on Cryptiana, a website compiled by Japanese patent engineer and hobby cryptographer Satoshi Tomokiyo.

GPT-6 Astra found a partial key among records on a French cryptography website, and tried an incremental approach to tackle the unsolved message. It used a common decoding strategy called simulated annealing, in which a deciphering key is tweaked iteratively according to whether the output is more comprehensible than that from the previous key. GPT-6 Astra hit on a successful key in about six hours, and Church sent the decoded message — which turned out to describe troop locations — to Tomokiyo, based in Tokyo, for verification.

Carter Church used GPT-6 Astra to decode this 1809 letter, intended for a general in the French emperor Napoleon’s army.Credit: Persée/French Ministry of National Education, Higher Education and Research

Church notes that this message could have been solved without AI, but the LLM’s ability to transcribe the symbols in the image, find the partial key and determine how to apply it greatly reduced the time and effort required.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03338-y

Correction 16 October 2026: An earlier version of this story said that Carter Leffen works at Bloomberg Law. He works at Bloomberg.

#367. World’s timekeepers upend how they adjust time to avoid catastrophic ‘negative second’

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Metrologists retire the leap second immediately, instead of by 2035. Credit: Alejandro Martinez Velez/Europa Press via Getty

Time discrepancies that used to be adjusted by a jump of a second around once every 1.5 years will now wait until an hour needs correcting instead.

Leap seconds serve to align time given by the sun’s position in the sky, which is based on Earth’s unsteady natural rotation, with the more stable ticking of atomic clocks, known as Universal Coordinated Time (UTC). But the rogue seconds have been a thorn in timekeepers' sides, disrupting computing systems and causing misalignment between clocks on the day they are implemented.

Their replacement — a shift of an hour once Earth time and atomic time drift apart by 3,600 seconds — likely won’t be needed for thousands of years, effectively pushing the issue onto future generations.

The leap second is dead. Long live the leap hour?

The leap second is dead. Long live the leap hour?

Member states of the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) voted to pass the resolution at their 28th meeting, outside Paris, on 15 October.

“This decision will ensure the continuity and relevance of UTC for centuries to come,” says Georgette Macdonald, director general of the National Research Council of Canada’s Metrology Research Centre in Halifax, Canada. Canada backed the resolution, which was not supported unanimously but only needed a majority to pass, she says.

“This is a historical moment, a decisive step for UTC”, says Noël Dimarcq, a metrologist at the Côte d'Azur Observatory in Nice, France, who formally introduced the resolution. "We now have an international reference time scale [that is] continuous for the next millennia", he adds.

#369. Daily briefing: Bleached corals revived by healthy neighbour’s touch

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

In stressful conditions, corals expel the symbiotic algae that give them their colour from their tissues. Putting a bleached coral in contact with a healthy one (left) can restore it to full health within eight weeks (right).Credit: Danny Collins

Scientists have successfully restored bleached coral in the lab by placing it in contact with a healthy fragment. Researchers found that when a healthy piece of Pocillopora damicornis coral rested against a bleached piece, the two fused together to create a bridge across which algal symbionts can spread. This transfer fully restored the bleached coral within eight weeks, even if the healthy piece was removed after a week. The result “can inspire solutions that eventually may be scalable” to reverse widespread coral decline, says marine ecologist and study co-author Fiorenza Micheli.

The preprint server arXiv has introduced a cap of two papers per month for each submitting researcher in a bid to clampdown on a deluge of submissions, many generated by artificial intelligence. The limit is the latest measure to prevent its voluntary moderators from being overwhelmed by submissions, says astrophysicist Steinn Sigurðsson, scientific director of arXiv. Some researchers support the cap; others counter that it doesn’t solve the root problem. AI slop will “simply go somewhere else and become someone else’s problem”, says Natalie Khalil, the founder of AI-assisted peer-review platform Reviewer3.

A study of more than 100,000 people has revealed some surprising benefits of brown fat — a type that burns calories to generate heat. Researchers found that people with ‘active’ brown fat are less affected by health issues — such as type 2 diabetes, depression and anxiety — than those without it. The risk of these conditions decreased the more active brown fat a person had. The study is retrospective, so can’t confirm that brown fat is causing these benefits, but “it’s still a very interesting and surprising study”, says molecular biologist Irfan Lodhi.

When presented with two shapes, one with spikes and one rounded, and asked to designate them ‘bouba’ and ‘kiki’, people tend to agree that kiki is the spiky one — and so do dogs. Researchers found that when presented with images of these shapes, domestic dogs (Canis familiaris) more often looked at and moved toward the round shape when the word ‘bouba’ was played from a speaker, and vice versa. The results could suggest that dogs make similar connections between visual information and sounds to humans.

Reference: Proceedings of the Royal Society B paper

Nature’s latest collection of stories selected to bring readers joy includes the newest penguin species described by science, and news that the island nation of Mauritius has become the first country in the world to reduce its number of people with type 2 diabetes — an impressive feat with diabetes rates rising globally, researchers say.

A technique called metagenomic testing can screen for every microorganism that might be present in a sample, rather than searching for one in particular. Now hospitals are trialling ways of using these tests to quickly identify whether acute illnesses that cause neurological symptoms are bacterial, viral or autoimmune in origin to inform more effective treatment. Interpreting the results of metagenomic tests — which pick up pathogens, harmless microbes and contamination alike — can be a rate-limiting step, but advances in AI have enabled a faster sort of useful data from noise.

The US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine has updated On Being a Scientist, its bible for graduate students and early career researchers first published in 1989. Things have changed since the last edition, in 2009, note engineer Mitul Luhar, chemist and dean Emily Pentzer and psychologist Alan Leshner, who was formerly head of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. “Shifts in research priorities and funding place new expectations and pressures on scientists,” they write. “Early-career researchers feel the consequences most acutely.”

Issues in Science and Technology | 9 min read

Reference: On Being a Scientist: A Guide to the Responsible and Ethical Conduct of Research

After a student asked him ‘what’s the point of doing mathematics if an AI can do it better?’, mathematician Steven Strogatz ponders why we bother with being creative and doing what is meaningful in the short time between the cradle and the grave. (The New York Times Daily podcast | 36 min listen or 2:20 video excerpt)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03336-0

Today I’m celebrating Sgiath, the black labrador named Animal of the Year by the International Fund for Animal Welfare. Raised as a mountain rescue dog, Sgiath (pronounced Skee-ah) has now been trained to sniff out carpet sea squirts or ‘sea vomit’ (Didemnum vexillum), marine organisms that can outmuscle native species in coastal ecosystems.

While I put on my party hat, please send any feedback you have on this newsletter to briefing@nature.com.

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing

#370. Nearly half of reef-building corals face elevated relative risk of extinction

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Coral reefs are diverse marine ecosystems that provide ecological functions and economic and social benefits across over 100 tropical countries. Warming driven by climate change is a primary threat to coral reefs and is increasing the frequency of global coral bleaching events. Here we reassessed the IUCN Red List status of 892 reef-building coral species, first assessed in 2008 1. Because species-level population trends are unavailable for most reef-building corals, population reductions were inferred using proxies based on global coral cover trends and projected annual severe bleaching under SSP2-4.5, both over three decades, adjusted using trait-based estimates of species vulnerability. Of the 774 species with sufficient data to be assessed, 340 (44%) were classified as threatened under IUCN Red List criteria. Thirty-three species were assessed as Critically Endangered, 251 as Endangered, and 56 as Vulnerable, most due to risk of population reduction associated with projected thermal stress. These findings predate the three hottest years on record and the fourth global coral bleaching event (2023-2025), and the first exceedance for an annual mean of the 1.5oC global warming threshold. The findings reinforce the importance of limiting further warming to maintain coral biodiversity and reef ecosystem function. The Red List assesses the relative extinction risk of species, whereby species are placed in categories of increasing risk by comparing their population size, decline and geographic range against standardised thresholds. The Red List does not predict whether or when a species may go extinct. As the ranges of coral species remain under-surveyed, future assessments would be strengthened by species-level population data and thermal-stress and recovery metrics that better capture range-representative dynamics.

Supplementary text, Supplementary Tables 1–10 and references supporting the reassessment of extinction risk for 892 reef-building coral species. The text describes the methodological updates from the 2008 assessment: coral taxonomy, the interpretation of coral abundance and extinction risk under the IUCN Red List framework, coral cover as a proxy for population reduction, projected thermal stress, generation length, species traits and the Red List Index. It also reports supporting results on Red List criteria applied, genuine and non-genuine changes in classification, and geographic and taxonomic differences.

Species-level results and supporting data for all 892 species assessed. The workbook has two sheets. “Metadata” defines each variable, as in Supplementary Table 10. “Supplementary Dataset 1” gives, for each species: family, current and 2008 species names; Red List category and criteria for 2024, with recalculated categories for 2008 and pre-1998; realm, number of ecoregions, extent of occurrence and coral reef area within range; total and preferred depth ranges; projected population decline under SSP2-4.5 and past coral cover decline (GCRMN); scores for each vulnerability trait; mean, mode and final vulnerability scores.

#371. Give me the good news: four science stories to brighten your day

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

A new species of sea spider, Tanystylum kiixin, has been discovered.Credit: Cormac Toler-Scott

Amid wars, AI doom and a super El Niño, good news can seem in short supply. But it is there if you go looking. In Nature’s latest collection of stories selected to bring readers joy, learn about a country that has reversed its rates of diabetes and umbrellas that keep corals cool.

But first, you might have heard about reports of the first new wild cat species in a century, announced last month1. The spotted feline, called Leopardus tilcayo, was found in the forested Yungas region of Bolivia.

The news is not all bad: five inspiring science stories to lift your mood

The news is not all bad: five inspiring science stories to lift your mood

But did you know that a new member has also been inducted into the penguin family this year? A population of penguins on the remote Kerguelen Islands — around 2,000 kilometres north of Antarctica in the Indian Ocean — has been designated as a new species, the southeastern gentoo (Pygoscelis kerguelensis)2. This addresses a long-running debate about whether the gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua) is one species or several. Using genetic analysis, scientists say the southeastern gentoo is its own species and that three populations previously identified as subspecies of gentoo should also be considered their own species.

Meanwhile, two new species of sea spider3 have been found in the Salish Sea, off the west coast of the United States and Canada. Sea spiders are a type of marine arthropod related to horseshoe crabs and arachnids. One of the new species, Callipallene pilosuspedes, has four bright red eyes, legs three times as long as its body, a triangular mouth and a short proboscis with claws that it uses to grab food. It also uses spiny appendages at the bottom of its head, called ovigers, to groom itself. The other species, called Tanystylum kiixin, has stubby legs, an hourglass-shaped body and black eyes.

Mauritius has become the first country in the world to reduce its number of people with type 2 diabetes4. Researchers say this is impressive, given that rates of the disease are rising globally.

The island nation off the east coast of Africa has been surveying how many people have type 2 diabetes or raised blood sugar levels — an indicator of being at risk of developing diabetes — since 1987. The number of people with the condition went up between 1987 and 2009, but had decreased by 11% for men and 16% for women by 2021. Rates of raised blood sugar also decreased by roughly one-third between 2009 and 2021.

The trend is striking, write Shukri Mohamed and Andre Pascal Kengne at the African Population and Health Research Center in Nairobi in a commentary5 accompanying the study in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology. It is probably the result of improved awareness of diabetes, they say, as well as better screening and access to health care.

Improvised umbrellas made from cloth resistant to ultraviolet light protected a small section of coral reef in the Florida Keys from heat stress during extreme temperatures in 20246. Scientists made umbrella-like canopies using PVC pipes, filled with spray foam, and shade cloth; the structures floated about 30 centimetres above the coral.

Researchers assemble a cover to shade coral in the Florida Keys.Credit: Arelys Chaparro

This shading reduced the amount of solar radiation the coral was exposed to, minimizing the heat stress that often causes coral bleaching by killing tiny, coloured organisms that live inside the coral. Nearby unshaded corals, by comparison, continued to get paler over time. The research team says that similar shades could be a cheap, effective way to protect coral against heat stress.

#372. Margaret Hamilton obituary: computer scientist who pioneered software engineering and helped us get to the Moon

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Maia Weinstock is deputy editorial director at MIT News, a lecturer on the history of women in STEM at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, and an author.

Margaret Hamilton — a titan of computer science — has died aged 90. She is best known for her work in developing the software for NASA’s Apollo project, which landed the first humans on the Moon.

Hamilton’s influence on the field of computing was vast. A specialist in systems engineering and human–computer interaction, she helped to develop pioneering techniques for reliable computer programming and is often credited with coining the term ‘software engineering’. Her work on logical procedures and systems that worked even in the presence of errors helped to give software development comparable stature to the development of computer hardware.

The Moon belongs to all of us — not just countries that can afford to reach it

The Moon belongs to all of us — not just countries that can afford to reach it

In addition to her work on Apollo at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, Hamilton ventured out on her own as a software entrepreneur, founding companies that specialized in programming languages and systems used in numerous fields, from space and defence to energy, communications and more.

Hamilton was born Margaret Heafield in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936. Her parents later moved the family to Michigan and encouraged her to explore her considerable talents in both technical and humanities subjects. She began undergraduate studies at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor before transferring to Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, where she completed a bachelor of arts in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958.

The next year, Hamilton moved with her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, to Boston, Massachusetts. The two had met at Earlham — he a chemist and the student-body president; she a maths whiz and the homecoming queen, according to their daughter, Lauren. Forgoing her original plan to attend graduate school, Margaret began working with Edward Lorenz, the founder of modern chaos theory — in which tiny variations in large systems can cause major unpredictable changes — in the MIT meteorology department, while James attended law school. With no previous programming experience, Hamilton helped to develop weather-prediction software using the LGP-30, a 31-bit computer with a 4,096-word memory.

In 1961, by then a working mother, Hamilton moved to a new project at the MIT Lincoln Laboratory: coding for the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE), a defence system being developed to ward off air attacks by the Soviet Union. Her stellar work on SAGE paid off. When she heard a few years later that a lab on MIT’s main campus was recruiting programmers to send men to the Moon, her application was swiftly advanced. She became the first programmer hired for the Apollo project at MIT, at a time when women made up just a tiny fraction of the workforce in US science and engineering. Although the vast majority of NASA’s Apollo project team was male, Hamilton was joined by a number of women who made key contributions in maths, coding, engineering and more.

First photos from Artemis II: see stunning ‘Earthset’ and more

First photos from Artemis II: see stunning ‘Earthset’ and more

Hamilton was tapped to head the team tasked with writing and testing software for the Apollo Guidance Computer. The space race was in full swing, and engineers and programmers at the MIT Instrumentation Lab were under high pressure to achieve what had only ever been dreamt of before, both quickly and safely. Hamilton stated in subsequent years that “there was no choice but to be pioneers”.

#373. ArXiv versus AI slop: will capping preprint submissions work?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dalmeet Singh Chawla is a freelance science journalist based in London.

Some preprint servers report being flooded with submissions.Credit: Michael Szebor/Nature

In a bid to tackle the deluge of manuscripts it now receives, the preprint server arXiv has announced a cap of two papers per month for each submitting researcher, which began on 1 October.

The move follows a steep rise in submissions driven mainly by the slop generated by artificial-intelligence tools, says Steinn Sigurðsson, an astrophysicist at Pennsylvania State University in University Park and scientific director of arXiv. In September, 40,000 preprints were uploaded to arXiv, up from about 30,000 between March and July.

The cap is the latest measure introduced by arXiv to prevent its nearly 300 voluntary moderators from being completely overwhelmed by submissions, says Sigurðsson. They are now collectively checking about 1,000 manuscripts per day. This step is “holding up too many legitimate papers,” Sigurðsson says, noting that nearly 4,000 submissions are currently waiting to be posted on the site.

Some see the limit as entirely reasonable. Siddhesh Zādéy, an epidemiologist at Columbia University in New York City, says that it is not “stunting anyone's productivity”, because posting two preprint articles per month already requires a substantial amount of work.

Surge in fake citations uncovered by audit of 2.5 million biomedical-science papers

Surge in fake citations uncovered by audit of 2.5 million biomedical-science papers

Others think that arXiv’s new policy should be stricter. Victor Galitski, a theoretical physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park, says that the limit can be circumvented by co-authors taking turns to submit studies.

Another preprint server, the social-sciences repository SocArXiv, now also restricts submissions to one article per author per week. “Sometimes there are good reasons to upload three papers at once, such as dissertation chapters,” notes Philip Cohen, a sociologist and demographer at the University of Maryland, who is director of SocArXiv. But most of the time, several submissions in rapid succession are “a good tip-off for AI slop”, he says.

Other venues are dealing with a rapid surge in submissions, and some major AI conferences and journals have turned to similar submission quotas.

Some say that the issue of AI slop can’t be solved by rejecting more articles. “If arXiv turns those papers away, they’ll simply go somewhere else and become someone else’s problem,” says Natalie Khalil, the founder of Reviewer3, a platform run from San Francisco, California, which uses AI to help researchers conduct peer review.

#374. Catalytic transfer of carbon atoms enables spirofusion of C–C σ-bonds

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Spirocyclic frameworks, polycyclic structures in which two rings share a single carbon atom, constitute key structural motifs across diverse areas, including optoelectronic and hole-transporting materials1–3, ligand design for coordination complexes4–6, and numerous natural products7. In a spiro skeleton, the two molecular units adopt an orthogonal arrangement, generating a rigid three-dimensional (3D) architecture. Introducing a single carbon atom to join two components to form the spiro centre therefore represents a direct strategy for constructing such frameworks. Previous carbon-atom-transfer approaches have largely relied on π-bond reactivity, whereas controlled insertion of a carbon atom into C–C σ-bonds remains challenging8–11. Here we report a rhodium-catalysed spiro-carbon-atom insertion reaction that converts biphenylene substrates into spirocyclic structures through sequential C–C bond activation. Using N-isocyanoiminophosphorane (PINC)12–14 as an atomic carbon equivalent, the reaction forms four new C–C bonds at a spiro centre. The transformation enables both homo- and cross-spirofusion of biphenylenes and can be extended to reactions combining σ- and π-bond activation. These results establish a catalytic strategy for constructing structurally complex spirocyclic frameworks through C–C σ-bond activation, with a single carbon atom serving as a central linchpin.

Butterfly wing patterns in flight create powerful illusory motion cues Butterflies are incredibly evasive insects, with no predators that specialize in hunting them as they fly. Why this is has been a bit of a mystery, but now new research suggests that the patterns on their wings create optical illusions to mislead predators. This finding not only explains butterflies nimble dodging but may also help researchers understand why many animals have stripes and patterns.

#380. Becoming real

Dadui Yao is a comparative literature professor at Hainan University, a Harvard visiting scholar and a recently selected Humboldt Fellow with an interest in the intersection of science and philosophy.

After they had enclosed the humans, they did not make the wall very high.

“Why not build it higher?” the child asked.

“High walls are for those who want to escape,” the old man said. “We don’t.”

The child sat on the threshold and stared at the pale line in the distance. Beyond the wall, the light never went out. It looked like another sky, one that had forgotten how to sleep.

“No people coughing through winter. No clocks losing time. No old men who forget names,” the old man said. “And no peaches that will rot by tomorrow.”

The child thought about that. “That sounds good.”

The old man did not answer. He broke the peach in his hands. Juice ran through his fingers, and the air filled at once with sweetness. At the edges, the flesh had already begun to brown, as though dusk had touched it.

“Why do things smell better when they’re about to go bad?”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

That was when the figure appeared. It came monthly to the village entrance. It had the shape and voice of a person, but was simply too complete — symmetrical, unmarred and terrifyingly still.

The child made a face. “You always get those two words mixed up.”

The figure fell quiet, then turned to the old man. “The knife-grinder died yesterday. I saw him three days ago, sharpening an old blade. If he knew he was ending, why bother with a tool he would never use again?”

“Did you come to ask about the grinder, or yourself?” the old man asked.

A brittle leaf drifted onto the figure’s shoulder. It lifted it, studying it like a rare manuscript. “We can manufacture this. The fractals, the insect marks. But we cannot create this specific instance of loss.”

“Because it was not made; it was lived,” the old man said. “What you are looking at is time. Not the time of your servers, but the kind that settles onto things and makes them worn and unique. In your world, nothing is ever ‘now’ because everything is forever.”

“There is a sickness where I come from,” the figure said. “More of us are refusing back-ups. Some deliberately preserve cracks in their chassis. They are seeking something called The Single-Life Accord.”

“To become nonrepeatable?” the old man asked.

Silence fell. A distant cough, the creak of a laundry line. Sounds of a world constantly wearing itself out.

“We thought preservation was victory,” the figure said. “But what is preserved does not come closer to being alive. It becomes only an exhibit. We have no fate.”

“Fate means reaching for a thing knowing it will end,” the old man said. “Living this hour carefully because it can never be retrieved from a cloud server. You have infinity. But without a frame, a painting is just an endless smear of colour.”

The child tossed his peach pit. “Without school, vacation wouldn’t be fun.”

The figure looked at the child. “But death brings terror. It brings the cessation of the ‘I’.”

“Of course,” the old man said. “That fear is the price of the ticket. Without the risk of losing yourself, you never truly possessed yourself.”

The light beyond the wall flared sharply. The figure straightened. “The Accord has been ratified. The system will allow the transition for those who confirm.”

“I am terrified,” the figure said. “Which is how I know I am moving in the right direction.”

#382. Will my lack of country-specific grants limit my chances of employment abroad?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

After more than 20 years of academic research, supervision and contributions to engineering technology in Latin America, I’ve been pursuing faculty positions at universities in North America and Europe. The advertised positions match my expertise closely, but my applications have been consistently unsuccessful.

The reason only became clear through a candid exchange with a colleague who had served on a selection committee for one such position. My scientific qualifications, he noted, were competitive. The factor that stopped the committee choosing me was that I hadn’t obtained grant funding from the national research system of the country I wanted to move to.

This is a problem with how funding is structured in most research-intensive countries. Grant mechanisms are often national and tied to taxpayer-supported programmes that do not enable researchers based abroad to be awarded principal-investigator status. International collaboration is actively encouraged in research, but international leadership of funded projects is another matter entirely. The practical consequence is that no amount of scientific output or achievement by an individual can compensate for this gap.

Is there anything that an applicant can do to combat this bias? — An excluded international scholar

César Marín, an ecologist at Santo Tomás University in Santiago, Chile, agrees with you. “Demonstrating experience and success on getting national funds seem to be the main hiring criteria in many countries — regardless of strong publication and supervision record,” he affirms.

In general, experience of a local system “can be an implicit metric in academia”, notes Laura Ación, co-executive director of MetaDocencia, a capacity-building organization for researchers from Spanish-speaking communities. MetaDocencia’s research on the career paths of Latin American scientists1 suggests that, as Ación says, “a lack of competitiveness for European or US funding constitutes a structural disadvantage”.

This can take a toll on academic jobseekers. “I believe that, as a foreigner, I am behind the competition for many reasons,” explains Renan Lyra, a Brazilian psychology researcher who is currently searching for positions in the United Kingdom. He suspects that one of the reasons is that researchers doing UK degrees are trained to put together domestic grant applications, and are more likely to be involved in such applications with senior researchers. Experience in bringing in money is what hiring organizations really care about, Lyra thinks.

Even researchers moving between well-resourced systems notice the gap between them. Caroline Lynn Kamerlin started her independent career in Sweden before moving to the United States as a professor. She’s now a computational chemist at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta.

During the transition, she encountered what you describe: “When US hiring committees saw my CV, the biggest thing they saw was that I had no US funding, and the fact that I had clearly been able to get funding from several sources in Europe was not something they considered.”

One reason for hiring managers’ funding bias might be that they are familiar with certain grants, which come with a kind of brand recognition that is associated with high quality. But this can be problematic if the assumption is “that global-south grant processes are not as strict as those from the global north”, Marín comments. “On my own experience of reviewing grants for European and Latin American countries, this is not always the case.”

As you identify, this is a structural problem, so there are limits to what a single person can do. Still, there are ways for individuals to increase their chances of being hired, even in an unjust system.

One way of boosting your grant track record is by forming international collaborations. But as you note, collaboration doesn’t necessarily build to leadership. And in the United States, restrictions on grants involving foreign researchers are making international collaborations of all types more challenging.

How a spreadsheet helped me to land my dream job

How a spreadsheet helped me to land my dream job

Marco Seeber, a science-policy researcher at the University of Agder in Kristiansand, Norway, says you shouldn’t underestimate the importance of trust and personal connections in the systems you’re trying to break into. The first stage could be attending and presenting at conferences, and using that as a jumping-off point for collaboration.

“I cannot emphasize strongly enough how vital it is to cultivate a diverse, robust network and community throughout a scientific career,” Ación adds. This should be reciprocal, not transactional. For instance, it can include service to scientific associations. That kind of network-building could eventually pave the way for entry into another country’s research system.

Even if you aren’t successful in getting a grant on which you’re a principal investigator (PI) in the desired country, that might not be a deal-breaker. “I think being a PI on international grants is always helpful, but it’s not absolutely necessary, just because there are so few international grants and those that exist are incredibly competitive,” Kamerlin says. If it’s still important to you to be a PI, it’s possible that the other collaborators in your consortium would be happy to have that administrative burden taken off their hands, and for you to take on the leadership role.

Some funding calls are geared towards foreign researchers of different levels, which could help you to develop a track record in the research system you’re interested in. Kamerlin highlights the European Research Council (ERC) funding schemes. “The ERC specifically wants to attract and retain the best talent in Europe, and actively encourages non-Europeans to apply to move to Europe,” she says. Admittedly, success rates are low. ERC starting grants, which are geared towards early-career researchers and can come with extra funding for researchers moving to the European Union, had a success rate of about 12% in 2025.

More broadly, in 2025, the European Commission kicked off the Choose Europe initiative to attract researchers to the EU. Although one impetus was to draw in researchers from the United States who are disillusioned with the cuts to science funding there, in principle, applicants can be of any nationality.

#383. A guide to the Nature Index

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The Nature Index is a database of author affiliations and institutional relationships. The index tracks contributions to research articles published in high-quality natural-science and health-science journals, chosen based on reputation by an independent group of researchers.

The Nature Index provides absolute and fractional counts of article publication at the institutional and national level and, as such, is an indicator of global high-quality research output and collaboration. Data in the Nature Index are updated regularly, with the most recent 12 months made available under a Creative Commons licence at natureindex.com. The database is compiled by Nature Portfolio.

The Nature Index uses Count and Share to track research output. A country/territory or an institution is given a Count of 1 for each article that has at least one author from that country/territory or institution. This is the case regardless of the number of authors an article has, and it means that the same article can contribute to the Count of multiple countries/territories or institutions.

To glean a country’s, territory’s, region’s or an institution’s contribution to an article, and to ensure that they are not counted more than once, the Nature Index uses Share, a fractional count that takes into account the share of authorship on each article. The total Share available per article is 1, which is shared among all authors under the assumption that each contributed equally. For instance, an article with 10 authors means that each author receives a Share of 0.1. For authors who are affiliated with more than one institution, the author’s Share is split equally between each institution. The total Share for an institution is calculated by summing the Share for individual affiliated authors. The process is similar for countries/territories, although complicated by the fact that some institutions have overseas labs that will be counted towards host country/territory totals.

Adjusted Share accounts for the annual variation in the total number of articles in the Nature Index journals. It is arrived at by calculating the percentage difference in the total number of articles in the Index in a given year relative to the number of articles in a base year and adjusting Share values to the base year levels.

The bilateral collaboration score (CS) between two institutions A+B is the sum of each of their Shares on the papers to which both have contributed. A bilateral collaboration can be between any two institutions or countries/territories co-authoring at least one article in the journals tracked by the Nature Index.

natureindex.com users can search for specific institutions or countries and generate their own reports, ordered by Count or Share.

#384. Nature Index reveals the four countries to watch in biomedical engineering

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Elliot Yates is an intern on the Nature Careers and Supplements team.

Biomedical-engineering research output has grown rapidly in the Nature Index. Between 2021 and 2025, the number of papers related to the field increased by 70%, a higher rate of increase than the growth of the database as a whole. This is also reflected by the subject’s proportion of all articles in the database, which rose from 2.4% to 2.7%. Within this expansion, however, the field’s research landscape has also shifted, with countries’ relative contributions reflecting changing patterns of international collaboration and research specialization.

The clearest trend is that between 2021 and 2025, biomedical-engineering research — in keeping with many other disciplines — moved decisively towards the leading nation, China. The country’s contribution to global output rose from 28.9% to 50.9%, while the field went from representing 2.8% of its total Nature Index output in 2021 to 3.5% in 2025.

The United States and Germany retained second and third place, respectively, throughout the period, but their focus on the field remained relatively static at around 2.3% to 2.5% of all output.

Here, we focus on four other countries among the leading ten in 2025 whose performance in biomedical engineering reveals more nuanced trends.

South Korea seems to have held a top-five position by developing and maintaining a strong specialization in the subject; Switzerland stands out for drawing on private-sector research and international collaboration to remain a leading European centre; Canada is one of the field’s fastest-rising countries; and the Netherlands has recorded more modest growth but retains a highly international network.

Leading university in biomedical engineering, 2021–25: Yonsei University

Most cited paper, 2021–25: ‘Superstrong, superstiff, and conductive alginate hydrogels’ (2022)1

South Korea is an outlier among the leading nations in biomedical engineering in the Nature Index. Its research is unusually concentrated in the field, with 4.8% of its overall database output from 2021 to 2025 being in the subject, the highest percentage among the leading 25 countries. South Korea is also relatively less reliant on international collaboration compared with the three other countries featured in this article, with a little over half its papers in 2021–25 co-authored by researchers outside the country.

This clear specialization in biomedical engineering has helped South Korea to cement itself as one of the top-five contributors to the field, consistently ranking fourth in Share, a position that is three places higher than its overall ranking in the Nature Index. It was also the third-fastest growing nation by increase in Share in biomedical engineering between 2021 and 2025.

The country’s most cited paper in the field over the period, produced by a group from Sungkyunkwan University in Seoul and published in Nature Communications1 in 2022, explains the development of an exceptionally strong and electrically conductive seaweed-derived hydrogel. Although the paper gained almost 450 citations up to July 2026, it was not as highly cited as the top papers from the three other countries featured here. There might be multiple reasons for this, but one possible factor might be that the paper was authored solely by researchers from one institution, whereas the other research articles featured authors based in a mix of different institutions and locations.

Leading university in biomedical engineering, 2021–25: University of Toronto

Most cited paper, 2021–25: ‘A proximity-dependent biotinylation map of a human cell’ (2021)2

Canada’s Share in biomedical engineering rose by almost 60% between 2021 and 2025, making it the country with the second-largest growth in output over the period among the leading ten nations, after China. Most of Canada’s growth occurred between 2021 and 2022, when its Share rose by 51% in one year alone. Part of this rise might have been due to the addition of health-sciences journals to the database in 2022. However, these new journals grew the Nature Index overall by 13%, suggesting that Canada still excelled that year in biomedical engineering.

Unlike South Korea, however, Canada’s growth is unlikely to be related to heavy specialization: biomedical engineering was a relatively small focus of Canada’s entire output in the Nature Index, at about 2.3% of overall Share from 2021 to 2025.

Canada’s broader growth coincides with a major funding push in the life sciences that was designed to address a decline in the country’s research and biomanufacturing capacity. The decline was identified by the federal government as a reason why it was unable to produce its own COVID-19 vaccine. The government’s 2021 budget allocated Can$2.2 billion (US$1.6 billion) to a Biomanufacturing and Life Science Strategy, with money going to a mix of life-sciences and biomanufacturing companies, research institutes and universities over seven years.

Canada’s most-cited biomedical-engineering paper2 in the Nature Index from 2021 to 2025 was produced by researchers based at the Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute in Ontario, the University of Toronto and McGill University, in Montreal. Published in Nature in 2021, the researchers showed how they constructed a detailed map of a human cell by placing molecular labels throughout the cell.

Leading university in biomedical engineering, 2021–25: Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich

Most cited paper, 2021–25: ‘Tissue geometry drives deterministic organoid patterning’ (2022)3

Switzerland’s biomedical-engineering Share rose from 41.5 to 49.2 between 2021 and 2025, a gain of 19%. Although its growth was modest, contributions from private-sector research have arguably helped Switzerland to maintain a spot in the top 10 each year.

From 2021 to 2025, corporate organizations were responsible for 7.2% of the country’s biomedical engineering output in the Nature Index, the highest proportion among the leading ten nations. This fits a wider pattern: Switzerland’s gross domestic expenditure on R&D stood at 3.2% of GDP in 2023, with business sector R&D alone accounting for 2.2%, well above the EU average of 1.5% — although still below South Korea’s 3.9% — according to Eurostat.

#385. Is this idea from AI or humans? A detector claims it can tell

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Researchers have developed a detector that aims to tell the difference between ideas made by humans and those conjured by artificial intelligence.

Used with care, IdeaLens could help to gauge the extent of AI use in submissions to conferences and journals, which have become “overwhelmed” with artificially generated content, says Rishanth Rajendhran, a computer scientist at the University of Maryland in College Park and co-author of the preprint1 describing IdeaLens.

Using AI to write scientific papers is becoming increasingly acceptable, but only “as long as the core idea” is the researcher’s own, he says.

Is it OK for AI to write science papers? Nature survey shows researchers are split

Is it OK for AI to write science papers? Nature survey shows researchers are split

The detector works by analysing the ‘outline’ of a work rather than the text itself. First, it distils a text — for example, a scientific paper — into an outline, stripping it of style. Then it looks for patterns that are characteristic of either AI- or human-generated ideas, such as those in arguments and flow.

The detector was able to spot AI-derived ideas 91% of the time. It “surprised me that they can detect AI-written arguments” from just the outlines, says Nikhil Garg, a computer scientist at Cornell Tech in New York City, who calls the detector impressive.

Garg cautions that because the tool is fallible, it should not be used to judge the human authenticity of individual cases, and that the detector might become inaccurate when used on types of data that are different from those used in training. “An AI ‘tell’ in one domain may simply be good human writing in another,” he says.

The group’s earlier work2 found that human-written stories differ structurally from those written by AI and that different chatbots tend to use the same arguments when writing essays. Together, this suggested that it might be possible to make a detector for AI ideas, says Rajendhran.

#388. Daily briefing: China’s extraordinary rise in science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Illustration: Jasiek Krzysztofiak. Photos: Qilai Shen/Bloomberg/Getty; Shawn Thew/EPA/Bloomberg/Getty; AFP via Getty; Inst. Plasma Physics at Hefei Insts of Phys. Sci., Chinese Academy of Sciences; S. L. Chen et al./Sci. Rep. (CC BY 4.0); VCG via Getty(2)

In less than 50 years, China has gone from having almost no scientific presence on the global stage to a scientific powerhouse that is on course to lead the world in research and development. But before that happens, China will have to deal with some systemic concerns: a widespread scientific misconduct problem, questions about regulations and ethics in cutting-edge biomedical research and an academic culture that researchers say makes it hard for individuals to pursue long-term, curiosity-based projects.

Artificial-intelligence graduates in China are increasingly choosing to stay instead of pursuing opportunities abroad, a move that could help the country catch up to the United States in AI research. China-based researchers now dominate global AI-related publications, and the rise of firms such as DeepSeek and MoonshotAI has proven the capability of Chinese AI models. Competition for jobs is fierce and the pressure to publish is intense. But if China can retain its top talent, it’s possible that it could become the world leader in AI by the end of the decade.

After huge successes with GLP-1 obesity drugs, several pharmaceutical companies are turning their efforts to developing similar drugs to treat brain disorders. For example, pharma giant Eli Lilly has presented early clinical trial results of a compound related to tirzepatide for treatment of alcohol use disorder. And biotech company Kariya Pharmaceuticals has done the same for a GLP-1-like compound for Parkinson’s disease. But it’s not clear how exactly GLP-1 drugs might curb addiction, and past attempts to treat Parkinson’s with GLP-1 have failed.

Archaeologists say that amphorae and other artefacts discovered off the Mediterranean coast of Turkey are from the oldest shipwreck ever found. The team says that, on the basis of the pottery, the ship sailed during the Early Bronze Age, between 4,700 and 4,400 years ago. And the pots still had some goo inside. “I looked inside and nearly fainted,” says archaeologist Karin Sowada. “It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins.”

Reference: Journal of Maritime Archaeology paper & Journal of Maritime Archaeology paper

Photographer James Lewin used an infrared camera to render the harsh sunlight at a watering hole in Kenya into dreamy black and white. It won the ‘Animals in their Environment’ category of Wildlife Photographer of the Year, developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London. (BBC | 10 min read) (James Lewin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

Birds that are moved, or bred in captivity, for conservation reasons might not have the chance to learn from their elders. But research suggests it is possible to teach birds lost songs. For example, in Argentina, researchers taught rufous-collared sparrows (Zonotrichia capensis) songs from hand-drawn annotations made in the 1960s. Someday, songs recorded by hobbyist birders could help restore lost aural diversity, says physicist Gabriel Mindlin, who co-authored the sparrow study. “One day we’ll be grateful to have all those records,” he says.

Reference: Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena paper & Scientific Reports paper

Whistleblowers who report misconduct at universities need greater protections against retaliation, and any resulting investigations should be handled by independent experts, argues astrophysicist N. Wyn Evans. “Challenge the institution, and you might spend years paying the personal, professional and financial price,” writes Evans, who experienced just such a drawn-out saga at Cambridge University’s Institute of Astronomy.

The bright and intricate patterns on butterflies might serve to create visual illusions that baffle birds — making it easier for the insects to avoid capture. By analysing slow-motion videos of butterflies taking off, researchers found that the insects’ markings can create the appearance of movement in one direction, when in fact they’re going the other.

Magdalena Skipper, the editor-in-chief of Nature, joined the editors-in-chief of Science and Cell to discuss disclosure and peer review in the age of artificial intelligence. (Broad Institute | 1 hour 26 min video — or jump straight to that bit)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03322-6

Today my hat’s off to NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover, which has officially broken the distance record on the Red Planet. It has driven 45.22 kilometres (28 miles) in less than six years — surpassing the mileage that took Opportunity nearly 15 years. “The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving,” says project manager Steven Lee. “We’ve blown well past that” — and there should be many more to come.

Let me know your favourite long drive, cycle or hike — plus any other feedback on this newsletter — at briefing@nature.com.

Flora Graham, chief editor, Nature Briefing
