(a) IPF maps and (b) band contrast (BC) maps of Nb45Ta25Ti15Hf15 showing a microstructure consisting of equiaxed grains ~259 μm in diameter. Some grains are not fully recrystallized because they contain sub-grain boundaries of partially recrystallized kink bands formed during rolling. (c) IPF maps and (d) BC maps of Nb70Ti30 showing the heterogeneous microstructure consisting of smaller, fully recrystallized grains ~51 μm in diameter and larger grains containing partially recrystallized kink bands and rotational twins. (E) and (F) show EDX maps indicating homogeneous composition.

(a) R-curves showing that the fracture toughness from 298 K to 20 K gradually decreases. (b) Representative stress-strain curves across the same set of temperatures show a gradual reduction in ductility as well as twinning-induced stress drops at temperatures at and below 77 K. (c) Instantaneous strain-hardening curves demonstrate similar strain-hardening behavior as Nb45Ta25Ti15Hf15: hardening becomes less sustained at progressively decreasing temperatures as a result of twin activation at yielding.

The effect of stress-state is illustrated by the differences in fracture morphology observed between C(T) and uniaxial tensile samples. Whereas in C(T) specimens in (a) fracture occurs by crystallographic microvoids on grain boundaries, in tensile specimens in (b) it occurs by microvoid coalescence. This is further exemplified by IPF and BC EBSD maps that show profuse {112} < 111> twinning in (c) compact-tension and (d) tensile specimens, but with significantly more deformation by dislocation glide in tension in (d). The intergranular fracture can also be noted in (c), where the crack travels along the high-angle grain boundary between two large grains.

(a) Orientation maps of twins at 20 K taken from a 4D-STEM scan. (b) Corresponding virtual dark-field reconstructions of the same twins in (a) with the virtual dark-field detector highlighted in red. (c) TEM micrograph of twins encased by ω. The corresponding diffraction pattern of the \([\bar{1}13]\) bcc zone axis (ZA) shows significantly higher intensities from peaks shared by twins and ω (circled in blue) than those solely from ω. (d) Another instance of twinning at 20 K. Dislocations can be seen impinging on the twin boundaries. At 77 K, orientation maps reconstructed from 4D-STEM micrographs show two instances of twinning in (e) and (g) with corresponding virtual dark-field images reconstructed in (f) and (h).

(a) Shows twinning at the onset of yielding, which progressively gives way to deformation by dislocation glide in (d). (b)-(c) A simple Schmidt factor analysis of the microstructure shows that the twins can orient each lamella into directions with varying critical resolved shear stress for both a0/2{110} < 111> and a0/2{112} < 111> slip systems. While in a typical TWIP material, this would generate strain hardening, here dislocation glide is difficult and plastic deformation has already begun, so only dislocations with the lowest barriers to glide (those with the highest critical resolved shear stresses) will move, causing strain to localize in the material. Severe deformation in the region that necked and directly adjacent to the fracture surface can be seen in (e). Note that the kink band-like features in (d) are part of the original microstructure.

(a) Overview EBSD map of crack-tip deformation structure with kink bands boxed in (b), (c), and (d). Pole figure maps of the kink bands in the selected areas in (a) (that contain kink bands) show that all have <110> poles, indicating that they are formed by a0/2 < 111 > {112} edge dislocations. The bands have variable rotation: those in (b) 8–15°, those in (c) 5–17°, and those in (d) 10–22°. These kink bands can also have gradient boundaries, indicating imperfect edge dislocation alignment, and can be micrometer-scale in size, as shown in (b). (e)-(f) show TKD micrographs of twins impinging on fractured grain boundaries at the fracture surface. The twin in (e) has an unusual morphology characterized by branching.

(a) A plot of the HRR field at 20 K as a function of distance from the crack tip normalized by the crack-tip opening displacement, δ. These values are compared with twinning growth stresses and screw and edge glide stresses. As can be seen, the applied stress at the critical stress intensity exceeds the twinning stress across a critical microstructural length-scale - a single grain size. The same occurs at 77 K in (b), demonstrating that the crack-initiation toughness is insensitive to temperature. However, at 77 K, screw glide stresses are lower, which causes this mechanism to activate during crack growth when the stress intensity increases. (c)-(d) show the local equivalent plastic strain as a function of distance from the crack tip. In Nb70Ti30, fracture is strain-controlled because both twinning stresses and dislocation glide stresses are lower than the fracture stress across a critical microstructural length-scale.

(a) HAADF-STEM overview micrograph of a twin-grain boundary intersection site ahead of a crack tip. (b) Virtual dark-field 4D-STEM scans reconstructed from the circled diffraction disk indicated in (b) inset show that the deformation at the grain boundary is produced by twinning; a phase map in (c) reconstructed from a virtual detector (highlighted in red) placed over an ω diffraction disk that shows the hexagonal phase on twin boundaries. Unlike in Nb45Ta25Ti15Hf15, the dislocation density is significantly higher, indicating that chemical complexity can substantially increase barriers to dislocation glide and restrict crack-tip plasticity.

(a) Atom probe tomography (APT) of a grain boundary in this alloy shows an enrichment of group IV elements in a ~ 4 nm range around the grain boundary. An alloy composition plot in (b) shows that the Ti and Hf concentrations are ~42 at.%, compared with their background of 30 at.%. Additional EDS maps of a region where twins and omega impact a grain boundary (from Fig. 3) are shown in element maps in (c)- (f) and in an HAADF-STEM overview image in (g). A line profile composition shown in (g) is plotted in (h) and shows a ~ 4 nm range with slight enrichment of group IV elements and a depletion of group V elements.

#405. Parity-dependent coupling of molecular spin chains to a superconductor

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 658, pages 617–622 (2026) Cite this article

Collective behaviour in quantum materials can produce excitations carrying only a fraction of the quantum numbers of their constituents. A notable case occurs in chains of spin-1 units1, in which a topological gap protects the interior of the chain, whereas spin-1/2 states, half the spin of the units that form it, emerge at the ends2. In short chains, these fractional edge spins couple to each other and their topological protection makes them attractive for hybrid spin–superconductor devices. Whether such fractionalization survives the proximity of a superconducting condensate, however, remains an open question. Here we grow molecular Haldane chains of antiferromagnetically coupled spin-1 triangulene units on a proximitized Au(111)/Nb(110) surface and resolve a parity-dependent coupling of their spin-1/2 edge states to the superconductor by scanning tunnelling spectroscopy. Odd-length chains host Yu–Shiba–Rusinov (YSR) bound states inside the superconducting gap, originating from a global S = 1 ground state, whereas even-length chains form an S = 0 ground state decoupled from the superconductor. A two-site model attributes this alternation to the sign and strength of inter-edge interactions, independently confirmed by extra-gap spin excitations in tunnelling spectra. Many-body spin excitations of the S = 1 chain are also detected, decoupled from the superconductor by the much larger Haldane gap. The length-tunable coupling of the edge spins to superconductors opens a route towards molecular spin qubits based on π-conjugated carbon architectures.

Spectra on the chain termini show YSR peaks developing inside the dGSJ excitations. c, Bond-resolved current image of triangulene chain with four units (V = 8.5 mV, constant-height at RT ≈ 16 MΩ). d, Low-energy dI/dV spectra over the termini. a, Bond-resolved current STM image of the N = 14 chain. The insets show a zoomed image of the end triangulene unit n = 14 before and after applying a bias pulse over the marked C site. The pulse produces dehydrogenation of the targeted C site, after which the triangulene appears with characteristic orbital shape in the images (V = 5 mV). b, Differential conductance spectra on the end unit n = 1 before and after the dehydrogenation in a. The YSR peak of Extended Data Fig. 8 over the n = 1 triangulene shifts to a binding energy δEYSR = 0.36 meV when the opposite end is dehydrogenated (V = 5 mV, I = 500 pA). c, Differential conductance spectral map versus tip–sample resistance over the n = 1 triangulene unit. The YSR state shifts towards the gap edges and merges with dGSJ resonances as the tip approaches, indicating that the edge spin lies in the weak interaction regime (JK ≪ Δ; Supplementary Information section 5).

a, Constant-current STM image of a N = 8 chain before and after dehydrogenation of the lower triangulene end. b, Comparison of spectra on the top triangulene before and after the dehydrogenation in a. The passivation of the lower edge state leads to disappearance of ST features and the emergence of an in-gap YSR state. As shown in Supplementary Information section 4, the H atom removal removes intra-chain exchange correlations and results in a free-like edge spin on the opposite end.

a, STM image of the surface of a 25-monolayer Au(111) film, exhibiting the herringbone reconstruction. b, dI/dV spectra measured at 1.2 K, showing the characteristic onset of its surface state close to −0.5 V sample bias. This value is close to the surface state onset on bulk Au(111) substrates.

#406. Capillary-selective vasodilation through myosin inhibition halts ischaemic cascades

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

In acute myocardial infarction and acute kidney injury, capillary no-reflow denotes that capillary blood flow is still blocked despite successful arterial reperfusion. This is associated with substantially increased mortality and reinfarction risk; nevertheless, no targeted therapy exists so far1,2. Because capillary no-reflow is driven by smooth muscle myosin-mediated hypercontraction of capillary pericytes, we developed R(+)2501, a myosin-specific and capillary-selective vasodilator. In reperfused animal models of acute myocardial infarction and acute kidney injury, direct in vivo imaging showed that R(+)2501 rapidly restored capillary flow, an effect sustained even after rapid drug clearance. Ex vivo experiments confirmed reversal of pericyte constriction directly. Restoration of capillary blood flow, together with clearance of trapped neutrophils, linked resolution of capillary no-reflow to attenuation of an early driver of reperfusion injury. R(+)2501 enhanced capillary perfusion while preserving coronary autoregulation and systemic haemodynamics, and markedly improved survival during acute reperfusion. We further found that acute myocardial infarction induced renal capillary no-reflow, which was reversed by R(+)2501, suggesting that capillary no-reflow contributes to the pathophysiology of cardiorenal syndrome type I. These findings establish pericyte-targeted smooth muscle myosin inhibition as a therapeutic strategy to restore microvascular perfusion and halt the ischaemic cascade across organs, while defining a specific physiological role for capillaries and pericytes in circulatory regulation.

a-b, Kidney can tolerate only ~10 min of occlusion before significant CNR develops. Beyond this threshold, reperfusion did not restore RBC velocity or flux to pre-ischemic levels (green shadow lane) when RBC velocity and flux were measured 30 min after reperfusion start (n10,R = 60, n10,T = 90, n30,R = 40, n30,T = 27, n60,R = 84, n60,T = 34, n120,R = 60, n120,T = 79 capillaries, R means reperfusion, T means R(+)2501 treatment). c, Renal artery occlusion time dependence of RBC velocity (orange) and flux (purple) values after reperfusion normalized to the healthy blood flow parameters, and representation of the non-moving RBC fractions (pink) as a function of occlusion-time (pink). Steep occlusion time dependence suggests that regenerative potentials are maintained only for a very limited time (cca. 10 min of occlusion) and beyond a threshold of 20–30 min the capillary flow deficit becomes refractory to reperfusion alone. Complete blockage of capillaries without R(+)2501 treatment becomes dominant after 60 min of occlusion, indicating that pericytes remain completely constricted and refractory to reperfusion alone (i.e. to restoration of large-artery flow). Kinetics of RBC velocity (d) and flux (e) in intravenous bolus 5 mg/kg R(+)2501 treated renal capillaries following 10, 30, 60 and 120 min of occlusion. Gray line indicates the reperfusion level of 60-minute non-treated capillaries as a reference. In all cases, both RBC velocity and flux increased back to the healthy range (green shadow lane) within 6 min of treatment. Both velocity and flux parameters increased above the healthy range in an occlusion time-dependent manner, suggesting that R(+)2501 is capable of opening the capillaries to a greater extent than the healthy regulated range (n10min = 3 animals, n30min = 2 animals, n60min = 3 animals, n120min = 3 animals). Thus, we also tested the effect of intravenous bolus 5 mg/kg R(+)2501 on the RBC velocity (f) and flux (g) of healthy animals and confirmed that R(+)2501 is capable of full relaxation of capillaries, increasing capillary blood flow to a higher than baseline level (nHealthy = 2, n5 = 2 animals). This confirms that this effect is not RAO-dependent but an inherent feature of the system, confirming that our effect is on the capillary pericytes maintaining regulated baseline capillary blood flow level by SMM-mediated contraction. h, Survival rate of animals after AKI of bilateral-90 min-RAO-operated rats (nV = 32, n5 = 33, n10 = 33, n20 = 3 animals). i, Addition of 100 mg/kg Vitamin C (n = 3 animals), 100 mg/kg allopurinol (n = 3 animals) or 10 mg/kg carprofen (Rimadyl) (n = 3 animals) into the 10 mg/kg R(+)2501 (n = 33 animals) treatment solution did not increase the survival rate of the bilateral-90 min-RAO-operated rats over the 10 mg/kg R(+)2501 treatment baseline. Concentration of creatinine and carbamide in blood plasma of RAO operated rats 24 h after occlusion (j), and calculated kidney function (eGFR) (k) as a function of renal artery occlusion time in RAO operated rats 24 h after occlusion (n0,15,30,120min = 3, n60min = 9, n90min = 6, n240min = 2 animals). Both carbamide and creatinine levels showed large variance among the animals resulting in high standard error of the calculated eGFR between 60-90-minute occlusion times. eGFR levels showed similar behavior as RBC velocity and flux (c.f. Extended Data Fig. 4c) suggesting that capillary blood flow and kidney functions are two closely interrelated parameters. This close correlation between capillary blood flow level and kidney function demonstrates that efficient capillary relaxation can directly influence long-term kidney functions.

In vivo micronucleus test using intravenous bolus 10 and 100 mg/kg doses showed that R(+)2501 does not induce chromosome aberrations neither in blood (a) nor in the bone marrow (b) even at extremely high doses (nVehicle = 6, nPos = 6, n10mg/kg = 6, n100mg/kg = 6 animals). c, Hierarchy of gates applied during the flow cytometric analysis of blood and bone marrow samples collected during the in vivo micronucleus test (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b) is demonstrated on the example of a bone marrow sample. Gates are shown as rectangles or ellipses draw around the gated subpopulation of events. Arrows mark hierarchical relationships between the subpopulations. Ames reverse mutagenicity test using TA98 (d) (n2501-SO4 Xtreme 10% = 2, n2501-SO4 Xtreme 30% = 1, n2501 humS9 = 2, n2501-SO4 humS9 = 2, n2501 Xtreme = 1, n2501-SO4-S9 = 1 sample(s)) and TA100 (e) (n2501-SO4 Xtreme 10% = 1, n2501-SO4 Xtreme 30% = 1, n2501-SO4-S9 = 1 sample) S.typhimurium strains shows that R(+)2501 does not induce frameshift and base-substitution mutations, respectively, in the absence and presence of human liver S9 fractions from different sources including the 200-donor, mixed-gender extreme-pool liver S9 fraction.

This file contains further methodological details, including structural analysis of the R(+)2501 and S(−)2501 crystal structures, characterization of the AKI rat model, and safety pharmacology studies supporting the findings of the main manuscript. This file also contains Supplementary Table 1.

The R(+)2501 binding site undergoes significant conformational changes during the myosin cycle. Trajectories were obtained using ChimeraX ‘morph’ command with different Myo2 structures as starting points: (1) Rigor (PDB 6BIH); (2) Smm2 actin-bound Strong-ADP (PDB 8SYF); (3) Post-rigor (PDB 3I5F); and (4) PPS (S(−)2501-bound, PDB 29ZZ). In all sequences, the R(+)2501-bound recovery stroke intermediate (PDB 29ZY) was used as the end-point structure. For simplification, the side chains of only a few key residues of the interface are shown.

Representative time-lapse fluorescence video of a capillary segment ensheathed by a pericyte. Capillaries were labelled with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated WGA, and pericytes were visualized in transgenic NG2-DsRed BAC mice, in which they exhibit red fluorescence enabling unambiguous identification. Application of ET-1 elicits a rapid and marked pericyte contraction, accompanied by constriction of the capillary lumen. Subsequent addition of compound R(+)2501 induces an immediate relaxation of the pericyte, restoring capillary diameter and flow. These observations also support a direct, pericyte-specific action of R(+)2501.

Acute effect of R(+)2501 after 60 min of renal ischaemia. Within 10 s of intravenous injection, R(+)2501 dilates the peritubular renal capillaries and restores healthy perfusion to the pre-ischemic state (video speed 7 fps). The apparent streaks observed under normal flow conditions arise from the interaction between rapid RBC movement and raster scanning during image acquisition, which can elongate fluorescent signals within a single frame. As RBC velocity decreases during ischaemia and early reperfusion, individual cells become clearly resolved within the vessel lumen, eliminating this apparent streaking artefact.

#407. Evaluating space-based methane detection through a one-year blind test

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 658, pages 673–681 (2026) Cite this article

Space-based remote sensing allows detection and monitoring of large, concentrated methane sources worldwide1. However, independent evaluation of instruments and algorithms is limited, and new satellites and artificial intelligence techniques have not been tested under controlled, single-blind conditions2. Here we conduct a year-long, single-blind test involving 746 events: 481 methane releases of 9.5–1,183.7 kg h−1 and 265 blank controls. We released metered methane quantities in Arizona, USA, coinciding with overpasses from 12 government, commercial and non-profit satellites. Fifteen analysis teams from nine countries generated more than 2,250 estimates, making this, to our knowledge, the largest controlled test so far and one of the first evaluations of the instruments EMIT, Tanager-1 (Carbon Mapper) and GHOSt. Performance is heterogeneous: ‘built-for-purpose’ instruments designed to target methane demonstrate excellent detection performance (92–100% true positive rate, 0–11% false positive rate) and quantification accuracy (slope 0.83–1.00, 44% mean absolute percentage error). Instruments repurposed for methane sensing perform more variably (detection rates 62–88%, 46% mean absolute percentage error); still, many demonstrate significant skill. Broad land scanners detect poorly at tested rates but have consistent global coverage and historical archives, motivating additional work. Artificial intelligence-based methods show promise, but caution is warranted; 79% of false positives emerge from these methods. Ground-measured cloud cover >20% degraded performance across systems, raising concerns for use in some locations. Our findings show that satellite-based measurements can achieve accurate detection and quantification of methane point sources when the source location is approximately known.

#408. De novo design of cysteine proteases

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Despite advances in de novo enzyme design, success has been largely limited to low-energy-barrier model reactions. Amide bonds such as those linking amino acids along the peptide backbone are stable for hundreds of years in neutral aqueous solution because of the high energy barrier to hydrolysis1. Here we describe the de novo design of enzymes that use an activated cysteine nucleophile to hydrolyse the polypeptide backbone in a sequence-dependent manner, with a success rate of 13/69 = 19% and rate enhancements over the background reaction (kcat/kuncat) of up to 3 × 107. The designed proteases have folds that are very different from proteases in nature (TM score < 0.50), and six crystal structures are very close to the design models (Cα root mean squared deviation of <1.2 Å), highlighting the capacity for generalization and the accuracy of the design methodology. Experimental and computational analyses suggest that the remaining gap in activity to the most active native cysteine proteases arises from imperfections in active-site preorganization and substrate positioning. The designed proteases efficiently cleave their targets in mammalian cells, opening the door to a wide range of synthetic biology applications.

#409. Computational design of metalloproteases

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

De novo design of enzymes that cleave amide bonds represents a major challenge1,2. Here we use RFdiffusion methods3,4 to de novo design proteins with water-activating zinc-based active sites adjacent to a peptide substrate binding pocket. Of 135 designs tested, 36% catalyse cleavage of their cognate peptide substrates at the targeted scissile bond. The best design accelerates peptide-bond hydrolysis by more than 108-fold relative to the uncatalysed reaction; four substitutions increase this acceleration to more than 1010-fold by improving active-site preorganization5. We use this approach to design metalloproteases that selectively cleave the human disease-associated proteins TDP-43, amyloid-β and serum amyloid A, with rate enhancements of up to 109-fold. We further design caged cytokines and receptor antagonists that are selectively activated by the designed proteases, enabling bioorthogonal control of cell state. Thus, de novo design can yield highly active, programmable proteases with applications in therapeutics, biotechnology and bioremediation.

The generation process involves one round of initial motif-scaffolded backbone generation, followed by sequence design and AF3 filtering, two rounds of partial diffusion refinement, followed by sequence design and AF3 filtering and one round of iteration between sequence design and AF3 filtering. See Supplementary Methods for all details of the computational pipeline.

a, The cis construct used for the screen of functional active sites. b, The substrate chain of the trans constructs used for the screen of active proteases. c, The protease chain of the trans constructs used for the screen of active proteases. d, Substrate construct with an N terminal sfGFP and a C terminal mScarlet used in the validation and characterization of active designs.

a, The heatmap pattern for experimental specificity shown in Fig. 4a, where the diagonal elements and the elements in the last row are highlighted, is observed with multiple computational metrics from AF3 predictions of the [Zn+2].O ES complex, plotted in the same heatmap format as Fig. 4a. b, Correlation between experimentally measured normalized digested fraction and computational metrics. High chain C (Zn(II) ion) pLDDT, high complex pLDDT, high iptm, low mean interface PAE and low minimum interface PAE all are predictive of high cross reactivity.

a, Apo crystal structure of Zn5 (red) superimposed with the design model (grey) and zoomed in view of the active site. b, Crystal structure of Zn5 E75Q-Zn(II) complex (red) superimposed with the design model (grey) and zoomed in view of the active site. c, Crystal structure of apo TDPr3 E45Q (green) superimposed with the design model (grey) and zoomed in view of the active site. d, Crystal structure of Zn48 E75Q-Zn(II) complex (red) superimposed with the design model (grey) and zoomed in view of the active site.

a, Design model of Zn45 and the substrate of S_ZnO36 showing 21 residue positions chosen for single site saturation in sticks in blue. The five catalytic residues are shown in wheat. b, Reaction progress curves for the 378 single variants with WT (blue) and buffer (black) controls. All variants were purified by strep-tag affinity chromatography and concentrations were normalized. Variants in red were further purified using HPLC, tested again to confirm improvements before mutations were recombined (Supplementary Methods 3.19). c, Activity heatmap of all single variants. d, Michaelis-Menten kinetics measurements for six improved single variants, each being the most active variant at the corresponding residue position in the activity screen. v0: reaction rate in the initial linear region (nM/s). [E0]: enzyme concentration, 500 nM. Measurements were made in triplicate. Black dots and error bars represent mean ± std. e, Single mutations selected for recombination. f, MPNN probabilities for residues where beneficial mutations are discovered. Blue: wild-type AA. Orange: the sum of probabilities for all beneficial substitutions. Individual measurements are represented as black dots and bars and error bars represent mean ± std; n = 5. g, Correlation between activity fold improvement and AF3 metrics. Many deleterious mutations can be predicted by metrics such as complex pLDDT, ipae min and pae interface.

a, Design model of Zn45 and the substrate of S_ZnO36 showing 6 residue positions chosen for combinatorial saturation in sticks in red. The five catalytic residues are shown in wheat. b, Reaction progress curves for the 148 combinatorial variants with WT and base KO controls. c, The relationship between activity and number of mutations. Box plots show the median (centre line), 25th and 75th percentiles (box limits), and whiskers extending to the most extreme values within 1.5× the interquartile range. Points represent individual observations. The number of variants with mutation numbers 1-6: 11, 38, 52, 34, 10, 1. d, Total turnover number (TTN) for Zn45_v2. A series of substrate concentrations of 160 µM, 80 µM, 40 µM, 20 µM, 10 µM, 5 µM, were incubated with or without 20 nM Zn45_v2 at 37 °C for 5 h and the TTN was determined by densitometry. This experiment was performed three times with similar results. Full gel image in Supplementary Fig. S13. e, Reaction progress curves of Zn45_v2 and the individual catalytic residue knockout variants. Measurements were made in triplicate. Solid lines and shaded regions represent the mean ± std. f, pH dependence of the activity of Zn45_v2 in the low substrate concentration regime (3 µM). Measurements were made in triplicate. Black dots and error bars represent mean ± std. g, Michaelis Menten kinetics of three other combinatorial variants. Measurements were made in triplicate. Black dots and error bars represent mean ± std. h, Correlation between activity fold improvement and AF3 metrics. Overall the correlation between activity improvement and AF3 metrics is weak.

a, TDP-43 contains structured domains (NTD, RRM1, RRM2) essential for nuclear function and a long disordered C-terminal domain (CTD) that governs liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) and oligomerization/aggregation. Full-length degradation risks loss of essential functions, whereas cleavage in the CTD can modulate LLPS and/or oligomerization without ablating function. b, Redesigning existing scaffold to target TDP43. c, Substrate specificity of the TDP43 redesign, TDPr3. Experiments were performed in triplicates. The solid line and the shaded area represent the mean ± std. d, Dynamic light scattering (DLS) determined the average size of oligomeric TDP-43 (Peak 1) as dozens of molecules solubly clustered together, while monomeric TDP-43 (Peak 2) remains monomeric; measurements were made in triplicate. Dots and error bars represent mean ± std. e, TDP-43 form aggregates after incubation at 37C 6h, 12h, 24 and monomeric TDP-43 at 37C 6h, 12, 24h in buffer 50 mM HEPES, 100 mM NaCl, 50 uM ZnSO4 samples in under microscope, monomers started to aggregate while oligomers remained unchanged. f, SDS-PAGE gel analysis after incubating human TDP-43 with TDPn3 or the base knockout (KO). In the WT, the band intensities of the C and N fragments (CO, NO for oligomer, CM, NM for monomer) gradually increase and the full-length (FLO for oligomer, FLN for monomer) is depleted in time. In base KO, no products are detected. The loss of full-length intensity likely is a result of precipitation as shown by the high molecular weight smears. This experiment was performed three times independently with similar results.

a,d, Design model of a de novo zinc protease, SAAc8, against serum amyloid A (SSRSFFSFLG, a) and a de novo zinc protease, AbetaF3, against amyloid-β peptide (KGAIIGLMVG, d). b,e, Reaction progress curves of SAAc8 and AbetaF3 on their cognate substrates, and on other substrates presented in this work. Measurements were made in triplicate. Solid lines and shaded regions represent the mean ± std. c, Kinetics of SAAc8 and AbetaF3 each on their cognate substrates. v0: reaction rate in the initial linear region (nM/s). [E0]: enzyme concentration, 500 nM. Measurements were made in triplicate. Black dots and error bars represent mean ± std.
